|  | Status Test <br> Rough (quick test) | Complete (functional test) | Operation <br> Monitoring |
| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
| $\begin{aligned} & \text { Properties } \\ & \text { r } \end{aligned}$ | - Testing of all important functions, if necessary with help of external test equipment <br> - Initiated by the operating personnel, then runs automatically | - Periodic testing of all important functions <br> - Initiated by the operating personnel, then runs automatically or semi-autom. (possibly without external stimulation or test equipment) | - Monitoring of all important functions and automatic display of complete and partial faults <br> - Performed with built-in means (BIT/BITE) |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | - Lower cost <br> - Allows fast checking of the functional conditions down to subsystem level | - Gives a clear status of the functional conditions of the item <br> - Allows fault localization down to subsystem (e.g. LRU) level | - Runs automatically on-line, i. e. in background <br> - Allows fault localization down to LRU level |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | - Limited fault localization (isolation and diagnosis) capability | - Relatively expensive <br> - Runs generally off-line (i. e. not in background) | - Expensive |

$\mathrm{LRU}=$ line replaceable unit; $\mathrm{BIT}=$ built-in test; $\mathrm{BITE}=$ built-in test equipmentstandard solutions. For such a selection, the following aspects are important:

1. Simplicity: Test sequences, procedures, and documentation should be as easy as possible.
2. Standardization: The greatest possible standardization should be striven for, in hardware and software.
3. Reliability: Built-in facilities should have a failure rate of at least one order of magnitude lower than that of the equipment or system in which they are used; their failure should not influence the item's operation (FMEA/FMECA).
4. Maintenance: The maintenance of BIT/BITE must be simple and should not interfere with that of the equipment or system; the user should be connected to the field data change service of the manufacturer.

For some applications, it is important that fault localization (or at least part of the diagnosis) can be remotely controlled. Such a requirement can often be satisfied, if stated early in the design phase. Remote diagnosis must be investigated on a case-by-case basis, using results from a careful failure modes \& effects analysis (FMEA).

A further step on above considerations leads to maintenance concepts which allow automatic or semiautomatic reconfiguration of the item after failure (see Section 6.8.6 for some applications). Preliminary investigations on a new, approach for mission oriented high safety systems (Active System Control ASC, superimposing a periodic check to preventive maintenance) are introduced in [4.26], with practical realizations in [4.4].

Design guidelines for maintainability are given in Section 5.2. Effects of imperfect switching and incomplete coverage are investigated in Sections 6.8.3 \& 6.8.4.

# 4.2.3 User Documentation 

User (or product) documentation for complex equipment and systems can include all of the following Manuals or Handbooks

- General Description
- Operating Manual
- Preventive Maintenance (Service) Manual
- Corrective Maintenance (Repair) Manual
- Illustrated Spare Parts Catalog
- Logistic Support.

The content of the user documentation must be, of course, consistent with the actual hardware and software status of the item considered. Emphasis must be placed on a clear and concise presentation, with block diagrams, flow charts, check lists. The language should be easily understandable to non specialized personnel. Procedures should be self sufficient and contain checkpoints to prevent the skipping of steps.# 4.2.4 Training of Operation and Maintenance Personnel 

Suitably equipped, well trained, and motivated maintenance personnel are an important prerequisite to achieve short maintenance times and to avoid human errors. Training must be comprehensive enough to cover present needs. However, for complex systems it should be periodically updated to cover technological changes introduced in the system and to further motivate operation and maintenance personnel.

### 4.2.5 User Logistic Support

For complex equipment and systems, customers (users) generally expect from the manufacturer a logistic support during the useful life of the item under consideration. This can range from support on an on-call basis up to a maintenance contract with manufacturer's personnel located at the user site. One important point in such a logistic support is the definition of responsibilities. For this reason, maintenance is often subdivided into different levels (four for military applications (Table 4.2) and three for industry, in general). The first level concerns simple maintenance work such as the status test, fault detection and fault localization down to the subsystem level. This task is generally performed by operating personnel. At the second level, fault localization is refined, the defective LRU is replaced by a good one, and the functional test is performed. For this task first line maintenance personnel is often required. At the third level, faulty LRUs are repaired by maintenance personnel and stored for reuse. The fourth level deals with overhaul or revision (essentially for mechanical parts) and is performed by specialized personnel.

1. Has the equipment or system been conceived with modularity in mind? Are the modules functionally independent and separately testable?
2. Has a concept for fault detection and localization been planned and realized? Is fault detection automatic? Which kind of faults are detected? How does fault localization work? Is localization down to line replaceable units (LRUs) possible? How large are values for fault detection and fault localization (coverage)? How have they been calculated/estimated?
3. Can redundant elements be repaired on-line?
4. Are enough test points provided? Do they have pull-up/pull-down resistors?
5. Have hardware adjustments (or alignments) been reduced to a minimum? Are the adjustable elements clearly marked and easily accessible? Is the adjustment uncritical?
6. Has the amount of external test equipment been kept to a minimum?
7. Has the standardization of components, materials, and maintenance tools been considered?
8. Are line replaceable units (LRUs) identical with spare parts? Are they easily accessible? Can they be easily tested? Is a spare parts provisioning concept available? What does it include?
9. Are all elements with limited useful life clearly marked and easily accessible?
10. Are access flaps (and doors) easy to open (without special tools) and self-latching? Have plug-in unit guide rails self-blocking devices? Can a standardized extender for PCBs be used?
11. Have indirect connectors been used? Is the plugging-out/plugging-in of PCBs (LRUs) easy? Are power supplies and ground distributed across different contacts?
12. Have wires and cables been conveniently placed? Also with regard to maintenance ?
13. Are sensitive elements sufficiently protected against mishandling during maintenance?
14. Can preventive maintenance be performed on-line? Does preventive maintenance also allow the detection of hidden faults? How? Also for software? In which amount and how?
15. Have maintainability tests been planned? What does this test program include? Has a test strategy from incoming inspection to system test been conceived? It is appropriate?
16. Which part of the item (system) can be considered as-good-as-new after a maintenance action?
17. Have man-machine, ergonomic \& human aspects been sufficiently considered to avoid mistakes at operation\&maintenance? Also with respect to safety (accident prevention\&critical failures)?
18. Have all other design guidelines for maintainability been respected? Without any deviation?
19. Has a fail-safe procedure been realized? For which failures or external events? Has a risk management plan been established? What does this plan include? (Points 23 p. 79, 5 p.423, 5p.424.)
20. Is remote control, detection, diagnosis, maintenance possible? Which of them and how?
21. Has the predicted maintainability been calculated? How? Taking care of redundancies?# 4.3 Maintainability Aspects in Design Reviews 

Design reviews are important to point out, discuss, and eliminate design weaknesses. Their objective is also to decide about continuation or stopping of the project on the basis of objective considerations (feasibility check in Table A3.3 (p. 419), Table 5.3 (p.161), and Fig. 1.6 (p.19)). The most important design reviews are described in Tables A3.3 for hardware and Table 5.5 (p. 165) for software. To be effective, design reviews must be supported by project specific checklists. Table 4.3 gives a catalog of questions which can be used to generate project specific checklists for maintainability aspects in design reviews (see Table 2.8 (p. 79) for reliability and Appendix A4 (pp. 421-25) for other aspects). As shown in Table 4.3, checking maintainability during a design review deals with all involved aspects, including adherence to given design guidelines, testability, coverage, man-machine \& human factors, logistic support, remote maintenance, and predicted maintainability.

### 4.4 Predicted Maintainability

Knowing the reliability structure of a system and the reliability \& maintainability of its elements, it is possible to calculate the maintainability of the system considered as a one-item structure. For instance, calculating reliability function \& point availability at system level and extracting $\mathrm{g}(x)$ as the density of the system down time using Eqs. (6.14) and (6.18) or (6.19). This method, used in Tables 6.9 and 6.10 for constant failure \& repair rates, can become laborious for arbitrary $\mathrm{g}(x)$.

However,
in practical applications it is often sufficient to know the mean of all repair times $M T T R_{S}$ or the system mean down time in steady-state $M D T_{S}{ }^{* 3}$
as a function of the system reliability structure and the mean time to failure $M T T F_{i}$ $\&$ mean time to repair $M T T R_{i}$ of its elements. Such a calculation is discussed in Section 4.4.1. Section 4.4.2 deals then with mean times to preventive maintenance. Use of statistical methods to estimate or demonstrate a maintainability or an MTTR are discussed in Sections 7.2.1 and 7.3 (see also Sections 7.5 and 7.6).

### 4.4.1 Calculation of $M T T R_{S} \& M D T_{S}$

Let's first consider a system without redundancy (series structure) with elements

T / M T T F_{i}

The mean of the total repair time necessary to restore the $T / M T T F_{i}$ failures follows then from

$$

From Eqs. (4.4) and (4.5) it follows for the mean of all repair (restoration) times $M T T R_{S}$, the final value (see footnote on p. 121 for $M D T_{S}$ )

$$
M T T R_{S}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} M T T R_{i} / M T T F_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 / M T T F_{i}}

(for series stuctures with no further failures at system down).

Equation (4.6) gives the mathematically exact mean of all repair times $M T T R_{S}$ for a series structure with elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, under the assumptions that a repaired element is as-good-as-new, switching on/off of not failed elements has no influence on their failure rates, and during a repair no further failures can occur (the system is down at each failure, and disconnected);
see Examples $4.1 \& 4.2$ for further considerations. From Eq.(4.6) one can verify that

$$
M T T R_{S}=M T T R, \quad \text { for } \quad M T T R_{1}=\ldots=M T T R_{n}=M T T R
$$

and

$$
M T T R_{S}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} M T T R_{i}, \quad \text { for } \quad M T T F_{1}=\ldots=M T T F_{n}
$$However,
it must be pointed out that when investigating other reliability figures (e.g. $M T T F_{S 0}$ in Examples $4.1 \& 4.2$ ), the system as a whole must be as-good-as-new after a repair, implying, in particular, constant failure rates for all elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$ to avoid restoration at each failure of all the not failed elements with time dependent failure rates.

If each element $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$ exhibits a const. failure rate $\lambda_{i}=1 / M T T F_{i}$, Eq. (4.6) yields

$$
M T T R_{S}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{S 0}} M T T R_{i}, \quad \lambda_{S 0}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}, M T T R_{i}=1 / \mu_{i} \text { for const.repair rate. }
$$

For series structures with no further failures at system down, Eqs. (4.6) \& (4.7) give also the system mean down time in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty M D T_{S}$ (Example 4.1);
however, in the presence of redundancy, distinction between $M T T R_{S}$ and $M D T_{S}$ is in general necessary (see footnote on p. 121 and Example 4.2).

a good approximate value of the system mean down time $M D T_{S}$, by summing only over all elements without redundancy (series elements); see Example 4.2 for an application, and footnote to Tables 6.9 \& 6.10 and pp. 393, 394 \& 278 - 79 or 515-16 for further comments.

# Example 4.2 

How does the mean of all repair (restoration) times $M T T R_{S}$ of the system in Example 4.1 change, if an active redundancy is introduced to the element with $M T T F=100 \mathrm{~h}$ ?


Under the assumption that the redundancy is repaired on-line (without interruption of operation at system level), is there a difference between $M T T R_{S}$ and the system mean down time in steadystate or for $t \rightarrow \infty M D T_{S}$ ?

## Solution

Because of the assumed active redundancy, operating elements and reserve elements show the same mean number of failures. $M T T R_{S}$ follows thus from Eq. (4.6) by summing over all system elements, yielding

$$
M T T R_{S}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~h} / 500 \mathrm{~h}+2.5 \mathrm{~h} / 400 \mathrm{~h}+1 \mathrm{~h} / 250 \mathrm{~h}+0.5 \mathrm{~h} / 100 \mathrm{~h}+0.5 \mathrm{~h} / 100 \mathrm{~h}}{1 / 500 \mathrm{~h}+1 / 400 \mathrm{~h}+1 / 250 \mathrm{~h}+1 / 100 \mathrm{~h}+1 / 100 \mathrm{~h}}=\frac{0.02425}{0.0285 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}} \approx 0.85 \mathrm{~h}
$$

However,
the system mean down time in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty M D T_{S}$, differs now from $M T T R_{S}$ (see footnote on p. 121 for $M D T_{S}=M T T R_{S}$ ). Assuming for the redundancy an availability equal to one, ${ }^{+}$the system down time is practically defined by the series elements in the reliability block diagram (see Eqs. (6.295) or (A7.179) for exact results in the cases of arbitrary systems described by Markov or semi-Markov processes). Thus,

$$
M D T_{S} \approx \frac{2 \mathrm{~h} / 500 \mathrm{~h}+2.5 \mathrm{~h} / 400 \mathrm{~h}+1 \mathrm{~h} / 250 \mathrm{~h}}{1 / 500 \mathrm{~h}+1 / 400 \mathrm{~h}+1 / 250 \mathrm{~h}}=\frac{0.01425}{0.0085 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}} \approx 1.68 \mathrm{~h}
$$

Supplementary result: As for example 4.1, the mean of the total system down time during $(0, t]$ for $t \rightarrow \infty$ follows (assuming constant failure rates) as $t \cdot\left(1-A A_{S}\right)$ $\approx t \cdot M D T_{S} / M U T_{S} \approx t \cdot 1.68 \mathrm{~h} \cdot 0.0085 \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \approx 0.014 t$ (see bottom of p.123).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+}$For constant failure rate $\lambda=1 / M T T F$, constant repair rate $\mu=1 / M T T R$, and one repair crew, Table 6.6 on p. 201 gives for the 1-out-of-2 active redundancy $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\mu(2 \lambda+\mu) /$ $\left(2 \lambda(\lambda+\mu)+\mu^{2}\right) \approx 1-2(\lambda / \mu)^{2}$ yielding $A A \approx 0.99995$ for this example.# 4.4.2 Calculation of Mean Time to Preventive Maintenance 

For the preventive maintenance, following two cases must be distinguished:

1. Preventive maintenance is carried out at once for the entire system, one element after the other. If the system consists of elements $E_{1}, \ldots . E_{n}$ (arbitrarily grouped on the reliability block diagram) and the mean time to perform a preventive maintenance of $E_{i}$ is $M T T P M_{i}$, then the system mean time to preventive maintenance (for the whole system) is (Eq. (A6.68))

$$
M T T P M_{S y s t}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} M T T P M_{i}
$$

2. Each element $E_{i}$ of the system is serviced for preventive maintenance independently of all other elements and has a mean time to perform a preventive maintenance $M T T P M_{i}$. In this case, to obtain the mean of all preventive maintenance times $M T T P M_{S}$, Eq. (4.6) can be used with $M T B P M_{i}$ instead of $M T T F_{i}$ and $M T T P M_{i}$ instead of $M T T R_{i}$ (where $M T B P M_{i}$ is the mean time between preventive maintenance for the element $E_{i}$ ), summing over all elements for the case of active redundancy (as in Example 4.2).

Case 2 applies when preventive maintenance can be performed without interruption of the operation or, approximately, during periodic non operating times.

### 4.5 Basic Models for Spare Parts Provisioning

Spare parts provisioning is important for systems with long useful life or when short repair times and / or independence from the manufacturer is required (spare part is used here e. g. for line replaceable unit (LRU), see p.116). Basically, a distinction is made between centralized and decentralized logistic support. Also important is to take into account whether spare parts are repairable or not. This section presents the basic models for the provision of nonrepairable and of repairable spare parts. For nonrepairable spare parts, the cases of centralized and decentralized logistic support are considered in order to quantify the advantage of a centralized logistic support with respect to a decentralized one. More general maintenance strategies are discussed in Section 4.6, and cost specific aspects in Sections 4.5-4.7.

### 4.5.1 Centralized Logistic Support, Nonrepairable Spare Parts

In centralized logistic support, spare parts are stocked at one place. The basic problem can be formulated as follows,at time $t=0$, the first part is put into operation, it fails at time $t=\tau_{1}$ and is replaced (in a negligible time) by a second part which fails at time $t=\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}$ and so forth; asked is the number $n$ of parts which must be stocked in order that the requirement for parts during the cumulative operating time $T$ is met with a given (fixed) probability $\gamma$.

To answer this question, the smallest integer $n$ must be found for which

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}>T\right\} \geq \gamma
$$

holds. In general, $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ are assumed to be independent positive random variables with the same distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)(\mathrm{F}(0)=0$, density $\mathrm{f}(x)) \&$ finite mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=\mathrm{E}[\tau]=$ MTTF $\& \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=\operatorname{Var}[\tau]$. If the number of parts is calculated from

$$
n=T / M T T F
$$

the requirement can only be covered (for $T$ large) with a probability of 0.5 . Thus, more than $T / M T T F$ parts are necessary to meet the requirement with $\gamma>0.5$.

According to Eq. (A7.12), valid for renewal processes, the probability as per Eq. (4.9) can be expressed by the $(n-1)$ th convolution of the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ with itself, i. e.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}>T\right\}=1-\mathrm{F}_{n}(T) \\
& \text { with } \quad \mathrm{F}_{1}(T)=\mathrm{F}(T) \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{F}_{n}(T)=\int_{0}^{T} \mathrm{~F}_{n-1}(T-x) \mathrm{f}(x) d x, \quad n>1
\end{aligned}
$$

Of the distribution functions $\mathrm{F}(x)$ used in reliability theory, a closed, simple form for the function $\mathrm{F}_{n}(x)$ exists only for the exponential, gamma, and normal distribution functions, yielding a Poisson, gamma, and normal distribution, respectively. In particular, the exponential distribution $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ leads to (Eq. (A7.39))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}>T\right\}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\lambda T)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda T}
$$

The important case of the Weibull distribution $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-(\lambda x)^{\beta}}$ must be solved numerically. Figure 4.3 shows the results with $\gamma$ and $\beta$ as parameters [4.2 (1974)].

For $n$ large, approximate solutions for a wide class of distribution functions $\mathrm{F}(x)$ can be obtained using the central limit theorem (Eq.(A6.148); $\mathrm{E}[\tau], \operatorname{Var}[\tau]<\infty$ ). ${ }^{*}$ )

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\tau_{i}-\mathrm{E}[\tau]}{\sqrt{n \operatorname{Var}[\tau]}}>x\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{x}^{\infty} e^{-y^{2} / 2} d y=1-\Phi(x)=\Phi(-x)
$$

and thus, using $x \sqrt{n \operatorname{Var}[\tau]}+n \mathrm{E}[\tau]=T$,

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ A solution is basically also possible using the central limit theorem for renewal proc. (Eq. (A7.34)).$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}>T\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{\left(T-n \mathrm{E}[\tau]\right) / \sqrt{n \operatorname{Var}[\tau]}}^{\infty} e^{-y^{2} / 2} d y=\gamma
$$

Setting $(T-n \mathrm{E}[\tau]) / \sqrt{n \operatorname{Var}[\tau]}=-d$ it follows that for $n \rightarrow \infty$

$$
n=\left[\kappa d / 2+\sqrt{(\kappa d / 2)^{2}+T / \mathrm{E}[\tau]}\right]^{2}, \quad \text { with } \kappa=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[\tau]} / \mathrm{E}[\tau]
$$

The number of spare parts $n_{s p}$ follows then as $n_{s p}=n-1$, considering that one part is operating in the system (see remark to Eq. (4.17)).


Figure 4.3 Number $n$ of parts necessary to cover a cumulative operating time $T$ with probability $\geq \gamma$, i. e. smallest $n$ for which $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}>T\right\} \geq \gamma$ holds, with $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i} \leq x\right\}=1-e^{-(\lambda x)^{\beta}}$ (Weibull distribution) and $M T T F=T(1+1 / \beta) / \lambda$ (dashed the results given by the central limit theorem as per Eq. (4.15); $\beta=1$ yields the exponential distribution function)

Figure 4.4 Coefficient of variation for the Weibull distribution for $1 \leq \beta \leq 3$

From Eqs. (4.13) to (4.15) one recognizes that $d$ is the $\gamma$ quantile of the standard normal distribution $(\gamma=1-\Phi(-d)=\Phi(d))$, yielding for instance (Table A9.1)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \gamma=0.99 \quad 0.95 \quad 0.90 \quad 0.75 \quad 0.5 \\
& d \approx 2.33 \quad 1.64 \quad 1.28 \quad 0.67 \quad 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, for $\gamma=0.5$ and $n$ large, it follows that $n=T / E[\tau]$ (as per Eq. (4.10)). $\kappa=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[\tau]} / E[\tau]$ is the coefficient of variation ( 1 for the exponential distribution, $\sqrt{\Gamma(1+2 / \beta) /(\Gamma(1+1 / \beta))^{2}-1}$ for the Weibull distribution (Fig. 4.4, pp. 459)).

As shown dashed in Fig. 4.3, for a Weibull distribution with $\beta \geq 1$, approximate values for $n$ obtained using the central limit theorem (Eq. (4.15)) are for $\gamma \leq 0.95$ good down to low values of $n$ (for $\beta=1$, deviation from the exact value is $<1$ for $\gamma \leq 0.95$ and $n \geq 5$; this deviation drops off rapidly for increasing values of $\beta$ ).

Let's now consider the case in which the same part occurs $k$ times in a series structure. For $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$, i. e. $\mathrm{E}[\tau]=1 / \lambda \& \kappa=1$, Eq. (4.12) holds with

$$
\lambda^{\prime}=k \lambda, \quad k=1,2, \ldots
$$

instead of $\lambda$. This is because the sum of independent Poisson processes is a Poisson process (Eq. (7.27)) and $k$ parts must be operating for the required function (the same holds if $l$ systems use the same part, one or more per system with total $k$ parts of the same type, and storage is centralized (Example 4.3)). As for $k=1$, a system failure occurs at the $\left(n_{s p}+1\right)$ th failure and the number of spare parts is thus given by

$$
n_{s p}=n-1, \quad \text { series structure, } n \text { from Eq. (4.12) with } \lambda^{\prime}=k \lambda, k=1,2, \ldots
$$

see Examples $4.3 \& 4.4$ for practical applications ( $n_{s p}=n-1+k$ holds for arbitrary failure rate of the part, if at time $T$ all $k$ operating parts must be replaced by new).

For the case of a $i$-out-of- $j$ standby redundancy, at $t=0$ i parts are operating and $j-i$ in standby; $\lambda^{\prime}=i \lambda$ and the smallest number of spare parts is given by

$$
n_{s p}=n-1-(j-i), \quad i \text {-out-of-j standby redundancy ( } i, j \text { instead of } k, n \text { as usual). (4.17a) }
$$

For an active redundancy, $\lambda^{\prime}=j \lambda$ and Eq. (4.17a) can be used as an approximation for $j-i$ small (exact calculation using an appropriate death process (p. 61)).Finally, Eq. (4.15) applies to arbitrary distributions $\mathrm{F}(x)$ of the failure-free time $\tau$ considered. However, if the same part appears $k$ times in a series structure, Eq. (4.15) can be used with $k T / E[\tau]=k T / M T T F$ as a preliminary result; for a refinement one can consider that the total number of failures of $k$ parts is for large $T$ and $k$ normally distributed with mean $k T / M T T F$ and variance $k \sigma^{2} T / M T T F^{3}$ (Eqs. (A7.34) \& (A7.214) and Example A6.17 on p. 463, see also remarks on p. 537).

# Example 4.3 

A part with constant failure rate $\lambda=10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ is used three times in a system ( $k=3$, series structure). Give the number of spare parts $n_{s p}$ which must be stored to cover a cumulative operating time $T=10,000 \mathrm{~h}$ with a probability $\gamma \geq 0.90$.

## Solution

Considering $k \lambda T=30$, the exact solution is given by the smallest integer $n_{s p}=n-1$ for which

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{30^{i}}{i!} e^{-30} \geq 0.9
$$

holds (Eq. (4.12)). From Table A9.2 it follows, for $q=1-0.9=0.1$ and $t_{v, q}=2 \cdot 30=60$, the value $v \approx 75.2$ (lin. interpolation); thus, $v=76$ and (Appendix A9.2 \& Eq. (4.12)) $n=v / 2=38$ (same results from Fig. 7.3 for $m=30 \& \gamma=0.9$, yielding $n=c+1=38$, and with Eq. (4.15) for $\kappa=1$ and $d \approx 1.28$, yielding $n=38\left(\left[0.64+\sqrt{0.64^{2}+30}\right]^{2} \approx 37.9\right)$ ). Thus, from Eq. (4.17) it follows that $n_{s p}=38-1=37$.

### 4.5.2 Decentralized Logistic Support, Nonrepairable Spare Parts

For users who have the same system located at different places, spare parts are often stored decentralized, i. e. separately at each location (decentralized means that spare parts cannot be transferred from one location to another location). If there are $l$ systems, each with a given part, and the storage of spare parts is decentralized at each system (or location), a first approach could be to store with each system the same number of spare parts obtained using Eqs. (4.9) \& (4.17). In this case, the total number of parts would be $n \cdot l$, i. e. $(n-1) \cdot l$ spare parts. This number $n$ of parts, which would be sufficient to meet, with probability $>\gamma$ (often $>\gamma$ ) the needs of the $l$ systems with a centralized storage, would now in general be too small to meet all the individual needs at each location, see Example 4.4. In fact, assuming that failures at each location are independent, and that with $n$ parts the probability of meeting the needs at any location individually is $\gamma$, the probability of meeting the need at all locations is $\gamma^{l}$. Thus, to meet the need at the $l$ locations with a probability $\gamma$

$$
n_{d e c}=l \cdot n_{l}
$$

parts are required, where $n_{l}$ is computed for each location individually with

$$
\gamma_{l}=\sqrt[l]{\gamma}
$$

e. g. using Eq.(4.15) with $d_{l}$ instead of $d\left(\Phi(d)=\gamma, \Phi\left(d_{l}\right)=\sqrt[l]{\gamma}\right)$.To make a comparison between a centralized and a decentralized logistic support, let's assume that the part considered appears $k$ times in a series structure in each of the $l$ locations, has constant failure rate $\lambda$, and $k \lambda T \gg d_{l}^{2} / 4>d^{2} / 4$ holds. In this case, Eqs. (4.15) \& (4.16) lead to

$$
n \approx k \lambda T+d \sqrt{k \lambda T}, \quad k \lambda T \gg d^{2} / 4, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, \text { probability } \gamma
$$

For centralized logistic support, Eq. (4.20) yields

$$
n_{c e n} \approx l k \lambda T+d \sqrt{l k \lambda T}, \quad l k \lambda T \gg d^{2} / 4, k, l=1,2, \ldots, \text { probability } \gamma
$$

For decentralized logistical support, Eq. (4.20) yields

$$
n_{d e c} \approx l\left(k \lambda T+d_{l} \sqrt{k \lambda T}\right), \quad k \lambda T \gg d_{l}^{2} / 4, k, l=1,2, \ldots, \text { probability } \gamma
$$

where $d_{l}$ is obtained as for $d$ in Eq. (4.15) with $\gamma_{i}=\sqrt[3]{\gamma}$ (for example, $d \approx 1.64$ for $\gamma=0.95$ and $d_{l} \approx 2.57$ for $l=10$ i. e. for $\gamma_{l} \approx 0.9949$, see Table A9.1). From the above considerations it follows that for $k \lambda T \gg d_{l}^{2} / 4 \geq d^{2} / 4$ (see Example 4.4)

$$
\frac{n_{d e c}}{n_{c e n}} \approx \frac{1+d_{l} / \sqrt{k \lambda T}}{1+d / \sqrt{l k \lambda T}} \quad \text { or } \quad \frac{n_{s p_{d e c}}}{n_{s p_{c e n}}} \approx \frac{1+\left(d_{l} / \sqrt{k \lambda T}\right)-1 / k \lambda T}{1+(d / \sqrt{l k \lambda T})-1 / l k \lambda T}
$$

# Example 4.4 

Let $\lambda=10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ be the constant failure rate of a part in a given system. The user has 6 locations $(l=6)$ and would like to achieve a cumulative operating time $T=50,000 \mathrm{~h}$ at each location with a probability $\gamma \geq 0.95$. How many spare parts can be saved using a centralized logistic support?

## Solution

From Fig. $4.3(T / M T T F=5, \gamma=\sqrt[6]{0.95} \approx 0.99)$, Fig $7.3\left(m=5, \gamma=0.99, c=n_{l}-1\right)$, or from a $\chi^{2}$-Table $\left(t_{v, q}=10, q=1-0.99=0.01, v=2 n_{l}\right)$ each user would need $n_{l}=12$ parts ( $n_{l}=14$ using Eq. (4.15) with $d=d_{l} \approx 2.33$ and $\lambda T=5$ ); thus $n_{d e c}=6 \cdot 12=72$ parts and (Eq. (4.17)) $n_{s p_{d e c}}=(12-1) 6=72-6=66$ spare parts. Combining the storage $(l=6)$, it follows from Fig. $7.3\left(m=30, \gamma=0.95, c=n_{c e n}-1\right)$ or from Table A9.2 $\left(t_{v, q}=60, q=0.05, v=2 n_{c e n}\right)$ that $n_{c e n}=40\left(n_{c e n}=41\right.$ using Eq. (4.15) with $d \approx 1.64$ and $\lambda T=30$ ); thus, $n_{s p_{c e n}}=40-1=39$. A centralized storage would save $66-39=27$ spare parts (Eq. (4.23) gives 1.57 instead of 1.8 (left) and 1.45 instead of 1.69 (right), because $k \lambda T=5$ is not $\gg d_{l}^{2} / 4 \approx 1.36$ ).
Supplementary result: Provisioning each location separately with $\gamma=0.95$ yields $n=6 \cdot 10=60$.

### 4.5.3 Repairable Spare Parts

In Sections $4.5 .1 \& 4.5 .2$ it was assumed that spare parts (e.g. LRUs) were nonrepairable. In many cases, spare parts can be repaired and stored for reuse. Calculation of the number of spare parts can be performed in a way similar to the investigation of a $k$-out-of-n standby redundancy, where $k$ is the number of parts used in the system and $n$ is the smallest integer to be determined such that the requirement is met with a given probability $\gamma$. Following two cases have to be considered:1. $\gamma$ is the probability that a request for a spare part at a time point $t$ can be met without time delay; in this case, $\gamma$ can be considered as the point availability $P A_{S}$ (in steady-state to simplify investigations) and $n$ is the smallest integer such that $P A_{S} \geq \gamma$ for a given (fixed) $\gamma$.
2. $\gamma$ is the probability that any request for a spare part during the time interval $(0, t]$ will be met without time delay; in this case, $\gamma$ can be considered as the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ ( $n$ as for Case 1 above but referred to $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \geq \gamma$ ).
If the spare parts have constant failure rate $\lambda=1 /$ MTTF and constant repair rate $\mu=1 / M T T R$, birth-and-death processes can be used (Appendix A7.5.5).*) To simplify investigations and to agree with results in Chapter 6, it is assumed that only one spare part at a time can be repaired (only 1 repair crew is available) and no further failures are considered when a request for a spare part cannot be met (corresponds to the assumption no further failure at system down (Fig. 6.13)).

For Case 1 above, Eq. (6.138) with $\lambda_{r} \cong 0$ and Eq. (6.140) yield

$$
P A_{S}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k} P_{j}=1-P_{n-k+1} \geq \gamma
$$

and

$$
P_{j}=\frac{\pi_{j}}{\sum_{i=0}^{n-k+1} \pi_{i}} \quad \text { and } \quad \pi_{i}=(k \lambda / \mu)^{i}, \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k+1
$$

Asked is the smallest integer $n$ which satisfies Eq. (4.24) for given (fixed) $\gamma, k$, $\lambda$, and $\mu$. Often $n=k+1$ (one spare part) or $n=k+2$ (two spare parts) will be sufficient. In these cases, results of Table 6.8 (or Eq. (6.140)) with $v_{i}=k \lambda$ yield

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P A_{S_{1}}=\frac{1}{1+k^{2} \lambda^{2} /\left(k \lambda \mu+\mu^{2}\right)} \approx 1-(k \lambda / \mu)^{2} \\
& n_{s p}=n-k=1 \text { spare part, } 1 \text { repair crew, Case } 1 \\
& P A_{S_{2}}=\frac{1}{1+k^{3} \lambda^{3} /\left(k^{2} \lambda^{2} \mu+k \lambda \mu^{2}+\mu^{3}\right)} \approx 1-(k \lambda / \mu)^{3} \\
& n_{s p}=n-k=2 \text { spare parts, } 1 \text { repair crew, Case } 1
\end{aligned}
$$

If $P A_{S_{2}}$ is still $<\gamma$, more than 2 spare parts are necessary, and a good approximation for the number $n_{s p}$ of spare parts can be obtained using the smallest integer $n_{s p}=n-k$ satisfying (Table 6.8 with $v_{i}=k \lambda$ )

$$
P A_{S n_{s p}} \approx 1-(k \lambda / \mu)^{n_{s p}+1} \geq \gamma, \quad n_{s p}=n-k \text { spare parts, } 1 \text { repair crew, Case } 1
$$

The approximations per Eqs. (4.26) - (4.28) assume $k \lambda<\mu$ and hold practically also if the assumption "no further failures are considered when a request for a spare part cannot be met" is not used. The case in which $n_{s p}+1$ repair crews are available (instead of 1 repair crew) is considered by Eq. (4.32) for comparative investigations.

[^0]
[^0]:    *) See p. 133 for arbitrary repair rates.For Case 2 above, the reliability function can be approximated by an exponential function (Eq. (6.93)), yielding (Table 6.8 or Eqs. (6.144) \& (6.145) with $v_{i}=k \lambda$ )

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{1}}(t) \approx e^{-t(k \lambda)^{2} / \mu}, & n_{s p}=n-k=1 \text { spare part, } 1 \text { repair crew, Case } 2 \\
\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{2}}(t) \approx e^{-t(k \lambda)^{3} / \mu^{2}}, & n_{s p}=n-k=2 \text { spare parts, } 1 \text { repair crew, Case } 2
\end{array}
$$

If $\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{2}}(t)$, with $t$ as mission time, is still $<\gamma$, more than 2 spare parts are necessary, and a good approximation for the number $n_{s p}$ of spare parts can be obtained using the smallest integer $n_{s p}=n-k$ satisfying (Table 6.8 with $v_{i}=k \lambda$ )

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{n_{s p}}}(t) \approx e^{-t \mu(k \lambda / \mu)^{n_{s p}+1}} \geq \gamma, \quad n_{s p}=n-k \text { spare parts, } 1 \text { repair crew, Case } 2
$$

For Eqs. (4.29) to (4.31) it holds necessarily that no further failures are considered when a request for a spare part cannot be met (system down states are made absorbing for reliability calculations). The case in which $n_{s p}$ repair crews are available is considered by Eq. (4.33) for comparative investigations. Example 4.5 gives a practical application.

Assuming for comparative investigations, that each of the $n$ parts can be repaired independently from each other ( $n_{s p}+1$ repair crew) and no further failures are considered when a request for a spare part cannot be met, results of Section A7.5.5 (Fig. A7.9 with $v_{i}=k \lambda, i=0, \ldots, n-k \&\theta_{i}=i \mu, i=1, \ldots, n-k+1\left(n-k\right.$ for $\left.\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)\right)$ ) yield

$$
P A_{S_{n_{s p}} \approx 1-(k \lambda / \mu)^{n_{s p}+1} /\left(n_{s p}+1\right)!,} \quad \begin{aligned}
& n_{s p}=n-k \text { spare parts, } \\
& n_{s p}+1 \text { repair crews, Case } 1
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{n_{s p}}}(t) \approx e^{-t \mu(\lambda / \mu)^{n_{s p}+1} / n_{s p}!}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& n_{s p}=n-k \text { spare parts, } \\
& n_{s p} \text { repair crews, Case } 2
\end{aligned}
$$

# Example 4.5 

A system contains $k=100$ identical parts (LRUs) with a constant failure rate $\lambda=10^{-5} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and which can be repaired with a constant repair rate $\mu=10^{-1} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. (i) Give the number of spare parts which must be stored in order to meet without any time delay and with a probability $\gamma \geq 0.99$ a request for a spare part at a time point $t$ (consider the steady-state only, one repair crew, and no further failure when a request for a spare part cannot be met). (ii) If one spare part is stored $(n=k+1)$, how large is the probability that any request for a spare part during the time interval $\left(0,10^{4} \mathrm{~h}\right]$ will be met without any time delay?

## Solution

(i) Taking $n=k+1$ (1 spare part), Eq. (4.26) yields

$$
P A_{S_{1}}=\frac{1}{1+10^{4} \cdot 10^{-10} /\left(100 \cdot 10^{-5} \cdot 10^{-1}+10^{-2}\right)} \approx 1-\left(\frac{100 \cdot 10^{-5}}{10^{-1}}\right)^{2} \approx 0.9999
$$

Thus only one spare part $\left(n_{s p}=1\right)$ must be stored.
(ii) For $n=k+1$, Eq. (4.29) yields $\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{1}}(t) \approx e^{-0.00001 t}$ and thus $\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{1}}\left(10^{4} \mathrm{~h}\right) \approx e^{-0.1} \approx 0.91$.

Supplementary result: To reach $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(10^{4}\right) \geq 0.99$ one needs $n_{s p}=2$ spare parts $\left(\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{2}}\left(10^{4}\right) \approx 0.999\right)$.The approximation per Eq. (4.32) assumes $k \lambda<<\mu$ and is good also if the assumption "no further failures are considered when a request for a spare part cannot be met" is not used; i. e. for the case of totally independent elements (p.61) considered by Eq. (6.149). For Eq. (4.33), it holds necessarily that no further failures are considered when a request for a spare part cannot be met (down states absorbing).

Generalization of the repair rate leads to semi-regenerative processes with $n-k+1$ regeneration and $n-k$ nonregeneration states, see Fig. A7.11 and Section 6.4.2 for $n-k=1$ (Eqs. (A7.182), (A7.182a), (6.105) - (6.110) with $k \lambda$ instead of $\lambda$ ), and Fig. A7.13 (Eqs. (A7.184) - (A7.186)) for $n-k=2$. For instance, assuming for the repair time $\tau^{\prime}>0$ a density $\mathrm{g}(x)$ with $\overline{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ per Eq. (6.113) and $M T T R=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right], \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]<\infty$, Eq. (6.110) with $k \lambda$ instead of $\lambda \& \lambda_{r} \equiv 0$, yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
P A_{S_{1}}=\frac{k \lambda}{(k \lambda)^{2} M T T R+k \lambda \overline{\mathrm{~g}}(k \lambda)} & \approx \frac{1}{1+(k \lambda)^{2}\left(M T T R^{2}+\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right) / 2} \\
\approx 1-(k \lambda M T T R)^{2} & \left(1+\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / M T T R^{2}\right) / 2 \geq 1-(k \lambda M T T R)^{2} \\
n_{s p} & =n-k=1 \text { spare part, } 1 \text { repair crew, Case } 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, Eq. (6.108) with $\overline{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ per Eq. (6.114), $k \lambda$ instead of $\lambda \& \lambda_{r} \equiv 0$, leads to

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{1}}(t) \approx e^{-t k \lambda(1-\overline{\mathrm{g}}(k \lambda))} \approx & e^{-t(k \lambda)^{2} M T T R} \\
& n_{S P}=n-k=1 \text { spare part, } 1 \text { repair crew, Case } 2
\end{aligned}
$$

For the approximation in Eq. (4.34) it was necessary to use Eq. (6.113), i. e . $\overline{\mathrm{g}}(k \lambda) \approx 1-k \lambda M T T R+(k \lambda)^{2}\left(M T T R^{2}+\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right) / 2$, and the last part of the approximation implies that

$$
\kappa^{2}=\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / E^{2}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / M T T R^{2} \leq 1
$$

which holds for distribution functions used for repair times (with strictly increasing repair rate [2.34 (1965)]). Assuming $M T T R=1 / \mu$, i. e. the same mean time to repair disregarding the distribution of the repair time, the last approximations in Eqs. (4.34) and (4.35) yield the same result as given by Eqs. (4.26) and (4.29), showing, once more,
the small influence of the repair time distribution on results at system level.
Taking $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{-t / M U T_{S}}$ in Eqs. (4.31), (4.33) \& (4.35), $P A_{S}$ per Eqs. (4.28), (4.32) \& (4.34) can be expressed as (Eq. (6.295) or (A7.146))

$$
P A_{S} \approx 1-M D T_{S} / M U T_{S}
$$

with $M D T_{S}=1 / \mu, 1 /(n-k+1) \mu \& M T T R$, respectively.
With respect to Eqs. (4.34) \& (4.35), the case with $n-k=2$ is solved on p. 529 (Eqs. (A7.185) \& (A7.186)).

Results of Sections 4.5.1-4.5.3, in particular those on decentralized logistic support, can be extended to cover the case of systems with different spare parts.# 4.6 Maintenance Strategies 

Maintenance strategies can be very different according to the objective to be reached (type of maintenance policies, minimization of system down time or spare parts, availability maximization by given cost and / or logistic support, etc.). Among possible maintenance strategies [2.34, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2, 4.6, 4.8, 4.14, 4.18, 4.30, 6.3, A7.4(1962)], this section unifies and extends basic repair/replacement policies. Preliminary investigations on a new, approach for mission oriented high safety systems (Active System Control ASC, superimposing a periodic check to preventive maintenance) are introduced in [4.26], with practical realizations in [4.4], see also [5.77]. Cost aspects related to maintenance strategies and to spare parts provisioning are considered in this section and in Section 4.7. For undetected fault times one can refer to Eqs. (A6.30) and (6.223) for a practical application.

In the following it is assumed that the item considered is new at $t=0$, its failurefree time $\tau>0$ has distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)$, density $\mathrm{f}(x)$, and finite mean $\mathrm{E}[\tau] \&$ variance $\operatorname{Var}[\tau]$. Furthermore, in Sections 4.6.1 \& 4.6.2, repairs/replacements are performed in a negligible time. Section 4.6.1 considers the case in which the item is as-good-as-new after each maintenance action, planned (preventive maintenance) or at failure (repair). In section 4.6.2, the item is as-good-as-new only after planned maintenance actions, but as-bad-as-old after repairs (minimal repair at failure). Considerations with finite repair/replacement times are in Sections 4.6.3 \& 6.8.2. ${ }^{+)}$

### 4.6.1 Complete renewal at each maintenance action

This section assumes that each maintenance action, planned or at failure, is of negligible length and brings the item considered to as-good-as-new, as a whole, yielding a renewal point for the underlying point process. ${ }^{*+1}$

Among possible strategies to avoid wear-out failures or effects of sudden failures, replacements can be performed, basically, ${ }^{*++1}$
(a) at a given (fixed) operating time $T_{P M}$ or at failure if the operating time is shorter than $T_{P M}$ (age replacement, Fig. 4.5a),
(b) at given (fixed) time points $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ or at failure (block replacement, Fig. 4.5b),
(fix) only at given time points $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ (fix replacement, Fig. 4.5c),
(of) only at failure (ordinary renewal process without truncation).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$Considering the remarks to Eqs. (A6.27) - (A6.29), preventive maintenance is useful/ necessary only for items with increasing failure rate, tacitly assumed here.
    ${ }^{*+1}$ Note, that for a complex item (system) this assumption is valid only if at the end of each maintenance action the system enters the regeneration state entered at $t=0$, see footnote on p. 386 and the discussion on pp. 387 \& 395 on corrective \& preventive maintenance
    ${ }^{*++1}$ Replacement is used here instead of renewal, to agree with established literature.

Figure 4.5 Possible time schedules for a repairable item with preventive maintenance (PM) and negligible repair and PM times (item new at $t=0$ and at each repair or $P M, x$ starts by 0 at each renewal point): a) At a given operating time $T_{P M}$ or at failure (age replacement); b) At given times $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ or at failure (block replacement); c) At given times $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ (fix replacement)

Consider first the case of age replacement (Fig. 4.5a). Results of Appendix A7.2 and Section 4.5.1 for renewal processes can be used, taking for the failure-free time $\tau_{\text {repl }_{a}}$ the truncated distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{\text {repl }_{a}}(x)$ (Eq. (A6.33a) with $a=0$ )

$$
\mathrm{F}_{\text {repl }_{a}}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{\text {repl }_{a}} \leq x\right\}=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
\mathrm{F}(x) & \text { for } 0 \leq x<T_{P M}, & \mathrm{~F}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq x\} \\
1 & \text { for } x \geq T_{P M}, & \mathrm{~F}(0)=\mathrm{F}_{\text {repl }_{a}}(0)=0
\end{array}\right.
$$

Considering $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{\text {repl }_{a}}=T_{P M}\right\}=1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right)$, the mean time to replacement follows as (see Problem 4.6 in Appendix A11)

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{\text {repl }_{a}}\right]=\int_{0}^{T_{P M}} x \mathrm{f}(x) d x+\left(1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right)\right) T_{P M}=\int_{0}^{T_{P M}}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x \leq T_{P M}
$$

Defining as $v_{a}(t)$ the number of renewals in $(0, t]$ on age replacement policy (replacements at failure \& preventive maintenance), it follows from Eq. (A7.15) that

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{a}(t)\right]=\mathrm{H}_{a}(t), \quad t>0, \mathrm{v}_{a}(0)=\mathrm{H}_{a}(0)=0
$$

with $\mathrm{F}_{1}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=\mathrm{F}_{\text {repl }_{a}}(x)$ in Eq. (A7.15). Furthermore, Eq. (A7.27) yields

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{a}(t)\right]=t / \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{\text {repl }_{a}}\right]=t / \int_{0}^{T_{P M}}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x
$$

in the proportion $\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right)$ for replacements at failure and $1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right)$ for replacements at age. Thus, with $c_{f}$ and $c_{a r}$ as cost for replacement at failure and at age, the mean total cost per unit time (cost rate) on age replacement policy is

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}\left[c_{a} / t\right]=\left[c_{f} \mathrm{~F}\left(T_{P M}\right)+c_{a r}\left(1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right)\right)\right] / \int_{0}^{T_{P M}}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x
$$From Eq. (4.42) one recognizes that $\mathrm{E}\left[c_{a} / t\right] \rightarrow \infty$ for $T_{P M} \rightarrow 0$ and $\rightarrow c_{f} / \mathrm{E}[\tau]$ for $T_{P M} \rightarrow \infty$; with $\mathrm{E}[\tau]$ as mean of the failure-free time $\tau$ of the item considered (Eq. (A6.38)). Optimization of $c_{a} / t$ is considered with Eq. (4.49). Reliability and availability is investigated in Section 6.8.2 (Eqs. (6.192) - (6.195)).

For the case of block replacement (Fig 4.5b), one or more failures can occur during an interval $\left(k T_{P M},(k+1) T_{P M}\right](k=0,1, \ldots)$, with consequent repair. For the expected total number of renewals in $\left(0, n T_{P M}\right]$ on block replacement policy (replacements at failure and at preventive maintenance) it follows that

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{b}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right]=n \mathrm{H}\left(T_{P M}\right)+n, \quad n=1,2, \ldots, T_{P M}>0, \mathrm{v}_{b}(0)=\mathrm{H}(0)=0
$$

where $\mathrm{H}\left(T_{P M}\right)$ is the renewal function at $T_{P M}$ (Eq.(A7.15) with $\mathrm{F}_{1}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)$ as distribution function of the failure-free time of the item considered). With $c_{f} \& c_{b r}$ as cost for replacement at failure and at $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$, respectively, the mean total cost per unit time on block replacement policy is

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[c_{b} / n T_{P M}\right]=\left[c_{f} \mathrm{H}\left(T_{P M}\right)+c_{b r}\right] / T_{P M}, \quad T_{P M}>0, \mathrm{H}(0)=0
$$

From Eq. (4.44) one recognizes that $\mathrm{E}\left[c_{b} / n T_{P M}\right] \rightarrow \infty$ for $T_{P M} \rightarrow 0$ and, using Eq. (A7.27), $\mathrm{E}\left[c_{b} / n T_{P M}\right] \rightarrow c_{f} / \mathrm{E}[\tau]$ for $T_{P M} \rightarrow \infty$; with $\mathrm{E}[\tau]$ as mean of the failure free time $\tau$ of the item considered. Optimization of $c_{b}$ is considered with Eq. (4.52).

For fix replacement (Fig.4.5c), i. e. replacement only at times $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ (taking in charge that for a failure in $\left(k T_{P M},(k+1) T_{P M}\right](k=0,1, \ldots)$ the item is down from failure time to $(\mathrm{k}+1) T_{P M}$ ), the expected number of renewals in $\left(0, n T_{P M}\right]$ is

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{f i x}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right]=n, \quad n=1,2, \ldots, T_{P M}>0, \mathrm{v}_{f i x}(0)=0
$$

With $c_{f i x}$ as cost for replacement at $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$, the mean total cost per unit time on fix replacement policy is

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[c_{f i x} / n T_{P M}\right]=c_{f} / T_{P M}
$$

The number of failures in $\left(0, n T_{P M}\right]$ has a binomial distribution. Setting $c_{d}=$ cost per unit down time, Eq. (A6.30) yields $\mathrm{E}\left[c_{f i x} / n T_{P M}\right]=\left[c_{f}+c_{d}\right]_{0}^{T_{P M}} \mathrm{~F}(x) d x] / T_{P M}$.

The replacement only at failure leads to an ordinary renewal process (Appendix A7.2), yielding results of Section 4.5.1 on spare parts provisioning, in particular,

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{o f}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right]=n T_{P M} / \mathrm{E}[\tau], \quad n=1,2, \ldots, T_{P M}>0, \mathrm{v}_{o f}(0)=0
$$

with $\mathrm{E}[\tau]$ as mean of the failure-free time $\tau$ of the item considered, and

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}\left[c_{o f} / n T_{P M}\right]=c_{f} / \mathrm{E}[\tau], \quad n=1,2, \ldots, T_{P M}>0
$$

One recognizes that for large $n T_{P M}, \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{o f}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right] \leq \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{a}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right] \leq \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{b}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right]$. This follows for $\mathrm{v}_{o f}$ versus $\mathrm{v}_{a}$ by comparing Eqs. (4.41) and (4.47), and for $\mathrm{v}_{a}$ versus $\mathrm{v}_{b}$ by considering that for increasing failure rate $\mathrm{H}(t) \geq(t / \int_{0}^{t}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x)-1$ [2.34(1965)], or from Fig. 4.5 (for each $0<\tau_{i}<T_{P M}, \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i+1}>T_{P M}-\tau_{i}\right\} \geq \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i+1}>T_{P M}\right\}$ ).For age and block replacement policy it is basically possible to optimize $T_{P M}$. Setting the derivative with respect to $T_{P M}$ equal to 0 , Eq. (4.42) yields for $T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}}$

$$
\lambda\left(T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}}\right) \int_{0}^{T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}}} \mathrm{~d} x-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}}\right)=\frac{c_{a r}}{c_{f}-c_{a r}}, \quad c_{f}>c_{a r}
$$

(with $\lambda(x)$ per Eq. (2.10) or (A6.25)), and thus (Eq. (4.42) with $T_{P M}=T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}}$ )

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}\left[c_{a_{\text {opt }}} / t\right]=\left(c_{f}-c_{a r}\right) \lambda\left(T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}}\right)
$$

if $T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}<\infty}$ exist. For strictly increasing failure rate $\lambda(x), T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}<\infty}$ exist for

$$
\lambda(\infty)>c_{f} /\left(\mathrm{E}[\tau]\left(c_{f}-c_{a r}\right)\right)
$$

see Example 4.6. $\quad \lambda(\infty) \leq c_{f} /\left(\mathrm{E}[\tau]\left(c_{f}-c_{a r}\right)\right), \lambda(x)=\lambda$, or $c_{f} \leq c_{a r}$ leads to a replacement only at failure $\left(T_{P M}=\infty\right)$. Similarly, Eq. (4.44) yields

$$
T_{P M b_{\text {opt }}} \mathrm{~h}\left(T_{P M b_{\text {opt }}}\right)-\mathrm{H}\left(T_{P M b_{\text {opt }}}\right)=c_{b r} / c_{f}
$$

with $\mathrm{h}(x)=d \mathrm{H}(x) / d x$ (Eq. (A7.18)), and thus (Eq. (4.44) with $T_{P M}=T_{P M b_{\text {opt }}}$ )

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[c_{b_{\text {opt }}} / n T_{P M b_{\text {opt }}}\right]=c_{f} \mathrm{~h}\left(T_{P M b_{\text {opt }}}\right)
$$

if $T_{P M b_{\text {opt }}<\infty}$ exist. Equation (4.52) is a necessary condition only. For strictly increasing failure rate, at least one $T_{P M b_{\text {opt }}<\infty}$ exist for

$$
1-\operatorname{Var}[\tau] / \mathrm{E}^{2}[\tau]>2 c_{b r} / c_{f}, \quad \text { implying also } \quad c_{f}>2 c_{b r}
$$

see Example 4.6. $1-\operatorname{Var}[\tau] / \mathrm{E}^{2}[\tau] \leq 2 c_{b r} / c_{f}$ or $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ leads to a replacement only at failure $\left(T_{P M}=\infty\right)$.

# Example 4.6 

Investigate Eqs. (4.49) and (4.52).

## Solution

(i) To Eq. (4.49), with $T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}}$ replaced by $T$ for simplicity, one can recognize that for strictly increasing failure rate $\lambda(x), \lambda(T) \int_{0}^{T}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x-\mathrm{F}(T)$ is strictly increasing in $T$, from 0 to $\lambda(\infty) \mathrm{E}[\tau]-1$. In fact, for $T_{2}>T_{1}$ it holds that

$$
\lambda\left(T_{2}\right) \int_{0}^{T_{1}}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x+\lambda\left(T_{2}\right) \int_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{1}\right)-\int_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}} \mathrm{f}(x)) d x>\lambda\left(T_{1}\right) \int_{0}^{T_{1}}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{1}\right)
$$

considering $\lambda\left(T_{2}\right)>\lambda\left(T_{1}\right)$ and $\int_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}} \mathrm{f}(x)) d x=\int_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}} \lambda(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x<\lambda\left(T_{2}\right) \int_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x$. Thus, $T<\infty$ exist for $\lambda(\infty) \mathrm{E}[\tau]-1>c_{a r} /\left(c_{f}-c_{a r}\right)$, i.e. for $\lambda(\infty)>c_{f} /\left(\mathrm{E}[\tau]\left(c_{f}-c_{a r}\right)\right)$. However, an analytical expression for $T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}}$ is rarely possible, see e. g. [4.8] for numerical solutions.
(ii) To Eq. (4.52), one can recognize that for strictly increasing failure rate $\lambda(x), T \mathrm{~h}(T)-\mathrm{H}(T)$ $\rightarrow\left(1-\operatorname{Var}[\tau] / \mathrm{E}^{2}[\tau]\right) / 2>0$ for $T \rightarrow \infty$ and thus, considering $\mathrm{H}(0)=0$, at least one $T<\infty$ exist for $\left(1-\operatorname{Var}[\tau] / \mathrm{E}^{2}[\tau]\right) / 2>c_{b r} / c_{f}$. This follows from Eqs. (A7.28) \& (A7.31) by considering $\operatorname{Var}[\tau]<\mathrm{E}^{2}[\tau]$ for strictly increasing failure rate [2.34 (1965)], see e. g. Fig. 4.4.Comparison of cost per unit time is easy for fix replacement versus replacement only at failure (Eqs. (4.46), (4.48)), but laborious for age replacement versus block replacement or replacement only at failure (Eqs. (4.42), (4.44), (4.48)). In general, it must be performed on a case-by-case basis, often taking care that $c_{f}>c_{a r}>c_{b r}$ and of other aspects like e.g. the importance to avoid wear-out or sudden failures. Besides remarks to Eqs. (4.51) \& (4.54), following general results can be given:

1. For strictly increasing failure rate $\lambda(x)$ and $\lambda(\infty)>c_{f} /\left(\mathrm{E}\left[\tau\right]\left(c_{f}-c_{a r}\right)\right)$ (Eq.(4.51)), $T_{P M a_{\text {opt }}<\infty}$ exist (see e. g. [4.8] for numerical solutions) and, for large $t$, optimal age replacement (Eq. (4.50)) is better (cheaper) than replacement only at failure ( $\mathrm{E}\left[c_{a} / t\right]$ per Eq. (4.42) crosses from above $\mathrm{E}\left[c_{o f} / t\right]=c_{f} / \mathrm{E}[\tau]$ ).
2. Considering Eq. (A7.28) for an ordinary renewal process $\left(M T T F_{A}=M T T F=\mathrm{E}[\tau]\right)$, it follows that $\mathrm{H}\left(T_{P M}\right) \rightarrow T_{P M} / \mathrm{E}[\tau]+\left(\operatorname{Var}[\tau] / \mathrm{E}^{2}[\tau]-1\right) / 2$ for $T_{P M} \rightarrow \infty$. Thus, considering Eqs.(4.53) \& (4.48), for $c_{b r} / c_{f}<\left(1-\operatorname{Var}[\tau] / \mathrm{E}^{2}[\tau]\right) / 2$ optimal block replacement can be better (cheaper) than replacement only at failure; however, this implies $\operatorname{Var}[\tau] / \mathrm{E}^{2}[\tau]<1$ (strictly increasing failure rate) and $c_{f}>2 c_{b r}$.
3. For $c_{f}>c_{b r} \geq c_{a r}$ optimal age replacement is better (cheaper) than optimal block replacement [4.1]; however, often one has $c_{b r}<c_{a r}$.
4. For $c_{a r}=c_{b r}=c_{f}, \mathrm{E}\left[c_{o f} / n T_{P M}\right] \leq \mathrm{E}\left[c_{a} / n T_{P M}\right] \leq \mathrm{E}\left[c_{b} / n T_{P M}\right]$ (follows from $\left.\mathrm{E}\left[v_{o f}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right] \leq \mathrm{E}\left[v_{a}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right] \leq \mathrm{E}\left[v_{b}\left(n T_{P M}\right)\right]$, see remarks to Eq. (4.48)).

# 4.6.2 Block replacement with minimal repair at failure 

Let's now consider the situation in which the item (system) is as-good-as-new after planned maintenance actions, but as-bad-as-old after repairs; i. e. minimal repair is performed at repair, and the system's failure rate after repair is assumed to be the same as just before failure [2.34, 6.1]. Minimal repair means thus, basically,
that only the failed part of the system is repaired to as-good-as-new.
However,
it must be noted that even if no influence of on/off switching for not failed elements is assumed, the system's failure rate cannot be (exactly) the same as just before failure if $\lambda(x) \neq \lambda(0)$ holds for the repaired part.

One can recognize that with minimal repair, maintenance only at failure leads (theoretically) to a nonhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)$ equal the failure rate $\lambda(t)$ of the item (system) considered; i. e. for $\mathrm{F}(0)=0$,

$$
\mathrm{m}(t)=\lambda(t)=\frac{\mathrm{f}(t)}{1-\mathrm{F}(t)} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{M}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~m}(x) d x=-\ln (1-\mathrm{F}(t))
$$

see Point 2 on p. 535. For this reason, minimal repair cannot be considered for a maintenance only at failure, because for strictly increasing failure rate the system continue to degenerate and at a given time it will be necessary to reestablish the as.good.as.new situation for the whole system.Similar is for age replacement, in particular for $T_{P M}$ large. For an exact evaluation, results from pp. 495 and 530 on regenerative processes can be used (consecutive occurrence of replacements at age (i. e. $P M$ actions) constitute a cycle).

For block replacement with minimal repair, different with respect to Section 4.6.1 is the fact that between consecutive replacements at $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ the involved point process is a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (Eq.(4.55), Appendix A7.8.2). Defining $c_{b r}$ and $c_{f_{m r}}$ as cost for replacement at block and minimal repair, respectively, the total cost per unit time follows as (Eqs. (4.44) \& (4.55))

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[c_{b_{m r}} / n T_{P M}\right]=\frac{c_{f_{m r}} \mathrm{M}\left(T_{P M}\right)+c_{b r}}{T_{P M}}=\frac{-c_{f_{m r}} \ln \left(1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right)\right)+c_{b r}}{T_{P M}}
$$

From Eq. (4.56) one recognizes that $\mathrm{E}\left[c_{b_{m r}} / n T_{P M}\right] \rightarrow \infty$ for $T_{P M} \rightarrow 0$ and $\rightarrow c_{f_{m r}} \lambda(\infty)$ for $T_{P M} \rightarrow \infty$. Optimization of $T_{P M}$ yields (considering $\partial / \partial T_{P M}=0$ and Eq. (4.55))

$$
T_{P M b m r_{o p t}} \lambda\left(T_{P M b m r_{o p t}}\right)^{T_{P M b m r_{o p t}}}-\int_{0}^{T_{P M b m r_{o p t}}} \lambda(t) d t=c_{b r} / c_{f m r}
$$

and thus (Eqs. (4.55) \& (4.56))

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[c_{b m r_{o p t}} / n T_{P M b m r_{o p t}}\right]=c_{f_{m r}} \lambda\left(T_{P M b m r_{o p t}}\right)
$$

if $T_{P M b_{m r, o p t}}<\infty$ exist. For $\lambda(t)$ strictly increasing, $T \lambda(T)-\int_{0}^{T} \lambda(t) d t$ is strictly increasing in $T$ and can cross from below $c_{b r} / c_{f_{m r}}$ at $T=T_{P M b_{m r o p t}}<\infty$. This occurs for $\lambda(\infty)=\infty$; for $\lambda(\infty)=\lambda<\infty, T_{P M b m r o p t}<\infty$ exist for

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}\left[\lambda t-\int_{0}^{t} \lambda(x) d x\right]>c_{b r} / c_{f_{m r}}, \quad \lambda=\lambda(\infty)
$$

No solution exist for $\lambda(t)$ constant. Taking as an example a Weibull distribution (Eq. (A.6.89)), for which $\lambda(t)=\beta \lambda^{\beta} t^{\beta-1}$ and $\mathrm{E}[\tau]=\Gamma(1+1 / \beta)) / \lambda$ one obtains for $\beta>1$

$$
T_{P M b m r o p t}=\frac{\int \sqrt{c_{b r} /\left(\left(\beta-1\right) c_{f_{m r}}\right)}}{\lambda} \quad \& \mathrm{E}\left[c_{b m r_{o p t}} / n T_{P M b m r_{o p t}}\right]=\frac{\beta c_{b r}}{\left(\beta-1\right) T_{P M b m r_{o p t}}}
$$

Cost comparison with results of Section 4.6.1 has to be performed on a case-bycase basis. For the Weibull distribution, Eqs. (4.60) and (4.48) show, for instance, that for $c_{f_{m r}}>\left(\left(\beta-1\right) / c_{b r}\right)^{\beta-1}\left(c_{f} / \Gamma(1 / \beta)\right)^{\beta}$ replacement only at failure is better (cheaper) than block replacement with minimal repair (using $\Gamma(1+1 / \beta)=\Gamma(1 / \beta) / \beta$ ).

# 4.6.3 Further considerations on maintenance strategies 

For the case of non negligible repair and preventive maintenance times, with mean MTTR and MTTPM, asymptotic and steady-state overall availability $O A_{S}$ per Eq. (6.196) can be optimized with respect to preventive maintenance period $T_{P M}$.

(6.196) with $M L D=0$ leads to $O A_{S a}=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{\text {repl } a}\right] /\left[\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{\text {repl } a}\right]+\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right) M T T R\right.$ $\left.+\left(1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right)\right) M T T P M\right], O A_{S b}=T_{P M} /\left[T_{P M}+\mathrm{H}\left(T_{P M}\right) M T T R+M T T P M\right]$, and $O A_{S b m r}=T_{P M} /$ [ $T_{P M}+M T T M R \int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2 m r}} d s+M T T P M$ ] for age replacement, block replacement, and block replacement with minimal repair, respectively ( $M T T M R=$ mean time to minimal repair). Optimization follows using $\partial P A_{S} / \partial T_{P M}=0$, and leads to Eqs. (4.49), (4.52) $\&(4.57)$ with $c_{a r} \& c_{b r}$ replaced by $M T T P M, c_{f}$ by $M T T R$, and $c_{f m r}$ by $M T T M R$. An alternative solution would be to consider $t$ as calendar time.

Besides the previous replacement strategies, a further possibility is to assume that at times $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ the system is inspected, and replacement at $(k+1) T_{P M}$ is performed only if a failure is occurred between $k T_{P M}$ and $(k+1) T_{P M}$. If the failurefree time $\tau$ is $>0$ with $\mathrm{F}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq x\}$, the replacement time $\tau_{\text {repl }}$ has distribution

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{\text {repl }}=k T_{P M}\right\}=\mathrm{F}\left(k T_{P M}\right)-\mathrm{F}\left((k-1) T_{P M}\right), \quad k=1,2, \ldots, \mathrm{~F}(0)=0
$$

This case has been investigated in [6.17] with cost considerations. If $c_{i}=$ inspection cost, $c_{r}=$ cost for replacement, and $c_{d}=$ cost for unit down time $\left(c_{i}, c_{r}, c_{d}>0\right)$, the total cost $C$ per unit time is for $t=n T_{P M} \rightarrow \infty$ given by

$$
C=\frac{n c_{i}}{n T_{P M}}+\frac{c_{r} n T_{P M} / \mathrm{E}\left\{\tau_{r e p l}\right\}}{n T_{P M}}+\frac{c_{d} \mathrm{E}\left\{\tau_{r e p l}-\tau\right\}}{\mathrm{E}\left\{\tau_{r e p l}\right\}}=\frac{c_{i}}{T_{P M}}+\frac{c_{r}}{\mathrm{E}\left\{\tau_{r e p l}\right\}}-\frac{c_{d} M T T F}{\mathrm{E}\left\{\tau_{r e p l}\right\}}+c_{d}
$$

where $M T T F=\mathrm{E}[\tau]$. For $T_{P M} \rightarrow \infty, \mathrm{E}\left\{\tau_{\text {repl }}\right\} \rightarrow \infty$ and $C \rightarrow c_{d}$. Thus, inspection is useful for $C<c_{d}$. For given $\mathrm{F}(x)$ it is possible to find a $T_{P M}$ which minimizes $C$ [6.17].

For the mission availability and work-mission availability, as defined by Eqs. (6.28) and (6.31), it can be asked in some applications that the number of repairs (replacements) be limited to $N$ (e. g. because only $N$ spare parts are available). In this case, the summation in Eqs. (6.29) and (6.32) goes up to $n=N+1$. If $k$ elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{k}$ with constant failure rates $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{k} \&$ constant repair rates $\mu_{1}, \ldots, \mu_{k}$ are in series, a good approximation for the work-mission availability with limited repairs is obtained by multiplying the probability for total system down time $\leq x$ for unlimited repairs (Eq. (7.22) with $\lambda=\lambda_{S 0}$ and $\mu=\mu_{S}$ from Table 6.10 (2 nd row)) with the $k$ probabilities that $N_{i}$ spare parts will be sufficient for element $E_{i}$ [6.11].

A strategy can also be based on the repair time $\tau^{\prime}$ itself. Assuming, for instance, that if the repair is not finished at time $\Delta$ the failed element is replaced at time $\Delta$ by a new one in a negligible time, the distribution function $\mathrm{G}(x)$ of the repair times $\tau^{\prime}$ is truncated at $\Delta$ (Eq. (4.38)). For the case of const. repair rate $\mu$, the Laplace transform of $\mathrm{G}_{\text {trunc }}(x)$ is given by (Table A9.7b) $\tilde{\mathrm{G}}_{\text {trunc }}(s)=\left(\mu+s \cdot e^{-(s+\mu) \Delta}\right) / s(s+\mu)$, yielding $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\left(1-e^{-\mu \Delta}\right) / \mu$ (Eq. (4.39)).

Further maintenance strategies are e. g. in [2.34, 4.18, 4.30, A7.4 (62)]. A comparison between some different maintenance strategies with respect to reliability \& availability is given in Table 4.4 for a basic reliability structure (Fig. 6.15 on p. 221). Expression for $M T T F_{S 0}$ is the same for all cases in Table 4.4 and given by Eq. Cost considerations are important in practical applications and apply, in particular, to system effectiveness (Section 1.2.9), reliability allocation (Section 2.4), spare parts provisioning (Section 4.5), maintenance strategies (Section 4.6), and test strategies (Section 8.4). In addition to the considerations in Sections 4.5 and 4.6, this section considers two basic models based on homogeneous Poisson processes (HPP) with fixed and random costs.

As a first example consider the case in which a constant cost $c_{0}$ is related to each repair of a given item (system). Assuming that repair duration is negligible and times between consecutive failures are independent and exponentially distributed with parameter $\lambda$, the failure flow is a homogeneous Poisson process and the probability for $n$ failures during the operating time $t$ is given by (Eq. (A7.41))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{n \text { failures in }(0, t] \mid \lambda\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t)=n \mid \lambda\}=\frac{(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!} e^{-\lambda t}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& n=0,1,2, \ldots \\
& t>0, v(0)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Eq. (4.63) is also the probability that the cumulated repair cost over $t$ is $C=n c_{0}$. Mean and variance of $C$ are (Eqs. (A6.40) and (A6.46) with Eq. (A7.42))

$$
\mathrm{E}[C]=c_{0} \lambda t \quad \text { and } \quad \operatorname{Var}[C]=c_{0}^{2} \lambda t
$$

For large $\lambda t, C$ is approximately normally distributed (Eqs. (A6.105)) with mean and variance as per Eq. (4.64), see e.g. [A8.8].

If repair cost is a random variable $\xi_{i}>0$ distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{i} \leq x\right\}$ $(\mathrm{F}(0)=0, i=1,2, \ldots), \xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \ldots$ are mutually independent and independent of the count function $v(t)$ giving the number of failures in the operating time interval $(0, t]$, and $\xi_{t}$ is the sum of $\xi_{i}$ over $(0, t]$, it holds that (Eq. (A7.218))

$$
\xi_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{v(t)} \xi_{i}, \quad v(t)=1,2, \ldots, t>0, v(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0, \xi_{t}=0 \text { for } v(t)=0
$$

$\xi_{t}$ is distributed as the (cumulative) repair time for failures occurred in a total operating time $t$ of a repairable item (system), and is thus given by the workmission availability $\mathrm{WMA}_{\mathrm{S} 0}\left(T_{0}, x\right)$ (Eq. (6.32) with $T_{0}=t$ ). Assuming that the failures flow is a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) with parameter $\lambda$, all $\xi_{i}$ are mutually independent, independent of $v(t)$, and have the same exponential distribution with parameter $\mu$, Eq. (6.32) with constant failure and repair rates $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ and $\mu(x)=\mu$ and $T_{0}=t$ yields (Eqs.(6.33), (A7.219))

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{t} \leq x\right\}=\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}(t, x)=e^{-\lambda t}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!} e^{-\lambda t}\left(1-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\mu x)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\mu x}\right)\right] \\
& =1-e^{-(\lambda t+\mu x)} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\mu x)^{k}}{k!}\right], \quad t>0 \text { given, } x>0, \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{t}=0\right\}=e^{-\lambda t}
\end{aligned}
$$Mean and variance of $\xi_{t}$ follow as (Eqs. (4.66), (A6.38), (A6.45), (A6.41), Problem A7.11 in Appendix A11)

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=\lambda t / \mu \quad \text { and } \quad \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=2 \lambda t / \mu^{2}
$$

Furthermore, for $t \rightarrow \infty$ the distribution of $\xi_{t}$ approach a normal distribution with mean and variance as per Eq. (4.67). Moments of $\xi_{t}$ can also be obtained for arbitrary $\mathrm{F}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{i} \leq x\right\}$, with $\mathrm{F}(0)=0$ (Eq. (A7.221), Example A7.14)

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)] \mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right] \& \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)] \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{i}\right]+\operatorname{Var}[\mathrm{v}(t)] \mathrm{E}^{2}\left[\xi_{i}\right]
$$

Of interest in some practical applications can also be the distribution of the time $\tau_{C}$ at which the cumulative $\operatorname{cost} \xi_{t}$ crosses a give (fixed) barrier $C$. For the case given by Eq. (4.66) (in particular for $\xi_{i}>0$ ), the events

$$
\left\{\tau_{C}>t\right\} \quad \text { and } \quad\left\{\xi_{t} \leq C\right\}
$$

are equivalent. Form Eq. (4.66) it follows then (Eq. (A7.223))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{C}>t\right\}=1-e^{-(\lambda t+\mu C)} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\mu C)^{k}}{k!}\right], \quad C>0 \text { given, } t>0
$$

(in Eq. (4.70), $C$ has dimension of $\mu^{-1}$ ).
More general cost optimization strategies are often necessary in practical applications. For example, spare parts provisioning has to be considered as a parameter in the optimization between performance, reliability, availability, logistic support and cost, taking care of obsolescence aspects as well. In some cases, one parameter is given (e. g. cost) and the best logistic structure is sought to maximize system availability or system performance. Basic considerations, as discussed above and in Sections 1.2.9, 8.4, A6.10.7, A7.5.3.3, apply. However, even assuming constant failure and repair rates, numerical solutions can become necessary (see e.g. [4.32]).# 5 Design Guidelines for Reliability, Maintainability, and Software Quality 

Reliability, maintainability, safety, and software quality have to be built into complex equipment \& systems during the design and development phase. This has to be supported by analytical investigations (Chapters 2, 4, 6) as well as by design guidelines and tests (Chapters 5, 3, 7, 8). Developing design guidelines demands practical experience and engineering feeling. Adherence to such guidelines limits the influence of those aspects which can invalidate the models assumed for analytical investigations, and improve the inherent reliability, maintainability, and safety of both hardware \& software. Each industry producing equipment and systems with high reliability (RAMS) requirements is aware of the necessity for such guidelines. This chapter gives a comprehensive list of design guidelines for reliability, maintainability (incl. human and safety aspects), and software quality of complex electronic and electromechanical equipment \& systems, harmonized with industry's needs [1.2 (1996)] (see e. g. also [1.22, 1.23, 5.0-5.20, 5.21-5.33, 5.40-5.85, 6.82], in particular $[1.22,1.23,5.0,5.5,5.14,5.29,6.82]$ for military and space applications).

### 5.1 Design Guidelines for Reliability

Reliability analysis in the design and development phase (Chapter 2) gives an estimate of the item's (system's) true reliability, based on some assumptions regarding data used, interface problems, dependence between components, materials compatibility, environmental influences, transients, EMC, ESD, etc., as well as on the quality of manufacture and the user's skill level. To consider exhaustively all these aspects is difficult. The following design guidelines can be used to alleviate intrinsic weaknesses and improve inherent reliability of complex equipment and systems.

### 5.1.1 Derating

Thermal and electrical stresses greatly influence the failure rate of electronic components. Derating is mandatory to improve the inherent reliability of equipment and systems (see critical remark on p. 106). Table 5.1 gives recommended stress factors $S$ (Eq. # 5.1.2 Cooling 

As a general rule, the junction temperature $\theta_{J}$ of semiconductor devices should be kept as near as possible to the ambient temperature $\theta_{A}$ of the equipment or system in which they are used; if not possible,$$
\begin{aligned}
& \theta_{J} \leq 100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { (desirable } \leq 65^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { for optoelectronic devices, } \leq 80^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { for ICs, } \\
& \leq 120^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { for power devices) is recommended for a reliable design. }
\end{aligned}
$$

In a steady-state situation, i. e. with constant power dissipation $P$, the following relationships

$$
\theta_{J}=\theta_{A}+R_{J A} P
$$

or

$$
\theta_{J}=\theta_{A}+\left(R_{J C}+R_{C S}+R_{S A}\right) P
$$

can be established and used to define the allowed thermal resistance

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
R_{J A} \text { for junction - ambient } & R_{J C} \text { for junction - case } \\
R_{C S} \text { for case - surface } & R_{S A} \text { for surface - ambient, }
\end{array}
$$

where surface is used for heat sink, see Example 5.1 for an application.

# Example 5.1 

Determine the thermal resistance $R_{S A}$ of a heat sink by assuming $P=400 \mathrm{~mW}, \theta_{J}=70^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, $\theta_{A}=40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, and $R_{J C}+R_{C S}=35^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{W}$.

## Solution

From Eq. (5.2) it follows that

$$
R_{S A}=\frac{\theta_{J}-\theta_{A}}{P}-R_{J C}-R_{C S} \quad \text { and thus } \quad R_{S A}=\frac{30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}{0.4 \mathrm{~W}}-35^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{W}=40^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{W}
$$

For many practical applications, thermal resistance can be assumed to be independent of the temperature. However, $R_{J C}$ generally depends on the package used (lead frame, packaging form and type), $R_{C S}$ varies with the kind and thickness of thermal compound between the device package and the heat sink (or device support), and $R_{S A}$ is a function of the heat-sink dimensions and form as well as of the type of cooling used (free convection, forced air, liquid-cooled plate, etc.). Indicative thermal resistance values $R_{J C}$ and $R_{J A}$ for free convection in ambient air without heat sinks are given in Table 5.2. The values of Table 5.2 are indicative and have to be replaced with specific values for exact calculations.

Cooling problems should not only be considered locally at the component level, but be integrated into a thermal design concept (thermal management). In defining the layout of an assembly, care must be taken in placing high power dissipation parts away from temperature sensitive components like wet Al capacitors and optoelectronic devices (the useful life is reduced by a factor of 2 for a $10-20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ increase of the ambient temperature). In placing the assemblies in a rack, the cooling flow should be directed from the parts with low toward those with high power dissipation.Table 5.2 Indicative thermal resistance values for semiconductor component packages
