For large seriesparallel structures, approximate expressions are carefully developed in Section 6.7. Procedures for repairable systems with complex structure (for which a reliability block diagram often does not exist) are given in Section 6.8 on the basis of practical examples, including imperfect switching, incomplete coverage, more than 2 states, phased-mission systems, common cause failures, and fault tolerant reconfigurable systems with reward \& frequency/duration aspects. It is shown that tools developed in Appendix A7 can be used to solve many of the problems occurring in practical applications, on a case-by-case basis working with a diagram of transition rates or a time schedule (Sections 6.8, A7.7). Alternative investigation methods, as well as computer-aided analyses are discussed in Section 6.9, where a Monte Carlo approach useful for rare events is given. Human reliability and risk management are considered in Sections 6.10 and 6.11.

From the results of Sections 6.2-6.11, the following conclusions can be drawn:

1. As long as MTTR $<<$ MTTF holds for each element, shape of distribution functions of repair times has small influence on $M T T F_{S i} \& P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ (pp. 206-07).
2. As a consequence of Point 1 , it is preferable to start investigations by assuming Markov models (constant failure \& repair rates for all elements, Table 6.2); in a second step, more appropriate distribution functions can be considered (p. 277).
3. The assumption (6.2) of no further failure at system down has no influence on the reliability function; it support the existence of regeneration states (even better if also (6.3) holds, see p. 240) and allows a reduction of the state space.
4. Already for moderately large systems, use of Markov models can become timeconsuming (up to $e \cdot n$ ! states for a rel. block diagram with $n$ elements, p. 226); approximate expressions are thus important, and the macro-structures introduced in Section 6.7 (Table 6.10) adheres well to many practical applications.
5. For large systems or complex structures, following possibilities are available:

- work with a diagram of transition rates or a time schedule,
- calculate only the mean time to failure and steady-state availability at system level (Table 6.2, Eqs. (A7.126), (A7.173), (A7.131), (A7.178)),
- use approximate expressions (Sections 6.7 \& 6.9.7, Tables 6.9 \& 6.10),
- use alternative methods or Monte-Carlo simulation (Section 6.9).

6. Human reliability and risk management (Sections 6.10 and 6.11) have to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis; having in mind, as far as possible, to bypass or greatly support dangerous human decisions.# 6.2 One-Item Structure 

A one-item structure is an unit of arbitrary complexity, generally considered as an entity for investigations. Its reliability block diagram is a single element (Fig. 6.1). Considering that in practical applications a repairable one-item structure can have the complexity of a system, and also to use the same notation as in the following sections of this chapter,
reliability figures are given with indices $S$ or $S i$ (e.g. $P A_{S}, \mathrm{R}_{S i}(t), M T T F_{S i}$ ), where $S$ stands for system and i specifies the state $Z_{i}$ entered at $t=0$ ( $S$ alone for steady-state $\left(P A_{S}=A A_{S}\right)$ and $Z_{0}$ for item (system) new at $\left.t=0\right)$; see also the footnote on p. 279.

Under the assumptions (6.1)-(6.3) and (6.5) - (6.7), the repairable one-item structure is completely characterized by the distribution function of the failure-free times $\tau_{0}>0, \tau_{1}>0, \ldots$

$$
\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{0} \leq x\right\} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{F}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i} \leq x\right\}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& i=1,2, \ldots, x>0 \\
& \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

with densities

$$
\mathrm{f}_{A}(x)=\frac{d \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)}{d x} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{f}(x)=\frac{d \mathrm{~F}(x)}{d x}
$$

the distribution function of the repair (restoration) times $\tau_{0}^{\prime}>0, \tau_{1}^{\prime}>0, \ldots$

$$
\mathrm{G}_{A}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{0}^{\prime} \leq x\right\} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{G}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i}^{\prime} \leq x\right\}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& i=1,2, \ldots, x>0 \\
& \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{G}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

with densities

$$
\mathrm{g}_{A}(x)=\frac{d \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)}{d x} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{g}(x)=\frac{d \mathrm{G}(x)}{d x}
$$

and the probability $p$ that the one-item structure is up at $t=0$

$$
p=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { at } t=0\}
$$

or

$$
1-p=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { down (i.e. under repair) at } t=0\}
$$

respectively. $\tau_{0} \& \tau_{0}^{\prime}$ belong to the same item, as $\tau_{i} \& \tau_{i}^{\prime}$; all are interarrival times, and $x$ is used instead of $t . M T T F=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right], M T T R=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}^{\prime}\right], \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau_{i}\right], \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau_{i}^{\prime}\right](i \geq 1)$ are tacitly assumed $<\infty$. With these assumptions, the time behavior of the one-item structure can be investigated with an alternating renewal process (Appendix A7.3).


Figure 6.1 Reliability block diagram for a one-item structure

Figure 6.2 Possible time schedule for a repairable one-item structure new at $t=0 \&$ after each repair (repair times greatly exaggerated, alternating renewal process with regeneration points 0 and $S_{\text {duu1 }}, S_{\text {duu } 2}, \ldots$ for a transition from down to up state, given item up (here new) at $t=0$, marked by $\bullet$ )

Section 6.2.1 considers the one-item structure new at $t=0$, i. e. the case $p=1$ and $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)$, with arbitrary $\mathrm{F}(x)$ and $\mathrm{G}(x)$. Generalization of the initial conditions at $t=0$ (Sections 6.2.3) allows in Sections $6.2 .4 \& 6.2 .5$ a depth investigation of the asymptotic and steady-state behavior.

# 6.2.1 One-Item Structure New at Time $t=0$ 

Figure 6.2 shows the time behavior of a one-item structure new at $t=0 . \tau_{1}, \tau_{2}, \ldots$ are the failure-free times. They are statistically independent and distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(x)$ as per Eq. (6.8). Similarly, $\tau_{1}^{\prime}, \tau_{2}^{\prime}, \ldots$ are the repair times, distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)$ as per Eq. (6.10). Considering assumption (6.5), the time points $0, S_{\text {duul }} \ldots$ are regeneration points (see footnote on p. 480) and constitute an ordinary renewal process embedded in the original alternating renewal process. Investigations of this Section are based on this property ( $S_{\text {duu }}$ means a transition from down (repair) to up (operating) starting up at $t=0$ ).

### 6.2.1.1 Reliability Function

The reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ gives the probability that the item operates failure free in $(0, t]$ given item new at $t=0$

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { up in }(0, t] \mid \text { new at } t=0\} .^{*}\}
$$

Considering Fig. 6.2 \& Eq. (6.8) it holds that

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}>t\right\}=1-\mathrm{F}(t)
$$

yielding $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for the case of constant failure rate $\lambda$. The mean time to failure given item new at $t=0$ follows from Eq. (A6.38)

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t, \quad\left(\text { for } M T T F_{S 0}<\infty\right)
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    *) Equation (6.13) follows form $\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ in $[0, t]\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ new at $t=0 \cap u p$ in $(0, t]\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ new at $t=0\}$ $\cdot \operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ in $(0, t] \mid$ new at $t=0\}=1 \cdot R_{S 0}(t)=R_{S 0}(t)$ (see also pp. 39-40 and 184).with upper limit of the integral $T_{L}$ should the useful life of the item be limited to $T_{L}$, see comment to Eq. (2.8) on p. 39. In the following, $T_{L}=\infty$ is tacitly assumed.

For the case of constant failure rate $\lambda_{S 0}$, Eq. (6.15) yields $M T T F_{S 0}=1 / \lambda_{S 0}$;
$\lambda_{S 0}=$ item (system) failure rate for item new at $t=0$, often tacitly designated as $\lambda$ in practical applications $\left(\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}\right.$, see pp.390-91).

# 6.2.1.2 Point Availability 

The point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ gives the probability of finding the item operating at time $t$ given item new at $t=0$ (see footnote on p. 176)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { at } t \mid \text { new at } t=0\}
$$

For $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ it holds that

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {duu }}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t-x)) d x
$$

$\mathrm{A}(t)$ is often used instead of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$, see remark on p. 386. Equation (6.17) is derived in Appendix A7.3 (Eq. (A7.56)) using the theorem of total probability. $1-\mathrm{F}(t)$ is the probability of no failure in $(0, t], \mathrm{h}_{\text {duu }}(x) d x$ gives the probability that any one of the regeneration points $S_{\text {duu } 1}, S_{\text {duu } 2}, \ldots$ lies in $(x, x+d x]$, and $1-\mathrm{F}(t-x)$ is the probability that no further failure occurs in $(x, t]$. Using Laplace transform (Appendix A9.7) and considering Eq. (A7.50) with $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=F(x)$, Eq. (6.17) yields

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{1-\widehat{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s(1-\widehat{\mathrm{f}}(s) \widehat{\mathrm{g}}(s))}
$$

$\widehat{\mathrm{f}}(s)$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{g}}(s)$ are the Laplace transforms of the failure-free time and repair time densities, respectively (Eqs. (6.9) and (6.11)), see Example 6.1 for an application.

## Example 6.1

a) Give the Laplace transform of the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for the case of a constant failure rate $\lambda\left(\lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}\right)$.
b) Give the Laplace transform and the corresponding time function of the point availability for the case of constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda \& \mu\left(\lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0} \& \mu(x)=\mu \equiv \mu_{S}\right)$.

## Solution

a) With $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ or $\mathrm{f}(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, Eq. (6.18) yields

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=1 /(s+\lambda(1-\widehat{\mathrm{g}}(s))
$$

Supplementary results: $\mathrm{g}(x)=\alpha(\alpha x)^{\beta-1} e^{-\alpha x} / \Gamma(\beta)$ (Eq. (A6.98)) yields (Tab. A9.7b)

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{g}}(s)=\frac{\alpha^{\beta}}{(s+\alpha)^{\beta}} \quad \& \quad \widehat{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{(s+\alpha)^{\beta}}{(s+\lambda)(s+\alpha)^{\beta}-\lambda \alpha^{\beta}}
$$b) With $\mathrm{f}(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ and $\mathrm{g}(x)=\mu e^{-\mu x}$, Eq. (6.18) yields

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{s+\mu}{s(s+\lambda+\mu)}
$$

and thus (Table A9.7b)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}+\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu} e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t} \approx(1-\lambda / \mu)+\frac{\lambda}{\mu} e^{-\mu t} \approx 1-\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\left(1-e^{-\mu t}\right)
$$

$\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ converges rapidly, exponentially with a time constant $1 /(\lambda+\mu) \approx 1 / \mu=M T T R$ to the asymptotic value $\mu /(\lambda+\mu)=P A_{S} \approx 1-\lambda / \mu$, see Section 6.2 .4 for an extensive discussion.
Supplementary results: Because of $\lambda(t)=\lambda$, the probability to be up at time $t$ and have a failure in $(t, t+\delta t]$ is given by $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \lambda \delta t$, see also the footnote on p. 491.
$\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can also be obtained using renewal theory arguments (Appendices A7.2, A7.3, A7.6): After the first repair the item is as-good-as-new, $S_{\text {duul }}$ is a regeneration point and from this time point the process restarts anew as at $t=0$. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { up at } t \mid S_{\text {duul }}=x\right\}=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t-x)
$$

Considering that the event

$$
\{u p \text { at } t\}
$$

occurs with exactly one of the following two mutually exclusive events

$$
\{\text { no failure in }(0, t]\}
$$

or

$$
\left\{S_{\text {duul }}<t \cap u p \text { at } t\right\}
$$

it follows that

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}(\mathrm{f}(x) * \mathrm{~g}(x)) \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t-x) d x
$$

where $\mathrm{f}(x) * \mathrm{~g}(x)$ is the density of the sum $\tau_{1}+\tau_{1}^{\prime}$ (see Fig 6.2 and Eq. (A6.75)). Equation (6.22) is the integral equation for $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$, and leads also to Eq. (6.18).

# 6.2.1.3 Average Availability 

The average availability $\mathrm{AA}_{S 0}(t)$ is defined as the expected proportion of time in which the item is operating in $(0, t]$ given item new at $t=0$

$$
\mathrm{AA}_{S 0}(t)=\frac{1}{t} \mathrm{E}[\text { total up time in }(0, t] \mid \text { new at } t=0]
$$

Considering $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(x)$ from Eq. (6.17), it holds that$$
\mathrm{AA}_{S 0}(t)=\frac{1}{t} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(x) d x
$$

Eq. (6.24) has a great intuitive appeal. It can be proved by considering that the time behavior of the repairable item can be described by an indicator (binary process) $\zeta(t)$ taking values 1 for $u p$ and 0 for down. From this, $\mathrm{E}\{\zeta(t)\}=0 \cdot\left(1-\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)\right)+$ $1 \cdot \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ and, taking care of ${ }^{t} \int_{0} \zeta(x) d x=$ total $u p$ time in $(0, t]$, it follows that (by Fubini's theorem [A6.7 (Vol.II)] and assuming existence of the integrals)

$$
\mathrm{AA}_{S 0}(t)=\frac{1}{t} \mathrm{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t} \zeta(x) d x\right]=\frac{1}{t} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{E}[\zeta(x)] d x=\frac{1}{t} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(x) d x
$$

# 6.2.1.4 Interval Reliability 

The interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ gives the probability that the item operates failure free during an interval $[t, t+\theta]$ given item new at $t=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta) & =\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { (up at } t \cap u p \text { for } t<x \leq t+\theta) \mid \text { new at } t=0\} \\
& =\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { in }[t, t+\theta] \mid \text { new at } t=0\}
\end{aligned}
$$

The same method used to obtain Eq. (6.17) leads to

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=1-\mathrm{F}(t+\theta)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t+\theta-x)) d x
$$

see Example 6.2 for an application.

## Example 6.2

Give the interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ for the case of a constant failure rate $\lambda \quad\left(\lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}\right)$.

## Solution

With $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ it follows that

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=e^{-\lambda(t+\theta)}+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(x) e^{-\lambda(t+\theta-x)} d x=\left[e^{-\lambda t}+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(x) e^{-\lambda(t-x)} d x\right] e^{-\lambda \theta}
$$

Comparison with Eq. (6.17) for $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ yields

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \cdot e^{-\lambda \theta}, \quad \text { for } \lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}
$$

It must be pointed out that the product rule in Eq. 6.27, expressing $\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ in $[t, t+\theta]$ | new at $t=0\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ at $t \mid$ new at $t=0\} \cdot \operatorname{Pr}\{$ no failure in $(t, t+\theta] \mid u p$ at $t\}$,
only holds because of const.failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ (memoryless property, p.458);
in the general case, the 2 nd term is $\operatorname{Pr}\{$ no failure in $(t, t+\theta] \mid$ (up at $t \cap$ new at $t=0)\}$, which differs from $\operatorname{Pr}\{$ no failure in $(t, t+\theta] \mid u p$ at $t\}$ for $\lambda(x) \neq \lambda$;
also should the use of $\operatorname{IR}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$ as reliability $\mathrm{R}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$, as in [A1.4], be dropped, to avoid misuses (see also remarks on pp. 40, 397, 442).# 6.2.1.5 Special Kinds of Availability 

In addition to the point and average availability (Sections 6.2.1.2 and 6.2.1.3), there are several other kinds of availability useful for practical applications [6.5 (1973)]:

1. Mission Availability: The mission availability $\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{o}\right)$ gives the probability that in a mission of total operating time (total up time) $T_{o}$ each failure can be repaired within a time span $t_{o}$, given item new at $t=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{o}\right)= & \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { each individual failure occuring in a mission with total op- } \\
& \text { erating time } T_{o} \text { can be repaired in a time } \leq t_{o} \mid \text { new at } t=0\} \text {. }
\end{aligned}
$$

Mission availability is important in applications where interruptions of length $\leq t_{o}$ can be accepted. Its calculation considers all cases with $n=0,1, \ldots$ failures, taking care that at the end of the mission the item is operating (to reach the given (fixed) operating time $T_{o}$ ). Thus, for given (fixed) $T_{o}, t_{o}>0$

$$
\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{o}\right)=1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{o}\right)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\mathrm{F}_{n}\left(T_{o}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}\left(T_{o}\right)\right)\left(\mathrm{G}\left(t_{o}\right)\right)^{n,+1}
$$

holds. $\mathrm{F}_{n}\left(T_{o}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}\left(T_{o}\right)$ is the probability for $n$ failures during the total operating time $T_{o}$ (Eq. (A7.14) with $\left.\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)\right) ;\left(\mathrm{G}\left(t_{o}\right)\right)^{n}$ is the probability that all $n$ repair times will be shorter than $t_{o}$. For constant failure rate $\lambda$ it holds that $\mathrm{F}_{n}\left(T_{o}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}\left(T_{o}\right)=\left(\lambda T_{o}\right)^{n} e^{-\lambda T_{o}} / n$ ! (Eq. (A7.41)) and thus

$$
\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{o}\right)=e^{-\lambda T_{o}\left(1-\mathrm{G}\left(t_{o}\right)\right)}, \quad \text { for } \lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}
$$

2. Work-Mission Availability: The work-mission availability $\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, x\right)$ gives the probability that the sum of the repair times for all failures occurring in a mission of total operating time (total up time) $T_{o}$ is $\leq x$, given item new a $t=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, x\right)= & \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { sum of the repair times for all failures occurring in a mis - } \\
& \text { sion of total operating time } T_{o} \text { is } \leq x \mid \text { new at } t=0\} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly as for Eq. (6.29) it follows that for given (fixed) $T_{o}, x>0$ +

$$
\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, x\right)=1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{o}\right)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\mathrm{F}_{n}\left(T_{o}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}\left(T_{o}\right)\right) \mathrm{G}_{n}(x),^{(+)}
$$

where $\mathrm{G}_{n}(x)$ is the distribution function of the sum of $n$ repair times with distribution $\mathrm{G}(x)$ (per Eq. (A7.12)). As for the mission availability, the item is up at the end of the mission (to reach the given (fixed) operating time $T_{o}$ ). For constant failure \& repair rates $(\lambda, \mu)$, it follows that (Eq.(4.66) or (A7.219))

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$An unlimited number $n$ of repair is assumed here, see e.g. Section 4.6 (p. 140) for $n$ limited.
    ${ }^{+ \text {+ })}$ See e. g. p. 538 for a possible application of Eq. (6.32) to a cumulative damage model.$$
\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, x\right)=1-e^{-\left(\lambda T_{0}+\mu x\right) \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left\{\frac{\left(\lambda T_{0}\right)^{n}}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\mu x)^{k}}{k!}\right\}}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& T_{0}>0 \text { given, } \quad \mathrm{x}>0 \\
& \mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}\left(T_{0}, 0\right)=e^{-\lambda T_{0}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Defining $D T$ as total down time and $U T=t-D T$ as total up time in $(0, t]$, one recognizes that for given $t, \operatorname{Pr}\{D T$ in $(0, t] \leq x \mid$ new at $t=0\}=\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}(t-x, x)$ holds for an item described by Fig. $6.2(t>0,0<x<t)$. However, the item can now be up or down at $t$, and the situation differs thus from that defined by Eq. (6.31), for which the item is up at the given cumulative operating time $T_{o}$. $\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}(t-x, x)$ has been investigated in [A7.29 (1957)]; besides a closed analytical expression for constant failure and repair rates $(\lambda, \mu)$, it is shown that the distribution of $D T$ converges for $t \rightarrow \infty$ to a normal distribution with mean $t \lambda /(\lambda+\mu) \approx t \lambda / \mu$ and variance $t 2 \lambda \mu /(\lambda+\mu)^{3} \approx t 2 \lambda / \mu^{2}$. It can be noted that referred to Eqs. (6.32) and (6.33), mean and variance of the total repair time are given exactly by $T_{0} \lambda / \mu$ and $T_{0} 2 \lambda / \mu^{2}$, respectively (Eq. (A7.220)).
3. Joint Availability: The joint availability $\mathrm{JA}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ gives the probability of finding the item operating at the time points $t$ and $t+\theta$, given item new at $t=0 \quad(t, \theta$ given (fixed), see e.g. [6.15 (1999), 6.28] for stochastic demand)

$$
\mathrm{JA}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\operatorname{Pr}\{(\text { up at } t \cap \text { up at } t+\theta) \mid \text { new at } t=0\}
$$

For the case of constant failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$, Eq. (6.27) yields

$$
\mathrm{JA}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \cdot \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(\theta), \quad \text { for } \lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}
$$

For arbitrary failure rate, $\{u p$ at $t \cap u p$ at $t+\theta \mid$ new at $t=0\}$ occurs with

$$
\{u p \text { in }[t, t+\theta] \mid \text { new at } t=0\}
$$

yielding the interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ given by Eq. (6.26), or

$$
\{(\text { up at } t \cap \text { next failure occurs before } t+\theta \cap u p \text { at } t+\theta) \mid \text { new at } t=0\}
$$

for which it is necessary to consider the distribution function of the forward recurrence time in the up state $\tau_{R u}(t)$. As shown in Fig. 6.3a, $\tau_{R u}(t)$ can only be defined if the item is up at time $t$, hence

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R u}(t)>x \mid \text { new at } t=0\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { in }(t, t+x] \mid(u p \text { at } t \cap \text { new at } t=0)\}
$$

and thus, as for Example A7.2 and considering Eqs. (6.16) \& (6.25),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R u}(t)>x \mid \text { new at } t=0\right\} & =\frac{\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { in }[t, t+x] \mid \text { new at } t=0\}}{\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { at } t \mid \text { new at } t=0\}} \\
& =\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+x) / \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}_{\tau_{R u}(t)}(x)
\end{aligned}
$$

it can be noted that for constant failure rate $\lambda, 1-\mathrm{F}_{\tau_{R u}(t)}(x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ (Eq. (6.27)).Considering Eq. (6.36) it follows that [6.5 (1973)]

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{JA}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)+\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \int_{0}^{\theta} \mathrm{f}_{\tau_{R u}(t)}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(\theta-x) d x \\
& =\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)-\int_{0}^{\theta} \frac{\partial \operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+x)}{\partial x} \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(\theta-x) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ up at $t \mid$ a repair begins at $t=0\}$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} h_{d u d}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t-x)) d x
$$

with $\mathrm{h}_{\text {dud }}(t)=\mathrm{g}(t)+\mathrm{g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t)+\mathrm{g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t)+\ldots$ (Eq. (A7.50)). $\mathrm{JA}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ can also be obtained in a similar way to $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ in Eq. (6.17), by considering the alternating renewal process starting up at the time $t$ with $\tau_{R u}(t)$ distributed according to $\mathrm{F}_{\tau_{R u(t)}}(x)$ as per Eq. (6.36). This leads directly to

$$
\mathrm{JA}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)+\int_{0}^{\theta} \mathrm{h}_{\text {duu }}^{\prime}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(\theta-x)) d x
$$

with $\mathrm{h}_{\text {duu }}^{\prime}(x)=\mathrm{f}_{\tau_{R u}(t)}^{\prime}(x) * g(x)+\mathrm{f}_{\tau_{R u}(t)}^{\prime}(x) * \mathrm{~g}(x) * \mathrm{f}(x) * \mathrm{~g}(x)+\ldots$, see Eq. (A7.50), and $\mathrm{f}_{\tau_{R u}(t)}^{\prime}(x)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \mathrm{f}_{\tau_{R u}(t)}(x)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) d \mathrm{~F}_{\tau_{R u}(t)}(x) / d x=-\partial \operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+x) / \partial x$, see Eqs. (6.36) and (6.37). To complete the discussion, the distribution function for the forward recurrence time in the down state $\tau_{R d}(t)$ follows as for $\tau_{R u}(t)$, considering Fig. 6.3b,

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R d}(t) \leq x \mid \text { new at } t=0\right\}=1-\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {udu }}(y)(1-\mathrm{G}(t+x-y)) d y /\left(1-\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)\right)
$$

with $\mathrm{h}_{\text {udu }}(t)=\mathrm{f}(t)+\mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t)+\ldots$ (Eq. (A7.50)). For constant failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$, Eq. (6.37) or (6.39) leads to Eq. (6.35), by considering Eq.(6.19).

Other kinds of availability are possible. For instance, availability by omitting down times for repair shorter than a given fixed or random time $\Delta$ has been investigated in [6.48], yielding for the case of fixed $\Delta$ to $\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{\Delta}(t)=1-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}(1+\mu \Delta) e^{-\mu_{\Delta}}$.


Figure 6.3 Forward recurrence times $\tau_{R u}(t)$ and $\tau_{R d}(t)$ in an alternating renewal process# 6.2.2 One-Item Structure New at $t=0$ with Const. Failure Rate $\lambda$ 

In many practical applications, a constant failure rate $\lambda$ can be assumed. In this case, the expressions of Section 6.2 .1 can be simplified making use of the memoryless property given by the constant failure rate. Table 6.3 summarizes the results for the cases of constant failure rate $(\lambda)$ and constant or arbitrary repair rate $(\mu$ or $\mu(x)=\mathrm{g}(x) /(1-\mathrm{G}(x)))$. Approximations in Table 6.3 are valid for $\lambda \ll \mu$ and $t>10 / \mu=10$ MTTR. For points 4 in Table 6.3, $\mathrm{AA}_{S 0}(0)=1$ and the convergence of $\mathrm{AA}_{S 0}(t)$ toward $A A_{S}=P A_{S}$ is (at least for $\mu(x)=\mu$ ) slightly slower than that of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$. The product rule for $\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ and $\mathrm{JA}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ is valid only because of the constant failure rate $\lambda$.

Mission availability $\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{f}\right)$ | $e^{-\lambda T_{o}\left(1-\mathrm{G}\left(t_{f}\right)\right)}$ | $e^{-\lambda T_{o} e^{-\mu t_{f}}}$ | $\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{f}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ each failure in a mission with total operating time $T_{o}$ can be repaired in a time $\leq t_{f} \mid$ new at $t=0\}$ |

see Eq. (6.33) for the work-mission availability \& Eq. (6.196) for the overall availability; up = operating state; * Markov process; ** approximation valid for $\lambda \ll \mu$ and $t>10 / \mu=10$ MTTR# 6.2.3 One-Item Structure with Arbitrary Conditions at $t=0$ 

Generalization of the initial conditions at time $t=0$, i. e. the introduction of $p$, $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)$ and $\mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$ as defined by Eqs. (6.12), (6.8), and (6.10), leads to a time behavior of the one-item repairable structure described by Fig. A7.3 and to the following results:

1. Reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S}(t)$

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { in }(0, t] \mid u p \text { at } t=0\}=1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t), \quad t>0, \mathrm{R}_{S}(0)=1
$$

Equation (6.41) follows from $\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ in $\{0, t\}\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ at $t=0 \cap u p$ in $(0, t]\}$ $=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ at $t=0\} \cdot \operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ in $(0, t] \mid u p$ at $t=0\}=p \cdot\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t)\right)=p \cdot R_{S}(t)$.
2. Point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)= & \operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { at } t\}=p\left[1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t-x)) d x\right] \\
& +(1-p) \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u d}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t-x)) d x, \quad t>0, \mathrm{PA}_{S}(0)=p
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\mathrm{h}_{\text {duu }}(t)=\mathrm{f}_{A}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t)+\mathrm{f}_{A}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t)+\ldots$ and $\mathrm{h}_{\text {dud }}(t)=\mathrm{g}_{A}(t)+$ $\mathrm{g}_{A}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t)+\mathrm{g}_{A}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t)+\ldots$ (see also Eq. (A7.50)).
3. Average availability $\mathrm{AA}_{S}(t)$

$$
\mathrm{AA}_{S}(t)=\frac{1}{t} \mathrm{E}[\text { total } u p \text { time in }(0, t])=\frac{1}{t} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(x) d x, \quad t>0, \mathrm{AA}_{S}(0)=p
$$

4. Interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+\theta)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+\theta)= & \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { up in }[t, t+\theta]\} \\
= & p\left[1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t+\theta)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {duu }}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t+\theta-x)) d x\right] \\
& +(1-p) \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {dud }}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t+\theta-x)) d x, \quad t, \theta>0, \operatorname{IR}_{S}(0,0)=p
\end{aligned}
$$

5. Joint availability $\mathrm{JA}_{S}(t, t+\theta)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{JA}_{S}(t, t+\theta) & =\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { at } t \cap u p \text { at } t+\theta\}=\operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+\theta) \\
& -\int_{0}^{\theta} \frac{\partial \operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+x)}{\partial x} \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(\theta-x) d x, \quad t, \theta>0, \mathrm{JA}_{S}(0,0)=p
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+\theta)$ from Eq. (6.44) and $\mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t)$ from Eq. (6.38).6. Forward recurrence times $\left(\tau_{R u}(t)\right.$ and $\left.\tau_{R d}(t)\right)$ as in Fig. 6.3)

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R u}(t) \leq x\right\}=1-\operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+x) / \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)
$$

with $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+x)$ according to Eq. (6.44) and $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ from Eq. (6.42), and

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R d}(t) \leq x\right\}=1-\frac{\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { down in }[t, t+x]\}}{1-\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)}
$$

with $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ from Eq. (6.42), and

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { down in }[t, t+x]\}=p \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{u d u}(y)(1-\mathrm{G}(t+x-y)) d y \\
& \quad+(1-p)\left[1-\mathrm{G}_{A}(t+x)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{u d d}(y)(1-\mathrm{G}(t+x-y)) d y\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\mathrm{h}_{u d u}(t)=\mathrm{f}_{A}(t)+\mathrm{f}_{A}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t)+\mathrm{f}_{A}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t)+\ldots$ and $\mathrm{h}_{u d d}(t)=\mathrm{g}_{A}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t)+\mathrm{g}_{A}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t) * \mathrm{~g}(t) * \mathrm{f}(t)+\ldots$ (see also Eq. (A7.50)).

Expressions for mission availability and work-mission availability are generally only used for items new at time $t=0$ (see [6.5 (1973)] for a generalization).

# 6.2.4 Asymptotic Behavior 

As $t \rightarrow \infty$ expressions for the point availability, average availability, interval reliability, joint availability, and distribution functions of the forward recurrence times (Eqs. (6.42)-(6.47)) converge to quantities which are independent of $t$ and of the initial conditions at $t=0$. Using the key renewal theorem (Eq. (A7.29)) it follows that (see also Example 6.3 and Eqs. (A7.58) - (A7.63))

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=P A_{S}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R} \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{AA}_{S}(t)=A A_{S}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}=P A_{S} \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+\theta)=\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R} \int_{\theta}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{JA}_{S}(t, t+\theta)=\mathrm{JA}_{S}(\theta)=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R} \mathrm{PA}_{S e}(\theta) \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R u}(t) \leq x\right\}=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R d}(t) \leq x\right\}=\frac{1}{M T T R} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{G}(y)) d y
\end{aligned}
$$where $M T T F=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right], M T T R=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}^{\prime}\right], i=1,2, \ldots$ (Fig. 6.2), and $\mathrm{PA}_{S e}(\theta)$ is the point availability per Eq. (6.42) with $p=1 \& \mathrm{~F}_{A}(t)$ from Eq. (6.52) or (6.57). In practical applications, $P A$ and $A A\left(P A_{S}, A A_{S}\right.$ at system level) are often referred as availability and denoted by $A$; this should be avoided, considering the different existing kind of availability (Eqs. (6.16), (6.23, (6.28), (6.31), (6.34), (6.196)). The use of $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=(M T B F-M T T R) / M T B F$ is to reject, as it implies $M T B F=M T T F+M T T R$.

# Example 6.3 

Show that for a repairable one-item structure in continuous operation (Assumption (6.1)), the limit

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=P A_{S}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}
$$

is valid for any distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x), \mathrm{F}_{A}(x), \mathrm{G}(x), \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$ satisfying conditions (6.8) (6.12), and for which $\mathrm{f}(x), \mathrm{f}_{A}(x), \mathrm{g}(x), \mathrm{g}_{A}(x)$ go to 0 as $x \rightarrow \infty$.

## Solution

Using the renewal density theorem Eq. (A7.31), by considering Fig. A7.3 (p. 491), it follows that

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {duu }}(t)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {dud }}(t)=\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R}
$$

Furthermore, applying the key renewal theorem Eq.(A7.29) to $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ given by Eq.(6.42) yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t) & =p\left(1-1+\frac{\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x}{M T T F+M T T R}\right)+(1-p) \frac{\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x}{M T T F+M T T R} \\
& =p \frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}+(1-p) \frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}
\end{aligned}
$$

The limits $1 /(M T T F+M T T R)$ and $M T T F /(M T T F+M T T R)$ can also be obtained from the final value theorem of the Laplace transform (Table A9.7a), considering for $s \rightarrow 0$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\hat{\mathrm{f}}(s)=1-s M T T F+\mathrm{o}(s), & \hat{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)=1-s \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{0}\right]+\mathrm{o}(s) \\
\hat{\mathrm{g}}(s)=1-s M T T R+\mathrm{o}(s), & \hat{\mathrm{g}}_{A}(s)=1-s \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{0}^{\prime}\right]+\mathrm{o}(s)
\end{array}
$$

with $\mathrm{o}(s)$ as per Eq. (A7.89) and using Eq. (A7.50). When considering $\hat{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ for availability calculations, the approximation given by Eq. (6.54) often leads to $P A_{S}=1$, already by simple redundancy structures. In these cases, Eq. (6.113) has to be used.
Supplementary results: For $t \rightarrow \infty, 1 /(M T T F+M T T R)$ holds also for $h_{\text {udu }}(t), h_{\text {udd }}(t), h_{\text {ud }}(t)$ $=p h_{\text {udu }}(t)+(1-p) h_{\text {udd }}(t) \& h_{d u}(t)=p h_{\text {duu }}(t)+(1-p) h_{\text {dud }}(t)$ (see also Eqs. (A7.60) \& (A7.177)).

In the case of constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0} \& \mu(x)=\mu \equiv \mu_{S}\right)$ Eq. (6.42) yields (Eq. (A7.50), Table A9.7b)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}+\left(p-\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}\right) e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t}=P A_{S}+\left(p-P A_{S}\right) e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t}
$$

Thus, for this important case, the convergence of $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ toward $P A_{S}=\mu /(\lambda+\mu)$is exponential with a time constant $1 /(\lambda+\mu)<1 / \mu=M T T R$. In particular, for $p=1$, i. e. for $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(0)=1$ and $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t) \equiv \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$, it follows that

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)-P A_{S}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu} e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t} \leq \frac{\lambda}{\mu} e^{-\mu t}=\lambda M T T R e^{-t / M T T R}
$$

Generalizing the distribution function $\mathrm{G}(x)$ of the repair time and/or $\mathrm{F}(x)$ of the failure-free time, $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can oscillate damped (as in general for the renewal density $\mathrm{h}(t)$ given by Eq. (A7.18)). However, for constant failure rate $\lambda$ and providing $\lambda M T T R$ sufficiently small and some rather weak conditions on the density $\mathrm{g}(x)$, lower and upper bounds on $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can be found [6.25]

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \geq \frac{1}{1+\lambda M T T R}-c_{l} \frac{\lambda M T T R}{1+\lambda M T T R} e^{-(\lambda+1 / M T T R) t}, \quad t \geq 0
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \leq \frac{1}{1+\lambda M T T R}+c_{u} \frac{\lambda M T T R}{1+\lambda M T T R} e^{-(\lambda+1 / M T T R) t}, \quad t \geq 0
$$

$c_{l}=1$ holds for many practical applications ( $\lambda M T T R \ll 0.1$ ). Sufficient conditions for $c_{u}=1$ are given in [6.25]. However, conditions on $c_{u}$ are less important as on $c_{l}$, since $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \leq 1$ is always true. The case of a gamma distribution with density $\mathrm{g}(x)=\alpha^{\beta} x^{\beta-1} e^{-\alpha x} / \Gamma(\beta)$, mean $\beta / \alpha$, and shape parameter $\beta \geq 3$, leads, for instance, to $\left|\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)-P A_{S}\right| \leq \lambda M T T R e^{-t / M T T R}$ at least for $t \geq 3 M T T R=3 \beta / \alpha\right.$.

# 6.2.5 Steady-State Behavior 

For

$$
p=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}, \quad \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y, \quad \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)=\frac{1}{M T T R} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{G}(y)) d y
$$

as initial conditions / distribution at $t=0$, the alternating renewal process describing the time behavior of a one-item repairable structure is stationary (in steadystate), see Appendix A7.3. With $p, \mathrm{~F}_{A}(t)$, and $\mathrm{G}_{A}(t)$ as per Eq. (6.57), the expressions for the point availability (6.42), average availability (6.43), interval reliability (6.44), joint availability (6.45), and the distribution functions of the forward recurrence times (6.46) \& (6.47) take the values given by Eqs. (6.48) - (6.53) for all $t \geq 0$, see Example 6.4 for the point availability $P A_{S}$. This relationship between asymptotic \& steady-state (stationary) behavior is important in practical applications because it allows the following interpretation (see also remarks on pp. 488, 493, 495, $514 \& 525$ as well as p. 530),
a one-item repairable structure is in steady-state (stationary behavior) if it began operating at the time $t=-\infty$ and will be considered only for $t \geq 0$, the time $t=0$ being an arbitrary time point (see also p.188).Table 6.4 Results for a repairable one-item in asymptotic \& steady-state (stationary) behavior

|  | Failure and repair rates Arbitrary |  | Remarks, assumptions |
| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
| 1. $\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ at $t=0\}$ $(p)$ | $\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}$ | $\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}$ | $\begin{aligned} & M T T F=\mathrm{E}\left\{\tau_{i}\right\}, \quad i \geq 1 \\ & M T T R=\mathrm{E}\left\{\tau_{i}\right\}, \quad i \geq 1 \end{aligned}$ |
| 2. Distribution of $\tau_{0}$ $\left(\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{0} \leq x\right\}\right)$ | $\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y$ | $1-e^{-\lambda x}$ | $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)$ is also the distribution function of $\tau_{R u}(t)$ as in Fig. 6.3 |
| 3. Distribution of $\tau_{0}^{\prime}$ $\left(\mathrm{G}_{A}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{0}^{\prime} \leq x\right\}\right)$ | $\frac{1}{M T T R} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{G}(y)) d y$ | $1-e^{-\mu x}$ | $\mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$ is also the distribution function of $\tau_{R d}(t)$ as in Fig. 6.3 |
| 4. Renewal densities $\mathrm{h}_{u d}(t)=\mathrm{h}_{d u}(t)$ <br> (i. e. failure frequency $=$ repair frequency) | $\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R}$ | $\frac{\lambda \mu}{\lambda+\mu}$ | $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{h}_{d u}(t)=p \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(t)+(1-p) \mathrm{h}_{d u d}(t) \\ & \mathrm{h}_{u d}(t)=p \mathrm{~h}_{u d u}(t)+(1-p) \mathrm{h}_{u d d}(t) \\ & t \geq 0 \quad \text { (see Example } 6.3 \text { on p. } 186 \\ & \text { or pp. } 492 \text {-93) } \end{aligned}$ |
| 5. Point availability $\left(P A_{S}\right)$ | $\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}$ | $\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}$ | $P A_{S}=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ at $t\}, \quad t \geq 0$ |
| 6. Average availability $\left(A A_{S}\right)$ | $\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}$ | $\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}$ | $\begin{aligned} & A A_{S}=\frac{1}{t} \mathrm{E}[\text { total up time in }(0, t]] \\ & t \geq 0 \end{aligned}$ |
| 7. Interval reliability $\left(\mathrm{IR}_{S}(\theta)\right)$ | $\frac{\int_{\theta}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x}{M T T F+M T T R}$ | $\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu} e^{-\lambda \theta}$ | $\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p \text { in }[t, t+\theta]\}, \\ & t \geq 0, \theta>0 \end{aligned}$ |
| 8. Joint availability $\left(\mathrm{JA}_{S}(\theta)\right)$ | $\frac{M T T F \cdot \mathrm{PA}_{S e}(\theta)}{M T T F+M T T R}$ <br> $=P A_{S} \cdot \mathrm{PA}_{S e}(\theta)$ | $\begin{aligned} & \frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}\left(\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}\right. \\ & \left.\quad+\frac{\lambda e^{-(\lambda+\mu) \theta}}{\lambda+\mu}\right) \end{aligned}$ | $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{JA}_{S}(\theta)=\operatorname{Pr}(u p \text { at } t \cap u p \text { at } t+\theta) \\ & \mathrm{PA}_{S e}(\theta)=\mathrm{PA}_{S}(\theta) \text { as per } \\ & \text { Eq. (6.42) with } p=1 \text { and } \mathrm{F}_{A}(t) \\ & \text { as in point } 2, t \geq 0, \theta>0 \end{aligned}$ |

$\lambda=$ failure rate, $\mu=$ repair rate; $u p=$ operating state; * Markov process

For constant failure rate $\lambda$ and repair rate $\mu$, the convergence of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ to $\mathrm{PA}_{S}$ is exponential with time constant $\approx 1 / \mu=M T T R$ (Eqs. (6.20) \& (6.55)). Extrapolating the results of Section 6.2.4, one can assume that for practical applications, the function $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ is captured at least for some $t>t_{0}>0$ in the band $\left|\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)-P A_{S}\right| \approx$ $\lambda$ MTTR $e^{-t / M T T R}$ when generalizing the distribution function of repair times. Thus,
for practical purposes one can assume that after a time $t \approx 10$ MTTR, the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ has reached its steady-state (stationary) value $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$
this, considering $e^{-10} \approx 5 \cdot 10^{-5}$ and $\lambda M T T R \leq 10^{-2}$, yielding $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)-\mathrm{PA}_{S} \leqq 5 \cdot 10^{-7}$, see Eq. (6.56). Important results for the steady-state behavior of a repairable one-item structure are summarized in Table 6.4.# Example 6.4 

Show that for a repairable one-item structure in steady-state, i.e. with $p, \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)$, and $\mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$ as per Eq. (6.57), the point availability is $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=P A_{S}=M T T F /(M T T F+M T T R)$ for all $t \geq 0$.

## Solution

Applying the Laplace transform to Eq. (6.42) and using Eqs. (A7.50) and (6.57) yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S}(s)=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}\left(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s^{2} M T T F}+\frac{\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s M T T F} \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}(s)}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)} \cdot \frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s}\right) \\
& +\frac{M T T R}{M T T F+M T T R} \cdot \frac{\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)}{s M T T R}}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)} \cdot \frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s},
\end{aligned}
$$

and finally

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S}(s)=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}\left(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s^{2} M T T F}\right)+\frac{[1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)][\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)+1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)]}{s^{2}(M T T F+M T T R)[1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)]} ;
$$

from which

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S}(s)=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R} \cdot \frac{1}{s}=\frac{P A_{S}}{s}
$$

and thus $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=P A_{S}$ for all $t \geq 0$.

### 6.3 Systems without Redundancy

The reliability block diagram of a system without redundancy (series structure/ system/model) consists of the series connection of all its elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, see Fig. 6.4. Each element $E_{i}$ in Fig. 6.4 is characterized by the distribution functions $\mathrm{F}_{i}(x)$ for the failure-free time and $\mathrm{G}_{i}(x)$ for the repair time. ${ }^{*}$

### 6.3.1 Series Structure with Constant Failure and Repair Rates

In this section, constant failure and repair rates are assumed, i. e.

$$
\mathrm{F}_{i}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda_{i} x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{~F}_{i}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{G}_{i}(x)=1-e^{-\mu_{i} x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{G}_{i}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    *) It can be noted that for a series structure, assumption (6.2) of no further failures at system down implies also assumption (6.3) of only one repair crew.

Figure 6.4 Reliability block diagram for a series structure (system without redundancy)
holds for $i=1, \ldots, n$. Because of Eqs. (6.58) and (6.59), the stochastic behavior of the system is described by a time-homogeneous Markov process (Appendix A7.5). Let $Z_{0}$ be the system up state and $Z_{i}$ the state in which element $E_{i}$ is down. Taking assumption (6.2) into account, i. e. of no further failures at system down, the corresponding diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ (p.503) is given by Fig. 6.5 (see also footnote on p. 189). Equations of Table 6.2 can be used to obtain the expressions for the reliability function, point availability and interval reliability. With $U=\left\{Z_{0}\right\}, \widetilde{U}=\left\{Z_{1}, \ldots, Z_{n}\right\}$ and the transition rates according to Fig. 6.5, the reliability function (see Table 6.2 on p. 173 for notation) follows from

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t}, \quad \text { with } \quad \lambda_{S 0}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}
$$



Figure 6.5 Diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a repairable series structure with elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{i} \& \mu_{i}$, ideal failure detection and switch, no further failures at system down (and thus also only one repair crew; $Z_{1}, \ldots, Z_{n}$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), arbitrary $t, \delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process)and thus, for the mean time to failure,

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=1 / \lambda_{S 0}
$$

The point availability is given by

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{P}_{00}(t)
$$

with $\mathrm{P}_{00}(t)$ from (Table 6.2)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{00}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{i} e^{-\lambda_{S 0} x} \mathrm{P}_{i 0}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{P}_{i 0}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \mu_{i} e^{-\mu_{i} x} \mathrm{P}_{00}(t-x) d x, \quad i=1, \ldots, n
\end{aligned}
$$

yielding for the Laplace transform (Table A9.7) of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{00}(s)=\frac{1}{s\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{s+\mu_{i}}\right)}
$$

From Eq. (6.64) there follows the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)$

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}} \approx 1-\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}
$$

Because of the constant failure rate of all elements, the interval reliability can be directly obtained from Eq. (6.27) by

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) e^{-\lambda_{S 0} \theta}
$$

with the asymptotic \& steady-state value

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=P A_{S} e^{-\lambda_{S 0} \theta}
$$

where (Eq. (6.60))

$$
\lambda_{S 0}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}
$$

According to pp. 278 - 79, the asymptotic \& steady-state system failure frequency $f_{u d S}$, repair frequency $f_{d u S}$, mean up time $M U T_{S} \&$ mean down time $M D T_{S}$ are given as $f_{u d S}=f_{d u S}=P A_{S} \lambda_{S 0}, M U T_{S}=1 / \lambda_{S 0}=M T T F_{S 0}$, and $M D T_{S}=1 / \mu$ for $\mu_{i}=\mu$. Same results for the case of p. 192 with $M D T_{S}=M T T R$ for $M T T R_{i}=M T T R$.# 6.3.2 Series Structure with Constant Failure and Arbitrary Repair Rates 

Generalization of the repair time distribution functions $\mathrm{G}_{i}(x)$, with densities $\mathrm{g}_{i}(x)$ and $\mathrm{G}_{i}(0)=0$, leads to a semi-Markov process (see pp. 521 - 22) with state space $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{n}$, as in Fig. 6.5; this because of Assumption (6.2) of no further failures at system down (implying also (6.3) of only one repair crew). The reliability function and the mean time to failure are still given by Eqs. (6.60) and (6.61). For the point availability let's first calculate the semi-Markov transition probabilities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ using Table 6.2

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Q}_{0 i}(x) & =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{0 i} \leq x \cap \tau_{0 k}>\tau_{0 i}, \quad k \neq i\right\} \\
& =\int_{0}^{x} \lambda_{i} e^{-\lambda_{i} y} \prod_{k \neq i} e^{-\lambda_{k} y} d y=\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{S 0}}\left(1-e^{-\lambda_{S 0} x}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n \\
\mathrm{Q}_{i 0}(x) & =\mathrm{G}_{i}(x), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
\end{aligned}
$$

The system of integral Equations for the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ follows then from Table 6.2

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{00}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{i} e^{-\lambda_{S 0} x} \mathrm{P}_{i 0}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{P}_{i 0}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}_{i}(x) \mathrm{P}_{00}(t-x) d x, \quad i=1, \ldots, n
\end{aligned}
$$

For the Laplace transform of the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{P}_{00}(t)$ one obtains finally, from Eq. (6.69),

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{00}(s)=\frac{1}{s+\lambda_{S 0}-\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i} \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}_{i}(s)}=\frac{1}{s+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}_{i}(s)\right)}
$$

from which, the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i} M T T R_{i}}
$$

obtained using $\lim _{s \rightarrow 0}(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s))=s \cdot M T T R$, as per Eq. (6.54), and (Eq. (A6.38))

$$
M T T R_{i}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(1-\mathrm{G}_{i}(x)\right) d x
$$

The interval reliability can be calculated from Eq. (6.66), with $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ per Eq. (6.70), or Eq. (6.67) with $P A_{S}$ per Eq. (6.71), see Example 6.5 for an application. Results for $f_{u d S}, f_{d u S}, M U T_{S}$, and $M D T_{S}$ are given at the bottom of p. 191.# Example 6.5 

A system consists of elements $E_{1}$ to $E_{4}$ which are necessary for the fulfillment of the required function (series structure). Assume constant failure rates $\lambda_{1}=10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \lambda_{2}=0.5 \cdot 10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \lambda_{3}=$ $10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \& \lambda_{4}=2 \cdot 10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, and that for all elements the repair time is lognormally distributed with parameters $\lambda=0.5 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and $\sigma=0.6$. Considering that no further failures can occur at system down (the system is disconnected), give the reliability function for a mission of duration $t=168 \mathrm{~h}$, the mean time to failure, the asymptotic \& steady-state values of the point and average availability, and the asymptotic \& steady-state values of the interval reliability for $\theta=12 \mathrm{~h}$.

## Solution

The system failure rate is $\lambda_{S 0}=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}+\lambda_{4}=36 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, according to Eq. (6.60). The reliability function follows as $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-0.0036 t}$, from which $R_{S 0}(168 \mathrm{~h}) \approx 0.55$. The mean time to failure is $M T T F_{S 0}=1 / \lambda_{S 0} \approx 278 \mathrm{~h}$. The mean time to repair is obtained from Table A6.1 as $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\left(e^{\sigma^{2} / 2}\right) / \lambda=M T T R \approx 2.4 \mathrm{~h}$. For the asymptotic \& steady-state values of the point and average availability as well as for the interval reliability for $\theta=12 \mathrm{~h}$ it follows from Eqs. (6.71) and (6.67) that $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=1 /\left(1+36 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 2.4\right) \approx 0.991$ and $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(12) \approx 0.991 \cdot e^{-0.0036 \cdot 12} \approx 0.95$

### 6.3.3 Series Structure with Arbitrary Failure \& Repair Rates

Generalization of repair and failure-free time distribution functions leads to a nonregenerative stochastic process. This model can be investigated using supplementary variables, or by approximating the distribution functions of the failure-free time in such a way that the involved stochastic process can be reduced to a regenerative process. Using for the approximation an Erlang distribution function (Eq. (A6.102)) leads to a semi-Markov process (Appendix A7.6). As an example, let's consider the case of a two-element series structure ( $E_{1}, E_{2}$ ) and assume that the repair times are arbitrary, with densities $\mathrm{g}_{1}(x)$ and $\mathrm{g}_{2}(x)$, and the failure-free times have densities

$$
\mathrm{f}_{1}(x)=\lambda_{1}^{2} x e^{-\lambda_{1} x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{f}_{1}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{f}_{2}(x)=\lambda_{2} e^{-\lambda_{2} x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{f}_{2}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

Equation (6.73) is the density of the sum of two exponentially distributed random time intervals with density $\lambda_{1} e^{-\lambda_{1} x}$ (see Eq. (A6.102)). Under these assumptions, the two-element series structure corresponds to a 1-out-of-2 standby redundancy $E_{1^{\prime}} \& E_{1^{\prime \prime}}$ with constant failure rate $\lambda_{1}$ and repair only at the failure of both elements $E_{1^{\prime}} \& E_{1^{\prime \prime}}\left(\mathrm{g}_{1}(x)\right.$ is the density of the repair function for $E_{1^{\prime}} \& E_{1^{\prime \prime}}$ ), in series with an element $\left(E_{2}\right)$ with constant failure rate $\lambda_{2}$. Figure 6.6 gives the equivalent reliability block diagram and the corresponding state transitions diagram. This diagram only visualizes the possible transitions. $Z_{0}$ and $Z_{1^{\prime}}$ are the system up states, $Z_{1^{\prime}}$ and $Z_{2^{\prime}}$ are supplementary states necessary for calculation (all five states are regeneration states, as required for a semi-Markov process). For thesemi-Markov transition probabilities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ one obtains (Table 6.2, Fig. 6.6)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Q}_{01^{\prime}}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{1^{\prime} 1}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \lambda_{1} e^{-\lambda_{1} y} e^{-\lambda_{2} y} d y=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}}\left(1-e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) x}\right) \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{02}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{1^{\prime} 2^{\prime}}(x)=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}}\left(1-e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) x}\right) \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{20}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{2^{\prime} 1^{\prime}}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~g}_{2}(y) d y \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{10}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~g}_{1}(y) d y
\end{aligned}
$$

From Eq. (6.75) it follows that (Tables 6.2 \& A9.7, and Eq. (6.54) for $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ )

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\left(1+\lambda_{1} t\right) e^{-\lambda_{1} t} e^{-\lambda_{2} t}=\left(1+\lambda_{1} t\right) e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) t} \\
& M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{2 \lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}}{\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)^{2}} \\
& \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{00}(s)+\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{01^{\prime}}(s)=\frac{\left[s+\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}_{2}(s)\right)\right]+\lambda_{1}}{\left[s+\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}_{2}(s)\right)\right]^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2} \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}_{1}(s)} \\
& P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{2}{2+2 \lambda_{2} M T T R_{2}+\lambda_{1} M T T R_{1}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Because of constant failure rates $\lambda_{1} \& \lambda_{2}$ and standby redundancy $\left(E_{1^{\prime}} . E_{1^{\prime \prime}}\right)$, the interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ can be obtained (as for a Markov process) from

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\mathrm{P}_{00}(t) \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)+\mathrm{P}_{01^{\prime}}(t) \mathrm{R}_{S 1^{\prime}}(\theta)
$$



Figure 6.6 Equivalent reliability block diagram and state transitions diagram for a two-element series structure ( $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ ) with arbitrarily distributed repair times, constant failure rate for $E_{2}$, and Erlangian ( $n=2$ ) distributed failure-free time for $E_{1}$ (yielding $E_{1^{\prime}} \& E_{1^{\prime \prime}}$ ), ideal failure detection \& switch, repair of $E_{1^{\prime}}$ and $E_{1^{\prime \prime}}$ only at the failure of both $E_{1^{\prime}} \& E_{1^{\prime \prime}}$ (state $Z_{1}$ ), no further failures at system down $\left(Z_{1}, Z_{2}, Z_{2}\right.$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), semi-Markov process)with $\mathrm{R}_{S 1} \cdot(\theta)=e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) \theta}$ and $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)$ per Eq. (6.76) with $\theta$ instead of $t$, yielding

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=\frac{\left(2+\lambda_{1} \theta\right) e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) \theta}}{2+2 \lambda_{2} M T T R_{2}+\lambda_{1} M T T R_{1}}
$$

obtained using Eq. (6.54).
Important results for repairable series structures are summarized in Table 6.5. Asymptotic results for arbitrary failure and repair rates are investigated e. g. in [2.34 (1975)] yielding $A A_{S}=P A_{S}=1 /\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} M T T R_{i} / M T T F_{i}\right) \approx 1-\sum_{i=1}^{n} M T T R_{i} / M T T F_{i}$ for the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability (Point 4 of Table 6.5). $A A_{S}=P A_{S}=1 /\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} M T T R_{i} / M T T F_{i}\right)$ follows also in a way similar to the development of Eq. (4.6).

[^0]:    * Supplementary results: For totally independent elements ( $n$ repair crews and possible failures also at system down) it holds that (Table 6.9) $P A_{S}=\Pi_{i}\left(1 /\left(1+\lambda_{i} / \mu_{i}\right)\right) \approx 1-\Sigma_{i} \lambda_{i} / \mu_{i}$.# 6.4 1-out-of-2 Redundancy (Warm, one Repair Crew) 

The 1-out-of-2 redundancy (also known as 1-out-of-2: $G$ ) is the simplest redundant structure in practical applications. It consists of two elements $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$, one of which is in the operating state and the other in reserve, when not under repair or waiting for repair. When a failure occurs, one element is repaired while the other continues operation. The system is down when an element fails when the other is being repaired or waiting for repair. Assuming ideal failure detection \& switching, the reliability block diagram is a parallel connection of elements $E_{1} \& E_{2}$ (Fig. 6.7).

Investigations in this section are based on assumptions (6.1)-(6.7). This implies that the system has only one repair crew, repair of a redundant element is performed on-line \& begins at failure occurrence, and repaired elements are as-good-as-new. Distribution functions of repair and failure-free times are generalized step by step, beginning with exponential, up to the case in which the process involved has only one regeneration state. Preventive maintenance, switching, incomplete coverage \& common cause failures are considered in Section 6.8, travel time on pp. 204 \& 528.

### 6.4.1 1-out-of-2 Redundancy with Const. Failure \& Repair Rates

Because of the constant failure and repair rates, the time behavior of the 1-out-of-2 redundancy can be described by a time-homogeneous Markov process. The number of states is 3 if elements $E_{1} \& E_{2}$ are identical and 5 if they are different, see Figs. $6.8 \& 6.9$ for the corresponding diagrams of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ (see e. g. also pp. 226, $235 \& 506$ for comments on the number of states and footnote * on p. 503 for considerations on the memoryless property).

Let's consider the case of identical elements $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$ (see Example 6.6 for different elements) and assume as distribution function of the failure-free time

$$
\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{~F}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

in the operating state and

$$
\mathrm{F}_{r}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda_{r} x}, \quad x>0, \quad \mathrm{~F}_{r}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

in the reserve state. This includes active (parallel) redundancy for $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$, warm redundancy for $\lambda_{r}<\lambda$, and standby redundancy for $\lambda_{r} \equiv 0$. Repair times are


Figure 6.7 1-out-of-2 redundancy reliability block diagram (ideal failure detection and switch)

Figure 6.8 Diagrams of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a repairable 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with two identical elements, constant failure and repair rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \mu\right)$, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew $\left(Z_{2}\right.$ down state, arbitrary $t, \delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov proc. (see footnotes on pp. $510 \& 513$ for b)): a) For point availability; b) For reliability function ( $Z_{2}$ absorbing state)
assumed to be independent of failure-free times and distributed according to

$$
\mathrm{G}(x)=1-e^{-\mu x}, \quad x>0, \quad \mathrm{G}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

Refinements are in Examples 6.6 (different elements) and 6.7 (travel time). For more general situations (load sharing, two repair crews, etc.), a birth \& death process (Appendix A7.5.5) can be used (see e.g. p. 62 for load sharing). For all these cases, investigations are generally performed using the method of differential equations (Table 6.2 and Appendix A7.5.3.1). Figure 6.8 gives the diagrams of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for the point availability (Fig. 6.8a) and the reliability function (Fig. 6.8b), respectively.

Considering the memoryless property of exponential distributions (Eq. (A6.87)), the system behavior at times $t$ and $t+\delta t$ can be described by following difference equations for the state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\right.$ process in $\left.Z_{i} \text { at } t\right\}, i=0,1,2$ (Fig. 6.8a)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{0}(t+\delta t)=\mathrm{P}_{0}(t)\left(1-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \delta t\right)+\mathrm{P}_{1}(t) \mu \delta t \\
& \mathrm{P}_{1}(t+\delta t)=\mathrm{P}_{1}(t)(1-(\lambda+\mu) \delta t)+\mathrm{P}_{0}(t)\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \delta t+\mathrm{P}_{2}(t) \mu \delta t \\
& \mathrm{P}_{2}(t+\delta t)=\mathrm{P}_{2}(t)\left(1-\mu \delta t\right)+\mathrm{P}_{1}(t) \lambda \delta t
\end{aligned}
$$

For $\delta t \downarrow 0$, it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \stackrel{\circ}{\mathrm{P}}_{0}(t)=-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{P}_{0}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{1}(t) \\
& \stackrel{\circ}{\mathrm{P}}_{1}(t)=-(\lambda+\mu) \mathrm{P}_{1}(t)+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{P}_{0}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{2}(t) \\
& \stackrel{\circ}{\mathrm{P}}_{2}(t)=-\mu \mathrm{P}_{2}(t)+\lambda \mathrm{P}_{1}(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

The system (6.84) can also be obtained directly from Table 6.2 and Fig. 6.8a. Its solution leads to the state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i}(t), i=0,1,2$. Assuming as initial conditions at $t=0, \mathrm{P}_{0}(0)=1 \& \mathrm{P}_{1}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2}(0)=0$, the above state probabilities are identical to the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{0 i}(t), i=0,1,2$; i.e. $\mathrm{P}_{00}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{0}(t), \mathrm{P}_{01}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{1}(t)$, $\mathrm{P}_{02}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{2}(t)$. The point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ follows as (Table 6.2 for notation)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{P}_{00}(t)+\mathrm{P}_{01}(t)
$$

$\mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t), \mathrm{PA}_{S 2}(t)$ could have been determined for suitable initial conditions at $t=0$.From Eq. (6.85) it follows for the Laplace transform of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ that

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{00}(s)+\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{01}(s)=\frac{\left((s+\mu)^{2}+s \lambda\right)+(s+\mu)\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{s\left[\left(s+\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(s+\lambda+\mu)+\mu(s+\mu)\right]}
$$

Thus, for $t \rightarrow \infty$ (Table A9.7a)

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=P A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}=\frac{\mu^{2}+\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(\lambda+\mu)+\mu^{2}} \approx 1-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{\mu^{2}}
$$

with $P_{i}=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{P}_{i}(t)=\lim _{i \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{P}_{i i}(t), i, j=0,1,2$ (Eq. (A7.129)). If $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=P A_{S}$ for $t \geq 0$, then $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is also the point \& average availability in steady-state. Obviously, $P_{2}=1-P A_{S}$. Investigation of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$ leads to (Eq. (6.86), Tab. A9.7b)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=P A_{S}+2 \lambda^{2}\left(a_{2} e^{a_{1} t}-a_{1} e^{a_{2} t}\right) / a_{1} a_{2}\left(a_{2}-a_{1}\right)
$$

with

$$
a_{1,2}=-\mu(1+3 \lambda / 2 \mu) \pm \mu \sqrt{\lambda / \mu+(\lambda / 2 \mu)^{2}} \approx-\mu(1 \mp \sqrt{\lambda / \mu})
$$

and $P A_{S}$ per Eq. (6.87). Using $a_{1} a_{2}=\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu+2 \lambda^{2}$, it follows that $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(0)=1$. Furthermore, $d \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) / d t=0$ at $t=0$, yielding $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=1$ for some $t,{ }^{+}$) and $a_{1,2} \rightarrow-\mu$ for $\lambda \rightarrow 0$. From these results, and considering $\lambda \ll \mu$, following approximation can be used for practical applications $\left(e^{a_{1} t}=e^{a_{2} t}=e^{-\mu t}, a_{1} a_{2}=\mu^{2}\right)$

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \approx P A_{S}+\left(1-P A_{S}\right) e^{-\mu t},{ }^{+)} \quad t>0, \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(0)=1
$$

Equation (6.88) is similar to Eq.(6.20) and holds also for $0 \leq \lambda_{r} \leq \lambda$; it is
an important result in developing with Eq. (6.94) approximate expressions for large series-parallel systems based on macro-structures (Table 6.10).

To calculate the reliability function it is necessary to consider that the 1-out-of-2 redundancy will operate failure free in $(0, t]$ only if in this time interval the down state at system level (state $Z_{2}$ ) will not be visited. To recognize if $Z_{2}$ has been entered before $t$ it is sufficient to make $Z_{2}$ absorbing (Fig. 6.8b). In this case, if $Z_{2}$ is entered the process remains there indefinitely. Thus, the probability of being in $Z_{2}$ at $t$ is the probability of having entered $Z_{2}$ before the time $t$, i. e. the unreliability $1-\mathrm{R}_{S}(t)$. To avoid ambiguities, the state probabilities in Fig. 6.8b are marked by an apostrophe (see also footnotes on pp. $510 \& 513$ ). The procedure is similar to that for Eq. (6.84) and leads to

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{0}^{\prime}(t)=-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t) \\
& \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{1}^{\prime}(t)=-(\lambda+\mu) \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t)+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(t) \\
& \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{2}^{\prime}(t)=\lambda \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

and to the corresponding state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(t), \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t)$, and $\mathrm{P}_{2}^{\prime}(t)$. With the initial

(6.88) \& (6.94) are basic for macro-structures).conditions at $t=0, \mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0)=1$ and $\mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2}^{\prime}(0)=0$, the state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(t), \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t)$ and $\mathrm{P}_{2}^{\prime}(t)$ are identical to the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{00}^{\prime}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{0}(t), \mathrm{P}_{01}^{\prime}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t)$ and $\mathrm{P}_{02}^{\prime}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{2}^{\prime}(t)$. The reliability function is then given by (Table 6.2 for notation)

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{P}_{00}^{\prime}(t)+\mathrm{P}_{01}^{\prime}(t)
$$

Equations (6.89) \& (6.90) yield following Laplace transform for $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{(s+\lambda+\mu)+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{\left(s+\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(s+\lambda)+s \mu}
$$

from which the mean time to failure $\left(M T T F_{S 0}=\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0)\right.$, Eq. (2.61)) follows as

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)} \approx \frac{\mu}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}
$$

Investigation of $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ for $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$ leads to (Eq. (6.91), Table A9.7b)

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\left(r_{2} e^{r_{1} t}-r_{1} e^{r_{2} t}\right) /\left(r_{2}-r_{1}\right)
$$

with

$$
r_{1,2}=-\left[(3 \lambda+\mu) / 2\right] \pm \sqrt{((3 \lambda+\mu) / 2)^{2}-2 \lambda^{2}}
$$

For $\lambda \ll \mu$, it follows that $r_{1} \approx-\mu$ and $r_{2} \approx 0\left(r_{1} r_{2}=2 \lambda^{2}\right)$, yielding

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{r_{2} t}
$$

Using $\sqrt{1-\varepsilon} \approx 1-\varepsilon / 2$ for $2 r_{2}=-(3 \lambda+\mu)\left(1-\sqrt{1-8 \lambda^{2} /(3 \lambda+\mu)^{2}}\right)$ leads to $r_{2} \approx-2 \lambda^{2} /(3 \lambda+\mu)$. $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ can thus be approximated by a decreasing exponential function with time constant $\approx M T T F_{S 0}=(3 \lambda+\mu) / 2 \lambda^{2}$. Considering $\lambda \ll \mu$, extension to any redundancy type $\left(0 \leq \lambda_{r} \leq \lambda\right)$ leads to

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t}, \quad t>0, \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(0)=1, \lambda_{S 0} \equiv \frac{1}{M T T F_{S 0}}=\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu}=\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{\mu} .^{* *}
$$

Similarly as for $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t), d \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) / d t=0$ at $t=0$, and thus $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1$ for some $t$. ${ }^{+)}$ Concluding the above investigations, results of Eqs. (6.88) \& (6.94) show that, for $\lambda, \lambda_{r} \ll \mu$, a repairable 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \mu\right)$, and one repair crew, behaves approximately like a one-item structure with constant failure rate $\lambda_{S 0} \approx \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu$ and repair rate $\mu_{S} \approx \mu$; result on which the macro structures method (Table 6.10 on p.233) can be based $\left(\mu_{S} \approx 2 \mu\right.$ for two repair crews (Tab. 6.9)). ${ }^{++}$)

Because of the memoryless property of the time-homogeneous Markov process, the interval reliability follows directly as (Table 6.2, $\mathrm{P}_{0}(0)=1$ )

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\mathrm{P}_{00}(t) \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)+\mathrm{P}_{01}(t) \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(\theta), \quad \operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(0,0)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(0)=1
$$

with $\mathrm{P}_{00}(t), \mathrm{P}_{01}(t)$ as in Eq. (6.85). The asymptotic \& steady-state value follows as

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=P_{0} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)+P_{1} \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(\theta)=\frac{\mu^{2} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)+\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(\theta)}{\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(\lambda+\mu)+\mu^{2}} \approx \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)
$$

with $P_{0}$ and $P_{1}$ as for Eq. (6.87).
Further results for a 1-out-of-2 redundancy are in Sections 6.8.3 (imperfect switching), 6.8.4 (incomplete coverage), and 6.8.7 (common cause failures).

To compare the effectiveness of calculation methods, let's now express the reliability function, point availability, and interval reliability using the method of integral equations (Appendix A7.5.3.2). Table 6.2, and Fig. 6.8a yield

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Q}_{01}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{01} \leq x\right\}=1-\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{01}>x\right\}=1-e^{-\lambda x} e^{-\lambda_{r} x}=1-e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) x} \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{10}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{10} \leq x \cap \tau_{12}>\tau_{10}\right\}=\int_{0}^{x} \mu e^{-\mu y} e^{-\lambda y} d y=\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}\left(1-e^{-(\lambda+\mu) x}\right) \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{12}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{12} \leq x \cap \tau_{10}>\tau_{12}\right\}=\int_{0}^{x} \lambda e^{-\lambda y} e^{-\mu y} d y=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda+\mu) x}\right) \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{21}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{21} \leq x\right\}=1-e^{-\mu x}
\end{aligned}
$$

From Table 6.2 it follows then that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) t}+\int_{0}^{t}\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) x} \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t)=e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t}+\int_{0}^{t} \mu e^{-(\lambda+\mu) x} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t-x) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

for the reliability functions $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ and $\mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t)$, as well asTable 6.6 Reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$, point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$, mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$, steady-state point \& average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$, and interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)$ for a repairable 1-out-of-2 redundancy with two identical elements, constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \mu\right)$, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew (Markov process, approximations valid for $\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)<<\mu$ )
