# Example 6.6 

Give the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability $P A_{S}$ for a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two different elements $E_{1} \& E_{2}$, constant failure and repair rates $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \mu_{1}, \mu_{2}$ (one repair crew, ideal failure detection \& switch).

## Solution

Figure 6.9 gives the reliability block diagram and the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t] . \quad M T T F_{S 0}$ and $P A_{S}$ can be calculated from appropriate systems of algebraic equations. According to Table 6.2 and considering Fig. 6.9 it follows for the mean time to failure that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T F_{S 0}=\left(1+\lambda_{1} M T T F_{S 1}+\lambda_{2} M T T F_{S 2}\right) /\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) \\
& M T T F_{S 1}=\left(1+\mu_{1} M T T F_{S 0}\right) /\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}\right), \quad M T T F_{S 2}=\left(1+\mu_{2} M T T F_{S 0}\right) /\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

which leads to

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}\right)+\lambda_{1}\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)+\lambda_{2}\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}\right)}{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)}
$$

and in particular for $\lambda_{1} \ll \mu_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2} \ll \mu_{2}$,

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx \mu_{1} \mu_{2} /\left(\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)\right)
$$

As for Eq. (6.93), the reliability function can be expressed by

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t} \quad \text { with } \quad \lambda_{S 0} \equiv \frac{1}{M T T F_{S 0}} \approx \frac{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)}{\mu_{1} \mu_{2}}=\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{1}}+\frac{1}{\mu_{2}}\right)
$$

$\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\lambda \& \mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu$ yield results as per Table 6.6 (for active redundancy). For the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability and average availability, $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{2}$ holds with $P_{0}, P_{1}$, and $P_{2}$ as solution of (Table 6.2)

Figure 6.9 Reliability block diagram and diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two different elements, constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \mu_{1}, \mu_{2}\right)$, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew with repair as per first-in first-out ( $Z_{3} \& Z_{4}$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), arbitrary $t, \delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process; see Fig. A7.4 on p. 504 for further possibilities)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) P_{0}=\mu_{1} P_{1}+\mu_{2} P_{2}, \quad\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}\right) P_{1}=\lambda_{1} P_{0}+\mu_{2} P_{4} \\
& \left(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{2}\right) P_{2}=\lambda_{2} P_{0}+\mu_{1} P_{3}, \quad \mu_{1} P_{3}=\lambda_{2} P_{1}, \quad \mu_{2} P_{4}=\lambda_{1} P_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

One (arbitrarily chosen) of the five equations must be dropped and replaced by $P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{2}+P_{3}+P_{4}=1$. The solution yields $P_{0}$ through $P_{4}$, from which

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{2}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left[\mu_{1}^{2}+\mu_{2}^{2}+\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)\right]}{\mu_{1} \mu_{2}\left[\mu_{1} \mu_{2}+\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)\right]}}
$$

yielding, for $\lambda_{1} \ll \mu_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2} \ll \mu_{2}$,

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=1-\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\mu_{1}} \cdot \frac{\lambda_{2}}{\mu_{2}} \cdot\left(\frac{\mu_{1}}{\mu_{2}}+\frac{\mu_{2}}{\mu_{1}}\right)
$$

$\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\lambda \& \mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu$ yield results as per Table 6.6 (for active redundancy).

# Example 6.7 

As a refinement of the case investigated with Fig. 6.8 assume that to the repair time, distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)=1-e^{-\mu} \mathrm{e}^{x}$, a wait time for travel distributed according to $\mathrm{W}(x)=1-e^{-\mu} \mathrm{W}^{x}$ has to be added to the repair time for a failure occurred when both units are up (one operating, the other in reserve; i. e. in $Z_{0}$ ). Repairs for failures occurred during the travel time or a repair do not need to wait for a further travel time. As before, the system has only one repair crew. Investigate the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the steady sate availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$.# Solution 

The system behavior can be described by a 5 states Markov process (graph). $M T T F_{S 0}$ follows as solution of (Table 6.2, $M_{i}=M T T F_{S i}$ ): $M_{0}=M_{1}+1 /\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) ; \quad M_{1}=\left(1+\mu_{W} M_{1^{\prime}}\right) /\left(\lambda+\mu_{W}\right)$, $M_{1^{\prime}}=\left(1+\mu_{R} M_{0}\right) /\left(\lambda+\mu_{R}\right)$, yielding

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{1}{\lambda}+\frac{\left(\lambda+\mu_{R}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu_{W}\right)}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu_{R}+\mu_{W}\right)}=\frac{1 /\left(1 / \mu_{R}+1 / \mu_{W}\right)}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}
$$

$P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ follows as solution of (Table 6.2, graph): $\mu_{W} P_{2}=\lambda P_{1}, \quad\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) P_{0}=\mu_{R} P_{1^{\prime}}, \quad\left(\lambda+\mu_{W}\right) P_{1}=\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) P_{0}$, $\left(\lambda+\mu_{R}\right) P_{1}=\mu_{W} P_{1}+\mu_{R} P_{2^{\prime}}, P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{1}+P_{2}+P_{2^{\prime}}=1$, yielding


$$
\begin{aligned}
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{1^{\prime}} & =\frac{1}{1+\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left[\lambda+\mu_{R}+\mu_{W}+\mu_{R}^{2} / \mu_{W}\right]}{\mu_{R}\left[\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu_{W}+\mu_{R}\right)+\left(\lambda+\mu_{W}\right) \mu_{R}\right]} } \\
& \approx 1-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{\mu_{R}^{2}}\left(1+\frac{\mu_{R}}{\mu_{W}}+\frac{\mu_{R}^{2}}{\mu_{W}^{2}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

For $\mu_{W}=\infty$ and $\mu_{R}=\mu$, Eqs. (6.103) \& (6.104) yield Eqs. (6.92) \& (6.87); $\mu_{W}=0$ yields results for the nonrepairable case; $\mu_{W}=\mu_{R}=\mu$ yields $M T T F_{S 0}=\mu / 2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right), P A_{S}=1-3 \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu^{2}$.
Supplementary results: Addition of a travel time to each repair has no practical significance. Generalization of the distribution functions for repair and travel time leads to a 4 states process with 3 regeneration states (Fig. A7.12, p.528).

### 6.4.2 1-out-of-2 Redundancy with Constant Failure and Arbitrary Repair Rates

Consider now a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with 2 identical elements $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$, one repair crew, failure-free times distributed according to Eqs. (6.81) \& (6.82), and repair time with mean $M T T R<\infty$, distributed according to an arbitrary distribution function $\mathrm{G}(x)$ with $\mathrm{G}(0)=0 \&$ density $\mathrm{g}(x)$. The time behavior of this system can be described by a process with states $Z_{0}, Z_{1}$, and $Z_{2}$ (Fig. A.7.11a on p. 527). Because of the arbitrary repair rate, only states $Z_{0}$ and $Z_{1}$ are regeneration states. ${ }^{+)}$ These states constitute a semi-Markov process embedded in the original semiregenerative process. The semi-Markov transition probabilities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ are given by Eq. (A7.182). Setting these quantities in the equations of Table 6.2 (SMP), by considering $\mathrm{Q}_{0}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{01}(x)$ and $\mathrm{Q}_{1}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{10}(x)+\mathrm{Q}_{12}^{\prime}(x)$ as per Eq. (A7.182a), it follows for the reliability functions $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) t}+\int_{0}^{t}\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) x} \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}(1-\mathrm{G}(\mathrm{t}))+\int_{0}^{t} g(x) e^{-\lambda x} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t-x) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$Only $Z_{0}$ if 2 repair crews were available (see Fig. A7.11a on p. 527).and for the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ of the embedded semi-Markov process

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{00}(t)=e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) t}+\int_{0}^{t}\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) x} \mathrm{P}_{10}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{P}_{10}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x) e^{-\lambda x} \mathrm{P}_{00}(t-x) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x)\left(1-e^{-\lambda x}\right) \mathrm{P}_{10}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{P}_{11}(t)=(1-\mathrm{G}(t)) e^{-\lambda t}+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x) e^{-\lambda x} \mathrm{P}_{01}(t-x) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x)\left(1-e^{-\lambda x}\right) \mathrm{P}_{11}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{P}_{01}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) x} \mathrm{P}_{11}(t-x) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

The solution of the systems of integral equations (6.105) leads, in particular, to

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{s+\lambda+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s+\lambda))}{(s+\lambda)\left[\left(s+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s+\lambda))\right]\right.}
$$

and, considering $M T T F_{S 0}=\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0)$ as per (Eq. (2.61),

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{\lambda+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda))}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda))}, \quad\left(\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu} \text { for } \mathrm{g}(x)=\mu e^{-\mu x}\right)
$$

The Laplace transform of the point availability follows from Eqs. (6.106) \& (A7.112)

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{00}(s)+\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{01}(s)=\frac{(s+\lambda)[1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)+\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s+\lambda)]+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s+\lambda))}{(s+\lambda)\left[\left(s+\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s))+s \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}(s+\lambda)\right]}
$$

and leads to the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$, considering $\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}(s)=1-s M T T R+\mathrm{o}(s)$ as per Eq. (6.54),

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=-\frac{\lambda \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda))}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) M T T R+\lambda \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)}=\frac{\lambda+\lambda_{r}(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda))}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) M T T R+\lambda \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)}
$$

where

$$
M T T R=\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mathrm{~g}(x) d x=\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{G}(x)) d x
$$

and $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ is the Laplace transform of the density $\mathrm{g}(x)$ for $s=\lambda$, + ) see Examples 6.8 - 6.10 for approximations on $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ and p. 530 (bottom) for an alternative derivation of Eq. (6.110). Calculation of the interval reliability is difficult because state $Z_{1}$ is regenerative only at its occurrence point (Fig. A7.11). However, for $\lambda M T T R \ll 1$, $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda) \rightarrow 1$ and the asymptotic value of the state probability for $Z_{1}$ becomes very small with respect to that for $Z_{0}\left(P_{0}=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{P}_{00}(t)\right) .{ }^{++}$) From this (Eq.(6.96)),

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta) \approx P_{0} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)=\frac{\lambda \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda) \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) M T T R+\lambda \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)} \approx \frac{1-\lambda M T T R}{1+\lambda_{r} M T T R} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)
$$

In practical applications, $\lambda M T T R<0.01$ and Eq. (6.112) yields $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta) \approx \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)$.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$Note that $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{g}(x) e^{-\lambda x} d x=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\right.$ failure-free time $\left.>\tau_{\text {repair }}\right\}$.
    ${ }^{++}$) Considering Eq. (A7.170) and $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{Z_{0}\right.$ is entered at $\left.t=0\right\}=1$.# Example 6.8 

Let the density $\mathrm{g}(x)$ of the repair time $\tau^{\prime}$ of a system with constant failure rate $\lambda>0$ be continuous and assume furthermore that $\lambda \mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\lambda M T T R \ll 1$ and $\lambda \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]<M T T R$. Investigate the quantity $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ for $\lambda \rightarrow 0$.

## Solution

For $\lambda \rightarrow 0, \lambda M T T R<<1 \& \lambda \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]<M T T R$, the 3 first terms of the series expansion of $e^{-\lambda t}$ lead to

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{g}(t) e^{-\lambda t} d t=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{g}(t)\left(1-\lambda t+\frac{(\lambda t)^{2}}{2}\right) d t=1-\lambda \mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]+\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime 2}\right] \lambda^{2} / 2
$$

From this, follows the approximate expression (Eq. (A6.45))

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=1-\lambda M T T R+\lambda^{2}\left(M T T R^{2}+\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right) / 2
$$

In many practical applications,

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=1-\lambda M T T R
$$

is a sufficiently good approximation, however not in calculating steady-state availability (Eq. (6.114) would give for Eq. (6.110) $P A_{S}=1$, thus Eq. (6.113) has to be used).
Supplementary results: $\mathrm{g}(x)=\mu e^{-\mu x}$ leads to $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\mu /(\lambda+\mu)=1-\lambda / \mu+(\lambda / \mu)^{2}$ which agree with Eq. (6.113), considering $M T T R=1 / \mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=1 / \mu^{2}$.

## Example 6.9

In a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$ let the failure rates in the operating and reserve state be constant ( $\lambda$ and $\lambda_{r}$ ). For the repair time let us assume that it is distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)=1-e^{-\mu^{\prime}(x-\psi)}$ for $x>\psi$ and $\mathrm{G}(x)=0$ for $x \leq \psi$, with $M T T R \equiv 1 / \mu>\psi$. Assuming $\lambda \psi \ll 1$, investigate the influence of $\psi$ on the mean time to failure $M T T R_{S 0}$ and on the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability $P A_{S}$.

## Solution

With

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\int_{\psi}^{\infty} \mu^{\prime} e^{-\mu^{\prime}(t-\psi)-\lambda t} d t=\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\lambda+\mu^{\prime}} e^{-\lambda \psi}=\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\lambda+\mu^{\prime}}(1-\lambda \psi)
$$

and considering $M T T R=\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mathrm{~g}(x) d x=\int_{\psi}^{\infty} x \mu^{\prime} e^{-\mu^{\prime}(x-\psi)} d x=\psi+\frac{1}{\mu^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\mu}$; i. e. $\mu^{\prime}=\mu /(1-\mu \psi)$ and thus $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\mu(1-\lambda \psi)^{\prime} /(\lambda+\mu(1-\lambda \psi))$, Eq. (6.108) and Eq. (6.110) lead to the approximate expressions

$$
M T T F_{S 0, \psi>0}=\frac{2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}
$$

and

$$
P A_{S, \psi>0}=\frac{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)}{\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)+\mu^{2}(1-\lambda \psi)}=1-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\mu \psi))}{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)}
$$

On the other hand, $\psi=0$ leads to $1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$ and thus (Eqs. (6.92) and (6.87))

$$
M T T F_{S 0, \psi=0}=\frac{2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)} \quad \text { and } \quad P A_{S, \psi=0}=\frac{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu\right)}{(\lambda+\mu)\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\mu^{2}}
$$

Assuming $\mu \gg \lambda, \lambda_{r}$, yields (considering $\lambda \psi<\lambda / \mu<<1$ )

$$
\frac{M T T F_{S 0, \psi>0}}{M T T F_{S 0, \psi=0}}=1-\lambda \psi \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{P A_{S, \psi>0}}{P A_{S, \psi=0}}=1+\lambda \psi \frac{\lambda+\lambda_{r}}{\mu}=1
$$Equation (6.115) allows the conclusion to be made that,
for $\lambda$ MTTR $<<1$, the shape of the distribution function of the repair time has (for unchanged MTTR) a small influence on results at system level, in particular on the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and on the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ of a 1-out-of-2 redundancy.

Above conclusion can often be extended to more complex structures. Example 6.10 shows a numerical comparison for the case of a 1-out-of-2 parallel redundancy.

# Example 6.10 

A 1-out-of-2 parallel redundancy with identical elements $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ has failure rate $\lambda=10^{-2} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and lognormally distributed repair times with mean $M T T R=2.4 \mathrm{~h}$ and variance $0.6 \mathrm{~h}^{2}$ (Eqs. (A6.112), (A6.113) with $\lambda=0.438 \mathrm{~h}^{-3}, \sigma=0.315$ ). Compute the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}$ with approximate expressions: (i) $\hat{g}(\lambda)$ from Eq. (6.114); (ii) $\hat{g}(\lambda)$ from Eq. (6.113); (iii) $\mathrm{g}(t)=\mu^{\prime} e^{-\mu^{\prime}(t-\psi)}$, $t \geq \psi, \psi=1.3 \mathrm{~h}, 1 / \mu^{\prime}=1.1 \mathrm{~h}, 1 / \mu=2.4 \mathrm{~h}$ (Eq. (4.2)); (iv) $\mathrm{g}(t)=\mu e^{-\mu t}$ and $1 / \mu=2.4 \mathrm{~h}$.

## Solution

(i) With $\hat{g}(\lambda)=0.976$ it follows (Eq. (6.108)) that $M T T F_{S 0} \approx 2183 \mathrm{~h}$ and (Eq. (6.110)) $P A_{S}=1$. (ii) With $\hat{g}(\lambda) \approx 0.9763$ it follows (Eq. (6.108)) that $M T T F_{S 0} \approx 2210 \mathrm{~h}$ and (Eq. (6.110)) $P A_{S} \approx 0.9994$. (iii) Example 6.9 yields $M T T F_{S 0, \psi=1.3 \mathrm{~h}} \approx 2206 \mathrm{~h}$ and $P A_{S, \psi=1.3 \mathrm{~h}} \approx$ 0.9995 . (iv) From Eqs. (6.92) and (6.87) it follows that $M T T F_{S 0} \approx 2233 \mathrm{~h}$ and $P A_{S} \approx 0.9989$.

Supplementary results: Numerical computation with the lognormal distribution ( $M T T R=2.4 \mathrm{~h}$, $\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=0.6 \mathrm{~h}^{2}$ ) yields $M T T F_{S 0} \approx 2186 \mathrm{~h}$ and $P A_{S} \approx 0.9995$. For a failure rate $\lambda=10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, results were: $209^{\prime} 333 \mathrm{~h}, 1 ; 209^{\prime} 611 \mathrm{~h}, 0.999997$; 209'563h, 0.999995; 209'833, 0.999989; 209'513h, 0.999994.

### 6.4.3 1-out-of-2 Redundancy with Constant Failure Rate only in the Reserve State, Arbitrary Repair Rates

Generalization of repair and failure rates for a 1-out-of-2 redundancy leads to a nonregenerative stochastic process. However, in many practical applications it can be assumed that the failure rate in reserve state is constant. If this holds, and the 1 -out-of-2 redundancy has only one repair crew, then the process involved is regenerative with exactly one regeneration state [A7.2 (Ph. D. thesis 1974), 6.5(1975)].

To see this, consider a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy, satisfying assumptions (6.1) - (6.7), with failure-free times distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(x)$ in operating state $\& \mathrm{V}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda_{r} x}$ in reserve state, and repair times distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)$ for repair of failures in operating state and $\mathrm{W}(x)$ for repair of failures in reserve state $(\mathrm{F}(x)=\mathrm{V}(x)=\mathrm{G}(x)=\mathrm{W}(x)=0$ for $x \leq 0$, densities $\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}), \mathrm{v}(x), \mathrm{g}(x), \mathrm{w}(x) \rightarrow 0$ for $x \rightarrow \infty$, means and variances $<\infty$ ). Figure 6.10a shows a possible time schedule and Fig. 6.10b gives the state transitions diagram of the involved stochastic process.

Figure 6.10 Repairable 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with constant failure rate $\lambda_{r}$ in reserve state, arbitrary failure rate in operating state, arbitrary repair rates, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew $\left(Z_{3} \& Z_{4}\right.$ down states, absorbing for rel. calculation, $Z_{1}$ regeneration state): a) Possible time schedule (rep. times exag.); b) State transitions diagram to visualize state transitions

States $Z_{0}, Z_{1}, Z_{2}$ are up states. $Z_{1}$ is the only regeneration state $\left(Z_{0}, Z_{2}, Z_{3}, Z_{4}\right.$ are not regeneration states, see footnotes on pp. 210 and 386). At its occurrence, a failure-free time of the operating element and a repair time for a failure in the operating state are started (Fig. 6.10a). The occurrence of $Z_{1}$ is a regeneration point (a renewal point for the whole process with respect to $Z_{1}$ ) and brings the process to a situation of total independence from previous development, the process restarts anew from $Z_{1}$. From this, it is sufficient to investigate the behavior between two consecutive regeneration points, and from $t=0$ up to the first regeneration point (Appendix A7.4).

Let's consider first the case in which the regeneration state $Z_{1}$ is entered at $t=0$ $\left(S_{R P 0}\right)$, and let $S_{R P 1}$ be the first regeneration point after $t=0$. The reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\right.$ up in $\left.(0, t] \mid Z_{1}\right.$ entered at $\left.t=0\right\}$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{1}(x) \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t-x) d x
$$

with
$1-\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ failure-free time of the operating element $\left.\left.>t \mid Z_{1}\right\rvert\,$ entered at $\left.t=0\right\}{ }^{+)}$
and

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{1}(x) \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t-x) d x=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(S_{R P 1} \leq t \cap \text { system not failed in }\left(0, S_{R P 1}\right]\right.\right. \\
& \cap \text { up in }\left(S_{R P 1}, t\right]) \mid Z_{1} \text { entered at } t=0\} .
\end{aligned}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)} Z_{1}$ entered at $t=0$ implies that at $t=0$ the operating element is new or as-good-as-new and a repair for failure in operating state begins (holds at each occurrence of $Z_{1}$ ).

Figure 6.11 Possible time schedules for the 1-out-of-2 redundancy according to Fig. 6.10 for the cases in which state $Z_{1}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})$ or state $Z_{0}$ with both elements new $(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d})$ is entered at $t=0$

The first regeneration point $S_{R P 1}$ occurs at the time $x$ (within the interval $(x, x+d x]$ ) only if at this time the operating element fails (for the first time) and the reserve element is ready to enter the operating state (Fig. 6.11a). $u_{1}(x)$, defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& u_{1}(x)=\lim _{\delta x \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\delta x} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(x<S_{R P 1} \leq x+\delta x \cap \text { system not failed in }(0, x]\right)\right. \\
& \left.\mid Z_{1} \text { entered at } t=0\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

follows from (Fig. 6.11a, see also Example A7.2)

$$
\mathrm{u}_{1}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{d}(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{PA}_{d}(x) & =\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { reserve element } u p \text { at time } x \mid Z_{1} \text { entered at } t=0\} \\
& =\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {dud }}^{\prime}(y) e^{-\lambda_{r}(x-y)} d y
\end{aligned}
$$

and (with $*$ as convolution (Eq. (A6.75)))

$$
\mathrm{h}_{\text {dud }}^{\prime}(y)=\mathrm{g}(y)+\mathrm{g}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y)+\mathrm{g}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y)+\ldots
$$

The point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\right.$ up at $\left.t \mid Z_{1}\right.$ entered at $\left.t=0\right\}$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{1}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t-x) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{2}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t-x) d x
$$

with $1-\mathrm{F}(t)$ as for Eq. (6.116),$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{1}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t-x) d x=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(S_{R P 1} \leq t \cap \text { system not failed in }\left(0, S_{R P 1}\right]\right.\right. \\
& \left.\cap \text { up at } t) \mid Z_{1} \text { entered at } t=0\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{2}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t-x) d x=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(S_{R P 1} \leq t \cap \text { system failed in }\left(0, S_{R P 1}\right]\right.\right. \\
& \cap \text { up at } t) \mid Z_{1} \text { entered at } t=0\} .
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{u}_{2}(x)$, defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{u}_{2}(x)=\lim _{\delta x \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\delta x} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(x<S_{R P 1} \leq x+\delta x \cap \text { system failed in }(0, x]\right)\right. \\
& \left.\mid Z_{1} \text { entered at } t=0\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

follows from (Fig. 6.11b, see also Example A7.2)

$$
\mathrm{u}_{2}(x)=\mathrm{g}(x) \mathrm{F}(x)+\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~h}_{u d d}^{\prime}(y) \mathrm{w}(x-y)(\mathrm{F}(x)-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y
$$

with

$$
\mathrm{h}_{u d d}^{\prime}(y)=\mathrm{g}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y)+\mathrm{g}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y)+\ldots
$$

One recognizes that $\mathrm{u}_{1}(x)+\mathrm{u}_{2}(x)$ is the density of the interval times $S_{R P_{i+1}}-S_{R P_{i}}$ separating consecutive regeneration points $S_{R P_{i}}\left(i=0,1, \ldots, S_{R P 0} \equiv 0\right)$, i. e. separating consecutive renewal points of the embedded renewal process.

Consider now the case in which at $t=0$ the state $Z_{0}$ with both elements new is entered. ${ }^{+)}$The reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { up in }(0, t] \mid Z_{0}$ with both elements new is entered at $t=0\}$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{3}(x) \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t-x) d x
$$

with (Fig. 6.11c)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{u}_{3}(x)= & \lim _{\delta x \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\delta x} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(x<S_{R P 1} \leq x+\delta x \cap \text { system not failed in }(0, x]\right)\right. \\
& \left.\mid Z_{0} \text { with both elements new is entered at } t=0\right\}=\mathrm{f}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{0}(x)
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{PA}_{0}(x) & =\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { reserve element } u p \text { at time } x \mid Z_{0} \text { with both elem. new is entered at } t=0\} \\
& =e^{-\lambda_{r} x}+\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}^{\prime}(y) e^{-\lambda_{r}(x-y)} d y
\end{aligned}
$$

with

$$
\mathrm{h}_{d u u}^{\prime}(y)=\mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y)+\mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y)+\ldots
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$Contrary to the general case, $Z_{0}$ is defined here as the state in which both elements are operating, but not necessarily new or as-good-as-new at its occurrence; it is not a regeneration state (Fig. 6.10 , footnote on p.386), and " $\mid Z_{0}$ with both elements new" is necessary for $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \& \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$.The point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\right.$ up at $t \mid Z_{0}$ with both elements new is entered at $\left.t=0\right\}$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{3}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t-x) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{u}_{4}(x) \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t-x) d x
$$

with (Fig. 6.11d)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{u}_{4}(x)=\lim _{\delta x \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\delta x} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(x<S_{R P 1} \leq x+\delta x \cap \text { system failed in }(0, x]\right) \mid Z_{0} \text { with both }\right. \\
& \left.\quad \text { elements new is entered at } t=0\right\}=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~h}_{u d u}^{-}(y) \mathrm{w}(x-y)(\mathrm{F}(x)-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{h}_{u d u}^{-}(y)=\mathrm{v}(y)+\mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y)+\mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y) * \mathrm{w}(y) * \mathrm{v}(y)+\ldots
$$

One recognizes that
$\mathrm{u}_{3}(x)+\mathrm{u}_{4}(x)$ is the density of the time from $t=0$, when the state $Z_{0}$ is entered with both elements new, to the first regeneration point $S_{R P 1}$, i.e. to the first renewal point of the embedded renewal process with renewal density $\mathrm{u}_{1}(x)+\mathrm{u}_{2}(x)$ for the time intervals separating consecutive renewal points.

Equations (6.116), (6.120), (6.123), and (6.127) can be solved using Laplace transforms (LT). However, analytical difficulties can arise when calculating LT for $\mathrm{F}(x), \mathrm{G}(x), \mathrm{W}(x), \mathrm{u}_{1}(x), \mathrm{u}_{2}(x), \mathrm{u}_{3}(x), \mathrm{u}_{4}(x)$ or at the inversion of final equations. Easier is the calculation of the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}=\overline{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0)$ (Eqs. (2.59), (2.61)) and of the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\lim _{s \rightarrow s} s \overline{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow s} s \overline{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 1}(s)$, for which following expressions can be found using Laplace Transforms (Eqs. (6.123) \& (6.116) for $M T T F_{S 0}$ and Eq. (6.120) for $P A_{S}$ ), and considering (Eq. (6.54)) $\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \overline{\mathrm{f}}(s)=1-s M T T F+\mathrm{o}(s)$ )

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=M T T F\left[1+\frac{\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{u}_{3}(x) d x}{1-\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{u}_{1}(x) d x}\right]
$$

and

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t)=P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{M T T F}{\int_{0}^{\infty} x\left(\mathrm{u}_{1}(x)+\mathrm{u}_{2}(x)\right) d x}
$$

with

$$
M T T F=\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x
$$

Eq. (6.131) considers that $P A_{S}$ exists (p. 494-95) and that $\mathrm{u}_{1}(x)+\mathrm{u}_{2}(x)$ is the density of a random variable with finite mean (and thus $\left.{ }^{\infty} \int_{0}\left(\mathrm{u}_{1}(x)+\mathrm{u}_{2}(x)\right) d x=1\right)$; same for $\mathrm{u}_{3}(x)+\mathrm{u}_{4}(x)$.It must be pointed out that $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ and $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ apply only to the case in which at $t=0$ both elements are new (Fig. $6.11 \mathrm{c} \& \mathrm{~d}$ ). Situations with arbitrary initial conditions at $t=0$ (e.g. entering state $Z_{0}$ with the operating element not new or entering state $Z_{2}$ ) are not considered here because their calculation requires the knowledge of the time spent in the operating state before $t=0$.

The model investigated in this section has as special cases that of Section 6.4.2 $\left(\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}, \mathrm{~W}(x)=\mathrm{G}(x)\right)$ and the 1-out-of-2 standby redundancy with identical elements and arbitrarily distributed failure-free and repair times (Example 6.11).

Table 6.7 summarizes the results for the 1-out-of-2 redundancy with arbitrary repair rates, and failure rates as general as possible within a regenerative process (Appendix A7.4, pp. 494-95).

# Example 6.11 

Using the results of Section 6.4.3, give the expressions for the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ and the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for a 1-out-of-2 standby redundancy with 2 identical elements, one repair crew, failure-free time distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(x)$, with density $\mathrm{f}(x)$, and repair time distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)$ with density $\mathrm{g}(x)$.

## Solution

For a standby redundancy, $\mathrm{u}_{1}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x) \mathrm{G}(x), \mathrm{u}_{2}(x)=\mathrm{g}(x) \mathrm{F}(x), \mathrm{u}_{3}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x)$, and $\mathrm{u}_{4}(x) \equiv 0$ (Eqs. (6.117), (6.121), (6.124), and (6.128)). The Laplace transforms of $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ and $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ are then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s}+\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s))}{s\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{u}}_{1}(s)\right)} \\
& \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s}+\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)(1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s))}{s\left[1-\left(\tilde{\mathrm{u}}_{1}(s)+\tilde{\mathrm{u}}_{2}(s)\right)\right]}
\end{aligned}
$$

with

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{u}}_{1}(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}(t) \mathrm{G}(t) e^{-s t} d t \quad \text { and } \quad \tilde{\mathrm{u}}_{2}(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{g}(t) \mathrm{F}(t) e^{-s t} d t
$$

The mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ follows from Eq. (6.133) as $M T T F_{S 0}=\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0)$, or directly from Eq. (6.130),

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=M T T F+\frac{M T T F}{1-\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}(x) \mathrm{G}(x) d x}
$$

The asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ follows from Eq. (6.134) as $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \widetilde{P A}_{S 0}(s)$ or directly form Eq. (6.131),

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{M T T F}{\int_{0}^{\infty} x d(\mathrm{~F}(x) \mathrm{G}(x))}
$$Table 6.7 Mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$, steady-state point \& average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$, and steady-state interval reliability $\mathrm{IR}_{S}(\theta)$ for a repairable 1-out-of-2 redundancy with two identical elements, arbitrary repair rates, failure rates as general as possible within a regenerative process, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew (Figs. 6.10 \& A7.11; see Table 6.6 for const. f. \& r. rates)

# 6.5 $k$-out-of- $n$ Redundancy (Warm, Identical Elements, one Repair Crew) 

A $k$-out-of-n redundancy, also known as $k$-out-of-n: $G$, consists of $n$ often identical elements, of which $k$ are necessary for the required function and $n-k$ are in reserve state, when not under repair or waiting for repair. Assuming ideal failure detection and switching, the reliability block diagram is as given in Fig. 6.12. Investigations in this Section assume identical elements $E_{1}=E_{2}=\ldots .=E_{n}=E$, only one repair crew,

Figure 6.12 $k$-out-of- $n$ redundancy reliability block diagram (ideal failure detection \& switch)
and no further failures at system down (failures during repair at system level are not considered, as per assumption (6.2)). Section 6.5 .1 considers the case of warm redundancy with constant failure rate $\lambda$ in operation state, $\lambda_{r}<\lambda$ in reserve state, and constant repair rate $\mu$ (active redundancy for $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$, standby for $\lambda_{r} \equiv 0$ ). An extension to cover other situations in which the failure rate is modified at state changes (e. g. for load sharing) is possible using equations for the birth and death process developed in Appendix A7.5.5 (see also pp. 61-62). Section 6.5.2 investigates a 2-out-of-3 active redundancy with constant failure rate, arbitrary repair rate, one repair crew, and no further failures at system down, opening the way to general $n-k=1$ cases (Fig A7.11 on p. 527). Reliability and availability for $n-k=2$ are considered on pp. 528-29. The influence of a series element, imperfect switching, incomplete coverage \& common cause failures are investigated in Sections 6.6-6.8.

# 6.5.1 k-out-of-n Redundancy with Const. Failure \& Repair Rates 

Assuming constant failure and repair rates, the time behavior of the $k$-out-of- $n$ redundancy with identical elements can be investigated using a birth and death process (Appendix A7.5.5). Figure 6.13 gives the corresponding diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t\}$. From Fig. 6.13 and Table 6.2, the following system of differential equations can be established for the state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)=$ $\operatorname{Pr}\{$ in state $Z_{j}$ at $t\}$ of a $k$-out-of- $n$ warm redundancy with one repair crew and no further failures at system down (constant failure rates $\lambda \& \lambda_{r}$ and repair rate $\mu$ )

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{0}(t)=-\nu_{0} \mathrm{P}_{0}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{1}(t) & \\
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{j}(t)=\nu_{j-1} \mathrm{P}_{j-1}(t)-\left(\nu_{j}+\mu\right) \mathrm{P}_{j}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{j+1}(t), & j=1, \ldots, n-k \\
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{n-k+1}(t)=\nu_{n-k} \mathrm{P}_{n-k}(t)-\mu \mathrm{P}_{n-k+1}(t)
\end{array}
$$

with

$$
v_{j}=k \lambda+(n-k-j) \lambda_{r}, \quad j=0, \ldots, n-k
$$

Figure 6.13 Diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a repairable $k$-out-of-n warm redundancy with $n$ identical elements, constant failure and repair rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \mu\right)$, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew, no further failures at system down $\left(Z_{n-k+1}\right.$ down state (absorbing for reliability calculation), arbitrary $t, \delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process (birth and death))

For the investigation of more general situations (arbitrary load sharing, more than one repair crew, or other cases in which failure and / or repair rates change at a state transition) one can use the birth and death process introduced in Appendix A7.5.5 (see also pp. 61-64). The solution of the system (6.137) - (6.138) with the initial conditions at $t=0, \mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=1$ and $\mathrm{P}_{j}(0)=0$ for $j \neq i$, yields the point availability (see Table 6.2 for notations)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k} \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t), \quad\left(\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{j}(t) \text { from Eq. (6.137) with } \mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=1\right)
$$

In many practical applications, only the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability $P A_{S}$ is required. This can be obtained by setting $\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{j}(t)=0$ and $\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)=P_{j}(j=0, \ldots, n-k+1)$ in Eq. (6.137). The solution yields (Eqs. (A7.134) \& (A7.151))

$$
P A_{S}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k} P_{j}=1-P_{n-k+1}, \quad \text { with } P_{j}=P_{0} \pi_{j}=\frac{\pi_{j}}{\sum_{i=0}^{n-k+1} \pi_{i}}, \pi_{i}=\frac{v_{0} \cdots v_{i-1}}{\mu^{i}}, \pi_{0}=1
$$

i.e.,

$$
P A_{S}=\frac{\mu^{n-k+1}+v_{0} \mu^{n-k}+v_{0} v_{1} \mu^{n-k-1}+\ldots+v_{0} \ldots v_{n-k-1} \mu}{\mu^{n-k+1}+v_{0} \mu^{n-k}+v_{0} v_{1} \mu^{n-k-1}+\ldots+v_{0} \ldots v_{n-k-1} \mu+v_{0} \ldots v_{n-k}}=1-\frac{v_{0} \ldots v_{n-k}}{\mu^{n-k+1}}
$$

$P A_{S}$ is also the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the average availability $A A_{S}$. As shown in Example A7.11 (Eq. (A7.157)), for $2 v_{j} \leq \mu, j=0, \ldots, n-k$, it holds that

$$
P_{j}>\sum_{i=j+1}^{n-k+1} P_{i}, \quad j=0, \ldots, n-k
$$

From this, the following bounds on $P A_{S}$ can be used in many practical applications (considering $2 v_{j} \leq \mu, j=0, \ldots, n-k$ ) to obtain an approximate expression for $P A_{S}$ (see also Point 4 on p. 229)

$$
\sum_{j=0}^{i} P_{j} \leq P A_{S}<P_{i}+\sum_{j=0}^{i} P_{j}, \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k
$$The reliability function follows from Table 6.2 and Fig. 6.13

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\mathrm{v}_{0} t}+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{v}_{0} e^{-\mathrm{v}_{0} x} \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{R}_{S j}(t)=e^{-\left(\mathrm{v}_{j}+\mu\right) t}+\int_{0}^{t}\left[\mathrm{v}_{j} \mathrm{R}_{S j+1}(t-x)+\mu \mathrm{R}_{S j-1}(t-x)\right] e^{-\left(\mathrm{v}_{j}+\mu\right) x} d x \\
& \mathrm{R}_{S n-k}(t)=e^{-\left(\mathrm{v}_{n-k}+\mu\right) t}+\int_{0}^{t} \mu \mathrm{R}_{S n-k-1}(t-x) e^{-\left(\mathrm{v}_{n-k}+\mu\right) x} d x
\end{aligned}
$$

with $v_{i}$ as in Eq. (6.138). Similar results hold for the mean time to failure

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T F_{S 0}=M T T F_{S 1}+1 / v_{0} \\
& M T T F_{S j}=\left(1+v_{j} M T T F_{S j+1}+\mu M T T F_{S j-1}\right) /\left(v_{j}+\mu\right), \quad j=1, \ldots, n-k-1 \\
& M T T F_{S n-k}=\left(1+\mu M T T F_{S n-k-1}\right) /\left(v_{n-k}+\mu\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The solution of Eqs. (6.142) and (6.143), shows that $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$ and $M T T F_{S i}$ depend on $n-k$ only. This leads for $n-k=1$ to

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0_{1}}(s)=\frac{s+\mathrm{v}_{0}+\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mu}{\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{0}\right)\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{1}\right)+s \mu}, \quad M T T F_{S 0_{1}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{0}+\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mu}{\mathrm{v}_{0} \mathrm{v}_{1}} \approx \frac{\mu}{\mathrm{v}_{0} \mathrm{v}_{1}}
$$

and for $n-k=2$ to

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0_{2}}(s)=\frac{\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{0}+\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mu\right)\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{2}+\mu\right)+\mathrm{v}_{1}\left(\mathrm{v}_{0}-\mu\right)}{s\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{0}+\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mu\right)\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{2}+\mu\right)+\mathrm{v}_{0} \mathrm{v}_{1} \mathrm{v}_{2}+s \mathrm{v}_{1}\left(\mathrm{v}_{0}-\mu\right)} \\
& M T T F_{S 0_{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{2}\left(\mathrm{v}_{0}+\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mu\right)+\mu\left(\mathrm{v}_{0}+\mu\right)+\mathrm{v}_{0} \mathrm{v}_{1}}{\mathrm{v}_{0} \mathrm{v}_{1} \mathrm{v}_{2}} \approx \frac{\mu^{2}}{\mathrm{v}_{0} \mathrm{v}_{1} \mathrm{v}_{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

This property holds for the point availability $P A_{S}$ as well, see Table 6.8 for results.
Because of the constant failure rate, the interval reliability follows directly from

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S i}(t, t+\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k} \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t) \mathrm{R}_{S j}(\theta), \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k
$$

with $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ as in Eq. (6.139) and $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(\theta)$ from Eq. (6.142) with $t=\theta$. The asymptotic \& steady-state value is then given by

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k} P_{j} \mathrm{R}_{S j}(\theta)
$$

with $P_{j}$ from Eq. (6.140). (6.149) can be expressed as $P A_{S} \approx 1-M D T_{S} / M U T_{S}$ with $M D T_{S} \approx 1 /(n-k+1) \mu \& M U T_{S}=M T T F_{S n-k} \approx M T T F_{S 0}$; the same holds for results of Tables $6.6 \& 6.8$ with $M D T_{S}=M T T R=1 / \mu$ (see remark ${ }^{* *}$ to Table 6.8). Comparing results of Eq. (6.148) or Table 6.9 with those of Table 6.10 one recognizes that $M T T F_{S 0}{ }_{I E} / M T T F_{S 0}{ }_{M S} \approx(n-k)$ ! and $\overline{P A}_{S_{I E}} / \overline{P A}_{S_{M S}} \approx 1 /(n-k+1)$ !, where $\overline{P A}_{S}=1-P A_{S}, I E$ stands for totally independent elements (Eq. (6.148) or Table 6.9) \& MS for macro-structures (Tables $6.8 \& 6.10$ ), see also Eqs. (6.314) and (6.315).

# 6.5.2 $k$-out-of- $n$ Redundancy with Constant Failure and Arbitrary Repair Rates 

Generalization of the repair rate, by conserving constant failure rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}\right)$, only one repair crew, and no further failure at system down, leads to stochastic processes with $2(n-k)+1$ states, of which $n-k+1$ are regeneration $\& n-k$ are not regeneration states (see Fig. A7.11 on p. 527 for $n-k=1$ and Fig. A7.13 on p. 529 for $n-k=2$ ).

As an example let's consider a 2-out-of-3 active redundancy, i. e. a majority redundancy with 3 identical elements, constant failure rate $\lambda$ and repair time distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)$ with $\mathrm{G}(0)=0$ and density $\mathrm{g}(x)$. Because of the assumption of no further failure at system down, results of Section 6.4.2 for the 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy can be used for $n-k=1$ by setting $k \lambda$ instead of $\lambda$ (see Example A7.12 on pp. 526-27 and also Tab. 6.8 row $n-k=1$ ). For the 2-out-of-3 active redundancy one has to set $2 \lambda$ instead of $\lambda(k=2)$ and $\lambda$ instead of $\lambda_{r}$ (active redundancy) in Eqs. (6.108) \& (6.110) to obtain Eqs. (6.152) \& (6.155). However, in order to show the utility of time schedules, an alternative derivation is given below.

Using Fig. 6.14a, the following integral equation can be established for the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ (see Table 6.2 for notations)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-3 \lambda t}+ & \int_{0}^{t} 3 \lambda e^{-3 \lambda x} e^{-2 \lambda(t-x)}(1-\mathrm{G}(t-x)) d x \\
& +\int_{0}^{t} \int_{0}^{y} 3 \lambda e^{-3 \lambda x} \mathrm{~g}(y-x) e^{-2 \lambda(y-x)} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t-y)) d x d y
\end{aligned}
$$

The Laplace transform of $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ follows as

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{s+5 \lambda-3 \lambda \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}(s+2 \lambda)}{(s+2 \lambda)(s+3 \lambda)-3 \lambda(s+2 \lambda) \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s+2 \lambda)}
$$and (considering $M T T F_{S 0}=\widehat{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0)$ ) the mean time to failure as

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{5-3 \hat{\mathrm{~g}}(2 \lambda)}{6 \lambda(1-\hat{\mathrm{g}}(2 \lambda))}
$$

For the point availability, Fig. 6.14b yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-3 \lambda t}+\int_{0}^{t} 3 \lambda e^{-3 \lambda x} \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t)=e^{-2 \lambda t}(1-\mathrm{G}(t))+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x) e^{-2 \lambda x} \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t-x) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x)\left(1-e^{-2 \lambda x}\right) \mathrm{PA}_{S 1}(t-x) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

from which,

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{(s+2 \lambda)[1+\hat{\mathrm{g}}(s+2 \lambda)-\hat{\mathrm{g}}(s)]+3 \lambda(1-\hat{\mathrm{g}}(s+2 \lambda))}{s(s+2 \lambda)[1+\hat{\mathrm{g}}(s+2 \lambda)-\hat{\mathrm{g}}(s)]+3 \lambda(s+2 \lambda)(1-\hat{\mathrm{g}}(s))}
$$

Asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability follows from

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \widehat{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{3-\hat{\mathrm{g}}(2 \lambda)}{2 \hat{\mathrm{~g}}(2 \lambda)+6 \lambda M T T R}
$$

considering $\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \hat{\mathrm{~g}}(s)=1-s M T T R+\mathrm{o}(s)$ as per Eq. (6.54) or (6.114). For Eq. (6.155), Eq. (6.113) must be used to approximate $\hat{\mathrm{g}}(2 \lambda)$. For the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the interval reliability, Eq. (6.112) with $2 \lambda$ instead of $\lambda$ and $\lambda$ instead of $\lambda_{r}$ can be used in practical applications. Generalization of failure and repair rates leads to non-regenerative stochastic processes.

The general case of a $k$-out-of-n warm redundancy with $n-k=1$, constant failure rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}\right)$, arbitrary repair rates, one repair crew, and no further failures at system down follows easily from the considerations on p. 527 (Fig. A7.11). For the case $n-k=2, M T T F_{S 0} \& P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ are given by Eqs. (A7.185) \& (A7.186), Fig. A7.13.


Figure 6.14 Possible time schedule for a repairable 2-out-of-3 active redundancy with 3 identical elements, constant failure rate, arbitrary repair rate, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew, and no further failures at system down (repair times exaggerated)# 6.6 Simple Series - Parallel Structures (one Repair Crew) 

A series-parallel structure with independent elements is an arbitrary combination of series and parallel models, see e.g. Table 2.1 on p.31. Such a structure is generally investigated on a case-by-case basis using methods of Sections 6.3 - 6.5. If the time behavior can be described by a Markov or semi-Markov process, Table 6.2 can be used to establish equations for reliability function, point availability \& interval reliability (inclusive mean time to failure and asymptotic \& steady-state values).

As a first example, let's consider a repairable 1 -out-of-2 active redundancy with elements $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$ in series with a switching element $E_{v}$ (see case a in Table 6.11 on p. 248 for a warm redundancy). Failure rates $\lambda, \lambda_{v}$ and repair rates $\mu, \mu_{v}$ are constant. The system has only one repair crew, repair priority on $E_{v}$ (a repair on $E_{1}$ or $E_{2}$ is stopped as soon as a failure of $E_{v}$ occurs, see Example 6.12 for the case of no priority), and no further failures at system down (failures during a repair at system level are not considered). ${ }^{*}$ Figure 6.15 gives the reliability block diagram and the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t\}$. The reliability function can be calculated using Table 6.2, or directly by considering that for a series structure the reliability at system level is the product of the reliability of its elements

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{\text {1-out-of- } 2}}(t) e^{-\lambda_{v} t}
$$

Because of the term $e^{-\lambda_{v} t}$, the Laplace transform of $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ follows directly from the Laplace transform of the reliability function for the 1-out-of-2 parallel redundancy (Eq. (6.91) with $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$ ), by replacing $s$ with $s+\lambda_{v}$ (Table A9.7a)

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{s+3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu}{\left(s+2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\left(s+\lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)+\left(s+\lambda_{v}\right) \mu}
$$

The mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ follows from $M T T F_{S 0}=\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0)$

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu}{\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\left(\lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)+\mu \lambda_{v}}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{v}+2 \lambda^{2} /\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)} \approx \frac{1}{\lambda_{v}+2 \lambda^{2} / \mu}
$$

The last part of Eq. (6.157) clearly shows the effect of the series element $E_{v}$ (see Eq. (6.160) for a discussion). The asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is obtained as solution of (Fig. 6.15 and Table 6.2)

$$
P_{0}=\frac{\left(\mu_{v} P_{1}+\mu P_{2}\right)}{2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}}, P_{1}=\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu_{v}} P_{0}, P_{2}=\frac{\left(\mu_{v} P_{3}+\mu P_{4}+2 \lambda P_{0}\right)}{\lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu}, P_{3}=\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu_{v}} P_{2}, P_{4}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu} P_{2}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ Repair priority implies that a running repair is stopped at failure of an element with higher repair priority $\left(Z_{3} \rightarrow Z_{2}\right.$ in Fig. 6.15) and assumes, as in Fig. 6.15, that the stopped repair will be restarted anew after the repair priority; this may hold for constant repair rates (memoryless property) but not necessarily for arbitrary repair rates (a running repair can be advanced when stopped, implying that repair will not be restarted anew but continued \& repair resumption is not a regeneration point).

Figure 6.15 Reliability block diagram and diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with a series (switch) element $E_{\mathrm{v}}, E_{1}=E_{2}=E$, constant failure and repair rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{\mathrm{v}}, \mu, \mu_{\mathrm{v}}\right)$, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew, repair priority on $E_{\mathrm{v}}$, no further failures at system down $\left(Z_{1}, Z_{3}, Z_{4}\right.$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), arbitrary $t, \delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process, see footnote on p. 220 for repair priority)
Note: The diagram of transition probabilities would have 8 states $\left(2^{3}\right)$ for the case of totally independent elements ( $E_{1} \neq E_{2}, 3$ repair crews, failures at system down allowed), 9 states for the case as in Fig. A7.6c on p. 506, and 16 states (p.226) for $E_{1} \neq E_{2}$, one repair crew \& repair as per first-in first-out (see also the footnote ${ }^{+}$on p.503).

For the solution of the system given by Eq. (6.158), one (arbitrarily chosen) equation must be dropped and replaced by $P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{2}+P_{3}+P_{4}=1$. The solution yields $P_{0}$ through $P_{4}$, from which (considering $\lambda_{i}<<\mu_{i}$ for the approximation)

$$
\begin{aligned}
P A_{S} & =A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{2}=\frac{\mu^{2} \mu_{v}+2 \lambda \mu \mu_{v}}{\mu^{2} \mu_{v}+2 \lambda \mu \mu_{v}+2 \lambda\left(\lambda \mu_{v}+\lambda_{v} \mu\right)+\mu^{2} \lambda_{v}} \\
& =\frac{1}{1+\lambda_{\mathrm{v}} / \mu_{\mathrm{v}}+2(\lambda / \mu)^{2} /(1+2 \lambda / \mu)}=1-\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{v}}}-\frac{2(\lambda / \mu)^{2}}{1+2 \lambda / \mu}
\end{aligned}
$$

As for the mean time to failure (Eq. (6.157)), the last part of Eq. (6.159) shows the influence of the series element $E_{\mathrm{v}}$. This influence becomes negligible for

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{v}} \ll 2 \lambda^{2} / \mu^{+)}$

$$
\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}<<\left(2 \lambda^{2} / \mu\right)\left(\mu_{\mathrm{v}} / \mu\right) \text { for } P A_{S}=A A_{S}\right)
$$

For the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the interval reliability it follows (Tab. 6.2)

$$
\mathrm{IR}_{S}(\theta)=P_{0} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)+P_{2} \mathrm{R}_{S 2}(\theta) \approx \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)} \lambda_{\mathrm{v}} \ll 2 \lambda^{2} / \mu$ or $\lambda_{\mathrm{v}} / \lambda \ll 2 \lambda / \mu$ shows that a compromise must be found between the requirement for a small $\lambda / \mu$ to reach high $M T T F_{S 0} \& P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ values (Table 6.6 on p. 201), and a large $\lambda / \mu$ to simplify the achievement of the condition on $\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}$.# Example 6.12 

Give the reliability function and the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability for a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy in series with a switching element, as in Fig. 6.15, but without repair priority on the switching element.

## Solution

The diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ of Fig. 6.15 can be used by changing the transition from state $Z_{3}$ to state $Z_{2}$ to one from $Z_{3}$ to $Z_{1}$ and $\mu_{v}$ in $\mu$. The reliability function is still given by Eq. (6.156). For the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$, the system of algebraic equations (6.158) is modified to

$$
P_{0}=\frac{\left(\mu_{v} P_{1}+\mu P_{2}\right)}{2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}}, \quad P_{1}=\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu_{v}} P_{0}+\frac{\mu}{\mu_{v}} P_{3}, \quad P_{3}=\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu} P_{2}, \quad P_{2}=\frac{\mu P_{4}+2 \lambda P_{0}}{\lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu}, \quad P_{4}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu} P_{2}
$$

and the solution yields (considering $P_{1}+\ldots+P_{4}=1$ and $\lambda_{i}<<\mu_{i}$ for the approximation)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S}=\mathrm{AA}_{S}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{v}}}+\frac{2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}\right) / \mu^{2}}{1+\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}\right) / \mu}} \approx 1-\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{v}}}-\frac{2 \lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\left(1-\frac{2 \lambda}{\mu}\right)-\frac{2 \lambda \lambda_{\mathrm{v}}}{\mu^{2}}\left(1-\frac{3 \lambda+\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}}{\mu}\right)
$$

Comparison of Eq. (6.159) with Eq. (6.162) shows the advantage $\left(\approx 2 \lambda \lambda_{\mathrm{V}} / \mu^{2}\right)$ of the repair priority on $E_{\mathrm{v}}$ on the availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ (no change for $M T T F_{50}$ ).

As a second example let's consider a 2-out-of-3 majority redundancy (2-out-of-3 active redundancy in series with a voter $E_{\mathrm{v}}$ ) with arbitrary repair rate. Assumptions (6.1) - (6.7) on pp. 170-171 hold also here, in particular (6.2), i. e. no further failures at system down. The system has constant failure rates ( $\lambda$ for the 3 redundant elements $\& \lambda_{v}$ for the series element $E_{v}$ ), repair time distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)$ with $\mathrm{G}(0)=0 \&$ density $\mathrm{g}(x)$, one repair crew, and no repair priority. Figure 6.16 shows the reliability block diagram and the state transitions diagram. $Z_{0} \& Z_{1}$ are up states. $Z_{0}, Z_{1}, Z_{4}$ are regeneration states and constitute a semi-Markov process embedded in the original process. This property will be used for the investigations. From Fig. 6.16 and Table 6.2 there follows for the semi-Markov transition probabilities $\mathrm{Q}_{01}(x), \mathrm{Q}_{10}(x), \mathrm{Q}_{04}(x), \mathrm{Q}_{40}(x), \mathrm{Q}_{121}(x), \mathrm{Q}_{134}(x)$ (as for Figs. A7.11 - A7.13 on pp. 527-29)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Q}_{01}(x) & =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{01} \leq x \cap \tau_{04}>\tau_{01}\right\}=\int_{0}^{x} 3 \lambda e^{-3 \lambda y} e^{-\lambda_{v} y} d y=\frac{3 \lambda\left(1-e^{-\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x}\right)}{3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}} \\
\mathrm{Q}_{10}(x) & =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{10} \leq x \cap\left(\tau_{12}>\tau_{10} \cap \tau_{13}>\tau_{10}\right)\right\}=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~g}(y) e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) y} d y \\
& =\mathrm{G}(x) e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x}+\int_{0}^{x}\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) y} \mathrm{G}(y) d y \\
\mathrm{Q}_{121}(x) & =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{121} \leq x\right\} \\
& =\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~g}(y) \int_{0}^{y} 2 \lambda e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) z} d z d y=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~g}(y) \frac{2 \lambda}{2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}}\left(1-e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) y}\right) d y
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure 6.16 Reliability block diagram and state transitions diagram for a repairable 2-out-of-3 majority redundancy with constant failure rates $\lambda$ for E and $\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}$ for $E_{\mathrm{v}}$, arbitrary distributed repair times, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew, no repair priority, no further failures at system down $\left(Z_{2}, Z_{3}, Z_{4}\right.$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), $Z_{0}, Z_{1}, Z_{4}$ constitute an embedded semi-Markov process, $Z_{2}$ and $Z_{3}$ are not regeneration states)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Q}_{134}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{134} \leq x\right\}=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~g}(y) \int_{0}^{y} \lambda_{v} e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) z} d z d y=\frac{\lambda_{v}}{2 \lambda} \mathrm{Q}_{121}(x) \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{04}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{04} \leq x \cap \tau_{01}>\tau_{04}\right\}=\int_{0}^{x} \lambda_{v} e^{-\left(\lambda_{v}+3 \lambda\right) y} d y=\frac{\lambda_{v}}{3 \lambda} \mathrm{Q}_{01}(x) \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{40}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{40} \leq x\right\}=\mathrm{G}(x)
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{Q}_{121}(x)$ is used to calculate the point availability. It accounts for the process returning from state $Z_{2}$ to state $Z_{1}$ and that $Z_{2}$ is not a regeneration state (probability for the transition $Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2} \rightarrow Z_{1}$, see also Fig. A7.11a); similar is for $\mathrm{Q}_{134}(x) . \quad \mathrm{Q}_{12}^{\prime}(x)$ and $\mathrm{Q}_{13}^{\prime}(x)$ as given in Fig 6.16 are not semi-Markov transition probabilities ( $Z_{2}$ and $Z_{3}$ are not regeneration states). However,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Q}_{12}^{\prime}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{12} \leq x \cap\left(\tau_{13}>\tau_{12} \cap \tau_{10}>\tau_{12}\right)\right\}=\int_{0}^{x} 2 \lambda e^{-2 \lambda y} e^{-\lambda_{v} y}(1-\mathrm{G}(\mathrm{y})) d y \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{13}^{\prime}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{13} \leq x \cap\left(\tau_{12}>\tau_{13} \cap \tau_{10}>\tau_{13}\right)\right\}=\mathrm{Q}_{12}^{\prime}(x) \lambda_{v} / 2 \lambda
\end{aligned}
$$

yields an equivalent $\mathrm{Q}_{1}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{10}(x)+\mathrm{Q}_{12}^{\prime}(x)+\mathrm{Q}_{13}^{\prime}(x)$ useful for the calculation of the reliability function. Considering that $Z_{0}$ and $Z_{1}$ are up states and regeneration states, as well as the above expressions, the following system of integral equations can be established for the reliability functions $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \& \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t)$, as per Eq. (A7.172),

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) t}+\int_{0}^{t} 3 \lambda e^{-\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x} \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t)=e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) t}(1-\mathrm{G}(t))+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x) e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t-x) d x
\end{aligned}
$$The system of equations (6.164) for $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \& \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(t)$ has a great intuitive appeal and could have been written without the use of $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$. Its solution yields, in particular,

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{s+5 \lambda+\lambda_{v}-3 \lambda \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}\left(s+2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)}{\left(s+2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\left[s+\lambda_{v}+3 \lambda\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}\left(s+2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\right)\right]}
$$

and (considering $M T T F_{S 0}=\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0)$ )

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{5 \lambda+\lambda_{v}-3 \lambda \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)}{\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\left[\lambda_{v}+3 \lambda\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\right)\right]}
$$

$\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)$ and $M T T F_{S 0}$ could have been obtained as for Eq. (6.157) by setting $s=s+\lambda_{v}$ in Eq (6.151). For the point availability, calculation of the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ with Table 6.2 (or Eq. (A7.169)) and Eq. (6.163) leads to

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{P}_{00}(t)= & e^{-\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) t}+\int_{0}^{t} 3 \lambda e^{-\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x} \mathrm{P}_{10}(t-x) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{v} e^{-\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x} \mathrm{P}_{40}(t-x) d x \\
\mathrm{P}_{10}(t)= & \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x) e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x} \mathrm{P}_{00}(t-x) d x \\
& +\int_{0}^{t} \frac{2 \lambda}{2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}}\left(1-e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x}\right) \mathrm{g}(x) \mathrm{P}_{10}(t-x) d x \\
& +\int_{0}^{t} \frac{\lambda_{v}}{2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}}\left(1-e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x}\right) \mathrm{g}(x) \mathrm{P}_{40}(t-x) d x \\
\mathrm{P}_{40}(t)= & \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x) \mathrm{P}_{00}(t-x) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{P}_{01}(t)= & \int_{0}^{t} 3 \lambda e^{-\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x} \mathrm{P}_{11}(t-x) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{v} e^{-\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x} \mathrm{P}_{41}(t-x) d x \\
\mathrm{P}_{11}(t)= & e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) t}(1-\mathrm{G}(t))+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x) e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x} \mathrm{P}_{01}(t-x) d x \\
& +\int_{0}^{t} \frac{1}{2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}}\left(1-e^{-\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) x}\right) \mathrm{g}(x)\left[2 \lambda \mathrm{P}_{11}(t-x)+\lambda_{v} \mathrm{P}_{41}(t-x)\right] d x \\
\mathrm{P}_{41}(t)= & \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}(x) \mathrm{P}_{01}(t-x) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

From the two systems of integral equations (6.167) it follows the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{P}_{00}(t)+\mathrm{P}_{01}(t)$ and (using Laplace transform) the asymptotic \& steadystate value$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}-2 \lambda\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\right)\right)+3 \lambda\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\right)}{\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\left[1+\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) M T T R\right]+\lambda\left(\lambda_{v} M T T R-2\right)\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\right)}
$$

with MTTR as per Eq. (6.111). For $\lambda_{v}=0$, Eqs. (6.166) \& (6.168) yield Eqs. (6.152) \& (6.155). For the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the interval reliability, the following approximate expression can often be used for practical applications

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta) \approx \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)
$$

Example 6.13 investigate the case of Fig. 6.16 for constant repair rate $\mu \gg \lambda, \lambda_{v}$.
To give a feeling for the mutual influence of the different parameters involved, Figs. 6.17 and 6.18 compare the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the asymptotic \& steady-state unavailability $1-P A_{S}$ of some basic series - parallel structures.

# Example 6.13 

(i) Give using Eqs. (6.166) and (6.168) the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the asymptotic $\&$ steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{\mathrm{S}}$ for the case of a constant repair rate $\mu \gg \lambda, \lambda_{v}$. (ii) Compare for the case of constant repair rate the true value of the interval reliability $1 \mathrm{R}_{S}(\theta)$ with the approximate expression given by Eq. (6.169).

## Solution

(i) With $\mathrm{G}(x)=1-e^{-\mu x}$ it follows that $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)=\mu /\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)$ and thus from Eq. (6.166)

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{5 \lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu}{\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)+\mu \lambda_{v}}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{v}+6 \lambda^{2} /\left(5 \lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)} \approx \frac{1}{\lambda_{v}+6 \lambda^{2} / \mu}
$$

and from Eq. $(6.168)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
P A_{S}=A A_{S} & =\frac{\mu\left(\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)+3 \lambda \mu}{\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)\left(\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)+3 \lambda\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu}+\frac{3 \lambda\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)}{\mu\left(\mu+3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)}} \\
& \approx 1-\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu}-\frac{3 \lambda\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) / \mu^{2}}{1+\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right) / \mu} \approx 1-\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu}-\frac{6(\lambda / \mu)^{2}}{1+3 \lambda / \mu}
\end{aligned}
$$

(Eqs. (6.170) and (6.171) follow also from Eqs. (6.157) and (6.162) by replacing $2 \lambda$ with $3 \lambda, 1 \cdot \lambda$ with $2 \lambda, \mu_{v}$ with $\mu$ ). The influence of the series element $E_{v}$ becomes negligible for

$$
\lambda_{v} \ll 6 \lambda^{2} / \mu
$$

(ii) With $\mathrm{P}_{0}$ and $\mathrm{P}_{1}$ as for $P A_{S}=A A_{\mathrm{S}}$ in Eq. (6.171), it follows for the asymptotic \& steadystate value of the interval reliability that (Table 6.2)

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=\frac{\mu\left(\lambda_{v}+\mu\right) \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)+3 \lambda \mu \mathrm{R}_{S 1}(\theta)}{\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)\left(\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)+3 \lambda\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{v}\right)} \approx\left[\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)+\mathrm{R}_{S 1}(\theta) 3 \lambda / \mu\right]\left[1-\left(3 \lambda+2 \lambda_{v}\right) / \mu\right]
$$

Considering $\mathrm{R}_{S 1}(\theta) \lesssim \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta)$ and assuming $\mu \gg 3 \lambda$, the approximate expression given by Eq. (6.173) is practically the same as that given by Eq. (6.169).Equations for Figs. $6.17 \& 6.18$ are taken from Table 6.10 which summarizes results of Sections 6.2-6.6 for constant failure \& repair rates. Comparison with Figs. 2.8 \& 2.9 (non-repairable case) confirms that the most important gain is obtained by the first step (structure b), and shows that the influence of series elements is much greater in the repairable than in the nonrepairable case. With reference to the structures a, b, and c of Figs. 6.17 and 6.18 the following design rule can be formulated,
to approach the $\mu / 2 \lambda_{1}$ MTTF gain given by the redundancy (p. 202), the failure rate $\lambda_{2}$ of the series element to a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy should not be greater than $1 \%$ ( $0.2 \%$ for $\mu / \lambda_{1}>200$ ) of the failure rate of the redundant elements; i.e.

$$
\lambda_{2}<0.01 \lambda_{1} \text { in general, and } \lambda_{2}<0.002 \lambda_{1} \text { for } \mu / \lambda_{1}>200
$$

# 6.7 Approximate Expressions for Large Series Parallel Structures ${ }^{+)}$ 

### 6.7.1 Introduction

Reliability and availability calculation of large series - parallel structures rapidly becomes time consuming, even if constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{i}, \mu_{i}$ is assumed for each element $E_{i}$ of the reliability block diagram and only mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ or steady-state availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is required; this because of the large number of states involved, which for a reliability block diagram with $n$ elements
can reach $1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \Pi_{k=n-i+1}^{n} \underline{k}=n!\sum_{i=0}^{n} 1 / i!\leqq e \cdot n!$ by $n$ different elements, one repair crew \& repair as per first-in first-out (see e.g. Fig. A7.4b on p. 504 \& captions to Figs. 6.15, 6.20); $2^{n}$ states holds for nonrepairable systems or for repairable system with totally independent elements (Point 1 below).

Use of approximate expressions becomes thus important. Thereby, assumptions involved muss be clearly specified to fix limits (e.g. constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{i}$ $\& \mu_{i} \gg \lambda_{i}$ for each element $E_{i}$, one repair crew, no further failure at system down). The following are some important possibilities to yield approximate expressions:

1. Totally independent elements (totally IE): If each element of the reliability block diagram operates and is repaired independently from each other (active redundancy, independent elements, one repair crew per element, failures at system down allowed), series or parallel structures can be reduced to one-item structures, which are themselves integrated into further series or

To each of the one-item structure obtained, mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and steady-state availability $P A_{S}$, calculated for the underlying series or parallel structure,
are used to compute an equivalent $\mu_{S}$ from $P A_{S}=\mu_{S} /\left(\lambda_{S 0}+\mu_{S}\right)$,
with $\lambda_{S 0} \equiv 1 / M T T F_{S 0}$. To simplify calculations, and considering comments to Eq. (6.94), constant failure rate $\lambda_{S 0} \equiv 1 / M T T F_{S 0}$ and constant repair rate $\mu_{S}$ are assumed for each of the one-item structures obtained. Table 6.9 (p.232) summarizes basic series or parallel structures based on totally independent elements (see Section 6.7.2 for a selected example). ${ }^{*}$ )
2. Macro-structures (MS): A macro-structure is a series, parallel, or simple series - parallel structure, considered as a one-item structure for calculations at higher levels and integrated into further macro-structures up to system level [6.5 (1991)]. It satisfies assumptions (6.1) - (6.7), in particular one repair crew for each macro-structure and no further failures during a repair at the macrostructure level. The procedure is similar to that of point 1 above (see remarks to Eqs. (6.94) \& (4.37)). Table 6.10 (p.233) summarizes basic macro-structures useful for practical applications (see Section 6.7.2 for a selected example).*)
3. One repair crew \& no further failures at system down ( $1 R \&$ noFF): It is valid for all models of Sections 6.2-6.7 (except Eqs. (6.148) \& (6.149)) and applies to many practical situations. No further failures at system down means that failures during a repair at system level are not considered (e.g. the system is disconnected). This assumption facilitates the existence of regeneration states, simplifies calculation, has no influence on $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$, and a limited influence on $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ if $\lambda_{i}<<\mu_{i}$ holds for each element $E_{i}$ (see p.240).
4. Cutting states: Removing states with more than $k$ failures from the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ (or from the state transitions diagram) produces in general an important reduction of the state diagram. The choice of $k$ (often $k=2$ ) is based on the required precision. An upper bound on the error for the asymptotic \& steady-state availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ based on the mapping of states with $k$ failures at system level in state $Z_{k}$ of a birth $\&$ death process and using $P_{k}>\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} P_{i}$ (Eq. (A7.157)), has been introduced in [2.50 (1992)].
5. Clustering of states: Grouping of elements in the reliability block diagram or of states in the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ (or state transitions) produces in general an important reduction of the state diagram.
Combination of the above methods is possible, see also Sections $6.8 .9 \& 6.9 .7$, as well as the footnote on p. 226, for further considerations. However, as a basic rule, series elements must be grouped before any analysis (2nd row of Table 6.10).

[^0]:    *) Methods $1 \& 2$ apply for constant failure \& repair rates for each element, yielding approximately constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{S 0}, \mu_{S}\right)$ for the reduced structure (Eqs. (6.88), (6.94), (6.48)).

Figure 6.19 Basic reliability block diagram for a repairable uninterruptible electrical power supply

Considering that the steady-state probability for states with more than one failure decreases rapidly as the number of failures increases ( $\sim \lambda / \mu$ for each failure, see e.g. Eq. (6.87) or pp. $237 \& 269$ with Figs. $6.20 \& 6.34$ ), all methods given above yield good approximate expressions for $M T T F_{S 0}$ and $P A_{S}$ in practical applications. However, with reference to the unavailability $1-P A_{S}$, method 1 above can deliver lower values, for instance a factor 2 with an order of magnitude $(\lambda / \mu)^{2}$ for a 1-outof-2 active redundancy (compare Tables $6.9 \& 6.10$ ). Analytical comparison of the above methods is difficult, in general. Numerical investigations show a close convergence of the results given by the different methods, as illustrated for instance in Section 6.7.2 (p. 237) for a practical example with low values for $\mu / \lambda$.

# 6.7.2 Application to a Practical Example 

To illustrate how methods 1 to 3 of Section 6.7.1 work, let's consider the system with a reliability block diagram as in Fig. 6.19, and assume system new at $t=0$, active redundancy, constant failure rates $\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{3}$, constant repair rates $\mu_{1}-\mu_{3}$, $\lambda_{i} \ll \mu_{i}$, repair priority $E_{1}, E_{3}, E_{2}$ (see caption to Fig. 6.20) [6.5 (1988)]. Except for some series elements (to be considered separately in a final step), the reliability block diagram of Fig. 6.19 describes an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) used for instance to buffer electrical power network $\left(E_{1}\right)$ failures in computer systems. ${ }^{43}$

Although limited to 4 elements, the stochastic process describing the system of Fig. 6.19 could contain up to 65 states if the assumption of no further failure at system down were dropped (pp. 226, 235). Assuming no further failure at system down, the state space is reduced to 12 states (Fig. 6.20). In the following, the mean time to failure ( $M T T F_{S 0}$ ) and the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $\left(P A_{S}=A A_{S}\right)$ of the system given by Fig. 6.19 is investigated using method 1 (Table 6.9), method 2 (Table 6.10), and method 3 (Table 6.2) of Section 6.7.1. For a numerical comparison, results are given on p. 237, also for method 4 and for the exact solution obtained by dropping the assumption of no further failure at system down, showing that all methods used deliver good approximate expressions.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{1}=\frac{1}{\rho_{4}}+\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\rho_{4} \rho_{5}}\left(1+\mu_{3} \frac{\lambda_{3}+\rho_{5}}{\rho_{5} \rho_{6}-\lambda_{3} \mu_{3}}\right), \quad a_{2}=\frac{\lambda_{2} \mu_{2} \mu_{3}}{\rho_{4}\left(\rho_{5} \rho_{6}-\lambda_{3} \mu_{3}\right)}+\frac{\mu_{3}}{\rho_{4}}, \\
& a_{3}=\frac{1}{\rho_{3}}\left(1+2 \lambda_{2} a_{1}\right), \quad a_{4}=\frac{2 \lambda_{2}}{\rho_{3}} a_{2}, \quad a_{5}=\frac{1+\lambda_{3} a_{3}}{\rho_{0}-\lambda_{3} \mu_{3} / \rho_{3}}, \\
& a_{6}=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\rho_{0}-\lambda_{3} \mu_{3} / \rho_{3}}, \quad a_{7}=\frac{2 \lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3} a_{4}}{\rho_{0}-\lambda_{3} \mu_{3} / \rho_{3}}, \quad a_{8}=\frac{1+2 \lambda_{2} / \rho_{7}}{\rho_{1}}, \\
& a_{9}=\frac{2 \lambda_{2} \mu_{1}}{\rho_{1} \rho_{7}}, \quad a_{10}=\frac{1+\lambda_{3} a_{1}+\left(\lambda_{2} \lambda_{3}+\lambda_{2} \rho_{5}\right) /\left(\rho_{5} \rho_{6}-\lambda_{3} \mu_{3}\right)+\lambda_{1} / \rho_{7}}{\rho_{2}-\lambda_{3} a_{2}-\lambda_{2} \mu_{2} \rho_{5} /\left(\rho_{5} \rho_{6}-\lambda_{3} \mu_{3}\right)-\lambda_{1} \mu_{1} / \rho_{7}}, \\
& a_{11}=\frac{\mu_{2}}{\rho_{2}-\lambda_{3} a_{2}-\lambda_{2} \mu_{2} \rho_{5} /\left(\rho_{5} \rho_{6}-\lambda_{3} \mu_{3}\right)-\lambda_{1} \mu_{1} / \rho_{7}}, \quad a_{12}=\frac{\mu_{1}}{\rho_{1}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\rho_{i}$ as in Eq. (6.185). One (arbitrarily chosen) of the Eqs. (6.188) must be dropped and replaced by $P_{0}+P_{1}+\ldots+P_{11}=1$. The solution yields $P_{0}$ to $P_{11}$, from which
