Structures and models investigated in the previous sections were based on the existence of a reliability block diagram (RBD) and on some simplifying assumptions ((6.1)-(6.7)). In particular, independent elements with only two states, repaired as-good-as-new at failure, and ideal fault coverage \& switching. This was, so far, good to understand basic investigation methods and tools (see e. g. Figs. 6.9, 6.10, 6.15). However, in practical applications more complex situations can arise. This section uses tools of Appendix A7 (summarized in Table 6.2 for Markov \& semi-Markov processes) to investigate complex fault tolerant repairable systems for which an RBD does not exist as series-parallel structure with independent elements, or cannot easily be found. Constant failure and in general also constant repair rates are assumed. It is shown that many practical problems can be solved on a case-by-case basis using a diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ or a time schedule;
however, to improve readability, $\delta t$ and $1-\rho_{i} \delta t$ are omitted from the diagrams of transition probabilities, yielding diagrams of transition rates.

After some general considerations, Section 6.8.2 deals with aspects of preventive maintenance. Sections $6.8 .3 \& 6.8 .4$ consider imperfect switching \& incomplete coverage (see also Eqs. (A6.30), (6.223) for undetected fault time). Elements with more than 2 states or one failure mode are discussed in Section 6.8.5. Section 6.8.6 investigates fault tolerant reconfigurable systems by considering also reward and frequency/duration aspects. Section 6.8.7 deals with systems with common cause failures. Section 6.8.8 presents basic considerations on network reliability, and Section 6.8.9 summarizes the procedure for modeling systems with complex structure. Alternative investigation methods (dynamic FTA, BDD, ETA, Petri nets, computeraided analysis) are discussed in Section 6.9, and a Monte Carlo procedure for rare events is given in Section 6.9.6.2. Tools and models useful for human reliability \& risk management are introduced in Sections $6.10 \& 6.11$. However, as a general rule,
modeling complex systems is a task which must be solved in close cooperation between project and reliability engineers on a case-by-case basis.

### 6.8.1 General Considerations

In this book, a structure is complex if the reliability block diagram either does not exist or cannot be reduced to a series-parallel structure with independent elements.

If the reliability block diagram exists, but not as series-parallel structure, reliability and availability analysis can be performed using, for instance, one or more of the following assumptions in extension/refinement to assumptions (6.1)-(6.7):

1. All failure-free (operating) and repair (restoration) times are independent, $>0$, and continuous with finite mean \& variance (6.6).2. Failure \& repair rates of each element are constant (time indep.) during the sojourn time in each state; not necessarily at a state change (e.g. load sharing).
3. Each element has constant failure rate (as in assumption 2).
4. The flow of failures is a Poisson process (homogeneous or nonhomogeneous).
5. No further failures are considered (can occur) at system down (no FF, (6.2)).
6. No common cause failures can occur \& redundant elements are repaired on-line.
7. After each repair, the repaired element is as-good-as-new (6.5).
8. After a repair the system is as-good-as-new with respect to the regeneration state considered.
9. Only one repair crew is available for the system, and repair is performed according to a stated strategy, first-in first-out or given repair priority (6.3).
10. Totally independent elements (totally IE); i. e. each element operates and is repaired independently of every other element ( $n$ repair crews for $n$ elements).
11. Ideal failures detection and localization; in particular, no hidden failures.
12. For each element $E_{i}, M T T R_{i} \ll S M T T F_{i}(6.6)$.
13. Switches \& switching operations are $100 \%$ reliable (have no aftereffect).
14. Preventive maintenance is not considered and logistic support is ideal (6.7).

Often it is tacitly assumed that each element has only 2 states (good/failed), one failure mode (e.g. shorts or opens), and a time invariant required function (e.g. continuous operation). Elements with more than 2 states or one failure mode are discussed in Section 6.8.5. A time dependent operation and/or required function can be investigated by assuming constant failure rates (Section 6.8.6.2). However,
to avoid ambiguities, a careful formulation of assumptions made is important to fix the validity of results obtained.

The following is a brief discussion of above assumptions. Assumption 1 often holds in practical applications. With assumption 2, time behavior of the system can generally be described by a time-homogeneous Markov process with finite number of states (pp.496,503). Equations can be established using a diagram of transition rates and Table 6.2. Difficulties can arise for the large number of states involved (p. 226). In such cases, a first possibility is to limit investigations to the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S i}$ and the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$. A second possibility is to use approximate expressions (Section 6.7) or special software tools (Section 6.9.6). Assumption 3 assures the existence of a regenerative process with at least one regeneration state (footnote on p. 386). Assumption 4 often applies to large systems. As shown in Sections 6.3-6.7, assumption 5 simplifies calculation of the point availability \& interval reliability, it has
no influence on reliability function \& $M T T F_{S i}$, and can be used for approximate expressions for $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ when assumption 12 holds (Section 6.7.2).
Assumptions $6 \& 11$ must be met during system design (pp.259, 274); if not satisfied, improvements given by redundancy are questionable (Sections 4.2.1, 6.8.4).Assumption 7 is often used, but its validity must be verified (satisfied if 2 or 3 holds). Assumption 8 can be used with 2 for Markov, in some case with $3,5 \& 9$ for semiMarkov (Fig. 6.5, Figs. 6.46-6.53 as a particular application), and with $3 \& 9$ for semi-regenerative processes. ${ }^{4}$ However, repair priority can become a problem for arbitrary repair rates (footnote on p.220). Assumption 9 often holds in practical applications (considering 12); it is often used with $3 \& 5$ and greatly facilitates the
existence of regeneration states, simplifying calculation \& verification of 8; assumption 3 alone assure only that the process is regenerative with at least one regeneration state (see footnote on p. 386 \& Table 6.1 on p.171).

With assumption 10, the point availability can be computed from the reliability for the nonrepairable case (Eq. (2.48)). This assumption rarely applies in practical applications, but it allows simple calculation of an upper bound on the point availability. Assumption 12 is generally met; it leads to approximate expressions, as illustrated in Section 6.7 or using asymptotic expansions [6.19, A7.26]. As shown in Examples 6.8-6.10 (pp. 206-07), the shape of repair time distribution functions has small influence on results at system level, if assumption 12 holds. Assumptions $13 \& 14$ simplify investigations, they are valid for all models in Sections 6.2-6.7.

If the reliability block diagram does not exists, stochastic processes introduced in Appendix A7 can be used to investigate reliability \& availability of fault tolerant systems, on the basis of a diagram of transition rates or a time schedule, see Sections 6.8.3-6.8.7 for systems with imperfect switching, incomplete coverage, more than two states or one failure mode, reconfigurable structure, and common cause failures.

However, investigation of large series-parallel structures is often time-consuming and that of complex structures can become mathematically difficult. As a first step it is thus useful to operate with Markov models; refinements can be considered on a case-by-case basis; see pp. 277-79, 293-94 for general procedures. Alternative investigation methods are discussed in Section 6.9, and a Monte Carlo procedure for rare events is presented in Section 6.9.6.2. Tools and models useful for human reliability and risk management are introduced in Sections 6.10 and 6.11.

# 6.8.2 Preventive Maintenance 

Preventive maintenance $(P M)$ is necessary to
avoid wear-out failures and identify \& repair hidden failures and defects (e. g. failures of redundant elements not detected during operation).

This section investigates a one-item repairable structure with $P M$ at $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$. Results are basic for complex structures and will be useful in investigating fault tolerant repairable systems in Section 6.8.6 (see also Section 4.6 for further strategies).

[^0]:    ${ }^{4}$ Constant failure rates, no further failures at system down and only one repair crew, is not sufficient, in general, to assure that all states are regeneration states (as required for SMP); see e.g. Fig. A7.13.

Figure 6.21 Reliability functions for a one-item structure with preventive maintenance (of negligible duration) at times $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ for 2 distribution functions $\mathrm{F}(t)=1-\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ of the failurefree times; item new at $t=0, T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ (left strictly increasing, right constant failure rate)

The one-item considered is new at $t=0$ and new, or as-good-as-new, after each $P M$ or repair. Failure-free \& repair times are distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(x) \& \mathrm{G}(x)$, densities $\mathrm{f}(x) \& \mathrm{~g}(x), \mathrm{F}(0)=\mathrm{G}(0)=0$. Preventive maintenance is of negligible time duration (specialized personnel, no logistic delays). For availability considerations, if a $P M$ is due at a time in which the item is under repair, following cases can apply:

1. Preventive maintenance will not be performed (included in the running repair, considering that after each repair the item is as-good-as-new).
2. Preventive maintenance is performed; i. e. a running repair is terminated with the $P M$ in a negligible time.

Both situations can occur in practical applications. In case 2, times $0, T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ and end of a repair are renewal points. This case will be considered in the following.

The reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)$ can be calculated from

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)=\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t), & \text { for } 0<t \leq T_{P M}, \mathrm{R}_{S 0_{P M}}(0)=\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(0)=1 \\
\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)=\mathrm{R}_{S 0}^{n}\left(T_{P M}\right) \mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(t-n T_{P M}\right), & \text { for } n T_{P M}<t \leq(n+1) T_{P M}, n \geq 1
\end{array}
$$

with $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(x)=1-\mathrm{F}(x)$ (Eq. (6.14)). Figure 6.21 shows the shape of $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ and $\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)$ for an item with strictly increasing (left) and constant (right) failure rate. Because of the memoryless property of the exponential distribution function,

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)=\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\lambda t} \quad \text { holds for } \quad \mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}
$$

From Eq. (6.192), the mean time to failure with preventive maintenance $M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{R}_{S 0_{P M}}(t) d t=\left[1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}^{n}\left(T_{P M}\right)\right] \int_{0}^{T_{P M}} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t \\
& =\int_{0}^{T_{P M}} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t /\left[1-\mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(T_{P M}\right)\right]=\int_{0}^{T_{P M}}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x / \mathrm{F}\left(T_{P M}\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

see Example 6.14 for an application. For $\lambda(x)=\lambda$, i. e. for $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$. Eq. (6.194)

Figure 6.22 Point availability for a repairable one-item structure with preventive maintenance (of negligible duration) at times $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$; item new at $t=0, T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ and after each repair
yields $M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}=1 / \lambda=\mathrm{E}[\tau]$. However, for a strictly increasing failure rate $\lambda(x)$ it follows that $M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}>\mathrm{E}[\tau]$. To see this, consider that

$$
\int_{0}^{T_{P M}} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t-\int_{T_{P M}}^{\infty} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t=\mathrm{E}[\tau]-\mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(T_{P M}\right) \mathrm{E}\left[\tau-T_{P M} \mid \tau>T_{P M}\right]
$$

with $\tau$ as failure-free time of the item considered and $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau-T_{P M} \mid \tau>T_{P M}\right]$ as per Eq. (A6.28); the rest of the proof follows from remark 2 to Eq. (A6.28). Optimization of preventive maintenance period must consider Eq. (6.194) as well as cost, logistic support, and other relevant aspects ( $M T T F_{S 0_{P M}} \rightarrow \infty$ for $T_{P M} \rightarrow 0$ and $\mathrm{f}(+0)=0$ ).

Calculation of the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)$ for case 2 above leads to

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t), & \text { for } 0<t<T_{P M}, \quad \mathrm{PA}_{S 0_{P M}}(0)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(0)=1 \\
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}\left(t-n T_{P M}\right), & \text { for } n T_{P M} \leq t<(n+1) T_{P M}, n \geq 1,^{+}
\end{array}
$$

with $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ from Eq. (6.17). Figure 6.22 shows a typical shape of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0_{P M}}(t)$.
If the time duration for the preventive maintenance is not negligible, it is useful to define, in addition to the availability introduced in Section 6.2.1, the overall (or operational) availability $O A_{S}$, defined for $t \rightarrow \infty$ as ratio of the total up time to the sum of total up and down time in $(0, t]$. Defining for a series structure (with no further failures at system down) $M U T_{S}=$ system mean up time, $M D T_{S}=$ system mean down time (for repair only), ${ }^{++1} M L D_{S}=$ system mean logistic delay, MTTPM = mean time to preventive maintenance, and $T_{P M}=$ preventive maintenance period (referred to up time) it follows that (similar as for Eq. (4.6))

$$
O A_{S}=\frac{M U T_{S}}{M U T_{S}+M D T_{S}+M L D_{S}+M T T P M\left(M U T_{S} / T_{P M}\right)}
$$

$M L D_{S}=0$ yields the technical availability. In some cases, standby times are added to operating time. Other figures are possible, see e.g. [6.12] for railway applications.

Further strategies are investigated in Section4.6; undetected fault time on p. 443.

Assume a nonrepairable (up to system failure) 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two identical elements with constant failure rate $\lambda$. Give the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}$ by assuming a preventive maintenance with period $T_{P M} \ll 1 / \lambda$. The preventive maintenance is performed in a negligible time span and restores the 1-out-of-2 active redundancy to as-good-as-new.

## Solution

For a nonrepairable (up to system failure) 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two identical elements with constant failure rate $\lambda$, the reliability function is given by Eq. (2.22)

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=2 e^{-\lambda t}-e^{-2 \lambda t}
$$

with time dependent failure rate $\lambda_{S 0}(t)=2 \lambda\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right) /\left(2-e^{-\lambda t}\right)$ as per Eqs. (2.10), (2.22). The mean time to failure with preventive maintenance follows from Eq. (6.194) as

$$
M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}=\frac{\int_{0}^{T_{P M}} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t}{1-\mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(T_{P M}\right)}=\frac{\frac{2}{\lambda}\left(1-e^{-\lambda T_{P M}}\right)-\frac{1}{2 \lambda}\left(1-e^{-2 \lambda T_{P M}}\right)}{1-2 e^{-\lambda T_{P M}}+e^{-2 \lambda T_{P M}}}
$$

Considering $\lambda T_{P M} \ll 1$, and using $e^{-x} \approx 1-x+x^{2} / 2$, it follows that

$$
M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}=\frac{2 T_{P M}-T_{P M}}{\lambda^{2} T_{P M}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\lambda^{2} T_{P M}} \quad\left(=M T B F \cdot M T B F / T_{P M} \text { for } M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda\right)
$$

Without preventive maintenance, Eq. (2.22) yields $M T T F_{S 0}=3 / 2 \lambda=1.5 M T B F($ for $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda)$. Equation (6.197) clearly shows the gain $1 / \lambda T_{P M}=M T B F / T_{P M}$ given by the preventive maintenance.

### 6.8.3 Imperfect Switching

In practical applications, switching is necessary for powering down failed elements and powering up repaired elements. In some cases it is sufficient to locate the switching element in series with the redundancy on the reliability block diagram, yielding a series-parallel structure as investigated in Section 6.6. However, such an approach is often too simple to cover real situations. This section investigates some practical examples. Further considerations are given in Sections 6.8.4 dealing with incomplete coverage and 6.8 .5 dealing with two failure modes (see also Section 6.8.6.3 (Fig 6.34 on p. 267) for a practical application).

As a first example, Fig. 6.23 shows a situation in which measurement points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$, switches $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$, as well as a control unit $C$ must be considered. To simplify, let's consider only the reliability function in the nonrepairable case (up to system failure). From a reliability point of view, switch $S_{i}$, element $E_{i}$, and measurement point $M_{i}$ in Fig. 6.23 are in series $(i=1,2)$. Let $\tau_{b 1}$ and $\tau_{b 2}$ be the corresponding failure-free times with distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{b}(x)$ and density $\mathrm{f}_{b}(x)$. $\tau_{c}$ is the failure-free time of the control device with distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{c}(x)$ and density $\mathrm{f}_{c}(x)$. Consider first the case of standby redundancy and assume that at $t=0$ element $E_{1}$ is switched on. A system failure in the interval $(0, t]$ occurs with

Figure 6.23 Functional block diagram for a 1-out-of-2 redundancy with switches $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$, measurement points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$, and control device $C$
one of the following mutually exclusive events

$$
\left\{\tau_{c}>\tau_{b 1} \cap\left(\tau_{b 1}+\tau_{b 2}\right) \leq t\right\} \quad \text { or } \quad\left\{\tau_{c}<\tau_{b 1} \leq t\right\}
$$

It is implicitly assumed here that a failure of the control device has no influence on the operating element, and does not lead to a commutation to $E_{2}$. A verification of these conditions by an FMEA (Section 2.6) is necessary. With these assumptions, the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ of the system described by Fig. 6.23 is given by (nonrepairable case, system new at $t=0$ )

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1-\left[\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{f}_{b}(x)\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{c}(x)\right) \mathrm{F}_{b}(t-x) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{f}_{b}(x) \mathrm{F}_{c}(x) d x\right]
$$

Assuming further $\mathrm{f}_{b}(x)=\lambda_{b} e^{-\lambda_{b} x}$ and $\mathrm{f}_{c}(x)=\lambda_{c} e^{-\lambda_{c} x}$, Eq. (6.198) yields

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{b} t}+\left(1-e^{-\lambda_{c} t}\right) \frac{\lambda_{b}}{\lambda_{c}} e^{-\lambda_{b} t}
$$

and

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{2 \lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}}{\lambda_{b}\left(\lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}\right)}
$$

$\lambda_{c} \equiv 0$ leads to the results of Section 2.3.5 for the 1-out-of-2 standby redundancy (Eqs. (2.63), (2.64)). Assuming now an active redundancy (at $t=0, E_{1}$ is put into operation and $E_{2}$ into the reserve state), a system failure occurs in $(0, t]$ with one of the following mutually exclusive events

$$
\left\{\tau_{b 1} \leq t \cap \tau_{c}>\tau_{b 1} \cap \tau_{b 2} \leq t\right\} \quad \text { or } \quad\left\{\tau_{c}<\tau_{b 1} \leq t\right\}
$$

( $\tau_{b 2} \leq t$ because of active redundancy). The reliability function is then given by (nonrepairable case, system new at $t=0$ )

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1-\left[\mathrm{F}_{b}(t) \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{f}_{b}(x)\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{c}(x)\right) d x+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{f}_{b}(x) \mathrm{F}_{c}(x) d x\right]
$$

From Eq.(6.201) and assuming $\mathrm{f}_{b}(x)=\lambda_{b} e^{-\lambda_{b} x}$ and $\mathrm{f}_{c}(x)=\lambda_{c} e^{-\lambda_{c} x}$ it follows that$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\frac{2 \lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}}{\lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}} e^{-\lambda_{b} t}-\frac{\lambda_{b}}{\lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}} e^{-\left(2 \lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}\right) t}
$$

and

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{2 \lambda_{b}+\lambda_{r}}{\lambda_{b}\left(\lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}\right)}-\frac{\lambda_{b}}{\left(\lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}\right)\left(2 \lambda_{b}+\lambda_{c}\right)}
$$

$\lambda_{c} \equiv 0$ leads to the results of Section 2.2.6.3 for the 1-out-of-2 active redundancy (Eq. (2.22)). From Eqs. (6.200) and (6.203) one recognizes that for $\lambda_{c} \gg \lambda_{b}$

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx 1 / \lambda_{b}, \quad \text { for } \lambda_{c} \gg \lambda_{b}
$$

for both standby and active redundancy, i. e. to a situation as where no redundancy.
As a second example consider a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with constant failure rates $\lambda, \lambda_{r} \&$ repair rate $\mu \gg \lambda, \lambda_{r}$. The switching element can fail with constant failure rate $\lambda_{\sigma}$ and failure mode stuck at the state occupied just before failure.

At first, let's consider the case in which the failure of the switch can be immediately detected and repaired with constant repair rate $\mu_{\sigma} \gg \lambda_{\sigma}$, the system has only one repair crew with repair priority on switch, and no further failure at system down are considered. Asked are mean time to system failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ for system new at $t=0$ (state $Z_{0}$ ) and asymptotic \& steady-state (stationary) point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$. The involved process is a time-homogeneous Markov process. Figure 6.24 gives the diagrams of transition rates for reliability and availability calculation, respectively (down states $Z_{2}, Z_{2}, Z_{2}$.). $M T T F_{S 0}$ follows as solution of ( $M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}$. Fig. 6.24a, Table 6.2)

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\rho_{0} M_{0}=1+\lambda_{\sigma} M_{0} \cdot+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) M_{1}, & \rho_{0} \cdot M_{0} \cdot=1+\lambda_{r} M_{1} \cdot+\mu_{\sigma} M_{0} \\
\rho_{1} M_{1}=1+\lambda_{\sigma} M_{1} \cdot+\mu M_{0}, & \rho_{1} \cdot M_{1} \cdot=1+\mu_{\sigma} M_{1}
\end{array}
$$

yielding

$$
\begin{aligned}
M T T F_{S 0} & =\frac{\left(\rho_{1} \rho_{1} \cdot-\lambda_{\sigma} \mu_{\sigma}\right)\left[\rho_{0} \cdot \rho_{1} \cdot+\lambda_{\sigma}\left(\rho_{1}+\lambda_{r}\right)\right]+\left(\rho_{1}+\lambda_{\sigma}\right)\left[\lambda_{r} \lambda_{\sigma} \mu_{\sigma}+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \cdot \rho_{0} \cdot \rho_{1}\right]}{\left(\rho_{1} \rho_{1} \cdot-\lambda_{\sigma} \mu_{\sigma}\right)\left(\rho_{0} \rho_{0} \cdot \rho_{1} \cdot-\rho_{1} \cdot \lambda_{\sigma} \mu_{\sigma}\right)-\mu \rho_{1}\left[\lambda_{r} \lambda_{\sigma} \mu_{\sigma}+\rho_{0} \cdot \rho_{1}\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\right]} \\
& \approx \frac{\mu+2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma} \mu / \mu_{\sigma}}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\lambda \lambda_{\sigma} \mu / \mu_{\sigma}} \approx \frac{\mu}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\lambda \lambda_{\sigma} \mu / \mu_{\sigma}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Approximations assume $\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \lambda_{\sigma} \ll \mu \approx \mu_{\sigma}$ From the last approximation it follows that the effect of imperfect switching with failure mode stuck at the state occupied just before failure "immediately detected and repaired" becomes negligible for

$$
\lambda_{\sigma}<<\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mu_{\sigma} / \mu, \quad\left(\mu \approx \mu_{\sigma} \gg \lambda, \lambda_{r}, \lambda_{\sigma}\right)
$$

A more severe condition as that of Eq. (6.207) is given by Eq. (6.212). $\lambda_{\sigma}=0$ yields results as for an ideal switch (Table 6.6). Per contra $\lambda_{\sigma} \gg\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mu_{\sigma} / \mu$ yields $M T T F_{S 0} \approx \mu \mu_{\sigma} / \lambda \lambda_{\sigma} \mu$, i. e. similar as for a 1 -out-of-2 active redundancy with 2 different elements $\lambda, \mu \& \lambda_{\sigma}, \mu_{\sigma}$ (see Eq.(6.100)). From Fig. 6.24b and Table 6.2 it follows that $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is given as solution of

a) For reliability
$\rho_{00^{\prime}}=\rho_{11^{\prime}}=\lambda_{\sigma} ; \rho_{01}=\lambda+\lambda_{r} ; \rho_{0^{\prime} 0}=\rho_{1^{\prime} 1}=\mu_{\sigma} ;$
$\rho_{10}=\mu ; \rho_{0^{\prime} 1^{\prime}}=\lambda_{r} ; \rho_{0^{\prime} 2}=\rho_{12}=\rho_{1^{\prime} 2}=\lambda$
$\rho_{0}=\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma} ; \rho_{0^{\prime}}=\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu_{\sigma}$
$\rho_{1}=\lambda+\lambda_{\sigma}+\mu ; \rho_{1^{\prime}}=\lambda+\mu_{\sigma} ; \rho_{2}=0$
b) For availability
$\rho_{00^{\prime}}=\rho_{11^{\prime}}=\lambda_{\sigma} ; \rho_{01}=\lambda+\lambda_{r} ; \rho_{10}=\rho_{21}=\mu ; \rho_{0^{\prime} 1^{\prime}}=\lambda_{r} ;$
$\rho_{0^{\prime} 0}=\rho_{1^{\prime} 1}=\rho_{2^{\prime} 2}=\rho_{2^{\prime \prime} 1}=\mu_{\sigma} ; \rho_{0^{\prime} 2^{\prime \prime}}=\rho_{12}=\rho_{1^{\prime} 2^{\prime}}=\lambda$
$\rho_{0}=\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma} ; \rho_{0^{\prime}}=\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu_{\sigma} ; \rho_{1}=\lambda+\lambda_{\sigma}+\mu ;$
$\rho_{1^{\prime}}=\lambda+\mu_{\sigma} ; \rho_{2}=\mu ; \rho_{2^{\prime}}=\rho_{2^{\prime \prime}}=\mu_{\sigma}$

& \rho_{1^{\prime}} P_{1^{\prime}}=\lambda_{r} P_{0^{\prime}}+\lambda_{\sigma} P_{1}, \quad \rho_{2} P_{2}=\lambda P_{1}+\mu_{\sigma} P_{2^{\prime}}, \quad \rho_{2^{\prime}} P_{2^{\prime}}=\lambda P_{1^{\prime}}, \quad \rho_{2^{\prime \prime}} P_{2^{\prime \prime}}=\lambda P_{0^{\prime}}
\end{aligned}
$$

One of the Eq. (6.208), arbitrarily chosen, must be replaced by $\Sigma_{i} P_{i}=1$. The asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability follows then from

$$
\begin{aligned}

& 1 \\
& 1+\frac{\rho_{1^{\prime}} \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(\rho_{0}+\mu_{\sigma}\right) / \mu+\left(\lambda / \mu+\lambda / \mu_{\sigma}\right)\left(\mu \lambda_{r} \lambda_{\sigma}+\rho_{0} \rho_{0^{\prime}} \lambda_{\sigma}-\lambda_{\sigma}^{2} \mu_{\sigma}\right)+\rho_{1^{\prime}} \lambda \lambda_{\sigma} \mu / \mu_{\sigma}}{\mu \rho_{0^{\prime}} \rho_{1^{\prime}}+\mu \lambda_{\sigma}\left(\rho_{1^{\prime}}+\lambda_{r}\right)+\left(\rho_{0} \rho_{0^{\prime}}-\lambda_{\sigma} \mu_{\sigma}\right)\left(\rho_{1^{\prime}}+\lambda_{\sigma}\right)} \\
& \approx 1-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{a}+\lambda_{\sigma} \lambda\left[\mu+\lambda_{r}\left(1+\mu / \mu_{\sigma}\right)+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(1+\mu_{\sigma} / \mu\right)\right] \mu / \mu_{\sigma}^{2}}{\mu\left(\mu+\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{a}}, \quad \mathrm{a}=1+\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma}\right) / \mu_{\sigma}=1

For $\mu_{\sigma} \approx \mu \& \lambda, \lambda_{r}, \lambda_{\sigma} \ll \mu$, Eq. (6.209) allows similar conclusions as given by Eq. (6.207) $\lambda_{\sigma} \ll\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mu_{\sigma}^{2} / \mu^{2} . \lambda_{\sigma}=0$ yields results as for an ideal switch (Table 6.6).

# Example 6.15 

Compute the mean time to system failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ for the 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy as per Fig. $6.25\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \lambda_{\sigma} \ll \mu, \mu_{g}\right)$.

## Solution

From Fig. 6.25a and Table 6.2, $M T T F_{S 0}$ is given as solution of $\left(M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}\right)$

$$
\rho_{0} M_{0}=1+\lambda_{\sigma} M_{0}+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) M_{1}, \quad \rho_{1} M_{1}=1+\mu M_{0}, \quad \rho_{0^{\prime}} M_{0^{\prime}}=1
$$

yielding

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu\right)+\lambda_{\sigma}(\lambda+\mu) / \lambda}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\lambda_{\sigma}(\lambda+\mu)}=\frac{\mu\left(1+\lambda_{\sigma} / \lambda\right)}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\lambda_{\sigma} \mu}
$$

Because of the not detected failure of the switch, the condition on $\lambda_{\sigma}$ to approach results as for an ideal switching (Table 6.6) is more severe as Eq. (6.207) and given by

$$
\lambda_{\sigma} \ll \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu, \quad \text { (which implies } \lambda_{\sigma} / \lambda \ll 1, \text { considering } \mu \gg \lambda \text { ). }
$$

Equation (6.212), as also (6.214), shows that in this case the switch acts as a series element (see Eq. (6.160) \& footnote on p.221). From Fig. 6.25b and Table 6.2, $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ follows as solution of

$$
\rho_{0} P_{0}=\mu P_{1}+\mu_{g} P_{2}, \quad \rho_{0^{\prime}} P_{0^{\prime}}=\lambda_{\sigma} P_{0}, \quad \rho_{1} P_{1}=\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) P_{0}, \quad \rho_{2} P_{2}=\lambda P_{1}+\lambda P_{0^{\prime}}
$$

One of the Eq. (6.213), arbitrarily chosen, must be replaced by $P_{0}+P_{0^{\prime}}+P_{1}+P_{2}=1$. The asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{0^{\prime}}+P_{1}$ follows then from

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma}\right)+\mu \lambda_{\sigma}}{\mu_{g}\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma}\right)+\mu \mu_{g}\left(1+\lambda_{\sigma} / \lambda\right)}}=1-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\lambda_{\sigma} \mu}{\mu \mu_{g}}=1-\lambda_{\sigma} / \mu_{g} \\
& -\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu \mu_{g}
\end{aligned}
$$

For $\mu_{g} \approx \mu$, Eq. (6.214) allows the same conclusions for $\lambda_{\sigma}$ as from Eq. (6.211). $\lambda_{\sigma}=0$ yields results as for an ideal switch (Table 6.6, $\mu_{g}=\mu$ and $2 \lambda$ instead of $\lambda$ for $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ because of the transition $Z_{2} \rightarrow Z_{0}$ ). $\lambda_{\sigma} \gg \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu$ yields $M T T F_{S 0} \approx 1 / \lambda_{\sigma}+1 / \lambda$ as for a nonrepairable 1 -out-of-2 standby redundancy with $\lambda_{\sigma} \& \lambda$, and $P A_{S}=A A_{S} \approx 1-\lambda_{\sigma} / \mu_{g}$ as for a repairable one-item.Table 6.11 resumes basic models for the investigation of imperfect switch in a repairable 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with constant failure and repair rates $\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \mu$ (see pp. 257-58 for 2 failure modes for the switch and Table 6.6 for ideal switch).

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{v}+\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) /\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{v}+\mu\right)} \approx \frac{1}{\lambda_{v}+\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu} \\
& P A_{S}{ }^{*}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu_{v}}+\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu\right)}} \approx 1-\frac{\lambda_{v}}{\mu_{v}}-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{\mu^{2}\left(1+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu\right)} \\
& \lambda_{v}=0 \text { yields results as for an ideal switch (Table 6.6) }
\end{aligned}
$$

| :--: | :--: |

$$

& \lambda_{\sigma} \ll \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu \text { yields for } \mu_{g} \approx \mu \text { results as for an ideal switch (Table 6.6) }

$$

& P A_{S}{ }^{*} \approx 1-\lambda_{o} / \mu_{o}-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \lambda / \mu^{2}-\lambda \lambda_{\sigma} / \mu_{\sigma}^{2}-\left(\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu+\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu_{\sigma}\right) \lambda_{o} / \mu_{o} \\
& \text { (see Eq. (6.240) for a more complete approximation) } \\
& \lambda_{o} \ll \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu \text { and } \lambda_{\sigma} \ll\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mu_{\sigma} / \mu \\
& \text { yield for } \mu_{o}, \mu_{\sigma} \approx \mu \text { results as for an ideal switch (Table 6.6) }
\end{aligned}
$$

d) Switch with failure modes stuck at the state occupied \& no connection, constant failure and repair rates $\lambda_{\sigma}, \mu_{\sigma} \& \lambda_{o}, \mu_{o}$, ideal failure detection \& localization, repair priority on switch (Eqs. (6.238), (6.240))
in general $\lambda_{\sigma}, \lambda_{o}<\lambda \& \mu_{\sigma}, \mu_{o} \geq \mu ;{ }^{*} P A_{S}$ used for $P A_{S}=A A_{S} ;{ }^{* *}$ considering $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$# 6.8.4 Incomplete Coverage 

Incomplete faults (failures \& defects) coverage occurs because of lack or failure in the fault detection and /or localization (pp. 113 \& 116). Fault coverage is defined as the proportion of faults that can be detected and localized under given conditions. ${ }^{+)}$ It applies in particular to redundant structures. A fault coverage greater as 0.95 is often required for complex equipment. Lacks in the detection and/or localization lead to hidden faults, often not covered by automatic or semi-automatic diagnosis, and thus localizable only at a repair or preventive maintenance. Hidden faults
can cause a serious reduction of the advantage given by a redundancy,
see e.g. Eqs. (6.220) \& (6.222) or (6.228) \& (6.229)). As a general rule, fault coverage has to be investigated on a case-by-case basis, considering the aspects of false detection and /or localization (or alternatively false alarm), and no detection and/or localization possible (or alternatively no alarm emitted).

Following an illustrative example, this section discusses some basic models for incomplete coverage. ${ }^{*+}$ A way to compensate incomplete coverage is given at the end of the 3 th footnote on this page and illustrated with 2 new models $\mathbf{c} \& \mathbf{d}$ of Table 6.12 (p. 256), implying the realization of an operation monitoring as per Table 4.1 with suitable BIT/BITE (see remarks on pp. $250 \& 255$ ). However,
for critical applications, majority redundancy remains the best way to compensate incomplete coverage (in a 2-out-of-3 redundancy, the first failure is captured on line and no switch is necessary, see pp. 49, 31, 222-25).

Consider first the case of a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two different elements $E_{1} \& E_{2}$, and assume that failures of $E_{1}$ can be localized and repaired only at a repair of $E_{2}$ or at a preventive maintenance (PM). Elements $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ have constant failure rates ( $\lambda_{1} \neq \lambda_{2}$, still with $\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}$ ), the repair time of $E_{2}$ is distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)(\mathrm{G}(0)=0$, density $\mathrm{g}(x))$, and $P M$, incl. repair of $E_{1}$ and/or $E_{2}$, takes a negligible time (see Example 6.17 for const. repair rate). ${ }^{*+4}$ After a repair or a $P M, E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ are as-good-as-new. If no $P M$ is performed, Fig. 6.26a shows a possible time schedule (system new at $t=0$ ), yielding for the reliability function

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) t}+\int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{1} e^{-\lambda_{1} x} e^{-\lambda_{2} t} d x+\int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{2} e^{-\lambda_{2} x} e^{-\lambda_{1} t}(1-\mathrm{G}(t-x)) d x \\
&+\int_{0}^{t} \int_{0}^{x} \lambda_{2} e^{-\lambda_{2} x} e^{-\lambda_{1} y} \mathrm{~g}(y-x) \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t-y) d x d y
\end{aligned}
$$

    ${ }^{*+4}$ ) It is tacitly assumed, that at each regeneration point ( $t=0$, end of a repair or $P M$ ), $E_{2}$ is put in operation and $E_{1}$ in reserve; moreover no common cause failures occur, and automatic failure detection in $E_{1} \& E_{2}$ and localization in $E_{2}$, as well as switching operations, are ideal. A suitable procedure being that at a failure (output $E_{2} \neq$ output $E_{1}$ ), operation is continued with $E_{1}$ in the case of failure localized in $E_{2}$, or with $E_{2}$ if not (Table 6.12 cases $\mathbf{c} \& \mathbf{d}$ ).

The Laplace transform of $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ follows as

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{\left(s+\lambda_{1}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)+\lambda_{2}\left(s+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}\left(s+\lambda_{1}\right)\right)}{\left(s+\lambda_{1}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)-\left(s+\lambda_{1}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{2}\right) \lambda_{2} \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}\left(s+\lambda_{1}\right)}
$$

and the mean time to failure becomes

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\left[\lambda_{1}\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)+\lambda_{2}^{2}\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}\left(\lambda_{1}\right)\right)\right] /\left[\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)-\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}^{2} \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}\left(\lambda_{1}\right)\right]
$$

Example 6.16 discusses Eq. (6.217). The point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ is investigated in Example 6.17 for the case of constant repair rates. If preventive maintenance is performed at times $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ and after each preventive maintenance (assumed of negligible duration, also considering a possible repair of $E_{2}$ and/or $E_{1}$ ) the system is as-good-as-new, the times $0, T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ are regeneration points for the system. $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}{ }_{P M}(t)$ and $M T T F_{S 0}{ }_{P M}$ follow from Eqs. (6.192) \& (6.194), with $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ as per Eq. (6.215). For $T_{P M} \gg M T T R, \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}{ }_{P M}(t) \approx \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \approx P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ can often be used. Optimization of $T_{P M}$ must consider cost and logistic aspects too.

Equations (6.217), (6.218), (6.220) and (6.222) show that a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with hidden failures in one element $\left(E_{1}\right)$, which can be localized and repaired only at a repair of the second element or at a preventive maintenance, behaves like a nonrepairable 1-out-of-2 standby redundancy. However, if failure localization and repair of element $E_{1}$ can start at failure occurrence (after checking $E_{2}$ as per the 3th footnote on p.249), the situation of an ideal active 1-out-of-2 repairable redundancy is reestablished, see case c of Tab.6.12 (this remains true also by considering a travel time for specialized personnel (Eqs. (6.103) \& (6.104));
this bears out, how important it is, in the presence of redundancy to investigate failure modes, failure localization \& check strategy at failure (FMEA).# Example 6.16 

Give approximate expressions for the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ per Eq. (6.217).

## Solution

For $\hat{\mathrm{g}}\left(\lambda_{1}\right) \rightarrow 1$, it follows from Eq. (6.217) that

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) / \lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}=1 / \lambda_{1}+1 / \lambda_{2}
$$

A better approximation using $\hat{\mathrm{g}}\left(\lambda_{1}\right)=1-\lambda_{1} M T T R$ yields (with $M T T R$ as per Eq. (6.111))

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2} M T T R\right) /\left(\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(1+\lambda_{2} M T T R\right)\right)
$$

## Example 6.17

Investigate $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ per Eq. (6.216), $M T T F_{S 0}$ and $M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}$ per Eqs. (6.217) and (6.194), $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ and $P A_{S_{P M}}=A A_{S_{P M}}$, and the undetected fault time $\tau_{U F T}$ for the case of constant repair rate $\mu$ for $E_{2}$ and $\mu_{g}$ for $E_{1}$ together with $E_{2}\left(\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2} \ll \mu, \mu_{g}\right)$.

## Solution

With $\hat{\mathrm{g}}\left(s+\lambda_{1}\right)=\mu /\left(s+\lambda_{1}+\mu\right)$ it follows from Eq. (6.216) that

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\left[\left(s+\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{1}+\mu\right)+\lambda_{2}\left(s+\lambda_{2}\right)\right] /\left(s+\lambda_{1}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu\right)
$$

and thus (Table A9.7b) $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=A e^{-\lambda_{1} t}+B e^{-\lambda_{2} t}+C e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu\right) t}$ with

$$
A=\frac{\lambda_{2}\left(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}+\mu\right)}{\left(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}\right)\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu\right)} \approx \frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}}, \quad B=\frac{-\lambda_{1}\left(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}+\mu\right)}{\left(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}\right)\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu\right)} \approx \frac{-\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}}, \quad C=\frac{-\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}}{\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu\right)\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu\right)} \approx 0
$$

The mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ follows as

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\hat{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0)=\frac{\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu\right)+\lambda_{2}^{2}}{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu\right)} \approx \frac{\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}}=1 / \lambda_{1}+1 / \lambda_{2}
$$

Equation (6.220) follows also from Eq. (6.217) $\left(\hat{\mathrm{g}}\left(\lambda_{1}\right)=\mu /\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu\right)\right)$. Note that $\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}<<\mu$ yields

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx\left(\lambda_{2} e^{-\lambda_{1} t}-\lambda_{1} e^{-\lambda_{2} t}\right) /\left(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}\right) \quad \text { and } M T T F_{S 0} \approx 1 / \lambda_{1}+1 / \lambda_{2}
$$

The point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ (as well as $\left.\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)\right)$ can be investigated using a 4 states Markov process with up states $Z_{0}, Z_{1}, Z_{1} \&$ down state $Z_{2}$ (absorbing for $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ ), see graph and the 3 th footnote on p. 249. The asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is obtained by solving (Table 6.2) $\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) P_{0}=\mu P_{1}+\mu_{g} P_{2}, \quad \lambda_{2} P_{1}=\lambda_{1} P_{0}$, $\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu\right) P_{1}=\lambda_{2} P_{0}, P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{1}+P_{2}=1$, yielding


$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S}=A \mathrm{~A}_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{1^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu\right)}{\mu_{g}\left[\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu\right)\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)+\lambda_{2}^{2}\right]}} \approx 1-\frac{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}}{\mu_{g}\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)}
$$

The undetected fault time $\tau_{U F T}$ is here the stay time in $Z_{1}$, thus (Eqs. (A7.166) \& (A7.132))

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{U F T}\right]=1 / \lambda_{2} \quad \& \quad \mathrm{E}[\text { total undetected time in }(0, t]]=t \cdot P_{1^{\prime}} \approx t \cdot \lambda_{1} /\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)
$$

In the case of preventive maintenance at $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ (regeneration points at $t=0, T_{P M}$, $2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ ), Eq. (6.194) with $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ per Eq. (6.221) yields

$$
M T T F_{S 0_{P M}} \approx \frac{\lambda_{2}\left(1-e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{P M}}\right) / \lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}\left(1-e^{-\lambda_{2} T_{P M}}\right) / \lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{2}\left(1-e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{P M}}\right)-\lambda_{1}\left(1-e^{-\lambda_{2} T_{P M}}\right)} \approx \frac{2}{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2} T_{P M}}
$$

The last part of Eq. (6.224) follows with $e^{-\lambda x} \approx 1-\lambda x+(\lambda x)^{2} / 2$. For $T_{P M} \gg 1 / \mu=M T T R$ $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0_{P M}}(t) \approx \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \approx P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ with $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ per Eq. (6.222) can often be used.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Q}_{0 \Gamma}(x)=1-e^{-2 \lambda x} ; \quad \mathrm{Q}_{\Gamma 2}(x)=(1-c) \mathrm{u}(x) \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{11}(x)=c \mathrm{u}(x) ; \mathrm{Q}_{10}(x)=\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}\left(1-e^{-(\lambda+\mu) x}\right) \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{12}(x)=\frac{\lambda}{\mu} \mathrm{Q}_{10}(x) ; \quad \mathrm{Q}_{21}(x)=1-e^{-\mu x} \\
& \mathrm{u}(x)=0 \text { for } x<0 \quad \text { and } 1 \text { for } x \geq 0 ; \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(\infty)=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure 6.27 State transitions diagram for a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with const. failure \& repair rates $(\lambda, \mu)$, incomplete coverage (identification of failed element with probability $c$ ), one repair crew ( $Z_{2}$ down state (absorbing for rel. calculation), semi-Markov proc.; see also Fig. 6.28)

A model often used to consider incomplete coverage assumes that a failure can be localized only with a probability $c$ (coverage $c$ ). This will be investigated in the following for the case of a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with identical elements and const. failure \& repair rates $\lambda \& \mu$. At a failure, outputs of both elements differ and with probability $1-c$ the failed element can't be identified, yielding a system failure. This case is similar to that of Fig. 6.25 and is also known as no start at call [6.34]. Figure 6.27 gives the state transitions diagram of the involved semi-Markov process. The transition from state $Z_{1}$, occurs instantaneously to $Z_{1}$ with probability $\varphi_{\Gamma 1}=c$ or to $Z_{2}$ with $\varphi_{\Gamma 2}=1-c$. Because of the constant failure \& repair rates, investigation can also be based on a Markov process with the diagram of transition rates given in Fig. 6.28 (see Examples $6.18 \& 6.19$ ). However, weak points of this model are
the assumption of c constant over time \& failures, and that at system down caused by non coverage, both elements must be repaired ( $Z_{2} \rightarrow Z_{1}$ in Figs. $6.27 \& 6.28$ ); solutions for the second aspect are in Example 6.20 and in Table $6.12 \boldsymbol{c} \& \boldsymbol{d}$ on p. 256 with share of the failure rate in $\lambda=\lambda_{c}+\lambda_{u}$.

# Example 6.18 

Give the mean time to system failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ for the 1-out-of-2 active redundancy as per Fig. $6.27(\lambda<<\mu)$.

## Solution

From Fig. 6.27 and Table 6.2, $M T T F_{S 0}$ is given as solution of $\left(M_{j} \equiv M T T F_{S j}\right) \quad M_{1}=T_{\Gamma}+c M_{1}$, $M_{0}=T_{0}+M_{1}, M_{1}=T_{1}+(\mu /(\lambda+\mu)) M_{0}$, with $T_{i} \equiv{ }_{0}^{\infty}\left(1-Q_{i}(x)\right) d x \& Q_{i}(x)=\Sigma_{j} Q_{i j}(x)$ (Eqs. (A7.166) \& (A7.165)). Considering Fig. 6.27 it follows $T_{0}=1 / 2 \lambda, T_{1}=0, T_{1}=1 /(\lambda+\mu), T_{2}=1 / \mu$, yielding

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{T_{0}+T_{1}+c T_{1}}{1-c \mu /(\lambda+\mu)}=\frac{\lambda+\mu+2 \lambda c}{2 \lambda(\lambda+\mu-\mu c)}=\frac{\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu(1-c)}
$$

From Fig. 6.27 and Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.178), $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{\Gamma}+P_{1}$ is given as

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\left(\varphi_{0} T_{0}+\varphi_{1} T_{\Gamma}+\varphi_{1} T_{1}\right) /\left(\varphi_{0} T_{0}+\varphi_{1} T_{\Gamma}+\varphi_{1} T_{1}+\varphi_{2} T_{2}\right)
$$

Thereby, $\varphi_{j}$ are the state probabilities of the embedded Markov chain, obtained as solution of (Table 6.2) $\quad \varphi_{0}=\varphi_{1} \mu /(\lambda+\mu), \quad \varphi_{1}=\varphi_{0}, \quad \varphi_{1}=\varphi_{1} c+\varphi_{2}, \quad \varphi_{2}=\varphi_{1}(1-c)+\varphi_{1} \lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$, yielding (considering $\left.\varphi_{0}+\varphi_{1}+\varphi_{1}+\varphi_{2}=1\right) \quad \varphi_{1}=(\lambda+\mu) /\left(2(\lambda+2 \mu)-\mu c\right), \quad \varphi_{2}=(\lambda+\mu-\mu c) /\left(2(\lambda+2 \mu)-\mu c\right)$, $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{1}=\mu /\left(2(\lambda+2 \mu)-\mu c\right)$. From Eq. (6.226) it follows then

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\left(\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu\right) /\left(\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu+2 \lambda(\lambda+\mu-\mu c)\right)=1-\left(2 \lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu(1-c)\right) /\left(\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu\right)
$$

See Eq. (6.231) for a discussion of Eqs. (6.225) \& (6.227).

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\rho_{01}=2 \lambda c ; & \rho_{02}=2 \lambda(1-c) ; \quad \rho_{10}=\mu ; \\
\rho_{12}=\lambda ; & \rho_{21}=\mu\left(\rho_{21}=0 \text { for reliability }\right) \\
\rho_{0}=2 \lambda ; & \rho_{1}=\lambda+\mu ; \quad \rho_{2}=\mu\left(\rho_{2}=0 \text { for reliability }\right)
\end{array}
$$

Figure 6.28 Diagram of the transition rates for a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with const. failure \& repair rates $(\lambda, \mu)$, incomplete coverage (identification of failed element with probability $c$, i. e. with prob. $1-c$ the system goes down whenever outputs of both elements differ), one repair crew ( $Z_{2}$ down state (absorbing for rel. calculation), Markov process; see Tab. 6.12 for other models)

# Example 6.19 

Give the mean time to system failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ for the 1-out-of-2 active redundancy as per Fig. $6.28(\lambda<<\mu)$.

## Solution

From Fig. 6.28 \& Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.126), $M T T F_{S 0}$ is given as solution of $\left(M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}\right)$ $2 \lambda M_{0}=1+2 \lambda c M_{1}$ and $(\lambda+\mu) M_{1}=1+\mu M_{0}$, yielding

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=[\lambda+\mu+2 \lambda c] /[2 \lambda(\lambda+\mu-\mu c)] \approx \mu /\left[2 \lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu(1-c)\right]
$$

From Fig. 6.28 and Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.127), $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is given as solution of $2 \lambda P_{0}=\mu P_{1}$, $(\lambda+\mu) P_{1}=2 \lambda c P_{0}+\mu P_{2}$, and $P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{2}=1$, yielding

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{2 \lambda(\lambda+\mu-\mu c)}{\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu}}=1-\frac{2 \lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu(1-c)}{\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu}
$$

See Eq. (6.231) for a discussion of Eqs. (6.228) \& (6.229).

## Example 6.20

Investigate $M T T F_{S 0}$ and $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ for the model given by Fig. 6.28 by assuming that a repair for a hidden failure (transition $Z_{0} \rightarrow Z_{2}$ ) brings the system to state $Z_{0}$ and not to $Z_{1}(\lambda<<\mu)$.

## Solution

$M T T F_{S 0}$ is given by Eq. (6. 228). The point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can be obtained using a 4 states Markov process with up states $Z_{0}$ and $Z_{1}$ and down states $Z_{1}$. and $Z_{2}$, see graph. The asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is obtained by solving (Table 6.2) $2 \lambda P_{0}=\mu P_{1}+\mu P_{1},(\lambda+\mu) P_{1}=2 \lambda c P_{0}+\mu P_{2}, \mu P_{1}=2 \lambda(1-c) P_{0}$, and $P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{1}+P_{2}=1$, yielding


$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S}=A \mathrm{~A}_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{2 \lambda[\lambda c+\mu(1-c)]}{\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu c}}=1-\frac{2 \lambda[\lambda c+\mu(1-c)]}{\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu c}
$$

Comparison of Eqs. (6.225) with (6.228) \& (6.227) with (6.229) shows the equivalence of the models of Figs. $6.27 \& 6.28$. For $c=1$, Eqs. (6.228), (6.229), (6.230) yield results of Table 6.6 for an ideal 1-out-of-2 active redundancy. For $c=0$, Eqs. (6.228) - (6.230) yield results for a one-item with failure rate $2 \lambda$ and repair rate $\mu$ (most unfavorable case, because the first failure leads to a system down). Comparison of Eqs. (6.92) with (6.228) and (6.87) with (6.229) or (6.230) showsthat the effect of incomplete coverage is negligible for

$$
2 \lambda \mu(1-c)<<2 \lambda^{2} \quad \text { or } \quad c \gg 1-\lambda / \mu, \quad \text { (e.g. } c=1-0.1 \lambda / \mu)
$$

Condition (6.231) can be hard to realize for complex equipment and remains the same also if repair of a hidden failure brings the system to state $Z_{0}$ (Example 6.20).

A further possibility is investigated in Example 6.21 by assuming that at the occurrence of a hidden failure, one of the two elements is selected to continue operation and the selected element is not failed with probability $p$. All
above investigations show that for critical applications, majority redundancy or a check strategy as described on pp. 249 \& 255, realized in the models $\boldsymbol{c} \& \boldsymbol{d}$ of Table 6.12 on p. 256, has to be preferred.

# Example 6.21 

Investigate $M T T F_{S 0}$ and $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ for the model considered in Example 6.20 by assuming that at the occurrence of a hidden failure (outputs of both elements differ and failed element cannot be detected), one of the two elements is selected to continue operation and the selected element is with probability $p$ not failed (safety is not primary objective).

## Solution

$\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ and $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can be obtained using a 5 states Markov process with up states $Z_{0}, Z_{1}, Z_{1}$, and down states $Z_{2}, Z_{2} \cdot\left(Z_{2}, Z_{2}\right.$. absorbing for $\left.\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)\right)$, see graph. $M T T F_{S 0}$ is given as solution of $\left(M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}\right)$ $2 \lambda M_{0}=1+2 \lambda c M_{1}+2 \lambda(1-c) p M_{1} \cdot,(\lambda+\mu) M_{1}=1+\mu M_{0}$, $(\lambda+\mu) M_{1}=1+\mu M_{0}$, yielding


$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{\lambda+\mu+2 \lambda(c+(1-c) p)}{2 \lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu(1-c)(1-p)} \approx \frac{\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu(1-c)(1-p)}
$$

The asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is obtained by solving (Table 6.2) $2 \lambda P_{0}=\mu\left(P_{1}+P_{1}+P_{2} \cdot\right), \quad(\lambda+\mu) P_{1}=2 \lambda c P_{0}+\mu P_{2}, \quad(\lambda+\mu) P_{1}=2 \lambda(1-c) p P_{0}$, $\mu P_{2}=\lambda\left(P_{1}+P_{1}\right), P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{1}+P_{2}+P_{2} .=1$, yielding

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S}=A \mathrm{~A}_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{1}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{2 \lambda[\lambda+(\mu-\lambda)(1-c)(1-p)]}{\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu[p(1-c)+c]}} \approx 1-\frac{2 \lambda[\lambda+\mu(1-c)(1-p)]}{\mu^{2}}
$$

Comparison of Eq. (6.232) with (6.228) and Eq. (6.233) with (6.230) shows, for instance, that

$$
\frac{M T T F_{S 0}}{M T T F_{S 0}}=\frac{2 \lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu(1-c)}{2 \lambda^{2}+\lambda \mu(1-c)} \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{\left(1-P A_{S}\right)_{p=0}}{\left(1-P A_{S}\right)_{p=0.5}} \approx \frac{\lambda \mathrm{c}+\mu(1-c)}{\lambda+\mu(1-c) / 2}
$$

Both ratios are 1 for a coverage $c=1$. One recognizes also that results of Example 6.20 are those of Example 6.21 for $p=0$, and that for $p=1$ Eqs. (6.232) \& (6.233) yield results as for an ideal coverage (Table 6.6), as for $c=1$.

Influence of preventive maintenance at $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ (yielding regeneration points at $t=0, T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ ) can be investigated as discussed in Example 6.17,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_{01}=\lambda_{D D} ; \rho_{03}=\lambda_{C} ; \rho_{04}=\lambda_{N C} ; \rho_{05}=\lambda_{D F} ; \\
& \rho_{12}=\lambda_{C}+\lambda_{N C}=\lambda ; \rho_{20}=\rho_{30}=\rho_{40}=\rho_{50}=\mu \\
& \rho_{0}=\left(\lambda_{C}+\lambda_{N C}\right)+\left(\lambda_{D F}+\lambda_{D D}\right)=\lambda+\lambda_{D} ; \\
& \rho_{1}=\lambda_{C}+\lambda_{N C}=\lambda ; \rho_{2}=\rho_{3}=\rho_{4}=\rho_{5}=\mu \\
& C=\text { covered }, N C=\text { uncovered } \\
& D F=\text { false alarm, } D D=\text { alarm defection }
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure 6.29 Diagram of the transition rates for a one-item structure with incomplete coverage and 2 failures modes for the diagnosis, const. failure and repair rates $\lambda_{C}, \lambda_{N C}, \lambda_{D F}, \lambda_{D D}, \mu$, ideal failure localization $\left(Z_{2}, Z_{3}, Z_{4}, Z_{5}\right.$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), Markov process)
often using

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{-t / M T T F_{S 0}} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \approx \mathrm{PA}_{S}+\left(1-\mathrm{PA}_{S}\right) e^{-\mu t}
$$

or $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \approx P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ (see Eqs. (6.94) \& (6.88) and the discussion to Eq. (6.56)).
Other possibilities to consider for incomplete coverage are conceivable. Assuming, for instance, that in a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy at a failure of one element (outputs of both elements differ), one element is instantaneously selected (without any check) to continue operation and with probability $p$ the selected element is not failed, leads to the model of Example 6.20 with $c=p$.

A further possibility, which considers false alarm with failure rate $\lambda_{D F}$ and alarm defection with failure rate $\lambda_{D D}$, shown in Fig. 6.29 with a repair rate $\mu$ for all failure modes, has been proposed in [6.42] and yields $\left(\lambda_{D}=\lambda_{D D}+\lambda_{D F}, \lambda=\lambda_{C}+\lambda_{N C}\right)$

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{\lambda+\lambda_{D D}}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{D}\right)} \quad \& \quad P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}=\frac{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{D D}\right)}{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{D D}\right)+\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{D}\right)}
$$

see also Fig. 3 of [6.42] and Fig. 1 of [1.13] for further refinements.
However,
if the design allows that at a failure in a 1-out-of-2 repairable redundancy (output $E_{2} \neq$ output $E_{1}$ ) an appropriate test signal is automatically started (BIT/BITE, as necessary for an acceptance test) and operation is continued with the not failed element, the situation of an ideal active 1-out-of-2 repairable redundancy (Table 6.6) is reestablished (as per the 3th footnote on p. 249 \& remark on p. 250), by assuming no common cause failures and thus that only one element is failed; see cases $\boldsymbol{c} \& \boldsymbol{d}$ in Table 6.12 on p. 256.

This bears out, again, how important it is, in presence of redundancy to investigate
failure modes, failure localization, and check strategy at failure (FMEA).

$c$ and $u$ refer to $100 \%$ and $0 \%$ coverage, respectively; * $P A_{S}$ is used for $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$# 6.8.5 Elements with more than two States or one Failure Mode 

Elements with more than two states (good / failed) or one failure mode (open / short) often arise in practical applications. Some considerations have been given in Sections 2.3.6 \& 6.8.4. This section shows, on the basis of two practical examples, that items with more than 2 states or one failure mode can often be investigated using a diagram of transition rates, see also pp. 266-69 for a further practical application.

As a first example consider an item with the three states good, waiting for repair, repair [6.14]. Figure 6.30 shows this model. From Fig. 6.30 \& Table 6.2 it holds that

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=1 / \lambda \quad \text { and } \quad P A_{S}=A A_{S}=1 /\left(1+\lambda\left(1 / \mu+1 / \mu^{\prime}\right)\right)
$$

The item of Fig. 6.30 is a one-item structure with failure rate $\lambda$ and mean repair time $M T T R=1 / \mu+1 / \mu^{\prime}$. More complex structures can also be investigated, see e. g. [6.14].

As a second example consider a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with constant failure rate $\lambda, \lambda_{r}$ and repair rate $\mu$. The switching element can fail with constant failure rate $\lambda_{\sigma}$ for failure mode stuck at the state occupied just before failure or $\lambda_{0}$ for failure mode no connection (or open). Failure of the switch can be immediately detected and repaired with constant repair rate $\mu_{\sigma}$ or $\mu_{0}$. Furthermore, assume only one repair crew, repair priority on the switch, and no further failure at system down (also for the switch, no further failure is possible after a failure with one of the two possible failure modes). Asked is the mean time to system failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ for system new (in state $Z_{0}$ ) at $t=0$. The involved process is a time-homogeneous Markov process. Figure 6.31 gives the diagrams of transition rates for reliability calculation (see Example 6.22 for availability). Comparing Fig. 6.31 with Fig. 6.24a, one recognizes that $M T T F_{S 0}$ is given by Eq. (6.206) with $\rho_{0}=\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma}+\lambda_{0}$ and $\rho_{1}=\lambda+\lambda_{0}+\lambda_{\sigma}+\mu$ (i. e. adding $\lambda_{0}$ to $\rho_{0}$ and $\rho_{1}$ ). From this,

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx \frac{\mu+2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{0}+\lambda_{\sigma} \mu / \mu_{\sigma}}{\lambda_{0}\left[\mu+2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{0}+\left(3 \lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mu / \mu_{\sigma}\right]+\lambda \lambda_{\sigma} \mu / \mu_{\sigma}+\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}
$$

The approximation assumes $\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \lambda_{\sigma}, \lambda_{0} \ll \mu \approx \mu_{\sigma}$. Comparison of Eq. (6.238) with (6.92) shows that the effect of imperfect switching becomes negligible for

$$
\lambda_{0} \ll \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu \text { and } \lambda_{\sigma} \ll\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mu_{\sigma} / \mu, \quad\left(\mu \approx \mu_{\sigma} \gg \lambda, \lambda_{r}, \lambda_{\sigma}, \lambda_{0}\right)
$$

One recognizes that the failure mode no connection (or open) is dominant and acts like a series element (see Eq. (6.160) and footnote on p. 221). $\lambda_{0}=0$ leads to Eq. (6.206). $\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{\sigma}=0$ yields results as for an ideal switching (Table 6.6).


$$
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_{01}=\rho_{0}=\lambda ; \quad \rho_{11^{\prime}}=\rho_{1}=\mu^{\prime} ; \quad \rho_{1^{\prime} 0}=\rho_{1^{\prime}}=\mu \\
& \lambda=\text { failure rate, } \mu=\text { repair rate, } \\
& \mu^{\prime}=\text { failure detection rate (including possible travel time) }
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure 6.30 Diagram of the transition rates for an item with 3 states: good, waiting for repair, repair (const. failure, failure localization \& repair rates $\left(\lambda, \mu^{\prime} \& \mu\right), Z_{1} \& Z_{1^{\prime}}$ down states, Markov proc.)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_{00^{\prime}}=\lambda_{\sigma} ; \quad \rho_{01}=\lambda+\lambda_{r} ; \quad \rho_{0^{\prime} 0}=\mu_{\sigma} ; \\
& \rho_{02}=\lambda_{o} ; \quad \rho_{0^{\prime} 1}=\lambda_{r} ; \quad \rho_{0^{\prime} 2}=\lambda ; \quad \rho_{10}=\mu ; \\
& \rho_{11^{\prime}}=\lambda_{\sigma} ; \quad \rho_{12}=\lambda+\lambda_{o} ; \quad \rho_{1^{\prime} 1}=\mu_{\sigma} ; \quad \rho_{1^{\prime} 2}=\lambda \\
& \rho_{0}=\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma}+\lambda_{o} ; \quad \rho_{0^{\prime}}=\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu_{\sigma} ; \\
& \rho_{1}=\lambda+\lambda_{o}+\lambda_{\sigma}+\mu ; \quad \rho_{1^{\prime}}=\lambda+\mu_{\sigma} ; \quad \rho_{2}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure 6.31 Diagram of the transition rates for reliability calculation of a repairable 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \mu$, switch with failure modes stuck at the state occupied and no connection with constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{\sigma}, \mu_{\sigma}$ and $\lambda_{0}, \mu_{0}$, respectively, ideal failure detection and localization, one repair crew, repair priority on switch ( $Z_{2}$ down state (absorbing for reliability calculation), Markov process)

Example 6.22 investigates $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ for the system described by Fig. 6.31 by assuming a repair rate $\mu_{\mathrm{o}}$ for failure mode no connection and $\mu_{\sigma}$ for failure mode stuck at the state occupied just before failure, one repair crew, and repair priority for switch failures (only a failure mode can occur). Equation (6.240) shows that imperfect switching acts for $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ in a similar way as for $M T T F_{S 0}$ (Eq. (6.239)).

A more complex, practical application, is considered in Section 6.8.6.3 (pp.26669). Further models for systems with more than two states or one failure mode are conceivable.

# Example 6.22 

Investigates the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ for the model considered in Fig. 6.31 by assuming no further failures at system down $\left(\lambda_{i} \ll \mu_{i}\right)$.

## Solution

$P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ (as well as $\left.\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)\right)$ can be obtained using a 9 states Markov process with up states $Z_{0}, Z_{0^{\prime}}, Z_{1}, Z_{1^{\prime}}$ and down states $Z_{1^{\prime \prime}}, Z_{1^{\prime \prime \prime}}, Z_{2}, Z_{2^{\prime}}, Z_{2^{\prime \prime}}$ (absorbing for reliability calculation), see graph, by solving (Table 6.2) $\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma}+\lambda_{o}\right) P_{0}+\mu_{\sigma} P_{0^{\prime}}+\mu P_{1}+\mu_{0} P_{1^{\prime \prime}}, \mu_{0} P_{1^{\prime \prime}}=\lambda_{0} P_{0}$, $\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu_{\sigma}\right) P_{0^{\prime}}=\lambda_{\sigma} P_{0},\left(\lambda+\mu_{\sigma}\right) P_{1}=\lambda_{r} P_{0^{\prime}}+\lambda_{\sigma} P_{1}, \mu_{0} P_{1^{\prime}}$ $=\lambda_{o} P_{1}, \mu P_{2}=\lambda P_{1}+\mu_{\sigma} P_{2^{\prime}}, \mu_{\sigma} P_{2^{\prime}}=\lambda P_{1^{\prime}}, \mu_{\sigma} P_{2^{\prime \prime}}=\lambda P_{0^{\prime}}$, and $P_{0}+P_{0^{\prime}}+P_{1}+P_{1^{\prime}}+P_{1^{\prime \prime}}+P_{2}+P_{2^{\prime}}+P_{2^{\prime \prime}}=1$, yielding


$$
\begin{aligned}
& P \mathrm{~A}_{S}=A \mathrm{~A}_{S}=P_{0}+P_{0^{\prime}}+P_{1}+P_{1^{\prime}}= \\
& \frac{1}{1+\frac{\mathrm{bd} \mu_{o} \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(\mu_{\sigma}+\mathrm{c} \lambda_{\sigma}\right)+\mathrm{b} \mu_{o} \mu \lambda \lambda_{\sigma}\left(\mathrm{c} \lambda_{r}+\mu\right)+\lambda_{o} \mu \mu_{\sigma}\left[\mathrm{bd}\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\mathrm{b} \mu\left(\mathrm{~b}+\lambda_{r}\right)\right]}{\mu \mu_{o} \mu_{\sigma}\left(\lambda+\lambda_{\sigma}+\mu_{\sigma}\right)\left[\mu \mu_{\sigma}+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(\mu+\mu_{\sigma}\right)+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma}\right)\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\right]} \\
& \approx 1-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{a}+\lambda_{\sigma} \lambda\left[\mu+\lambda_{r}\left(1+\mu / \mu_{\sigma}\right)+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(1+\mu_{\sigma} / \mu\right)\right] \mu / \mu_{\sigma}^{2}+\lambda_{o}\left[\mu^{2} / \mu_{o}+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{a} \mu / \mu_{o}+\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\right.}{\mu\left(\mu+\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \mathrm{a}} \\
& \approx 1-\lambda_{o} / \mu_{o}-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) \lambda / \mu^{2}-\lambda \lambda_{\sigma} / \mu_{\sigma}^{2}-\left(\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu+\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) / \mu_{\sigma}\right) \lambda_{o} / \mu_{o}, \\
& \quad \mathrm{a}=1+\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma}\right) / \mu_{\sigma}, \quad \mathrm{b}=\lambda+\mu_{\sigma}, \quad \mathrm{c}=\left(\mu+\mu_{\sigma}\right) / \mathrm{b}, \quad \mathrm{~d}=\mathrm{b}+\lambda_{r}+\lambda_{\sigma} .
\end{aligned}
$$

For $\mu_{o}=\mu_{\sigma}=\mu$, Eq.(6.240) allows similar conclusions as for Eq.(6.239). $\lambda_{0}=0$ leads to Eq. (6.209); $\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{\sigma}=0$ yields results as for an ideal switch.# 6.8.6 Fault Tolerant Reconfigurable Systems 

Fault tolerant (resilient) structures are able to detect and localize faults (failures \& defects) and reconfigure themselves to continue operation with minimum loss of performance and / or safety (graceful degradation); see e. g. [2.36, 4.4, 4.26, 5.77]. Such a characteristic must be built in during design \& development. Typical examples of fault tolerant systems are safety circuits and power \& telecommunication networks. Following a short discussion on ideal reconfiguration, this section deals with reconfiguration occurring at given fixed times (phased-mission systems) or at failure by considering also imperfect switching in Section 6.8.6.3. Investigation is based on tools introduced in Appendix A7, summarized in Table 6.2;
constant failure and repair rates are assumed, yielding to Markov processes.
Procedures are illustrated on a case-by-case basis using diagrams of transition rates.

### 6.8.6.1 Ideal Case

Each redundant structure belongs to a fault tolerant reconfigurable structure and must be validated for this purpose during design \& development, for instance with an FMEA (Section 2.6). For the redundant structures investigated in Sections 2.2, 2.3.1-2.3.5, 6.4-6.7 and Appendix A7, independent elements (p.52), ideal fault coverage, ideal switching, and no reduction of system performance at failure of a redundant element was assumed. Because of these assumptions, investigations often lead to series - parallel structures (Sections $6.6 \& 6.7$ ). Imperfect switching, incomplete coverage, and items (systems) with more than two states or failure modes are considered in Sections 2.3.6, 6.8.3-6.8.5, 6.8.6.3. Sections 6.8.6.2 and 6.8.6.3 investigate time and failure censored reconfiguration, and Section 6.8.6.4 considers reward \& frequency/duration aspects. In addition, Sections 6.8.7-6.8.9 deal with common cause failures, basic considerations on reliability networks, and a general procedure for complex repairable systems. Alternative investigation methods for complex systems and aspects of human reliability \& risk management are introduced in Sections $6.9,6.10$ and 6.11 , respectively.

### 6.8.6.2 Time Censored Reconfiguration (Phased-Mission Systems)

In some practical applications, systems are used for different required functions. If each required function can be considered separately from one another, investigation is performed by considering a reliability block diagram (if it exist) for each required function (p. 29). Otherwise, if mission phases follow each other, investigation must consider the system reconfiguration at the end of each phase and one define this as a phased-mission system. Investigation of phased-mission systems can be more time-consuming as stated e. g. in [2.7,2.18,6.24,6.33,6.41], dealing with binary state assignment (basically limited to totally independent elements (p. 52)),considering time dependent failure or repair rates (breaking the Markov property), using semi-Markov processes (of limited validity), or missing Assumption 4 below (important when transferring state probabilities at the end of phase $k$ to initial probabilities for phase $k+1$ ). A lower bound $R_{S 0_{I}}$ on the reliability $R_{S 0}$ for the whole mission is obtained by connecting the reliability block diagrams for each phase in series for the whole mission duration. An upper bound on $R_{S 0}$ is given by the smaller of the reliability for each phase, taken separately, by assuming that all elements involved are as-good-as-new at begin of the phase considered; thus,

$$
R_{S 0_{I}} \leq R_{S 0} \leq R_{S 0_{u}}=\min \left(R_{S 0, k}\right)^{*)} \quad k=1, \ldots, n \text { (for } n \text { phases) }
$$

Examples 6.23-6.25 illustrate basic aspects. For the availability, Eq.(6.246) applies.
Following some general assumptions in Point (i), a practice oriented procedure for reliability and availability analysis of repairable phased-mission systems, which considers standby redundancy and arbitrary repair strategy, is given in Point (ii).
(i) General assumptions:

1. Failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{i} \& \mu_{i}\right)$ of all elements are constant during the sojourn time in any state within each phase, but can change (stepwise) at a state (or phase) change because of change in configuration, component use, stress, repair strategy or other; for all elements it holds that $\lambda_{i} \ll \mu_{i}$.
2. At the beginning of the phased-mission all elements are as-good-as-new.
3. Phase duration $T_{1}, \ldots, T_{n}$ are given (fixed) values, each of them so large that asymptotic \& steady-state values for availability can be assumed for each phase $\left(T_{1}, \ldots, T_{n} \gg \max \left(10 / \mu_{i}\right)\right.$ for all elements (Section 6.2.5 \& Eq. (6.88)).
4. For availability investigation, not used elements in a phase are either as-good-as-new and put in standby (failure rate $\lambda \equiv 0$ ) at begin of the phase, or repaired (Assumption 3) and then put in standby (repair priority on elements used); for reliability investigation, down states at system level are absorbing states and the above rule holds for elements which have not caused system down.
5. The system has only one repair crew and no further failures can occur at system down; system down is an absorbing state for reliability; for availability, the system is restored to an operating state according to a given repair strategy.
6. Fault coverage, switch \& logistic support are ideal, no preventive maintenance.
7. For each phase, a reliability block diagram exists.

Reduction of above assumptions is possible, for instance, on the basis of the models discussed in Sections 6.8.2-6.8.5.
