(6.29)); $R_{S 0} \&$ $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ are thus numbers within [0,1], not time functions, this applies also to Example 6.25.

Figure 6.32 Reliability block diagrams and diagrams of the transition rates for reliability calculation of a one-item used in a mission with phase 1 followed by phase 2 ; constant failure rate $\lambda_{1} \& \lambda_{2}$, duration $T_{1} \& T_{2}$, respectively $\left(Z_{1,1}, Z_{2,1}\right.$ down states; $E_{1} \& E_{2}$ used to point out $\left.\lambda_{2} \neq \lambda_{1}\right)$

# Example 6.23 

A one-item is used in a mission with phase 1 (duration $T_{1}$, const. failure rate $\lambda_{1}$ ), followed by phase 2 (duration $T_{2}$, const. failure rate $\lambda_{2}$ ). Calculate the reliability function for item new at $t=0$.

## Solution

Considering $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ constant (time independent), it holds that (see Eq. (2.14) or (A6.29))

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{S 0}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { phase } 1 \text { failure free } \cap \text { phase } 2 \text { failure free }\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { phase } 1 \text { failure free }\} \cdot \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { phase } 2 \\
\text { failure free }\} \text { phase } 1 \text { failure free }\}=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} \cdot e^{-\lambda_{2} T_{2}}=e^{-\left(\lambda_{1} T_{1}+\lambda_{2} T_{2}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Example 6.24

Show that Eq. (6.242) can be obtained using a Markov approach (with two separate transition rate diagrams and setting final state probabilities from phase 1 as initial-state probabilities for phase 2).

## Solution

Figure 6.32 gives the diagrams of transition rates for phase 1 and 2 (separately). For phase 1, the state probability $\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}(t)$ follows from $\stackrel{\circ}{\mathrm{P}}_{1,0}^{-}(t)=-\lambda_{1} \mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}(t)$ (Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.115), yielding $\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{1} t}$, for $\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}(0)=1$. Thus,

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(T_{1}\right)=\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}\left(T_{1}\right)=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{-}\left(T_{1}\right)=1-e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}}
$$

$\mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{-}(t)$ follows from $\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}(t)+\mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{-}(t)=1$. Similarly, for phase 2 with $t$ starting at $t=T_{1}$,

$$
\stackrel{\circ}{\mathrm{P}}_{2,0}^{-}\left(t-T_{1}\right)=-\lambda_{2} \mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{-}\left(t-T_{1}\right), \quad \text { with } \quad \mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{-}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}\left(T_{1}\right)=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}}
$$

yielding $\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{-}\left(t-T_{1}\right)=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} e^{-\lambda_{2}\left(t-T_{1}\right)}, \quad T_{1}<t \leq T_{1}+T_{2}$, and thus

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(T_{1}+\mathrm{T}_{2}\right)=\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{-}\left(T_{1}+T_{2}\right)=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} e^{-\lambda_{2} T_{2}}=e^{-\left(\lambda_{1} T_{1}+\lambda_{2} T_{2}\right)}=R_{S 0}
$$

## Example 6.25

A one-item system with reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ is used for a mission of random duration $\tau_{W}>0$ distributed according to $\mathrm{F}_{W}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{W} \leq t\right\}$ with $\mathrm{F}_{W}(0)=0 \&$ density $\mathrm{f}_{W}(t)$. Give $R_{S 0}$ for the general case and by assuming constant failure rate $\lambda$ and $\mathrm{f}_{W}(t)=\delta e^{-\delta t}$.

## Solution

As mission duration can take any time between $(0, \infty)$, reliability takes a constant value given by

$$
R_{S 0}=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{w}(t) \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t
$$

(see also Eq. (2.76)). For $\mathrm{f}_{W}(t)=\delta e^{-\delta t}$ and constant failure rate $\lambda$, Eq. (6.244) yields

$$
R_{S 0}=\delta /(\delta+\lambda), \quad \text { and thus } \quad R_{S 0} \approx 1 \text { for } \delta \gg>\lambda \& R_{S 0} \approx \delta / \lambda \text { for } \delta \ll<\lambda
$$

Supplement. results: If the mission is limited to $T_{W}, \tau_{W}>0$ is a truncated random variable (Eq. (A6.33a)), $R_{S 0}={ }^{T_{W}=0} \int_{0} \mathrm{f}_{w}(t) \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) d t+\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{W}=T_{W} \cap \tau>T_{W}\right\}$ and Eq. (6.245) becomes $R_{S 0}=\left(\delta+\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\delta+\lambda\right) T_{w}}\right) /(\delta+\lambda)$.(ii) Procedure for reliability \& availability calculation of repairable phased-mission systems with fixed phase duration $T_{1}, \ldots, T_{n}$, satisfying the general assumptions (i):

1. Group series elements used in all phases (power supply, cooling, etc.) in one element to be considered in final results (Table 6.10, Eqs. (6.257), (6.258)).
2. Draw the diagram of transition rates for reliability evaluation, separately for each phase $(1, \ldots, n)$, beginning by phase 1 with $Z_{1,0}$ ( 1 referring to phase 1 and 0 being the state in which all elements are as-good-as-new); down states at system level are absorbing states; use the same state numbering for the same state appearing in successive phases; however, state $Z_{k, i}$ corresponding to a state $Z_{c, i}$ in a phase $c$ preceding phase $k$ can also contain as-good-as-new elements appearing in phase $k$ but not in a pervious phase, or standby elements (not used in phase $k$ ) with failure rate $\lambda \equiv 0$; for $k>1$, state $Z_{k, 0}$ contains all as-good-as-new elements used in phase $k$ and (as necessary) elements not used in phase $k$ which are standby with failure rate $\lambda \equiv 0$ (as-good-as-new is same as operating or ready to operate, because of $\lambda_{i}$ const.).
3. For availability investigation, use results of Tables $6.10,6.6$ or 6.8 to calculate the asymptotic $\&$ steady-state availability for each phase separately, taking care of elements which are not used in the phase considered and can act as redundancy (active or standby) for working elements, to obtain a good approximation (considering $\lambda_{i} \ll \mu_{i}$ and assumption 3 on p. 260) of $P A_{S, k}=A A_{S, k}$ for phase $k$; for the whole mission it holds then

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S} \geq \min \left(P A_{S, k}=A A_{S, k}\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, n(\text { for } n \text { phases })
$$

4. For reliability investigation, calculate the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{1,0}\left(T_{1}\right)$ at the end of phase 1 starting in state $Z_{1,0}$ at $t=0$ in the same way as for a one mission system (Table 6.2), as well as states probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{1, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)$ for all up states $Z_{1, j}$; if $Z_{1, j}$ (possibly with further as-good-as-new elements used inphase 2) is an up state in phase $2, \mathrm{P}_{1, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)$ becomes the probability $\mathrm{P}_{2, j}^{\prime}(0)$ to start phase 2 in $Z_{2, j}$; if $Z_{1, j}$ is a (system) down state in phase $2, \mathrm{P}_{1, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)$ adds to the initial probability of starting phase 2 in the (system) down state; if $Z_{1, j}$ does not appear in phase $2, \mathrm{P}_{1, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)$ adds to the initial probability in state $Z_{2,0}$ to give $\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}(0)$ (from rule 2 above and verifying that for each phase the sum of all states probabilities is 1 ); reliability calculation must take care of elements which are not used in the phase considered and can act as standby redundancy $(\lambda \equiv 0)$ for working elements; continuing in this way, the reliability $R_{S 0}$ for the whole mission starting phase 1 in $Z_{1,0}$, follows as

$$
R_{S 0}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U_{n}} \mathrm{P}_{n, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{n}\right), \quad U_{n}=\text { set of up states in phase } n
$$

5. If a state $Z_{k, i}$ does not appear in the phase $k+1$, the general rule 4 applies.
6. To avoid ambiguities, $x$ starting by $x=0$ at the begin of each phase has to be used.

Figure 6.33 Reliability block diagrams and diagrams of the transition rates for reliability calculation of a phased-mission system with 3 phases (the diagram for phase 2 takes care that one element $E_{2}$ is put in standby with $\lambda_{2} \equiv 0$ as soon as available); dashed are indicated to which states the final state probabilities of phase 1 and phase 2 are transferred as initial probabilities for phase 2 and phase 3, respectively (constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{i}, \mu_{i}\right)$, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew, repair as per first-in first-out, $Z_{1,1}, Z_{2,1}, Z_{3,1}$ down states, Markov process)

As an example, let's consider the phased-mission system with 3 phases of given (fixed) duration $T_{1}, T_{2}$ and $T_{3}$, described by the 3 reliability block diagrams and the corresponding diagrams of transition rates for reliability investigation given in Fig. 6.33. The diagram of transition rates for phase 2 considers that in phase 2 only one element $E_{2}$ is used and assumes that the second element $E_{2}$ is put in standby redundancy with failure rate $\lambda_{2} \equiv 0$ (either from state $Z_{1,0}$ or as soon as repaired if from state $Z_{1,2}$, step 4 on p. 262). Dashed is given to which states the final state probabilities at time $T_{1}$ for phase 1 and $T_{2}\left(T_{1}+T_{2}\right.$ with respect to time $\left.t\right)$ for phase 2 are transferred as initial probabilities for the successive phase. Let's first consider the asymptotic \& steady-state availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ for the whole mission. From Tables 6.10 and 6.6, it follows for the 3 phases (taken separately) that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P A_{S, 1}=A A_{S, 1} \approx 1-\left(\lambda_{1} / \mu_{1}\right)-2\left(\lambda_{2} / \mu_{2}\right)^{2} \approx 1-\left(\lambda_{1} / \mu_{1}\right) \\
& P A_{S, 2}=A A_{S, 2} \approx 1-\left(\lambda_{2} / \mu_{2}\right)^{2}-2\left(\lambda_{3} / \mu_{3}\right)^{2} \\
& P A_{S, 3}=A A_{S, 3} \approx 1-\left(\lambda_{1} / \mu_{1}\right)-2\left(\lambda_{2} / \mu_{2}\right)^{2}-2\left(\lambda_{3} / \mu_{3}\right)^{2} \approx 1-\left(\lambda_{1} / \mu_{1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The 2 nd equation assumes that in phase 2 one of the elements $E_{2}$ acts as standby redundancy (approximation based on assumptions $3 \& 4$ on p. 260) and uses results from Table 6.6 (standby redundancy for $E_{2}$, active redundancy for $E_{3}$ ) \& Table 6.10 (4th row); similar is for the 3 th equation. Equation (6.246) yields then

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S} \geq 1-\left(\lambda_{1} / \mu_{1}\right)-2\left(\lambda_{2} / \mu_{2}\right)^{2}-2\left(\lambda_{3} / \mu_{3}\right)^{2}
$$For the reliability $R_{S 0}$, for the whole mission starting in state $Z_{1,0}$ (elements news) at $t=0$, the diagrams of transition rates of Fig. 6.33 yield for phases 1, 2, 3 the following coupled system of differential equations for the state probabilities (Table 6.2; $\mathrm{P}_{i, j}^{\prime}$ is used instead of $\mathrm{P}_{i, j}^{\prime}(x), x$ starts by $x=0$ at the beginning of each phase)

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{1,0}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{1}+2 \lambda_{2}\right) \mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{\prime}+\mu_{2} \mathrm{P}_{1,2}^{\prime}, & \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{1,2}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu_{2}\right) \mathrm{P}_{1,2}^{\prime}+2 \lambda_{2} \mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{\prime} \\
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{1,1}^{\prime}=\lambda_{1} \mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{\prime}+\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) \mathrm{P}_{1,2}^{\prime}, & \text { with } \mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{\prime}(0)=1, \mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{1,2}^{\prime}(0)=0 \\
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{2,0}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{2}+2 \lambda_{3}\right) \mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}+\mu_{2} \mathrm{P}_{2,2}^{\prime}+\mu_{3} \mathrm{P}_{2,3}^{\prime}, & \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{2,4}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}+\mu_{2}\right) \mathrm{P}_{2,4}^{\prime}+2 \lambda_{3} \mathrm{P}_{2,2}^{\prime} \\
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{2,2}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{2}+2 \lambda_{3}+\mu_{2}\right) \mathrm{P}_{2,2}^{\prime}+\lambda_{2} \mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}+\mu_{3} \mathrm{P}_{2,5}^{\prime}, & \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{2,5}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}+\mu_{3}\right) \mathrm{P}_{2,5}^{\prime}+\lambda_{2} \mathrm{P}_{2,3}^{\prime} \\
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{2,3}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}+\mu_{3}\right) \mathrm{P}_{2,3}^{\prime}+2 \lambda_{3} \mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}+\mu_{2} \mathrm{P}_{2,4}^{\prime}, & \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{2,1}^{\prime}=\lambda_{2} \mathrm{P}_{2,2}^{\prime}+\lambda_{3} \mathrm{P}_{2,3}^{\prime}+\left(\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}\right)\left(\mathrm{P}_{2,4}^{\prime}+\mathrm{P}_{2,5}^{\prime}\right) \\
\text { with } \mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right), \quad \mathrm{P}_{2,2}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{1,2}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right), \quad \mathrm{P}_{2,1}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right), \quad \mathrm{P}_{2,3}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,4}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,5}^{\prime}(0)=0
\end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{3,0}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{1}+2 \lambda_{2}+2 \lambda_{3}\right) \mathrm{P}_{3,0}^{\prime}+\mu_{2} \mathrm{P}_{3,2}^{\prime}+\mu_{3} \mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime}, \quad \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{3,3}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{1}+2 \lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}+\mu_{3}\right) \mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime}+2 \lambda_{3} \mathrm{P}_{3,0}^{\prime}+\mu_{2} \mathrm{P}_{3,4}^{\prime} \\
& \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{3,2}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+2 \lambda_{3}+\mu_{2}\right) \mathrm{P}_{3,2}^{\prime}+2 \lambda_{2} \mathrm{P}_{3,0}^{\prime}+\mu_{3} \mathrm{P}_{3,5}^{\prime}, \quad \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{3,5}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}+\mu_{3}\right) \mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime}+2 \lambda_{2} \mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime} \\
& \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{3,4}^{\prime}=-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}+\mu_{2}\right) \mathrm{P}_{3,4}^{\prime}+2 \lambda_{3} \mathrm{P}_{3,2}^{\prime}, \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{3,1}^{\prime}=\lambda_{1} \mathrm{P}_{3,0}^{\prime}+\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) \mathrm{P}_{3,2}^{\prime}+\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{3}\right) \mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime}+\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}\right)\left(\mathrm{P}_{3,4}^{\prime}+\mathrm{P}_{3,5}^{\prime}\right) \\
& \text { with } \mathrm{P}_{3,0}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right), \mathrm{P}_{3,2}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,2}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right), \mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,3}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right), \mathrm{P}_{3,4}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,4}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right) \\
& \mathrm{P}_{3,5}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,5}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right), \quad \mathrm{P}_{3,1}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,1}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

From Eq. (6.247) it follows then

$$
R_{S 0}=\mathrm{P}_{3,0}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right)+\mathrm{P}_{3,2}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right)+\mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right)+\mathrm{P}_{3,4}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right)+\mathrm{P}_{3,5}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right)
$$

Analytical solution of the system given by Eq. (6.250) is possible, but time-consuming. A numerical solution is in Example 6.26. A lower bound $R_{S 0_{l}}$ on the reliability $R_{S 0}$ for the whole mission is obtained by connecting the reliability block diagrams for each phase in series (Eq. (6.241)). For Fig. 6.33, this corresponds, nearly, to consider phase 3 for a time $T_{1}+T_{2}+T_{3}$ (per assumption 4 on p.260, for element $E_{2}$ a second element $E_{2}$ in standby redundancy is available in phase 2). Using $R_{S 0_{l}} \approx$ $e^{-\left(T_{1}+T_{2}+T_{3}\right) / M T T F_{S 0}}$ with $M T T F_{S 0}$ as per Table 6.10 ( $2 \mathrm{nd} \& 3 \mathrm{rd}$ row), it follows that

$$
R_{S 0}>R_{S 0_{l}} \approx e^{-\left(T_{1}+T_{2}+T_{3}\right)\left(\lambda_{1}+2 \lambda_{2}^{2} / \mu_{2}+2 \lambda_{3}^{2} / \mu_{3}\right)}
$$

An upper bound on $R_{S 0}$ follows from Eq. (6.241), see Example 6.26.
If the second element $E_{2}$ were not available in phase 2 as standby redundancy, $P A_{S, 2}=A A_{S, 2} \approx 1-\lambda_{2} / \mu_{2}$ and, from Eq. (6.249), $P A_{S}=A A_{S} \approx 1-\lambda_{2} / \mu_{2}$, since $\lambda_{1} / \mu_{1}<\lambda_{2} / \mu_{2}$ can be assumed when considering the reliability block diagram for phase 1. In this case, and assuming that the second element $E_{2}$ would be repaired before the end of phase 2 (if in a failed state at the end of phase 1), the diagram of transition rates for phase 2 would be equal to that for phase 1 , with $\lambda_{1} \rightarrow \lambda_{2}, \lambda_{2} \rightarrow \lambda_{3}, \mu_{2} \rightarrow \mu_{3}, Z_{1,0} \rightarrow Z_{2,0}, Z_{1,1} \rightarrow Z_{2,1}, Z_{1,2} \rightarrow Z_{2,3}$, and

$$
\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)+\mathrm{P}_{1,2}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right), \quad \mathrm{P}_{2,1}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right), \quad \mathrm{P}_{2,3}^{\prime}(0)=0
$$# Example 6.26 

Give the numerical solution of Eqs. (6.250) and (6.251) for $\lambda_{1}=10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \lambda_{2}=10^{-2} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, $\lambda_{3}=10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu_{3}=0.5 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, T_{1}=168 \mathrm{~h}, T_{2}=336 \mathrm{~h}$, and $T_{3}=672 \mathrm{~h}$.

## Solution

Numerical solution of the 3 coupled systems of differential equations given by Eq. (6.250) yields

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{P}_{3,0}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right) \approx 0.598655, & \mathrm{P}_{3,2}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right) \approx 0.023493, \quad \mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right) \approx 0.002388 \\
\mathrm{P}_{3,4}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right) \approx 0.000092, & \mathrm{P}_{3,5}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right) \approx 0.000094, \quad \mathrm{P}_{3,1}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right) \approx 0.375278
\end{array}
$$

(with 6 digits because of $\mathrm{P}_{3,4}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right)$ and $\mathrm{P}_{3,5}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right)$ ). $R_{S 0}$ follows then from Eq. (6.251)

$$
R_{S 0}=1-\mathrm{P}_{3,1}^{\prime}\left(T_{3}\right) \approx 0.625
$$

Supplementary results: Computing lower and upper bound on $R_{S 0}$ as per Eqs. (6.252) and (6.241), yields for the above example $0.55 \leq R_{S 0} \leq 0.71$ (considering assumption 4 on p. 260 for $R_{S 0_{1}}$ ).

The corresponding initial probabilities for phase 3 would be

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{3,0}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right), \quad \mathrm{P}_{3,1}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,1}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right), \quad \mathrm{P}_{3,3}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2,3}^{\prime}\left(T_{2}\right), \\
& \mathrm{P}_{3,2}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{3,4}^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{3,5}^{\prime}(0)=0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

If an element $E_{\text {ser }}$ where common to all 3 phases in Fig. 6.33 (i. e. in series with all 3 reliability block diagrams), Table 6.10 ( 2 nd row) can be used to find

$$
P A_{S_{\text {tot }}}=A A_{S_{\text {tot }}}=1-\lambda_{\text {ser }} / \mu_{\text {ser }}-\left(\lambda_{1} / \mu_{1}\right)-2\left(\lambda_{2} / \mu_{2}\right)^{2}-2\left(\lambda_{3} / \mu_{3}\right)^{2}
$$

(considering Eq. (6.249)) and, with $R_{S 0}$ from Eq. 6.251,

$$
R_{S 0_{\text {tot }}} \approx R_{S 0} \cdot e^{-\lambda_{\text {ser }}\left(T_{1}+T_{2}+T_{3}\right)}
$$

The above procedure can be extended to consider more than one repair crew at system level or any kind of repair (restore) strategy. Other procedures (models) are conceivable. For instance, for nonrepairable systems (up to system failure) of complex structure, and with independent elements (parallel redundancy), it can be useful to number the states using binary considerations.

For randomly distributed phase duration, Eq. (6.246) can be used for availability. Reliability can be obtained by expanding results in Examples 6.23-6.25.

An alternative approach for phased-mission systems is to assume that at the beginning of each mission phase, the system is as-good-as-new with respect to the elements used in the mission phase considered (required elements are repaired in a negligible time at the begin of the mission phase, if they are in a failed state, and not required elements can be repaired during a phase in which they are not used). This assumption can be reasonable for some repairable systems and highly simplifies investigation. For this case, results developed in Section 6.8.2 for preventive maintenance lead to (for phases $1,2, \ldots, n$ )$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{S 0}(t)= & R_{S 0_{1}}(t), \\
= & R_{S 0_{1}}\left(T_{1}^{*}\right) R_{S 0_{2}}\left(t-T_{1}^{*}\right), \\
= & R_{S 0_{1}}\left(T_{1}^{*}\right) R_{S 0_{2}}\left(T_{2}^{*}-T_{1}^{*}\right) R_{S 0_{3}}\left(t-T_{2}^{*}\right), \\
& \vdots
\end{aligned}
$$

for the reliability function, and (see footnote ${ }^{+}$on p. 242)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P A_{S 0}(t)=P A_{S 0_{1}}(t), \\
& =P A_{S 0_{2}}\left(t-T_{1}^{*}\right), \\
& =P A_{S 0_{3}}\left(t-T_{2}^{*}\right), \\
& \text { for } 0<t<T_{1}^{*}, \quad P A_{S 0_{k}}(0)=1, k=1,2, \ldots, n, \\
& T_{1}^{*}<t \leq T_{2}^{*}, \\
& \text { for } T_{2}^{*} \leq t<T_{3}^{*},
\end{aligned}
$$

for the point availability. $S 0_{k}$ is the state from which the $k$ th mission phase starts; $T_{i}^{*}=T_{0}+\ldots+T_{i}(i=0,1, \ldots, n-1, T_{0}=0)$ are the time points on the time axis at which mission phases $i+1$ begin.

# 6.8.6.3 Failure Censored Reconfiguration 

In most applications, reconfiguration occurs at the failure of a redundant element. Besides cases with ideal fault coverage, ideal switching, and no system performance reduction at failure (Sections 2.2, 2.3, and 6.4-6.7), more complex structures often arise in practical applications (see Sections 6.8.3-6.8.5 for some examples). Such structures must be investigated on a case-by-case basis, and an FMEA/FMECA (Section 2.6) is mandatory to validate investigations. Often it is necessary to consider that after a reconfiguration, the system performance is reduced, i. e. reward and frequency/duration aspects have to be involved in the analysis.

A reasonably simple and comprehensive example is a power system substation. Figure 6.34 gives the functional block diagram and the diagram of transition rates $\left(\mu_{g} \equiv 0\right.$ for reliability investigation, the down state $Z_{12}$ appears twice for convenience only). ${ }^{+)}$The substation is powered by a reliable network and consists of:

- Two branch designated by $A_{1} \& A_{2}$ and capable of performing $100 \%$ load, each with HV switch, HV circuit breaker and control elements, transformer, measurement \& control elements, and LV switch.
- Two busbars designated by $C_{1} \& C_{2}$ and capable of performing $100 \%$ load (failure rate basically given by double contingency of faults on control elements).
- A coupler between the busbars, designated by B, capable of performing $100 \%$ load; failure modes does not open \& does not close, failure rates $\lambda_{B \sigma} \& \lambda_{B o},{ }^{++}$ )
Load is distributed between $C_{1} \& C_{2}$ at $50 \%$ rate each. The diagram of transition rates is based on an extensive FMEA/FMECA [6.20(2002)] showing in particular the key position of the coupler $B$ in the reconfiguration strategy. Coupler $B$ is normally open. A failure of $B$ is recognized only at a failure of A or $C$. From state $Z_{0}$,

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$A refinement to consider also common cause failures has been investigated in [6.20 (2010)].
    ${ }^{++}$Does not open and does not close apply here because $B$ is a coupler normally open (not a switch).

Figure 6.34 Functional block diagram and diagram of the transition rates for a repairable power system substation with active redundancy, constant failure and repair rates $\left(\lambda_{A 1}, \lambda_{A 2}, \lambda_{B \sigma}, \lambda_{B o}\right.$, $\left.\lambda_{C 1}, \lambda_{C 2}, \mu_{A}, \mu_{C}, \mu_{g}\right)$, imperfect switching of $B$ (failure modes does not open $\left(\lambda_{B \sigma}\right.$, from $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ ) or does not close ( $\lambda_{B o}$, from $Z_{0}$ )), failure of $B$ recognized only at failure of $A$ or $C$, ideal failure detection \& localization for $A$ and $C$, one repair crew, repair priority on $C$, no further failure at system down $\left(Z_{12}\right.$ down state for a load loss of $100 \%$, absorbing for reliability calculation (only one state $Z_{12}$ exists in the system); $Z_{6}-Z_{12}$ down states for a load loss of $50 \%$ (see Example 6.27); Markov process)
$B$ can fail only with failure mode does not close, from $Z_{1}$ or $Z_{2}$ only with does not open. Constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{A 1}, \lambda_{A 2}, \lambda_{B \sigma}, \lambda_{B o}, \lambda_{C 1}, \lambda_{C 2} \& \mu_{A}, \mu_{C}, \mu_{g}$ are assumed. $\mu_{A} \& \mu_{C}$ are the same also if a repair of $B$ is necessary; $\mu_{g}$ is smaller than $\mu_{A} \& \mu_{C}$. From the down state $\left(Z_{12}\right)$ the system returns to state $Z_{0}$. Furthermore, only one repair crew, repair priority on $C$ (followed by $C+B, A, A+B$ ), and no further failure at system down are assumed. Asked are mean time to system failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ for system new (in state $Z_{0}$ ) at $t=0$ and asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$. The involved process is a timehomogeneous Markov process. For a load loss of $100 \%$ (Fig. 6.34), states with $50 \%$ load are up states with reduced performance (if results are required only for a $100 \%$ load, $Z_{6}-Z_{12}$ are down states), see pp.270-71 for reward considerations. To simplify investigation, $\lambda_{A 1}=\lambda_{A 2}=\lambda_{A} \& \lambda_{C 1}=\lambda_{C 2}=\lambda_{C}$ are assumed. To increase readability, series elements have been grouped in the functional block diagram.From Fig. 6.34 and Table 6.2 it follows that $M T T F_{S 0}$ is given as solution of the following system of algebraic equations $\left(M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}\right)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_{0} M_{0}=1+\lambda_{B 0} M_{5}+\lambda_{A}\left(M_{1}+M_{2}\right)+\lambda_{C}\left(M_{6}+M_{7}\right), \quad \rho_{5} M_{5}=1+\lambda_{A}\left(M_{10}+M_{11}\right)+\lambda_{C}\left(M_{6}+M_{7}\right), \\
& \rho_{1} M_{1}=1+\mu_{A} M_{0}+\lambda_{C} M_{8}+\lambda_{B \sigma} M_{3}, \quad \rho_{2} M_{2}=1+\mu_{A} M_{0}+\lambda_{C} M_{9}+\lambda_{B \sigma} M_{4}, \quad \rho_{3} M_{3}=1+\mu_{A} M_{0}, \\
& \rho_{4} M_{4}=1+\mu_{A} M_{0}, \quad \rho_{6} M_{6}=1+\lambda_{A} M_{8}+\mu_{C} M_{0}, \quad \rho_{7} M_{7}=1+\lambda_{A} M_{9}+\mu_{C} M_{0}, \quad \rho_{8} M_{8}=1+\mu_{C} M_{1}, \\
& \rho_{9} M_{9}=1+\mu_{C} M_{2}, \quad \rho_{10} M_{10}=1+\mu_{A} M_{0}+\lambda_{C} M_{8}, \quad \rho_{11} M_{11}=1+\mu_{A} M_{0}+\lambda_{C} M_{9} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Because of $\lambda_{A 1}=\lambda_{A 2}=\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}, \lambda_{C 1}=\lambda_{C 2}=\lambda_{C}$ and the symmetry in Fig. 6.34 it follows that $\rho_{2}=\rho_{1}, \rho_{4}=\rho_{3}, \rho_{7}=\rho_{6}, \rho_{9}=\rho_{8}, \rho_{11}=\rho_{10} \& M_{2}=M_{1}, M_{4}=M_{3}, M_{7}=M_{6}, M_{9}=M_{8}, M_{11}=M_{10}$. This has been considered in solving the system of algebraic equations (6.261). From Eq. (6.261) it follows that (for a load loss of 100\%)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T F_{S 0}= \\
& \frac{a_{1} a_{2}+2 a_{1} a_{3} \lambda_{A}+2 a_{2} \lambda_{C} \rho_{5} \rho_{10}\left(\rho_{8}+\lambda_{A}\right)+2 a_{3} \lambda_{A} \lambda_{C} \mu_{C} \rho_{5} \rho_{10}+\lambda_{B 0}\left(a_{2} a_{4}+a_{3} a_{6}\right)}{a_{1} a_{2} \rho_{0}-2 \lambda_{A} \mu_{A} \rho_{8}\left(\rho_{3}+\lambda_{B \sigma}\right)\left(a_{1}+\lambda_{C} \mu_{C} \rho_{5} \rho_{10}\right)-2 a_{2} \lambda_{C} \mu_{C} \rho_{5} \rho_{8} \rho_{10}-\lambda_{B 0}\left(a_{2} a_{5}+a_{6} \mu_{A} \rho_{8}\left(\rho_{3}+\lambda_{B \sigma}\right)\right)},
\end{aligned}
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{1}=\rho_{5} \rho_{6} \rho_{8} \rho_{10}, \quad a_{2}=\rho_{8} \rho_{5} \rho_{8}-\rho_{3} \lambda_{C} \mu_{C}, \quad a_{4}=\rho_{6} \rho_{8} \rho_{10}+2 \lambda_{A} \rho_{6}\left(\rho_{8}+\lambda_{C}\right)+2 \lambda_{C} \rho_{10}\left(\rho_{8}+\lambda_{A}\right), \\
& a_{3}=\rho_{8}\left(\rho_{3}+\lambda_{B \sigma}\right)+\rho_{3} \lambda_{C}, a_{5}=2 \lambda_{A} \mu_{A} \rho_{6} \rho_{8}+2 \lambda_{C} \mu_{C} \rho_{8} \rho_{10}, \quad a_{6}=2 \lambda_{A} \lambda_{C} \mu_{C}\left(\rho_{6}+\rho_{10}\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_{0}=2 \lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}+\lambda_{B 0}, \quad \rho_{1}=\rho_{2}=\lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}+\lambda_{B \sigma}+\mu_{A}, \quad \rho_{3}=\rho_{4}=\lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}+\mu_{A}, \quad \rho_{5}=2\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right), \\
& \rho_{6}=\rho_{7}=2 \lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}+\mu_{C}, \quad \rho_{8}=\rho_{9}=\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}+\mu_{C}, \quad \rho_{10}=\rho_{11}=\lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}+\mu_{A}, \quad \rho_{12}=\mu_{g} .
\end{aligned}
$$

$M T T F_{S 0}$ per Eq. (6.262) can be approximated by

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx \frac{\mu_{A}+5\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)+\left(4 \lambda_{A}+5 \lambda_{C}\right) \mu_{A} / \mu_{C}+\lambda_{B \sigma}+\lambda_{B 0}\left(\mu_{A}+\lambda_{B \sigma}\right) / 2\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)}{\left(2 \lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}+\lambda_{B 0}\right)\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C} \mu_{A} / \mu_{C}\right)}
$$

yielding $M T T F_{S 0} \approx \mu / 2\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)^{2}$ for $\lambda_{B \sigma}, \lambda_{B 0}<<\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)$ and $\mu=\mu_{C}=\mu$ (1-out-of-2 active redundancy with $A$ and $C$ in series, as per Table $6.10,2 \mathrm{nd} \& 3 \mathrm{rd}$ row).

From Fig. 6.34 and Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.127) it follows that the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is given as solution of

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_{0} P_{0}=\mu_{A}\left(P_{1}+P_{2}+P_{3}+P_{4}+P_{10}+P_{11}\right)+\mu_{C}\left(P_{6}+P_{7}\right)+\mu_{g} P_{12}, \quad \rho_{1} P_{1}=\lambda_{A} P_{0}+\mu_{C} P_{8}, \\
& \rho_{2} P_{2}=\lambda_{A} P_{0}+\mu_{C} P_{9}, \quad \rho_{3} P_{3}=\lambda_{B \sigma} P_{1}, \quad \rho_{4} P_{4}=\lambda_{B \sigma} P_{2}, \quad \rho_{5} P_{5}=\lambda_{B 0} P_{0}, \\
& \rho_{6} P_{6}=\lambda_{C}\left(P_{0}+P_{5}\right), \quad \rho_{7} P_{7}=\lambda_{C}\left(P_{0}+P_{5}\right), \quad \rho_{8} P_{8}=\lambda_{A} P_{6}+\lambda_{C}\left(P_{1}+P_{10}\right), \\
& \rho_{9} P_{9}=\lambda_{A} P_{7}+\lambda_{C}\left(P_{2}+P_{11}\right), \quad \rho_{10} P_{10}=\lambda_{A} P_{5}, \quad \rho_{11} P_{11}=\lambda_{A} P_{5}, \\
& \rho_{12} P_{12}=\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)\left(P_{1}+P_{2}+P_{6}+P_{7}+P_{8}+P_{9}+P_{10}+P_{11}\right)+\left(\lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}\right)\left(P_{3}+P_{4}\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

One of the Eq. (6.266) must be dropped and replaced by $\sum P_{i}=1$. The solution yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{1}=P_{2}=b_{1} P_{0}, \quad P_{3}=P_{4}=b_{1} P_{0} \lambda_{B \sigma} / \rho_{3}, \quad P_{5}=P_{0} \lambda_{B o} / \rho_{5}, \quad P_{8}=P_{9}=b_{2} P_{0}, \\
& P_{6}=P_{7}=P_{0} \lambda_{C}\left(\rho_{5}+\lambda_{B o}\right) / \rho_{5} \rho_{6}, \quad P_{10}=P_{11}=P_{0} \lambda_{A} \lambda_{B o} / \rho_{5} \rho_{10}, \quad P_{12}=b_{3} P_{0},
\end{aligned}
$$with

$$
P_{0}=\frac{1}{1+2 b_{2}+2 b_{1}\left(1+\lambda_{B \sigma} / \rho_{3}\right)+\lambda_{B o} / \rho_{5}+2 \lambda_{C}\left(\rho_{5}+\lambda_{B o}\right) / \rho_{5} \rho_{6}+2 \lambda_{A} \lambda_{B o} / \rho_{5} \rho_{10}+b_{3}}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b_{1}=\frac{\rho_{5} \rho_{6} \rho_{8} \rho_{10} \lambda_{A}+\rho_{10} \lambda_{A} \lambda_{C} \mu_{C}\left(\rho_{5}+\lambda_{B o}\right)+\rho_{6} \lambda_{A} \lambda_{C} \lambda_{B o} \mu_{C}}{\rho_{8} \rho_{5} \rho_{6} \rho_{10}-\rho_{5} \rho_{6} \rho_{10} \lambda_{C} \mu_{C}} \\
& b_{2}=b_{1} \frac{\lambda_{C}}{\rho_{8}}+\frac{\lambda_{A} \lambda_{C}\left(\rho_{5}+\lambda_{B o}\right)}{\rho_{6} \rho_{8} \rho_{5}}+\frac{\lambda_{A} \lambda_{C} \lambda_{B o}}{\rho_{5} \rho_{8} \rho_{10}} \\
& b_{3}=\frac{2\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)}{\rho_{12}}\left[b_{1}+b_{2}+\frac{\lambda_{C}\left(\rho_{5}+\lambda_{B o}\right)}{\rho_{5} \rho_{6}}+\frac{\lambda_{A} \lambda_{B o}}{\rho_{5} \rho_{10}}\right]+2\left(\lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}\right) \frac{\lambda_{B \sigma}}{\rho_{3} \rho_{12}}
\end{aligned}
$$

From Eqs. (6.267) - (6.269) it follows that (for a load loss of 100\%)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\sum_{i=0}^{11} P_{i}=1-P_{12}=1-b_{3} P_{0} \\
& =\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{1+2 b_{2}+2 b_{1}\left(1+\lambda_{B \sigma} / \rho_{3}\right)+\lambda_{B o} / \rho_{5}+2 \lambda_{C}\left(\rho_{5}+\lambda_{B o}\right) / \rho_{5} \rho_{6}+2 \lambda_{A} \lambda_{B o} / \rho_{5} \rho_{10}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

$P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ per Eq. (6.270) can be approximated by

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S} \approx 1-\frac{2\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)\left(\lambda_{C} \mu_{A}+\mu_{C}\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{B \sigma}\right)\right)+\lambda_{B o}\left(\lambda_{A} \mu_{C}+\lambda_{C}\left(\mu_{A}+\mu_{C} \lambda_{B \sigma} / \lambda_{B o}\right)\right)}{\mu_{\mathrm{g}}\left[\mu_{A} \mu_{C}+2\left(\lambda_{A} \mu_{C}+\lambda_{C} \mu_{A}\right)\left(1+\lambda_{B o} /\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)\right)+2 \lambda_{A} \lambda_{B \sigma} \mu_{C} / \mu_{A}\right]}
$$

yielding $P A_{S}=A A_{S} \approx 1-2\left(\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right) / \mu\right)^{2}$ for $\lambda_{B \sigma}, \lambda_{B o}<<\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right), \mu_{A}=\mu_{C}=\mu_{g}=\mu$ (1-outof-2 active redundancy with $A$ and $C$ in series, as per Table 6.10). Equations (6.265) and (6.271) show the small influence of the coupler $B$. A numerical evaluation with

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\lambda_{A 1}=\lambda_{A 2}=\lambda_{A}=4 \cdot 10^{-6} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} & (\approx 0.035 \text { mean expected failures per year }) \\
\lambda_{C 1}=\lambda_{C 2}=\lambda_{C}=0.12 \cdot 10^{-6} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} & (\approx 0.001 \text { mean expected failures per year }) \\
\lambda_{B \sigma}=0.08 \cdot 10^{-6} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} & (\approx 0.0007 \text { meanexpected failures per year }) \\
\lambda_{B o}=0.6 \cdot 10^{-6} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} & (\approx 0.005 \text { mean expected failures per year }) \\
\mu_{A}=\mu_{C}=1 / 4 \mathrm{~h}, \mu_{g}=1 / 12 \mathrm{~h} &
\end{array}
$$

yields (for a load loss of $100 \%$ )

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx 7.364 \cdot 10^{9} \mathrm{~h} \quad \& \quad P A_{S}=A A_{S} \approx 1-1.63 \cdot 10^{-9}
$$

from Eqs.(6.262) \& (6.270), and $M T T F_{S 0} \approx 7.36 \cdot 10^{9} \mathrm{~h} \& P A_{S}=A A_{S} \approx 1-1.78 \cdot 10^{-9}$ from Eqs. (6.265) \& (6.271); moreover,

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
P_{0} \approx 0.932096, & P_{1}=P_{2} \approx 1.4913 \cdot 10^{-5}, & P_{3}=P_{4} \approx 4.772 \cdot 10^{-12}, & P_{5} \approx 0.067871, \\
P_{6}=P_{7} \approx 4.80 \cdot 10^{-7}, & P_{8}=P_{9} \approx 1.54 \cdot 10^{-11}, & P_{10}=P_{11} \approx 1.09 \cdot 10^{-6}, & P_{12} \approx 1.63 \cdot 10^{-9}
\end{array}
$$

Considering the substation as a macro-structure (first row in Table 6.10), it holds that $P A_{S}=A A_{S} \approx 1-\lambda_{S 0} / \mu_{S}$ and $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t}$, with $\mu_{S}=\mu_{g}$ and $\lambda_{S 0} \equiv 1 / M T T F_{S 0}$.# 6.8.6.4 Reward and Frequency/Duration Aspects 

For some applications, e. g. in power and communication systems, it is important to consider system's performance also in presence of failures. Reward and frequency/ duration aspects are of interest to evaluate system's performability. For systems described by Markov processes (implying constant failure \& repair rates for all elements, p. 503 or 277), asymptotic \& steady-state system failure frequency $f_{u d S}$, system repair (restoration) frequency $f_{d u S}$, system mean up time $M U T_{S}$, and system mean down time $M D T_{S}$ are given as (Eqs. (6.290)-(6.295) or (A7.141)-(A7.146)) ${ }^{*}$ )

$$
f_{u d S}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}\left(\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}}\right)=f_{d u S}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}} P_{i}\left(\sum_{Z_{j} \in U}\right)=1 /\left(M U T_{S}+M D T_{S}\right)
$$

and

$$
M D T_{S}=M U T_{S}\left(1-P A_{S}\right) / P A_{S}=\left(1-P A_{S}\right) / f_{d u S}, \quad P A_{S}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}
$$

respectively (Eq. (6.273) can be heuristically explained, considering that for $T \rightarrow \infty$, $\left(1-P A_{S}\right) T$ is the mean of the total system down time and $T \cdot f_{d u S}$ the mean number of repairs at system level in $(0, T]) . U$ is the set of states considered as up states for $f_{u d S}$ and $M D T_{S}$ calculation, $\bar{U}$ is the complement to the totality of states considered. ${ }^{*+1} P_{j}$ is the asymptotic \& steady-state probability of state $Z_{j}$ and $\rho_{j i}$ the transition rate from $Z_{j}$ to $Z_{i}$. In Eq.(6.272), all transition rates $\rho_{j i}$ leaving state $Z_{j} \in U$ toward $Z_{i} \in \bar{U}$ are considered (cumulated states). Example 6.27 gives an application to the substation of Fig. 6.34.

## Example 6.27

Give the failure frequency $f_{u d S}$ and the mean (expected) failure duration $M D T_{S}$ in steady-state for the substation of Fig. 6.34 for failures referred to a load loss of $100 \%$ and $\geq 50 \%$, respectively.

## Solution

From Eq. (6.272), and considering $U \cup \bar{U}=\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{12}\right\}$, Fig. 6.34 yields for a load loss of $100 \% U=\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{11}\right\} \& \bar{U}=\left\{Z_{12}\right\}$, and thus (with $P_{j}$ as per Eq. (6.267))

$$
f_{u d S \operatorname{loss} 100 \%}=2\left(P_{1}+P_{6}+P_{8}+P_{10}\right)\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)+2 P_{3}\left(\lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}\right)
$$

For load loss $\geq 50 \%$, Fig. 6.34 with $U=\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{5}\right\} \& \bar{U}=\left\{Z_{6}, \ldots, Z_{12}\right\}$ yields

$$
f_{u d S \operatorname{loss} \geq 50 \%}=P_{0} 2 \lambda_{C}+2 P_{1}\left(\lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}\right)+2 P_{3}\left(\lambda_{A}+2 \lambda_{C}\right)+P_{5} 2\left(\lambda_{A}+\lambda_{C}\right)
$$

From Eq. (6.273) it follows then

$$
M D T_{S \operatorname{loss} 100 \%}=P_{12} / f_{u d S \operatorname{loss} 100 \%}, \quad M D T_{S \operatorname{loss} \geq 50 \%}=\left(1-\left(P_{0}+2 P_{1}+2 P_{3}+P_{5}\right)\right) / f_{u d S \operatorname{loss} \geq 50 \%}
$$

The numerical example on p. 269 yields $f_{u d S \operatorname{loss} 100 \%} \approx 136 \cdot 10^{-12} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}\left(\approx 10^{-6}\right.$ expected failures per year), $f_{u d S \operatorname{loss} 50 \%} \approx 783 \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}\left(\approx 7 \cdot 10^{-3}\right.$ expected failures per year), $M D T_{S \text { loss } 100 \%}$ $=12 \mathrm{~h}=1 / \mu_{S}$, and $M D T_{\mathrm{S} \text { loss } \geq 50 \%} \approx 4.3 \mathrm{~h}$.
Supplementary results: For $M U T_{S}=M D T_{S} \cdot P A_{S} /\left(1-P A_{S}\right)$, the numerical example on p. 269 yields

$$
M U T_{S \operatorname{loss} 100 \%} \approx(12 / 1.63) 10^{9} \mathrm{~h} \approx 7.362 \cdot 10^{9} \mathrm{~h} \leqq M T T F_{S 0} \approx 7.364 \cdot 10^{9} \mathrm{~h}
$$

    ${ }^{*+1}$ See remark at the top of p. 279.# Example 6.28 

Give the mean (expected) reward rate in steady-state for the substation of Fig. 6.34.

## Solution

Considering Fig. 6.34 and the numerical example on p. 269 it follows that

$$
M I R_{S}=1 \cdot\left(P_{0}+2 P_{1}+2 P_{3}+P_{5}\right)+0.5 \cdot\left(2 P_{6}+2 P_{8}+2 P_{10}\right) \approx 0.9999984
$$

The reward rate $r_{i}$ takes care of the performance reduction in the state considered ( $r_{i}=0$ for down states, $0<r_{i}<1$ for partially down states, and $r_{i}=1$ for up states with $100 \%$ performance). From this, the mean reward rate in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty, M I R_{S}$, is given as (Eq. (A7.147))

$$
M I R_{S}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} r_{i} P_{i}
$$

see Example 6.28 for an application. The mean accumulated reward in steady-state (or for $t \rightarrow \infty$ ) follows as $M A R_{S}(t)=M I R_{S} \cdot t . P_{i}$ in Eq. (6.274) is the asymptotic \& steady-state probability of state $Z_{i}$, giving also the expected percentage of time the system stays at the performance level specified by $Z_{i}$ (Eq. (A7.132)).

### 6.8.7 Systems with Common Cause Failures

In some practical applications it is necessary to consider that common cause failures can occur. Common cause failures $(C)$ are multiple failures resulting from a single cause. They must be distinguished from common mode failures, which are multiple failures showing the same symptom. Common cause failures can occur in hardware as well as in software. Their causes can be quite different. Some possible causes for common cause failures in hardware are:

- overload (electrical, thermal, mechanical),
- technological weakness (material, design, production),
- misuse (e. g. caused by operating or maintenance personnel),
- external event.

Similar causes can be found for software.
In the following, a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy is used as a basic example for investigating effects of common cause failures. Results (Eqs. (6.276) \& (6.278)) show that common cause failure acts (in general) as a series element in the system's reliability structure, with failure rate equal the occurrence rate $\delta_{C}$ of the common cause failure and repair (restoration) rate equal the remove rate $\mu_{C}$ of the common cause failure. Design rules ((6.280) or (6.174)) and design guidelines (Chapter 5) are useful to avoid secondary failures or limit effects of common cause failures.
a) Common cause failures $(C)$ only on working elements, repair for $C$ includes that for a failure

c) $C$ on elements in working or repair state, repair as for case a

b) $C$ only on working elements, repair priority on $C$ without inclusion of other failures

d) $C$ on elements in working or repair state, repair as for case $\mathbf{b}$

Figure 6.35 Diagram of the transition rates for a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with common cause failures $(C)$ for 4 possible basic situations, const. failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda, \mu, \mu_{C}, \mu_{C i}\right)$, constant occurrence rates for $C\left(\delta_{C}, \delta_{C i}\right.$ (often $\left.\delta_{C i}=\delta_{C}\right)$ ), ideal failure detection and switch, one repair crew, repair priority on $C$, no further failures at system down except for $\delta_{C 41} \& \delta_{C 45}$ $\left(Z_{1}, Z_{3}, Z_{4}, Z_{5}\right.$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), Markov processes)

Figure 6.35 gives the diagrams of transition rates for a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with common cause failures for 4 possible basic situations ( $C$ refers to common cause failures, repair priority on $C$, one repair crew, no further failures at system down except for $\delta_{C 41} \& \delta_{C 45}$ ). To clarify results, occurrence rates $\delta_{C i}$ and repair rates $\mu_{C i}$ for common cause failures are assumed to be each other different when moving from one state to the other $\left(\delta_{C 01} \equiv \delta_{C}\right.$ and $\mu_{C 10} \equiv \mu_{C}$ is used to simplify the interpretation of Eqs. (6.276) \& (6.279)). The 4 possibilities of Fig. 6.35 are resumed in Fig. 6.36 for investigation. From Fig. 6.36 and Table 6.2, MTTF $_{S 0}$ is given as solution of the following system of algebraic equations (all down states $\left(Z_{1}, Z_{3}, Z_{4}, Z_{5}\right)$ are absorbing for reliability investigation)

$$
\left(2 \lambda+\delta_{C}\right) M T T F_{S 0}=1+2 \lambda M T T F_{S 2},\left(\lambda+\delta_{\mathrm{C} 21}+\delta_{\mathrm{C} 23}+\mu\right) M T T F_{S 2}=1+\mu M T T F_{S 0}
$$

From Eq. (6.275), $M T T F_{S 0}$ follows as

Figure 6.36 Reliability block diagram and diagram of the transition rates for a repairable 1 -out-of-2 active redundancy with common cause failures $(C)$ for different possibilities as per Fig. 6.35 (one repair crew, $Z_{1}, Z_{3}, Z_{4}, Z_{5}$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), Markov process)

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{3 \lambda+\delta_{C 21}+\delta_{C 23}+\mu}{\left(2 \lambda+\delta_{C}\right)\left(\lambda+\delta_{C 21}+\delta_{C 23}\right)+\mu \delta_{C}} \approx \frac{1}{\delta_{C}}
$$

Furthermore, from Fig. 6.36 and Table 6.2, the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is given as solution of the following system of algebraic equations

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\rho_{0} P_{0}=\mu_{C} P_{1}+\mu P_{2}, & \rho_{1} P_{1}=\delta_{C} P_{0}+\delta_{C 21} P_{2}+\delta_{C 41} P_{4}, \quad \rho_{5} P_{5}=\delta_{C 45} P_{4} \\
\rho_{3} P_{3}=\delta_{C 23} P_{2}, & \rho_{4} P_{4}=\lambda P_{2}+\mu_{C 54} P_{5}, \quad \rho_{2} P_{2}=2 \lambda P_{0}+\mu_{C 32} P_{3}+\mu P_{4}
\end{array}
$$

One of the Eq. (6.277) must be dropped and replaced by $P_{0}+\ldots+P_{5}=1$ (the first equation because of the particular cases investigated below). The solution yields

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{2}=\frac{1+a_{2}}{a_{3}+\delta_{C} / \rho_{1}+a_{1} a_{2} \delta_{C 41} / \rho_{1}+a_{2} \delta_{C 21} / \rho_{1}} \approx 1-\frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{1}=\lambda \rho_{5} /\left(\rho_{4} \rho_{5}-\delta_{C 45} \mu_{C 54}\right), \quad a_{2}=2 \lambda \rho_{3} /\left(\rho_{2} \rho_{3}-\delta_{C 23} \mu_{C 32}-a_{1} \mu \rho_{3}\right), \\
& a_{3}=1+a_{2}\left(1+\delta_{C 23} / \rho_{3}\right)+a_{1} a_{2}\left(1+\delta_{C 45} / \rho_{5}\right), \quad \rho_{0}=2 \lambda+\delta_{C}, \quad \rho_{1}=\mu_{C}, \\
& \rho_{2}=\lambda+\delta_{C 21}+\delta_{C 23}+\mu, \quad \rho_{3}=\mu_{C 32}, \quad \rho_{4}=\delta_{C 41}+\delta_{C 45}+\mu, \quad \rho_{5}=\mu_{C 54} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Approximations in Eqs. (6.276) and (6.278) assume

$$
\mu_{C}, \mu_{C 32}, \mu_{C 54} \geq \mu \quad \& \quad \mu \gg \lambda \gg \delta_{C}, \delta_{C 21}, \delta_{C 23}, \delta_{C 41}, \delta_{C 45}
$$

and are refined on p. 274. From these refinements, and as for Eqs. (6.157) \& (6.159), the effect of common cause failures becomes negligible for

$$
\delta_{C} \ll 2 \lambda^{2} / \mu
$$Equations (6.276) \& (6.278) are useful to investigate Fig. 6.35, yielding

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{1}{\delta_{C}+\frac{2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\delta_{C 21}-\delta_{C}\right)}{3 \lambda+\delta_{C 21}+\mu}}=\frac{1}{\delta_{C}} & M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{1}{\delta_{C}+\frac{2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\delta_{C 23}-\delta_{C}\right)}{3 \lambda+\delta_{C 23}+\mu}}=\frac{1}{\delta_{C}} \\
P A_{S} \approx 1-\frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}-\frac{2 \lambda}{2 \lambda+\delta_{C 21}+\mu}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\frac{\delta_{C 21}}{\mu_{C}}-\frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}\right) & P A_{S} \approx 1-\frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}-\frac{2 \lambda}{2 \lambda+\mu}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\frac{\delta_{C 23}}{\mu_{C 32}}-\frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}\right)
\end{array}
$$

a) Common cause failures $(C)$ only on working elements, repair for $C$ includes that for a failure
b) $C$ only on working elements, repair priority on $C$ without inclusion of other failures
$\operatorname{MTTF}_{S 0}=\frac{1}{\delta_{C}+\frac{2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\delta_{C 21}-\delta_{C}\right)}{3 \lambda+\delta_{C 21}+\mu}}=\frac{1}{\delta_{C}}$
$\operatorname{MTTF}_{S 0}=\frac{1}{\delta_{C}+\frac{2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\delta_{C 23}-\delta_{C}\right)}{3 \lambda+\delta_{C 23}+\mu}}=\frac{1}{\delta_{C}}$
$P A_{S} \approx 1-\frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}-\frac{2 \lambda}{2 \lambda+\delta_{C 21} \mu}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\frac{\delta_{C 21}}{\mu_{C}} \cdot \frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}+\frac{\lambda \delta_{C 41}}{\mu \mu_{C}}\right)$
$P A_{S} \approx 1-\frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}-\frac{2 \lambda}{2 \lambda+\mu}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\frac{\delta_{C 23}}{\mu_{C 32}}-\frac{\delta_{C}}{\mu_{C}}+\frac{\lambda \delta_{C 45}}{\mu \mu_{C 34}}\right)$
c) $C$ on elements in working or repair state, repair as for case $\mathbf{a}$
d) $C$ on elements in working or repair state, repair as for case $\mathbf{b}$

Often $\delta_{C 21}=\delta_{C 23}=\delta_{C 41}=\delta_{C 45}=\delta_{C} \& \mu_{C 32}=\mu_{C 54}=\mu_{C}$ can be assumed. Case $\mathbf{b}$ corresponds then to a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy in series with a switch (Eqs. (6.157), (6.159)). Further approximations are possible using $1-P A_{S}=\overline{P A}_{S}=P_{1}+P_{3}+P_{4}+P_{5}$.

Equations (6.276), (6.278) \& (6.280) show that
for a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy, the common cause failure acts as a series element with failure rate equal the occurrence rate $\delta_{C}$ of the common cause failure and repair (restoration) rate $\mu_{C}$ equal the removal rate of the common cause failure; this effect becomes negligible for $\delta_{C} \ll 2 \lambda^{2} / \mu$ (Eq. (6.280), see also Eqs. (6.160), (6.212)\& (6.239) for a similar situation, footnote on p. 221 for a compromise, and design rule (6.174) \& Fig.6.17).

These considerations remains basically true for more complex structures. From this, good protection against common cause failures can only be obtained if each element of a redundant structure is realized independently from each other (different designers for software and hardware, and different technologies \& manufacturing processes, as well as electrically, mechanically \& thermally separated for hardware); moreover, an FMEA/FMECA (Section 2.6) is mandatory to verify effectiveness.

Concrete protection against common cause failures must be worked out on a case-by-case basis. In some applications, common cause failures can occur with a time delay on elements of a redundant structure (e. g. drop of a cooling ventilator); in such cases, automatic fault detection can avoid secondary failures. Some practical considerations on failure rates for common cause failures in electronic equipment are in [A2.6(61508-6)], giving $\delta_{C} / \lambda \approx 0.005$ as achievable value (see design rules (6.280) \& (6.174) and footnote on p. 221).# 6.8.8 Basic Considerations on Network Reliability 

A network (telecommunication, power, neuronal, or other) can often be regarded, for modeling purposes, as a graph with $N$ nodes and up to $\binom{N}{2}$ edges (or links). Edges can be directed or bi-directional. Nodes and/or edges can fail and can have two or more states. Furthermore, for reliability investigations, distinction is made between 2-terminal and $k$-terminal $(2<k \leq N)$ connections. Networks can thus have very complex (meshed) reliability structures, some of which have been investigated since the 1950s, with increasing interest in the last years, seee.g. [2.32, 6.51-6.70].

For the case of only two states for nodes and edges, small networks can be investigated with methods introduced in Sections 2.3.1-2.3.3 (nonrepairable) or 6.2 -6.8.7 (repairable). For large networks, solutions using minimal path or cut sets, i. e. based on Boolean functions (Section 2.3.4), are possible, manually using binary decision diagrams (Section 6.9.3), or with help of dedicated computer programs, see e.g. $[6.53(2007,2009), 6.56,6.58,6.59]$. Multi-states for nodes and / or edges have to be considered when dealing with capacity problems, and some results for 2-terminal networks are known, see e. g. [6.53(2009), 6.56-6.60, 6.64].

In the following, two basic network structures are investigated using the key item method introduced in Section 2.3.1 (see Points 7 of Table 2.1 for a basic example).

Figure 6.37a shows a network with 3 nodes $N_{1}, N_{2}, N_{3}$ and 3 bi-directional edges $E_{12}, E_{13}, E_{23}$. The reliability block diagram (RBD) for connection $N_{1}, N_{2}$ is given in Fig. 6.37b if only edges can fail and in Fig. 6.37c if nodes and edges can fail. The reliability function (nonrepairable) related to Fig. 6.37c follows as for Eq. (2.26)

$$
R_{S 0_{N_{1}, N_{2}}}=R_{N_{1}} R_{N_{2}}\left[R_{E_{12}}+R_{E_{13}} R_{E_{23}} R_{N_{3}}-R_{E_{12}} R_{E_{13}} R_{E_{23}} R_{N_{3}}\right]
$$

with $R_{S 0_{N_{1}, N_{2}}}=R_{S 0_{N_{1}}, N_{2}}(t), R_{i}=R_{i}(t), R_{i}(0)=1$. Figure 6.37 d gives the RBD for all-terminal. For this case, all nodes are in series and $\left\{\left(N_{1}, N_{2}\right) \cap\left(N_{1}, N_{3}\right) \cap\left(N_{2}, N_{3}\right)\right\}$ $=\left\{\left(N_{1}, N_{2}\right) \cap\left(N_{1}, N_{3}\right)\right\}$ is used. The reliability function (nonrepairable case) can be calculated using e.g. $E_{12}$ as key item (Eq. (2.29)), yielding

R_{S 0_{a l l}}=R_{N_{1}} R_{N_{2}} R_{N_{3}}\left[R_{E_{12}}\left(R_{E_{13}}+R_{E_{23}}-R_{E_{13}} R_{E_{23}}\right)+\bar{R}_{E_{12}} R_{E_{13}} R_{E_{23}}\right]
$$

with $\bar{R}_{i}=1-R_{i}, R_{S 0}$ all $=R_{S 0}$ all $(t), R_{i}=R_{i}(t), R_{i}(0)=1$. Considering Eq. (2.48), $P A_{i}(t)$ instead of $R_{i}(t)$ in Eqs. (6.281) and (6.282) leads to the point availability $P A_{S 0}(t)$ for the case of totally independent elements $N_{1}, N_{2}, N_{3}, E_{12}, E_{13}, E_{23}$ (p. 52). To investigate the reliability for the repairable case or the point availability for non totally independent elements, a diagram of transition rates can be used.

Figure 6.38a shows a network with 4 nodes $N_{1}, N_{2}, N_{3}, N_{4}$ and 6 bi-directional edges $E_{12}, E_{13}, E_{14}, E_{23}, E_{24}, E_{34}$. Assuming that nodes and edges can fail, the reliability block diagram is given in Fig. 6.38b for connection $N_{1}, N_{2}$ and Fig. 6.38c for all-terminal. Successively use of the key item method on $E_{12}, E_{34}, N_{3}, N_{4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S 0_{N_{1}, N_{2}}}=R_{N_{1}} R_{N_{2}}\left[R_{E_{12}}+\bar{R}_{E_{12}}\left[R_{E_{34}}\left[R_{N_{3}}\left\{R_{N_{4}}\left(R_{E_{13}}+R_{E_{14}} R_{E_{13}} R_{E_{14}}\right)\left(R_{E_{23}} R_{E_{24}} R_{E_{23}} R_{E_{24}}\right)\right.\right.\right. \\
& \left.\left.\left.+\bar{R}_{N_{4}} R_{E_{13}} R_{E_{23}}\right\}+\bar{R}_{N_{3}} R_{N_{4}} R_{E_{14}} R_{E_{24}}\right\}+\bar{R}_{E_{34}}\left(R_{N_{3}} R_{E_{13}} R_{E_{23}}+R_{N_{4}} R_{E_{14}} R_{E_{24}} R_{N_{3}} R_{E_{13}} R_{E_{23}}\left[N_{4} R_{E_{14}} R_{E_{24}}\right)\right]\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, Fig. 6.38c leads to (key item method on $E_{12}, E_{13}, E_{14}, E_{24} ; R_{i j}=R_{E_{i j}}$ )

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{S 0_{a l l}}= & R_{N_{1}} R_{N_{2}} R_{N_{3}} R_{N_{4}}\left[R_{12}\left\{R_{13}\left[1-\left(1-R_{14}\right)\left(1-R_{24}\right)\left(1-R_{34}\right)\right\}+\bar{R}_{13}\left[R_{14}\left(R_{23}+R_{34}-R_{23} R_{34}\right)\right.\right.\right. \\
& \left.\left.+\bar{R}_{14} R_{b}\right]\right\}+\bar{R}_{12}\left[R_{13}\left[R_{14}\left(R_{23}+R_{24}-R_{23} R_{24}\right)+\bar{R}_{14} R_{b}\right]+\bar{R}_{13} R_{14} R_{b}\right\}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

with $R_{b}=R_{24}\left(R_{23}+R_{34}-R_{23} R_{34}\right)+\bar{R}_{24} R_{23} R_{34}$; from this $R_{S 0_{a l l}}=R_{N}^{4}\left[16 R^{3}-33 R^{4}+24 R^{5}-6 R^{6}\right]$ for $R_{N_{i}}=R_{N}, R_{E_{i j}}=R$ (see also the remark to Eq. (6.282) for the repairable case).

Besides deterministic networks, some kinds of stochastic and evolving networks have been investigated, for instance by assuming that for bi-directional edges, every pair of nodes has a probability $p$ to be connected (Erdös-Renyi) or there is a probability $p(k)$ that a randomly selected node has $k$ edges ( $p(k)$ can be a Poisson distribution (Erdös-Renyi) or a given power law), see e. g. [6.51-6.55] for greater details. However, because of their complexity, investigation of networks is still in progress.


Figure 6.38 a) Network with 4 nodes \& bi-directional connection from each node to all other node; b) 2-terminal RBD for connection $N_{1}, N_{2}$, edges and nodes can fail; c) RBD for all-terminal reliability, edges and nodes can fail ( $\mathrm{RBD}=$ reliability block diagram)# 6.8.9 General Procedure for Modeling Complex Systems 

On the basis of the tools introduced in Appendix A7 and results in Sections 6.8.16.8.8, following procedure can be given for reliability and availability investigations of complex systems, both when a reliability block diagram exists or not (for seriesparallel structures, Section 6.7 applies, in particular Table 6.10 on p.233; see also pp. 293-94 for further approximate expressions).

1. As a first step operate with time-homogeneous Markov processes, i. e. assume that all involved times are exponentially distributed (in particular, that failure \& repair rates of all elements are constant during the stay time in each state and can change (stepwise) only at a state transition, e.g. because of load sharing (p.62)). This will be assumed for steps 2, 4-10; dropping this assumption leads to non-Markovian processes. In a further step, refinements can be considered on a case-by-case basis using more complex regenerative processes (Tab. 6.1 on p.171), see e.g. pp. 204-12, 526-30, as well as footnote on p.220.
2. Group series elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, and assign to each macro-structure a failure rate $\lambda_{S 0}=\lambda_{1}+\ldots+\lambda_{n}$ and repair (restoration) rate $\mu_{S}=\lambda_{S 0} /\left(\lambda_{1} / \mu_{1}+\ldots+\lambda_{n} / \mu_{n}\right)$ as per Table 6.10 (a further reduction of a diagram of transition rates is possible in some cases, see e.g. [6.32, 6.40], p. 229, Figs. 6.27 \& 6.28, 6.30, 6.39).
3. Perform an FMEA (Section 2.6) to fix all relevant failure modes and to verify actual system capability for detection, localization, reconfiguration, graceful degradation at failure, and protection against common cause/mode failures.
4. Draw the diagram of transition rates and verify its correctness (see Fig. 6.20 on p. $235 \&$ Fig. 6.34 on p. 267 for two comprehensive examples); important is the identification of up states having a direct transition to a down state at system level ( $Z_{1}, Z_{3}-Z_{7}$ in Fig. 6.20), i. e. of critical operating states.
5. Identify the transition rates between each state (combination of failure and repair rates), by considering assumed repair (restoration) priorities, retained failure modes, and particularities specific to the system considered (dependence between elements, sequence of failure, failure modes, etc.).
6. For reliability calculation, the mean time to system failure $M T T F_{S i}$ for system entering state $Z_{i}$ at $t=0$ is obtained by solving (Eq. (A7.126))

$$
\rho_{i} M T T F_{S i}=1+\sum_{Z_{j} \in U, j \neq i} \rho_{i j} M T T F_{S j}, \quad Z_{i} \in U, \quad \rho_{i}=\sum_{j=0, j \neq i}^{m} \rho_{i j}
$$

thereby, $U$ is the set of up states ( $\bar{U}$ that of down states, $U \cup \bar{U}=\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}$ ),


Figure 6.39 Example for the reduction of a diagram of transition rates for $M T T F_{S 0}$ calculation (note that $\left(\lambda_{0}+\lambda_{2}\right) /\left(1+\lambda_{0} / \lambda_{1}\right)=\left(1+\lambda_{2} / \lambda_{0}\right) /\left(1 / \lambda_{0}+1 / \lambda_{1}\right)$ )$\rho_{i j}$ the transition rate from state $Z_{i} \in U$ to state $Z_{j} \in U$, and $\rho_{i}$ the sum of all transition rates leaving $Z_{i}$. The system (6.285) delivers all $M T T F_{S i}$ for any $Z_{i} \in U$ entered at $t=0$ (note that for Markov processes, the condition " $Z_{i}$ is entered at $t=0$ " can be replaced by "system in $Z_{i}$ at $t=0$ "). At system level, the reliability function (Eq. (A7.117))

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{-t / M T T F_{S 0}}=e^{-t \lambda_{S 0}}, \quad t>0, \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(0)=1, \lambda_{S 0} \equiv 1 / M T T F_{S 0}
$$

can often be used in practical applications (see e. g. Eq. (6.94)); in general, in $Z_{0}$ all elements are new or as-good-as-new (however, for non Markovian processes it can occur that $Z_{0}$ is not a regeneration state (footnote on p.210)).
7. The asymptotic $(t \rightarrow \infty) \&$ steady-state (stationary) point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ is given as (Eqs. (A7.112), (A7.134))

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}
$$

with $P_{j}$ as solution of (Eq.(A7.127), irreducible embedded Markov chain)

$$
\rho_{j} P_{j}=\sum_{i=0, i \neq j}^{m} P_{i} \rho_{i j}, \quad \text { with } P_{j}>0, \sum_{j=0}^{m} P_{j}=1, \quad \rho_{j}=\sum_{i=0, i \neq j}^{m} \rho_{j i}, \quad j=0, \ldots, m
$$

one equation for $P_{j}$, arbitrarily chosen, must be replaced by $\sum P_{j}=1$ (see p. 513, and e. g. pp. 180-82, 242, 514 for further availability figures).
8. Considering the constant failure \& repair rates for all elements, the asymptotic \& steady-state interval reliability follows as (Eqs. (6.27), (A7.119), (A7.129))

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j} \mathrm{R}_{S j}(\theta) \approx P A_{S} e^{-\theta / M T T F_{S 0}}, \quad \theta>0, \operatorname{IR}_{S}(0)=P A_{S}
$$

9. The asymptotic \& steady-state system failure frequency $f_{u d S}$ and system mean up time $M U T_{S}$ are given as (Eqs. (A7.141) \& (A7.142))

$$
f_{u d S}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U, Z_{i} \in \bar{U}} P_{j i} \rho_{j i}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}\left(\sum \rho_{j i}\right), \quad\left(f_{i j}=h_{i}=1 / T_{i j}=P_{j} \rho_{j} \text { for } U=Z_{j}\right)
$$

and

$$
M U T_{S}=\left(\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}\right) / f_{u d S}=P A_{S} / f_{u d S}, \quad\left(M U T_{j}=T_{j}=1 / \rho_{j}=P_{j} T_{i j} \text { for } U=Z_{j}\right)
$$

respectively; $U$ is the set of states considered as up states for $f_{u d S} \& M U T_{S}$ calculation, $\bar{U}$ the complement to system states $\left(U \cup \bar{U}=\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}\right)$. Similar is for the system repair (restoration) frequency $f_{d u S}$ and the system mean down time $M D T_{S}$, given as (Eqs. (A7.143) \& (A7.144))

$$
f_{d u S}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}, Z_{j} \in U} P_{i} \rho_{i j}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}} P_{i}\left(\sum \rho_{i j}\right), \quad\left(f_{i i}=h_{i}=1 / T_{i i}=P_{i} \rho_{i} \text { for } \bar{U}=Z_{i}\right)
$$

and

$$
M D T_{S}=\left(\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}} P_{i}\right) / f_{d u S}=\left(1-P A_{S}\right) / f_{d u S}, \quad\left(M D T_{i}=T_{i}=1 / \rho_{i}=P_{i} T_{i i} \text { for } \bar{U}=Z_{i}\right)
$$$M U T_{S}$ is the mean of the times in which, after a transition from a down state, the system is moving in the set of up states $Z_{i} \in U$ before a transition to the set of down states $Z_{i} \in \bar{U}$ occurs, in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty ;{ }^{+)}$similar is for $M D T_{S}, f_{u d S} \& f_{d u S}$.
For practical applications, $M U T_{S} \approx M T T F_{80}$ can often be used (pp.200, 237, 270), but $M T B F_{S}$ instead of $M U T_{S}$ should be avoided (pp.392-94, 515-16). Furthermore, $\sum_{Z_{i} \in U} P_{i} M T T F_{S i}$ cannot be used for $M U T_{S}$ (p.516, Ex. 6.29), and for systems with redundancy, $M D T_{S}$ differs from the mean of all repair (restoration) times $M T T R_{S}$ (Example 4.2(p.124)). Finally, one recognizes that

$$
f_{u d S}=f_{d u S}=z_{S}=1 /\left(M U T_{S}+M D T_{S}\right)
$$

and Eqs. (6.291), (6.293), (6.294) lead to the following important relation

$$
M D T_{S}=M U T_{S}\left(1-P A_{S}\right) / P A_{S} \quad \text { or } \quad P A_{S}=M U T_{S} /\left(M U T_{S}+M D T_{S}\right)
$$

10. The asymptotic \& steady-state mean reward rate $M I R_{S}$ is given by (Eq. (A7.147) and with $P_{i}$ as per Eq. (6.288))

$$
M I R_{S}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} r_{i} P_{i}
$$

thereby, $r_{i}=0$ for down states, $0<r_{i}<1$ for partially down states, and $r_{i}=1$ for up states with $100 \%$ performance. The asymptotic \& steady-state mean accumulated reward $M A R_{S}$ follows as (Eq. (A7.148))

$$
M A R_{S}(t)=M I R_{S} \cdot t
$$

For Points 6, 7, 9,10, similar relations exist for semi-Markov processes (pp.524-25). If the process involved is non-Markovian, it can be useful to use a time schedule (Figs. 6.10,A7.11-13). Alternative investigation methods are given in Section 6.9.

# Example 6.29 

Investigate $M U T_{S}, M D T_{S}, f_{u d S}$, and $f_{d u S}$ for the 1-out-of-2 redundancy of Fig. 6.8a.

## Solution

The solution of Eq. (6.84) with $\hat{\mathrm{P}}_{i}(t)=0, i=0,1,2$, yields (Eq. (6.87))

$$
P_{0}=\mu^{2} /\left[\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(\lambda+\mu)+\mu^{2}\right] \quad \text { and } \quad P_{1}=\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) /\left[\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(\lambda+\mu)+\mu^{2}\right]
$$

From Fig. 6.8a and Eqs. (6.290)-(6.293) it follows that

$$
M U T_{S}=\frac{\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}, \quad M D T_{S}=\frac{1}{\mu}, \quad f_{u d S}=f_{d u S}=\frac{1}{M U T_{S}+M D T_{S}}=\frac{\mu \lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}{\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(\lambda+\mu)+\mu^{2}}
$$

For this example it holds that $M U T_{S}=M T T F_{S 1}$ (with $M T T F_{S 1}$ from Eq. (6.89) with $P_{1}^{\prime}(0)=1$, see also Eq. (A7.154)); this because the system enters $Z_{1}$ after each system down and $Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2}$ is the unique transition to $Z_{2}$ (Fig. 6.8a); furthermore, one repair crew yields $M D T_{S}=1 / \mu=M T T R$.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$The use of "mean of the times" and not of "mean time" implies that times between consecutive system failures will be, in general, dependent \& have different distribution functions (footnote p.512, p.394); this further motivates the use of indices $S_{i}$ for reliability figures ( $i$ for the state $Z_{i}$ entered at $t=0$ ).# 6.9 Alternative Investigation Methods 

The methods given in sections 6.1 to 6.8 are based on Markov, semi-Markov and semi-regenerative processes, according to the involved distributions for failure-free and repair times. They have the advantage of great flexibility (type of redundancy and repair strategy, incomplete coverage or switch, common cause failures, etc.). Further tools are known to model repairable systems, e. g. based on dynamic fault trees or Petri nets. For very large or complex systems, a numerical solution or Monte Carlo simulation can become necessary. Many of these tools are similar in performance and versatility (Petri nets are equivalent to Markov models), other have limitations (fault trees apply basically to totally independent elements, and Monte Carlo simulations delivers only numerical solutions), so that choice of the tool is related to the personal experience of the analyst (see e. g. [A2.6 (61165, 60300-3-1), 6.103 (31010), 6.39 (2005)] for comparisons). However, modeling large complex systems
requires a close cooperation between project and reliability engineers.
After a review of totally independent elements, Sections 6.9.2-6.9.5 discuss dynamic fault trees, BDD, event trees \& Petri nets. Sections 6.9.6-6.9.7 consider then numerical solutions \& approximate expressions for large systems. Tools and models for human reliability \& risk management are introduced in Sections 6.10 \& 6.11.

### 6.9.1 Systems with Totally Independent Elements

Totally independent elements (totally IE) assumes that there is only active redundancy and each element operates, and if repairable is repaired to as-good-as-new, independently from each other. Elements are boxes in the reliability block diagram and total independence implies that each element has its own repair crew and continues operation during repair of failed elements. This does not exclude that the (physically) same element can appear more times in a reliability block diagram (Examples $2.2 \& 2.3$ ). The reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ of nonrepairable (up to system failure) systems with totally independent elements has been investigated in Section 2.3.4. As stated with Eq. (2.48), equations for $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ are also valid for the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ of repairable systems, substituting $\mathrm{PA}_{i}(t)$ to $\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$. This rule gives an upper bound on $\mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ if each element does not have its own repair crew. Except for series structures, $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ for repairable systems cannot be obtained using Boolean methods, see pp. 293-94 for a possible approximation.

### 6.9.2 Static and Dynamic Fault Trees

A fault tree (FT) is a graphical representation of the conditions or other factors causing or contributing to the occurrence of a defined undesirable event, referred astop event. In its original form, as introduced in Section 2.6 (p. 76), a fault tree contains only static gates (essentially AND \& OR for coherent systems) and is termed static fault tree. Such a fault tree can handle combinatorial events, qualitatively (similar as for an FMEA, Section 2.6) or quantitatively (with Boolean functions, Section 2.3.4). As in the current literature [2.85, 6.38, A2.6(IEC61025)],
" 0 " will be used also here for operating and " 1 " for failure (this in contrast to the notation used in Sections $2.2 \& 2.3$ for reliability investigations based on the reliability block diagram with 1 for up and 0 for down).

With this notation, AND gates represent in fault trees a parallel structure with active redundancy and OR gates a series structure (Figs. 2.14, 6.40-6.42). In setting up a fault tree, a reliability block diagram can be useful. However, fault trees can also consider external events. Figure 6.40 gives two examples with corresponding static fault trees (see Table 2.1 and Example 6.30 for calculations based on the reliability block diagram, Section 6.9.3 for calculations based on binary decision diagrams).

Static fault trees can be used to calculate reliability and point availability for the case of totally independent elements (see discussion on p. 280). For instance, reliability calculation leads to (nonrepairable up to system failure)

$$
1-\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1-\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{R}_{i}(t) \quad \text { or } \quad \overline{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(t)=1-\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1-\overline{\mathrm{R}}_{i}(t)\right), \quad \mathrm{R}_{i}(0)=1
$$

for the series structure with independent elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, and to

$$
1-\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1-\sum_{i=k}^{n}\binom{n}{i} \mathrm{R}^{i}(t)(1-\mathrm{R}(t))^{n-i} \quad \text { or } \quad \overline{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(t)=1-\sum_{i=k}^{n}\binom{n}{i}(1-\overline{\mathrm{R}}(t))^{i} \overline{\mathrm{R}}(t)^{n-i}
$$

for the $k$-out-of-n active redundancy with identical and independent elements $E_{1}=$ $\ldots=E_{n}=E$ (Eqs. (2.17) \& (2.23), $\overline{\mathrm{R}}_{i}(t)=1-\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)=$ failure probability). For complex structures, calculation uses binary decision diagrams (based on the Shannon decomposition of the fault tree structure function, see Section 6.9.3) or minimal path or cut sets (Eqs. (2.42), (2.44)), often supported by computer programs.

However, because of their basic structure, static fault trees cannot handle states or time dependencies, in particular standby redundancy \& repair strategy. For these cases, it is necessary to extend static fault trees, adding so called dynamic gates to obtain dynamic fault trees. Important dynamic gates are [2.85, 6.38, A2.6 (IEC 61025)]:

- Priority AND gate (PAND), the output event (failure) occurs only if all input events occur and in sequence from left to right.
- Sequence enforcing gate (SEQ), the output event occurs only if input events occur in sequence from left to right and there are more than two input events.
- Spare gate (SPARE), the output event occurs if the number of spares is less than required.
Further gates (choice gate, redundancy gate, warm spare gate) have been suggested,

Figure 6.40 a) Reliability block diagram and static fault tree for a 2-out-of-3 active redundancy with switch element; b) Functional block diagram \& static fault tree for a redund. computer system [6.30]; Notes: " 0 " holds for operating (up), " 1 " for failure (down)
e.g. in [6.38]. All above dynamic gates requires a Markov analysis, i. e. states probabilities must be calculated by a Markov approach (constant failures \& repair rates), yielding results used as occurrence probability for the basic event replacing the corresponding dynamic gate. Use of dynamic gates in dynamic fault tree analysis, with corresponding computer programs, has been carefully investigated, e. g. in $[2.85,6.36,6.38]$.

Fault tree analysis (FTA) is an established methodology for reliability and availability calculation emerging in the 1960's with investigations on nuclear power plants. However, it is basically limited to totally independent elements (active redundancy, nonrepairable up to system failure for reliability, repairable with a repair crew for each element for availability), and the necessity to use Markov approaches to solve dynamic gates can further reduce its utility in practical applications. Quite generally, FTA has the same limitations as those of methods based on binary considerations (fault trees, reliability block diagrams, binary decision diagrams, etc.). However, all these tools are sufficient for some applications, and can give a valid support in generating transition rates diagrams for Markov analysis. So once more,
combination of investigation tools is often a good way to solve difficult problems.# 6.9.3 Binary Decision Diagrams 

A binary decision diagram (BDD) is a directed acyclic graph obtained by successive Shannon decomposition (Eq. (2.38)) of a Boolean function. It applies in particular to the structure functions developed in Section 2.3.4 for coherent systems, using minimal path or cut sets. This allows for easy calculation of the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ for the nonrepairable case (Eqs. (2.45), (2.47)) or point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for repairable totally independent elements (Eqs. (2.45), (2.48)). Frequently, BDDs are used to calculate $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ or $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for systems completely described by a fault tree with corresponding fault tree structure function $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right) . \quad \phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$ follows from a fault tree, see e.g. Figs. $6.41 \& 6.42$, or from the corresponding reliability block diagram, considering " 0 " for operating (up) and " 1 " for failure (down).

In relation to fault trees, a BDD is created starting from the top event, i. e. from $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$, down to the sink boxes using the Shannon decomposition (Eq. (2.38)) of the fault tree structure function at the node considered. Each node refers to a variable of $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$ and has 2 outgoing edges, 0 -edge for operating and 1-edge for failure. Input to a node can be one or more outgoing edges from other nodes. The BDD terminates in 2 sink boxes labeled 0 for operating (up), 1 for failure (down). Indication 0 or 1 and an arrow help to identify the outgoing edge. Figure 6.41 gives two basic reliability block diagrams with corresponding fault trees, $\phi_{F T}$, and BDDs;
to obtain $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$, one moves from the top of the BDD following all possible paths down to the sink box " 0 ", taking in a multiplicative way $\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$ or $\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}_{i}(t)=1-\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$ according to the value 0 or 1 assumed by the variable $\zeta_{i}$ involved (similar is for $\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(t)$; for $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ consider Eq. (2.48)).


Figure 6.41 Basic reliability block diagrams with corresponding fault trees, $\phi_{F T} \&$ binary decision diagrams $\left(\zeta_{i}\right.$ refers to $E_{i}$, " 0 " to operating, " 1 " to failure; $R_{S 0}=\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t), R_{i}=R_{i}(t), R_{i}(0)=1, \widetilde{R}_{i}=1-R_{i}$; independent elem.; $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ for nonrepairable; availability per Eq. (2.48) for totally independent elem.)# Example 6.30 

Give the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ for the nonrepairable case and the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for the system of Fig. 6.40b, by assuming totally independent elements and using the reliability block diagram's method with $R_{D_{11}}=R_{D_{12}}=R_{D_{21}}=R_{D_{22}}=R_{D}, R_{M_{1}}=R_{M_{2}}=R_{M}, R_{P_{1}}=R_{P_{2}}=R_{P}, R_{i}=R_{i}(t)$.

## Solution

The reliability block diagram follows from the functional block diagram of Fig. 6.40b (Section 2.2.2), or from the corresponding fault tree (Fig. 6.40b, considering " 0 " for operating (up) and " 1 " for failure (down)). As element $M_{3}$ appears twice in the reliability block diagram, calculation of the reliability function (nonre-

pairable case) make use of the key item method given in Section 2.3.1, yielding

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{S 0}= & R_{M 3}\left\{2\left[\left(2 R_{D}-R_{D}^{2}\right) R_{P}\right]-\left[\left(2 R_{D}-R_{D}^{2}\right) R_{P}\right]^{2}\right\} R_{B} \\
& +\left(1-R_{M 3}\right)\left\{2\left[\left(2 R_{D}-R_{D}^{2}\right) R_{M} R_{P}\right]-\left[\left(2 R_{D}-R_{D}^{2}\right) R_{M} R_{P}\right]^{2}\right\} R_{B}
\end{aligned}
$$

with $R_{i}=\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$, and $\mathrm{R}_{i}(0)=1$. Following the assumed totally independence of the elements (each of the 10 elements has its own repair crew), the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ is also given by Eq. (6.300) substituting $R_{i}$ with $\mathrm{PA}_{i}(t)$ ( $\left.P A_{i}=A A_{i}\right)$ for steady-state or $\left.t \rightarrow \infty\right)$.
Supplementary results: $R_{D_{1}} \neq R_{D_{2}}, R_{M_{1}} \neq R_{M_{2}}, R_{P_{1}} \neq R_{P_{2}}$ yield results given by Eq. (6.301).

Figure 6.42 considers the basic structures given in Fig. 6.40. The reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ for the nonrepairable case follows, for the structure of Fig. 6.42b, from

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S 0}=R_{B}\left[R_{M_{3}}\left[R_{P_{1}} R_{D_{11}}+R_{P_{1}} \bar{R}_{D_{11}} R_{D_{12}}+R_{P_{1}} \bar{R}_{D_{11}} \bar{R}_{D_{12}} R_{P_{2}}\left(R_{D_{21}}+\bar{R}_{D_{21}} R_{D_{22}}\right)\right.\right. \\
& \left.+\bar{R}_{P_{1}} R_{P_{2}}\left(R_{D_{21}}+\bar{R}_{D_{21}} R_{D_{22}}\right)\right] \\
& +\bar{R}_{M_{3}}\left[R_{M_{1}} R_{M_{2}} R_{P_{1}}\left(R_{D_{11}}+\bar{R}_{D_{11}} R_{D_{12}}\right)+R_{M_{1}} R_{M_{2}} R_{P_{1}} \bar{R}_{D_{11}} \bar{R}_{D_{12}} R_{P_{2}}\left(R_{D_{21}}+\bar{R}_{D_{21}} R_{D_{22}}\right)\right. \\
& +R_{M_{1}} R_{M_{2}} \bar{R}_{P_{1}} R_{P_{2}}\left(R_{D_{21}}+\bar{R}_{D_{21}} R_{D_{22}}\right)+R_{M_{1}} \bar{R}_{M_{2}} R_{P_{1}}\left(R_{D_{11}}+\bar{R}_{D_{11}} R_{D_{12}}\right) \\
& \left.\left.+\bar{R}_{M_{1}} R_{M_{2}} R_{P_{2}}\left(R_{D_{21}}+\bar{R}_{D_{21}} R_{D_{22}}\right)\right]\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

with $R_{S 0}=\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t), R_{i}=\mathrm{R}_{i}(t), \mathrm{R}_{i}(0)=1, \bar{R}_{i}=1-R_{i}$ Setting $R_{M_{1}}=R_{M_{2}}=R_{M}, R_{P_{1}}=R_{P_{2}}=R_{P}$, $R_{D_{11}}=R_{D_{12}}=R_{D_{21}}=R_{D_{22}}=R_{D}$, one obtains Eq. (6.300). Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{R}_{S 0}=\bar{R}_{B}+ & R_{B}\left[R_{M_{3}}\left[\left(R_{P_{1}} \bar{R}_{D_{11}} \bar{R}_{D_{12}}+\bar{R}_{P_{1}}\right)\left(\bar{R}_{P_{2}}+R_{P_{2}} \bar{R}_{D_{21}} \bar{R}_{D_{22}}\right)\right]\right. \\
& +\bar{R}_{M_{3}}\left[\bar{R}_{M_{1}} \bar{R}_{M_{2}}+R_{M_{1}} R_{M_{2}}\left(\bar{R}_{P_{1}}+R_{P_{1}} \bar{R}_{D_{11}} \bar{R}_{D_{12}}\right)\left(\bar{R}_{P_{2}}+R_{P_{2}} \bar{R}_{D_{21}} \bar{R}_{D_{22}}\right)\right. \\
& \left.\left.\left.+R_{M_{1}} \bar{R}_{M_{2}}\left(\bar{R}_{P_{1}}+R_{P_{1}} \bar{R}_{D_{11}} \bar{R}_{D_{12}}\right)+\bar{R}_{M_{1}} R_{M_{2}}\left(\bar{R}_{P_{2}}+R_{P_{2}} \bar{R}_{D_{21}} \bar{R}_{D_{22}}\right)\right]\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

which verify $1-\bar{R}_{S 0}=R_{S 0}$. Assuming totally independent elements (Section 6.9.1), Eq. (6.301) delivers $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ by substituting $R_{i}$ with $\mathrm{PA}_{i}(t)$ (or with $P A_{i}$ for $P A_{S}$ ).

Evaluation of binary decision diagrams (and fault trees) is generally supported by dedicated computer programs. For hand evaluation, it is often more favorable to work directly with the key item method introduced in Section 2.3.1 (as in Example 6.30).
