(2.48) for totally independent elements)

To consider "1" for operating (up) and "0" for failure (down), as in Sections 2.2 and 2.3 , it is necessary to change AND with OR and $R_{i}$ with $\bar{R}_{i}$.# 6.9.4 Event Trees 

Event trees can be used to support and extend effectiveness of failure modes and effects analyses introduced in Section 2.6, see e.g. [A2.6 (IEC 62502)]. Event tree analysis (ETA) is a bottom-up (inductive) logic procedure combining advantages of FMEA/FMECA and FTA. It applies, in particular, for risk analysis of large complex systems of any type with interacting internal and external factors (technical, environmental, human). The basic idea is to give an answer to the question,
what happens if a given initiating event occurs?
The answer is given by investigating propagation of initiating events, in particular efficacy of mitigation barriers introduced to limit effects of the initiating event considered (col. 8 in Tab. 2.6). An initiating event can be a failure or an external event, and a comprehensive list of initiating events must be prepared before analysis begins.

Figure 6.43 shows the basic structure of an event tree for the case of two coupled systems ( $A$ and $B$ ), each with two mitigating factors (barriers) $\delta_{i}$ for the initiating event $\alpha$ considered. Each mitigation is successful with $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\delta_{i}\right\}$ and unsuccessful (failure) with $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\overline{\delta_{i}}\right\}=1-\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\delta_{i}\right\}$. The probability for the outcome $\omega$ in Fig. 6.43 is calculated following the path leading to $\omega$ and is given by (Eq. (A6.12))

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\{\omega\}= & \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\alpha \cap \delta_{A 1} \cap \delta_{A 2} \cap \bar{\delta}_{B 1} \cap \delta_{B 2}\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\alpha\} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\delta_{A 1} \mid \alpha\right\} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\delta_{A 2} \mid\left(\alpha \cap \delta_{A 1}\right)\right\} \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\bar{\delta}_{B 1} \mid\left(\alpha \cap \delta_{A 1} \cap \delta_{A 2}\right)\right\} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\delta_{B 2} \mid\left(\alpha \cap \delta_{A 1} \cap \delta_{A 2} \cap \bar{\delta}_{B 1}\right)\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Calculation of conditional probabilities can become laborious; however, independence (p. 437) of events $\omega, \delta_{1}, \ldots$ can often be assumed. Substituting $\lambda_{\alpha}$ to $\operatorname{Pr}\{\alpha\}$, Eq. (6.303) delivers the occurrence frequency $(\mathrm{h}(t)=\lambda$ per Eq. (A7.42)) of $\omega$.

As for FMEA/FMECA\&FTA, time evolution cannot be easily considered in ETA. An extension like for dynamic FT (Section 6.9.2) is possible. In particular, $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\delta_{i}\right\}$ can be issued from the top event of an FT, allowing handling of common cause events.

| Initiating event $(\alpha)$ | System A |  | System B |  | Outcome |
| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
|  | Mitigating factors $\delta_{\mathrm{A} 1} \quad \mid \quad \delta_{\mathrm{A} 2}$ |  | Mitigating factors $\delta_{\mathrm{B} 1} \quad \mid \quad \delta_{\mathrm{B} 2}$ |  |  |
|  | $\delta_{\text {A1 }} \quad \mid \quad \delta_{\text {A2 }}$ |  |  |  |  |

Figure 6.43 Basic structure of an event tree# 6.9.5 Petri Nets 

Petri nets (PN) were introduced 1962 [6.35,6.6] to investigate in, particular, synchronization, sequentiality, concurrency, and conflict in parallel working digital systems. They are well established in the literature, see e. g. [2.40, 6.0, 6.6, 6.8, 6.30, 6.39 (1999), A2.6 (IEC 62551)]. Important for reliability investigations was the possibility to create algorithmically the diagram of transition rates belonging to a given Petri net. With this, investigation of time behavior on the basis of time-homogeneous Markov processes was open (stochastic PN). Extension to semi-Markov process is easy [6.8]. This section introduces Petri nets from a reliability analysis point of view.

A Petri net (PN) is a directed graph involving 3 kind of elements:

- Places $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{n}$ (drawn as circles): A place $P_{i}$ is an input to a transition $T_{j}$ if an arc exist from $P_{i}$ to $T_{j}$, and is an output of a transition $T_{k}$ and input to a place $P_{l}$ if an arc exist from $T_{k}$ to $P_{l}$; places may contain token (black spots) and a PN with token is a marked PN.
- Transitions $T_{1}, \ldots, T_{m}$ (drawn as empty rectangles for timed transitions or bars for immediate transitions): A transition can fire, taking one token from each input place and putting one token in each output place.
- Directed arcs: An arc connects a place with a transition or vice versa and has an arrowhead to indicate the direction; multiple arcs are possible and indicate that by firing of the involved transition a corresponding number of tokens is taken from the involved input place (for input multiple arc) or put in the involved output place (for output multiple arc); inhibitor arcs with a circle instead of the arrowhead are also possible and indicate that for firing condition no token must be contained in the corresponding place.
Firing rules for a transition are:

1. A transition is enabled (can fire) only if all places with an input arc to the given transition contain at least one token (no token for inhibitor arcs).
2. Only one transition can fire at a given time; the selection occurs according to the embedded Markov chain describing the stochastic behavior of the PN.
3. Firing of a transition can be immediate or occurs after a time interval $\tau_{i j}>0$ (timed PN); $\tau_{i j}>0$ is in general a random variable (stochastic PN ) with distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)$ when firing occurs from transition $T_{i}$ to place $P_{j}$ (yielding a Markov process for $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda_{i j} x}$, i. e. with transition rate $\lambda_{i j}$, or a semi-Markov process for $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)$ arbitrary, with $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(0)=0$ ).
Considering Table 6.1 on p.171, practically only Markov processes (i. e. constant failure \& repair rates) will occur in Petri nets for reliability applications. Two further concepts useful when dealing with Petri nets are those of marking and reachability:

- A marking $M=\left\{m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}\right\}$ gives the number $m_{i}$ of token in the place $P_{i}$ at a given time point and defines thus the state of the PN.
- $M_{j}$ is immediately reachable from $M_{i}$, if $M_{j}$ can be obtained by firing a transition enabled by $M_{i}$.With $M_{0}$ as marking at time $t=0, M_{1}, \ldots, M_{k}$ are all the (different) marking reachable from $M_{0}$; they define the PN states and give the reachability tree, from which, the diagram of transition rates of the corresponding Markov model follows. Figure 6.44 gives two examples of reliability structures with corresponding PN.


Figure 6.44 Top: Reliability block diagram (a), diagram of the transition rates (c), Petri net (b), and reachability tree (d) for a repairable 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with two identical elements, const. failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}, \mu\right)$, one repair (restoration) crew $\left(Z_{2}\right.$ down state, Markov proc.) Bottom: Reliability block diagram (a), diagram of the transition rates (c), Petri net (b), and reachability tree (d) for a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two identical elements and switch in series, constant failure and repair rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{\mathrm{v}}, \mu, \mu_{\mathrm{v}}\right)$, one repair crew, repair priority on switch, no further failures at system down $\left(Z_{1}, Z_{3}, Z_{4}\right.$ down states, Markov process)# 6.9.6 Numerical Reliability and Availability Computation 

Investigation of large series-parallel structures or of complex systems (for which a reliability block diagram often does not exist) is in general time-consuming and can become mathematically difficult. A large number of computer programs for numerical solution of reliability and availability equations as well as for Monte Carlo simulation have been developed. Such a numerical computation can be, in some cases, the only way to get results. However, although appealing, numerical solutions can deliver only case-by-case solutions and can cause problems (instabilities in the presence of sparse matrices, prohibitive run times for Monte Carlo simulation of rare events or if confidence limits are required). As a general rule, analytically exact solutions (Sections 6.2-6.6, 6.8) or approximate expressions (Sections 6.7, 6.9.7) should be preferred, wherever possible.

Section 6.9.6.1 discusses requirements for a versatile program for the numerical solution of reliability \& availability equations. Section 6.9.6.2 gives basic considerations on Monte Carlo simulation and introduces an approach useful for rare events.

### 6.9.6.1 Numerical Computation of System's Reliability and Availability

Analytical solution of algebraic or differential/integral equations for reliability and availability computation of large or complex systems can become time-consuming. Software tools exist to solve this kind of problems. From such a software package one generally expects high completeness, usability, robustness, integrity, and portability (Table 5.4 on p.162). The following is a comprehensive list of requirements:

## General requirements:

1. Support interface with CAD/CAE and configuration management packages.
2. Provide a large component data bank with the possibility for manufacturer and company-specific labeling, and storage of non application-specific data.
3. Support different failure rate models [2.20 - 2.30].
4. Have flexible output (regarding medium, sorting capability, weighting), graphic interface, single \& multi-user capability, high usability \& integrity.
5. Be portable to different platforms.

Specific for nonrepairable (up to system failure) systems:

1. Consider reliability block diagrams (RBD) of arbitrary complexity and with a large number of elements $(\geq 1,000)$ and levels $(\geq 10)$; possibility for any element to appear more than once in the RBD; automatic editing of series and parallel models; powerful algorithms to handle complex structures; constant or time dependent failure rate for each element; possibility to handle as element macro-structures or items with more than one failure mode.
2. Easy editing of application-specific data, with user features such as:

- automatic computation of the ambient temperature at component level with freely selectable temperature difference between elements,- freely selectable duty cycle from the system level downwards,
- global change of environmental and quality factors, manual selection of stress factors for tradeoff studies or risk assessment, manual introduction of field data and of default values for component families or assemblies.

3. Allow reuse of elements with arbitrary complexity in a RBD (libraries).

# Specific for repairable systems: 

1. Consider elements with constant failure rate and constant or arbitrary repair rate, i. e. handle Markov and (as far as possible) semi-regenerative processes.
2. Have automatic generation of the transition rates $\rho_{i j}$ for Markov model and of the involved embedded semi-Markov transition probabilities $Q_{i j}(x)$ for systems with constant failure rates, one repair crew, and arbitrary repair rate (starting e. g. from a given set of successful paths); automatic generation and solution of the equations describing the system's behavior.
3. Allow different repair strategies (first-in first-out, one repair crew or other).
4. Use sophisticated algorithms for quick inversion of sparse matrices.
5. Consider at least 10,000 states for the exact solution of the asymptotic \& steady-state availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ and mean time to system failure $M T T F_{S i}$.
6. Support investigations yielding approximate expressions (macro-structures, totally independent elements, cutting states or other, see Section 6.7.1).

A scientific software package satisfying many of the above requirements has been developed at the Reliability Lab. of the ETH [2.50]. Refinement of the requirements is possible. For basic reliability computation, commercial programs are available [2.50-2.60]. Specialized programs are e.g. in [2.6,2.18,2.59,2.85,6.23,6.24, 6.43; considerations on numerical methods for reliability evaluation are e.g. in [2.56].

### 6.9.6.2 Monte Carlo Simulations

The Monte Carlo technique is a numerical method based on a probabilistic interpretation of quantities obtained from algorithmically generated random variables. It was introduced 1949 by N. Metropolis and S. Ulman [6.31]. Since this time, a large amount of literature has been published, see e.g. [6.4, 6.13, 6.50, A7.18]. This section deals with some basic considerations on Monte Carlo simulation useful for reliability analysis and gives an approach for the simulation of rare events which avoids the difficulty of time truncation because of amplitude quantization of the digital numbers used.

For reliability purposes, a Monte Carlo simulation can basically be used to estimate a value (e. g. an unknown probability) or simulate (reproduce) the stochastic process describing the behavior of a complex system. It can take care of (known or assumed) deterministic or aleatory variations of input variables or system parameters. In this sense, a Monte Carlo simulation is useful to achieve numerical results, verify numerically an analytical solution, get an idea of the possible time behavior of a complex system or determine interactions among variables (numerical sensitivityanalysis). Two main problems related to Monte Carlo simulation are the generation of uniformly distributed random numbers $\left(\zeta_{0}, \zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{2^{n}-1}\right.$ with $\left.p_{i}=1 / 2^{n}\right)$ scaled on $[0,1)$ and the transformation of these numbers in random variables with prescribed distribution functions. A congruential relation

$$
\zeta_{n+1}=\left(a \zeta_{n}+b\right) \quad \bmod c
$$

where mod is used for modulo, is frequently used to generate pseudorandom numbers [6.29] (for simplicity, pseudo will be omitted in the following). Transformation to an arbitrary distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)$ is often performed with help of the inverse function $\mathrm{F}^{-1}(x)$, see Example A6.18 on p. 464. The method of the inverse function is simple but not necessarily good enough for critical applications.

A further question arising with Monte Carlo simulation is that of how many repetitions $n$ must be run to have an estimate of the unknown quantity within a given interval $\pm \varepsilon$ at a given confidence level $\gamma$. For the case of an event with probability $p$ and assuming $n$ sufficiently large as well as $p$ or (1-p) not very small $(\min (n p, n(1-p)) \geq 5)$, Eq. (A6.152) yields for $p$ known

$$
n=\left(\frac{t_{(1+\gamma) / 2}}{\varepsilon}\right)^{2} p(1-p) \quad \text { i. e. } \quad n_{\max }=\left(\frac{t_{(1+\gamma) / 2}}{2 \varepsilon}\right)^{2} \text { for } p=0.5
$$

where $t_{(1+\gamma) / 2}$ is the $(1+\gamma) / 2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution; for instance, $t_{(1+\gamma) / 2} \approx 1.645$ for $\gamma=0.9$ and $\approx 1.96$ for $\gamma=0.95$ (Appendix A9.1). For $p$ totally unknown, the value $p=0.5$ has to be taken. Knowing the number of realizations $k$ in $n$ trials, Eq. (A8.43) can be used to find confidence limits for $p$.

To simulate (reproduce) a time-homogeneous Markov process, following procedure is useful, starting by a transition in state $Z_{i}$ at the arbitrary time $t=0$ :

1. Select the next state $Z_{j}$ to be visited by generating an event with probability

$$
\mathscr{P}_{i j}=\frac{\rho_{i j}}{\rho_{i}}, \quad j \neq i \quad\left(\mathscr{P}_{i i} \equiv 0\right), \quad \rho_{i}=\sum_{j=0, j \neq i}^{m} \rho_{i j}, \quad \sum_{j=0, j \neq i}^{m} \mathscr{P}_{i j}=1
$$

according to the embedded Markov chain (for uniformly distributed random numbers $\xi$ scaled on $[0,1)$ it holds that $\operatorname{Pr}\{\xi \leq x\}=x$, i.e . $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{x_{i}<\xi \leq x_{j}\right\}=x_{j}-x_{i}=p_{i j}$ ).
2. Find the stay time (sojourn time) in state $Z_{i}$ up to jump to the next state $Z_{j}$ by generating a random variable with distribution function (Example A6.18)

$$
\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)=1-e^{-\rho_{i} x}
$$

3. Jump to state $Z_{j}$.

Extension to semi-Markov processes is easy $\left(\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)\right.$ arbitrary, $\left.\mathrm{F}_{i j}(0)=0\right)$. For semi regenerative processes, states visited during a cycle must be considered (see e.g. Fig. A7.11 on p. 527). The advantage of this procedure is that transition sequence \& stay (sojourn) times are generated with only a few random numbers. A disadvantage is that stay times are truncated because of the amplitude quantization of $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)$.

Figure 6.45 Block diagram of the programmable generator for renewal processes

To avoid truncation problems, in particular when dealing with rare events distributed on the time axis, an alternative approach implemented as hardware generator for semi-Markov processes in [A7.2 (Ph. D. thesis 1974)] can be used. To illustrate the basic idea, Fig. 6.45 shows the structure of the generator for renewal processes. The generator is driven by a clock $\Delta t=\Delta x$ and consists of three main elements:

- a generator for uniformly distributed pseudorandom numbers $\zeta_{0}, \zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{2^{n}-1}$ with $p_{i}=1 / 2^{n}$ scaled on $\{0,1)$, for digital computers;
- a comparator, comparing at each clock the present random number $\xi_{i}$ with $\lambda_{k}$ and giving an output pulse, marking a renewal point, for $\xi_{i}<\lambda_{k}$;
- a function generator creating $\lambda_{k}$ and starting with $\lambda_{1}$ at each renewal point.

It can be shown ( $\lambda_{k} \equiv w_{k}$ in [A7.2 (1974 \& 1977)]) that for

$$
\lambda_{k}=(\mathrm{F}(k \Delta x)-\mathrm{F}((k-1) \Delta x)) /(1-\mathrm{F}((k-1) \Delta x)), \quad k=1,2, \ldots, \mathrm{~F}(0)=0
$$

the sequence of output pulses is a realization of an ordinary renewal process with distribution function $\mathrm{F}(k \Delta x)$ for times $(\tau)$ between consecutive renewal points. $\lambda_{k}$ is the failure rate related to the arithmetic random variable $(\tau)$ with distribution function $\mathrm{F}(k \Delta x), \lambda_{k} \equiv \lambda(k)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau=k \Delta x \mid \tau>(k-1) \Delta x\}$, as given on p.443. Generated random times $(\tau)$ are not truncated, because the last part of $\mathrm{F}(k \Delta x)$ can be approximated by a geometric distribution ( $\lambda_{k}=$ const., Eq. (A6.132)). A software realization of the generator of Fig 6.45 is easy, and hardware limitations can be avoided.

The homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) can be generated using $\lambda_{k}=$ constant, the generated random time interval have then a geometric distribution.

For a non-homogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) with mean value function $\mathrm{M}(t)$, generation can be based on considerations given on pp. 532 - 35: for fixed $t=T$, generate $k$ according to a Poisson distribution with parameter $\mathrm{M}(T)$ (Eq. (A7.190), similar as for Eq. (6.306)), and then $k$ random variables with density $\mathrm{m}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T)$; the ordered values are the $k$ occurrence times of the NHPP on $(0, T)$.

The extension to semi-Markov processes is easy [A7.2 (Ph. D. thesis 1974)].# 6.9.7 Approximate Expressions for Large, Complex Systems 

Approximate expressions for the reliability and availability of large series-parallel structures, whose elements $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots, E_{n}$ have constant failure and repair rates $\lambda_{i}, \mu_{i}, i=1, \ldots, n$, have been developed in Section 6.7, in particular using macrostructures (Table 6.10) or totally independent elements (Table 6.9). Thereby, based on the results obtained for the repairable 1-out-of-2 redundancy (Eqs. (6.88) and (6.94) with $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$ ), a series, parallel, or simple series - parallel structure is considered as a one-item structure with constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{S 0} \& \mu_{S}$ for calculations, and integrated into a further macro-structure bottom up to system level.

Expressions for small complex systems, for which a reliability block diagram either does not exist or can't be reduced to a series-parallel structure with independent elements, have been carefully investigated in Sections 6.8.2-6.8.7, assuming no further failures at system down and taking care of imperfect switching, incomplete coverage, more than 1 failure mode, reconfiguration strategy \& common cause failures. A general procedure for modeling such systems has been given on pp. 277-79.

For large, complex systems, investigation methods and tools are still in progress. Clustering of states (p.229) is often possible by conserving exact results. Cutting states with more than one failure (p.229) is applicable (see e.g. numerical evaluations on pp. $237 \& 269$ ). State merging in Markov transition diagrams is conceivable, but limited to the case in which transitions from a block of merged states to an unmerged state have same transition rates [6.40]. To give a feeling, consider elimination of $Z_{0}$. in Fig.6.25a by introducing between $Z_{0} \& Z_{2}$ the transition rate

$$
\lambda \lambda_{\sigma}(\lambda+\mu) /\left[\lambda\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu\right)+\lambda_{\sigma}(\lambda+\mu)\right]
$$

Also limited is the exploitation of symmetries in Markov transition diagrams [6.32].
A general procedure delivering often useful upper bounds on the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the asymptotic $\&$ steady-state availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ at system level is, for large, complex \& coherent systems (pp. 57-58, 531-32):

1. Assume totally independent elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$ (p.280) with constant failure rates $\lambda_{i}$ and constant repair rates $\mu_{i} \gg \lambda_{i}, i=1, \ldots, n$.
2. Calculate $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ per Eq. (2.48); i. e. substituting in the structure function $\phi\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$, given by Eqs. (2.42) or (2.44), $\zeta_{i}$ with

$$
P A_{S i}=\mu_{i} /\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

3. Calculate $M T T F_{S 0}$ from

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx M T T R_{S_{\text {series elem. }}} \cdot P A_{S} /\left(1-P A_{S}\right)
$$

i. e. using Eq. (6.295) by assuming

$$
M U T_{S} \approx M T T F_{S 0} \text { and } M D T_{S} \approx M T T R_{S_{\text {series elem. }}}
$$

with $M T T R_{S_{\text {series elem. }}}$ from Eq. (4.7) for the series elements only (pp. 121-24).4. Moreover, on the basis of results for the 1-out-of-2 redundancy (pp. 198 - 99)

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{-I / M T T F_{S 0}} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \approx P A_{S}
$$

can often be assumed in practical applications at system level.
$M U T_{S} \approx M T T F_{S 0}$ is generally valid. $M D T_{S} \approx M T T R_{S_{\text {series elem. }}}$ can often be used, as discussed on p.124. However, a $k$-out-of- $n$ active redundancy without series element (Tables 6.9 (IE, $n$ repair crews) \& 6.10 (MS, only one repair crew)) would lead to

$$
M T T F_{S 0}{ }_{I E} / M T T F_{S 0}{ }_{M S} \approx(n-k)!
$$

and

$$
\left(1-P A_{S 0}{ }_{I E}\right) /\left(1-P A_{S 0}{ }_{M S}=1 /(n-k+1)!\right.
$$

Nevertheless, considering that a system has practically always series elements, and $(n-k)$ remains small, the assumption of totally independent elements leads often to useful upper bounds on $M T T F_{S 0} \& P A_{S}=A A_{S}$.

# 6.10 Human Reliability 

For large and/or complex equipment \& systems, human and ergonomic aspects/factors can have a great influence on reliability, maintainability, availability, and safety. Disregarding of design or manufacturing flaws, experience shows that in emergency situations more than $80 \%$ of the safety related system failures are caused by human errors during operation or maintenance (false detection, diagnosis, action planing or execution). Although the behavior of a homogenous human population is often known, the reaction of a single person can become unpredictable, in particular when under stress or faced unexpected events (pp.10, 158). Thus,
wherever possible, humans should be bypassed in safety critical decisions or, at least, two-step actions should be introduced (first step reversible).

Moreover, although training and motivation of operators \& maintainers is important, extensive design guidelines \& design reviews are necessary to avoid human errors or limit their effect, e. g. in space, nuclear, military, medical applications [5.14, 6.82].

All tools discussed in Sections 2.6 and 6.1-6.9 are useful to investigate human reliability, in particular FMEA/FMECA, FTA, event trees (including human errors as possible causes), and stochastic models. Procedures to evaluate the probability of human errors, in view also of risk assessment, have been developed since the 1970's [6.83]; many computer supported, e.g. REHMS-D [6.78], and most of them for nuclear and aerospace applications, see e.g. [6.71] for a recent extensive review. These procedures can be grouped in two classes based on

- reliability techniques used for hardware (e. g.THERP \& SPAR [6.89 \& 6.75]),
- cognitive human models (e.g. REHMS-D [6.78] \& CREAM [6.76 (1998)]).The method used for the first class (known also as performance prediction) is to partition the task performed by human in subtasks and assign to each subtask a misleading probability; the human error probability can then be expressed as a function of misleading probabilities, from a simple product to elaborated expressions. An extension of this, is to assign constant failure \& repair rates to the human and integrate these in Markov models [6.73]. Cognitive models (known also as accident analysis) are more complex, and consider human functions as based on four subfunctions (sensing, information processing, decision, and response) assisted by a memory, taking care also of the variability of the human performance caused by temporary psychological, physical or environmental changes, see e. g. [6.76 (2009)].

Combination of both techniques is important. However,
modeling must be supported by extensive preventive actions during the development of complex equipment \& systems (as for hardware \& software) and, wherever possible, humans should be bypassed in safety critical decisions (e.g. using majority redundancy also for actuators, or two-step actions).

Section 5.2.5 (pp.158-59) deals with design guidelines useful to avoid human errors or limit their effects. In the following, three structurally new basic models, combining human error probability and time necessary to accomplish a task assigned to a human, are introduced. This, using semi-Markov processes (Appendix A7.6), characterized by the property that given a state $Z_{i}$ entered at time $t$, the next state $Z_{j}$ to be visited is selected with a probability $\mathcal{P}_{i j}$ and the stay time in $Z_{i}$ is a random variable $\tau_{i j}>0$ whose distribution depends only on $Z_{i} \& Z_{j}$, not on $t$ (for instance, $Z_{i}$ is a failure of a redundant element, $\mathcal{P}_{i j}$ an error probability, and $\tau_{i j}$ is lognormally distributed). Markov processes are less appropriate because of their memoryless property. Investigated is reliability, extension to availability is easy (Example 6.31). It turns out that these new models are refinements of those developed for imperfect switching \& incomplete coverage (Figs. $6.25 \& 6.27$ ). However, the processes used here constitute a new subclass of semi-Markov processes called in this book particular semi-Markov processes. For this purpose, all models of this section
assume that no further failure occurs during human intervention (i.e. $Z_{1}$, in Figs.6.46-6.48 \& Example 6.31 is an up state), and consider that reaction times are common to good and wrong decision (footnote on p.296).

similar to the influence of the series element $E_{\mathrm{v}}$ (see Eq. (6.160)). $p_{h}=M_{h}=\lambda_{a}=0$ leads to Eq. (6.157).# 6.11 Risk Management for Repairable Systems 

Besides natural accident/disasters, like earthquakes or floods, to which humankind is often inevitably and dramatically exposed, questions on risk and risk management practically arise in all human activities, at different degree and in a more or less objective form. Some basic considerations on risk, risk awareness \& risk acceptance have been given on pp. 9 - 11. After a short introduction, this section focuses on risk and risk management related to complex repairable equipment \& systems for which external influences (human or other) are important, discussing methods \& tools for risk assessment and risk mitigation with particular attention to new models for risk analysis, and by introducing the concept of mean time to accident/disaster (MTTA). Not considered is risk \& risk management in relation to project management, security, sociological, ethical \& communicational aspects, as well as in climate, health and financial fields; for all these one can refer e. g. to [6.102 (62198), 6.99, $6.105,6.106,6.108,6.109,1.26]$, as well as $[6.110,6.112,6.97]$, and pp. 9-11.

### 6.11.1 Introduction

From an engineering point of view, risk management can be defined as
all planned and systematic activities to assess (identify, analyze, evaluate) potential or real risks, to minimize or at least mitigate their effects/consequences, and to communicate risks (see also p.398).

Risk being an undesirable situation involving exposure to danger, i. e. to possible considerable harm (accident/disaster), with injury to persons or unacceptable consequences to material, environment or other. The magnitude of a risk is often measured in term of its probability of occurrence and the severity of its consequences (p. 10, Fig. 2.13). *) From these considerations, and for the purpose of this book,
risk management is closely related to safety management, and thus, risk analysis to safety (as technical safety, p. 9 or 399) analysis.

Exposure to risk appears everywhere with human activities, at different degree and in a more or less objective form. A broad literature is thus concerned with risk management, e. g. [1.3,1.21,1.26, 6.91-6.112] to begin with; often rather theoretically oriented and focused on technical [6.107], financial [6.97], health [6.112], and, more recently, psychological \& philosophical $[6.95,6.98,6.100,6.105,6.106,6.108,6.109]$ aspects. Also are international standards on risk management [6.102, 6.103], as well as STDs \& HDBKs on safety management, e.g. [A2.10 (MIL-STD-882), 5.51], available,

[^0]
[^0]:    *) Hazard is often used for risk or danger, to better point out the random character involved. However, if an efficient barrier exits, the hazard remain but the risk can disappear; thus, more appropriately, hazard is a potential cause for a risk or danger and can also be an event.This section focuses on risk management related to complex equipment and systems for which humans are an important part of. Basically, all aspects of human reliability discussed on pp. 158-59 and 294-98 apply here. However, more than in reliability analysis, uncertainties play an important role in risk management, because of the consequences that an undesirable event (hazard) can have and of the low number of statistically identical items often existing (e.g. in space or nuclear);
uncertainties are caused, basically, by lack of knowledge on the item or on external influence factors (epistemic uncertainties), or by the variability between statistically identical items \& situations (aleatory uncertainties).

For instance, for a large population of statistically identical items, the failure rate (pp. 4-5) is given by the shape of Fig. 1.2 (aleatory uncertainty); however, if for another set of similar items particular early failures are present, or an higher stress is applied, the shape of Fig. 1.2 will be changed (epistemic uncertainty). From this,
the necessity to use stochastic models for risk management, to carefully verify models validity, and, in particular, to support this with failure modes \& effects analysis tools (p.301) to investigate barriers able to avoid or at least mitigate risk causes or effects/consequences. ${ }^{*}$ )

Also important for risk management (analysis and mitigation) is the identification of which parts of the system are susceptible to cause critical failures (causing a safety problem), as intrinsic failure or as failure triggered by an external event. This lead to the concept of risk importance measures introduced in [6.94] as

$$
\mathrm{I}_{i}(t)=\partial \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) / \partial \mathrm{R}_{i}(t)
$$

where $\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$ is the reliability function of element $E_{i}$, yielding, for instance, $\mathrm{I}_{i}(t)=$ $\mathrm{R}_{1}(t) \cdot \mathrm{R}_{2}(t) \cdot \ldots \cdot \mathrm{R}_{i-1}(t) \cdot \mathrm{R}_{i+1}(t) \cdot \ldots \cdot \mathrm{R}_{n}(t)$ for a series structure with independent elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$ (Eqs.(2.17), (6.60)).

Risk situations yielding to an accident/disaster, often result from a concatenation of events (failure, external event, error, secondary failure). The environment (workplace, organization) has great influence on the propensity for human errors; however, even if shown by some accident analyses [6.76(1998)], it seem difficult to accept that human error is noise with respect to the influence of environment in which accident/disaster has occurred, this because human is often the main (final) cause.

In the context of complex equipment \& systems, risk management responsibility is with the project's manager; however, risk management requires
a close cooperation between all people involved in a project.
The risk management process defined in ISO 31000[6.103] focuses on: Communication \& Consultation, Establishing the Context, Risk Assessment, Risk Treatment, and Risk Monitoring \& Review. This process is general, and applies to products and

[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ For some epistemic uncertainties, Eq.(A6.32) can often be used.services as well. The 5 elements involved are considered in ISO/IEC 31010 [6.103], focused on the risk assessment process by considering carefully its main steps:

Risk Identification, Risk Analysis, and Risk Evaluation, as well as Risk Documentation, Monitoring \& Reviewing during all life cycle phases,
and the related assessment techniques (Sections 5 \& 6, Appendices A \& B of 31010).
Important risk analysis tools have been introduced in Chapters $2 \& 6$; in particular, FMEA / FMECA (pp.72-75), FTA \& BDD (pp.76, 280-82 \& 283-85) and ET (p. 286), as well as Markov, semi-Markov \& semi regenerative processes for modeling purposes. Basic models for risk analysis are introduced in Section 6.11.2. Section 6.11.3 deals then with barriers to avoid or mitigate risks;
to simplify models, only critical failures (affecting safety), intrinsic or triggered by external events, are considered.

# 6.11.2 Risk Modeling, MTTA, S(t) 

This section introduces five structurally new basic models useful for risk investigation, with the aim to calculate the mean time to accident / disaster MTTA and the related safety function $\mathrm{S}(t)$ (reliability function with respect to accident /disaster) ${ }^{*}$ ) as function of failure \& repair rates for critical failures $\left(\lambda_{c r} \& \mu_{c r}\right)$, frequencies $f_{e i}$ of external events (attacks, natural catastrophes), success probabilities $p_{b i}$ of related barriers, success probability $p_{f s}$ of a fail-safe procedure, probability $p_{h}$ of human error, and corresponding reaction times. This, to support sensitivity analyses. To simplify models it will be assumed
that elements causing critical failures, possible human errors or other external events (attacks, natural catastrophes) affecting system's safety, as well as barriers to avoid or at least mitigate risk causes or effects/ consequences have been assessed, in particular using FMEA / FMECA, FTA, BDD and ETA (pp.72-75, 76 \& 280-82, 283-85 and 286), and that only these elements and events are considered.

These preliminary investigations are important to reduce or limit uncertainties. However, it must be pointed out that transfer of knowledge or lack of knowledge into probabilities muss remain as objective as possible, and expert judgments can help.

As for human reliability (pp. 295 - 98) the models used here are based on semiMarkov processes (Appendix A7.6, remark on p. 522), characterized by the property that given a state $Z_{i}$ entered at time $t$, the next state $Z_{j}$ to be visited is selected with a probability $\mathcal{P}_{i j}$ and the stay time in $Z_{i}$ is a random variable $\tau_{i j}>0$ whose distribution depends only on $Z_{i}$ and $Z_{j}$, not on $t$. For instance, $Z_{i}$ is a failure of a redundant element, $\mathcal{P}_{i j}$ an error probability, and $\tau_{i j}$ is lognormally distributed (use

[^0]

turns out that these processes constitute a new subclass of semi-Markov processes called in this book particular semi-Markov processes (allowing thus the use of the simple mathematical tools known for Markov processes).

For this purpose, all models of this section consider that reaction times are common (as for human reliability on pp. 295-96), and assume
that neither failures nor external events occur during human intervention (state $Z_{1}$ ), fail-safe procedure $\left(Z_{2} \cdot\right)$, restart $\left(Z_{F S}\right)$, and barriers activation $\left(Z_{E}, Z_{E}, Z_{E_{1}}, Z_{E_{2}}\right) ;{ }^{*}$ moreover, fail-safe state $Z_{F S}$, entered after a successful fail-safe procedure, is an up state for safety (independently if fail-safe has been activated by intrinsic failure $\left(Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2} \cdot\right)$, human error $\left(Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2} \cdot\right)$, or not stopped external event $\left(Z_{E}, Z_{E}, Z_{E_{1}}, Z_{E_{2}} \rightarrow Z_{2} \cdot\right)$ ), and a restart (distribution $\mathrm{F}_{r}(x)$, mean $M_{r}$ ) is necessary to bring the system in the operating state $\mathrm{Z}_{1} .{ }^{* *}$ )

Consider first the case of Fig. 6.46 on p. 296, i. e. a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with possible human error at failure (two identical elements, const. failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{c r} \& \mu_{c r}$, probability $p_{h}$ for false action causing failure or disconnection of not failed element and $\tau_{h}>0$ (distribution $\left.\mathrm{F}_{h}(x)$, mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{h}\right]=M_{h}<\infty\right)$ as time to take the decision and make the corresponding action). Furthermore, let $p_{f s}$ be the success probability of the fail-safe procedure (duration $\tau_{f s}>0$, distribution $\mathrm{F}_{f s}(x)$, mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{f s}\right]=M_{f s}<\infty$ ) and $\tau_{r}>0$ the restart time after a successful fail-safe procedure (distribution $\mathrm{F}_{r}(x)$, mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{r}\right]=M_{r}<\infty$ ). Considering above general assumption and constant failure \& repair rates ( $\lambda_{c r} \& \mu_{c r}$ ), the system can be investigated using a particular semi-Markov process (footnote on p. 296). Figure 6.49 gives the corresponding state transitions diagram for safety calculation. In $Z_{A}$ the system is down for accident/disaster; $\mathrm{Z}_{F S}$ is a system down state for reliability, not for safety; in $Z_{2}$. the fail-safe $\&$ in $\mathrm{Z}_{F S}$ the restart procedure is running. From Fig. 6.49 and Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.173), $M T T A_{S 0}$ (mean time to accident/disaster for system entering $Z_{0}$ at $t=0$ ) follows as solution of

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M_{0}=T_{0}+M_{1} \cdot, M_{1} \cdot=T_{1} \cdot+\left(1-p_{h}\right) M_{1}+p_{h} M_{2} \cdot, M_{2} \cdot=T_{2} \cdot+p_{f s} M_{F S} \\
& M_{1}=T_{1}+\left(M_{0} \mu_{c r}+M_{2} \cdot \lambda_{c r}\right) /\left(\lambda_{c r}+\mu_{c r}\right), M_{F S}=T_{F S}+M_{1}
\end{aligned}
$$

with $M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}, T_{i} \stackrel{\infty}{\leftarrow}_{0}\left(1-\mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)\right) d x, \mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)=\Sigma_{j} \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ (Eqs. (A7.166) \& (A7.165)). Considering Fig. 6.49 it follows that $T_{0}=1 / 2 \lambda_{c r}, T_{1} \cdot=M_{h}, T_{1}=1 /\left(\lambda_{c r}+\mu_{c r}\right), T_{2} \cdot=M_{f s}$ $\& T_{F S}=M_{r}$, yielding

$$
\begin{aligned}
M T T A_{S 0} & =\frac{(\lambda+\mu)\left(1+2 \lambda M_{h}\right)+2 \lambda\left(1-p_{h}\right)+2 \lambda\left(M_{f s}+M_{r} p_{f s}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu p_{h}\right)-\lambda p_{f s}\left(1+2 \lambda M_{h}-2 p_{h}\right)}{2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\mu p_{h}\right)\left(1-p_{f s}\right)} \\
& \approx \frac{\mu\left(1+2 \lambda\left(M_{h}+p_{h} M_{f s}+p_{h} p_{f s} M_{r}\right)\right)}{2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\mu p_{h}\right)\left(1-p_{f s}\right)} \approx \frac{\mu}{2 \lambda\left(\lambda+\mu p_{h}\right)\left(1-p_{f s}\right)}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& \lambda=\lambda_{c r} \\
& \mu=\mu_{c r}^{\prime}
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure 6.49 State transitions diagram for safety calculation of a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy (only critical failures, 2 identical elements, constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{c r} \& \mu_{c r}$ ) with incomplete human performance (probability $p_{h}$ for a false action yielding $Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2}$ ) and failsafe procedure (success probability $p_{f s}$ yielding $Z_{2} \rightarrow Z_{F S}$ ); $Z_{A}$ down state (accident/disaster), $Z_{F S}$ fail-safe state (down for reliability, not for safety), particular semi-Markov process

Approximations consider $0 \leq p_{h}, p_{f s} \leq 1,2 \lambda M_{f s}, 2 \lambda M_{h}, 2 \lambda M_{r} \ll 1$, and $2 \lambda \ll \mu$. $p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ yields Eq. (6.317), see Eq. (6.318) for a discussion. $p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ and $p_{h}=M_{h}=0$ yield Eq. (6.92) with $\lambda_{r}=\lambda . \quad p_{f s}=1$ leads to

$$
M T T A_{S 0}=\infty \text {, assuring that an accident/disaster cannot occur. }
$$

The safety function $S(t)$ (reliability function with respect to accident/disaster, i. e. referred to critical failures) can be obtained from Fig. 6.49 \& Tab. 6.2 or Eq. (A7.172); however,

$$
\mathrm{S}(t) \approx e^{-t / M T T A_{S 0}}
$$

can often be used in practical applications (see e.g. Eq. (6.94)).
As a second example consider the case of Fig. 6.49 by assuming no human error, but that an external event (e.g. attack or natural catastrophe) can occur with frequency $f_{e}$ and the success probability of the corresponding barrier is $p_{b}$, with a reaction time $\tau_{b}>0$ with distribution $\mathrm{F}_{b}(x)$ and mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{b}\right]=M_{b}<\infty$; $\tau_{b}$ includes external event reaction time. Because of the constant (time independent) frequency, occurrence of the external event can be described by a timehomogeneous Poisson process, and $f_{e}$ can be replaced by a failure rate $\lambda_{e}=f_{e}$. The external event acts with $f_{e} \& p_{b}$ on $Z_{0}$ (both elements operating) or $f_{e} \cdot \& p_{b^{\prime}}$ on $Z_{1}$ (one element operating, the other under repair); often one can assume $f_{e^{\prime}}=f_{e} \&$ $p_{b^{\prime}}=p_{b}$. It causes system down for reliability, not for safety ( $Z_{E} \rightarrow Z_{2} \cdot$ or $Z_{E} \cdot \rightarrow Z_{2} \cdot$ ), and activates the fail-safe procedure. Considering the general assumption on p. 302, constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{c r} \& \mu_{c r}\right)$, constant event frequencies $\left(f_{e} \& f_{e^{\prime}}\right)$, and that $\tau_{b} \& \tau_{b^{\prime}}$ are common to barriers success and failure, similar for $\tau_{f s}$, the system can be investigated using a particular semi-Markov process (footnote on p. 296). Figure 6.50 gives the corresponding state transitions diagram for safety calculation. In $Z_{A}$ the system is down for accident/disaster; $\mathrm{Z}_{F S}$ is a system down state for reliability, not for safety; in $Z_{2}$. the fail-safe \& in $Z_{F S}$ the restart procedure is running. From Fig. 6.50 and Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.173), $M T T A_{S 0}$ (mean time to

& M_{F S}=T_{F S}+M_{1}, \quad M_{2^{\prime}}=T_{2^{\prime}}+p_{f s} M_{F S}, \quad M_{E^{\prime}}=T_{E^{\prime}}+p_{b^{\prime}} M_{1}+\left(1-p_{b^{\prime}}\right) M_{2^{\prime}} \\
& M_{1}=T_{1}+\left(M_{0} \mu_{c r}+M_{2^{\prime}} \lambda_{c r}+M_{E^{\prime}} \lambda_{e^{\prime}}\right) /\left(\lambda_{c r}+\lambda_{e^{\prime}}+\mu_{c r}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}, T_{i} \stackrel{\leftrightarrow}{\leftrightarrow} \mathrm{Q}_{i}\left(1-\mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)\right) d x, \mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)=\Sigma_{j} \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ (Eqs.(A7.166) \& (A7.165)). Considering Fig. 6.50 it follows that $T_{0}=1 /\left(2 \lambda_{c r}+\lambda_{e}\right), T_{1}=1 /\left(\lambda_{c r}+\lambda_{e^{\prime}}+\mu_{c r}\right)$, $T_{2} \cdot=M_{f s}, T_{E}=M_{b}, T_{E^{\prime}}=M_{b}, \& T_{F S}=M_{r}$, yielding

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T A_{S 0}=\frac{a d+b c}{e b-\mu d} \\
& \text { with } a=1+\lambda\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right)+\lambda_{e^{\prime}}\left(M_{b^{\prime}}+\left(1-p_{b^{\prime}}\right)\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right)\right) \\
& b=\lambda+\lambda_{e^{\prime}}+\mu-\lambda p_{f s}-\left(p_{b^{\prime}}+p_{f s}\left(1-p_{b^{\prime}}\right)\right) \lambda_{e^{\prime}}, \quad d=p_{f s}\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e}+2 \lambda \\
& \mathrm{c}=1+\lambda_{e}\left(M_{b}+\left(1-p_{b}\right)\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right)\right), \quad e=2 \lambda+\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e}, \quad \lambda=\lambda_{c r}, \mu=\mu_{c r}
\end{aligned}
$$

$p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
M T T A_{S 0} & =\frac{2 \lambda\left(1+\lambda_{e^{\prime}} M_{b^{\prime}}\right)+\left(1+\lambda_{e} M_{b}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu+\left(1-p_{b^{\prime}}\right) \lambda_{e^{\prime}}\right)}{\left(2 \lambda+\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu+\left(1-p_{b^{\prime}}\right) \lambda_{e^{\prime}}\right)-2 \lambda \mu} \\
& \approx \frac{3 \lambda+\mu+\left(1-p_{b^{\prime}}\right) \lambda_{e^{\prime}}}{2 \lambda^{2}+\mu\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e}} \approx \frac{\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}+\mu\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Approximations consider $\lambda_{e}, \lambda_{e^{\prime}} \ll \lambda \ll \mu / 3$ and $\lambda_{e^{\prime}} M_{b^{\prime}}, \lambda_{e} M_{b} \ll 1 . \quad p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ and $\lambda_{e}=\lambda_{e^{\prime}}=0$ or $p_{b}=p_{b^{\prime}}=1 \& M_{b}=M_{b^{\prime}}=0$ yield Eq. $$

Eq. (6.157) with the external event on $Z_{0}$ or $Z_{1}$ acting as a series element.

The safety function $\mathrm{S}(t)$ (reliability function with respect to accident/disaster, i. e. referred to critical failures) can be obtained from Fig. 6.50 \& Tab. 6.2 or Eq. (A7.172); however, Eq. (6.330) can often be used in practical applications (see e.g. Eq.(6.94)).

As a third example consider the system of Fig. 6.50 by assuming that two independent external events (attacks or natural catastrophes) can occur with frequencies $f_{e_{1}} \& f_{e_{2}}$, with success probabilities of the corresponding barriers $p_{b_{1}} \& p_{b_{2}}$ and reaction times $\tau_{b_{1}} \& \tau_{b_{2}}>0$ with distributions $\mathrm{F}_{b_{1}}(x) \& \mathrm{~F}_{b_{2}}(x)$ and means $M_{b_{1}} \& M_{b_{2}}<\infty$ ( $\tau_{b_{l}}$ include external events reaction times). Because of constant (time independent) frequencies $f_{e_{1}} \& f_{e_{2}}$, occurrences of external events can be described by an homogeneous Poisson processes, and $f_{e_{i}}$ can be replaced by a failure rate $\lambda_{e_{i}}=f_{e_{i}}, i=1,2$. It is assumed that external events act only for system in state $Z_{0}$ (both elements operating); extension to the case in which external events act also for system in state $Z_{1}$ (one element operating, the other under repair) is easy (as for Fig. 6.50). Considering the general assumption on p. 302, constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{c r} \& \mu_{c r}\right)$, constant events frequencies $f_{e_{1}} \& f_{e_{2}}$, and that $\tau_{b_{1}} \& \tau_{b_{2}}$ are common to barriers success and failure, similar for $\tau_{f s}$, the system can be investigated using a particular semi-Markov process (footnote on p. 296). Figure 6.51 gives the corresponding state transitions diagram for safety calculation. In $Z_{A}$ the system is down for accident/disaster; $\mathrm{Z}_{F S}$ is a system down state for reliability, not for safety; in $Z_{2}$. the fail-safe \& in $\mathrm{Z}_{F S}$ the restart procedure is running. FromFig. 6.51 and Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.173), $M T T A_{S 0}$ (mean time to accident/disaster for system entering $Z_{0}$ at $t=0$ ) follows as solution of

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M_{0}=T_{0}+\left(M_{1} 2 \lambda_{c r}+M_{E_{1}} \lambda_{e_{1}}+M_{E_{2}} \lambda_{e_{2}}\right) /\left(2 \lambda_{c r}+\lambda_{e_{1}}+\lambda_{e_{2}}\right), \quad M_{F S}=T_{F S}+M_{1} \\
& M_{2^{\prime}}=T_{2^{\prime}}+p_{f s} M_{F S}, \quad M_{E_{i}}=T_{E_{i}}+p_{b_{i}} M_{0}+\left(1-p_{b_{i}}\right) M_{2^{\prime}}, i=1,2 \\
& M_{1}=T_{1}+\left(M_{0} \mu_{c r}+M_{2^{\prime}} \lambda_{c r}\right) /\left(\lambda_{c r}+\mu_{c r}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}, T_{i}={ }_{0}^{i}\left(1-\mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)\right) d x, \mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)=\Sigma_{j} \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ (Eqs.(A7.166) \& (A7.165)). Considering Fig. 6.51 it follows that $T_{0}=1 /\left(2 \lambda_{c r}+\lambda_{e_{1}}+\lambda_{e_{2}}\right), T_{1}=1 /\left(\lambda_{c r}+\mu_{c r}\right)$, $T_{2}=M_{f s}, T_{E_{1}}=M_{b_{1}}, T_{E_{2}}=M_{b_{2}} \& T_{F S}=M_{r}$, yielding

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T A_{S 0}=\frac{a f+b e}{(d-c) f-\mu b} \\
& \text { with } a=1+\lambda_{e_{1}}\left(M_{b_{1}}+\left(1-p_{b_{1}}\right)\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right)\right)+\lambda_{e_{2}}\left(M_{b_{2}}+\left(1-p_{b_{2}}\right)\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right)\right) ; \\
& b=2 \lambda+\lambda_{e_{1}} p_{f s}\left(1-p_{b_{1}}\right)+\lambda_{e_{2}} p_{f s}\left(1-p_{b_{2}}\right), \quad c=\lambda_{e_{1}} p_{b_{1}}+\lambda_{e_{2}} p_{b_{2}}, \\
& d=2 \lambda+\lambda_{e_{1}}+\lambda_{e_{2}}, \quad e=1+\lambda\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right), \quad f=\mu+\left(1-p_{f s}\right) \lambda, \quad \lambda=\lambda_{c r}, \mu=\mu_{c r} .
\end{aligned}
$$

$p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T A_{S 0}=\frac{\left(1+\lambda_{e_{1}} M_{b_{1}}+\lambda_{e_{2}} M_{b_{2}}\right)(\lambda+\mu)+2 \lambda}{(\lambda+\mu)\left(2 \lambda+\lambda_{e_{1}}+\lambda_{e_{2}}-\lambda_{e_{1}} p_{b_{1}}-\lambda_{e_{2}} p_{b_{2}}\right)-2 \lambda \mu} \quad p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0, \lambda=\lambda_{c r}, \mu=\mu_{c r} \\
& \approx \frac{3 \lambda+\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}+\mu\left(\lambda_{e_{1}}\left(1-p_{b_{1}}\right)+\lambda_{e_{2}}\left(1-p_{b_{2}}\right)\right)} \approx \frac{\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}+\mu\left(\lambda_{e_{1}}\left(1-p_{b_{1}}\right)+\lambda_{e_{2}}\left(1-p_{b_{2}}\right)\right)} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Approximations consider $\lambda_{e_{i}}<<\lambda<<\mu / 3$ and $\lambda_{e_{i}} M_{b_{i}}<<1, i=1,2 . \quad p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ and $\lambda_{e_{1}}=\lambda_{e_{2}}=0$ or $p_{b_{1}}=p_{b_{2}}=1 \& M_{b_{1}}=M_{b_{2}}=0$ yield Eq. (6.92) with $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$; however, for $p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ and $p_{b_{1}}=p_{b_{2}}=M_{b_{1}}=M_{b_{2}}=0$, Eqs. (6.336) \& (6.337) yield only approximately Eq. (6.157) with external events on $Z_{0}$ acting as a series element $\lambda_{v}=\lambda_{e_{1}}+\lambda_{e_{2}}$ (Eq. (6.157) if external events act also on $Z_{1}$ (Fig. 6.50)).

$M T T A_{S 0}=\infty$, assuring that an accident/disaster cannot occur.
The safety function $S(t)$ (reliability function with respect to accident / disaster, i. e. referred to critical failures) can be obtained from Fig. 6.51 \& Tab. 6.2 or Eq.(A7.172); however, Eq. (6.330) can often be used in practical applications (see e.g. Eq.(6.94)).

As a fourth example consider the system of Fig. 6.50 by assuming that two independent barriers are available for the external event (attack or natural catastrophe) with occurrence frequency $f_{e}$, success probabilities of corresponding barriers $p_{b_{1}}, p_{b_{2}}$ and reaction times $\tau_{b_{1}}, \tau_{b_{2}}>0$ with distributions $\mathrm{F}_{b_{1}}(x), \mathrm{F}_{b_{2}}(x) \&$ means $M_{b_{1}}, M_{b_{2}}<\infty$ ( $\tau_{b_{i}}$ include external event reaction time).
