& \approx \frac{\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}+\lambda_{e}\left(1-p_{b_{1}}\right)\left(1-p_{b_{2}}\right) \mu}, \quad p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0, \lambda=\lambda_{c r}, \mu=\mu_{c r} \text {. }
\end{aligned}
$$The approximation considers $\lambda_{e}<<\lambda<<\mu / 3$ and $\lambda_{e} M_{b_{1}}<<1, i=1,2 . \quad p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ and $\lambda_{e}=0$ or $p_{b_{1}}=1 \& M_{b_{1}}=0$ or $p_{b_{2}}=1 \& M_{b_{1}}=M_{b_{2}}=0$ yield Eq. (6.92) with $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$; however, for $p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ and $p_{b_{1}}=1$ or $p_{b_{2}}=1$, Eq. (6.92) holds only approximately. $p_{b_{2}}=M_{b_{2}}=0$ yields Eq. (6.332) with $\lambda_{e^{\prime}}=0, p_{b}=p_{b_{1}}$, and $M_{b}=M_{b_{1}}$ (i. e. Eq. (6.334) with $p_{b}=p_{b_{1}}$, and $M_{b}=M_{b_{1}}$ ). $p_{f s}=1$ leads to $c e-\mu b=0$ and

$$
M T T A_{S 0}=\infty \text {, assuring that an accident/disaster cannot occur. }
$$

The safety function $\mathrm{S}(t)$ (reliability function with respect to accident/disaster, i. e. referred to critical failures) can be obtained from Fig. 6.52 \& Tab. 6.2 or Eq. (A7.172); however, Eq. (6.330) can often be used in practical applications (see e.g. Eq.(6.94)).

As a fifth and last basic example consider the combination of the models of Figs. 6.49 and 6.50, i. e. human error with probability $p_{h}$, external event with occurrence frequency $f_{e} \&$ success probability $p_{b}$ of the barrier, and fail-safe procedure with success probability $p_{f s}\left(\tau_{h}, \tau_{b}, \tau_{f s}>0\right.$ as reactions times with distributions $\mathrm{F}_{h}(x), \mathrm{F}_{b}(x), \mathrm{F}_{f s}(x)$ and means $M_{h}, M_{b}, M_{f s}<\infty$ ). Because of the constant (time independent) frequency, occurrence of the external event can be described by an homogeneous Poisson process, and $f_{e}$ can be replaced by a failure rate $\lambda_{e}=f_{e}$. It is assumed that the external event acts only for system in $Z_{0}$ (both elements operating), extension is easy (as for Fig. 6.50). Considering the general assumption on p. 302, constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{c r} \& \mu_{c r}\right)$, constant event frequency $f_{e}$, and that $\tau_{b}$ is common to barrier success and failure, similar for $\tau_{h}$ and $\tau_{f s}$, the system can be investigated using a particular semi-Markov process (footnote on p.296). Figure 6.53 gives the corresponding state transitions diagram for safety calculation. In $Z_{A}$ the system is down for accident/disaster; $\mathrm{Z}_{F S}$ is a system down state for reliability, not for safety; in $Z_{2}$. the fail-safe \& in $Z_{F S}$ the restart procedure is running. From Fig. 6.53 \& Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.173), MTTA $_{S 0}$ (mean time to accident/disaster for system entering $Z_{0}$ at $t=0$ ) follows as solution of

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M_{0}=T_{0}+\left(M_{1} \cdot 2 \lambda_{c r}+M_{E} \lambda_{e}\right) /\left(2 \lambda_{c r}+\lambda_{e}\right), \quad M_{F S}=T_{F S}+M_{1}, \quad M_{2^{\prime}}=T_{2^{\prime}}+p_{f s} M_{F S} \\
& M_{E}=T_{E}+p_{b} M_{0}+\left(1-p_{b}\right) M_{2^{\prime}}, \quad M_{1^{\prime}}=T_{1^{\prime}}+\left(1-p_{h}\right) M_{1}+p_{b} M_{2^{\prime}} \\
& M_{1}=T_{1}+\left(M_{0} \mu_{c r}+M_{2} \cdot \lambda_{c r}\right) /\left(\lambda_{c r}+\mu_{c r}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $M_{i} \equiv M T T F_{S i}, T_{i} \stackrel{\rightharpoonup}{\leftarrow}_{0}\left(1-\mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)\right) d x, \mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)=\Sigma_{j} \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ (Eqs.(A7.166) \& (A7.165)). Considering Fig. 6.53 it follows that $T_{0}=1 /\left(2 \lambda_{c r}+\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}\right), \quad T_{1}=1 /\left(\lambda_{c r}+\mu_{c r}\right), \quad T_{1^{\prime}}=M_{h}$, $T_{2}=M_{f s}, T_{E}=M_{b} \& T_{F S}=M_{r}$, yielding

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T A_{S 0}=\frac{a e+b d}{c e-\mu b} \\
& \text { with } a=1+2 \lambda\left(M_{h}+p_{h}\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right)\right)+\lambda_{e}\left(M_{b}+\left(1-p_{b}\right)\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right)\right) \\
& b=2 \lambda\left(1-p_{b}\right)+2 \lambda p_{h} p_{f s}+p_{f s}\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e}, \quad c=2 \lambda+\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e} \\
& d=1+\lambda\left(M_{f s}+p_{f s} M_{r}\right), \quad e=\mu+\left(1-p_{f s}\right) \lambda, \quad \lambda=\lambda_{c r}, \mu=\mu_{c r}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\lambda_{e}=0$ or $p_{b}=1 \& M_{b}=0$ yield Eq. (6.329). $p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$ yields

Figure 6.53 State transitions diagram for safety calculation of a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy (only critical failures, 2 identical elements, constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{c r} \& \mu_{c r}$ ) with incomplete human performance (probability $p_{h}$ for a false action yielding $Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2}$ ), external event on $Z_{0}$ (frequency $f_{e}=\lambda_{e} \&$ barrier with success probability $p_{b}$ yielding $Z_{E} \rightarrow Z_{0}$ ), and fail-safe procedure (success probability $p_{f s}$ yielding $Z_{2} \rightarrow Z_{F S}$ ); $Z_{A}$ down state (accident/disaster), $Z_{F S}$ fail-safe state (down for reliability, not for safety), particular semi-Markov process

$$
\begin{aligned}
M T T A_{S 0} & =\frac{\left(1+2 \lambda M_{b}+\lambda_{e} M_{b}\right)(\lambda+\mu)+2 \lambda\left(1-p_{b}\right)}{\left(2 \lambda+\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e}\right)(\lambda+\mu)-2 \lambda \mu\left(1-p_{b}\right)} \\
& \approx \frac{\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}+\mu\left(2 \lambda p_{h}+\left(1-p_{b}\right) \lambda_{e}\right)}, \quad p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0, \lambda=\lambda_{c r}, \mu=\mu_{c r}
\end{aligned}
$$

The approximation considers $\lambda_{e} \ll \lambda \ll \mu / 3$ and $\lambda_{e} M_{b}, 2 \lambda M_{b} \ll 1 . \quad p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0$, $\lambda_{e}=0$ or $p_{b}=1 \& M_{b}=0$ yields Eq. (6.317). $p_{f s}=M_{f s}=0, \lambda_{e}=0$ or $p_{b}=1 \& M_{b}=0$ and $p_{h}=M_{h}=0$ yield Eq. (6.92) with $\lambda_{r}=\lambda . \quad p_{f s}=1$ leads to $c e-\mu b=0$ and

$$
M T T A_{S 0}=\infty \text {, assuring that an accident/disaster cannot occur. }
$$

The safety function $S(t)$ (reliability function with respect to accident/disaster, i. e. referred to critical failures) can be obtained from Fig. 6.53 \& Tab. 6.2 or Eq. (A7.172); however, Eq. (6.330) can often be used in practical applications (see e.g. Eq. (6.94)).

Figures 6.49 - 6.53 can be considered as basic models for risk analysis. They can be combined or extended to cover availability (Example 6.31 on p.297), series elements (pp. 220-21, Eqs. (6.257) \& (6.258)), or other needs (still considering footnote on p. 296). Calculation of the safety function $S(t)$ (reliability function with respect to accident/disaster, i. e. referred to critical failures) using the corresponding state transitions diagram and Table 6.2 or Eq. (A7.172) can become time-consuming because of the distribution functions $\mathrm{F}_{h}(x), \mathrm{F}_{f s}(x), \mathrm{F}_{b}(x)$, and $\mathrm{F}_{r}(x)$; however, for practical applications Eq. (6.330) can often be used.

# 6.11.3 Risk Avoidance and Risk Mitigation 

Models as given in Section 6.11.2 can help to evaluate the safety level of a given system. However, considering the uncertainties involved in the risk assessmentprocess, and that risk acceptance has often an important subjective component, planing, realizing \& checking/monitoring barriers that avoid or at least mitigate risk causes or effects/consequences, during the life cycle of a system, is the most effective way to improve protection against harm.

Ideally, the system should be conceived to have a fail-safe behavior (pp. 66, 72, 158) with respect to system intrinsic critical failures and hazards triggered by system's personnel (operation, maintenance, support) or external events (attacks, natural catastrophes). For this purpose, besides appropriate control \& fail-safe procedures, barriers (hardware and/or software) are introduced to avoid or at least mitigate risk causes or effects. Barriers can be active or passive, and are realized for instance by

- observing design rules (Chapter 5), in particular to avoid failure propagation,
- realizing redundancy with different elements, to avoid common cause failures, and by performing a careful investigation of all possible failure modes (as a general rule, redundant elements of fault tolerant equipment and systems must be designed and realized independently from each other, in critical cases with different technologies, tools and personnel, for hardware and software),
- introducing majority redundancies (also for actuators),
- introducing efficient alarm and fail-safe procedures (e. g. shut-off circuitries),
- supporting/bypassing humans by critical decisions, at least with two-step actions,
- improving technical controls through preventive maintenance,
- improving administrative controls,
- improving risk awareness and communication (through motivation \& training),
- restricting access to sensitive parts, and/or reinforcing guarding.

Identification, realization, evaluation, and monitoring of barriers must be performed
during all life cycle phases, using tools for failures (fault) modes \& effects/ consequences analysis (Sections 2.6 \& 6.10), in particular FMEA / FMECA (pp. 72 - 75), FTA (pp. 76, 280-82), BDD (pp.283-85) \& ETA (p.286),
and experience shows that
combination of investigation tools is often necessary to improve solutions.
However, $100 \%$ risk mitigation (i. e. risk avoidance) is generally not possible ${ }^{*}$, and a compromise between conflicting needs must be found to fix the acceptable risk (or safety) level for a given system.

As often used for MTTR estimation or demonstration (p. 409), efficacy of barriers should be checked by introducing selected critical failures or external hazards; tests which can deliver important results useful to support modeling efforts.

[^0]
[^0]:    *) For instance, assuming failure as cause and fire as consequence, neither a redundancy as barrier for cause nor a firewall or sprinkler as barrier for consequence can reach a $100 \%$ risk mitigation.# 7 Statistical Quality Control \& Reliability Tests 

Statistical quality control \& reliability (RAMS) tests are performed to estimate or demonstrate quality and reliability characteristics on the basis of data collected from sampling tests. Estimation leads to point or interval estimate, marked with ${ }^{\wedge}$ in this book; demonstration is a test of a given hypothesis on an unknown characteristic. Estimation \& demonstration of an unknown probability is given in Section 7.1 for a defective probability $p$ and in Section 7.2.1 for some reliability figures. Procedures for steady-state availability estimation \& demonstration are in Section 7.2.2. Estimation \& demonstration of a constant failure rate $\lambda$ (or $M T B F$ for $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ) are discussed in depth in Sections 7.2.3. The case of an MTTR is considered in Section 7.3. Basic models for accelerated tests are introduced in Section 7.4, with regard also to multiple failure mechanisms. Goodness-of-fit tests based on graphical \& analytical procedures are summarized in Section 7.5. General reliability data analysis, including test on nonhomogeneous Poisson processes and trend tests, are discussed in Section 7.6; models for reliability growth in Section 7.7. A careful introduction to the mathematical foundations for this chapter is in Appendix A8. Selected examples illustrate the practical aspects, and
to simplify the notation, sample is used for random sample (taken from a very large, homogeneous lot), mean for expected value \& independent for mutually, statistically, stochastically independent; furthermore, indices $S_{i}$ (p.3) are omitted in this chapter ( $S_{0}$ is assumed for $R, R(t), P A, \lambda, M T B F$ ), and estimated (or empirical) values are marked with ^.

### 7.1 Statistical Quality Control

One of the main purposes of statistical quality control is to use sampling tests to estimate or demonstrate the defective probability $p$ of a given item, to a required accuracy and often on the basis of tests by attributes (i. e. tests of type good/bad). However, considering $p$ as an unknown probability, a broader field of applications can be covered by the same methods. Other topics, such as tests by variables and statistical processes control [7.1-7.5], are not considered in this book.

In this section, $p$ is considered as a defective probability (see footnote on p. 1). It will be assumed that all elements of the sample are independent and have the same defective probability (i. e. the lot is homogeneous and much larger than the sample), allowing the use of the binomial distribution (Appendix A6.10.7, pp. 465-67).# 7.1.1 Estimation of a Defective Probability $p$ 

Let $n$ be the size of a (random) sample from a large homogeneous lot. If $k$ defective items have been observed within the sample of size $n$, then (Eq. (A8.29))

$$
\hat{p}=k / n, \quad k=0,1,2, \ldots, n
$$

is the maximum likelihood point estimate of the defective probability $p$ for an item in the lot under consideration. $\hat{p}=k / n$ is unbiased ( $\mathrm{E}[\hat{p}]=\mathrm{E}[k] / n=p$, Eq. (A6.122)) and $k$ is a sufficient statistic (delivers the complete information about $p$, Appendix A8.2.1). Furthermore, $\operatorname{Var}[\hat{p}]=\operatorname{Var}[k] / n^{2}=p(1-p) / n$ (Eq. (A6.123)). For a given confidence level $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$, the lower $\hat{p}_{l}$ and upper $\hat{p}_{u}$ limit of the confidence interval for $p$ can be obtained from

$$
\sum_{i=k}^{n}\binom{n}{i} \hat{p}_{l}^{i}\left(1-\hat{p}_{l}\right)^{n-i}=\beta_{2} \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{n}{i} \hat{p}_{u}^{i}\left(1-\hat{p}_{u}\right)^{n-i}=\beta_{1}
$$

for $0<k<n$, and from

$$
\hat{p}_{l}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{p}_{u}=1-\sqrt[n]{\beta_{1}} \quad \text { for } \quad k=0 \quad\left(\gamma=1-\beta_{1}\right)
$$

or from

$$
\hat{p}_{l}=\sqrt[n]{\beta_{2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{p}_{u}=1 \quad \text { for } \quad k=n \quad\left(\gamma=1-\beta_{2}\right)
$$

see Eqs. (A8.37) to (A8.40) and the remarks given there. $\beta_{1}$ is the risk that the true value of $p$ is larger than $\hat{p}_{u}$ and $\beta_{2}$ the risk that the value of $p$ is smaller than $\hat{p}_{l}$, see Example 7.1 for an application. The confidence level is nearly equal to (but not less than) $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}$. It can be considered as the relative frequency of cases in which the interval $\left[\hat{p}_{l}, \hat{p}_{u}\right]$ overlaps (covers) the true value of $p$, in an increasing series of repetitions of the experiment of taking a random sample of size $n$ from the same homogeneous lot (p. 554).

In many practical applications, a graphical determination of $\hat{p}_{l}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}$ is sufficient. The upper diagram in Fig. 7.1 can be used for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0.05$, the lower diagram for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0.1$ ( $\gamma=0.9$ and $\gamma=0.8$, respectively). The continuous lines in Fig. 7.1 are the envelopes of the staircase functions ( $k, n$ integer) given by Eq. (7.2). They converge rapidly, for $\min (n p, n(1-p)) \geq 5$, to the confidence ellipses (dashed lines in Fig. 7.1). Using the confidence ellipses (Eq. (A8.42)), $\hat{p}_{l}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}$ can be calculated from (Eq. (A8.43))

$$
\hat{p}_{l, u}=\frac{k+0.5 b^{2} \pm b \sqrt{k(1-k / n)+b^{2} / 4}}{n+b^{2}}, \quad \beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2
$$

$b$ is the $1-(1-\gamma) / 2=(1+\gamma) / 2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution $\Phi(t)$, given for some typical values of $\gamma$ by (Table A9.1)

| $\gamma=$ | 0.6 | 0.8 | 0.9 | 0.95 | 0.98 | 0.99 |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| $b \approx$ | 0.84 | 1.28 | 1.64 | 1.96 | 2.33 | 2.58 |

Figure 7.1 Confidence limits $\hat{p}_{l}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}$ for an unknown probability $p$ (e. g. defective probability) as a function of the observed relative frequency $k / n$ ( $n=$ sample size, $k=$ observed events); $\gamma=$ confidence level $=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}$, here with $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}$ (continuous lines are the exact solution per Eqs. (7.2) - (7.4), dashed the confidence ellipses per Eq. (7.5))

Example: $n=25, k=5$ gives $\hat{p}=k / n=0.2$ and for $\gamma=0.9$ the confidence interval $[0.08,0.38]$ ([0.0823, 0.3754] using Eq. (7.2), and [0.1011, 0.3572] using Eq. (7.5))The confidence limits $\hat{p}_{1}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}$ can also be used as one-sided confidence intervals. In this case (Eq. (A8.44)),

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
0 \leq p \leq \hat{p}_{u} & \left(\text { or simply } p \leq \hat{p}_{u}\right), & \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{1} \\
\hat{p}_{l} \leq p \leq 1 & \left(\text { or simply } p \geq \hat{p}_{l}\right), & \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{2}
\end{array}
$$

# Example 7.1 

In a sample of size $n=25, k=5$ items were found to be defective. Determine for the underlying defective probability $p$, (i) the point estimate, (ii) the interval estimate for $\gamma=0.8\left(\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0.1\right)$, (iii) the upper bound on $p$ for a one sided confidence interval with $\gamma=0.9$.

## Solution

(i) Equation (7.1) yields the point estimate $\hat{p}=5 / 25=0.2$. (ii) For the interval estimate, the lower part of Fig. 7.1 leads to the confidence interval [0.10, 0.34], [0.1006, 0.3397] using Eq. (7.2) and $[0.1175,0.3194]$ using Eq. (7.5). (iii) With $\gamma=0.9$ it holds $p \leq 0.34$.

Supplementary result: The upper part of Fig. 7.1, would lead to $p \leq 0.38$ with $\gamma=0.95$.

Note that the role of $k / n$ and $p$ can be reversed and Eq. (7.5) can be used to calculate the limits $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ of the number of observations $k$ in $n$ independent trials (e. g. the number $k$ of defective items in a sample of size $n$ ) for given probability $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}$ (with $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}$ ) and known values of $p$ and $n$ (Eq. (A8.45))

$$
k_{1,2}=n p \pm b \sqrt{n p(1-p)}
$$

As in Eq. (7.5), the quantity $b$ in Eq. (7.7) is the $(1+\gamma) / 2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution (e.g. $b \approx 1.64$ for $\gamma=0.9$, Table A9.1). For a graphical solution, Fig. 7.1 can be used by taking the ordinate $p$ as known, and by reading $k_{1} / n$ and $k_{2} / n$ from the abscissa.

### 7.1.2 Simple Two-sided Sampling Plans for the Demonstration of a Defective Probability $p$

In the context of an acceptance test, demonstration of a defective probability $p$ is often required, instead of its estimation (Section 7.1.1). The main concern of this test is to check a zero hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$ against an alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: p>p_{1}$ on the basis of the following agreement between producer and consumer, the lot should be accepted with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\alpha$ if the true (unknown) defective probability $p$ is lower than $p_{0}$, but rejected with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\beta$ if $p$ is greater than $p_{1}\left(p_{0}, p_{1}>p_{0}\right.$, and $0<\alpha<1-\beta<1$ are given (fixed) values).$p_{0}$ is the specified defective probability and $p_{1}$ is the maximum acceptable defective probability. $\alpha$ is the allowed producer's risk (type I error), i. e. the probability of rejecting a true hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0} . \beta$ is the allowed consumer's risk (type II error), i. e. the probability of accepting the hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$ when the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: p>p_{1}$ is true. Verification of the agreement stated above is a problem of statistical hypothesis testing (Appendix A8.3) and can be performed, for instance, with a simple two-sided sampling plan or a sequential test. In both cases, the basic model is the sequence of Bernoulli trials, as introduced in Appendix A6.10.7 (pp. 465-66).

# 7.1.2.1 Simple Two-sided Sampling Plan 

The procedure (test plan) for the simple two-sided sampling plan is as follows (Appendix A8.3.1.1):

1. From $p_{0}, p_{1}, \alpha \& \beta$, determine the smallest integer $c$ and the value $n$ satisfying

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p_{0}^{i}\left(1-p_{0}\right)^{n-i} \geq 1-\alpha
$$

and

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p_{1}^{i}\left(1-p_{1}\right)^{n-i} \leq \beta
$$

2. Take a sample of size $n$, determine the number $k$ of defective items in the sample, and

- reject $H_{0}: p<p_{0}, \quad$ if $k>c$
- accept $H_{0}: p<p_{0}, \quad$ if $k \leq c$.

The graph of Fig. 7.2 visualizes the validity of the above rule (see Appendix A8.3.1.1 for a proof). It satisfies inequalities (7.8) \& (7.9), and is known as operating characteristic curve (or acceptance probability curve). For each value of $p$, it gives the probability of having no more than c defective items in a sample of size $n$. Since the operating characteristic curve decreases monotonically in $p$, the risk for a false decision decreases for $p<p_{0}$ and $p>p_{1}$, respectively. It can be shown that the quantities $c$ and $n p_{0}$ depend only on $\alpha, \beta$, and the ratio $p_{1} / p_{0}$ (discrimination ratio). Table 7.3 (p. 335) gives $c$ and $n p_{0}$ for some important values of $\alpha, \beta$ and $p_{1} / p_{0}$ for the case where the Poisson approximation (Eq. (A6.129)) holds, see Example 7.2 for an application.

Using the operating characteristic curve, the Average Outgoing Quality (AOQ) can be calculated. $A O Q$ represents the mean percentage of defective items that reach the customer, assuming that all rejected samples have been $100 \%$ inspected \& the defective items have been replaced by good ones, and is given by

Figure 7.2 Operating characteristic curve (acceptance probability curve) as a function of the defective probability $p$ for $p_{0}=2 \%, p_{1}=4 \%, \alpha=\beta \leqq 0.1, n=510, c=14$ as per Table 7.3 (see also Fig. 7.3)

$$
A O Q=\operatorname{Pr}\{p \cap \text { acceptance }\}=p \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { acceptance }|p\}=p \sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i}
$$

The maximum value of $A O Q$ is the Average Outgoing Quality Limit [7.4, 7.5].
Obtaining the solution of inequalities (7.8) and (7.9) is time-consuming. For small values of $p_{0} \& p_{1}$ (up to a few \%), the Poisson approximation (Eq. (A6.129))

$$
\binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i} \approx \frac{(n p)^{i}}{i!} e^{-n p}
$$

can be used. Introducing the Poisson approximation in Eqs. (7.8) and (7.9) leads to a Poisson distribution with parameters $m_{1}=n p_{1}$ and $m_{0}=n p_{0}$, which can be solved using a table of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution (Table A9.2). Alternatively, the curves of Fig. 7.3 provide graphical solutions, sufficiently good for practical applications. Exact solutions are in Table 7.3 (p.335).

# Example 7.2 

Determine, using the Poisson approximation, the sample size $n$ and the number of allowed defective items $c$ to test the null hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0}=1 \%$ against the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: p>p_{1}=2 \%$ with producer and consumer risks $\alpha=\beta=0.1$ (which means $\alpha \approx \beta \leqq 0.1$ ).

## Solution

Considering $\alpha=\beta=0.1 \& p_{1} / p_{0}=2$, Table 7.3 (p.335) yields $c=14$ and $n p_{0}=\lambda_{0} T=10.17$ from which $n=1017$, for $\alpha \approx \beta \approx 0.093$. The graph of Fig. 7.3 yields the same result: $c=14$, $m_{0} \approx 10.2$ and $m_{1} \approx 20.4$ for $\alpha \approx \beta \leq 0.1$. Results using Table A9.2 lead to $v=30$ $\left(t_{v, q_{2}} / t_{v, q_{1}}=2, q_{1}=\alpha \leq 0.1, q_{2}=1-\beta \geq 0.9\right), \mathrm{F}(20.34)=0.093 \leq \alpha . \mathrm{F}(40.68) \approx 0.906 \geq 1-\beta$ (linear interpolation); thus, $c=\mathrm{v} / 2-1=14$ and $n=20.34 /(2 \cdot 0.01)=1017$. Graphical and analytical methods require a solution by successive approximation: choice of $c$, starting at $c=0$, and check of conditions for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ by considering the ratio $p_{1} / p_{0}$.# 7.1.2.2 Sequential Test 

The procedure for a sequential test is as follows (Appendix A8.3.1.2):

1. In a Cartesian coordinate system draw the acceptance line $y_{1}(n)=a n-b_{1}$ and the rejection line $y_{2}(n)=a n+b_{2}$, with

$$
a=\frac{\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}, \quad b_{1}=\frac{\ln \frac{1-\alpha}{\beta}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}, \quad b_{2}=\frac{\ln \frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}
$$

2. Select one item after another from the lot, test the item, enter the test result in the diagram drawn in step 1 , and stop the test as soon as either the rejection or the acceptance line is crossed.


Figure 7.3 Poisson distribution per Table A9.2 ( $\cdot$ results for Examples $7.2(c=14), 7.4(7), 7.5(0)$, $7.6(2 \& 0)$, and $7.9(6))$Figure A8.8 shows acceptance and rejection lines for $p_{0}=1 \%, p_{1}=2 \% \& \alpha \approx \beta \approx 0.2$. The advantage of the sequential test is that on average it requires a smaller sample size than the corresponding simple two-sided sampling plan (Example 7.10 or Fig. 7.8). A disadvantage is that the sample size (test duration) is random.

# 7.1.3 One-sided Sampling Plans for the Demonstration of a Defective Probability $p$ 

The two-sided sampling plans of Section 7.1.2 are fair in the sense that for $\alpha=\beta$, both producer and consumer run the same risk of making a false decision. In practical applications however, one-sided sampling plans are often used, i. e. only $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ or $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ are specified. In these cases, the operating characteristic curve (acceptance probability curve) is not completely defined. For each value of $c$ $(c=0,1, \ldots)$ a largest $n(n=1,2, \ldots)$ exists which satisfies inequality (7.8) for given $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$, or a smallest $n$ exists which satisfies inequality (7.9) for given $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ (Fig.7.3). One recognizes that the operating characteristic curves become steeper as the value of $c$ increases (Figs. 7.4 or A8.9). Hence, for small values of $c$, the producer (if $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ are given) or the consumer (if $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ are given) can realize an advantage. Figure 7.4 (obtained from Fig. 7.3, $m=n p$ ) visualizes the reduction of the consumer risk (from $\beta \approx 0.88$ for $c=0$ or $\approx 0.98$ for $c=7$ ) by increasing values of the defective probability $p$ or values of $c$, see Fig 7.9 for a counterpart.

When only $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ or $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ are given, it is usual to set in these cases

$$
p_{0}=A Q L \quad \text { and } \quad p_{1}=L T P D
$$

respectively, where $A Q L$ is the Acceptable Quality Level and LTPD is the Lot Tolerance Percent Defective (Eqs. (A8.79) to (A8.82)).

A large number of one-sided sampling plans for the demonstration of $A Q L$ values are given in national and international standards (IEC 60410, ISO 2859, MIL-STD-105, DIN 40080 [7.3]). Many of these plans have been established empirically. Following remarks can be useful when evaluating such plans:

1. $A Q L$ values are given in $\%$.
2. The values for $n$ and $c$ are in general obtained using the Poisson approximation.
3. Not all values of $c$ are listed, the value of $\alpha$ often decreases with increasing $c$.
4. Sample size is related to lot size, and this relationship is empirical.
5. A distinction is made between reduced tests (level I), normal tests (level II) and tightened tests (level III); level II is normally used; transition from one level to another is often given empirically (e. g. transition from level II to level III is necessary if 2 out of 5 successive independent lots have been rejected and a return to level II follows if 5 successive independent lots are passed).
6. The value of $\alpha$ is not given explicitly (for $c=0$, for example, $\alpha$ is approximately 0.05 for level I, 0.1 for level II, and 0.2 for level III).

Figure 7.4 Operating characteristic curves (acceptance probability curves) as a function of the defective probability $p$ for $p_{0}=A Q L=0.65 \%$ with sample sizes $n=20,80,500$ as per Table 7.1 $(\alpha=0.12$ for $c=0, \approx 0.09$ for $c=1, \approx 0.02$ for $c=7$ per Fig. 7.3, Table A9.2 or [A9.1 - A9.6])

Table 7.1 presents some test procedures for $A Q L$ values from IEC 60410 [7.3] and Fig. 7.4 shows the corresponding operating characteristic curves for $A Q L=0.65 \%$ and sample size $n=20,80$, and 500 .

Test procedures for demonstration of $L T P D$ values with given (fixed) customer risk $\beta$ are for example in [3.12 (S-19500)]. They are often based on the Poisson approximation (Eq. (A6.129)) and can be easily established using a $\chi^{2}$ - table (Appendix A9.2) or Fig. 7.3. For given $\beta$ and $L T P D$, the values of $n$ and $c$ can be obtained taking in Fig. 7.3

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{c} \frac{(m)^{i}}{i!} e^{-m}=\beta
$$

and reading $m=n p=n L T P D$ for $c=0,1,2, \ldots$ (Example: $\beta=0.1 \& L T P D=2 \%$ yields $m \approx 3.9$ for $c=1$, and from this $n \approx 3.9 / 0.02=195$; the procedure is thus: test 195 items and reject $L T P D=2 \%$ if more than 1 defect occur).

In addition to the simple one-sided sampling plans described above, multiple one-sided sampling plans are often used to demonstrate $A Q L$ values. In a double one-sided sampling plan, the following procedure is used:

1. Take a first sample of size $n_{1}$ and accept definitely if no more than $c_{1}$ defects occur, but reject definitely if exactly or more than $d_{1}$ defects have occurred.
2. If after the first sample the number of defects is greater than $c_{1}$ but less than $d_{1}$, take a second sample of size $n_{2}$ and accept if there are totally (in the first and second sample) no more than $c_{2}$ defects; elsewhere reject.

The operating characteristic curve (acceptance probability curve) for a double onesided sampling plan can be calculated as$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { acceptance } \mid p\}= & \sum_{i=0}^{c_{1}}\binom{n_{\mathrm{i}}}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n_{1}-i} \\
& +\sum_{i=c_{1}+1}^{d_{1}-1}\left[\binom{n_{\mathrm{i}}}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n_{1}-i} \sum_{j=0}^{c_{2}-i}\binom{n_{2}}{j} p^{j}(1-p)^{n_{2}-j}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiple one-sided sampling plans are also given in national and international standards, see for example IEC 60410 [7.3] for the following double one-sided sampling plan to demonstrate $A Q L=1 \%$

| Lot size | $n_{1}$ | $n_{2}$ | $c_{1}$ | $d_{1}$ | $c_{2}$ |
| --: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
| $281-500$ | 32 | 32 | 0 | 2 | 1 |
| $501-1,200$ | 50 | 50 | 0 | 3 | 3 |
| $1,201-3,200$ | 80 | 80 | 1 | 4 | 4 |
| $3,201-10,000$ | 125 | 125 | 2 | 5 | 6 |

The advantage of multiple one-sided sampling plans is that on average they require smaller sample sizes than would be necessary for simple one-sided sampling plans. A disadvantage is that the test duration is not fixed in advance.

use the first sampling plan above for $\uparrow$ or below for $\downarrow, c=$ number of allowed defects# 7.2 Statistical Reliability (RAMS) Tests 

Statistical reliability (RAMS) tests are useful to evaluate the reliability, availability, maintainability, and safety achieved in a given item (system). Early initiation of these tests allows quick identification and cost-effective correction of weaknesses not discovered by reliability (RAMS) analyses. This supports a learning process, often related to a reliability growth program (Section 7.7). However, since reliability (RAMS) tests are generally time-consuming and expensive, they should be coordinated with other tests and performed with test conditions as close as possible to those experienced in the field. As for quality control, a distinction is made between estimation and demonstration of a specific reliability (RAMS) figure. Section 7.2.1 uses results of Section 7.1 for reliability and availability testing for the case of a given (fixed) mission; this applies also to maintainability and safety considered as a probability. In section 7.2.2 a unified method for availability estimation and demonstration for the case of continuous operation is introduced. Section 7.2.3 deals then carefully with estimation and demonstration of a constant failure rate $\lambda$ (or $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ); these results can be used for the safety function given by Eq. (6.330). Estimation and demonstration of an MTTR is discussed in Section 7.3. Accelerated tests (also for multiple failure mechanisms), goodness-of-fit tests, general reliability data analysis \& trend tests, and reliability growth are introduced in Sections 7.4-7.7, respectively. To simplify the notation, indices $S_{i}$ are omitted $\left(R, P A, \lambda, M T B F\right.$ are used for $R_{S 0}, P A_{S}, \lambda_{S 0}, M T B F_{S 0}$ ).

### 7.2.1 Reliability \& Availability Estimation and Demonstration for the Case of a given (fixed) Mission

Reliability $(R)$ and availability (asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A=A A$ ) are often defined as success probability for a given (fixed) mission. Their estimation and demonstration can thus be performed as for an unknown probability $p$ (Section 7.1) by setting, for convenience,

$$
p=1-R \quad \text { or } \quad p=1-P A=1-A A
$$

For a demonstration, the null hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$ is converted to $H_{0}: R>R_{0}$ or $H_{0}: A A>A A_{0}$, which adheres better to the concept of reliability or availability. The same holds for other reliability figure expressed as an unknown probability $p$.

Above considerations hold for given (fixed) mission, repeated $n$ times. However, for the case of continuous operation, estimation and demonstration of $\mathrm{R}(t)$ or $\mathrm{PA}(t)$ can leads to a difficulty in defining time points $t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots, t_{n}$ at which the $n$ observations have to be performed. Sections $7.2 .2 \& 7.2 .3$ deal with continuous operation. Examples 7.3 - 7.6 illustrate some cases of reliability tests for given (fixed) mission.# Example 7.3 

In a reliability test 95 of 100 items pass. Give the confidence interval for $R$ at $\gamma=0.9\left(\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}\right)$.

## Solution

With $p=1-R$ and $\hat{R}=0.95$ the confidence interval for $p$ follows from Fig. 7.1 as [0.03, 0.10]. The confidence interval for $R$ is then $[0.9,0.97]$; Eq. (7.5) leads to $[0.901,0.975]$ for $R$.

## Example 7.4

The reliability of a given subassembly was $R=0.9$ and should have been improved through constructive measures. In a test of 100 subassemblies, 94 of them pass the test. Check with a type I error $\alpha \leq 20 \%$ the hypothesis $H_{0}: R>0.95$.

## Solution

For $p_{0}=1-R_{0}=0.05, \alpha=20 \%$, and $n=100$, Eq. 7.8 delivers $c=7$ (see also the graphical solution from Fig. 7.3 with $m=n p_{0}=5$ and acceptance probability $\geq 1-\alpha=0.8$, yielding $\alpha \approx 0.15$ for $m=5$ and $c=7$ ). As just $k=6$ subassemblies have failed the test, the hypothesis $H_{0}: R>0.95$ cannot be rejected (i.e. has to be accepted) at the level $1-\alpha \approx 0.85$.
Supplement. results: Assuming as an alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: R<0.90$, or $p>p_{1} \approx 0.1$, the type II error $\beta$ were $\beta \approx 0.2$ (Eq. (7.9) or Fig. 7.3 with $c=7, n=100$, $p_{1}=0.1$ or $n p_{1}=10$ ). (A two-sided plan with $\alpha \approx \beta \approx 0.15, n=100, c=7$, $p_{0}=0.05$ would ask for $p_{1} \approx 0.11$, Fig.7.3.)

## Example 7.5

Determine the minimum number of tests $n$ that must be repeated to verify the hypothesis $H_{0}: R>R_{1}=0.95$ with a consumer risk $\beta=0.1$. What is the allowed number of failures $c$ ?

## Solution

$n$ and $c$ must satisfy the inequality (7.9) with $p_{1}=1-R_{1}=0.05$ and $\beta=0.1$, i. e.,

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} 0.05^{i} \cdot 0.95^{n-i} \leqq 0.1
$$

The number of tests $n$ is a minimum for $c=0$. From $0.95^{n} \leqq 0.1$, it follows that $n=45$, yielding $\beta \approx 0.099$ (calculation with the Poisson approximation (Eq. (7.12)) yields $n=46$, a graphical solution with Fig. 7.3 leads to $m \approx 2.3$ and then $n=m / p_{1} \approx 46$ ).

## Example 7.6

Continuing with Example 7.5, (i) find $n$ for $c=2$ and (ii) how large would the producer risk be for $c=0$ and $c=2$ if the true reliability were $R=0.97$ ?

## Solution

(i) From Eq. (7.9),

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{2}\binom{n}{i} 0.05^{i} \cdot 0.95^{n-i} \leqq 0.1
$$

and thus $n=105$ (Fig. 7.3 yields $m \approx 5.3$ and $n \approx 106$; from Table A9.2, $v=6, t_{6,0.9} \approx 10.645$ and $n=107$ ).
(ii) The producer risk is

$$
\alpha=1-\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} 0.03^{i} \cdot 0.97^{n-i}
$$

hence, $\alpha \approx 0.75$ for $c=0$ and $n=45, \alpha \approx 0.61$ for $c=2$ and $n=105$ (Fig. 7.3, yields $\alpha \approx 0.75$ for $c=0$ and $m \approx 1.35, \alpha \approx 0.62$ for $c=2$ and $m \approx 3.15$; from Table A9.2, $\alpha \approx 0.73$ for $v=2$ and $t_{2, \alpha} \approx 2.7, \alpha \approx 0.61$ for $v=6$ and $t_{6, \alpha} \approx 6.3$ linear interpolation $(0.74 \& 0.61$ from [A9.1])).# 7.2.2 Availability Estimation \& Demonstration for the Case of Continuous Operation (Asymptotic \& Steady-state Case) 

Availability estimation and demonstration for a repairable item in continuous operation could be based on results of Section 6.2 for the one-item repairable structure. Point estimate (with corresponding mean and variance) for the availability can be found for arbitrary distributions of failure-free and repair times (Section 7.2.2.3). However, interval estimation and demonstration tests can lead to some difficulties.

An unified approach for point \& interval estimation as well as for demonstration of the asymptotic and steady-state point and average availability $P A=A A$ for a repairable item in continuous operation with exponentially or Erlangian distributed failure-free and / or repair times is introduced in Appendices A8.2.2.4\& A8.3.1.4. Sections 7.2.2.1 and 7.2.2.2 deal with this approach. The case of exponentially distributed failure-free \& repair times, i. e. constant failure \& repair rates $(\lambda(x)=\lambda \&$ $\mu(x)=\mu)$ is considered in detail, extension to Erlangian distributions is given.

For constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda \& \mu$, the point unavailability $1-\operatorname{PA}(t)$ converge rapidly and exponentially with time constant $\approx 1 / \mu$ to the asymptotic \& steady-state value (similar for $1-\mathrm{AA}(t)$, Table 6.3)

$$
\widehat{P A}=1-P A=1-A A=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)=(\lambda / \mu) /(1+\lambda / \mu) \leqq \lambda / \mu
$$

To simplify considerations, it is assumed that the observed time interval $(0, t]$ is $>>1 / \mu$, terminates at the conclusion of a repair, and exactly $k$ (or $n$ ) failure-free times $\tau_{i}$ and repair times $\tau_{i}^{\prime}$ have occurred. Furthermore, considering $\lambda \ll \mu$,

$$
\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu
$$

is estimated instead of $\widehat{P A}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)\left(\widehat{P A}_{a}-(\lambda / \mu)^{2}<\widehat{P A}<\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu\right) . \lambda / \mu$ is a probabilistic value of the asymptotic \& steady-state unavailability and has his statistical counterpart in $D T / U T$, where $D T$ and $U T$ are the observed down and up times. The procedures developed in Appendices A8.2.2.4 and A8.3.1.4 are based on the fact that the quantity $\mu \cdot D T / \lambda \cdot U T$ has a Fisher distribution with $v_{1}=v_{2}=2 k$ (or $2 n$ ) degrees of freedom. Section 7.2.2.1 deals with estimation of $\widehat{P A}_{a}$, Section 7.2.2.2 with demonstration of $\widehat{P A}$. Alternative methods are discussed in Section 7.2.2.3.

### 7.2.2.1 Availability Estimation (Erlangian Failure-Free and/or Repair Times)

Having observed for an item as-good-as-new at $t=0$ and after each repair (Fig. 6.2), with constant failure\& repair rates $\lambda \& \mu$, an operating time $U T=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}$ and a repair time $D T=t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{k}^{\prime}$, the maximum likelihood point estimate for $\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu$ is

$$
\widehat{P A}_{a}=(\lambda / \mu)=D T / U T=\left(t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{k}^{\prime}\right) /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}\right)
$$

$D T / U T$ is biased, unbiased is $(1-1 / k) D T / U T, k>1$ (p.571). $\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu$ is an approximation for $\widehat{P A}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$, good for practical applications (abs. error $\left\langle(\lambda / \mu)^{2}\right)$.

Figure 7.5 Confidence limits $\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a \hat{\jmath}} / \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a} \approx \widehat{\widehat{P A}_{\hat{\jmath}}} / \widehat{\widehat{P A}} \& \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a_{\mu}} / \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a} \approx \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{u} / \widehat{\widehat{P A}}$ for an unknown asymptotic \& steady-state unavailability $\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)=\widehat{P A}=1-P A=1-A A=\widehat{P A}_{a} /(1+\lambda / \mu), \widehat{P A}_{a}=D T / U T=$ maximum likelihood estimate for $\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu, U T=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}, D T=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}, \quad \gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}=$ confidence level, here $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2 \quad$ (per Eq. (7.17) and Table A9.4; $\cdot$ result for Example A8.8)

For given $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$, lower $\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a_{\hat{\jmath}}}$ and upper $\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a_{\mu}}$ confidence limits for $\widehat{P A}_{a}$ are given by (Eq. (A8.65))

$$
\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a_{\hat{\jmath}}}=\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a} / \boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a_{\mu}}=\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{1}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{2}} \& \boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{1}}$ are the $1-\beta_{2} \& 1-\beta_{1}$ quantiles of the Fisher ( $\boldsymbol{F}$-) distribution with $2 k$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.4). Figure 7.5 gives confidence limits for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$, useful for practical applications. $\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a \hat{\jmath}} / \widehat{\widehat{P A}_{\hat{\jmath}}} \approx \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a_{\mu}} / \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{u}$ $\approx \widehat{P A}_{a} / \widehat{P A}=1+\lambda / \mu \approx 1$ can often be used, yielding

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \widehat{\widehat{P A}} \approx \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a}=D T / U T \\
& 0 \leq \widehat{P A} \leq \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{u} \approx \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a_{\mu}} \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a \hat{\jmath}} \approx \widehat{\widehat{P A}_{\hat{\jmath}}} \leq \widehat{P A} \leq 1 \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

for point estimate and one sided confidence intervals of $\widehat{P A}$ (see p. 562 for an application). Corresponding values for the availability follow from $P A=1-\widehat{P A}$.

If failure free and/or repair times are Erlangian distributed (Eq. (A6.102)) with $\beta_{\lambda}=n_{\lambda} \& \beta_{\mu}=n_{\mu}, \boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{2}}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{1}}$ have to be replaced by $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k \cdot n_{\mu}, 2 k \cdot n_{\lambda}, 1-\beta_{2}}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k \cdot n_{\lambda}, 2 k \cdot n_{\mu}, 1-\beta_{1}}$, for unchanged MTTF \& MTTR, see Example A8.11 on p. 571 $\left(\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a}=D T / U T\right.$ remains valid, $\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a}=\left(\lambda^{*} n_{\mu} / \mu^{*} n_{\lambda}\right)=(\lambda / \mu)$ ). Results based on the distribution of $D T$ (Eq. (7.22)) are not parameter free (see Section 7.2.2.3).# 7.2.2.2 Availability Demonstration (Erlangian Failure-Free and/or Repair Times) 

In the context of an acceptance test, demonstration of the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $(P A=A A)$ is often required. The item is assumed as-good-as-new at $t=0$ and after each repair, and for practical applications it is useful to work with the unavailability $\overline{P A}=1-P A$. The main concern of this test is to check a zero hypothesis $H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0}$ against an alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: \overline{P A}>\overline{P A}_{1}$ on the basis of the following agreement between producer and consumer,
items should be accepted with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\alpha$ if the true (unknown) unavailability $\overline{P A}$ is lower than $\overline{P A}_{0}$, but rejected with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\beta$ if $\overline{P A}$ is greater than $\overline{P A}_{1}\left(\overline{P A}_{0}, \overline{P A}_{1}>\overline{P A}_{0}, 0<\alpha<1-\beta<1\right.$ are given (fixed) values $)$.
$\overline{P A}_{0}$ is the specified unavailability and $\overline{P A}_{1}$ is the maximum acceptable unavailability. $\alpha$ is the allowed producer's risk (type I error), i. e. the probability of rejecting a true hypothesis $H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0} . \beta$ is the allowed consumer's risk (type II error), i. e. the probability of accepting the hypothesis $H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0}$ when the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: \overline{P A}>\overline{P A}_{1}$ is true. Verification of the agreement stated above is a problem of statistical hypothesis testing (Appendix A8.3) and different approach are possible. In the following, the method developed in Appendix A8.3.1.4 is given (comparison with other methods is in Section 7.2.2.3).

Assuming constant failure and repair rates $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ and $\mu(x)=\mu$, the procedure is as follows (Eqs. (A8.91)-(A8.93), see also [A8.29, A2.6 (IEC 61070)]):

1. For given $\overline{P A}_{0}, \overline{P A}_{1}, \alpha \& \beta(0<\alpha<1-\beta<1)$, find the smallest integer $n$ which satisfy

$$
\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\beta} \leq \frac{\overline{P A}_{1}}{\overline{P A}_{0}} \cdot \frac{P A_{0}}{P A_{1}}=\frac{\left(1-P A_{1}\right) P A_{0}}{\left(1-P A_{0}\right) P A_{1}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\beta}$ are the $1-\alpha$ and $1-\beta$ quantiles of the $\boldsymbol{F}$-distribution with $2 n$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.4), and compute the limiting value

$$
\delta=\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha} \overline{P A}_{0} / P A_{0}=\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha}\left(1-P A_{0}\right) / P A_{0}
$$

2. Observe $n$ failure free times $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n} \&$ corresponding repair times $t_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, t_{n}^{\prime}$, and

- reject $H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0}, \quad$ if $\left(t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{n}^{\prime}\right) /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)>\delta$
- accept $H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0}, \quad$ if $\left(t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{n}^{\prime}\right) /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right) \leq \delta$.

Example A8.9 on p. 570 shows a practical application, and Table 7.2 gives $n$ and $\delta$ for some useful values of $\overline{P A}_{1} / \overline{P A}_{0}$ (Table A9.4). It must be noted that test duration is not fixed in advance. However, results for fixed time sample plans are not free of parameters (see remark to Eq. (7.22)). Results based on the distribution of $D T$ are not parameter free (Section 7.2.2.3).

# 7.2.2.3 Further Availability Evaluation Methods for Continuous Operation 

The approach developed in Appendices A8.2.2.4 \& A8.3.1.4 and given in Sections 7.2.2.1 \& 7.2.2.2 yields to exact solutions based on the Fisher distribution for estimating and demonstrating an availability $P A=A A$, obtained by investigating $D T / U T$ for exponentially or Erlangian distributed failure-free and/or repair times. Exponentially distributed failure-free times can be assumed in many practical applications. The distribution of repair (restoration) times can often be approximated by an Erlang distribution (Eq. (A6.102)) with $\beta \geq 3$. Generalization of the distribution of failure-free or repair times can lead to difficulties. In the following alternative approaches for estimating and demonstrating an availability $P A=A A$ are briefly discussed and compared with the approach given in Sections 7.2.2.1 \& 7.2.2.2 (item's behavior still described by an alternating renewal process as per Fig. 6.2).

A first possibility is to consider only the distribution of the down time $D T$ (total repair (restoration) time) in a given time interval $(0, t]$. At the given (fixed) time point $t$ the item can be up or down, and Eq. (6.33) with $t-x$ instead of $T_{0}$ gives the distribution function of $D T$ (Eq. (7.22)). Moments of $D T$ have been investigated in [A7.29(1957)], mean and variance of the unavailability $\overline{P A}=1-P A=\mathrm{E}[D T / t]$ can thus be given for arbitrary distributions of failure-free and repair times. In particular, for the case of constant failure and repair rates $(\lambda(x)=\lambda, \mu(x)=\mu)$ it holds that$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { total down time } D T \text { in }(0, t] \leq x \mid \text { new at } t=0\}= \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\{D T / t \leq x / t \mid \text { new at } t=0\}=1-e^{-(\lambda(t-x)+\mu x)} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{(\lambda(t-x))^{n}}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\mu x)^{k}}{k!}\right), \quad 0<x<t \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}[D T / t]=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu} \approx \lambda / \mu, \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Var}[D T / t]=\frac{2 \lambda \mu}{t(\lambda+\mu)^{3}} \leqq 2 \lambda / t \mu^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

However, already for the case of constant failure and repair rates, results for interval estimation and demonstration test are not free of parameters (function of $\mu$ [A8.29] or $\lambda$ [A8.18]). The use of the distribution of $D T$, or $D T / t$ for fixed $t$, would bring the advantage of a test duration $t$ fixed in advance, but results are not free of parameters and the method is thus of limited utility.

A second possibility is to assign to the state of the item an indicator $\zeta(t)$ taking values $I$ for item up and 0 for item down (binary process, Boolean variable). In this case it holds that $\operatorname{PA}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta(t)=1\}$, and thus $\mathrm{E}[\zeta(t)]=\operatorname{PA}(t)$ and $\operatorname{Var}[\zeta(t)]=\mathrm{E}\left[\zeta(t)^{2}\right]-\mathrm{E}^{2}[\zeta(t)]=\operatorname{PA}(t)(1-\operatorname{PA}(t))$ (Eq. (A6.118)). Investigation on $\operatorname{PA}(t)$ reduces to that on $\zeta(t)$, see e.g. [A7.4(1962)]. In particular, estimation and demonstration of $\operatorname{PA}(t)$ can be based on observations of $\zeta(t)$ at time points $t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots$. A basic question here, is the choice of the observation time points (randomly, at constant time intervals $\Delta=t_{i+1}-t_{i}$, or other). For the case of constant failure \& repair rates $(\lambda \& \mu), \operatorname{PA}(t)$ convergence rapidly to $P A=A A=\mu /(\lambda+\mu) \approx 1-\lambda / \mu$ (Eq. (6.20)). Furthermore, because of the constant failure rate, the joint availability is given by (Eqs. (6.35)) $\mathrm{JA}_{S 0}(t, t+\Delta)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \cdot \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(\Delta)$, relation which can be extended to an arbitrary number of observation points (Eq.(A6.9)). Estimation and demonstration for the case of observations at constant time intervals $\Delta$ can thus be reduced to the case of an unknown probability $p=\widehat{\mathrm{PA}}(\Delta)=1-\operatorname{PA}(\Delta) \approx\left(1-e^{-\mu \Delta}\right) \lambda / \mu$ as per Eq. (6.20), yielding $p \approx \lambda \Delta$ for $\Delta \ll 1 / \mu$ or $p \approx \lambda / \mu$ for $\Delta \gg 1 / \mu$ (Section 7.1).

A further possibility is to estimate and demonstrate $\lambda \& \mu$ separately (Eqs. (7.28) - (7.30) and (7.33) - (7.35)), and consider $\widehat{P A}=\widehat{A A} \approx \lambda / \mu$.

A one-sided interval estimation $\widehat{P A}=\widehat{A A} \approx \lambda / \mu \leq \widehat{P A}_{u}$ for an item described by Fig. 6.2 and Eq. (7.22), using the Chebyshev's inequality (Eq. (A6.49), Fig. A8.3) in the form $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left|D T / t-\lambda / \mu\right|>\varepsilon\right\} \leq 2 \lambda /\left(t \mu^{2} \varepsilon^{2}\right)=\beta_{1}=1-\gamma$, i. e. for $\varepsilon=\sqrt{2 \lambda / t \mu^{2}(1-\gamma)}$, has been proposed in [7.14]. This leads to $\operatorname{Pr}\{D T / t>\lambda / \mu+\varepsilon\} \leq 1-\gamma$, or $\operatorname{Pr}\{D T / t \leq \lambda / \mu+\varepsilon\} \geq \gamma$; thus, $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\widehat{P A} \leq \widehat{P A}_{u}\right\} \geq \gamma$ with $\widehat{P A}_{u}=\hat{\lambda} / \hat{\mu}+\sqrt{2 \hat{\lambda} / t \hat{\mu}^{2}(1-\gamma)}$, $t$ as test time, $\hat{\lambda} \& \hat{\mu}$ estimates for $\lambda \& \mu$ (Eqs. (7.28), (7.23)-(7.25) as appropriate).

The different methods can basically be discussed by comparing Figs. 7.5 \& 7.6 and Tables $7.2 \& 7.3$. Analytical results based on the Fisher distribution yield broader confidence intervals and longer demonstration tests (which can be partly compensated by accepting higher values for $\widehat{P A}_{u} / \widehat{P A}_{i}$ or $\widehat{P A}_{1} / \widehat{P A}_{0}$, considering the low values of $\widehat{P A}$ and that $\lambda \& \mu$ are unknown); the advantage being an exact knowledge of the involved errors $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}\right)$ or risks $(\alpha, \beta)$. However, for some aspects (test duration, possibility to verify maintainability with selected failures) it can become more appropriate to estimate and demonstrate $\lambda \& \mu$ separately.# 7.2.3 Estimation \& Demonstration of a Constant Failure Rate $\lambda$ (or of $M T B F$ for the Case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ) 

A constant (time independent) failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ occurs in many practical applications for nonrepairable items, as well as for repairable items which are assumed new or as-good-as-new after repair; $x$ being the variable starting by $x=0$ at the beginning of the failure-free time considered, as for interarrival times. However, it must be noted that even with a constant failure rate for all elements, $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ at item (system) level holds for series structures (Eqs. (2.19) \& (6.60)), but only approximately for systems with redundancy (see remarks to Eqs. (2.22) \& (6.94)).

If a constant (or nearly so) failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ can be assumed at system level, all failure-free times are independent and exponentially distributed with same parameter $\lambda$ and mean time to failure $M T T F=1 / \lambda$ (pp. 40, 177).

Referred to repairable systems, $M T B F$ (mean operating time between failures) is frequently used instead of MTTF. However, to avoid ambiguities and also because often tacitly assumed in practical applications [1.22, A2.5, A2.6 (HDBK-781], in this book $M T B F$ is confined to the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ (see pp. 6, 40, 392-93, 394).

For both cases, repairable items (systems) considered as-good-as-new after repair or nonrepairable items replaced at failure, and considering only operating times,
$\lambda(x)=\lambda$ yields to a flow of failures described by a homogeneous Poisson process (p. 488); this property characterizes exponentially distributed failure-free times and highly simplifies investigations.

This section deals with estimation and demonstration of a constant failure rate $\lambda$, or of $M T B F$ for $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ (see Sections $7.5-7.7$ for further results). In particular, the case of a given cumulative operating time $T$, obtained with one or more statistically identical and independent items which are as-good-as-new after each repair or replacement at failure, is considered (footnote on p.330). Due to the relation between exponentially distributed failure-free times and homogeneous Poisson process (Eq. (A7.39)), and the additive property of Poisson processes (Example 7.7),
for constant failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$, the (fixed) cumulative operating time $T$ can be partitioned in an arbitrary way from failure-free times of statistically identical and independent items (see note to Table 7.3 on p. 335 for a rule).

Following situations can occur in practical applications:

1. Operation of a single item immediately renewed at failure, here $T=t$.
2. Operation of $n$ identical items, each of them being immediately renewed at failure, here $T=n t(n=1,2, \ldots)$.
As stated above, for constant failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ and immediate renewal, the failure process is a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$ for $n=1$, or $n \lambda$ for $n>1$, over the (fixed) time interval $(0, T]$ for $n=1$, or $(0, T / n]$ for $n>1$. Hence, the probability for $k$ failures within the cumulative operating time $T$ is (Eq. (A7.41))$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { failures within } T \mid \lambda\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { failures within } T / n \mid n \lambda\}=\frac{(\lambda T)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\lambda T}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& k=0,1, \ldots \\
& n=1,2, \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

Statistical procedures for the estimation and demonstration of a failure rate $\lambda$ (or for $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ) can thus be based on the evaluation of the parameter $(m=\lambda T)$ of a Poisson distribution.

In addition to the case of a given (fixed) cumulative operating time $T$, with immediate renewal, discussed above and investigated in Sections 7.2.3.1-7.2.3.3, for which the number $k$ of failures in $T$ is a sufficient statistic and $\hat{\lambda}=k / T$ is an unbiased estimate for $\lambda$, further possibilities are known. Assuming $n$ identical items new at $t=0$ and labeling the individual failure times as $t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots$, measured from $t=0$, also following censoring cases can occur in practical applications $(k>1)$ :

1. Fixed number $k$ of failures, the test is stopped at the $k$ th failure and failed items are not renewed; an unbiased point estimate of the failure rate $\lambda$ is (Eq (A8.35))

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \hat{\lambda}=(k-1) /\left[n t_{1}+(n-1)\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)+\ldots+(n-k+1)\left(t_{k}-t_{k-1}\right)\right] \\
& =(k-1) /\left[t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) t_{k}\right] .
\end{aligned}
$$

2. Fixed number $k$ of failures, the test is stopped at the $k$ th failure and failed items are instantaneously renewed; an unbiased point estimate for $\lambda$ is

$$
\hat{\lambda}=(k-1) /\left(n t_{1}+n\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)+\ldots+n\left(t_{k}-t_{k-1}\right)=(k-1) / n t_{k}\right.
$$

3. Fixed test time $T_{\text {test }}$, failed items are not renewed; a biased point estimate of the failure rate $\lambda$ (given $k$ items have failed in $\left.\left(0, T_{\text {test }}\right]\right)$ is

$$
\hat{\lambda}=k /\left[n t_{1}+(n-1)\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)+\ldots+(n-k)\left(T_{\text {test }}-t_{k}\right)\right]=k /\left[t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) T_{\text {test }}\right]
$$

# Example 7.7 

An item with constant failure rate $\lambda$ operates first for a fixed time $T_{1}$ and then for a fixed time $T_{2}$. Repair times are neglected. Give the probability that $k$ failures will occur in $T=T_{1}+T_{2}$.

## Solution

The item's behavior within each of the time periods $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ can be described by a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$. From Eq. (A7.39) it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{i \text { failures in the time period } T_{i} \mid \lambda\right\}=\frac{\left(\lambda T_{i}\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda T_{1}}
$$

and, because of the memoryless property of the homogeneous Poisson process

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{k \text { failures in } T=T_{1}+T_{2} \mid \lambda\right\} & =\sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\lambda T_{i}\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda T_{1}} \cdot \frac{\left(\lambda T_{2}\right)^{k-i}}{(k-i)!} e^{-\lambda T_{2}} \\
& =e^{-\lambda T} \lambda^{k} \sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{T_{i}^{i}}{i!} \cdot \frac{T_{2}^{k-i}}{(k-i)!}=\frac{(\lambda T)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\lambda T}
\end{aligned}
$$

The last part of Eq. (7.26) follows from the binomial expansion of $\left(T_{1}+T_{2}\right)^{k}$. Eq. (7.26) shows that for $\lambda$ constant, the cumulative operating time $T$ can be partitioned in an arbitrary way from failure-free times of statistically identical and independent items (see note to Table 7.3 for a rule).Supplementary result: The same procedure can be used to prove that the sum of two independent homogeneous Poisson processes with intensities $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ is a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}$; in fact,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{k \text { failures in }(0, T] \mid \lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}\right\} \\
& =\sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\lambda_{1} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda_{1} T} \frac{\left(\lambda_{2} T\right)^{k-i}}{(k-i)!} e^{-\lambda_{2} T}=\frac{\left(\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) T\right)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) T}
\end{aligned}
$$

This result can be extended to nonhomogeneous Poisson processes.

# 7.2.3.1 Estimation of a Constant Failure Rate $\lambda$ (or of $M T B F$ for $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda)^{*}$ 

Let's consider an item with a constant failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$. If during the given (fixed) cumulative operating time $T^{* \prime}$ exactly $k$ failures have occurred, the maximum likelihood point estimate for the unknown parameter $\lambda$ follows as (Eq. (A8.46))

$$
\hat{\lambda}=k / T, \quad k=0,1,2, \ldots
$$

$\hat{\lambda}=k / T$ is unbiased, i. e. $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\lambda}]=\lambda, k$ is a sufficient statistic $\& \operatorname{Var}[\hat{\lambda}]=\operatorname{Var}[k] / T^{2}=\lambda / T$ (Example A6.21, Eqs. (A6.40), (A6.46), Appendix A8.2.1). For a given confidence level (p.554) $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$ and $k>0$, lower $\hat{\lambda}_{l}$ and upper $\hat{\lambda}_{u}$ limits of the confidence interval for $\lambda$ can be obtained from (Eqs. (A8.47)-(A8.51))

$$
\sum_{i=k}^{\infty} \frac{\left(\hat{\lambda}_{l} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\hat{\lambda}_{l} T}=\beta_{2} \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\hat{\lambda}_{u} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\hat{\lambda}_{u} T}=\beta_{1}
$$

or from

$$
\hat{\lambda}_{l}=\frac{\chi_{2 k, \beta_{2}}^{2}}{2 T} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\lambda}_{u}=\frac{\chi_{2(k+1), 1-\beta_{1}}^{2}}{2 T}
$$

using the quantile of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution (Table A9.2). For $k=0$, Eq. (A8.49) yields

$$
\hat{\lambda}_{l}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\lambda}_{u}=\frac{\ln \left(1 / \beta_{1}\right)}{T} . \quad \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{1}
$$

Figure 7.6 gives confidence limits $\hat{\lambda}_{l} / \hat{\lambda} \& \hat{\lambda}_{u} / \hat{\lambda}$ for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$, with $\hat{\lambda}=k / T$, useful for practical applications; see Example 7.8 for an application.

For the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda, M T \bar{B} F=T / k, k \geq 1$, is biased; unbiased is, for $\lambda T \gg 1$, $M T \bar{B} F=T /(k+1) \quad(\mathrm{E}[T /(k+1)]=\left(1-e^{-\lambda T}\right) / \lambda$, Eqs. (A6.40), (A6.39), (A7.41)). For practical applications, $M T \bar{B} F_{l} \approx 1 / \hat{\lambda}_{u}$ and $M T \bar{B} F_{u} \approx 1 / \hat{\lambda}_{l}$ can often be used.

[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ The case considered in Sections 7.2.3.1-7.2.3.3 corresponds to a sampling plan with $n \geq 1$ statistically identical \& independent items and $k$ failures in the given (fixed,cumulative) operating time $T$ ( $T$ is often considered as time interval $(0, t=T / n]$ by assuming immediate repair or replacement to as-good-as-new of failed items, yielding a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) with intensity $n \lambda$ as flow of failures); fixed $T$ (or $t=T / n$ ) is known as Type I (time) censoring (fixed $k$ is the Type II (failure) censoring).

Figure 7.6 Confidence limits $\hat{\lambda}_{l} / \hat{\lambda} \& \hat{\lambda}_{u} / \hat{\lambda}$ for an unknown constant failure rate $\lambda, T=$ given (fixed) cumulative operating time (time censoring), $k=$ number of failures during $T, \gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}=$ confidence level, here $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$ (per Eqs. (7.28) \& (7.29); see footnote on p. 330; for $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda, M T B F_{l} \approx 1 / \hat{\lambda}_{u} \& M T B F_{u} \approx 1 / \hat{\lambda}_{l}$ can often be used; $\cdot$ result for Examples $7.8 \& 7.13$ )

Confidence limits $\hat{\lambda}_{l}, \hat{\lambda}_{u}$ can also be used to give one-sided confidence intervals:

$$
0 \leq \lambda \leq \hat{\lambda}_{u}, \quad \text { with } \quad \gamma=1-\beta_{1}
$$

and

$$
\lambda \geq \hat{\lambda}_{l}, \quad \text { with } \quad \gamma=1-\beta_{2}
$$

In practical applications, $M T B F \geq M T B F_{l} \approx 1 / \hat{\lambda}_{u} \& M T B F \leq M T B F_{u} \approx 1 / \hat{\lambda}_{l}$ can often be used, for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$.

# Example 7.8 

In testing a subassembly with constant failure rate $\lambda, 4$ failures occur during $T=10^{4}$ cumulative operating hours (footnote on p. 330). Find the confidence interval for $\lambda$ for a confidence level $\gamma=0.8\left(\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0.1\right)$.

## Solution

From Fig. 7.6 it follows that for $k=4$ and $\gamma=0.8, \hat{\lambda}_{l} / \hat{\lambda} \approx 0.44$ and $\hat{\lambda}_{u} / \hat{\lambda} \approx 2$. With $T=10^{4} \mathrm{~h}$, $k=4$, and $\hat{\lambda}=4 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, the confidence limits are $\hat{\lambda}_{l} \approx 1.7 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and $\hat{\lambda}_{u} \approx 8 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$.
Supplementary result: Corresponding one-sided conf. interval is $\lambda \leq 8 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ with $\gamma=0.9$.In the above considerations (Eqs. (7.28) - (7.32)), the cumulative operating time $T$ was given (fixed), independent of the individual failure-free times and the number $n$ of items involved (Type I (time) censoring, see also footnote on p. 330). The situation is different when the number of failures $k$ is given (fixed), i. e. when the test is stopped at the occurrence of the $k$ th failure (Type II (failure) censoring). Here, the cumulative operating time is a random variable (term $(k-1) / \lambda$ of Eqs. (7.23) \& (7.24)). Using the memoryless property of homogeneous Poisson processes, it can be shown that the quantities $\left(t_{i}-t_{i-1}\right), i=1,2, \ldots, k, t_{0}=0$, are independent observations of exponentially distributed random variables with parameters $n \lambda$ for Eq.(7.24) and $(n-i+1) \lambda$ for Eq.(7.23), respectively. This is necessary and sufficient to prove that the $\hat{\lambda}$ given by Eqs. (7.23) and (7.24) are maximum likelihood estimates for $\lambda$. For confidence intervals, results of Appendix A8.2.2.3 can be used (directly for the case of Eq. (7.24)).

In some practical applications, system's failure rate confidence limits as a function of component's failure rate confidence limits is asked. Monte Carlo simulation can help. However, for a series system with $n$ elements, constant failure rates $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}$, time censoring, and same observation time $T$, Eqs. (2.19), (7.28) \& (7.27) yield $\hat{\lambda}_{S 0}=\hat{\lambda}_{1}+\ldots+\hat{\lambda}_{n}$. Furthermore, for given (fixed) $T, 2 T \lambda_{i}\left(\lambda_{i}\right.$ considered here as random variable, Appendix A8.2.2.2) has a $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $2\left(k_{i}+1\right)$ degrees of freedom (Eqs. (A8.48) \& (A8.51), Table A9.2); thus, $2 T \lambda_{S 0}$ has a $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $\Sigma 2\left(k_{i}+1\right)$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.2, Example A6.15). From this, and considering the shape of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution (Tab. A9.2, [A9.2, A9.3]), it holds, empirically, that $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lambda_{S 0} \leq \hat{\lambda}_{1_{u}}+\ldots+\hat{\lambda}_{n_{u}}\right\} \geq \gamma$, with $\hat{\lambda}_{i_{u}}$ obtained from $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lambda_{i} \leq \hat{\lambda}_{i_{u}}\right\}=\gamma$ for $\gamma \approx 0.7, i=1, \ldots, n(\gamma \approx 0.78$ in [7.17]). Extensions to different observation times $T_{i}$, series-parallel structures, Erlangian distributed failure-free times are investigated in [7.17].

Estimation of $\lambda / \mu$ as approximation for unavailability is given in Section 7.2.2.1.

# 7.2.3.2 Simple Two-sided Test for the Demonstration of a Constant Failure Rate $\lambda$ (or of $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda)^{*}$ 

In the context of an acceptance test, demonstration of a constant failure rate $\lambda$ (or of $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ) is often required, not merely its estimation as in Section 7.2.3.1. The main concern of this test is to check a zero hypothesis $H_{0}: \lambda<\lambda_{0}$ against an alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: \lambda>\lambda_{1}$ on the basis of the following agreement between producer and consumer,
items should be accepted with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\alpha$ if the true (unknown) failure rate $\lambda$ is less than $\lambda_{0}$, but rejected with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\beta$ if $\lambda$ is greater than $\lambda_{1}$ $\left(\lambda_{0}, \lambda_{1}>\lambda_{0}\right.$, and $0<\alpha<1-\beta<1$ are given (fixed) values).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ ) See footnote on p. 330.$\lambda_{0}$ is the specified $\lambda$ and $\lambda_{1}$ is the maximum acceptable $\lambda\left(1 / m_{0} \& 1 / m_{1}\right.$ in IEC 61124 [7.19], and for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda, 1 / \theta_{0} \& 1 / \theta_{1}$ in MIL-HDBK-781 [7.23]). $\alpha$ is the allowed producer's risk (type I error), i. e. the probability of rejecting a true hypothesis $H_{0}: \lambda<\lambda_{0} . \beta$ is the allowed consumer's risk (type II error), i. e. the probability of accepting $H_{0}$ when the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: \lambda>\lambda_{1}$ is true. Evaluation of the above agreement is a problem of statistical hypothesis testing (Appendix A8.3), and can be performed e. g. with a simple two-sided test or a sequential test.

With the simple two-sided test (also known as fixed length test), the cumulative operating time $T$ (footnote on p. 330) and the number of allowed failure $c$ during $T$ are fixed quantities. The procedure (test plan) follows in a way similar to that developed in Appendix A8.3.1.1 as:

1. From $\lambda_{0}, \lambda_{1}, \alpha, \beta$ determine the smallest integer $c$ and the value $T$ satisfying

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{c} \frac{\left(\lambda_{0} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda_{0} T} \geq 1-\alpha
$$

and

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{c} \frac{\left(\lambda_{1} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda_{1} T} \leq \beta
$$

2. Perform a test with a total cumulative operating time $T$ (see footnote on p. 330), determine the number of failures $k$ during the test, and

- reject $H_{0}: \lambda<\lambda_{0}, \quad$ if $k>c$
- accept $H_{0}: \lambda<\lambda_{0}, \quad$ if $k \leq c$,
see Example 7.9 for an application. For the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$, the above procedure can be used to test $H_{0}: M T B F>M T B F_{0}$ against $H_{1}: M T B F<T B F_{1}$, by replacing $\lambda_{0}=1 / M T B F_{0}$ and $\lambda_{1}=1 / M T B F_{1}$.


# Example 7.9 

Following conditions have been specified for the demonstration (acceptance test) of the constant (time independent) failure rate $\lambda$ of an assembly: $\lambda_{0}=1 / 2000 \mathrm{~h}$ (specified $\lambda$ ), $\lambda_{1}=1 / 1000 \mathrm{~h}$ (minimum acceptable $\lambda$ ), producer risk $\alpha=0.2$, consumer risk $\beta=0.2$. Give: (i) the cumulative operating (test time) $T$ and the allowed number of failures $c$ during $T$; (ii) the probability of acceptance if the true failure rate $\lambda$ were $1 / 3000 \mathrm{~h}$.

## Solution

(i) From Fig. 7.3, $c=6$ and $m \approx 4.6$ for $\operatorname{Pr}\{$ acceptance $\} \approx 0.82, c=6$ and $m \approx 9.2$ for $\operatorname{Pr}\{$ acceptance $\} \approx 0.19$ (see Example 7.2 for the procedure); thus $c=6$ and $T \approx 9200 \mathrm{~h}$. These values agree well with those obtained from Table A9.2 $(v=14)$, as given also in Table 7.3.
(ii) For $\lambda=1 / 3000 \mathrm{~h}, T=9200 \mathrm{~h}, c=6$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { acceptance } \mid \lambda=1 / 3000 \mathrm{~h}\} \\
& \quad=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { no more than } 6 \text { failures in } T=9200 \mathrm{~h} \mid \lambda=1 / 3000 \mathrm{~h}\}=\sum_{i=0}^{6} \frac{3.07^{i}}{i!} e^{-3.07} \approx 0.96
\end{aligned}
$$

see also Fig. 7.3 for $m=3.07$ and $c=6$.

Figure 7.7 Operating characteristic curve as a function of the constant failure rate $\lambda$ for $\lambda_{0}=1 / 2000 \mathrm{~h}, \lambda_{1}=1 / 1000 \mathrm{~h}, \alpha=\beta \leqq 0.2 ; T=9200 \mathrm{~h}$ and $c=6$ as per Table 7.3, see also Fig. 7.3 ( $T=$ cumulative op. time; holds also for $M T B F_{0}=2000 \mathrm{~h} \& M T B F_{1}=1000 \mathrm{~h}$, for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ )

The graph of Fig. 7.7 visualizes the validity of the above agreement between producer and consumer (customer). It satisfies the inequalities (7.33) and (7.34), and is known as operating characteristic curve (or acceptance probability curve). For each value of $\lambda$, it gives the probability of having not more than $c$ failures during a cumulative operating time $T$. Considering that, for constant failure rate the operating characteristic curve as a function of $\lambda$ is strictly decreasing, the risk for a false decision decreases for $\lambda<\lambda_{0}$ and $\lambda>\lambda_{1}$, respectively. It can be shown that the quantities $c \& \lambda_{0} T$ only depend on $\alpha, \beta$, and the ratio $\lambda_{1} / \lambda_{0}$ (discrimination ratio).

Table 7.3 gives $c$ and $\lambda_{0} T$ for some values of $\alpha, \beta$ and $\lambda_{1} / \lambda_{0}$ useful for practical applications. For the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$, Table 7.3 holds for testing $H_{0}: M T B F>M T B F_{0}$ against $H_{1}: M T B F<M T B F_{1}$, by setting $\lambda_{0}=1 / M T B F_{0}$ and $\lambda_{1}=1 / M T B F_{1}$. Table 7.3 can also be used for the demonstration of an unknown probability $p$ (pp. 315 -16) in the case where the Poisson approximation applies. A large number of test plans are in international standards [7.19 (61124)].

In addition to the simple two-sided test described above, a sequential test is often used (see Appendix A8.3.1.2 \& Section 7.1.2.2 for an introduction and Fig.7.8 for an example). In this test, neither the cumulative operating time $T$ (footnote on p. 330), nor the number $c$ of allowed failures during $T$ are specified before the test begins;
the number of failures is recorded as a function of the (running) cumulative operating time (normalized to $1 / \lambda_{0}$ ), and the test is stopped as soon as the resulting staircase curve crosses the acceptance line or the rejection line.

Sequential tests offer the advantage that the test duration is on average shorter than with simple two-sided tests. Using Eq. (7.12) with $p_{0}=1-e^{-\lambda_{0} \delta t}, p_{1}=1-e^{-\lambda_{1} \delta t}$, $n=T / \delta t$, and $\delta t \rightarrow 0$ (continuous in time), the acceptance and rejection lines areTable 7.3 Number of allowed failures $c$ during the cumulative operating time $T$ (footnote p.330) and value of $\lambda_{0} T$ to demonstrate $\lambda<\lambda_{0}$ against $\lambda>\lambda_{1}$ for various values of $\alpha$ (producer risk), $\beta$ (consumer risk), and $\lambda_{1} / \lambda_{0}$ (Tab. # 7.2.3.3 Simple One-sided Test for the Demonstration of a Constant Failure Rate $\lambda$ (or of $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda)^{*}$ ) 

Simple two-sided tests (Fig. 7.7) and sequential tests (Fig. 7.8) have the advantage that, for $\alpha=\beta$, producer and consumer run the same risk of making a false decision. However, in practical applications often only $\lambda_{0}$ and $\alpha$ or $\lambda_{1}$ and $\beta$, i. e. simple one-sided tests, are used. The considerations of Section 7.1.3 (p.318) apply, and care should be taken with small values of $c$, as operating with $\lambda_{0} \& \alpha$ (or $\lambda_{1} \& \beta$ ) the producer (or consumer) can realize an advantage (see e. g. Problem 7.6 on p. 596). Figure 7.9 shows the operating characteristic curves for various values of $c$ as a function of $\lambda$ for the demonstration of $\lambda<1 / 1000 \mathrm{~h}$ against $\lambda>1 / 1000 \mathrm{~h}$ with consumer risk $\beta \approx 0.2$ for $\lambda=1 / 1000 \mathrm{~h}$, and visualizes the reduction of producer's risk ( $\alpha \approx 0.8$ for $\lambda \equiv 1 / 1000 \mathrm{~h}$ ) by decreasing $\lambda$ or increasing $c$ (counterpart of Fig.7.4).
