# 7.3 Estimation and Demonstration of an MTTR 

Maintainability is generally expressed as a probability (p. 392). In this case, results of Sections 7.1 and 7.2 .1 can be used to estimate or demonstrate maintainability. However, estimation and demonstration of specific parameters, for instance MTTR (mean time to repair, used for mean time to restoration in this book, see p. 113) is important for practical applications. If the underlying random variables are exponentially distributed (constant repair rate $\mu$ ), the results of Section 7.2.3 for a constant failure rate $\lambda$ can be used. This section deals with the estimation and demonstration of an MTTR by assuming that repair time is lognormally distributed (for Erlangian distributed repair times, results of Section 7.2.3 can be used, considering Eqs. (A6.102) - (A6.104)).

### 7.3.1 Estimation of an MTTR

Let $t_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, t_{n}^{\prime}$ be independent observations (realizations) of the repair time $\tau^{\prime}$ of a given item. From Eqs. (A8.6) and (A8.10), the empirical mean and variance of $\tau^{\prime}$ are given by

$$
\hat{\mathrm{E}}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\prime}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Vár}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}^{\prime}-\hat{\mathrm{E}}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{n-1}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\prime 2}-\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\prime}\right)^{2}\right]
$$Both estimates are unbiased, i. e. $\mathrm{E}\left[\hat{\mathrm{E}}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=M T T R \& \mathrm{E}\left[\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right]=\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]$; furthermore, $\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat{\mathrm{E}}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right]=\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / n$ (Appendix A8.1.2). As stated above, the repair time $\tau$ ' can often be assumed lognormally distributed with distribution function

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau^{\prime} \leq t\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\frac{\ln (\lambda t)}{\sigma}} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x
$$

(Eq. (A6.110)), and mean \& variance given by (Eqs. (A6.112) \& (A6.113))

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=M T T R=\frac{e^{\sigma^{2} / 2}}{\lambda}, \quad \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\frac{e^{2 \sigma^{2}}-e^{\sigma^{2}}}{\lambda^{2}}=M T T R^{2}\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right)
$$

Form Example A6.18 (p. 464) one recognizes that $\ln \tau^{\prime}$ is normally distributed with mean $\ln (1 / \lambda)$ and Variance $\sigma^{2}$. Using Eqs. (A8.24) and (A8.27), the maximum likelihood estimations of $\lambda$ and $\sigma^{2}$ follow as

$$
\hat{\lambda}=\left[\prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{t_{i}^{\prime}}\right]^{1 / n} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\ln \left(\hat{\lambda} t_{i}^{\prime}\right)\right]^{2}
$$

A point estimate for $\lambda$ and $\sigma$ can also be obtained by the method of quantiles. The idea is to substitute some particular quantiles with the corresponding empirical quantiles to obtain estimates for $\lambda$ or $\sigma$. For $t=1 / \lambda, \ln (\lambda t)=0$ and $\mathrm{F}(1 / \lambda)=0.5$, therefore, $1 / \lambda$ is the 0.5 quantile (median) $t_{0.5}$ of the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ given by Eq. (7.41). From the empirical 0.5 quantile $\hat{t}_{0.5}^{\prime}=\inf \left(t^{\prime}: \hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}\left(t^{\prime}\right) \geq 0.5\right)$ an estimate for $\lambda$ follows as

$$
\hat{\lambda} \approx 1 / \hat{t}_{0.5}^{\prime}
$$

Moreover, $t=e^{\sigma} / \lambda$ yields $\mathrm{F}\left(e^{\sigma} / \lambda\right) \approx 0.841(\ln (\lambda t) / \sigma=1$, Table A9.1); thus $e^{\sigma} / \lambda \approx t_{0.841}$ is the 0.841 quantile of $\mathrm{F}(t)$ given by Eq. (7.41). Using $\lambda=1 / t_{0.5}$ and $\sigma \approx \ln \left(\lambda t_{0.841}\right)=\ln \left(t_{0.841} / t_{0.5}\right)$, an estimate for $\sigma$ is obtained as

$$
\hat{\sigma} \approx \ln \left(\hat{t}_{0.841}^{\prime} / \hat{t}_{0.5}^{\prime}\right)
$$

Furthermore, considering $\mathrm{F}\left(e^{-\sigma} / \lambda\right) \approx 1-0.841 \approx 0.159$, i. e. $t_{0.159} \approx e^{-\sigma} / \lambda$, it follows that $e^{2 \sigma} \approx \lambda t_{0.841} / \lambda t_{0.159}$ and thus Eq. (7.45) can be replaced by

$$
\hat{\sigma} \approx \frac{1}{2} \ln \left(\hat{t}_{0.841}^{\prime} / \hat{t}_{0.159}^{\prime}\right)
$$

The possibility of representing a lognormal distribution function as a straight line, to simplify data interpretation, is discussed in Section 7.5.1 (Fig. 7.14, App. A9.8.1).

To obtain interval estimates for the parameters $\lambda$ and $\sigma$, note that the logarithm of a log normally distributed variable is normally distributed with mean $\ln (1 / \lambda)$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$. Applying the transformation $t_{i}^{\prime} \rightarrow \ln t_{i}^{\prime}$ to the individual observations $t_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, t_{n}^{\prime}$ and using the results known for the interval estimation ofthe parameters of a normal distribution [A6.1, A6.5], the confidence intervals

$$
\left[\frac{n \hat{\sigma}^{2}}{\chi_{n-1,(1+\gamma) / 2}^{2}}, \frac{n \hat{\sigma}^{2}}{\chi_{n-1,(1-\gamma) / 2}^{2}}\right]
$$

for $\sigma^{2}$, and

$$
\left[\hat{\lambda} e^{-\varepsilon}, \hat{\lambda} e^{\varepsilon}\right] \quad \text { with } \quad \varepsilon=\frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{n-1}} t_{n-1,(1+\gamma) / 2}
$$

for $\lambda$, can be found with $\hat{\lambda}$ and $\hat{\sigma}$ as in Eq. (7.43). $\chi_{n-1, q}^{2}$ and $\boldsymbol{t}_{n-1, q}$ are the $q$ quantiles of the $\chi^{2}$ and $\boldsymbol{t}$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom, respectively (Tables A9.2 and A9.3), see Example 7.11 for an application.

# Example 7.11 

Let $1.1,1.3,1.6,1.9,2.0,2.3,2.4,2.7,3.1$, and 4.2 h be 10 independent ordered observations (realizations) of a lognormally distributed repair time. Give the maximum likelihood estimate and, for $\gamma=0.9$, the confidence interval for the parameters $\lambda$ and $\sigma^{2}$, as well as the maximum likelihood estimate for MTTR.

## Solution

Equation (7.43) yields $\hat{\lambda} \approx 0.476 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and $\hat{\sigma}^{2} \approx 0.146$ as maximum likelihood estimates for $\lambda$ and $\sigma^{2}$. From Eq. (7.42), $M \hat{T} \hat{T} R \approx e^{0.073} / 0.476 \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \approx 2.26 \mathrm{~h}$. Using Eqs. (7.47) \& (7.48), as well as Tables A9.2 and A9.3, the confidence intervals are $[1.46 / 16.919,1.46 / 3.325] \approx[0.086,0.44]$ for $\sigma^{2}$ and $\left[0.476 e^{-0.127 \cdot 1.833}, 0.476 e^{0.127 \cdot 1.833}\right] \mathrm{h}^{-1} \approx[0.38,0.60] \mathrm{h}^{-1}$ for $\lambda$, respectively.

### 7.3.2 Demonstration of an MTTR

The demonstration of an MTTR (in an acceptance test) will be investigated here by assuming that the repair time $\tau^{\prime}$ is lognormally distributed with known $\sigma^{2}$ (method 1-A of MIL-HDBK-470 [7.23]). A rule is asked to test the null hypothesis $H_{0}: M T T R=M T T R_{0}$ against the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: M T T R=M T T R_{1}$ for given type I error $\alpha$ and type II error $\beta$ (Appendix A8.3). The procedure (test plan) is as follows:

1. From $\alpha$ and $\beta(0<\alpha<1-\beta<1)$, determine the quantiles $t_{\beta}$ and $t_{1-\alpha}$ of the standard normal distribution (Table A9.1)

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{t_{\beta}} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x=\beta \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{t_{1}} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x=1-\alpha
$$

From $M T T R_{0}$ and $M T T R_{1}$, compute the sample size $n$ (next highest integer)

$$
n=\frac{\left(t_{1-\alpha} M T T R_{0}-t_{\beta} M T T R_{1}\right)^{2}}{\left(M T T R_{1}-M T T R_{0}\right)^{2}}\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right)
$$2. Perform $n$ independent repairs and record the observed repair times $t_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, t_{n}^{\prime}$ (representative sample of repair times).
3. Compute $\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]$ according to Eq. (7.39) and reject $H_{0}: M T T R=M T T R_{0}$ if

$$
\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]>c=M T T R_{0}\left(1+t_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right) / n}\right)
$$

otherwise accept $H_{0}$.
The proof of the above rule implies a sample size $n>10$, so that the quantity $\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]$ can be assumed to have a normal distribution with mean MTTR and variance $\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / n$ (Eqs. (A6.148), (A8.7), (A8.8)). Considering the type I and type II errors

$$
\alpha=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]>c \mid M T T R=M T T R_{0}\right\}, \quad \beta=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] \leq c \mid M T T R=M T T R_{1}\right\}
$$

and using Eqs. (A6.105) and (7.49), the relationship

$$
c=M T T R_{0}+t_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{0}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / n}=M T T R_{1}+t_{\beta} \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{1}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / n}
$$

can be found, with $\operatorname{Var}_{i}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]$ for $M T T R=M T T R_{i}(i=0,1)$ according to Eq. (7.42) $\left(\operatorname{Var}_{i}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right) M T T R_{i}^{2}, i=0,1\right)$. The sample size $n$ (Eq. (7.50)) follows then from Eq. (7.52). The right hand side of Eq. (7.51) is equal to the constant $c$ as per Eq. (7.52). The operating characteristic curve can be calculated from

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { acceptance } \mid M T T R\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] \leq c \mid M T T R\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{d} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x
$$

with (Eqs. (A6.105), (7.42), (7.52))

$$
d=\frac{M T T R_{0}}{M T T R} t_{1-\alpha}-\left(1-\frac{M T T R_{0}}{M T T R}\right) \sqrt{n /\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right)}
$$

Considering $n /\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right)$ from Eq. (7.50), one recognizes that the operating characteristic curve is independent of $\sigma^{2}$ (rounding of $n$ neglected), see Example 7.12.

# Example 7.12 

Give the rejection conditions (Eq. (7.51)) and the operating characteristic curve (OC) for the demonstration of $M T T R=M T T R_{0}=2 \mathrm{~h}$ against $M T T R=M T T R_{1}=2.5 \mathrm{~h}$ with $\alpha=\beta=0.1 \& \sigma^{2}=0.2$.

## Solution

For $\alpha=\beta=0.1$, Eq. (7.49) and Table A9.1 yield $t_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.28, t_{\beta} \approx-1.28$. From Eq. (7.50) it follows $n=30$. The rejection condition is then given by

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{30} t_{i}^{\prime}>2 \mathrm{~h}\left(1+1.28 \sqrt{\left(e^{0.2}-1\right) / 30}\right) 30 \approx 66.6 \mathrm{~h}
$$

From Eq. (7.53), the OC follows as

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { acceptance } \mid M T T R\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{d} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x
$$

with $d \approx 25.84 \mathrm{~h} / M T T R-11.64$ (see graph).
# 7.4 Accelerated Testing 

The failure rate $\lambda$ of electronic components lies typically between $10^{-10}$ and $10^{-7} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, and that of assemblies in the range of $10^{-7}$ to $10^{-5} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. With such figures, cost and scheduling considerations demand the use of accelerated testing for $\lambda$ estimation and demonstration, in particular if reliable field data are not available. An
accelerated test is a test in which the applied stress is chosen to exceed that encountered in field operation, but still below the technological limits; this in order to shorten the time to failure of the item considered by avoiding an alteration of the involved failure mechanism (genuine acceleration).

In accelerated tests, failure mechanisms are assumed to be activated selectively by increased stress. The quantitative relationship between degree of activation and extent of stress, the acceleration factor $A$, is determined via specific tests. Generally,
it is assumed that the stress will not change the type of the failure-free time distribution function of the item under test, but only modify parameters; in the following, this hypothesis is assumed to be valid; however, its verification is mandatory before a statistical evaluation of data (see also p.102).

Many electronic component failure mechanisms are activated through a temperature increase. Calculating the acceleration factor $A$, the Arrhenius model can often be used over a reasonably large temperature range (about $0-150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for ICs ). The Arrhenius model is based on the Arrhenius law [7.10,3.43], which states that the rate $v$ of a simple (first-order) chemical reaction depends on temperature $T$ as

$$
v=v_{0} e^{-E_{a} / k T}
$$

$E_{a}$ and $v_{0}$ are parameters, $k$ is the Boltzmann constant ( $k=8.6 \cdot 10^{-5} \mathrm{eV} / \mathrm{K}$ ), and $T$ the absolute temperature in Kelvin degrees. $E_{a}$ is the activation energy and is expressed in eV . Assuming that the event considered (for example the diffusion between two liquids) occurs when the chemical reaction has reached a given threshold, and the reaction time dependence is given by a function $\mathrm{r}(t)$, the relationship between the times $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ necessary to reach at two temperatures $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}>T_{1}$ a given level of the chemical reaction considered can be expressed as

$$
v_{1} \mathrm{r}\left(t_{1}\right)=v_{2} \mathrm{r}\left(t_{2}\right)
$$

Furthermore, assuming $\mathrm{r}(t) \sim t$, i. e. a linear time dependence, it follows that

$$
v_{1} t_{1}=v_{2} t_{2}
$$

Substituting in Eq. (7.54) and rearranging, yields

$$
\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}}=e^{\frac{E_{a}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)}
$$By transferring this deterministic model to the mean times to failure $M T T F_{1}$ and $M T T F_{2}$ or to the constant failure rates $\lambda_{2}$ and $\lambda_{1}$ (using $M T T F=1 / \lambda$ ) of a given item at temperatures $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, it is possible to define an acceleration factor $A$

$$
A=M T T F_{1} / M T T F_{2}, \text { or, for time independent failure rate, } A=\lambda_{2} / \lambda_{1}
$$

expressed by

$$
A=e^{\frac{E_{a}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)+)}
$$

The right hand sides of Eq. (7.55) applies to the case of a constant (time independent but stress dependent) failure rate $\lambda(t)=\lambda$, for which $\mathrm{E}[\tau]=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[\tau]}=1 / \lambda$ holds with $\tau$ as time to failure (p. 457). Assuming that for time dependent failure rates, the left hand sides of Eq. (7.55) applies to mean time to failure $(E[\tau]=M T T F)$ and standard deviation ( $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[\tau]}$ ) as well, and that the type of the distribution function is the same at temperatures $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ (as stated on p.341), it can be shown that for the distribution functions frequently used in reliability engineering (Table A6.1) the following holds for the parameters: $\lambda_{2}=A \lambda_{1}$ for exponential, Gamma, Weibull, and lognormal; $\beta_{2}=\beta_{1}$ for Gamma and Weibull; $\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{1}$ for lognormal; $m_{2}=m_{1} / A$ $\& \sigma_{2}=\sigma_{1} / A$ for normal distribution (Problem 7.10 on p. 596). ${ }^{++}$This yields

$$
\mathrm{F}_{\tau_{1}}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{\tau_{2}}\left(\frac{t}{A}\right) \text { or } \mathrm{f}_{\tau_{1}}(t)=\mathrm{f}_{\tau_{2}}\left(\frac{t}{A}\right) / A \quad \text { and thus } \tau_{1}=A \tau_{2}
$$

where $\tau_{1} \& \tau_{2}$ are the (random) times to failure at temperatures $T_{1} \& T_{2}$, with distribution functions $\mathrm{F}_{\tau_{1}}(t) \& \mathrm{~F}_{\tau_{2}}(t)$ belonging (per assumption) to the same family (case viii in Example A6.18 on p. 464 and Eqs. (A6.40) \& (A6.46) with $C=A$ ).

Equation (7.56) can be reversed to give an estimate $\hat{E}_{a}$ for the activation energy $E_{a}$ based on the mean times to failure $M T T F_{1} \& M T T F_{2}$ (or the failure rates $\hat{\lambda}_{1} \&$ $\hat{\lambda}_{2}$ ) obtained empirically from two life tests at temperatures $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$. However,
at least three tests at $T_{1}, T_{2}$, and $T_{3}$ are necessary to verify the model.
The activation energy is highly dependent upon the particular failure mechanism involved (see Table 3.5 for indicative figures). For ICs, global values of $E_{a}$ lie between 0.3 and 0.7 eV , values which could basically be obtained empirically from the curves of the failure rate as a function of the junction temperature. However,
it must be noted that the Arrhenius model does not hold for all electronic devices and for any temperature range,
see e. g. also $[7.13,7.15,7.22]$ for further critical remarks on accelerated tests.
Figure 7.10 shows the acceleration factor $A$ from Eq. (7.56) as a function of $\theta_{2}$ in ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, for $\theta_{1}=35$ and $55^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and with $E_{a}$ as parameter $\left(\theta_{i}=T_{i}-273\right)$.

If the item (system) consists of $n$ independent series elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, each with its own failure mechanisms, the series model $\left(\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{R}_{i}(t)\right.$, Eq. (2.18))

\lambda_{S 0}\left(T_{2}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_{i} \lambda_{i}\left(T_{1}\right)
$$

(see also Eq. (8.1) on p. 376 for $A_{S}$ useful to calculate $\hat{\lambda}_{S 0}\left(T_{1}\right)=\hat{\lambda}_{S 0}\left(T_{2}\right) / A_{S}$ ). the series model can also be used to calculate the compound failure rate $\lambda_{C o}(t)$ for the case in which the item (device) considered exhibits $n$ different and independent (not mutually exclusive) failure mechanisms, each of which able to cause a failure of the item (multiple failure mechanisms, $\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$ referring to the ith of them; see p. 65 for an application and $p .354$ for a possible consequence)

$$
\lambda_{C o}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(t), \quad\left(\lambda_{i}(t)=\left(-d \mathrm{R}_{i}(t) / d t\right) / \mathrm{R}_{i}(t) \text { per Eq. }(2.10)\right)
$$

For two different devices, for instance, it follows that $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=$ $p_{a} \mathrm{R}_{a}(t)+\left(1-p_{a}\right) \mathrm{R}_{b}(t)$ per Eq. \lambda_{C o}(0)=p_{a} \lambda_{a}(0)+\left(1-p_{a}\right) \lambda_{b}(0), \quad \mathrm{R}_{i}(0)=1
$$

for $\lambda_{a}(t)=\lambda_{a} \& \lambda_{b}(t)=\lambda_{a}+\delta, \lambda_{C o}(t)$ decrease monotonically from $\lambda_{a}+\left(1-p_{a}\right) \delta$ to $\lambda_{a}$. This case correspond to the situation in which $n$ possible failure mechanisms appear in each item only with probabilities $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}$ (with $p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n}=1$ ). *)

# Example 7.13 

Four failures have occurred during $10^{7}$ cumulative operating hours (footnote on p. 330) of a digital CMOS IC at a chip temperature of $130^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Assuming $\theta_{1}=35^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, a constant failure rate $\lambda$, and an activation energy $E_{a}=0.4 \mathrm{eV}$, give the interval estimation of $\lambda$ for $\gamma=0.8$.

## Solution

For $\theta_{1}=35^{\circ} \mathrm{C}, \theta_{2}=130^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, and $E_{a}=0.4 \mathrm{eV}$ it follows from Fig. 7.10 or Eq. (7.56) that $A \approx 35$. The cumulative operating time at $35^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is thus $T=0.35 \cdot 10^{9} \mathrm{~h}$ and the point estimate for $\lambda$ is $\hat{\lambda}=k / T \approx 11.4 \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. With $k=4$ and $\gamma=0.8$, it follows from Fig. 7.6 that $\hat{\lambda}_{i} / \hat{\lambda} \approx 0.44$ and $\hat{\lambda}_{u} / \hat{\lambda} \approx 2$; the confidence interval for $\lambda$ is therefore $[5,22.8] \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$.

## Example 7.14

A PCB contains 10 metal film resistors with stress factor $S=0.1$ and $\lambda\left(25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)=0.2 \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, 5 ceramic cap. (class 1) with $S=0.4$ and $\lambda\left(25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)=0.8 \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, 2$ electrolytic cap. (Al wet) with $S=0.6$ and $\lambda\left(25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)=6 \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, and 4 ceramic-packaged linear ICs with $\Delta \theta_{J A}=10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $\lambda\left(35^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)=20 \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. Neglecting printed wiring and solder joints, give the PCB failure rate at a burn-in temperature $\theta_{A}$ of $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ on the basis of relationships given in Figs. $2.4 \& 2.5$.

## Solution

The resistor and capacitor acceleration factors can be obtained from Fig. 2.4 as

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text { resistor: } & A \approx 2.5 / 0.7 \approx 3.6 \\
\text { ceramic capacitor (class 1): } & A \approx 3.8 / 0.45 \approx 8.4 \\
\text { electrolytic capacitor (Al wet): } & A \approx 13.6 / 0.35 \approx 38.9
\end{array}
$$

Using Eq. (2.4) for the ICs, it follows that $\lambda-\Pi_{T}$; with $\theta_{J}=35^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $90^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, the acceleration factor for the linear ICs can then be obtained from Fig. 2.5 as $A \approx 10 / 0.9 \approx 11$. From Eqs. $(2.19) \&(7.57)$, the PCB failure rate follows as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lambda\left(25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right) \approx(10 \cdot 0.2+5 \cdot 0.8+2 \cdot 6+4 \cdot 20) 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \approx 100 \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \\
& \lambda\left(80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right) \approx(10 \cdot 0.2 \cdot 3.6+5 \cdot 0.8 \cdot 8.4+2 \cdot 6 \cdot 38.9+4 \cdot 20 \cdot 11) 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \approx 1.4 \cdot 10^{-6} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \approx 14 \cdot \lambda\left(25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{\text {*) }}$ See also p. 64 for mutually exclusive events, and p. 367 for an alternative possibility using nonhomogeneous Poisson processes.A further model for investigating the time scale reduction (time compression) resulting from an increase in temperature has been proposed by H. Eyring [3.43, 7.25]. The Eyring model defines the acceleration factor as

$$
A=\left(T_{2} / T_{1}\right) e^{\frac{B}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)}
$$

where $B$ is not necessarily an activation energy. Eyring also suggests the following model, which considers the influences of temperature $T$ and of further stresses $X_{i}$

$$
A=\left(T_{2} / T_{1}\right)^{m} e^{\frac{B}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)} e^{\left[X_{1}\left(C+\frac{D}{k T_{1}}\right)-X_{2}\left(C+\frac{D}{k T_{2}}\right)\right]}
$$

Equation (7.59a) is known as the generalized Eyring model. In this multiplicative model, a function of the normalized variable $x=X / X_{0}$ can also be used instead of the quantity $X$ itself (for example $x^{n}, 1 / x^{n}, \ln x^{n}, \ln \left(1 / x^{n}\right)$ ). $B$ is not necessarily an activation energy, $C \& D$ are constants. The generalized Eyring model led to accepted models, for electromigration (Black, $m=0, X_{1}=\ln \left(j_{2} / j_{1}\right)^{n}, B=E_{a}, C=1, D=X_{2}=0$ in Eq. (7.59a)), corrosion (Peck), and voltage stress (Kemeny) [3.34, 3.56, 3.67]

$$
A=\left(\frac{j_{2}}{j_{1}}\right)^{n} e^{\frac{E_{a}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)}, \quad A=\left(\frac{R H_{2}}{R H_{1}}\right)^{n} e^{\frac{E_{a}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)}, \quad A=e^{\left(C_{0}+\frac{E_{a}}{k T}+C_{1} V / V_{\max }\right)}
$$

where $j=$ current density, $R H=$ relative humidity, and $V=$ voltage, respectively (see also Eqs. (3.2) - (3.6) and Table 3.5). Refined models are e. g. in [3.67 \& 2.22].

For failure mechanisms related to mechanical fatigue, Coffin-Manson simplified models [2.73, 2.62] (based on the inverse power law) can often be used, yielding for the number of cycles to failure

$$
A=\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}=\left(\frac{\Delta T_{2}}{\Delta T_{1}}\right)^{\beta_{T}} \quad \text { or } \quad A=\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}=\left(\frac{G_{2}}{G_{1}}\right)^{\beta_{M}}
$$

where $\Delta T$ refers to thermal cycles, $G$ to vibration tests $\left(0.5<\beta_{T}<0.8,0.7<\beta_{M}<0.9\right.$ for practical applications). For cracks propagation, Paris Law [2.77, 2.79] applies in many situations. For damage accumulation, Miner's hypothesis of independent damage increments [3.52] can be used in some applications. Known for conductivefilament formation is the Rudra's model[3.62]. Models for solder joints are discussed e. g. in [3.79(2011), 3.90], see Section 3.4 (p.109) for some considerations.

Refinement of the above models is in progress in the context of physics of failures (PoF) [2.15, 3.49, 3.66, 3.67], in particular for ULSI ICs and considering stress dependent parameters and time dependent failure rates, with emphasis on:

1. New oxide \& package related, or externally induced failure mechanisms.
2. Identification and analysis of causes for early failures or premature wear-out.
3. Development of physical models for failure mechanisms and of simplified models for reliability predictions in practical applications.

Such efforts will increase physical understanding on components failure rates.In addition to the accelerated tests discussed above, a rough estimate of component life time can often be obtained through short-term tests under extreme stresses (HALT, HAST, etc.). Examples are humidity testing of plastic-packaged ICs at high pressure and nearly $100 \% \mathrm{RH}$, or tests of ceramic-packaged ICs at up to $350^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Experience shows that under high stress, life time is often lognormally distributed, thus with strong time dependence of the failure rate (Table A6.1 on p. 447). Highly accelerated stress tests (HAST) and highly accelerated life tests (HALT) can activate failure mechanisms which would not occur during normal operation, so
care is necessary in extrapolating results to situations exhibiting lower stresses.
Often, the purpose of such tests is to force (not only to activate) failures. They belong thus to the class of semi-destructive or destructive tests, often used at the qualification of prototype to investigate possible failure modes, mechanisms, and/or technological limits. The same holds for step-stress accelerated tests (often used as life tests or in screening procedures), for which, damage accumulation can be more complex as given e. g. by the Miner's hypothesis or in [7.20, 7.28];
a case-by-case investigation is mandatory for all this kind of tests (see also remarks on pp. 102, 341, 342, 406).

# 7.5 Goodness-of-fit Tests 

Let $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ be $n$ independent observations of a random variable $\tau$ distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(t)$, a rule is asked to test the null hypothesis $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$, for a given type I error $\alpha$ (probability of rejecting a true hypothesis $H_{0}$ ), against a general alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: \mathrm{F}(t) \neq \mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$. Goodness-of-fit tests deal with such testing of hypothesis and are often based on the empirical distribution function (EDF), see Appendices A8.3 for an introduction. This section shows the use of Kolmogorov-Smirnov and chi-square tests. Cramér -von Mises tests are summarized on pp. 572 - 73. Trend tests are discussed in Section 7.6.

### 7.5.1 Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (pp. 545-46, 572) is based on the convergence for $n \rightarrow \infty$ of the empirical distribution function (Eq. (A8.1))

$$
\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } t<t_{(1)} \\ i / n & \text { for } t_{(i)} \leq t<t_{(i+1)}, \\ 1 & \text { for } t \geq t_{(n)}\end{cases} \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n-1
$$

to the true distribution function, and compares the experimentally obtained $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ with the given (postulated) $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t) . \quad \mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is assumed here to be known and continuous, $t_{(1)}<\ldots<t_{(n)}$ are the ordered observations. The procedure is as follows:

Figure 7.11 Largest deviation $y_{1-\alpha}$ between a postulated distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ and the corresponding empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ at the level $1-\alpha\left(\operatorname{Pr}\left\{D_{n} \leq y_{1-\alpha} \mid \mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\right.\right.$ true $\left.]=1-\alpha\right)$

1. Determine the largest deviation $D_{n}$ between $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ and $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$

$$
D_{n}=\sup _{-\infty<t<\infty}\left|\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)-\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\right|
$$

2. From the given type 1 error $\alpha$ and the sample size $n$, use Table A9.5 or

Fig. 7.11 to determine the critical value $y_{1-\alpha}$.
3. Reject $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ if $D_{n}>y_{1-\alpha} ;$ otherwise accept $H_{0}$.

This procedure can be easily combined with a graphical evaluation of data. For this purpose, $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ and the band $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t) \pm y_{1-\alpha}$ are drawn using a probability chart on which $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ can be represented by a straight line. If $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ leaves the band $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t) \pm y_{1-\alpha}$, the hypothesis $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is to be rejected (note that the band width is not constant when using a probability chart). Probability charts are discussed in Appendix A.8.1.3, examples are in Appendix A9.8 and Figs. 7.12 - 7.14. Example 7.15 (Fig. 7.12) shows a graphical evaluation of data for the case of a Weibull distribution, Example 7.16 (Fig. 7.13) investigates the distribution function of a population with early failures and a constant failure rate using a Weibull probability chart, and Example 7.17 (Fig. 7.14) uses the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to check agreement with a lognormal distribution. If $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is not completely known, a modification is necessary (Appendix A8.3.3).

# Example 7.15 

Accelerated life testing of a wet Al electrolytic capacitor leads following 13 ordered observations of lifetime: $59,71,153,235,347,589,835,913,1185,1273,1399,1713$, and 2567 h . (i) Draw the empirical distribution function of data on a Weibull probability chart. (ii) Assuming that the underlying distribution function is Weibull, determine $\hat{\lambda} \& \hat{\beta}$ graphically (p. 547). (iii) The maximum likelihood estimation of $\lambda \& \beta$ yields $\hat{\beta}=1.12$, calculate $\hat{\lambda}$ and compare with (ii).

## Solution

(i) Figure 7.12 presents the empirical distribution function $\hat{F}_{n}(t)$ on Weibull probability paper. (ii) The graphical determination of $\lambda$ and $\beta$ leads to (straight line (ii)) $\hat{\lambda} \approx 1 / 840 \mathrm{~h}$ and $\hat{\beta} \approx 1.05$. (iii) With $\hat{\beta} \approx 1.12$, Eq. (A8.31) yields $\hat{\lambda} \approx 1 / 908 \mathrm{~h}$ (straight line (iii)) (see also Example A8.12).

Figure 7.12 Empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{0}(t)$ and estimated Weibull distribution functions ((ii) and (iii)) as per Example 7.15 (see Appendix A8.1.3, in particular the remark on p. 547)

Figure 7.13 S-shape of a weighted sum $\mathrm{F}(t)=p \mathrm{~F}_{a}(t)+(1-p) \mathrm{F}_{b}(t)$ of a Weibull distribution $\mathrm{F}_{a}(t)$ and an exponential distribution $\mathrm{F}_{b}(t)$ per Example 7.16, useful to detect (describe) early failures (wear-out failures for slope 1 at the beginning and $>1$ at the end, see also pp. 7, $367 \& 483$ for alternative possibilities and pp. $7 \& 444$ when early failures and wear-out can occur)# Example 7.16 

Investigate the mixed distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)=0.2\left[1-e^{-(0.1 t)^{0.5}}\right]+0.8\left[1-e^{-0.0005 t}\right]$ on a Weibull probability chart (describing a possible early failure period).

The weighted sum of a Weibull distribution (Eq. (A6.89) with $\beta=0.5, \lambda=0.1 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, MTTF $=20 \mathrm{~h}$ ) and an exponential distribution (with $\lambda=0.0005 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and $M T T F=1 / \lambda=2000 \mathrm{~h}$ ) represents the distribution function of a population of items with early failures up to about $t \approx 300 \mathrm{~h}$, see graph; $\lambda(t)=\left[0.01(0.1 t)^{-0.5} e^{-(0.1 t) 0.5}+0.0004 e^{-0.0005 t}\right] /$ $\left[0.2 e^{-(0.1 t)^{0.5}}+0.8 e^{-0.0005 t}\right]$ is nearly constant at $0.0005 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ for $t$ between 300 and 300.000 h , so that for $t>300 \mathrm{~h}$ a constant failure rate can be assumed $(1-F(300) \approx 0.69, \lambda(300) \approx 0.00051 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$; $\left.1-F(300.000) \approx 6 \cdot 10^{-66}, \lambda(300.000) \approx 0.0005 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}\right)$. Figure 7.13 gives the function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ on a Weibull probability chart, showing the typical $s$-shape.


## Example 7.17

Use the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to verify with a type I error $\alpha=0.2$, whether the repair time defined by the ordered observations $t_{(1)}, \ldots, t_{(10)}$, of Example 7.11 (p.339) are distributed according to a lognormal distribution function with parameters $\lambda=0.5 \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \& \sigma=0.4$ (hypothesis $H_{0}$ ).

## Solution

The lognormal distribution (Eq. (7.41)) with $\lambda=0.5 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and $\sigma=0.4$ is represented by a straight line on Fig. $7.14\left(\mathrm{~F}_{0}(t)\right)$. With $\alpha=0.2$ and $n=10$, Table A9.5 or Fig. 7.11 yields $y_{1-\alpha}=0.323$ and thus the band $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t) \pm 0.323$. Since the empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ does not leave the band $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t) \pm y_{1-\alpha}$, the hypothesis $H_{0}$ cannot be rejected.

### 7.5.2 Chi-square Test

The chi-square test ( $\chi^{2}$-test) can be used for continuous or non-continuous $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$. Furthermore, $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ need not to be completely known.

For $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ completely known, the procedure is as follows (pp. 573-74):

1. Partition the definition range of the random variable $\tau$ into $k$ intervals/ classes $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right],\left(a_{2}, a_{3}\right], \ldots,\left(a_{k}, a_{k+1}\right)$; the choice of the classes must be made independently of the observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ (made before test begin) and based on the rule: $n p_{i} \geqq 5$, with $p_{i}$ as per Eq. (7.64)).
2. Determine the number of observations $k_{i}$ in each class $\left(a_{i}, a_{i+1}\right]$, $i=1, \ldots, k\left(k_{i}=\right.$ number of $t_{j}$ with $a_{i}<t_{j} \leq a_{i+1}, k_{1}+\ldots+k_{k}=n$ ).
3. Assuming the hypothesis $H_{0}$, compute the expected number of observations for each class $\left(a_{i}, a_{i+1}\right]$

$$
n p_{i}=n\left(\mathrm{~F}_{0}\left(a_{i+1}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i}\right)\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, k, p_{1}+\ldots+p_{k}=1
$$

4. Compute the statistic

Figure 7.14 Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to check the repair time distribution as per Example 7.17 (the distribution function with $\hat{\lambda}$ and $\hat{\sigma}$ from Example 7.11 is shown dashed for information only)

$$
X_{n}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{\left(k_{i}-n p_{i}\right)^{2}}{n p_{i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{k_{i}^{2}}{n p_{i}}-n
$$

5. For a given type I error $\alpha$, use Table A9.2 or Fig. 7.15 to determine the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $k-1$ degrees of freedom $\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$.
6. Reject $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ if $X_{n}^{2}>\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2} ;$ otherwise accept $H_{0}$.

If $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is not completely known $\left(\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(t, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)\right.$, with $\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}$ as unknown parameters, $r<k-1$ ), modify the above procedure after step 2 as (pp. 575-76):
3'. On the basis of the observations $k_{i}$ in each class $\left(a_{i}, a_{i+1}\right], i=1, \ldots, k$ determine the maximum likelihood estimates for the parameters $\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}$ from the following system of (r) algebraic equations

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{k_{i}}{p_{i}\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)} \cdot\left.\frac{\partial p_{i}\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)}{\partial \theta_{j}}\right|_{\theta_{j}=\hat{\theta}_{j}}=0, \quad j=1, \ldots, r
$$

with $p_{i}=\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i+1}, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i}, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)>0, p_{1}+\ldots+p_{k}=1$, and for each class $\left(a_{i}, a_{i+1}\right]$ compute the expected number of observations

$$
n \hat{p}_{i}=n\left[\mathrm{~F}_{0}\left(a_{i+1}, \hat{\theta}_{1}, \ldots, \hat{\theta}_{r}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i}, \hat{\theta}_{1}, \ldots, \hat{\theta}_{r}\right)\right], \quad i=1, \ldots, k
$$4'. Calculate the statistic

$$
\hat{X}_{n}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{\left(k_{i}-n \hat{p}_{i}\right)^{2}}{n \hat{p}_{i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{k_{i}^{2}}{n \hat{p}_{i}}-n
$$

5'. For given type 1 error $\alpha$, use Table A9.2 or Fig. 7.15 to determine the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $k-1-r$ degrees of freedom.
6'. Reject $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ if $\hat{X}_{n}^{2}>\chi_{k-1-r, 1-\alpha}^{2} ;$ otherwise accept $H_{0}$.
Comparing the above two procedures, it can be noted that the number of degrees of freedom has been reduced from $k-1$ to $k-1-r$, where $r$ is the number of parameters of $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ which have been estimated from the observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ using the multinomial distribution (Example A8.13), see Example 7.18 for an application.

# Example 7.18 

Let $160,380,620,650,680,730,750,920,1000,1100,1400,1450,1700,2000,2200,2800$, $3000,4600,4700$, and 5000 h be 20 independent ordered observations (realizations) of the failure-free time $\tau$ for a given assembly. Using the chi-square test for $\alpha=0.1$ and the 4 classes $(0,500],(500,1000],(1000,2000],(2000, \infty)$, determine whether or not $\tau$ is exponentially distributed (hypothesis $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-\lambda t}, \lambda$ unknown).

## Solution

The given classes yield number of observations of $k_{1}=2, k_{2}=7, k_{3}=5$, and $k_{4}=6$. The point estimate of $\lambda$ is then given by Eq. (7.66) with $p_{i}=e^{-\lambda a_{i}}-e^{-\lambda a_{i+1}}$, yielding for $\hat{\lambda}$ the numerical solution $\hat{\lambda} \approx 0.562 \cdot 10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. Thus, the numbers of expected observations in each of the 4 classes are according to Eq. (7.67) $n \hat{p}_{1} \approx 4.899, n \hat{p}_{2} \approx 3.699, n \hat{p}_{3} \approx 4.90$, and $n \hat{p}_{4} \approx 6.499$. From Eq. (7.68) it follows that $\hat{X}_{20}^{2} \approx 4.70$ and from Table A9.2, $\chi_{2,0.9}^{2} \approx 4.605$. The hypothesis $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-\lambda t}$ must be rejected since $\hat{X}_{n}^{2}>\chi_{k-1-r, 1-\alpha}^{2}$.


Figure 7.15 $(1-\alpha)$ quantile ( $\alpha$ percentage point) of the chi-square distribution with $v$ degrees of freedom ( $\chi_{v, 1-\alpha}^{2}$, see also Table A9.2)# 7.6 Statistical Analysis of General Reliability Data 

### 7.6.1 General considerations

In Sections 7.2 - 7.5, data were issued from a sample of a random variable $\tau$, i. e. they were $n$ independent realizations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of $\tau>0$ distributed according to (a postulated) $\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}$, and belonging to one of the following situations:

1. Life times $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of $n$ statistically identical and independent items, all starting at $t=0$ when plotted on the time axis (Figs. 1.1, 7.12, 7.14, A8.1).
2. Failure-free times separating consecutive failure occurrences of a repairable item (system) with negligible repair times, repaired (restored) as a whole to as-good-as-new at each repair; i. e. statistically identical, independent interarrival times with common distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)$, yielding a renewal process.
To this data structure belongs also the case considered in Example 7.19.
A basically different situation arises when the observations are arbitrary points on the time axis, i. e. a general point process. To distinguish this case, the involved random variables are labeled $\tau_{1}^{*}, \tau_{2}^{*}, \ldots$, with $t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ for the corresponding realizations ( $t_{1}^{*}<t_{2}^{*}<\ldots$ tacitly assumed). This situation often occurs in reliability tests;
for instance, when only the failed part in a system is repaired to as-good-as-new (p.138-39), and at least one element in the system has a time dependent failure rate; in this case, failure-free times (interarrival times, by negligible repair times) are neither independent nor equally distributed.

Except for very large systems, for which the flow of failures can converge to a homogeneous Poisson process (p. 537), the only situation which leads to independent and equally distributed interarrival times is that of case 2 above,
which requires constant failure rate for all elements to avoid restoration at each repair of all not failed elements with time dependent failure rate.

## Example 7.19

Let $\mathrm{F}(t)$ be the distribution function of the failure-free time of a given item. Suppose that at $t=0$ an unknown number $n$ of items are put into operation and that at the time $T$ exactly $k$ item are failed (no replacement or repair has been done). Give a point estimate for $n$.

## Solution

Setting $p=\mathrm{F}(T)$, the number $k$ of failures in $(0, T)$ is binomially distributed (Eq. (A6.120))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { failures in }(0, T]\}=p_{k}=\binom{k}{k} p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}, \quad p=\mathrm{F}(T)
$$

An estimate for $n$ using the maximum likelihood method $\left(L=\binom{n}{k} p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}\right.$ per Eq. (A8.23) and $\partial \ln \mathrm{L} / \partial n=0$ for $\left.n=\hat{n}\right)$ yields, with $\binom{n}{k}=\left(e^{-k} / k!\right)\left(n^{n} /(n-k)^{(n-k)}\right.$ (Stirling's formula p. 582),

$$
\hat{n}=k / p=k / \mathrm{F}(T), \quad\left(p_{k} \approx e^{-n p}(n p)^{k} / k!\text { (Eq. (A6.129)) gives also } \hat{n}=k / p\right)
$$

Supplementary results: If $\mathrm{F}(t)$ is unknown, $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{k}(t)$ can be obtained using $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{k}$ and Eq. (7.62).Easy to investigate (when observing data on the time axis) are also cases involving nonhomogeneous Poisson processes (Sections 7.6.2, 7.6.3, 7.7, Appendix A7.8.2). However, more general situations can lead to difficulties, except for some general results valid for stationary point processes (Appendices A7.8.3-A7.8.5).

From the above considerations, following general rule should apply,
if neither a Poisson process (homogeneous or nonhomogeneous) nor a renewal process can be assumed for the underlying point process, care is necessary in identifying possible models; in any case, model validation (physical \& statistical aspects) must precede data analysis (see also p.102).

The homogeneous Poisson process (HPP), introduced in Appendix A7.2.5 as a particular renewal process, is the simplest point process. It is memoryless, and tools for a statistical investigation are well known. Nonhomogeneous Poisson processes (NHPPs) are without aftereffect (Appendix A7.8.2), and for investigation purposes they can be transformed into an HPP (Eqs. (7.76), (A7.200)). Investigations on renewal processes (Appendix A7.2) can be reduced to that of independent random variables with a common distribution function (cases 1 and 2 on p. 353). However, disregarding the last part of the above general rule can lead to mistakes, even in the presence of renewal processes or independent realizations of a random variable $\tau$. As an example, let's consider an item with two independent failure mechanisms, one appearing with constant failure rate $\lambda_{0}=10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and the second (wear-out) with a shifted Weibull distribution $\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda(t-\psi))^{\beta}}$ with $\lambda=10^{-2} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \psi=10^{4} \mathrm{~h}$, and $\beta=3(t>\psi, F(t)=0$ for $t \leq \psi)$. The failure-free time $\tau$ has the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-\lambda_{0} t}$ for $0<t \leq \psi$ and $\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-\lambda_{0} t} \cdot e^{-(\lambda(t-\psi))^{\beta}}$ for $t>\psi$ (failure rate $\lambda(t)=\lambda_{0}$ for $t \leq \psi$ and $\lambda(t)=\lambda_{0}+\beta \lambda^{\beta}(t-\psi)^{\beta-1}$ for $t>\psi$, similar to a series model with two independent elements (pp. 343-44));
if the presence of the two failure mechanisms is not known, neither suspected, and the test is stopped (censored) at $10^{4} \mathrm{~h}$, the wrong conclusion can be drawn that the item has a constant failure rate $\lambda_{0}=10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$.

Investigation of cases involving general point processes is beyond the scope of this book (only some general results are given in Appendices A7.8.3 - A7.8.5). A large number of ad hoc procedures are known in the literature, but they often only apply to specific situations and their use needs a careful validation of assumptions made.

After some basic considerations on tests for nonhomogeneous Poisson processes (Section 7.6.2), Sections 7.6.3.1 \& 7.6.3.2 deal with trend tests to check the assumption homogeneous Poisson process versus nonhomogeneous Poisson process with increasing or decreasing intensity. A heuristic test to distinguish a homogeneous Poisson process from a general monotonic trend is critically discussed in Section 7.6.3.3. However, as stated in above general rule, the validity of a model should be
checked also on the basis of physical considerations on the item considered, in particular about "without aftereffect", characterizing Poisson processes.# 7.6.2 Tests for Nonhomogeneous Poisson Processes 

A nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) is a point processes which count function $v(t)$ has unit jumps, independent increments (in nonoverlapping intervals), and satisfies for any $b>a \geq 0$ (Eq. (A7.195), see also the footnote on p. 481)

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { events in }(a, b]\}=\frac{(\mathrm{M}(b)-\mathrm{M}(a))^{k}}{k!} e^{-(\mathrm{M}(b)-\mathrm{M}(a))}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& k=0,1, \ldots \\
& 0 \leq a<b, \mathrm{M}(0)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

$a=0 \& b=t$ yields $\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t)=k\}=(\mathrm{M}(t))^{k} e^{-\mathrm{M}(t)} / k$ !. $\mathrm{M}(t)$ is the mean value function of the NHPP, giving the expected number of points (events) in $(0, t]$ (p. 532)

$$
\mathrm{M}(t)=\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)]
$$

$$
t>0, \mathrm{M}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

$\mathrm{M}(t)=\lambda t$ yields a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP). Assuming $\mathrm{M}(t)$ derivable,

$$
\mathrm{m}(t)=d \mathrm{M}(t) / d t \geq 0, \quad t>0, \mathrm{~m}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

is the intensity of the NHPP and has for $\delta t \downarrow 0$ following interpretation (Eq.(A7.194))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { one event in }(t, t+\delta t]\}=\mathrm{m}(t) \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t)
$$

Because of independent increments (in nonoverlapping intervals), the number of events (failures) in a time interval $(t, t+\theta]$ (Eq. (7.71) with $a=t \& b=t+\theta$ ) and the rest waiting time to the next event from an arbitrary time point $t$ (Eqs. (A7.196))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R}(t)>x\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { no event in }(t, t+x]\}=e^{-(\mathrm{M}(t+x)-\mathrm{M}(t))}, \quad t, x>0, \mathrm{M}(0)=0
$$

are independent of the process development up to time $t$; i. e. the Poisson process is a process without aftereffect, memoryless if homogeneous. The mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{R}(t)\right]$ is thus also independent of the process development up to time $t$ (Eq. (A7.197))

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{R}(t)\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(\mathrm{M}(t+x)-\mathrm{M}(t))} d x
$$

Furthermore, if $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\tau_{2}^{*}<\ldots$ are the occurrence times (arrival times) of the event considered (e.g. failures of a repairable system), measured from $t=0$, it holds for $\mathrm{m}(t)>0$ (i. e. $\mathrm{M}(t)$ derivable and strictly increasing) that the quantities

$$
\psi_{1}^{*}=\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{1}^{*}\right)<\psi_{2}^{*}=\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{2}^{*}\right)<\ldots
$$

are the occurrence times in a homogeneous Poisson processes with intensity one (Eq. (A7.200)). Moreover, for given (fixed) $T$ and $v(T)=n$, the occurrence times $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T$ have the same distribution as if they where the order statistic of $n$ independent identically distributed random variables with density

$$
\mathrm{m}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T), \quad 0<t<T
$$

and distribution function $\mathrm{M}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T)$ on $(0, T)$ (Eq. (A7.205)).Equation (7.74) gives the unconditional probability for one event in $(t, t+\delta t]$. Thus, $\mathrm{m}(t)$ refers to the occurrence of any one of the events considered. It corresponds to the renewal density $\mathrm{h}(t)$ and the failure intensity $\mathrm{z}(t)$, but differs basically from the failure rate $\lambda(t)$ (see remarks on pp. 7, 390-91, 482, 540).

Nonhomogeneous Poisson processes (NHPPs) are carefully introduced in Appendix A7.8.2. Some examples are discussed in Section 7.7 with applications to reliability growth. Assuming that the underlying process is an NHPP, estimation of the model parameters (parameters $\theta$ of $\mathrm{m}(t, \theta)$ ) can be performed using the maximum likelihood method on the basis of the observed data $0<t_{1}^{*}<t_{2}^{*}<\ldots<t_{n}^{*}<T$ (time censoring; $t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ are the observed values (realizations) of $\tau_{1}^{*}, \tau_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ and * is used to explicitly indicate that $t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ are points on the time axis and not independent realizations of a random variable $\tau$, e. g. as in Figs. 1.1, 7.12, 7.14, A8.1). Considering Eqs. (7.71) and (7.74), the likelihood function follows as (Eq. (7.102))

$$
\mathrm{L}=e^{-\mathrm{M}(T)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)
$$

and delivers the maximum likelihood estimate $\hat{\theta}$ for the parameters $\theta$ of $\mathrm{m}(t, \theta)$ by solving $\partial \mathrm{L} / \partial \theta=0$ for $\theta=\hat{\theta}$, where $\theta$ can be a vector (see e. g. Eq. (7.104) for the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of the NHPP with $\mathrm{m}(t)=\alpha \beta t^{\beta-1}$ ). Using the property stated by Eq. (7.76), statistical tests for exponential distribution or for homogeneous Poisson processes (Section 7.2.3, Appendices A8.2.2.2 \& A8.2.3.3) can be applied to NHPPs as well. Furthermore, using the property stated by Eq. (7.77), the goodness-of-fit tests introduced in Appendices A8.3.2 \& A8.3.3 and Section 7.5 (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, chi-square, Cramér-von Mises) can be used to verify agreement of observed data $t_{1}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*}<T$ with a postulated $\mathrm{M}_{0}(t)$. For the KolmogorovSmirnov test, the procedure given in Section 7.5.1 applies with (see p. 536)

$$
\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)=\mathrm{v}(t) / \mathrm{v}(T)
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)=\mathrm{M}_{0}(t) / \mathrm{M}_{0}(T)
$$

where $v(t)$ is the number of events in $(0, t]$, yielding $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ similar as in Fig. A8.1.
More difficult is the situation when the assumption that the model is an NHPP
must also be verified by a statistical data analysis,
for instance with a goodness-of-fit test. The problem in not completely solved (see Section 7.6.3 for some particular cases). However, the property given by Eqs. (7.76) \& (7.77) can be used for goodness-of-fit of the NHPP with incompletely specified (up to the parameters) mean function $\mathrm{M}_{0}(t)$. The chi-square test holds with the procedure given in Section 7.5.2 (pp. 350-52). For a first evaluation, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (and tests based on a quadratic statistic) can be used, taking half (randomly selected) of the observations $t_{1}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*}$ to estimate the parameters and continuing with the whole sample the procedure given in Section 7.5.1 for the goodness-of-fit test [A8.11, A8.32], considering Eqs (7.79) \& (7.80).# 7.6.3 Trend Tests 

In reliability engineering one is often interested to test if there is a monotonic trend in the times between consecutive failures (interarrival times) of a repairable system with negligible repair (restoration) times. For instance, in order to detect the end of an early failure period or the beginning of a wear-out period. Such tests extend the tests for exponentiality or for homogeneous Poisson processes introduced in Section 7.2.3 (see also Section 7.5 and Appendices A8.2.1, A8.2.2, A8.3.2, A8.3.3). If the underlying point process can be approximated by a renewal process, a graphical approach can be used in detecting the presence of trends, see e.g. Fig. 7.13 for the case of early failures. In the case of a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP), a trend is given by an increasing or decreasing intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)$, e. g. $\beta>1$ or $\beta<1$ in Eq. (7.99). Trend tests can also be useful in investigating what kind of alternative hypothesis should be considered when an assumption is to be made about the statistical properties of a given data set. However,
trend tests check, often, a postulated hypothesis $H_{0}$ against a more or less broad alternative hypothesis $H_{1} ;$ care is therefore necessary in drawing precise conclusions from these tests, and the general rule on p. 354 applies (see e. g. [A8.1 (1985)] for test power studies with defined $H_{1}$ ).

In the following, some trend tests used in reliability data analysis are discussed, among these the Laplace test (see e. g. [A8.1 (1991)] for greater details).

### 7.6.3.1 Tests of an HPP versus an NHPP with increasing intensity

The homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) is a point process which count function $v(t)$ has stationary and independent Poisson distributed increments in nonoverlapping intervals (Eqs. (A7.41)). Interarrival times in an HPP are independent and distributed according to the same exponential distribution $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ (occurrence times are Erlangian distributed, Eqs. (A6.102), (A7.39)). The parameter $\lambda$ characterizes completely the HPP. $\lambda$ is at the same time the intensity of the HPP and the failure rate $\lambda(x)$ for all interarrival times, $x$ starting by 0 at each occurrence time of the event considered (e. g. failure of a repairable system with negligible repair (restoration) times). This numerical equality has been the cause for misinterpretations and misuses in practical applications, see e. g. [6.1, 7.11, A7.30]. The homogeneous Poisson process has been introduced in Appendix A7.2.5 as a particular renewal process. Considering $v(t)$ as the count function giving the number of events (failures) in $(0, t]$, Example A7.13 (Eq. (A7.213)) shows that,
for given (fixed) $T$ and $v(T)=n$ (time censoring), the normalized arrival times $0<\tau_{1}^{n} / T<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{n} / T<1$ of a homogeneous Poisson process are distributed as if they where the order statistic of $n$ independent identically uniformly distributed random variables on $(0,1)$.Similar results hold for an NHPP (Eq. (A7.206)),
for given (fixed) $T$ and $\mathrm{V}(T)=n$ (time censoring), the quantities $0<\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{1}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)<\ldots<\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{n}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)<1$ of a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) with mean value function $\mathrm{M}(t)$ are distributed as if they where the order statistic of $n$ independent identically uniformly distributed random variables on $(0,1)$.

With the above transformations, properties of the uniform distribution can be used to support statistical tests on homogeneous and nonhomogeneous Poisson processes.

Let $\omega$ be a continuous uniformly distributed random variable with density

$$
\mathrm{f}_{\omega}(x)=1 \quad \text { on }(0,1), \quad \mathrm{f}_{\omega}(x)=0 \quad \text { outside }(0,1)
$$

and distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{\omega}(x)=x$ on $(0,1)$. Mean and variance of $\omega$ are given by (Eqs. (A6.37) and (A6.44))

$$
\mathrm{E}[\omega]=1 / 2 \quad \& \quad \operatorname{Var}[\omega]=1 / 12
$$

The sum of $n$ independent random variables $\omega$ has mean $n / 2 \&$ variance $n / 12$. The distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{\omega_{n}}(x)$ of $\omega_{1}+\ldots+\omega_{n}$ is defined on $(0, n)$ and can be calculated using Eq. (A7.12). $\mathrm{F}_{\omega_{n}}(x)$ has been investigated in [A8.8], yielding to the conclusion that $\mathrm{F}_{\omega_{n}}(x)$ rapidly approach a normal distribution. For practical applications one can assume that for given $T$ and $\mathrm{v}(T)=n \geq 5$, the sum of the normalized arrival times $0<\tau_{1}^{*} / T<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*} / T<1$ of an HPP has distribution (Eq. (A6.148))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}^{*} / T\right)-n / 2\right] / \sqrt{n / 12} \leq x\right\} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{x} e^{-y^{2} / 2} d y, \quad-\infty<x<\infty
$$

Equation (7.85) can be used to test an HPP $(\mathrm{m}(t)=\lambda)$ versus an NHPP. For the case of a strictly increasing intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)=d \mathrm{M}(t) / d t$, and considering the observations (realizations) $0<t_{1}^{*}<t_{2}^{*}<\ldots<t_{n}^{*}<T$, the corresponding test procedure is:

1. Compute the statistic

$$
\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{*} / T\right)-n / 2\right] / \sqrt{n / 12}, \quad t_{i}^{*}=i \text { th arrival time. }
$$

2. For given type I error $\alpha$ determine the critical value $t_{1-\alpha}$ ( $1-\alpha$ quantile of the standard normal distribution, e.g. $t_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.64$ for $\alpha=0.05$, Tab. A9.1).
3. Reject $H_{0}$ : the underlying point process is an HPP, against $H_{1}$ : the underlying process is an NHPP with a strictly increasing intensity, at $1-\alpha$ confidence, if $\left[\left(\Sigma_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{*} / T\right)-n / 2\right] / \sqrt{n / 12}>t_{1-\alpha} ;$ otherwise accept $H_{0}$.

A test based on Eqs. (7.86) - (7.87) is called Laplace test and was introduced by Laplace as a test of randomness. It can be noted that $\Sigma_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{*} / T$ is a sufficient statistic (Appendix A8.2.1), and tends to assume large values for $H_{1}$ true ( $\mathrm{m}(t)$ strictly increasing). Example 7.20 gives an application.A further possibility to test an HPP $(\mathrm{m}(t)=\lambda)$ versus an NHPP is to use the statistic

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right)
$$

Considering (Eq.(A7.213)) that for given (fixed) $T$ and $v(T)=n$, the normalized arrival times $0<\omega_{1}=\tau_{1}^{*} / T<\ldots<\omega_{n}=\tau_{n}^{*} / T<1$ of an HPP are distributed as if they where the order statistic of $n$ independent identically uniformly distributed random variables on $(0,1)$, and that (Example 7.21) $2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right)=2 \sum_{i=1}^{n}-\ln \omega_{i}$ has a $\chi^{2}$-distribution (Eq. (A6.103) with $2 n$ degrees of freedom

$$
\mathrm{F}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / \tau_{i}^{*}\right) \leq x\right\}=\frac{1}{2^{n}(n-1)!} \int_{0}^{x} y^{n-1} e^{-y / 2} d y
$$

the statistic given by Eq. (7.88) can be used to test an HPP $(\mathrm{m}(t)=\lambda)$ versus an NHPP. For the case of a strictly increasing intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)$ it is necessary to take care that $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right)$ tends to assume small values, for $H_{1}$ true. The corresponding test procedure is thus:

1. Compute the statistic

$$
2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right), \quad t_{i}^{*}=i \text { th arrival time. }
$$

2. For given type I error $\alpha$ determine the critical value $\chi_{2 n, \alpha}^{2}$ ( $\alpha$ quantile of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution, e. g. $\chi_{2 n, \alpha}^{2}=7.96$ for $n=8 \& \alpha=0.05$, Table A9.2).
3. Reject $H_{0}$ : the underlying point process is an HPP, against $H_{1}$ : the underlying process is an NHPP with a strictly increasing intensity, at $1-\alpha$ confidence, ${ }^{*}$ if $2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right)<\chi_{2 n, \alpha}^{2}$; otherwise accept $H_{0}$.

It can be noted that $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right)$ is a sufficient statistic (Appendix A8.2.1), and tends to assume small values for $H_{1}$ true ( $\mathrm{m}(t)$ strictly increasing). Example 7.22 gives an application.

# Example 7.20 

In a reliability test, 8 failures have occurred in $T=10,000 \mathrm{~h}$ at $850,1200,2100,3900,4950,5100$ $8300,9050 \mathrm{~h}\left(t_{1}^{*}+\ldots+t_{8}^{*}=35,450 \mathrm{~h}\right)$. Test at $95 \%$ confidence, using the rule (7.87), the hypothesis $H_{0}$ : the underlying point process is an HPP, against $H_{1}$ : the underlying process is an NHPP with increasing intensity.

## Solution

From Table A9.1 $t_{0.95}=1.64>(3.545-4) / 0.816=-0.56$ and $H_{0}$ cannot be rejected.

[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ As for the procedure (7.87), also for (7.91) it holds that $\alpha=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ sample in $\tilde{\mathcal{A}} \mid H_{0}$ true $\}$, with $\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=$ rejection set (Eq. (A8.67)), same for (7.94) \& (7.96).# Example 7.21 

Let the random variable $\omega$ be uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$. Show that $\eta=-\ln (\omega)$ is distributed according to $\mathrm{F}_{\eta}(t)=1-e^{-t}$ on $(0, \infty)$, and thus $2 \sum_{i=1}^{n}-\ln \left(\omega_{i}\right)=2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \eta_{i}=\chi_{2 n}^{2}$

## Solution

Considering that for $0<\omega<1,-\ln (\omega)$ is a decreasing function defined on $(0, \infty)$, it follows that the events $\{\omega \leq x\}$ and $\{\eta=-\ln (\omega)>-\ln (x)\}$ are equivalent. From this (see also Eq. (A6.31)), $x=\operatorname{Pr}\{\omega \leq x\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\eta>-\ln (x)\}$ and thus, using $-\ln (x)=t$, one obtains $\operatorname{Pr}\{\eta>t\}=e^{-t}$ and finally

$$
\mathrm{F}_{\eta}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\eta \leq t\}=1-e^{-t}
$$

From Eqs. (A6.102) - (A6.104), $2 \sum_{i=1}^{n}-\ln \left(\omega_{i}\right)=2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \eta_{i}$ has a $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $2 n$ degrees of freedom.

Continuing Example 7.20, test at $95 \%$ confidence, using the rule (7.91), the hypothesis $H_{0}$ : the underlying point process is an HPP, against the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}$ : the underlying process is an NHPP with increasing intensity.

## Solution

From Table A9.2, $\chi_{16,0.05}^{2} \approx 7.96<2\left(\ln \left(T / t_{1}^{*}\right)+\ldots+\ln \left(T / t_{8}^{*}\right)\right) \approx 17.5$ and $H_{0}$ cannot be rejected.

### 7.6.3.2 Tests of an HPP versus an NHPP with decreasing intensity

Tests of a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) versus a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) with a strictly decreasing intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)=d \mathrm{M}(t) / d t$ can be deduced from those for strictly increasing intensity given in section 7.6.3.1. Equations (7.85) and (7.89) remain true. However, if the intensity is strictly decreasing, most of the failures tend to occur before $T / 2$ and the procedure for the Laplace test (Eq. (7.87)) has to be changed in:

1. Compute the statistic

$$
\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{*} / T\right)-n / 2\right] / \sqrt{n / 12}, \quad t_{i}^{*}=i \text { th arrival time. }
$$

2. For given type I error $\alpha$ determine the critical value $t_{\alpha}$ ( $\alpha$ quantile of the standard normal distribution, e. g. $t_{\alpha} \approx-1.64$ for $\alpha=0.05$ (Tab. A9.1)).
3. Reject $H_{0}$ : the underlying point process is an HPP, against $H_{1}$ : the underlying process is an NHPP with a strictly decreasing intensity, at $1-\alpha$ confidence, if $\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{*} / T\right)-n / 2\right] / \sqrt{n / 12}<t_{\alpha} ;$ otherwise accept $H_{0}$.

It can be noted that $\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{*} / T$ is a sufficient statistic (Appendix A8.2.1), and tends to assume small values for $H_{1}$ true ( $\mathrm{m}(t)$ strictly decreasing). Example 7.23 gives an application.For the test according to the statistic (7.88), the test procedure becomes:

1. Compute the statistic

$$
2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right), \quad t_{i}^{*}=i \text { th arrival time. }
$$

2. For given type I error $\alpha$ determine the critical value $\chi_{2 n, 1-\alpha}^{2}(1-\alpha$ quantile of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution, e.g. $\chi_{2 n, 1-\alpha}^{2} \approx 26.3$ for $n=8 \& \alpha=0.05$ (Table A9.2)).
3. Reject $H_{0}$ : the underlying point process is an HPP, against $H_{1}$ : the underlying process is an NHPP with a strictly decreasing intensity, at $1-\alpha$ confidence, if $2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right)>\chi_{2 n, 1-\alpha}^{2}$; otherwise accept $H_{0}$.

It can be noted that $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right)$ is a sufficient statistic (Appendix A8.2.1), and tends to assume large values for $H_{1}$ true ( $\mathrm{m}(t)$ strictly decreasing). Example 7.24 gives an application.

Results of Examples 7.20, 7.22, 7.23 \& 7.24 are coherent (Eq. (7.97) yields approximately a straight line, and an empirical estimation of $\hat{F}_{n}(t)$ per Eq. (7.79) on a Weibull probability chart (Figs. 7.12 or A9.2) yields $\hat{\beta} \approx 1 \& \hat{\lambda} \approx 1 / 4,400 \mathrm{~h}$ ).

# 7.6.3.3 Heuristic Tests to distinguish between HPP and General Monotonic Trend 

In some applications, only little information is available about the underlying point process describing failures occurrence of a complex repairable system. As in the previous sections, it will be assumed that repair times are neglected. Asked is a test to identify a monotonic trend of the failure intensity against a constant failure intensity given by a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP).

Consider first, investigations based on consecutive interarrival times. Such an investigation should be performed at the beginning of data analysis, also because
