Figure A1.1 Terms most commonly used in reliability (RAMS) engineering# Availability, Point Availability $(\mathrm{PA}(t), P A)[\mathrm{A} 1.4]$ 

Probability that the item is in a state to perform as required at a given instant.
Instantaneous availability is used in [A1.4]. Perform as required means perform the required function under stated conditions, including environmental \& operation conditions, human factors \& logistic support, and state entered at $t=0$. To avoid ambiguities, at system level $\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)$ is used in this book, where PA stands for point availability, $S$ for system, and $i$ for the state $Z_{i}$ entered at $t=0$ (system referring to the highest integration level of the item considered and $i=0$ to system new or as-good-as-new, as often tacitly assumed at $t=0$; see also the footnote on p. 512, and p. 391 for item). Use of $\mathrm{A}(t)$ should be avoided, to elude confusion with other kinds of availability (average $\mathrm{AA}(t)$, mission $\mathrm{MA}\left(T_{0}, t_{0}\right)$, joint $\mathrm{JA}(t, t+0)$, overall $O A$, as given in Sections $6.2 \& 6.8 .2)$. Important for the stated conditions is also the state of the item after a repair (new, as-good-as-new, as-bad-as-old, or other). For an item (system) with more than one element,
as-good-as-new after repair refers in this book to the repaired element (in the reliability block diagram); this assumption is valid with respect to the state $Z_{i}$ considered only if $Z_{i}$ is a regeneration state (up or down for availability) and $x$ starting by 0 at each transition to $Z_{i}$ is used instead of $t$, as for interarrival times. ${ }^{*}$ )
Under weak conditions, the asymptotic \& steady-state value $P A_{S}$ of the point availability is given by $P A_{S}=M T T F /(M T T F+M T T R)$ for a one-item structure (pp. 9, 185-87) as well as for an arbitrary structure (with $M T T F=M U T_{S} \& M T T R=M D T_{S}$ for systems described by Markov or semi-Markov processes). $P A_{S}$ is also the steady-state value of the average availability $A A_{S}$. A qualitative definition of availability, focused on ability, is possible and belongs to the concept of dependability.

## Burn-in (nonrepairable items)

Type of screening test while the item is in operation.
For electronic devices, stresses during burn-in are often constant higher ambient temperature $\left(125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right.$ for ICs) \& constant higher supply voltage. Burn-in can be considered as a part of a screening procedure, performed to provoke early failures and to stabilize characteristics of the item (pp. 89, 101,373).

## Burn-in / Run-in (repairable items)

Operation of the item in a prescribed environment, with successive corrective maintenance at each failure, during the early failure period.

Stress conditions during burn-in/run-in have to be near field operation, in particular for SMT. Faults during burn-in/run-in can be deterministic (defects, systematic failures) during pilot production.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ ) $Z_{i}$ is a regeneration state if and only if at its occurrence there is no "running time" which is not exponentially distributed (pp. 442-43); this applies to all states for Markov and semi-Markov processes (p. 522), and to at least one state for the case of constant failure rates for all elements (to at least 2 states, i. e. for semi-regenerative processes, if in addition to constant failure rates also only one repair crew is available; see the footnote on p. 204, Table 6.1 on p.171, pp. 494-95, and footnotes on pp. $240 \& 220$ for refinements). Occurrence of $Z_{i}$ is then a regeneration point (a renewal point for the process with respect to $Z_{i}$, see p. 494).# Capability 

Ability to meet stated quantitative dependability characteristics under given conditions.

Performance (technical performance) is often used instead of capability.

## Concurrent Engineering

Systematic approach to reduce the time to develop, manufacture, and market the item, essentially by integrating production activities into the design \& development phase.

Concurrent engineering is achieved through intensive teamwork between all engineers involved in design, production, marketing of the item. It has positive influence on time to market \& life-cycle cost.

## Configuration Management

Procedure to specify, describe, audit, and release the configuration of the item, as well as to control it during modifications or changes.

Configuration includes all of the item's functional and physical characteristics as given in the documentation (to specify, produce, test, accept, operate, maintain, and logistically support the item) and as present in the hardware and / or software. In practical applications, it is useful to subdivide configuration management into configuration identification, auditing, control (design reviews), and accounting. Configuration management is of great importance during the design \& development phase.

## Corrective Maintenance [A1.4]

Maintenance carried out after fault detection to effect restoration.
Effect restoration means restore the item to a specified state, according to given procedures and resources. A fault is a state, and can result from a failure or a defect (p.391). Corrective maintenance is also known as repair and can include any or all of the following steps: detection (recognition), localization (isolation, diagnosis), correction (disassemble, remove, replace, reassemble, adjust), and function checkout (p.113). In this book, fault detection time as well as administrative, logistic \& technical delays are neglected (except for Example 6.7 on p. 203 \& Fig. A7.12 on p. 528),
repair is thus used for restoration; furthermore, to simplify calculations it is assumed that repaired element (in the reliability block diagram) is as-good-as-new after repair,
including a possible environmental stress screening of the corresponding spare parts. This assumption is valid with respect to the state $Z_{i}$ considered only if $Z_{i}$ is a regeneration state (up or down for $\mathrm{PA}(t)$, up for $\lambda(t)$, MTBF, MTTF, $\mathrm{R}(t)$ considerations) and $x$ starting by 0 at each transition to $Z_{i}$ is used instead of $t$, as for interarrival times (see footnotes on pp. 386, 240, 220 for refinements). The assumption that after repair the system failure rate is the same as just before failure (repair to as-bad-as-old) leads to the concept of minimal repair, critically discussed on pp. 138-39, $535-36$.# Cost Effectiveness 

Measure of the ability of the item to meet a service demand of stated quantitative characteristics, with the best possible usefulness to life-cycle cost ratio.

System effectiveness is often used instead of cost effectiveness (pp.11,13).

## Defect [A1.6]

Nonfulfillment of a requirement related to an intended or specified use.
From a technical point of view, defect is close to nonconformity (p.394). However, in relation to product liability, defect has to be used (because of "intended use" in the definition, see also the footnote on p.1). As for nonconformity, defects do not need to influence the item's functionality. They are caused by flaws (errors or mistakes) during design, development, production, or installation. Unlike failures, which always appear in time (randomly distributed), defects are present at $t=0$. However, some defects can only be recognized when the item is operating, and are referred to as dynamic defects (e.g. in software). Similar to defects, with regard to causes, are systematic failures (e.g. caused by a cooling or an interface problem); however, they are often not directly detectable (hidden) at $t=0$.

## Dependability [A1.4]

Ability to perform as and when required.
Dependability is generally used in a qualitative sense to describe the ability to perform the required function under stated conditions at a given instant or for a given time interval, including thus its influencing factors like reliability, maintainability, and logistic support.

## Derating [A1.4]

Employing components of higher capability than anticipated operating stresses.
The stress factor $S$ expresses the ratio of actual to rated stress under standard operating conditions (generally at $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ambient temperature, see p. 33).

## Design Review

Independent, documented, comprehensive examination of the design to evaluate the design's ability to meet all requirements, to identify deviations or problems, and to discuss solutions.

Design reviews are an important tool for quality assurance and $T Q M$ during the design and development of hardware and software (Tables A3.3, 5.3, 5.5, 2.8, 4.3, Appendix A4). An important objective of design reviews is also to decide about continuation or stopping the project, on the basis of objective considerations (feasibility check in Tables A3.3 \& 5.3 and Fig. 1.6).# Environmental Stress Screening (ESS) 

Test or set of tests intended to remove defective items, or those likely to exhibit early failures.

ESS is a screening procedure often performed at assembly (PCB) or equipment level on a 100\% basis to find defects and systematic failures during the pilot production (reliability growth), or to provoke early failures in a series production. For electronic items, it consists generally of temperature cycles and/or random vibrations (Sections $8.2 \& 8.3$ ). Stresses are in general higher than in field operation, but not so high as to stimulate new failure mechanisms. Experience shows that to be cost effective, ESS has to be tailored to the item and to the production processes. At component level, the term screening is often used.

## Failure [A1.4]

Loss of ability to perform as required.
Perform as required means perform the required function under stated conditions. Failure is an event leading to an inoperative state (down state). It should be considered (classified) with respect to the mode, cause, effect, and mechanism. The cause of a failure can be intrinsic (early failures, failures with constant failure rate, wear-out failures) or extrinsic (systematic failures, i. e. failures resulting from errors or mistakes in design, production or operation, which are deterministic and have to be considered as defects). The effect (consequence) of a failure can be different if considered on the directly affected item or on a higher level (pp. 4, 72). A failure is an event appearing in time (randomly distributed), in contrast to a defect which is present at $t=0$ (even if hidden); see also fault.

## Failure Intensity $(z(t)) \quad[A 1.4]$

Limit, if it exists, of the mean number of failures of a repairable item within time interval $(t, t+\delta t]$, to $\delta t$ when $\delta t \rightarrow 0$.

Instantaneous failure intensity is used in [A1.4]. At system level, $\mathrm{z}_{S}(t)$ is used in this book, where $S$ stands for system (system referring to the highest integration level of the item considered). Failure intensity applies to repairable items, in particular when repair times are neglected. It must be clearly distinguished from failure rate, and is investigated in Appendix A7 for Poisson processes (homogeneous $(\mathrm{z}(t)=\lambda$, p.489) and nonhomogeneous $(\mathrm{z}(t)=\mathrm{m}(t)$, p.532)), renewal processes $(\mathrm{z}(t)=\mathrm{h}(t)$, p. 482), and general point processes (p. 540). For practical applications and $\delta t \rightarrow 0$ it holds that $\mathrm{z}(t) \delta t=\operatorname{Pr}\{\mathrm{v}(t+\delta t)-\mathrm{v}(t)=1\}, \mathrm{v}(t)=$ number of failures in $(0, t]$. Other designations have been suggested for failure intensity, e.g. rate of occurrence of failures (ROCOF), failure frequency, unconditional failure intensity, etc.; all these terms should be avoided.

## Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) [A1.4]

Qualitative method of analysis that involves the study of possible failure modes in subitems, and their effects up to system level.

Effects is used also for consequences. See FMECA for comments.# Failure Modes, Effects, and Criticality Analysis (FMECA) [A1.4] 

Quantitative or qualitative method of analysis that involves failure modes and effects analysis together with considerations on the probability of the failure mode occurrence and the severity of the effects.

Goal of an FMECA is to identify all possible failure modes (taking an element after the other of the item considered), analyze their causes, and investigate possibilities for reducing failure effect and/or occurrence probability, bottom-up to system level (Table 2.5 on p. 79). An FMECA is mandatory for critical failures (affecting safety) and where redundancy appear. Often one distinguishes between design \& process FMECA. Fault should be used if failures and defects have to be considered.

## Failure Rate $(\lambda(t))$

Limit, if it exists, of the conditional probability that the failure occurs within time interval $(t, t+\delta t]$, to $\delta t$ when $\delta t \rightarrow 0$, given that the item was new at $t=0$ and did not fail in the interval $(0, t]$ (Eq. (A1.1)).

Instantaneous failure rate is used in [A1.4]; however, without specifying the item's state at $t=0$ (see the discussion to Eq. (A1.1)). $(0, t]$ is generally tacitly assumed as operating time interval. At system level, $\lambda_{S i}(t)$ is used in this book, where $S$ stands for system and $i$ for the up state $Z_{i}$ entered at $t=0$ (system referring to the highest integration level of the item considered, $i=0$ to system new or as-good-as-new, see footnote on p.512). Often $i=0$ is tacitly assumed and $\lambda_{S 0}(t) \equiv \lambda(t)$ is used. Referring to a nonrepairable item, if $\tau>0$ is the item's failure-free time (distribution $\mathrm{F}(t)$, density $\mathrm{f}(t), \mathrm{F}(0)=0$, reliability $\mathrm{R}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)$ ), the failure rate is given by (Eq.(A6.25))

$$
\lambda(t)=\lim _{\delta t \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\delta t} \operatorname{Pr}\{t<\tau \leq t+\delta t \mid \tau>t\}=\frac{\mathrm{f}(t)}{1-\mathrm{F}(t)}=-\frac{d \mathrm{R}(t) / d t}{\mathrm{R}(t)}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& t>0, \mathrm{~F}(0)=0 \\
& \mathrm{R}(t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

see Fig. 1.2 on p. 7 for a typical shape. At system level, $\lambda_{S i}(t)$ follows from Eq.(A1.1) using $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$. It can be noted that $\lambda_{S i}(t)=\lambda_{S i}$ holds for series structures with constant failure rates for all elements, but only approximately for redundant structures (see e.g. Eq. (2.22) on p. 43). If at $t=0$ the nonrepairable item has already operated for a time $x_{0}$, the conditional failure rate

$$
\lambda\left(t \mid x_{0}\right)=\lambda\left(t+x_{0}\right) \text { must be used, and } \lambda\left(t \mid x_{0}\right)=\lambda(t) \text { holds only for } \lambda(t)=\lambda(p .442)
$$

Considering item new at $t=0, \mathrm{R}(0)=1$ and Eq.(A1.1) yields $\mathrm{R}(t)=e^{-\int_{0}^{t} \lambda(x) d x}$, i. e. $\mathrm{R}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $\lambda(x)=\lambda$. This result characterizes the memoryless property of the exponential distribution;
only for $\lambda(t)=\lambda$ one can estimate $\lambda$ by $\hat{\lambda}=k / T$, as often done in practical applications, with $T$ as given cumulative operating time and $k \geq 0$ as number of failures during $T$.

From Eq. (A1.1) one can recognize that the concept of failure rate
applies also to repairable items which are new or as-good-as-new after repair, taking instead of $t$ the variable $x$ starting by 0 after each repair (renewal); in fact, at renewal a failure-free time statistically identical to the former one restarts at $x=0$.

Such an extension is necessary when investigating repairable systems in Chapter 6. However, for a system with more than one element, as-good-as-new after repair refers in this book to the repaired element in the rel. block diagram. As-good-as-new is then valid with respect to state $Z_{i}$ considered,
only if $Z_{i}$ is a regeneration up state, the system remains in the set of up states (i.e. only redundant elements can fail \& be repaired on-line), and $x$ starting by 0 at each transition to $Z_{i}$ is used instead of $t$, as for interarrival times (see footnote on p.386).If a repairable system cannot be restored to be as-good-as-new after repair with respect to the regeneration up state $Z_{i}$ considered, i. e., in particular, if at least one element with time dependent failure rate has not been renewed at each repair, failure intensity $\mathrm{z}(t)$ must be used. The distinction between failure rate $\lambda(t)$ and failure intensity $\mathrm{z}(t)$ or intensity $\mathrm{h}(t)$ or $\mathrm{m}(t)$ (for a renewal or Poisson process) is important. $\mathrm{z}(t), \mathrm{h}(t), \mathrm{m}(t)$ are unconditional intensities (Eqs. (A7.229), (A7.24), (A7.194)) and differ basically from $\lambda(t)$, even for the case of a homogeneous Poisson process, for which $\mathrm{z}(t)=\mathrm{h}(t)=\mathrm{m}(t)=\lambda$ holds (Eq. (A7.42), pp. 7, 482-83, 540). Also it is to note that $\lambda(t)$ is not a (probability) density (p. 442). For $\lambda(t)$, force of mortality [6.1, A7.30] and hazard rate have been suggested, both terms should be avoided.

# Fault $[A 1.4]$ 

Inability to perform as required, due to an internal state.
Perform as required means perform the required function under stated conditions. A fault is a state resulting from a failure or a defect, having as possible cause a failure mechanism for failures or a flaw (error or mistake) for defects \& systematic failures. Not considered as fault are down states caused by external actions or events (e. g. preventive maintenance or loss of resources). For software, a fault always results from a defect.

## Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) [A1.4 (FT+FTA)]

Deductive analysis using logic diagrams, showing the faults of subitems, external events, or combination thereof, which cause a predefined, undesired event.

Top event is the predefined, undesired event (generally at item (system) level). FTA is a top-down approach, which allows inclusion of external causes more easily than for an FMEA/ FMECA. However, it does not necessarily go through all possible fault modes. Combination of FMEA/ FMECA with FTA and event tree analysis leads to causes-to-effects charts, showing relationships between identified causes and their single or multiple consequences (Sections 2.6, 6.9.2, 6.9.3); such a combination of tools is necessary for items (systems) with high safety requirements.

## Item $[A 1.4]$

Subject being considered.
An item is a functional or structural unit, generally considered as an entity for investigations. It can consist of hardware and / or software and include human resources. For hardware it can be, for instance, a component (part, device), assembly, equipment, subsystem or system.

## Life-Cycle Cost (LCC) [A1.4]

Total cost incurred during the item's life cycle.
Life-cycle cost is the sum of cost for acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposal or recycling of the item. They have to consider also effects to the environment of production, use \& disposal or recycling of the item considered (sustainable development). Their optimization uses cost effectiveness or systems engineering tools and can be positively influenced by concurrent engineering.# Lifetime 

Time span between initial operation and failure of a nonrepairable item, if not limited (truncated) by technical or economical reasons.

## Logistic Support

All actions undertaken to provide effective and economical use of the item during its operating phase.

An emerging aspect in logistic support is that of obsolescence management [A2.6 (IEC 62402:2007)].

## Maintainability

Probability that a given maintenance action (preventive or corrective) to the item, performed under stated conditions and using specified procedures and resources, can be completed within a given time interval $(0, t]$.

Maintainability is an item's characteristic and refers to preventive \& corrective maintenance. A qualitative definition, focused on ability, is also possible. In specifying or evaluating maintainability, it is important to consider the available logistic support. Use of $\mathrm{M}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$ should be avoided (see p.397).
$\boldsymbol{M D T}_{S}\left(\right.$ see $\left.\boldsymbol{M U T}_{S}\right)$

## Mission Profile

Specific tasks, often time dependent, which must be fulfilled by the item under stated conditions during a given time interval $(0, t]$.

The mission profile defines the required function and the environmental conditions as a function of time. A system with a variable required function is termed a phased-mission system (Section 6.8.6.2).

## MTBF [A1.4]

Mean operating time between failures.
At system level, $M T B F_{S i}$ has to be used, where $S$ stands for system and $i$ for the up state $Z_{i}$ entered at $t=0$ (system referring to the highest integration level of the item considered, $i=0$ to system new or as-good-as-new); see footnote on p. $512 \&$ the remark at the top of p. 393. MTBF applies to repairable items. Often $i=0$ is tacitly assumed and $M T B F_{S 0} \equiv M T B F$ is used. Assuming that repaired elements are as-good-as-new after repair, no difficulties arises for a series structure $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$,
because it can be assumed that the system is disconnected at failure; in this case, for constant failure rates $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}$ and arbitrary repair rates, the involved process is a semiMarkov process (p.192), and the flow of failures at system level, referred to operating time, is a homogeneous Poisson process, for which consecutive interarrival times are independent, distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-x\left(\lambda_{1}+\ldots+\lambda_{n}\right)}=1-e^{-x \lambda_{50}}$, and with mean $M T B F_{S 0}=1 / \lambda_{50}$ (repaired elements are assumed as-good-as-new, yielding system as-good-as-new because of constant failure rates $\lambda_{i}$, and $x$ is used instead of $t$, as for interarrival times).However, for systems with redundancy, some difficulties can appear;
firstly, it is not always clear if only failures at system level or all failures causing a repair are considered; secondly, $M T B F_{S i} \neq M T B F_{S j}\left(Z_{i}, Z_{j}\right.$ being two different up states entered at $t=0$ ) and MTBF becomes the mean of different failure-free (operating) times between consecutive failures at system level, which are neither independent nor have the same distribution function (see the footnotes on pp. $512 \& 279$ and comments to MTTF).

For all this, and considering also the common usage of $M T B F$, the estimate $M \widehat{T B F}=T / k$ used in practical applications (see e. g. [1.22, A2.5, A2.6 (HDBK-781]) but valid only for $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ (p.330), and to avoid misuses [6.1, 7.11, A7.30],

MTBF should be confined to MTBF $\equiv 1 / \lambda$, as in this book \& often tacitly assumed in practical applications (pp. 6, 40); however, at component level, MTBF $=1 / \lambda$ should be avoided.

# MTBUR 

Mean time between unscheduled removals.

## MTTA

Mean time to accident/disaster.
MTTA is used in safety and risk management considerations (pp. 299 -310).

## MTTF

Mean time to failure.
Mean operating time to failure is used in [A1.4]; however, "operating", necessary for MTBF because of the sum of a repair and a failure-free time (p.176), can be confusing for MTTF. At system level, $M T T F_{S i}$ is used in this book, where $S$ stands for system and $i$ for the up state $Z_{i}$ entered at $t=0$ (system referring to the highest integration level of the item considered $\& i=0$ to system new or as-good-as-new); see the footnote on p. 512. Often $i=0$ is tacitly assumed and $M T T F_{S 0} \equiv M T T F$ is used. MTTF is the mean (expected value) of the item's failure-free time $\tau>0$. It can be calculated from the reliability function as $M T T F=\int_{0} \mathrm{R}(t) d t, M T T F_{S i}=\int_{0} \mathrm{R}_{S i}(t) d t$ at system level (p.39).
$M T T F_{S i}$ applies for both nonrepairable and repairable systems; for repairable systems it is necessary and sufficient that repaired elements are as-good-as-new after each repair, $Z_{i}$ is a regeneration up state, the system remains in the set of up states (i.e. only redundant elements can fail \& be repaired on-line), and $x$ starting by 0 at each transition to $Z_{i}$ is used instead of $t$, as for interarrival times (see the footnote on p.386).

For systems described by Markov processes (pp. 498, 503, 522), $M U T_{S}$ (system mean up time in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty$, see p. 394) is used instead of $M T T F_{S}$ (Eq. (6.291) or (A7.142)). For practical applications, $M U T_{S} \approx M T T F_{S 0}$ can often be used. However,
the use of $M T B F_{S}$ instead of $M U T_{S}$ can cause misunderstanding, because $M U T_{S}$ refers specifically to a steady-state or $t \rightarrow \infty$ situation (see the comments on MTBF \& MUT $T_{S}$ and the footnote on p. 512).
$M U T_{S}$ applies also to semi-Markov Processes (Eq.(A7.179)). An unbiased empirical estimate for $M T T F$ is $M \widehat{T} T F=\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right) / n$ where $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ are failure-free times of statistically identical items.

## MTTPM

Mean time to perform a preventive maintenance.# MTTR 

## Mean time to repair.

Mean time to restoration is to be used, if fault detection time as well as administrative, logistic, and technical delays must be considered [A1.4]. In this book,
all these times are neglected (except for Example 6.7 on p. 203 and Fig. A7.12 on p. 528), and repair is used for restoration.

To be representative, repairs have to be performed according to specified procedures and resources, inclusive personnel's skill level, spare parts, test facilities. MTTR is the mean of the item's repair time, given by the distribution function $\mathrm{G}(x)$ of the repair time as $M T T R=\int_{x}(1-\mathrm{G}(x)) d x$. As for $M T T F \& M T B F, M T T R$ implies that repaired elements are as-good-as-new after each repair. In statistical evaluations of $M T T R$, it is necessary to take care of logistic support (personnel, spare parts, test facilities), and that repair time is often lognormally distributed;
nevertheless, for reliability or availability calculation of repairable systems, a constant repair rate $\mu=1 / M T T R$ can often be used to get valid approximate results, as long as $M T T R_{i} \ll M T T F_{i}$ holds for each element (pp.206-07).
At system level, $M D T_{S}=M U T_{S}\left(1-P A_{S}\right) / P A_{S}$ holds for systems described by Markov or semiMarkov processes in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty$, with $M D T_{S}$ and $M U T_{S}$ as given below. However,
for systems with redundancy, $M D T_{S}$ differs, in general, from the mean of all repair (restoration) times, given in this book as $M T T R_{S}$, and is practically defined by the series elements in the reliability block diagram (see footnote on p. 121).
Based on results of pp. 198-99, $\mu_{S}=1 / M D T_{S}$ is used for the approximate expressions in Tables 6.9 and 6.10 for systems with constant failure and repair rates. As for $M T T F, M T T R=\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}^{\prime}\right) / n$ is an unbiased empirical estimate for $M T T R \quad\left(t_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, t_{n}^{\prime}=\right.$ repair times of statistically identical items).

## $M U T_{S}\left(M D T_{S}\right)$

System mean up (down) time in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty$.
$M U T_{S}$ is the mean of the times in which, after a transition from a down state, the system is moving in the set of up states $Z_{i} \in U$ before a transition to the set of down states $Z_{i} \in \bar{U}$ occurs, in steadystate or for $t \rightarrow \infty$; times which are, in general, dependent, see the footnote on p. 512. "Mean of the system up times in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty$ " could thus be more appropriate, but "in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty$ " implies the existence of different stay times in the up state set. This aspect,
further motivates the use of indices $S_{i}$ for reliability figures related to the state $Z_{i}$.
$M U T_{S}$ is given by Eq. (6.292) for systems described by Markov and semi-Markov processes. Similar is for $M D T_{S}, f_{u d S} \& f_{d u S}$. In practical applications, $M U T_{S}=M T T F_{50}$ can often be used,
but the use of $M T B F_{S}$ instead of $M U T_{S}$ should be avoided, since $M U T_{S}$ refers specifically to a steady-state (or $t \rightarrow \infty$ ) situation (see also pp. 6, 40, 392-93, 279).
For system with redundancy, $M D T_{S}$ differs from the mean of all repair times $M T T R_{S}$, and is practically defined by the series elements (footnote on p. 121 and pp. 123-24).

Nonconformity [A1.4, A1.6]
Nonfulfillment of a requirement.
See defect on p. 388 for comments.# Preventive Maintenance [A1.4] 

Maintenance carried out to mitigate degradation and reduce the probability of failure.

The aim of preventive maintenance $(P M)$ must also be to detect and remove hidden failures and defects (e. g. undetected failures in redundant elements). To simplify calculations, it is generally assumed that the element in the reliability block diagram for which a preventive maintenance has been performed is as-good-as-new after preventive maintenance. This assumption is valid with respect to the state $Z_{i}$ considered only if $Z_{i}$ is a regeneration state (up or down for $\mathrm{PA}(t)$, up for $\lambda(t), M T B F, M T T F, \mathrm{R}(t)$ considerations) and $x$ starting by 0 at each transition to $Z_{i}$ is used instead of $t$, as for interarrival times (see the footnote on p. 386). Preventive maintenance is generally performed at scheduled time intervals, according to given procedures \& resources, to the whole system or only to some elements (see pp. 125, 134-41 \& 240-43).

## Product Assurance

All planned and systematic activities necessary to provide adequate confidence that the item will meet all specified quality and reliability (RAMS) requirements.

Product assurance is used, in particular, in space programs. It includes quality assurance as well as reliability, maintainability, availability, safety, and logistic support engineering.

## Product Liability

Generic term used to describe the onus on a producer or others to make restitution for loss related to personal injury, property damage, or other harm caused by the product.

The manufacturer (producer) has to specify a safe operational mode for the product (item). If strict liability applies, the manufacturer has to demonstrate (at a claim) that the product was free from defects (see definition of defect \& nonconformity on pp. $388 \& 394$ ) and systematic failures when it left the production plant. This holds in the USA and partially also in Europe [1.10]. However, in Europe the causality between damage and defect has still to be demonstrated by the user and the limitation period is short (often 3 years after the identification of the damage, defect, and manufacturer, or 10 years after the appearance of the product on the market). A return to tort liability (the user has to demonstrate the presence of a defect in the product (item)) is not desirable. Moreover, it is hoped that liability will be refined to better cover software specific aspects.

## Quality [A1.6]

Degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfills specified or expected requirements.

This definition refers to products and services as well. It takes care of the definition of requirement given in the ISO 9000:2005 [A1.6], and follows closely the traditional definition of fitness for use.# Quality Assurance [A1.6] 

Part of quality management focused on providing confidence that quality requirements will be fulfilled.

Quality assurance is a part of quality management, as per ISO 9000 [A1.6]. It refers to hardware and software as well, and includes configuration management, quality tests, quality control during production (hardware), quality data reporting systems, and software quality (Fig. 1.3 on p.13). For complex equipment and systems, quality assurance activities are coordinated by a quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program (Appendix A3). An important target for quality assurance is to achieve the quality requirements with a minimum of cost and time. Concurrent engineering also strive to short the time to develop \& market the product.

## Quality Control During Production

Control of the production processes and procedures to reach a stated quality of manufacturing.

## Quality Data Reporting System

System to collect, analyze, and correct all defects and failures occurring during tests of the item, as well as to evaluate and feedback the corresponding quality and reliability (RAMS) data.

A quality data reporting system is generally computer aided. Its basic concept is illustrated in Fig. 1.8 on p. 22. Analysis of defects and failures must be traced to the cause in order to determine the best corrective action necessary to avoid repetition of the same problem. For complex systems, the quality data reporting system should remain active during the operating phase (at least during warranty). The quality data reporting system applies to hardware and software as well, and is also known as failure reporting, analysis, and corrective action system (FRACAS).

## Quality Management [A1.6]

Coordinated activities to direct \& control an organization with regard to quality.
Organization is defined as group of people and facilities (e. g. a company) with an arrangement of responsibilities, authorities, and relationships.

## Quality Test

Test to verify whether the item conforms to specified requirements.
Quality tests include incoming inspections, qualification tests, production \& acceptance tests, and cover performance, reliability, maintainability, safety, and software aspects. To optimize cost and time schedule, tests should be integrated in a test and screening strategy at system level. The terms inspection should be used only in the context of incoming inspections.# Redundancy [A1.4] 

Provision of more than one means for performing a function.
For hardware, distinction is made between active (hot, parallel), warm (lightly loaded), and standby (cold) redundancy, see pp. 42-43 for a discussion. Redundancy does not necessarily imply a duplication of hardware; it can, for instance, be implemented at the software level or as a time redundancy. To avoid common cause failures, redundant elements must be designed and realized independently from each other, in critical cases with different technologies, tools and personnel (p. 274). Where redundancy appear, failure mode investigation is mandatory (FMEA). Should the redundant elements fulfill only a part of the required function, a pseudo redundancy is present.

## Reliability $(R, \mathrm{R}(t))$

Probability that the item is able to perform as required for a time interval $(0, t]$.
Time interval $\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$ is given in [A1.4]; however, to avoid misuses $(0, t]$ has to be used (see below). Perform as required means perform the required function under stated conditions, including environment, operation, maintenance, and state entered at $t=0$. According to the above definition, reliability is a characteristic of the item, generally designated by $R$ for a fixed mission and $\mathrm{R}(t)$ for a mission with $t$ as parameter $(\mathrm{R}(t)$ is termed reliability function). At system level $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$ is used in this book, where $S$ stands for system and $i$ for the up state $Z_{i}$ entered at $t=0$ (system referring to the highest integration level of the item considered and $i=0$ to system new or as-good-as-new); see the footnote on p.512. Often, $i=0$ is tacitly assumed and $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \equiv \mathrm{R}(t)$ is used. To make sense,
a numerical statement on reliability must be accompanied by a clear definition of required function, mission duration, given conditions on operation \& maintenance (including environmental, human and logistic aspects), and state entered at mission begin (often tacitly assumed $Z_{0}$, i. e. system new or as-good-as-new).

A qualitative definition, focused on ability, is possible. $\mathrm{R}(T)$ is the probability that no operational interruption at item (system) level will occur during a mission of duration $T$. This does not mean that redundant parts may not fail, such parts can fail and be repaired on-line. Thus, considering $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$,
the concept of reliability applies for both nonrepairable and repairable systems; for repairable systems it is necessary and sufficient that repaired elements (in the reliability block diagram) are as-good-as-new after each repair, $Z_{i}$ is a regeneration up state, the system remains in the set of up states (i. e. only redundant elements can fail \& be repaired on-line), and $x$ starting by 0 at each transition to $Z_{i}$ is used instead of $t$, as for interarrival times (see the footnote on p.386).

If $\tau>0$ is the failure-free time, with $\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}$ and $\mathrm{F}(0)=0$, then $\mathrm{R}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau>t\}=1-\mathrm{F}(t)$ and $\mathrm{R}(0)=1\left(\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)\right.$ with $\left.\mathrm{R}_{S i}(0)=1\right.$ at system level). Furthermore, the probability for failure-free operation in $(0,1]$ given that at $t=0$ the item has already operated failure-free for a time $x_{0}>0$
is the conditional reliability $\mathrm{R}\left(t \mid x_{0}\right)$ (p.442); note that $\mathrm{R}\left(t \mid x_{0}\right)=\mathrm{R}(t)$ only holds for $\mathrm{R}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$, i. e. for constant failure rate $\lambda(p .442)$; to avoid misuses, $\mathrm{R}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$ should thus be reserved for interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$ as defined by Eq. (6.25) on p. 179 (see also pp. $492 \& 510$ ), not for the reliability $\mathrm{R}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$ (see p. 40 for a deeper discussion).

The concept of reliability can also be used for processes or services, although modeling human aspects can lead to some difficulties (pp. 10, 294-310).# Reliability Block Diagram [A1.4] 

Logical, graphical representation of the item showing how reliability of subitems (represented by blocks) \& combinations thereof, affect item's reliability.

The reliability block diagram (RBD) is an event diagram. It answers the question: Which elements of the item are necessary to fulfill the required function and which ones can fail without affecting it? The elements (blocks in the RBD) which must operate are connected in series (the ordering of these elements is not relevant for reliability calculation) and the elements which can fail (redundant elements) are connected in parallel (see pp. 30, 32, 51, 69 for some examples). Elements which are not relevant (used) for the required function are removed from the RBD and put into a reference list, after having verified (FMEA) that their failure does not affect elements involved in the required function. In a reliability block diagram, redundant elements always appear in parallel, irrespective of the failure mode; an FMEA is thus mandatory where redundancy appears. However, only one failure mode (e.g. short or open) and two states (good, failed) can be considered for each element.

## Reliability Growth [A1.4]

Iterative process for reliability improvement by addressing design and manufacturing weaknesses.

Reliability growth is performed during the pilot production, seldom for series-produced items. Faults detected during a reliability growth program are often deterministic (defects or systematic failures present in every item of a given lot), and less frequently caused by early failures or failures with constant failure rate. Investigation of the cause of each fault is important to select the most appropriate corrective action to avoid repetition of the same problem. As for environmental stress screening (ESS), stresses during reliability growth often exceed those expected in field operation, but are not so high as to stimulate new failure mechanisms. Models for reliability growth can also be used to investigate the occurrence of defects in software; however, even if software defects appear in time (dynamic defects), software quality should be preferred to software reliability (pp.159-60).

## Required Function [A1.4]

Function considered necessary to fulfill a given requirement.
Definition of the required function is starting point for every reliability analysis, as it defines failures. Difficulties can arise with complex systems, and parameters should be specified with tolerances.

## Risk Management [6.103 (31000:2009 or 73:2009)]

Coordinated activities to direct \& control an organization with regard to risk.
However, from an engineering point of view, risk management can be defined as
all planned and systematic activities to assess (identify, analyze, evaluate) potential or real risks, to minimize or at least mitigate their effects/consequences, and to communicate risks.

Risk being an undesirable situation (state) involving exposure to possible considerable harm (accident/disaster) with injury to persons or unacceptable consequences to material, environment or other; often expressed as a combination of an event and associated occurrence probability (pp.10, 299-310).# Run-in (see Burn-in/Run-in) 

## Safety

Ability of the item to cause neither injury to persons nor unacceptable consequences to material, environment or other during its use.

Safety expresses freedom from unacceptable harm. In practical applications, it is useful to subdivide safety into accident prevention (the item is safe working while it is operating correctly) and technical safety (the item has to remain safe even if a failure (fault) occurs). Technical safety can be defined as the probability that the item will not cause injury to persons nor consequences to material, environment, or other, above a stated (fixed) level for a given time interval, when operating under stated conditions. Methods and procedures used to investigate technical safety are similar to those used for reliability analyses, however with emphasis on fault/failure effects (consequences). In particular, safety analysis includes identification of potential hazards, identification of their causes, determination of their effect, classification of their effect \& probability of occurrence, and investigation of possibilities to avoid hazards or at least to mitigate their effects.

## Software Quality (SQ) [A1.7 (25000:2014)]

Capability of the software product to satisfy stated and implied needs when used under specified conditions.

This definition can also be given as the degree to which a software package fulfills a specified or expected combination of quality attributes; which would better agree to the definition of quality given on p.395. A fault in the software is always caused by a defect, also if it appears randomly in time (dynamic defect), the use of software reliability should thus be avoided.

## System

Set of interrelated elements that collectively fulfill a requirement.
A system generally includes hardware, software, services, and personnel (for operation \& support) to the degree that it can be considered self-sufficient in its intended operational environment. For calculations, ideal conditions for human aspects and logistic support are often assumed, leading to a technical system (system in this book, to simplify the notation). Elements of a system are e. g. components, assemblies, equipment \& subsystems, for hardware. For maintenance purposes, systems are partitioned into independent line replaceable units (LRUs), i. e. spare parts at systems level. In this book, system refers to the highest integration level of the item considered (investigated).

## Systematic Failure [A1.4]

Failure that consistently occurs under particular conditions of handling, storage or use.

Systematic failures are also known as dynamic defects, for instance in software quality, and have a deterministic character. However, they must not be present at $t=0$ (e.g. cooling or interface problems) and, because of the item's complexity, can appear as if they were randomly distributed in time.# Systems Engineering (SE) 

Broad area of engineering centered on how to manage complex products or systems over their life cycles, by considering also sustainability aspects.

Reliability (RAMS) engineering, value engineering, value analysis, concurrent engineering \& TQM amply support systems engineering.

## Total Quality Management (TQM)

Management approach of an organization centered on quality, based on the participation of all its members, and aiming at long-term success through customer satisfaction \& benefits to all members of the organization and to society.

Within TQM, everyone involved in the product (directly during development, production, installation, servicing, or indirectly with management activities) is jointly responsible for the product quality.

## Useful Life [A1.4]

Time interval, from first use until user requirements are no longer met, due to economics of operation and maintenance, or obsolescence.

Useful life refers to repairable equipment and systems (see lifetime on p. 392 for nonrepairable items). Economic aspects can be related to an unacceptable failure intensity or other causes. Typical values for useful life are 3 to 6 years for commercial applications, 5 to 15 years for military installations, and 10 to 30 years for distribution or power systems. However, facing increasing sustainability problems, longer useful life times should be considered (pp. 19, 405-06).

## Value Analysis (VA)

Optimization of the item's configuration, as well as of the production processes \& procedures, to provide the required item characteristics at the lowest cost without loss of capability, reliability, maintainability, and safety.

Value analysis is part of cost effectiveness and systems engineering.

## Value Engineering (VE)

Application of value analysis methods during the design phase to optimize the life-cycle cost of the item.

Value engineering is part of cost effectiveness and systems engineering.# A2 Quality and Reliability (RAMS) Standards, Story of Reliability Engineering 

For repairable items (equipment \& systems), reliability implies also availability, maintainability, and safety. RAMS is used in this book to point out this aspect, wherever necessary. To assure RAMS figures, besides quantitative requirements (e. g. MTBF, MTTR, PA), customers require a quality assurance/management system and often also the realization of an assurance program. Such general requirements are covered by national \& international standards, the most important of which are briefly discussed in this appendix. A procedure for setting up and realizing quality and reliability (RAMS) requirements for equipment \& systems, with related assurance program, is carefully discussed in Appendix A3. A skillful, allegorical story of reliability engineering is outlined in Appendix A2.4. The term management is used explicitly where the organization (company) is involved.

## A2.1 Introduction

Customer requirements for quality and reliability (RAMS) can be quantitative or qualitative. As with performance parameters, quantitative requirements are given in system specifications and contracts. They fix, in particular, targets for reliability, maintainability, availability, and safety, as necessary, along with associated specifications for required function, operating conditions, logistic support, and criteria for acceptance tests. Qualitative requirements are in national and international standards, and generally deal with quality assurance / management systems. Depending upon the application (aerospace, nuclear, defense, industrial), these requirements can be more or less stringent. Objectives of such standards are, in particular:

1. Harmonization of quality assurance/management systems, as well as of terms and definitions.
2. Enhancement of customer satisfaction.
3. Standardization of configuration, environmental \& operating conditions, logistic support, and test procedures, as well as of selection/ qualification criteria for components, materials, and production processes.
Important standards for quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance / management are given in Table A2.1, see [A2.0 - A2.12] for a comprehensive list. Some of the standards in Table A2.1 are briefly discussed in the following sections.# A2.2 General Requirements in the Industrial Field 

In the industrial field, the ISO 9000 family of standards [A1.6, A2.9] has opened since the 1990's a new era in quality management requirements. Many definitions of the ISO 8402 have been revised and integrated in the ISO 9000. Structure \& content of the ISO 9001 have evolved from the requirement to satisfy a standard (1987) to the necessity for a company to have a quality management system able to satisfy customer needs, reach company targets, and allow continuous effectiveness improvement; adhering better to industrial needs and to the concepts depicted on pp. $13 \& 19$ (see e. g. [1.0 (2015)] for a careful presentation of the ISO 9001:2015).

ISO 9000:2005 [A1.6] describes fundamentals of quality management systems and give the terminology involved.

ISO 9001:2015 [A2.9] specifies that for a company it is necessary to have a quality management system able to support its ability to provide products \& services that satisfy customer needs \& expectations, in agreement with applicable standards. It focus on seven aspects: Comprehension of real Firm's Possibilities, Definition of Management Responsibility, Definition of Realistic Targets, Resource Management, Product or Service Realization, Controls, Corrections. A quality management system must ensure that everyone involved with a product (development, production, installation, as well as management or staff) shares responsibility for the quality of that product, in accordance to $T Q M$. At the same time, the system must be cost effective and contribute to a reduction of time to market. Thus, bureaucracy must be avoided and such a system must cover all aspects related to quality, reliability, maintainability, availability, and safety, including management, organization, planning, and engineering activities. Customer expects today that delivered products and services will satisfy user's requirements and expectations.

ISO9004:2009 provides guidelines to consider efficiency \& effectiveness of quality management systems. ISO19011:2011 gives guidelines for internal \& external audits.

The ISO 9000 family deals with a broad class of products and services (technical and not technical), its content is thus lacking in details, compared with application specific standards used e. g. in aerospace, railway, defense, and nuclear industries (Appendix A2.3). ISO 9001 has been accepted as national standards in many countries, and international recognition of certification has been greatly achieved (over one million certificates worldwide).

Dependability aspects, focusing on reliability, maintainability, safety, and logistic support of systems are considered in IEC standards, in particular IEC 60300 for global requirements and IEC 60605, 60706, 60812, 61014, 61025, 61078, 61124, 61163, $61165,61508,61709,62380$, and 62628 for specific aspects, see [A2.6] for a comprehensive list. IEC 60300 deals with dependability programs (management, task descriptions, application guides). Reliability tests for constant failure rate $\lambda$, or of $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$, are considered in IEC 61124. System: Req. for Aviation, Space \& Defense Org. |For electronic equipment \& systems, IEEE Std 1332-2012 [A2.7] has been issued as a baseline for a reliability program for the development and production phases. This document, reinforced with IEEE Std 1413-2010, 1413.1-2002, 1624-2008 \& 16332008, gives in short form the basic requirements, putting an accent on an active cooperation between supplier (manufacturer) and customer, and focusing three main aspects: Determination of the Customer's Requirements, Determination of a Process that satisfy the Customer's Requirements, and Assurance that Customer's Requirements are met. Examples of comprehensive requirements for industry application are e. g. in[A2.2, A2.3]. Software aspects are considered in IEEE Stds [A2.8], ISO / IEC 12207 \& 25000 [A2.9], and IEC 62628 [A2.6]. To support a sustainable development by reusing hardware \& software parts, IEC 62309 \& 62814 have been issued [A2.6]. Risk management is considered in IEC 62198 [A2.6] and ISO / IEC 31010 \& 27005 [6.102, 6.103, A2.9]. Requirements for product liability are in national and international directives, see for instance [1.10].

# A2.3 Requirements in the Aerospace, Railway, Defense, and Nuclear Fields 

Requirements in space and railway fields generally combine the aspects of quality, reliability, maintainability, safety, and software quality in well conceived Product Assurance or RAMS documents [A2.3, A2.4, A2.12]. In the railway field, EN 50126 [A2.3] requires a RAMS program with particular emphasis on safety aspects (see also IEC 62278 [A2.6]). Similar is in the avionics field, where EN 9100 [A2.3] has been issued by reinforcing requirements of the ISO 9001 [A2.5, A2.6 (IEC 62396)], and now for software aspects the standard Do-178C/ED-12C [5.51].

MIL-Standards have played an important role in the last 40 years, in particular MIL-Q-9858, MIL-STD-470,-471,-781,-785, -882, and corresponding MIL-HDBK [A2.10]. MIL-Q-9858 (1st ed. 1959), now replaced by ISO 9001, was the basis for many quality assurance standards. However, as it does not cover specific aspects of reliability, maintainability \& safety, MIL-STD-785,-470 \& -882 were issued. MIL-STD-785 (1sted. 1965), now ANSI-GEIA-STD-0009 [A2.0], was the basis for most reliability programs. $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ acceptance (demonstration) tests in MIL-STD-781 (1sted. 1965) are now in MIL-HDBK-781. MIL-STD-470 (1st ed. 1966), now MIL-HDBK-470, requires the realization of a maintainability program, with emphasis on design rules, design reviews \& FMEA / FMECA. Maintainability demonstration is also covered by MIL-HDBK-470. MIL-STD-882 requires a safety program, in particular analysis of potential hazards. For NATO countries, AQAP Requirements, now ADMP, were issued starting 1968. MIL-STDs have dropped their importance since 1998. However, they can still be useful in developing procedures for industrial applications. ANSI-GEIA-STD-0009 [A2.0], focus on four main objectives: UnderstandCustomer/User Requirements & Constraints, Design & Redesign for Reliability, Produce Reliable Systems/Products, Monitor & Assess User Reliability. It opens a new era for MIL-Doc, insisting more on "what to do" rather than on "how do" (similar as the evolution of ISO 9001).

The *nuclear field* has its own specific, well established *standards* with emphasis on safety aspects, design reviews, configuration accounting, *traceability*, qualification of components/materials/production processes, and quality tests.

### A2.4 A Skillful, Allegorical Story of Reliability

Reliability (RAMS) engineering, like many other humankind activities, has gone through high and low, successes and failures, since its starting phase early in the 1960s. It is thus conceivable to describe reliability engineering's development as a tale, free from prejudices. A good way for this is to follow the story of Ulysses in the Odyssey. According to Greek mythology, Ulysses, King of Ithaca, unwilling involved in the Trojan War (ca. 1200 BC), after the defeat of Troy thanks the horse (wooden horse) attributed to him, on the return to Ithaca via sea was submitted to a large number of proofs (episodes) from which it comes out only thanks to his astuteness and courage. So far in the epic poem *Odyssey*, attributed to Homer.

Each of the 12 episodes of Ulysses can be transferred, as metaphor, to the development of many humankind activities. Giorgio Turconi has done this in his story of reliability engineering [1.25 (2002 & 2015)]. Some of these skillful interpretations are resumed here with the author's permission, to support these exiting and pertinent statements, in particular considering the exaggerated waste of resources and energy which characterizes present humankind, the thoroughly positive contribution of standardization, and the fact that many problems are not new at all:

- **Island of Aeolus**: the bag of winds offered to Ulysses is a dangerous gift, it's only good if used correctly; so, misuses frequently occur when innovative technologies/techniques/tools are made available to everybody (oversimplified analyses or cookbooks in reliability engineering and software reliability, to give just two examples);
- **Circe and the Siren's song**: there's always someone with the ultimate book, the unified theory, the general model, the close-form solution, or the comprehensive user-friendly software tool;
- **The home of lotus plant**: don't reinvent the wheel, but don't forget it just because it's old;
- **Calypso and the gift of immortality**: immortality doesn't exist for hardware, at least, and reliability problems are related to safety which has no price but only high cost;- encounter with Polyphemus: consumerism is a monster that will devour humankind, like Polyphemus with some Ulysses's men;
- Scylla and the whirlpool Charybdis: the challenge is to pass the straight represented by committed and future errors, and there's no way to get around;
- coming home: it will take a lot of multidisciplinary work to understand the new need for complexity \& flexibility, and to accept our responsibilities (also ethical) in building a more complex, difficult, and dynamic future.
Concluding his Reliability Odyssey: After 2001 [1.25 (2015)], Giorgio Turconi insists on the necessity that sustainability today should mainly refer to humankind, environmental sustainability being a consequence. Also, it would be necessary to stop those products with "programmed reliability" ${ }^{*}$ ) that are put on the marked with great marketing actions (or budgets) but less value added, just so they can be consumed. This also to limit the increasing division between rich and poor, with consequent social stresses.

Important for reliability engineering is thus, today more than before, the cooperation between all engineers involved in a project
to build sustainable, reliable, maintainable, long life and safe products, because it is time to remember that humankind needs nature, but nature does not need humankind (see also pp. 17-24 and the front-page).

This, making use of appropriate design guidelines (Chapter 5), failure modes/effects/mechanism analysis (Sections 2.6 \& 3.3), and design reviews (Appendix A4), as well as by developing suitable models. A model is a mathematical abstraction of a more or less complex entity, important to investigate and predict the entity's behavior (e.g. in relation to performance, reliability and safety) ${ }^{* *}$ ). Correct modeling of a technical entity, as material, structure, device, equipment or system is important for engineering purposes. Thereby, design of experiment can become unavoidable, and
experiment joined with experience greatly help in finding simplifications making the model just complex as necessary to contain all relevant parameters; however, oversimplified models should be avoided (as pointed out on pp.167-68, 252, 342, 346, 362, 365, 368 \& 536, 483), and validation of model assumptions (physical and statistical aspects) should always precede data analysis (see e.g.pp.102,239-40,341,342,354, $362,365)$.

[^0]:    *) Products which fail after a certain amount of time and are replaced instead as repaired.
    ${ }^{* *)}$ Of course, approach for lifeless or living entities/systems is quite different.# A3 Definition and Realization of Quality \& Reliability (RAMS) Requirements 

For repairable items (equipment \& systems), reliability implies also availability, maintainability, and safety. RAMS is used in this book to point out this aspect, wherever necessary. In defining quality and reliability (RAMS) requirements, it is important that besides real market needs, life-cycle cost, time to market and sustainability aspects, also development, production \& technological risks are considered with care. For complex equipment and systems with high quality \& reliability requirements, the realization of such requirements is then best achieved with
a quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program, integrated in the project activities and performed without bureaucracy.

Such a program (plan with a time schedule) defines the project specific activities for quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance and assigns responsibilities for their realization in agreement to $T Q M$. This appendix discusses important aspects in defining quality \& reliability (RAMS) requirements, and the content of a quality \& reliability (RAMS) assurance program for complex equipment and systems with high quality and reliability requirements for the case in which tailoring is not mandatory. It has been added to support managers in answering the question of
how to specify and achieve high RAMS targets for complex equipment \& systems.
For less stringent requirements, tailoring is necessary to meet real needs and to be cost and time effective. Software specific quality assurance aspects are considered in Section 5.3. Examples for check lists for design reviews are in Tables 2.8 \& 4.3, and Appendix A4. Requirements for a quality data system are in Appendix A5.

## A3.1 Definition of Quality and Reliability (RAMS) Requirements

In defining quantitative, project specific, quality \& reliability (RAMS) requirements, attention has to be paid to the actual possibility to realize them (development \& production), as well as to demonstrate them at a final or acceptance test. These requirements are derived from customer or market needs, taking care of limitations given by technical, cost, and sustainability aspects. This section deals with basic considerations by setting $M T B F, M T T R$, and steady-state availability $P A=A A$ requirements.$M T B F$ is used for $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the constant (time independent) failure rate of the item (system) considered, and $P A=A A$ for $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ ( $\$$ stand for system).

Tentative targets for $M T B F, M T T R, P A=A A$ are set by considering

- operational requirements relating to reliability, maintainability, and availability
- required function, expected environmental conditions, allowed logistic support
- experience with similar equipment or systems
- possibility for redundancy at higher integration level
- requirements for life-cycle cost, dimensions, weight, power consumption, etc.
- ecological consequences (sustainability, sustainable development).

Typical figures for failure rates $\lambda$ of electronic assemblies (PCBs) are between 100 and $1,000 \cdot 10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ at ambient temperature $\theta_{A}$ of $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and with a duty cycle $d$ of 0.3 , see Table A3.1 for some examples. The duty cycle $(0<d \leq 1)$ gives the mean of the ratio between operational time and calendar time. Assuming a constant failure rate $\lambda$ and no reliability degradation caused by power on/off, an equivalent failure rate

$$
\lambda_{d}=d \cdot \lambda
$$

can be used for practical purposes. Often it can be useful to operate with the mean expected number of failures per year and 100 items

$$
m_{\% / y}=\lambda_{d} \cdot 8,600 \mathrm{~h} \cdot 100 \% \approx \lambda_{d} \cdot 10^{6} \mathrm{~h}
$$

$m_{\% / y}<1$ is a good target for equipment and can influence acquisition cost.
Tentative targets are refined successively by performing rough analysis and comparative studies (allocation down to assemblies is often necessary (Eqs. (2.71), (2.72)).

For acceptance test (demonstration) of an MTBF for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$, the following data are important (Sections 7.2.3.2 and 7.2.3.3):

1. $M T B F_{0}=$ specified $M T B F$ and / or $M T B F_{1}=$ minimum acceptable $M T B F$.

Table A3.1 Indicative values of failure rates $\lambda$ and mean expected number $m_{\% / y}$ of failures per year and 100 items for a duty cycle $d=30 \%$ and $d=100 \%\left(\theta_{A}=40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$

|  | $d=30 \%$ |  | $d=100 \%$ |  |
| :-- | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
|  | $\lambda_{d}\left[10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}\right]$ | $m_{\% / y}$ | $\lambda\left[10^{-9} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}\right]$ | $m_{\% / y}$ |
| Telephone exchanger | 2,000 | 2 | 6,000 | 6 |
| Telephone receiver (multifunction) | 200 | 0.2 | 600 | 0.6 |
| Photocopier incl. mechanical parts | 30,000 | 30 | 100,000 | 100 |

3. Environmental conditions (thermal, mechanical, climatic).
4. Allowed producer's and/or consumer's risks ( $\alpha$ and/or $\beta$ ).
5. Cumulative operating time $T$ and number $c$ of allowed failures during $T$.
6. Number of systems under test $\left(T / M T B F_{0}\right.$ as a rule of thumb).
7. Parameters which should be tested and frequency of measurement.
8. Failures which should be ignored for the MTBF acceptance test.
9. Maintenance and screening before the acceptance test.
10. Maintenance procedures during the acceptance test.
11. Form and content of test protocols and reports.
12. Actions in the case of a negative test result.

For acceptance testing of an MTTR, following data are important (Section 7.3.2):

1. Quantitative requirements (MTTR, variance, quantile).
2. Test conditions (environment, personnel, tools, external support, spare parts).
3. Acceptance conditions (number of repairs and observed empirical MTTR).
4. Extent and type of repairs to be undertaken for introduced/simulated failures.
5. Allocation of the repair time (detection, localization, correction, checkout).
6. Form and content of test protocols and reports.
7. Actions in the case of a negative test result.

Availability usually follows from the relationship $P A=M T B F /(M T B F+M T T R)$. However, specific test procedures for $P A=A A$ are given in Section 7.2.2.

# A3.2 Realization of Quality \& Reliability (RAMS) Requirements for Complex Equipment \& Systems 

For complex items, in particular at equipment \& systems level, quality and reliability targets are best achieved with a quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program, integrated in the project activities and performed without bureaucracy. ${ }^{43}$ In such a program, project specific tasks and activities are clearly described and assigned. Table A3.2 can be used as a checklist by defining the content of a quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program for complex equipment and systems with high quality and reliability requirements, when tailoring is not mandatory (see also Section 5.3 \& [A2.8 (730 -2014)] for software specific quality assurance aspects). Tab. A3.2 is a refinement of Tab.1.2 and shows a possible task assignment in a company as per Fig. 1.7; it can be shortened or extended. The given responsibilities (R,C,I) can be modified to reflect the company's personnel situation. A description of reliability assurance tasks is e. g. in [A2.0, A2.2, A2.6(60300), A3.1].

|  | 3 Realization of the motivation and training program | C | C | C | R |# A3.3 Elements of a Quality and Reliability (RAMS) Assurance Program 

The basic elements of a quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program, as defined in Appendix A.3.2, can be summarized as follows:

1. Project organization, planning, and scheduling
2. Quality and reliability (RAMS) requirements
3. Reliability, maintainability, and safety analyses
4. Selection \& qualification of components, materials, and manufacturing processes
5. Software quality assurance
6. Configuration management
7. Quality tests
8. Quality data reporting system

These elements are discussed in this section for the case of complex equipment and systems with high quality \& reliability requirements (RAMS), when tailoring is not mandatory. In addition, Appendix A4 gives a catalog of questions useful to generate checklists for design reviews and Appendix A5 specifies the requirements for a quality data reporting system. As suggested in task 4 of Table A3.2, the realization of a quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program should be the responsibility of the project manager. It is appropriate to separate the quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program for the development phase and for the production phase.

## A3.3.1 Project Organization, Planning, and Scheduling

A clearly defined project organization and planning is necessary for the realization of a quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program. Organization and planning must also satisfy present needs for cost management and concurrent engineering.

The system specification is the basic document for all considerations at project level. The following is a typical outline for system specifications:

1. State of the art, need for a new product
2. Target to be achieved
3. Cost, time schedule
4. Market potential (turnover, price, competition)
5. Technical performance
6. Environmental conditions
7. Operational capabilities (reliability, maintainability, availability, logistic support)
8. Quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance, inclusive software quality assurance
9. Special aspects (new technologies, patents, value engineering, etc.)
10. AppendicesThe organization of a project begins with the definition of the main task groups. The following groups are usual for a complex system: Project Management, Systems Engineering, Life-Cycle Cost, Quality and Reliability (RAMS) Assurance (incl. software quality assurance), Software Development and Validation, Assembly Design, Prototype Qualification Tests, Production, Integration and Final Testing. Project organization, task lists, task assignment, and milestones can be derived from the task groups, allowing the quantification of the personnel, material, and financial resources needed for the project. The quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program must assess that the project is clearly and suitably organized and planned.

# A3.3.2 Quality and Reliability (RAMS) Requirements 

Important steps in defining quality and reliability (RAMS) targets for complex equipment and systems have been discussed in Appendix A.3.1.

## A3.3.3 Reliability, Maintainability, and Safety Analyses

Reliability and safety analyses include, in particular, failure rate analysis, failure modes analysis (FMEA/FMECA, FTA), sneak circuit analysis (to identify latent paths which can cause unwanted functions or inhibit desired functions, while all components are functioning properly), evaluation of concrete possibilities to improve reliability and safety (derating, screening, redundancy), as well as comparative studies; see Chapters 2-6 for methods and tools.

The quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program must consider tasks 5, 6, 9 of Table A3.2 and show what is actually being done for the project considered. In particular, it should be able to supply answers to the following questions:

1. Which derating rules are considered?
2. How are the actual component-level operating conditions determined?
3. Which failure rate data are used? Which are the associated factors $\left(\pi_{E} \& \pi_{Q}\right)$ ?
4. Which tool is used for failure modes analysis? To which items does it apply?
5. Which kind of comparative studies will be performed?
6. Which design guidelines for reliability, maintainability (incl. human, ergonomic \& safety aspects) and software quality are used? How will their adherence be verified?
7. How has been the predicted reliability calculated (models, data)?

Furthermore, interfaces to the selection and qualification of components and materials, design reviews, test and screening strategies, reliability tests, quality data reporting system, and subcontractor activities must be shown. The data used for components failure rates calculation should be critically evaluated (source, relevance, assumed environmental and quality factors $\pi_{E} \& \pi_{Q}$ ).# A3.3.4 Selection \& Qualification of Components, Materials, and Manufacturing Processes 

Components, materials, and production processes have a great impact on product quality and reliability. They must be carefully selected and qualified. Examples for qualification tests on electronic components and assemblies are given in Chapter 3. For production processes one may refer e.g. to [8.1-8.14, 3.70 - 3.93].

The quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program should give how components, materials, and processes are (or have already previously been) selected and qualified. In particular, the following questions should be answered:

1. Does a list of preferred components and materials exist? Will critical components be available on the market-place at least for the required production and warranty time?
2. How will obsolescence problems be solved?
3. Under what conditions can a designer use non qualified components/materials?
4. How are new components selected? What is the qualification procedure?
5. How have the standard manufacturing processes been qualified?
6. How are special manufacturing processes qualified?

Special manufacturing processes are those which quality can't be tested directly on the product, have high requirements with respect to reproducibility, or can have an important negative effect on the product quality or reliability.

## A3.3.5 Software Quality Assurance

For complex equipment and systems, software quality assurance can take a great portion of the effort devoted to the quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program. Considering that software faults are caused by defects, even if they appears randomly in time (dynamic defects), software problems are basically quality problems which have to be solved with quality assurance tools (defect prevention, configuration management, testing, and quality data reporting system), as described in Sections 5.3.1-5.3.3 and Appendices A3.3.6 -A3.3.8. Defects modeling can be useful in the context of software quality growth (Section 5.3.4).

The quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program should, in particular, answer the following questions (see e.g. also Section 5.3, Appendix A4.2 (p. 424), and [A2.8, A2.9 (29119)] for further specific questions):

1. What is the priority list of quality attributes (Table 5.4)? How will the customer (user) be involved in this list? How it is assured that this list will be consequently followed by all engineers involved in the project?
2. Which project specific written procedures (in particular design guidelines) will be worked out? From who? Who approves procedures? How it is assured that these procedures will be followed by all engineers in the project?

Fig. A3.1 Possible documentation outline for complex equipment and systems
3. How is the software life-cycle partitioned (Table 5.3)? Is each of these phases closed with a comprehensive design review (Tables 5.5)? Who takes part?
4. Is the software configuration management at the same level as that for hardware?
5. How is the software test strategy? Who is involved in its definition/approval?
6. How it is assured that software will be conceived \& developed to be defect tolerant?

# A3.3.6 Configuration Management 

Configuration management is an important tool for quality assurance, in particular during design and development. Within a project, it is often subdivided into configuration identification, auditing, control, and accounting.

The identification of an item is recorded in its documentation. A possible documentation outline for complex equipment and systems is given in Fig. A3.1.

Configuration auditing is done via design reviews (often also termed gate review), the aim of which is to assure/ verify that the item (system) will meet all requirements. In a design review, all aspects of design and development (selection and use of components and materials, dimensioning, interfaces (hardware and / or software), software aspects, etc.), production (manufacturability, testability, reproducibility), reliability, maintainability, safety, patent regulations, value engineering, and value analysis are critically examined with the help of checklists. The most important design reviews are described in Table A3.3 on p. 419, see also Table 5.5 on p. 165 for software aspects. For complex systems a preproduction design review or a review of the first production unit is often required. A further important objective of design reviews is to decide about continuation or stopping the project considered, on the basis of objective considerations (feasibility check in Tables A3.3\& 5.3 and Fig.1.6). About a week before the design review, participants should submit project specific checklists, see Appendix A4 and Tables $2.8 \& 4.3$ for some suggestions. Design reviews are chaired by the project manager and should cochaired by the project quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance manager. For complex equipment and systems, the review team may vary according to the following list:

- project manager (must),
- project quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance manager (must),
- designer(s) (must),
- independent design engineer or external expert (should),
- representatives from production, marketing, customer (as necessary/appropriate).

Configuration control includes evaluation, coordination, and release or rejection of all proposed changes and modifications. Changes occur as a result of mistakes, defects, or failures; modifications are triggered by a revision of system specifications.

Configuration accounting ensures that all approved changes and modifications have been implemented and recorded. This calls for a defined procedure, as changes/modifications must be realized in hardware, software, and documentation.

A faultless correspondence between hardware \& software and documentation is important during all life-cycle phases of a product. Complete records over all lifecycle phases become necessary if traceability is explicitly required, as e.g. in the aerospace or nuclear field. Partial traceability can also be required for products which are critical with respect to safety, or because of product liability.

Referring to configuration management, the quality and reliability (RAMS) assurance program should, in particular, answer the following questions:

1. Which documents will be produced by whom, when, and with what content?
2. Does document contents agree with quality and reliability (RAMS) requirements?
3. Is the release procedure for technical and production documentation compatible with quality requirements?
4. Are the procedures for changes/modifications clearly defined?
5. How is compatibility (upward and / or downward) assured?
6. How is configuration accounting assured during production?
7. Which items are subject to traceability requirements?

# A3.3.7 Quality Tests 

Quality tests are necessary to verify whether an item conforms to specified requirements. Such tests include incoming inspections, qualification tests, production \& acceptance tests, and cover performance, reliability, maintainability, safety, and software aspects. To optimize cost and time schedule, tests should be integrated in a test (and screening) strategy at system level.Table A3.3 Design reviews during definition, design\& development of complex equipment \& systems
