\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t)=n\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t) \leq n\}-\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t) \leq n-1\}= & \mathrm{F}_{n}(t)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}(t) \\
& n=0,1, \ldots, \mathrm{~F}_{0}(t) \equiv 1
\end{aligned}
$$

and thus, for the expected value (mean) of $v(t)$,

$$
\mathrm{E}[v(t)]=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n\left[\mathrm{~F}_{n}(t)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}(t)\right]=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathrm{F}_{n}(t)=\mathrm{H}(t), \quad t>0, \mathrm{H}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

The function $\mathrm{H}(t)$ defined by Eq. (A7.15) is the renewal function. Due to $\mathrm{F}_{A}(0)=\mathrm{F}(0)=0$ one has $\mathrm{H}(0)=0$. The distribution functions $\mathrm{F}_{n}(t)$ have densities

$$
\mathrm{f}_{1}(t)=\mathrm{f}_{A}(t) \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{f}_{n}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{f}_{n-1}(t-x) d x, \quad \begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{f}_{1}(t)=\mathrm{f}_{n}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0 \\
& n=2,3, \ldots, t>0
\end{aligned}
$$

and are thus the convolutions of $\mathrm{f}(x)$ with $\mathrm{f}_{n-1}(x)$. Changing the order of summation and integration one obtains from Eq. (A7.15)

$$
\mathrm{H}(t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{f}_{n}(x) d x=\int_{0}^{t} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{n}(x) d x, \quad t>0, \mathrm{H}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

The function

$$
\mathrm{h}(t)=\frac{d \mathrm{H}(t)}{d t}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{n}(t), \quad t>0, \mathrm{~h}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

is the renewal density, or renewal points frequency. $\mathrm{h}(t)$ is the failure intensity $\mathrm{z}(t)$ (Eq. (A7.228)) for the case in which failures of a repairable item with negligible repair times can be described by a renewal process (see also Eqs. (A7.24), (A7.229)).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ Half-open interval $(0, t]$ because $v(t)$ is continuous from the right (Fig. A7.1b).$\mathrm{H}(t)$ and $\mathrm{h}(t)$ per Eqs. (A7.15) \& (A7.18) satisfy

$$
\mathrm{H}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{A}(t)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{H}(x) \mathrm{f}(t-x) d x \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{h}(t)=\mathrm{f}_{A}(t)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}(x) \mathrm{f}(t-x) d x
$$

Equations (A7.19), known as renewal equations, have a solution with Laplace transforms (Appendix A9.7, see also [A7.9(1941)])

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{H}}(s)=\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{F}}_{A}(s)}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}=\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)}{s(1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s))} \quad \text { and } \quad \tilde{\mathrm{h}}(s)=\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}
$$

Furthermore, for $\mathrm{H}(t)$ it can be shown that

$$
\mathrm{H}(t) \geq \frac{t}{M T T F}-1
$$

with MTTF as per Eq. (A7.11) (see e. g. [2.34 (1965)] for a two sided bound).
For an ordinary renewal process $\left(\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)\right)$ it holds that

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{h}}_{o}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) /(1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s))
$$

Thus, an ordinary renewal process is completely characterized by its renewal density $\mathrm{h}_{o}(t)$ or renewal function $\mathrm{H}_{o}(t)$ (the index $o$ referring to an ordinary renewal process). In particular, it can be shown (see e. g. [6.3 (1983)]) that

$$
\operatorname{Var}\left[\mathrm{v}_{o}(t)\right]=\mathrm{H}_{o}(t)+2 \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{o}(x) \mathrm{H}_{o}(t-x) d x-\left(\mathrm{H}_{o}(t)\right)^{2}
$$

It is not difficult to recognize that $\mathrm{H}(t)=\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)]$ and $\operatorname{Var}[\mathrm{v}(t)]$ are finite for all $t<\infty$.

The renewal density $\mathrm{h}(t)$ has the following important meaning,
due to the assumption $\mathrm{F}_{A}(0)=\mathrm{F}(0)=0$, it follows that

$$
\lim _{\delta t \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\delta t} \operatorname{Pr}\{\mathrm{v}(t+\delta t)-\mathrm{v}(t)>1\}=0, \quad t>0
$$

and thus, for $\delta t \downarrow 0$,
$\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\right.$ any one of the renewal points $S_{1}$ or $S_{2}$ or $\ldots$ lies in $\left.(t, t+\delta t]\right\}=\mathrm{h}(t) \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t)$,
with $o \delta t$ as per Eq. (A7.89). Equation (A7.24) is the unconditional probability for one renewal point in $(t, t+\delta t] . \quad \mathrm{h}(t)$ corresponds thus to the failure intensity $\mathrm{z}(t)$ for an arbitrary point process (Eq. (A7.228)) or intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)$ for a Poisson process (homogeneous (Eq. (A7.42)) or nonhomogeneous (Eq. (A7.193))), but differs basically from the failure rate $\lambda(t)$ defined by Eq. (A6.25), which gives (for $\lambda(t) \delta t$ ) the conditional probability for a failure in $(t, t+\delta t]$ given item new at $t=0$ and no failure in $(0, t] . \lambda(t)$ can thus be used, as a function of $t$ only for $\tau_{0}$.This distinction is important also for the case of a homogeneous Poisson process $\left(\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}\right.$, p. 488), for which $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ holds for all interarrival times ( $x$ starting by 0 at each renewal point) and $\mathrm{h}(t)=\lambda$ holds for the whole process (see pp. 390-91, 441-42). Misuses are known, see e. g. [6.1].

Example A7.1 discusses the shape of $\mathrm{H}(t)$ for some practical applications.

# Example A7.1 

Give the renewal function $\mathrm{H}(t)$, analytically for
(i) $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x} \quad$ (Exponential)
(ii) $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x)=0.5 \lambda(\lambda x)^{2} e^{-\lambda x} \quad$ (Erlang with $n=3$ )
(iii) $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x)=\lambda(\lambda x)^{\beta-1} e^{-\lambda x} / \Gamma(\beta)$ (Gamma),
and numerically for $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ for $0<x \leq \Psi$ and $\lambda(x)=\lambda+\beta \lambda_{w}^{\beta}(x-\Psi)^{\beta-1}$ for $x>\Psi$, i. e. for
(iv) $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{y}) d y= \begin{cases}1-e^{-\lambda x} & \text { for } 0<x \leq \psi \\ 1-e^{-\left(\lambda x+\lambda_{w}^{\beta}(x-\Psi)^{\beta}\right)} & \text { for } x>\Psi\end{cases}$
with $\lambda=4 \cdot 10^{-6} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \lambda_{w}=10^{-5} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \beta=5, \psi=2 \cdot 10^{5} \mathrm{~h}$ (wear-out), and for
(v) $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)$ as in case (iv) but with $\beta=0.3$ and $\psi=0$ (early failures).

Give the solution in a graphical form for cases (iv) and (v) $\left(\mathrm{f}_{A}(0)=\mathrm{f}(0)=\mathrm{F}_{A}(0)=\mathrm{F}(0)=0\right)$.

## Solution

The Laplace transformations of $\mathrm{f}_{A}(t)$ and $\mathrm{f}(t)$ for the cases (i) to (iii) are (Table A9.7b)
(i) $\tilde{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)=\lambda /(s+\lambda)$
(ii) $\tilde{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)=\lambda^{3} /(s+\lambda)^{3}$
(iii) $\tilde{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)=\lambda^{\beta} /(s+\lambda)^{\beta}$,
$\tilde{\mathrm{h}}(s)$ follows from Eq. (A7.22) yielding $\mathrm{h}(t)$ and $\mathrm{H}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}(x) d x$
(i) $\tilde{\mathrm{h}}(s)=\lambda / s$ and $\mathrm{H}(t)=\lambda t$
(ii) $\tilde{\mathrm{h}}(s)=\lambda^{3} /\left[s\left(s^{2}+3 \lambda s+3 \lambda^{2}\right)\right]=\lambda^{3} / s\left[\left(s+\frac{3}{2} \lambda\right)^{2}+\frac{3}{4} \lambda^{2}\right]$
and $\mathrm{H}(t)=\frac{1}{3}\left[\lambda t-1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} e^{-3 \lambda t / 2} \sin \left(\sqrt{3} \lambda t / 2+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right] \quad \begin{aligned} & \text { (using } s \tilde{\mathrm{~h}}(s)=d^{2} \mathrm{H}(t) / d t_{c}^{2} \text {, and } \\ & \sin \left(\alpha+60^{\circ}\right)=0.5 \sin \alpha+0.5 \sqrt{3} \cos \alpha)\end{aligned}$
(iii) $\tilde{\mathrm{h}}(s)=\frac{\lambda^{\beta} /(s+\lambda)^{\beta}}{1-\lambda^{\beta} /(s+\lambda)^{\beta}}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[\lambda^{\beta} /(s+\lambda)^{\beta}\right]^{\mathrm{n}}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\lambda^{n \beta}}{(s+\lambda)^{n \beta}}$
and $\mathrm{H}(t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{t} \frac{\lambda^{n \beta} x^{n \beta-1}}{\Gamma(n \beta)} e^{-\lambda x} \mathrm{~d} x, \quad$ (Tab. A9.7b).
Cases (iv) and (v) can only be solved numerically or by simulation. Figure A7.2 gives the results for these two cases in a graphical form (see Eq. (A7.28) for the asymptotic behavior of $\mathrm{H}(t)$, dashed lines in Fig. A7.2a). Figure A7.2 shows that the convergence of $\mathrm{H}(t)$ to its asymptotic value is reasonably fast. However,
even if the shape of $\mathrm{H}(t)$ allows recognition of the presence of wear-out (case iv) or early failures (case v), it cannot deliver valid indications on the failure rate shape
(see Section 7.6.3.3 \& Problem A7.2 in Appendix A11). Cases iv \& v are also discussed on pp. 7, 349-50, and 367-68 \& Section 7.6 for considerations with nonhomogeneous Poisson processes.

Figure A7.2 a) Renewal function $\mathrm{H}(t)$ and b) Failure rate $\lambda(x)$ and density $\mathrm{f}(x)$ for cases (iv) \& (v) in Example A7.1 ( $\mathrm{H}(t)$ obtained by simulating 1000 failure-free times \& plotting $\mathrm{H}(t)=\ddot{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{v}(t))$ as a continuous curve (Eqs. (A7.15) \& (7.97)); $\delta=\left[(\sigma / M T T F)^{2}-1\right] / 2$ as per Eq. (A7.28))

# A7.2.2 Recurrence Times 

Consider now the distribution functions of the forward recurrence time $\tau_{R}(t)$ and the backward recurrence time $\tau_{S}(t)$. As shown in Fig. A7.1a, $\tau_{R}(t)$ and $\tau_{S}(t)$ are the time intervals from an arbitrary time point $t$ forward to the next renewal point and backward to the last renewal point (or to the time origin), respectively. From Fig. A7.1a it follows that the event $\tau_{R}(t)>x$ occurs with one of the following mutually exclusive events

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{0}=\left\{S_{1}>t+x\right\} & \\
A_{n}=\left\{\left(S_{n} \leq t\right) \cap\left(\tau_{n}>t+x-S_{n}\right)\right\}, & n=1,2, \ldots
\end{array}
$$Obviously, $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{A_{0}\right\}=1-F_{A}(t+x)$. The event $A_{n}$ means that exactly $n$ renewal points have occurred before $t$ and the $(n+1)$ th renewal point occurs after $t+x$. Considering that $S_{n}$ and $\tau_{n}$ are independent, it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{A_{n} \mid S_{n}=y\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{n}>t+x-y\right\}, \quad n=1,2, \ldots
$$

and thus, from the theorem of total probability (Eq. (A6.17))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R}(t)>x\right\}=1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t+x)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}(y)(1-\mathrm{F}(t+x-y)) d y, \quad t, x>0
$$

yielding finally, for the forward recurrence time $\tau_{R}(t)$,

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R}(t) \leq x\right\}=\mathrm{F}_{A}(t+x)-\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}(y)(1-\mathrm{F}(t+x-y)) d y, \quad t, x>0
$$

The distribution function of the backward recurrence time $\tau_{S}(t)$ can be obtained as

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{S}(t) \leq x\right\}= \begin{cases}\int_{t-x}^{t} \mathrm{~h}(y)(1-\mathrm{F}(t-y)) d y & \text { for } 0<x<t \\ 1 & \text { for } x \geq t\end{cases}
$$

Since $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{S_{0}>t\right\}=1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t)$, the distribution function of $\tau_{S}(t)$ makes a jump of height $1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t)$ at the point $x=t$.

# A7.2.3 Asymptotic Behavior 

Asymptotic behavior of a renewal process (generally of a stochastic process) is understood to be the behavior of the process for $t \rightarrow \infty$. The following theorems hold with MTTF and $\sigma$ as per Eq. (A7.11) (some of these theorems can be proved with less restrictive assumptions as conditions (A7.9) - (A7.11)):

1. Elementary Renewal Theorems [A7.9(1941), A7.24(1954)]: If conditions (A7.9) - (A7.11) are fulfilled, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}(\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)] / t)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}(\mathrm{H}(t) / t)=1 / M T T F \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}(\operatorname{Var}[v(t)] / t)=\sigma^{2} / M T T F^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

It can also be shown [6.17] that $\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}(\mathrm{v}(t) / t)=1 /$ MTTF holds with probability 1.
2. Tightened Elementary Renewal Theorem [A7.24 (1954)]: If conditions (A7.9) (A7.11) are fulfilled, then

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}\left(\mathrm{H}(t)-\frac{t}{M T T F}\right)=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2 M T T F^{2}}-\frac{M T T F_{A}}{M T T F}+\frac{1}{2}
$$3. Key Renewal Theorem [A7.24 (1954)]: If conditions (A7.9) - (A7.11) are fulfilled, $\mathrm{U}(z) \geq 0$ is bounded, nonincreasing, and Riemann integrable over the interval $(0, \infty)$, and $\mathrm{h}(t)$ is a renewal density, then

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{U}(t-y) \mathrm{h}(y) d y=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{U}(z) d z
$$

For any $a>0$, the key renewal theorem leads, with

$$
\mathrm{U}(z)= \begin{cases}1 & \text { for } 0<z<a \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
$$

to the Blackwell's Theorem [A7.24 (1954)]

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\mathrm{H}(t+a)-\mathrm{H}(t)}{a}=\frac{1}{M T T F}, \quad a>0
$$

4. Renewal Density Theorem [A7.9 (1941), A7.24 (1954)]: If conditions (A7.9) (A7.11) are fulfilled, $\mathrm{f}_{A}(x) \& \mathrm{f}(x)$ go to 0 as $x \rightarrow \infty$, then

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{~h}(t)=\frac{1}{M T T F}
$$

5. Recurrence Time Limit Theorems: Assuming $\mathrm{U}(z)=1-F(x+z)$ in Eq. (A7.29) and considering $\mathrm{F}_{A}(\infty)=1 \& M T T F=\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y$, Eq. (A7.25) yields

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R}(t) \leq x\right\}=1-\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x+z)) d z=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y
$$

For $t \rightarrow \infty$, the density of the forward recurrence time $\tau_{R}(t)$ is thus given by $\mathrm{f}_{\tau_{R}}(x)=(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) / M T T F$. Considering $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=M T T F<\infty \& \sigma^{2}=\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau_{i}\right]<\infty(i \geq 1)$ and $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{R}(t)\right]<\infty$, it follows that $\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}\left(x^{2}(1-\mathrm{F}(x))\right)=0$ (supplementary results in Example A6.9, p. 448). Integration by parts and Eq. (A6.45) lead to

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{R}(t)\right]=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{\infty} x(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x=\frac{M T T F}{2}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2 M T T F}
$$

The result of Eq. (A7.33) is important to clarify the waiting time paradox:
(i) $\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{R}(t)\right]=M T T F / 2$ holds for $\sigma^{2}=0$, i. e. for $\tau_{i}=M T T F, i \geq 0$, and
(ii) $\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{R}(t)\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=1 / \lambda=M T T F, i \geq 0$, holds for $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$.

Similar is for $\tau_{S}(t)$. For a simultaneous observation of $\tau_{R}(t) \& \tau_{S}(t)$, it must be noted that in this cases $\tau_{R}(t)$ and $\tau_{S}(t)$ belong to the same $\tau_{i}$ (Fig A7.1a) and are independent only for case (ii). Considering Eqs. (A7.37) \& (A7.32), Eq. (A7.33) holds for any $t>0$ in the case of a stationary renewal process.6. Central Limit Theorem for Renewal Processes [A6.7 (Vol. II), A7.24 (1955), A7.29 (1956)]: If conditions (A7.9) - (A7.11) are fulfilled, then

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\frac{v(t)-t / M T T F}{\sigma \sqrt{t / M T T F^{3}}} \leq x\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{x} e^{-y^{2} / 2} d y
$$

Equation (A7.34) can be heuristically explained by means of the central limit theorem (Eq. (A6.148)); it shows that $v(t)$ is for $t \rightarrow \infty$ normally distributed with mean $t / M T T F$ and variance $\sigma^{2} t / M T T F^{3}$.

Equations (A7.27) - (A7.34) show that renewal processes encountered in practical applications converge to a statistical equilibrium (steady-state) as $t \rightarrow \infty$, see Appendix A7.2.4 for a discussion on stationary renewal processes.

# A7.2.4 Stationary Renewal Processes 

The results of Appendix A7.2.3 allow a stationary renewal process to be defined as follows,
a renewal process is stationary (in steady-state) if for all $t \geq 0$ the distribution function of $\tau_{R}(t)$ in Eq. (A7.25) does not depend on $t$.

It is intuitively clear that such a situation can only occur if a particular relationship exists between the distribution functions $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)$ and $\mathrm{F}(x)$ given by Eqs. (A7.6) and (A7.7). Assuming, as initial distribution at $t=0$,

$$
\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y, \quad x>0, \mathrm{~F}(x)=\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

it follows that $\mathrm{f}_{A}(x)=(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) / M T T F, \dot{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)=(1-\dot{\mathrm{f}}(s)) /(s \cdot M T T F)$, and thus from Eq. (A7.20)

$$
\ddot{\mathrm{h}}(s)=\frac{1}{s \cdot M T T F}
$$

yielding

$$
\mathrm{h}(t)=\frac{1}{M T T F}, \quad t \geq 0
$$

With $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x) \& \mathrm{~h}(x)$ from Eqs. (A7.35) \& (A7.36), Eq.(A7.25) yields for $t \geq 0, x>0$

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R}(t) \leq x\right\}=\frac{1}{M T T F}\left[\int_{0}^{t+x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y-\int_{0}^{t}(1-\mathrm{F}(t+x-y)) d y\right]=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y
$$

(see also Eq. (A7.32)).Equation (A7.35) is thus a necessary and sufficient condition for stationarity of the renewal process with $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i} \leq x\right\}=\mathrm{F}(x), i \geq 1, x>0, \mathrm{~F}(x)=0$ for $x \leq 0$.

It is not difficult to show that the count process $v(t)$ given in Fig. 7.1b, belonging to a stationary renewal function, is a process with stationary increments. For any $t \geq 0, a>0$ and $n=1,2, \ldots$ it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t+a)-v(t)=n\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{v(a)=n\}=\mathrm{F}_{n}(a)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}(a)
$$

with $\mathrm{F}_{n+1}(a)$ as in Eq. (A7.13) and $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)$ as in Eq. (A7.35). Moreover, for a stationary renewal process, $\mathrm{H}(t)=t / M T T F$ and the mean number of renewals within an arbitrary interval $(t, t+a]$ is

$$
\mathrm{H}(t+a)-\mathrm{H}(t)=a / M T T F
$$

Comparing Eqs. (A7.32) and (A7.37) it follows that under weak conditions, as $t \rightarrow \infty$ each renewal process becomes stationary. For reliability applications,
a stationary renewal process can thus be regarded as a renewal process with arbitrary initial condition $\left(\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)\right)$ which has been started at $t=-\infty$ and will only be considered for $t \geq 0, t=0$ being an arbitrary time point;
in other words,
for reliability applications, asymptotic \& steady-state can be used for stationary (see e.g. also pp. 187, 493, 495, 514 \& 525 as well as p.530).

It can be noted that for a stationary renewal process, Eq. (A7.33) holds for $t \geq 0$. The important properties of stationary renewal processes are summarized in Table A7.1.

# A7.2.5 Homogeneous Poisson Processes (HPP) 

The renewal process, defined by Eq. (A7.8), with

$$
\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x>0, \lambda>0 \quad\left(\mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=0 \text { for } \mathrm{x} \leq 0\right)
$$

is a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP), and the contrary is true. $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)$ per Eq.(A7.38) fulfills Eq. (A7.35) and thus, the HPP is stationary. From Appendices A7.2.1 to A7.2.3 it follows that (see also Example A6.21)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{0}+\ldots+\tau_{n-1} \leq t\right\}=\mathrm{F}_{n}(t)=1-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\lambda t)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda t}=\int_{0}^{\lambda t} \frac{x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} e^{-x} d x, \quad n=1,2, \ldots \\
& \mathrm{f}_{n}(t)=d \mathrm{~F}_{n}(t) / d t=\lambda e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^{n-1} /(n-1)!, \quad n=1,2, \ldots \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\{v(t)=k\}=\mathrm{F}_{k}(t)-\mathrm{F}_{k+1}(t)=\frac{(\lambda t)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\lambda t}, \quad k=0,1,2, \ldots, \mathrm{~F}_{0}(t) \equiv 1
\end{aligned}
$$$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{H}(t)=\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)]=\lambda t, \quad \mathrm{~h}(t)=\lambda, \quad \operatorname{Var}[\mathrm{v}(t)]=\lambda t, \quad t \geq 0, \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R}(t) \leq x\right\}=1-e^{-\lambda x}, \quad t \geq 0, x>0, \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{S}(t) \leq x\right\}= \begin{cases}1-e^{-\lambda x} & \text { for } 0<x<t \\
1 & \text { for } x \geq t\end{cases} \quad t \geq 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

As a result of the memoryless property of the exponential distribution, the count function $v(t)$ (as in Fig A7.1b) has independent increments (Eq. (A7.2)). Quite generally, a point process is a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) with intensity $\lambda$ if the associated count function $v(t)$ has stationary independent increments and satisfy Eq. (A7.41). Alternatively, a renewal process satisfying Eq. (A7.38) is an HPP.

Substituting for $\lambda t$ in Eq. (A7.41) a nondecreasing function $\mathrm{M}(t)>0$, a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) is obtained (Appendix A7.8.2). The NHPP is a point process with independent Poisson distributed increments. Because of independent increments, the NHPP is a process without aftereffect (memoryless if HPP) and the sum of Poisson processes is a Poisson process (Eq. (7.27) for HPP). Moreover, the sum of $n$ independent renewal processes with low occurrence converge for $n \rightarrow \infty$ to an NHPP, to an HPP in the case of stationary (or for $t \rightarrow \infty$ ) independent renewal processes (p. 537). However, despite its simplicity,
the NHPP is not a regenerative process, and in statistical data analysis, the property of independent increments is often difficult to be proven (see p.368).

Nonhomogeneous Poisson processes are introduced in Appendix A7.8.2 and used in Sections $7.6 \& 7.7$ for reliability tests \& reliability grow modeling, respectively.

[^0]:    ${ }^{+} \mathrm{F}(x)=\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x)=\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(x)=0$ for $x \leq 0$# A7.3 Alternating Renewal Processes 

Generalization of the renewal process given in Fig. A7.1a by introducing a positive random replacement time $\left(\tau^{\prime}>0\right)$, distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)$, leads to the alternating renewal process. An alternating renewal process is a process with two states, which alternate from one state to the other after a stay (sojourn) time distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(x)$ and $\mathrm{G}(x)$, respectively (it is a 2 states semi-Markov process, see the footnote on p. 521). Considering the reliability and availability analysis of a repairable item in Section 6.2 and in order to simplify the notation, these two states will be referred to as the up state and the down state, abbreviated as $u$ and $d$, respectively.

To define an alternating renewal process, consider two independent renewal processes $\left\{\tau_{i}\right\}$ and $\left\{\tau_{i}^{\prime}\right\}, i=0,1, \ldots$. For reliability applications, $\tau_{i}$ denotes the $i$ th failure-free (operating) time and $\tau_{i}^{\prime}$ the $i$ th repair (restoration) time. These random variables are distributed according to

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{F}_{A}(x) \text { for } \tau_{0} \text { and } \mathrm{F}(x) \text { for } \tau_{i}, i \geq 1, & x>0, \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0, \\
\mathrm{G}_{A}(x) \text { for } \tau_{0}^{\prime} \text { and } \mathrm{G}(x) \text { for } \tau_{i}^{\prime}, i \geq 1, & x>0, \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{G}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0,
\end{array}
$$

with densities $\mathrm{f}_{A}(x), \mathrm{f}(x), \mathrm{g}_{A}(x), \mathrm{g}(x)$, and means

$$
M T T F=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x, \quad i \geq 1, \quad M T T F_{A}=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{0}\right]
$$

and

$$
M T T R=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}^{\prime}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{G}(x)) d x, \quad i \geq 1, \quad M T T R_{A}=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{0}^{\prime}\right]
$$

where MTTF and MTTR are used for mean time to failure and mean time to repair (restoration). $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right], \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}^{\prime}\right], \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau_{i}\right], \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau_{i}^{\prime}\right], i \geq 0$, are assumed $<\infty$. The sequences

$$
\tau_{0}, \tau_{1}^{\prime}, \tau_{1}, \tau_{2}^{\prime}, \tau_{2}, \tau_{3}^{\prime}, \ldots \quad \text { and } \quad \tau_{0}^{\prime}, \tau_{1}, \tau_{1}^{\prime}, \tau_{2}, \tau_{2}^{\prime}, \tau_{3}, \ldots
$$

form two modified alternating renewal processes, starting at $t=0$ with $\tau_{0}$ and $\tau_{0}^{\prime}$, respectively. Figure A7.3 shows a possible time schedule of these two alternating renewal processes (repair times greatly exaggerated). Embedded in every one of these processes are two renewal processes with renewal points $S_{\text {udui }}$ or $S_{\text {uddi }}$ marked with $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ and $S_{\text {duui }}$ or $S_{\text {dudi }}$ marked with $\cdot$,
where udu denotes a transition from up to down given up at $t=0$, i.e.

$$
S_{u d u 1}=\tau_{0} \quad \text { and } \quad S_{u d u i}=\tau_{0}+\left(\tau_{1}^{\prime}+\tau_{1}\right)+\ldots+\left(\tau_{i-1}^{\prime}+\tau_{i-1}\right), \quad i>1
$$

These four embedded renewal processes are statistically identical up to the time intervals starting at $t=0\left(\tau_{0}, \tau_{0}+\tau_{1}^{\prime}, \tau_{0}^{\prime}+\tau_{1}, \tau_{0}^{\prime}\right)$. The corresponding densities are

Figure A7.3 Possible time schedule for two alternating renewal processes starting at $t=0$ with $\tau_{0}$ and $\tau_{0}^{-}$, respectively; shown are also the 4 embedded renewal processes with renewal points $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ \& $\boldsymbol{A}$ (regeneration points for states up \& down of the alternating renewal process, see footnote on p. 480)

$$
\mathrm{f}_{A}(x), \quad \mathrm{f}_{A}(x) * \mathrm{~g}(x), \quad \mathrm{g}_{A}(x) * \mathrm{f}(x), \quad \mathrm{g}_{A}(x)
$$

for the time interval starting at $t=0$, and

$$
\mathrm{f}(x) * \mathrm{~g}(x)
$$

for all others. The symbol $*$ denotes convolution (Eq. (A6.75)).
Results of Appendix A7.2 can be used to investigate the embedded renewal processes of Fig. A7.3. Equation (A7.20) yields Laplace transforms of the renewal densities $\mathrm{h}_{u d u}(t), \mathrm{h}_{d u u}(t), \mathrm{h}_{u d d}(t)$, and $\mathrm{h}_{d u d}(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tilde{\mathrm{h}}_{u d u}(s)=\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)}, \quad \tilde{\mathrm{h}}_{d u u}(s)=\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s) \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)}, \\
& \tilde{\mathrm{h}}_{u d d}(s)=\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{g}}_{A}(s) \tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)}, \quad \tilde{\mathrm{h}}_{d u d}(s)=\frac{\tilde{\mathrm{g}}_{A}(s)}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)} .^{*}
\end{aligned}
$$

To describe the alternating renewal process defined above (Fig. A7.3), let's introduce the two-dimensional stochastic process $\left(\zeta(t), \tau_{R \zeta(t)}(t)\right)$ where $\zeta(t)$ denotes the state of the process (repairable item in reliability application)

$$
\zeta(t)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
u & \text { if the item is up at time } t \\
d & \text { if the item is down at time } t
\end{array}\right.
$$

$\tau_{R_{u}}(t)$ and $\tau_{R_{d}}(t)$ are thus the forward recurrence times in the up and down states, respectively, provided that the item is up or down at the time $t$, see Fig. 6.3 on p.182.

[^0]
[^0]:    *) It can be noted that $\mathrm{f}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, i. e. constant failure rate $\lambda$ and item new at $t=0$, yields $\mathrm{h}_{\text {udu }}(t)=\lambda\left(\mu+\lambda e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t}\right) /(\lambda+\mu)=\lambda \mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(\mathrm{t})$, as per Eq. (6.19); showing once more the memoryless property of exponentially distributed failure-free times.To investigate the general case, both alternating renewal processes of Fig. A7.3 must be combined. For this let

$$
p=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { item up at } t=0\} \quad \text { and } \quad 1-p=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { item down at } t=0\}
$$

In terms of the process $\left(\zeta(t), \tau_{R \zeta(t)}(t)\right)$,

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
p=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta(0)=u\}, & \mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R u}(0) \leq x \mid \zeta(0)=u\right\} \\
1-p=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta(0)=d\}, & \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R d}(0) \leq x \mid \zeta(0)=d\right\}
\end{array}
$$

Consecutive jumps from up to down form a renewal process with renewal density

$$
\mathrm{h}_{u d}(t)=p \mathrm{~h}_{u d u}(t)+(1-p) \mathrm{h}_{u d d}(t), \quad t>0, \mathrm{~h}_{u d u}(t)=\mathrm{h}_{u d d}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

Similarly, the renewal density for consecutive jumps from down to up is given by

$$
\mathrm{h}_{d u}(t)=p \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(t)+(1-p) \mathrm{h}_{d u d}(t), \quad t>0, \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(t)=\mathrm{h}_{d u d}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

Using Eqs. (A7.52) \& (A7.53), and considering Eq. (A7.25), it follows that for $\theta \geq 0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\zeta(t)=u\right. & \cap \tau_{R u}(t)>\theta\} \\
& =p\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t+\theta)\right)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t-x+\theta)) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\zeta(t)=d\right. & \left.\cap \tau_{R d}(t)>\theta\right\} \\
& =(1-p)\left(1-\mathrm{G}_{A}(t+\theta)\right)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{u d}(x)(1-\mathrm{G}(t-x+\theta)) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $\theta=0$ in Eq. (A7.54) yields

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta(t)=u\}=p\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{A}(t)\right)+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u}(x)(1-\mathrm{F}(t-x)) d x
$$

The probability $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta(t)=u\}$ is called point availability, and $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+\theta\}=$ $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\zeta(t)=u \cap \tau_{R_{u}}(t)>\theta\right\}$ interval reliability, of the given item (as per Eqs. (6.42) and (6.44), see also Section 6.2 for further considerations).

An alternating renewal process, characterized by the parameters $p, \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x), \mathrm{F}(x)$, $\mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$, and $\mathrm{G}(x)$ is stationary if the two-dimensional process $\left(\zeta(t), \tau_{R \zeta(t)}(t)\right)$ is stationary. As with the renewal process (pp. 487-88) it can be shown that an alternating renewal process is stationary if and only if (Eqs.(A7.51), (A7.45), (A7.46))

$$
p=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}, \quad \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y, \quad G_{A}(x)=\frac{1}{M T T R} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{G}(y)) d y
$$hold as initial condition/distributions at $t=0$, with MTTF \& MTTR as in Eqs. (A7.47) $\&$ (A7.48). In particular, for $t \geq 0$ the following relationships apply for the stationary alternating renewal process (see Examples $6.3 \& 6.4$ on p. $186 \& 189$ for $P A_{S}$, Eq. $(6.50)$ on p. 185 for $\left.\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)\right)$

$$
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{PA}_{S}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { item up at } t\}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}=P A_{S}, \quad t \geq 0 \\
\operatorname{IR}_{S}(t, t+\theta)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { item up at } t \text { and remains up until } t+\theta\} \\
\quad=\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R} \int_{\theta}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y=\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta), \quad t \geq 0, \theta>0, \operatorname{IR}_{S}(0)=P A_{S}
\end{gathered}
$$

Condition (A7.57) is equivalent to

$$
\mathrm{h}_{u d}(t)=\mathrm{h}_{d u}(t)=\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R} \cdot \quad t \geq 0
$$

Moreover, application of the key renewal theorem (Eq. (A7.29)) to Eqs. (A7.54) (A7.56) yields (for $\theta>0$ given (fixed), see Example 6.3 for $P A_{S}$ )

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\zeta(t)=u \cap \tau_{R u}(t)>\theta\right\}=\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R} \int_{\theta}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\zeta(t)=d \cap \tau_{R d}(t)>\theta\right\}=\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R} \int_{\theta}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{G}(y)) d y \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta(t)=u\}=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=P A_{S}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}
\end{aligned}
$$

Under weak conditions, irrespective of its initial conditions $p, \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)$, and $\mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$, an alternating renewal process has for $t \rightarrow \infty$ an asymptotic behavior which is identical to the stationary state (steady-state). Thus, for reliability applications,
a stationary alternating renewal process can be regarded as an alternating renewal process with arbitrary initial conditions $p, \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x), \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$ which has been started at $t=-\infty$ and will only be considered for $t \geq 0$, $t=0$ being an arbitrary time point;
in other words,
for reliability applications, asymptotic \& steady-state can be used for stationary (see also pp. 187, 488, 495, 514 \& 525 as well as p.530).

It can be noted that the results of this section remain valid even if independence between $\tau_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}^{\prime}$ within a cycle (e.g. $\tau_{0}+\tau_{1}^{\prime}, \tau_{1}+\tau_{2}^{\prime}, \ldots$ ) is dropped; only independence between cycles is necessary. For exponentially distributed $\tau_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}^{\prime}$, i. e. for constant failure rate $\lambda$ and repair rate $\mu$ in reliability applications, the convergence of $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ towards $P A_{S}$ stated by Eq. (A7.63) is of the form $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)-P A_{S}=(\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)) e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t} \approx(\lambda / \mu) e^{-\mu t}$, see Eq. (6.20). The case of general repair rate is discussed at the end of Section 6.2.4 on p.187.# A7.4 Regenerative Processes with a Finite Number of States 

A regenerative process with a finite number of states $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}$ is characterized by the property that there is a sequence of random points on the time axis, regeneration points, at which the process
forgets its foregoing evolution and, from a probabilistic point of view, restarts anew with respect to the regeneration state considered.

The times at which a regenerative process restarts, occur when the process returns to some states defined as regeneration states. The sequence of these time points
for a specific regeneration state is a renewal process embedded in the original process.

For instance, a renewal process is a regenerative process with one state, ${ }^{*}$ both states of an alternating renewal process (Fig. A7.3) and, by assuming irreducible embedded Markov chains, all states of time-homogeneous Markov and semiMarkov processes (Eqs. (A7.77), (A7.95) \& (A7.158)) are regeneration states. However, in practical applications there are processes in discrete state space with only few (Figs. 6.10, A7.11-A7.13) or even with no regeneration states;
a regenerative process must have at least one regeneration state (footnote on $p .386$ ), and the set of regeneration states (if $\geq 2$ ) constitutes a semiMarkov process embedded in the original process (remark on p. 522).

A regenerative process with states space $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}$ and an embedded semi-Markov process on the regeneration states $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{k}, 0<k<m$, is a semi-regenerative process (Appendix A7.7), and has $k+1$ (in general different) embedded renewal processes.

In the following, a basic result for regenerative processes is given focusing on an arbitrarily chosen regeneration state and the related embedded renewal process. So considered, the process consists of independent cycles which describe the time behavior of the process between two consecutive regeneration points. The $i$ th cycle is characterized by a positive random variable $\tau_{c_{i}}$ (duration of cycle $i$ ) and a stochastic process $\xi_{i}(x)$ defined for $0 \leq x<\tau_{c_{i}}$ (content of cycle). The pieces $\xi_{n}(x)$ $\left(n=0,1, \ldots, 0 \leq x<\tau_{c_{n}}\right)$ are independent, and for $n \geq 1$ identically distributed cycles. The time points $S_{1}=\tau_{c_{0}}, S_{2}=\tau_{c_{0}}+\tau_{c_{1}}, \ldots$ form a renewal process, for which we assume that $\tau_{c_{0}}$ and $\tau_{c_{i}}, i \geq 1$, have distribution functions $\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)$ for $\tau_{c_{0}} \& \mathrm{~F}(x)$ for $\tau_{c_{i}}$, densities $\mathrm{f}_{A}(x) \& \mathrm{f}(x)$, and finite means $T_{A} \& T_{c}$ and variances $\sigma_{A}^{2} \& \sigma_{c}^{2}$, respectively $\left(\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)=\mathrm{f}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x)=0\right.$ for $\left.x \leq 0\right)$. $\xi(t)$ is then given by

$$
\xi(t)= \begin{cases}\xi_{0}(t) & \text { for } 0 \leq t<S_{1} \\ \xi_{n}\left(t-S_{n}\right) & \text { for } S_{n} \leq t<S_{n+1}, \quad n=1,2, \ldots\end{cases}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    *) Renewal process is used instead of regenerative process because the whole process restarts anew.The regenerative structure is sufficient for the existence of an asymptotic behavior (limiting distribution) for the process as $t \rightarrow \infty$ (provided $T_{A}, T_{c}<\infty$ ). This limiting distribution is determined by the behavior of the process between two consecutive regeneration points (belonging to the same embedded renewal process) [A7.9 (1949), A6.7 (Vol. II), A7.24, 6.3 (1983)]. Defining $\mathrm{h}(t)$ as the renewal density of the embedded renewal process considered, and setting $\mathrm{V}(x, \mathrm{~B})=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{i}(x) \in \mathrm{B} \cap \tau_{c_{i}}>x\right\}$, $\left(i=1,2, \ldots, \mathrm{~B} \subseteq\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}\right)$, it follows, similarly to Eq. (A7.25), that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\xi(t) \in \mathrm{B}\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{0}(t) \in \mathrm{B} \cap \tau_{c_{0}}>t\right\}+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}(x) \mathrm{V}(t-x, \mathrm{~B}) d x
$$

For any given distribution of the cycle $\xi_{i}(x), 0 \leq x<\tau_{c_{i}}, i \geq 1$, with $T_{c}=E\left[\tau_{c_{i}}\right]<\infty$, there exists a stationary regenerative process $\xi_{e}(t)$ with regeneration points $S_{e_{i}}$, $i \geq 1$. The cycles $\xi_{e_{n}}(x), 0 \leq x<\tau_{e_{n}}$, have for $n \geq 1$ the same distribution law as $\xi_{i}(x), 0 \leq x<\tau_{c_{i}}$. The distribution law of the starting cycle $\xi_{e_{0}}(x), 0 \leq x<\tau_{e_{0}}$, can be calculated from the distribution law of $\xi_{i}(x), 0 \leq x<\tau_{c_{i}}$ (see e. g. Eq. (A7.57) for an alternating renewal process); in particular [A7.24 (1955), 6.3 (1983)],

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{e}(0) \in \mathrm{B}\right\}=\frac{1}{T_{c}} \int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{V}(x, \mathrm{~B}) d x
$$

with $T_{c}=E\left[\tau_{c_{i}}\right]<\infty, i \geq 1$. Furthermore, for $S_{1}=0$ and $\mathrm{u}(x)$ non-negative, strictly increasing, and continuous, it holds that [6.3(1983)]

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{u}\left(\xi_{e}(0)\right)\right]=\frac{1}{T_{c}} \mathrm{E}\left[\int_{0}^{\tau_{c_{i}}} \mathrm{u}\left(\xi_{1}(x)\right) d x\right]
$$

Equation (A7.66) is known as the stochastic mean value theorem for regenerative processes, and can be extended to any non-negative function $u(x)$. Assuming, for instance, $\xi_{i}(x)=1$ for item $u p$ and $\xi_{i}(x)=0$ for item down for the alternating renewal process, and $\mathrm{u}(x)=x$, Eq. (A7.66) yields $\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{e}(0)\right]=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{e}(0)=1\right\}=p$ (Eq. (A7.57)).

Considering $T_{c}<\infty, \quad \mathrm{V}(x, \mathrm{~B}) \geq 0$, nonincreasing and $\leq 1-\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{c_{i}} \leq x\right\}$ for all $x>0$, it follows from Eq. (A7.64) and the key renewal theorem (Eq. (A7.29)) that

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\{\xi(t) \in \mathrm{B}\}=\frac{1}{T_{c}} \int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{V}(x, \mathrm{~B}) d x, \quad T_{c}=E\left[\tau_{c_{i}}\right]<\infty, \quad i \geq 1
$$

Equations (A7.65) \& (A7.67) show that under weak conditions, as $t \rightarrow \infty$ a regenerative process becomes stationary (see e. g. p. 530 and Eqs. (6.110) \& (6.131) for practical applications). As for renewal, alternating renewal, Markov and semiMarkov processes (pp. 187, 488, 493, $514 \& 525$ as well as p. 530),
for reliability applications, a stationary regenerative process can be considered as a regenerative process with arbitrary distribution of the starting cycle, which has been started at $t=-\infty$ and will only be considered for $t \geq 0, t=0$ being an arbitrary time point.# A7.5 Markov Processes with a Finite Number of States 

Markov processes are processes without aftereffect. They are characterized by the property that for any (arbitrarily chosen) time point $t$, their evolution after $t$ depends on $t$ and on the state occupied at $t$, but not on the process evolution up to the time $t$. For time-homogeneous Markov processes, dependence on $t$ also disappears. In reliability theory, constant failure and repair rates for all elements is a necessary condition to have a time-homogeneous Markov process (necessary and sufficient is that in each state all involved times are exponentially distributed, see p. 503). After an introduction to Markov chains, time-homogeneous Markov processes with a finite number of states are introduced as basis for Chapter 6.

## A7.5.1 Markov Chains with a Finite Number of States

Let $\xi_{0}, \xi_{1}, \ldots$ be a sequence of random variables taking values in $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}, 0<m<\infty$, e. g. the sequence of consecutively occurring states of a given system. The sequence $\left\{\xi_{n}\right\}, n=0,1,2, \ldots$ constitutes a Markov chain with state space $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}, 0<m<\infty$, if for $n=0,1,2, \ldots$ and arbitrary $i, j, i_{0}, \ldots, i_{n-1} \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \mid\right. & \left(\xi_{n}=Z_{i} \cap \xi_{n-1}=Z_{i_{n-1}} \cap \ldots \cap \xi_{0}=Z_{i_{0}}\right)\} \\
& =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\}=\varphi_{i j}(n)
\end{aligned}
$$

holds. ${ }^{+)}$The quantities $\varphi_{i j}(n)$ are the (one step) transition probabilities of the Markov chain. Investigation will be limited here to time-homogeneous Markov chains, for which the transition probabilities $\varphi_{i j}(n)$ are independent of $n$

$$
\varphi_{i j}(n)=\varphi_{i j}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad n=0,1, \ldots
$$

To simplify the notation, Markov chain will be used in the following for timehomogeneous Markov chains. The probabilities $\varphi_{i j}$ satisfy the relationships

$$
\varphi_{i j} \geq 0 \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_{j=0}^{m} \varphi_{i j}=1, \quad i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m<\infty\}
$$

A matrix with elements $\varphi_{i j}$ as in Eq. (A7.70) is a stochastic matrix. The $k$-step transition probabilities are the elements of the $k$ th power of the stochastic matrix with elements $\varphi_{i j}$. For instance, $k=2$ leads to (Example A7.2, Eq. (A6.17))

$$
\begin{aligned}
\varphi_{i j}^{(2)} & =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+2}=Z_{j} \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\}=\sum_{k=0}^{m} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\xi_{n+2}=Z_{j} \cap \xi_{n+1}=Z_{k}\right) \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\} \\
& =\sum_{k=0}^{m} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+1}=Z_{k} \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+2}=Z_{j} \mid\left(\xi_{n}=Z_{i} \cap \xi_{n+1}=Z_{k}\right)\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)} \xi_{0}, \xi_{1}, \ldots$ identify only consecutive transitions (in the same state for $\varphi_{i j}(n)>0$ ) without relation to the time axis; this is important when considering Markov chains embedded in stochastic processes.# Example A7.2 

Assuming $\operatorname{Pr}\{C\}>0$, prove that $\operatorname{Pr}\{(A \cap B) \mid C\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{B \mid C\} \operatorname{Pr}\{A \mid(B \cap C)\}$.
Solution
For $\operatorname{Pr}\{C\}>0$ it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{(A \cap B) \mid C\}=\frac{\operatorname{Pr}\{A \cap B \cap C\}}{\operatorname{Pr}\{C\}}=\frac{\operatorname{Pr}\{B \cap C\} \operatorname{Pr}\{A \mid(B \cap C)\}}{\operatorname{Pr}\{C\}}=\operatorname{Pr}\{B \mid C\} \operatorname{Pr}\{A \mid(B \cap C)\}
$$

from which, considering the Markov property (Eqs. (A7.68)),

$$
\varphi_{i j}^{(2)}=\sum_{k=0}^{m} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+1}=Z_{k} \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+2}=Z_{j} \mid \xi_{n+1}=Z_{k}\right\}=\sum_{k=0}^{m} \varphi_{i k} \varphi_{k j}
$$

Results for $k>2$ follow by induction.
The transition probabilities $\varphi_{i j}$, together with the initial distribution

$$
A_{i}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{0}=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad i=0, \ldots, m, \sum A_{i}=1
$$

completely determine the distribution law of a Markov chain; in particular,

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{0}=Z_{i_{0}} \cap \xi_{1}=Z_{i_{1}} \cap \ldots \cap \xi_{n}=Z_{i_{n}}\right\}=A_{i_{0}} \varphi_{i_{0} i_{1}} \ldots \varphi_{i_{n-1} i_{n}}
$$

holds for arbitrary $i_{0}, \ldots, i_{n} \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$, and the state probability follows as

$$
\varphi_{j}(n)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n}=Z_{j}\right\}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} A_{i} \varphi_{i j}^{(n)}, \quad n=1,2, \ldots
$$

A Markov chain with transition probabilities $\varphi_{i j}$ is stationary (in steady-state) if the state probabilities $\varphi_{j}(n)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n}=Z_{j}\right\}, j=0, \ldots, m$, are independent of $n$, i. e. if the initial distribution $A_{i}$ (Eq. (A7.72)) is a solution ( $\varphi_{j}$ ) of the system

$$
\varphi_{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} \varphi_{i} \varphi_{i j}, \quad \text { with } \varphi_{j} \geq 0 \text { and } \sum_{j=0}^{m} \varphi_{j}=1, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

Furthermore, a Markov chain with a finite number of states $(m<\infty)$ is irreducible (irreducible and aperiodic, because of $m<\infty$ ) if every state can be reached from every other state, i. e. if for each $(i, j)$ there is an $n=n(i, j)$ such that

$$
\varphi_{i j}^{(n)}>0, \quad i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}, \quad n \geq 1
$$

It can be shown that the system (A7.74) possesses for $m<\infty$ a unique solution with

$$
\varphi_{j}>0 \quad \text { and } \quad \varphi_{0}+\varphi_{1}+\ldots+\varphi_{m}=1, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

only if the Markov chain is irreducible (Markov theorem [A7.12], see e. g. also [A6.7 (Vol. I)]); in this case, the stationary distribution is also an ergodic distribution, i. e. $\varphi_{j}=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \varphi_{i j}^{(n)}$. However, the system given by Eq. (A7.74)
must be solved by replacing one (freely chosen) equation by $\sum \varphi_{j}=1$.
Finally, Eq. (A7.74) expresses that in steady-state, the probability to be at the next step in $Z_{j}$ is equal to the probability to be and remain in $Z_{j}\left(\varphi_{i j}>0\right)$ or to be in any $Z_{i} \neq Z_{j}$ and to come to $Z_{j}$ (see p. 513 for Markov processes).# A7.5.2 Markov Processes with a Finite Number of States ${ }^{*}$ 

A stochastic process $\xi(t)$ with state space $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}, 0<m<\infty$, is a Markov process in continuous time $(t \geq 0)$ with a finite number of states, if for $n=0,1,2, \ldots$, arbitrary time points $t_{n}+a>t_{n}>\ldots>t_{0} \geq 0$, and arbitrary $i, j, i_{0}, \ldots, i_{n} \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi\left(t_{n}+a\right)=Z_{j} \mid\left(\xi\left(t_{n}\right)=Z_{i} \cap \xi\left(t_{n-1}\right)=Z_{i_{n-1}} \cap \ldots \cap \xi\left(t_{0}\right)=Z_{i_{0}}\right)\right\} \\
& =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi\left(t_{n}+a\right)=Z_{j} \mid \xi\left(t_{n}\right)=Z_{i}\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t+a)=Z_{j} \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

holds. $\xi(t)(t \geq 0)$ is a jump function (jump process), as visualized in Fig. A7.10 on p. 522. The conditional state probabilities in Eq. (A7.77) are the transition probabilities of the Markov process and they will be designated by $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t, t+a)$

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t, t+a)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t+a)=Z_{j} \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad t \geq 0, a>0
$$

Equations (A7.77) and (A7.78) give the probability that $\xi(t+a)$ will be $Z_{j}$ given that $\xi(t)$ was $Z_{i}$. Between $t$ and $t+a$ the Markov process can visit any other state (note that this is not the case in Eq. (A7.95), in which $Z_{j}$ is the next state visited after $Z_{i}$, as with Eq. (A7.158) for semi-Markov processes).

The Markov process is time-homogeneous if

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t, t+a)=\mathrm{P}_{i j}(a), \quad t \geq 0, a>0
$$

In the following only time-homogeneous Markov processes in continuous time $(t \geq 0)$ and with a finite number of states $(m+1)$ is considered. Equation (A7.79) expresses the memoryless property of the time-homogeneous Markov processes. From these property, for arbitrary $t \geq 0$ and given $a>0, \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t+a)$ satisfy the Chapman-Kolmogorov equations

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t+a)=\sum_{k=0}^{m} \mathrm{P}_{i k}(t) \mathrm{P}_{k j}(a), \quad t \geq 0, a>0, i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}
$$

whose demonstration is similar to $p_{i j}^{(2)}$ in Eq. (A7.71). Furthermore $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(a)$ satisfy

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(a) \geq 0 \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_{j=0}^{m} \mathrm{P}_{i j}(a)=1, \quad a>0, \quad i=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

and thus form a stochastic matrix. Together with the initial distribution

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad i=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(a)$ completely determine the distribution law of the

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{\text {*) }}$ Continuous (parameter) Markov chain is often used in the literature. Use of Markov process should help to avoid confusion with Markov chains embedded in stochastic processes (pp. 501 \& 522-23).Markov process. In particular, the state probabilities

$$
\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{j}\right\}, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty, \quad t>0
$$

follows as (theorem of total probability (Eq. (A6.17)) and Eq. (A7.82))

$$
\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{m} \mathrm{P}_{i}(0) \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t), \quad t>0
$$

Setting

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(0)=\delta_{i j}= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } i \neq j \\ 1 & \text { for } i=j\end{cases}
$$

and assuming that the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ are continuous at $t=0$, it can be shown that $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ are also differentiable at $t=0$ (see e.g. the discussion to Eqs. (A7.105)-(A7.106)). Thus, the limiting values

$$
\lim _{\delta t \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathrm{P}_{i j}(\delta t)}{\delta t}=\rho_{i j}, \quad \text { for } i \neq j, \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{\delta t \downarrow 0} \frac{1-\mathrm{P}_{i j}(\delta t)}{\delta t}=\rho_{i}
$$

exist and satisfy

$$
\rho_{i}=\sum_{\substack{j=0 \\ j \neq i}}^{m} \rho_{i j}, \quad i=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

Equation (A7.86) can be written in the form

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(\delta t)=\rho_{i j} \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t) \quad \text { and } \quad 1-\mathrm{P}_{i i}(\delta t)=\rho_{i} \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t)
$$

where $\mathrm{o}(\delta t)$ denotes a quantity having an order higher than that of $\delta t$, i. e.

$$
\lim _{\delta t \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathrm{o}(\delta t)}{\delta t}=0
$$

Considering for any $t \geq 0$ and $\delta t>0$

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(\delta t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t+\delta t]=Z_{j} \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}
$$

the following useful interpretation for $\rho_{i j}$ and $\rho_{i}$ can be obtained for arbitrary $t$ and $\delta t \downarrow 0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { jump from } Z_{\mathrm{i}} \text { to } Z_{\mathrm{j}} \text { in }(t, t+\delta t] \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}=\rho_{i j} \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t) \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { leave } Z_{i} \text { in }(t, t+\delta t] \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}=\rho_{i} \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t)
\end{aligned}
$$

It is thus reasonable to define $\rho_{i j}$ and $\rho_{i}$ as transition rates. It can be noted, that for a Markov process, $\rho_{i j}$ plays a similar role to that of the transition probability $\varphi_{i j}$ for a Markov chain.Setting $a=\delta t$ in Eq. (A7.80) yields

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t+\delta t)=\sum_{k=0, k \neq j}^{m} \mathrm{P}_{i k}(t) \mathrm{P}_{k j}(\delta t)+\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t) \mathrm{P}_{j j}(\delta t)
$$

or

$$
\frac{\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t+\delta t)-\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)}{\delta t}=\sum_{k=0, k \neq j}^{m} \mathrm{P}_{i k}(t) \frac{\mathrm{P}_{k j}(\delta t)}{\delta t}+\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t) \frac{\mathrm{P}_{i j}(\delta t)-1}{\delta t}
$$

and then, taking into account Eq. (A7.86), it follows that

$$
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{i j}(t)=-\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t) \rho_{j}+\sum_{k=0, k \neq j}^{m} \mathrm{P}_{i k}(t) \rho_{k j}, \quad t>0, \quad i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}
$$

Equations (A7.91) are the Kolmogorov's forward equations. With initial conditions $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(0)=\delta_{i j}$ as in Eq. (A7.85), they have a unique solution which satisfies Eq.(A7.81). In other words, the transition rates according to Eq. (A7.86) or Eq. (A7.90) uniquely determine the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$. Setting $a=\delta t$ in Eq. (A7.80) and using $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t+\delta t)=\sum_{k \neq i} \mathrm{P}_{i k}(\delta t) \mathrm{P}_{k j}(t)+\mathrm{P}_{i i}(\delta t) \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t), \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ also satisfy the Kolmogorov's backward equations

$$
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{i j}(t)=-\rho_{i} \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)+\sum_{k=0, k \neq j}^{m} \rho_{i k} \mathrm{P}_{k j}(t) \quad, \quad t>0, \quad i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}
$$

Equations (A7.91) \& (A7.92) can also be written in matrix form $\dot{\mathbf{P}}(t)=\mathbf{P}(t) \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \&$ $\dot{\mathbf{P}}(t)=\boldsymbol{\Lambda} \mathbf{P}(t)$ yielding, with $\mathbf{P}(0)=\mathbf{I}$, the (formal) solution $\mathbf{P}(t)=\boldsymbol{e}^{\mathbf{A} t}\left(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\left\|\rho_{i j}\right\|\right)$.

However,
the following description of the time-homogeneous Markov process with initial distribution $\mathrm{P}_{i}(0)$ and transition rates $\rho_{i j}, i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$, provides a better insight into the structure of a Markov process as a pure jump process; it is the basis for investigations of Markov processes using integral equations (pp.511-12), and is the motivation for the introduction of semi-Markov processes (pp.521-26) [A7.2 (1974 (Ph. D., Section 4.2)].
Let $\xi_{0}, \xi_{1}, \ldots$ be a sequence of random variables taking values in $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}$ denoting the states consecutively occupied and $\eta_{0}, \eta_{1}, \ldots$ a sequence of positive random variables denoting the stay times between two consecutive state transitions. Define

$$
\varrho_{i j}=\frac{\rho_{i j}}{\rho_{i}}, \quad i \neq j, \quad \text { and } \quad \varrho_{i i} \equiv 0, \quad i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}
$$

(see footnote ${ }^{++}$on p. 503 and the remark at the bottom of p. 522 for a discussion on $\varrho_{i i} \equiv 0$ ). Assume furthermore that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{0}=Z_{i}\right\}=\mathrm{P}_{i}(0), \quad i=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

and, for $n=0,1,2, \ldots$, arbitrary $i, j, i_{0}, \ldots, i_{n} \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$, and arbitrary $x, x_{0}, \ldots, x_{n}>0$,$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \cap \eta_{n} \leq x\right) \mid\left(\xi_{n}=Z_{i} \cap \eta_{n-1}=x_{n-1} \cap \ldots \cap \xi_{1}=Z_{i_{1}} \cap \eta_{0}=x_{0} \cap \xi_{0}=Z_{i_{0}}\right)\right\} \\
& =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \cap \eta_{n} \leq x\right) \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\}=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)=\varphi_{i j} \mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x)=\varphi_{i j}\left(1-e^{-\rho_{i} x}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in Eq. (A7.95), as well as in Eq. (A7.158) for semi-Markov processes,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& Z_{i} \text { is the next state visited after } Z_{i} \text { (this is not the case in Eqs. (A7.77) } \\
& \text { \& (A7.78)); and thus, } \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x) \text { is defined only for } j \neq i \quad\left(\mathrm{Q}_{i i}(x) \equiv 0\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ is also known as one-step transition probability. For Eq. (A7.95) one recognizes easily that (see Example A7.2 on p. 497)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \varphi_{i j}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad \text { with } \quad \varphi_{i i} \equiv 0, \\
& \mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\eta_{n} \leq x \mid\left(\xi_{n}=Z_{i} \cap \xi_{n+1}=Z_{j}\right)\right\} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The last part of Eq. (A7.95) is a consequence of the memoryless property of the time-homogeneous Markov process (see the discussion to Eq. (A7.79) and also Eq. (A7.102)). From this, and considering Eq. (A7.68),it follows that

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\xi_{0}, \xi_{1}, \ldots \text { is a Markov chain with initial distribution } \varphi_{i}(0)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{0}=Z_{i}\right\} \\
(i=0, \ldots, m) & \text { and transition probabilities } \varphi_{i j} \text {, embedded in the original } \\
\text { process. } &
\end{array}
$$

$\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ is a semi-Markov transition probability and will as such be discussed in Appendix A7.6. Now, define (see e.g. Fig. A7.10)

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
S_{0}=0, & S_{n}=\eta_{0}+\ldots+\eta_{n-1}, \\
\xi(t)=\xi_{n-1} & \text { for } \quad S_{n-1} \leq t<S_{n}, \\
S_{n}=1,2, \ldots
\end{array}
$$

From Eq. (A7.97) and the memoryless property of the exponential distribution (Eq. (A6.87)) it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \xi(t), t \geq 0 \text { is a Markov process with initial distribution } \mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\} \\
& (i=0, \ldots, m) \text { as per Eq. (A7.82), and transition rates } \\
& \rho_{i j}=\lim _{\delta t \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\delta t} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { jump from } Z_{i} \text { to } Z_{j} \text { in }(t, t+\delta t] \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad j \neq i, \\
& \rho_{i}=\lim _{\delta t \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\delta t} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { leave } Z_{i} \text { in }(t, t+\delta t] \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}=\sum_{\substack{j=0 \\
j \neq i}}^{m} \rho_{i j} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The evolution of a time-homogeneous Markov process with transition rates $\rho_{i j}$ and $\rho_{i}$ can thus be described in the following way,
if at $t=0$ the process enters the state $Z_{i}$, i. e. $\xi_{0}=Z_{i}$, the next state to be entered, say $Z_{j}(j \neq i)$ is selected according to the probability $\varphi_{i j} \geq 0\left(\varphi_{i i} \equiv 0\right)$, and the stay (sojourn) time in $Z_{i}$ is a random variable $\eta_{0}$ with distribution function

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\eta_{0} \leq x \mid\left(\xi_{0}=Z_{i} \cap \xi_{1}=Z_{j}\right)\right\}=1-e^{-\rho_{i} x}, \quad x>0
$$as the process enters $Z_{j}$, the next state to be entered, say $Z_{k}(k \neq j)$, will be selected with probability $\varphi_{j k} \geq 0\left(\varphi_{j j} \equiv 0\right)$ and the stay (sojourn) time $\eta_{1}$ in $Z_{j}$ will be distributed according to

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\eta_{1} \leq x \mid\left(\xi_{1}=Z_{j} \cap \xi_{2}=Z_{k}\right)\right\}=1-e^{-\rho_{j} x}, \quad x>0
$$

etc.
The sequence $\xi_{n}, n=0,1, \ldots$ of the states consecutively occupied by the process is that of the Markov chain embedded in $\xi(t)$, the so called embedded Markov chain. The random variable $\eta_{n}$ is the stay (sojourn) time of the process in the state defined by $\xi_{n}$. From the above description it becomes clear that each state $Z_{i}, i=0, \ldots, m$, is a regeneration state.

In practical applications, the following procedure can be used to find the quantities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ in Eq. (A7.95) for time-homogeneous Markov processes (MP) and in Eqs. (A7.158) for semi-Markov processes (SMP),
if the process enters the state $Z_{i}$ at an arbitrary time, say at $t=0$, then a set of independent random times $\tau_{i j}>0, j \neq i$, begin $\left(\tau_{i j}\right.$ is the stay (sojourn) time in $Z_{i}$ with the next jump to $Z_{j}$ ); the process will then jump to $Z_{j}$ at the time $x$ if $\tau_{i j}=x$ and $\tau_{i k}>\tau_{i j}$ for (all) $k \neq i, j$, $i, j, k \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$ (for SMP see also the remark at the bottom of $p .522$ ).

In this interpretation, the quantities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x), \varphi_{i j}$, and $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)$ are given by

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i j} \leq x \cap \tau_{i k}>\tau_{i j}, k \neq i, j\right\}, & j \neq i, x>0, \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0, \\
\varphi_{i j}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i k}>\tau_{i j}, k \neq i, j\right\}=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(\infty), & \varphi_{1 i} \equiv 0, \\
\mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i j} \leq x \mid \tau_{i k}>\tau_{i j}, k \neq i, j\right\}, & j \neq i, x>0, \mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0 . \text { (A7.101) }
\end{array}
$$

Assuming for the time-homogeneous Markov process (memoryless property)

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i j} \leq x\right\}=1-e^{-\rho_{i j} x}, \quad j \neq i, x>0
$$

it follows that (as for Eq. (A7.95)),

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \rho_{i j} e^{-\rho_{i j} y} \prod_{\substack{k=0 \\
k \neq i, j}}^{m} e^{-\rho_{i k} y} d y=\frac{\rho_{i j}}{\rho_{i}}\left(1-e^{-\rho_{i} x}\right), & j \neq i, x>0 \\
\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0, & \\
\varphi_{i j}=\frac{\rho_{i j}}{\rho_{i}}=Q_{i j}(\infty), & j \neq i, \quad \varphi_{i i} \equiv 0, \rho_{i}=\sum_{\substack{j=0 \\
j \neq i}}^{m} \rho_{i j}, \sum_{\substack{j=0 \\
j \neq i}}^{m} \varphi_{i j}=1 . \\
\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)=1-e^{-\rho_{i} x}, & j \neq i, x>0, \mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
\end{array}
$$

It should be emphasized that due to the memoryless property of the time-homogeneous Markov process, there is no difference whether at $t \equiv 0$ the process enters $Z_{i}$ or it is already there. However, this is not true for semi-Markov processes (Eq. (A7.158)).Quite generally, the time behavior of a system
can be described by a time-homogeneous Markov process if and only if in each state all involved random variables are exponentially distributed (implying in reliability theory, constant failure-free, repair, wait \& travel rates which can change only at a state transition, e.g. for load sharing).

In the case of Erlang distributed times (p. 461), a time-homogeneous Markov process with supplementary states can be used, see e. g. Fig. 6.6 on p. 194.

A powerful tool when investigating time-homogeneous Markov processes is the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$, where $\delta t \downarrow 0$ and $t$ is an arbitrary time point (e.g. $t=0$ ). This diagram is a directed graph with nodes labeled by states $Z_{i}, i=0, \ldots, m$, and arcs labeled by transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(\delta t)$, where terms of order $\mathrm{o}(\delta t)$ are omitted (p. 499). It is related to the state transitions diagram of the system involved, take care of particular assumptions (repair priority, change of failure or repair rates at a state change, etc.), and has often more than $2^{n}$ states, if $n$ elements in the reliability block diagram are involved (p. 226, Fig. A7.6). Examples A7.3 - A7.5 give the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for some typical structures in reliability applications (Figs. A7.4 - A7.6). The states in which the system is down are gray. In state $Z_{0}$ all elements are new (operating or in reserve). ${ }^{+)}$

Finally, considering Eqs. (A7.99) and (A7.102) it follows that for $\delta t \rightarrow 0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\xi(\delta t)=Z_{j} \cap \text { only one transition occurs in }(0, \delta t]\right) \mid \xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\} \\
& =\int_{0}^{\delta t_{t}}\left(d \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x) / d x\right)\left(1-\mathrm{Q}_{j}(\delta t-x)\right) d x=\int_{0}^{\delta t_{t}}\left(d \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x) / d x\right) e^{-\mathrm{p}_{j}(\delta t-x)} d x=\rho_{i j} \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t)=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(\delta t)
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { more than one transition in }(0, \delta t] \mid \xi(0)=Z_{i}\}=\mathrm{o}(\delta t)
$$

with $1-\mathrm{Q}_{j}(\delta t-x)=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ no transition in $(x, \delta t-x] \mid \xi(x)=Z_{j}\}$ (Eq. (A7.165), (A7.102)) and $\mathrm{o}(\delta t)$ as per Eq. (A7.89). To Eqs. (A7.105) and (A7.88) it must be pointed out that,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { although for } \delta t \rightarrow 0 \quad \mathrm{P}_{i j}(\delta t)=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(\delta t)=\rho_{i j} \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t), \quad \mathrm{P}_{i j}(\delta t) \text { per Eq.(A7.79) } \\
& \text { and } \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(\delta t) \text { per Eq. (A7.95) are basically different; with } \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x), Z_{j} \text { is the } \\
& \text { next state visited after } Z_{i} \text {, but this is not necessarily the case for } \mathrm{P}_{i j}(x) .^{++)}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Example A7.5

Figure A7.6 shows a series-parallel structure consisting of the series connection (in the reliability sense) of a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy, with elements $E_{2}=E_{3}=E$ and a switching element $E_{1}$. The system has only one repair crew. Since one of the redundant elements $E_{2}$ or $E_{3}$ can be down without having a system failure, in cases a) and b) the repair of element $E_{1}$ is given priority. This means that if a failure of $E_{1}$ occurs during a repair of $E_{2}$ or $E_{3}$, the repair is stopped and $E_{1}$ will be repaired. In cases c) and d) the repair priority on $E_{1}$ has been dropped.
