In reliability theory, two important quantities are the state probabilities and the distribution function of the stay (sojourn) times in the set of system up states. The state probabilities allow calculation of the point availability. The reliability function can be obtained from the distribution function of the stay time in the set of system up states. Furthermore, a combination of these quantities allows, for time-homogeneous Markov processes, a simple calculation of the interval reliability. ${ }^{+)}$

In such analyses, it is useful to partition the system state space $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}, m<\infty$, into two complementary sets $U$ and $\bar{U}\left(U \cup \bar{U}=\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}\right)$.
$U=$ set of the system up states (up states at system level)
$\bar{U}=$ set of the system down states (down states at system level).
Partition of the state space in more than two classes is possible, see e. g. [A7.28].
Calculation of state probabilities and stay (sojourn) times can be carried out for Markov processes using the method of differential or of integral equations.

## A7.5.3.1 Method of Differential Equations

The method of differential equations is the classical one used in investigating time-homogeneous Markov processes, and is based on the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$. Consider a time-homogeneous Markov process $\xi(t)$ with arbitrary initial distribution $\mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\}$ and transition rates $\rho_{i j}$ and $\rho_{i}$ (Eq. (A7.98)). The state probabilities defined by Eq. (A7.83)

$$
\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{j}\right\}, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty, \quad t>0
$$

satisfy the system of differential equations

$$
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{j}(t)=-\rho_{j} \mathrm{P}_{j}(t)+\sum_{\substack{i=0 \\ i \neq j}}^{m} \mathrm{P}_{i}(t) \rho_{i j}, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty, t>0, \rho_{j}=\sum_{\substack{i=0 \\ i \neq j}}^{m} \rho_{i i}
$$

Equation (A7.108) uses the memoryless property of the time-homogeneous Markov process \& Eq.(A7.90), and follows from $\mathrm{P}_{j}(t+\delta t)=\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)\left(1-\rho_{j} \delta t\right)+\sum_{i \neq j} \mathrm{P}_{i}(t) \rho_{i j} \delta t$, see also Example A7.6. The point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$, for arbitrary initial conditions at $t=0$, follows then from ${ }^{+)}$

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\xi(t) \in U\}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} \mathrm{P}_{j}(t), \quad t>0
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$Reliability figures at system level will have indices $S i$ (e.g. $M T T F_{S i}$ ), where $S$ stands for system and $i$ is the state $Z_{i}$ entered at $t=0$ (system referring in this book to the highest integration level of the item considered, $i=0$ to system new or as-good-as-new; see also the footnote on p.512).In reliability analysis, particular initial conditions (Eq.(A7.82)) are often of interest. Assuming

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=1 \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{P}_{j}(0)=0 \text { for } j \neq i
$$

i.e. that the system is in $Z_{i}$ at $t=0,{ }^{*}$ the state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)$, obtained as solution of Eq. (A7.108) with initial conditions per Eq. (A7.110), become the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ defined by Eqs. (A7.78) \& (A7.79)

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{j}(t), \quad i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}
$$

The point availability, designated with $\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)$ (footnote on p.507), is then given by

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t) \in U \mid \xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\}=\sum_{\substack{Z_{j} \in U}} \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t), \quad \begin{aligned}
& i=0, \ldots, m<\infty, t>0, \\
& \mathrm{PA}_{S i}(0)=1 \text { for } Z_{i} \in U .
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)$ is the probability that the system is in one of the up states at $t$, given it was in $Z_{i}$ at $t=0 ;{ }^{*}$ thus, $\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(0)=1$ holds only for $Z_{i} \in U$. Example A 7.6 illustrate calculation of the point-availability for a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy.

# Example A7.6 

Assume a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy, consisting of 2 identical elements $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$ with constant failure rate $\lambda$, constant repair rate $\mu$, and only one repair crew. Give the state probabilities of the involved Markov process ( $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ are new at $t=0$ ).

## Solution

Figure A7.7 shows the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for the investigation of the point availability. Because of the memoryless property of the involved Markov Process, Fig A7.7 and Eqs. (A7.83) \& (A7.90) lead to the following system of difference equations (by omitting the terms in $\mathrm{o}(\delta t)$ as per Eq. (A7.89))

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{0}(t+\delta t)=\mathrm{P}_{0}(t)(1-2 \lambda \delta t)+\mathrm{P}_{1}(t) \mu \delta t \\
& \mathrm{P}_{1}(t+\delta t)=\mathrm{P}_{1}(t)(1-(\lambda+\mu) \delta t)+\mathrm{P}_{0}(t) 2 \lambda \delta t+\mathrm{P}_{2}(t) \mu \delta t \\
& \mathrm{P}_{2}(t+\delta t)=\mathrm{P}_{2}(t)(1-\mu \delta t)+\mathrm{P}_{1}(t) \lambda \delta t
\end{aligned}
$$

and then, as $\delta t \downarrow 0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \stackrel{\bullet}{\mathrm{P}}_{0}(t)=-2 \lambda \mathrm{P}_{0}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{1}(t) \\
& \stackrel{\bullet}{\mathrm{P}}_{1}(t)=-(\lambda+\mu) \mathrm{P}_{1}(t)+2 \lambda \mathrm{P}_{0}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{2}(t) \\
& \stackrel{\bullet}{\mathrm{P}}_{2}(t)=-\mu \mathrm{P}_{2}(t)+\lambda \mathrm{P}_{1}(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

The system of differential equations (A7.113) also follows from Eq. (A7.108) with the $\rho_{i j}$ from Fig. A7.7. The solution for given initial conditions at $t=0$, e. g. $\mathrm{P}_{0}(0)=1, \mathrm{P}_{1}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{2}(0)=0$, leads to probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{0}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{00}(t), \mathrm{P}_{1}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{01}(t) \& \mathrm{P}_{2}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{02}(t)$, and to the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ (Eqs. (A7.111) \& (A7.112); see pp. 197 - 198 and Example A7.9 on p. 519 for a detailed solution, Eq. (6.88) for an approximation, and Table 6.6 (p. 201) for a summary of important results).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ ) Enters $Z_{i}$ at $t=0$ will be necessary for semi-Markov processes (in this book $Z_{0}$ denotes system new).

Figure A7.7 Diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t\}$ for availability calculation of a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$, constant failure rate $\lambda$, constant repair rate $\mu$, and one repair crew (ideal failure detection and switch, $Z_{2}$ down state, $t$ arbitrary, $\delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process with $\rho_{01}=2 \lambda, \rho_{10}=\mu, \rho_{12}=\lambda, \rho_{21}=\mu, \rho_{0}=2 \lambda, \rho_{1}=\lambda+\mu, \rho_{2}=\mu$ )

A further important quantity for reliability analyses is the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S}(t)$; i. e. the probability of no system failure (no failure at system level) in $(0, t]$. $\mathrm{R}_{S}(t)$ can be calculated using the method of differential equations if all states in $\bar{U}$ are declared to be absorbing states. This means that the process will never leave $Z_{k}$ if it jumps into a state $Z_{k} \in \bar{U}$. It is not difficult to see that in this case, the events
\{first system failure occurs before $t\}$
and
$\{$ system is in one of the states $\bar{U}$ at $t\}$
are equivalent, so that the probability to be in one of the states in $U$ is the required reliability function, i.e. the probability that up to the time $t$ the process has never left the set of up states $U$. To make this analysis rigorous, consider the modified Markov process $\xi^{\prime}(t)$ with transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}^{\prime}(t)$ and transition rates

$$
\rho_{i j}^{\prime}=\rho_{i j} \text { if } Z_{i} \in U, \quad \rho_{i j}^{\prime}=0 \text { if } Z_{i} \in \bar{U}, \quad \rho_{i}^{\prime}=\sum_{j=0, j \neq i}^{m} \rho_{i j}^{\prime}
$$

The state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{j}^{\prime}(t)$ of $\xi^{\prime}(t)$ satisfy the following system of differential equations (see Example A7.7 for an application)

$$
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{j}^{\prime}(t)=-\rho_{j}^{\prime} \mathrm{P}_{j}^{\prime}(t)+\sum_{i=0, i \neq j}^{m} \mathrm{P}_{i j}^{\prime}(t) \rho_{i j}^{\prime}, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty, t>0, \rho_{i}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=0, i \neq j}^{\infty} \rho_{i i}^{\prime}
$$

Assuming as initial conditions $\mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(0)=1$ and $\mathrm{P}_{j}^{\prime}(0)=0$ for $j \neq i$, with $Z_{i} \in U$, the solution of Eq. (A7.115) leads to the state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{j}^{\prime}(t)$ and from these to the transition probabilities (as for Eq. (A7.111))

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}^{\prime}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{j}^{\prime}(t)
$$

The reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$ is then given by (footnote on p.507)

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(x) \in U \text { for } 0<x \leq t \mid \xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} \mathrm{P}_{i j}^{\prime}(t), \quad \begin{aligned}
& Z_{i} \in U, t>0, \\
& \mathrm{R}_{S i}(0)=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure A7.8 Diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for reliability calculation of a $r e$ pairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$, const. failure \& repair rates $\lambda, \mu$, one repair crew (ideal failure detection \& switch, $Z_{2}$ down state (absorbing), $t$ arbitrary, $\delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process (footnote on p.513); $\rho_{01}=2 \lambda, \rho_{10}=\mu, \rho_{12}=\lambda, \rho_{0}=2 \lambda, \rho_{1}=\lambda+\mu, \rho_{2}=0 ; \rho_{i j}^{\prime}=\rho_{i j}$ as per Eq. (A7.114)) ${ }^{*}$ )

Example A7.7 illustrates the calculation of the reliability function for a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy. Finally,
the probabilities marked with ' (e.g. $\mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(t)$ ) are reserved for reliability calculation, when using the method of differential equations; this to avoid confusion with the corresponding quantities for the point availability. ${ }^{*}$ )

Equations (A7.112) and (A7.117) can be combined to determine the probability that the process is in an up state (set $U$ ) at $t$ and does not leave the set $U$ in the time interval $(t, t+\theta]$, given $\xi(0)=Z_{i}$. This quantity is the interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S i}(t, t+\theta)$. Due to the memoryless property of the involved Markov process,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IR}_{S i}(t, t+\theta) & =\operatorname{Pr}\{\xi(x) \in U \text { at } t \cap \text { for } t<x \leq t+\theta \mid \xi(0)=Z_{i}\} \\
& =\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t) \cdot \mathrm{R}_{S j}(\theta), \quad i=0, \ldots, m<\infty, t, \theta>0, \operatorname{IR}_{S i}(0,0)=\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(0)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ as given in Eq. (A7.111) and $\mathrm{R}_{S j}(\theta)$ as per Eq. (A7.117), see also p.179.

# Example A7.7 

Investigate the reliability function for the same case as in Example A7.6; i. e. the probability that the system has not left the states $Z_{0}$ and $Z_{1}$ up to time $t$.

## Solution

The diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ of Fig. A7.7 is modified as in Fig. A7.8 by making the down state $Z_{2}$ absorbing. ${ }^{*}$ ) For the state probabilities it follows that (Example A7.6)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \hat{\mathrm{P}}_{0}^{\prime}(t)=-2 \lambda \mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t) \\
& \hat{\mathrm{P}}_{1}^{\prime}(t)=-(\lambda+\mu) \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t)+2 \lambda \mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(t) \\
& \hat{\mathrm{P}}_{2}^{\prime}(t)=\lambda \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

The solution of Eq. (A7.118) with the given initial conditions at $t=0$, e. g. $\mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0)=1, \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(0)=0$, $\& \mathrm{P}_{2}^{\prime}(0)=0$, leads to state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{00}^{\prime}(t), \mathrm{P}_{1}^{\prime}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{01}^{\prime}(t) \& \mathrm{P}_{2}^{\prime}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{02}^{\prime}(t)$, and to the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ (Eqs. (A7.116) and (A7.117); see also pp. 198-99 \& 519).

[^0]
[^0]:    *) However, states designation is not changed in $Z_{i}^{\prime}$, because states remain the same (only their probabilities change, and often only the diagram for $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ is used, making down states absorbing).# A7.5.3.2 Method of Integral Equations 

The method of integral equations is based on the representation of the timehomogeneous Markov process $\xi(t)$ as a pure jump process by means of $\xi_{n}$ and $\eta_{n}$ as introduced in Appendix A7.5.2 (Eq.(A7.95), Fig. A7.10). From the memoryless property it uses only the fact that jump points (in any state) are regeneration points of $\xi(t)$.

The transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{j} \mid \xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\}$ can be obtained by solving the following system of integral equations

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)=\delta_{i j} e^{-\rho_{i} t}+\sum_{\substack{k=0 \\ k \neq i}}^{m} \int_{0}^{t} \rho_{i k} e^{-\rho_{i} x} \mathrm{P}_{k j}(t-x) d x, \quad i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m<\infty\}, t>0
$$

with $\rho_{i}=\Sigma_{j \neq i} \rho_{i j}, \delta_{i j}=0$ for $j \neq i, \delta_{i i}=1$, and $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(0)=\delta_{i j}$ per Eq. (A7.85). The first term of Eq. (A7.120) only holds for $j=i$ and gives the probability that the process will not leave the state $Z_{i}\left(e^{-\rho_{i} t}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i j}>t\right.\right.$ for all $\left.\left.j \neq i\right\}\right)$. To prove the second term of Eq. (A7.120), consider that it holds

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)=\sum_{\substack{k=0 \\ k \neq i}}^{m} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { first jump in } Z_{k} \text { at } x \text { for } 0<x \leq t \text { and } \xi(x)=Z_{k}\right.
$$

this term gives the probability that the process will first move from $Z_{i}$ to $Z_{k}$ at $x$ for $0<x \leq t, k \neq i$, and take into account that occurrence of $Z_{k}$ is a regeneration point $\left(\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\xi_{1}=Z_{k} \cap \eta_{0} \leq x\right) \mid \xi_{0}=Z_{i}\right\}=Q_{i k}(x)=\left(1-e^{-\rho_{i} x}\right) \rho_{i k} / \rho_{i}\right.$ (Eqs. (A7.95) \& (A7.102)), yields $d Q_{i k}(x) / d x=\rho_{i k} e^{-\rho_{i} x}$ and $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{j} \mid\left(\xi_{0}=Z_{i} \cap \eta_{0}=x \cap \xi_{1}=Z_{k}\right)\right\}=P_{k j}(t-x)$ ). Equation (A7.121) then follow from the theorem of total probability given by Eq. (A6.17).

In the same way as for Eq. (A.120), it can be shown that the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$, as defined in Eq. (A7.117), satisfies the following system of integral equations

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)=e^{-\rho_{i} t}+\sum_{\substack{Z_{j} \in U \\ j \neq i}}^{t} \int_{0}^{t} \rho_{i j} e^{-\rho_{i} x} \mathrm{R}_{S j}(t-x) d x, \quad \rho_{i}=\sum_{\substack{j=0 \\ j \neq i}}^{m} \rho_{i j}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& Z_{i} \in U, t>0, \\
& \mathrm{R}_{S i}(0)=1 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)$ and interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S i}(t, t+\theta)$ are given by Eqs. (A7.112) and (A7.119), with $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ per Eq. (A7.120); see, for instance, Eqs. (6.85) and (6.96) for a 1-out-of-2 redundancy. However, it must be noted that
the use of integral equations, as in Eq. (A7.122), for $\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)$ leads to mistakes, because $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$ and $\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)$ describe two basically different situations (summing for $\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)$ over all states $j \neq i$ yields $\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)=1$, as for Eq. (A7.112) with $j=0, \ldots, m)$.The systems of integral equations (A7.120) and (A7.122) can be solved using Laplace transform. Referring to Appendix A9.7,

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{i j}(s)=\frac{\delta_{i j}}{s+\rho_{i}}+\sum_{\substack{k=0 \\ k \neq i}}^{m} \frac{\rho_{i k}}{s+\rho_{i}} \tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{k j}(s), \quad \rho_{i}=\sum_{\substack{j=0 \\ j \neq i}}^{m} \rho_{i j}, i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m<\infty\}
$$

and

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S i}(s)=\frac{1}{s+\rho_{i}}+\sum_{\substack{Z_{j} \in U \\ j \neq i}} \frac{\rho_{i j}}{s+\rho_{i}} \tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S j}(s), \quad \rho_{i}=\sum_{\substack{j=0 \\ j \neq i}}^{m} \rho_{i j}, \quad Z_{i} \in U
$$

A direct advantage of the method based on integral equations appears in the calculation of $M T T F_{S i}$, i.e. of the system mean time to failure, provided the system is in state $Z_{i} \in U$ at $t=0$. Considering Eqs. (A6.38) \& (2.61) it follows that

$$
M T T F_{S i}=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{R}_{S i}(t) d t=\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S i}(0)
$$

and thus, $M T T F_{S_{i}}$ satisfies the following system of algebraic equations ${ }^{*}$ )

$$
M T T F_{S i}=\frac{1}{\rho_{i}}+\sum_{\substack{Z_{j} \in U \\ j \neq i}} \frac{\rho_{i j}}{\rho_{i}} M T T F_{S j}, \quad \rho_{i}=\sum_{\substack{i=0 \\ j \neq i}}^{m} \rho_{i j}, \quad Z_{i} \in U
$$

For the interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S i}(t, t+\theta)$, Eq. (A7.119) holds.

# A7.5.3.3 Stationary State and Asymptotic Behavior 

Determination of time-dependent state probabilities or of the point availability for a system whose elements have constant failure and repair rates is still possible using differential or integral equations. However, it can become time-consuming. The situation is easier when state probabilities are independent of time, i. e. when the process involved is stationary (yielding algebraic equations);
a time-homogeneous Markov process $\xi(t)$ with states $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}$ is stationary, if its state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}, i=0, \ldots, m<\infty$ do not depend on $t$.

This can be seen from the following relationship

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi\left(t_{1}\right)=Z_{i_{1}} \cap \ldots \cap \xi\left(t_{n}\right)=Z_{i_{n}}\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi\left(t_{1}\right)=Z_{i_{1}}\right\} \mathrm{P}_{i_{1} i_{2}}\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right) \ldots \mathrm{P}_{i_{n-1} i_{n}}\left(t_{n}-t_{n-1}\right)
$$

which, according to the Markov property (Eq. (A7.77)) must be valid for arbitrary $0 \leq t_{1}<\ldots<t_{n}$ and $i_{1}, \ldots, i_{n} \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$. For any $a>0$ this leads to

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi\left(t_{1}\right)=Z_{i_{1}} \cap \ldots \cap \xi\left(t_{n}\right)=Z_{i_{n}}\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi\left(t_{1}+a\right)=Z_{i_{1}} \cap \ldots \cap \xi\left(t_{n}+a\right)=Z_{i_{n}}\right\}
$$

From $\mathrm{P}_{i}(t+a)=\mathrm{P}_{i}(t)$ it follows that $\mathrm{P}_{i}(t)=\mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=P_{i}$, and $\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{i}(t)=0$. Consequently,

[^0]
[^0]:    *) Equation (A7.126) shows the dependence between $M T T F_{S i} \& M T T F_{S_{j}}$, reinforcing the necessity to use indices $S i$ (footnote on p. 507).the process $\xi(t)$ is stationary (in steady-state) if its initial distribution (initial conditions) $P_{i}=\mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\}, i=0, \ldots, m$, satisfy (Eq. (A7.108))

$$
P_{j} \rho_{j}=\sum_{i=0, i \neq j}^{m} P_{i} \rho_{i j}, \quad \text { with } P_{j} \geq 0, \sum_{j=0}^{m} P_{j}=1, \rho_{j}=\sum_{i=0, i \neq j}^{m} \rho_{j i}, j=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

Furthermore, a Markov process with a finite number of states $(m<\infty)$ is irreducible if every state can be reached from every other state, i. e. if for each pair $i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$ there exists a $t$ such that $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)>0$. A Markov process is
irreducible if and only if its embedded Markov chain is irreducible (irreducible and aperiodic, because of $m<\infty$, Eq. (A7.75)).

Similarly as on p. 497 for Markov chains, it can be shown that
the system (A7.127) possesses for $m<\infty$ a unique solution with $P_{j}>0$ $(j=0, \ldots, m) \& P_{0}+\ldots+P_{m}=1$, only if the Markov process is irreducible. ${ }^{*}$ )
In this case, the stationary distribution is also an ergodic distribution (Markov theorem [A7.12], see e.g. also [A6.7(Vol.I)]); i.e.

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} P_{i}(t)=P_{j}>0, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

For any $i=0, \ldots, m$ it follows then

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} P_{i j}(t)=P_{j}>0, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

$P_{0}, \ldots, P_{m}$ from Eq. (A7.128) is the limiting distribution of the Markov process. From Eq. (A7.129) it follows that for an irreducible Markov process the limiting distribution is the only stationary and ergodic distribution, i. e. the only solution of Eq. (A7.127) with $P_{j}>0 \& \Sigma P_{j}=1, j=0, \ldots, m<\infty .{ }^{*}$ ) However, the system (A7.127) **) must be solved by replacing one, freely chosen, equation by $\Sigma P_{j}=1$.

As for Eq. (A7.74), Eq.(A7.127) expresses that in steady-state and for $\delta t \downarrow 0, \operatorname{Pr}\{$ to be in state $Z_{j}$ and to leave $Z_{j}($ in $\delta t)\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\right.$ to be in any $Z_{i} \neq Z_{j}$ and to come to $\left.Z_{j}($ in $\delta t)\right\}$.

Further important results follow from Eqs. (A7.174)-(A7.180). In particular,

- the initial distribution in steady-state $\mathrm{A}_{i j}^{\mathrm{s}}(x)=\left(1-e^{-\rho_{i} x}\right) P_{i} \rho_{i j} / \rho_{i}$ (Eq.(A7.181))
- the frequency $h_{i}=P_{i} \rho_{i}$, of consecutive occurrences of state $Z_{i}$ (Eq.(A7.181))
- the relation between stationary values $\varphi_{i}$ per Eq.(A7.175) for the embedded Markov chain and $P_{i}$ per Eq. (A7.127) for the involved Markov process (see the remark at the bottom of p. 525)

$$
P_{i}=\frac{\varphi_{i} / \rho_{i}}{\sum_{k=0}^{m} \varphi_{k} / \rho_{k}}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ ) On the contrary, if the embedded Markov chain is not irreducible, e.g. because of absorbing states, $\sum_{Z_{i} \in U} P_{i}=0 \quad\left(P_{j}=0\right.$ for all $Z_{j} \in U$, e. g. as given by applying Eq.(A7.127) to Eq.(A7.118)).
    ${ }^{* *}$ ) Also known as generalized cut sets theorem.From the results given by Eqs. (A7.127) - (A7.129), the asymptotic \& steadystate value of the point availability $P A_{S}$ follows as

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)=P A_{S}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}, \quad i=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

For the interval reliability, Eq. (A7.119) holds with $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ as per Eq. (A7.129).
If $K$ is a subset of $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}$, the Markov process is irreducible, and $P_{0}, \ldots, P_{m}$ are the limiting probabilities obtained from Eq. (A7.127) then,

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\text { total sojourn time in states } Z_{j} \in K \text { in }(0, t]}{t}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in K} P_{j}\right\}=1
$$

irrespective of the initial distribution $\mathrm{P}_{0}(0), \ldots, \mathrm{P}_{m}(0)$. From Eq. (A7.132) it follows

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\text { total operating time in }(0, t]}{t}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}=P A_{S}\right\}=1
$$

The average availability of the system can be expressed as (see Eq. (6.24))

$$
\mathrm{AA}_{S i}(t)=\frac{1}{t} \mathrm{E}\left[\text { total operating time in }(0, t] \mid \xi(0)=Z_{i}\right]=\frac{1}{t} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{PA}_{S i}(x) d x
$$

The above considerations lead to (for any $i=0, \ldots, m<\infty$ )

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{AA}_{S i}(t)=A A_{S}=P A_{S}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}
$$

Expressions $\sum k P_{k}$ are useful in practical applications, e.g. for cost optimizations.
Except for investigations on the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S}(t)$ (footnote on p. 513), an irreducible embedded Markov chain can be assumed in reliability applications. For such cases, according to Eqs. (A7.127) and (A7.128),
asymptotic \& steady-state can be used for stationary (see e.g. also pp. 187, 488, 493, 495 \& 525 as well as p.530).

# A7.5.4 Frequency / Duration and Reward Aspects 

In some applications, it is important to consider the frequency with which failures at system level occur and the mean duration of system up (operating) or down time in stationary state. Also of interest is the investigation of fault tolerant systems for which a reconfiguration can take place after a failure, allowing continuation of operation with defined loss of performance (reward). Basic considerations on these aspects are given in this section. Some applications are in Section 6.8.6.

## A7.5.4.1 Frequency / Duration

To introduce the concept of frequency/duration let us consider the one-item structure discussed in Appendix A7.3 as application of the alternating renewal process.As in Appendix A7.3, assume an item (system) which alternates between operating state, with mean time to failure $M T T F$, and repair state, with complete renewal and mean repair time MTTR. In the stationary state, the frequency at which item failures $f_{u d}$ or item repairs (restorations) $f_{d u}$ occurs is given by (Eq. (A7.60))

$$
f_{u d}=f_{d u}=\mathrm{h}_{u d}(t)=\mathrm{h}_{d u}(t)=1 /(M T T F+M T T R), \quad t \geq 0
$$

Furthermore, for the one-item structure, the mean up time MUT is

$$
M U T=M T T F, \quad \text { (one item structure) }
$$

Consequently, considering Eq. (A7.58), the basic relation

$$
P A=M T T F /(M T T F+M T T R)=f_{u d} \cdot M U T, \quad \text { i. e. } M U T=P A / f_{u d}
$$

can be established, where $P A$ is the point availability (probability to be up) in the stationary state. Similarly, for the mean failure duration MDT one has

$$
M D T=M T T R, \quad \text { (one item structure) }
$$

and thus

$$
\overline{P A}=M T T R /(M T T F+M T T R)=f_{d u} \cdot M D T, \quad \text { i.e. } M D T=\overline{P A} / f_{d u}
$$

with $\overline{P A}=1-P A$. Constant failure \& repair rates $(\lambda=1 / M T T F \& \mu=1 / M T T R)$ leads to

$$
P A \cdot \lambda=\overline{P A} \cdot \mu=f_{u d}=f_{d u}, \quad \overline{P A}=1-P A
$$

which expresses the stationary property of time-homogeneous Markov processes, as particular case of Eq. (A7.127) with $m=\{0,1\}$.

For systems of arbitrary complexity with constant failure \& repair (restoration) rates, and described by time-homogeneous Markov processes (Appendix A7.5.2), generalization of Eqs. (A7.135) \& (A7.137) yields for the asymptotic \& steady-state system failure frequency $f_{u d S}$ and system mean up time $M U T_{S}$

$$
f_{u d S}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U, Z_{i} \in \bar{U}} P_{j} \rho_{j i}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}\left(\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}}\right), \quad\left(f_{i j}=h_{i}=1 / T_{i j}=P_{j} \rho_{j} \text { for } U=Z_{j}\right)
$$

and

$$
M U T_{S}=\left(\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j}\right) / f_{u d S}=P A_{S} / f_{u d S}, \quad\left(M U T_{j}=T_{j}=1 / \rho_{j}=P_{j} T_{j j} \text { for } U=Z_{j}\right)
$$

respectively (see also Eq. (A7.181) for $U=Z_{j}$ ). $U$ is the set of states considered as up states for $f_{u d S} \& M U T_{S}$ calculation, $\bar{U}$ the complement to system states. Thus,
$M U T_{S}$ is the mean of the times in which, after a transition from a down state, the system is moving in the set of up states $Z_{j} \in U$ before a transition to the set of down states $Z_{i} \in \bar{U}$ occurs, in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty$, similar is for $M D T_{S}, f_{u d S}, f_{d u S} ;$ for practical applications, $M U T_{S} \approx M T T F_{S 0}$ can often be used, $M T B F_{S}$ instead of $M U T_{S}$ should be avoided. ${ }^{*}$ )

[^0]
[^0]:    *) See remarks on pp. 279 and 392-94, as well as footnotes on pp. $512 \& 121$.In Eq. (A.7.141), all transition rates $\rho_{j i}$ leaving $Z_{j} \in U$ toward $Z_{i} \in \bar{U}$ are considered (cumulated states). Similar results hold for semi-Markov processes (Eq. (A7.179)). Equations (A7.141) \& (A7.142) have a great intuitive appeal: (i) Because of the memoryless property of the time-homogeneous Markov processes, the asymptotic $\&$ steady-state probability to have a failure in $(t, t+\delta t]$ is $f_{u d S} \delta t$; (ii) Setting $U T$ as (total) up time and $v(t)$ as (total) number of failures in $(0, t], \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}(U T / t)=P A_{S}$ and $\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}(v(t) / t)=f_{u d S}$ lead to $U T / v(t) \rightarrow M U T_{S}=P A_{S} / f_{u d S}$ for $t \rightarrow \infty$.

Similar results hold for the asymptotic \& steady-state system repair (restoration) frequency $f_{d u S}$ and system mean down time $M D T_{S}$

$$
f_{d u S}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}, Z_{j} \in U} P_{i} \rho_{i j}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}}\left(\sum_{Z_{j} \in U}\right), \quad\left(f_{i i}=h_{i}=1 / T_{i i}=P_{i} \rho_{i} \text { for } \bar{U}=Z_{i}\right)
$$

and

$$
M D T_{S}=\left(\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}} P_{i}\right) / f_{d u S}=\left(1-P A_{S}\right) / f_{d u S}, \quad\left(M D T_{i}=T_{i}=1 / \rho_{i}=P_{i} T_{i i} \text { for } \bar{U}=Z_{i}\right)
$$

(see also Eq. (A7.181) for $\bar{U}=Z_{i}$ and pp.124, 279, 392-94, 512-14 for a discussion).
$f_{u d S}$ is the system failure intensity $z_{S}(t)=z_{S}$ as per Eq. (A7.230) in steady-state or for $t \rightarrow \infty$. Considering that each failure at system level is followed by a repair (restoration) at system level, one has $f_{u d S}=f_{d u S}$ and thus (see also Eq. (A7.60))

$$
f_{d u S}=f_{u d S}=z_{S}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in \bar{U}, Z_{j} \in U} P_{i} \rho_{i j}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U, Z_{i} \in \bar{U}} P_{j} \rho_{j i}=1 /\left(M U T_{S}+M D T_{S}\right)
$$

The central part of Eq. (A7.145) is known as theorem of cuts.
Equations (A7.142), (A7.144), and (A7.145) yield to the following important relation between $M D T_{S}$ and $M U T_{S}$ (see also Eqs. (A7.137) \& A7.139))

$$
M D T_{S}=M U T_{S}\left(1-P A_{S}\right) / P A_{S}
$$

Equation (A7.146) satisfy $P A_{S}=M U T_{S} /\left(M U T_{S}+M D T_{S}\right)$ as per Eqs. (6.48) \& (6.49).
Calculation of the frequency of failures $f_{u d S} \&$ mean failure duration $\left(M D T_{S}\right)$ based on fault trees and minimal cut-sets is often used in power systems [6.4, 6.22].

Although appealing,
$\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} P_{j} M T T F_{S j}$, with $M T T F_{S j} \& P_{j}$ from Eqs.(A6.126) \& (A7.127), cannot be used to calculate $M U T_{S}$ (Eq. (A7.126) applies to a non irreducible Markov process, for which Eq.(A7.127) yields $P_{j}=0$ for all up states $Z_{j}$
(see the footnote on p. 513). However, $M U T_{S} \approx M T T F_{S 0}$ can often be used, see e. g. Example 6.29 on p. 279 and the numerical results on pp. 237 \& 270; approximations for $M U T_{S} \& M D T_{S}$ are also considered on pp.121-24, 191, 200, 217, 232, 233.

# A7.5.4.2 Reward 

Complex fault tolerant systems have been conceived to be able to reconfigure themselves at a failure and continue operation, if necessary with reduced performance.Such a feature is important for many systems, e. g. production, information \& power systems, which should continue operation after a system failure. Besides fail-safe aspects, investigation of such systems is based on the superposition of performance behavior (often assumed deterministic) and stochastic dependability behavior (including reliability, maintainability, availability, and logistic support). Considering that $P_{i}$ is the asymptotic \& steady-state probability to be in state $Z_{i}$, giving also the expected percentage of time the system stays at the performance level specified by $Z_{i}$ (Eq. (A7.132)), a straightforward possibility is to assign to each state $Z_{i}$ of the dependability model a reward rate $0 \leq r_{i} \leq 1$ which take care of the performance reduction in the state considered. From this, the mean reward rate $\mathrm{MIR}_{S}(t)$ can be calculated in stationary state as (see Example 6.27 on p. 270 for an application)

$$
M I R_{S}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} r_{i} \cdot P_{i}
$$

Thereby, $r_{i}=0$ for down states and $r_{i}=1$ for up states with $100 \%$ performance. The mean accumulated reward $\operatorname{MAR}_{S}(t)$ follows for the stationary state as

$$
\operatorname{MAR}_{S}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \operatorname{MIR}_{S}(x) d x=M I R_{S} \cdot t
$$

$\mathrm{MAR}_{S}(t)$ gives the reward over $(0, t]$ on the basis of the stay (sojourn) times in each state. Other metrics are possible, e. g. reward impulses at state transition, expected ratio of busy channels etc. (see e. g. [6.19(1995), 6.26, 6.34]). Of less importance for practical applications is the use of reward aspects for $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$ or $M T T F_{S i}$. For the purpose of this book, application in Section 6.8.6.4 will be limited to Eq. (A7.147).

# A7.5.5 Birth and Death Process 

A birth and death process is a Markov process characterized by the property that transitions from a state $Z_{i}$ can only occur to state $Z_{i+1}$ (birth) or $Z_{i-1}$ (death). In the time-homogeneous case, it is used to investigate $k$-out-of-n redundancies with identical elements and constant failure \& repair rates during the stay (sojourn) time in any given state (not necessarily at state transitions, e. g. for load sharing). The diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ is given in Fig. A7.9. $v_{i}$ and $\theta_{i}$ are the transition rates from state $Z_{i}$ to $Z_{i+1} \& Z_{i}$ to $Z_{i-1}$, respectively (transitions outside


Figure A7.9 Diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a birth and death process with $(n+1)<\infty$ states ( $t$ arbitrary, $\delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process)neighboring states can occur in $(t, t+\delta t]$ only with probability $\mathrm{o}(\delta t)$ ). The system of differential equations describing the birth and death process given in Fig. A7.9 is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{j}(t)=-\left(v_{j}+\theta_{j}\right) \mathrm{P}_{j}(t)+v_{j-1} \mathrm{P}_{j-1}(t)+\theta_{j+1} \mathrm{P}_{j+1}(t) \\
& \text { with } \theta_{0}=v_{-1}=v_{n}=\theta_{n+1}=0, \quad j=0, \ldots, n<\infty .
\end{aligned}
$$

The conditions $v_{j}>0 \quad(j=0, \ldots, n-1)$ and $\theta_{j}>0 \quad(j=1, \ldots, n<\infty)$ make the Markov process irreducible and are thus sufficient for the existence of the limiting probabilities (see Eqs. (A7 127) \& (A7.128))

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} P_{j}(t)=P_{j}, \quad \text { with } \quad P_{j}>0 \text { and } \sum_{j=0}^{n} P_{j}=1
$$

It can be shown (Example A7.8), that the probabilities $P_{j}$ are given by

$$
P_{j}=\pi_{j} P_{0}=\pi_{j} f \sum_{i=0}^{n} \pi_{i}, \quad \text { with } \pi_{0}=1, \pi_{i}=\frac{v_{0} \ldots v_{i-1}}{\theta_{1} \cdots \theta_{i}}, j=0, \ldots, n<\infty
$$

From Eq. (A7.151) one recognizes that

$$
P_{k} v_{k}=P_{k+1} \theta_{k+1}, \quad k=0, \ldots, n-1
$$

yielding the so called generalized cut sets theorem

$$
P_{k} \cdot\left(v_{k}+\theta_{k}\right)=P_{k-1} v_{k-1}+P_{k+1} \theta_{k+1}, \quad k=0, \ldots, n, \theta_{0}=v_{-1}=v_{n}=\theta_{n+1}=0
$$

The values of $P_{j}$ given by Eq. (A7.151) can be used in Eq. (A7.134) to calculate the stationary (asymptotic \& steady-state) value of the point availability. The system mean time to failure follows from Eq. (A7.126). Examples A7.9 and A7.10 are applications of the birth and death process (see also Table 6.8 on p. 217).

# Example A7.8 

Assuming Eq. (A7.150) prove Eq. (A7.151).

## Solution

Considering Eqs. (A7.149) \& (A7.150), $P_{j}$ are the solution of following system of algebraic eqs.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 0=-v_{0} P_{0}+\theta_{1} P_{1} \\
& \vdots \\
& 0=-\left(v_{j}+\theta_{j}\right) P_{j}+v_{j-1} P_{j-1}+\theta_{j+1} P_{j+1}, \quad j=1, \ldots, n-1 \\
& \vdots \\
& 0=-\theta_{n} P_{n}+v_{n-1} P_{n-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation it follows $P_{1}=P_{0} v_{0} / \theta_{1}$. With this $P_{1}$, the second equation leads to

$$
P_{2}=\frac{v_{1}+\theta_{1}}{\theta_{2}} P_{1}-\frac{v_{0}}{\theta_{2}} P_{0}=\left(\frac{v_{1}+\theta_{1}}{\theta_{2}} \cdot \frac{v_{0}}{\theta_{1}}-\frac{v_{0}}{\theta_{2}}\right) P_{0}=\frac{v_{0} v_{1}}{\theta_{1} \theta_{2}} P_{0}
$$

Recursively one obtains

$$
P_{j}=\frac{v_{0} \ldots v_{j-1}}{\theta_{1} \ldots \theta_{j}} P_{0}=\pi_{j} P_{0}, \quad j=1, \ldots, n, \quad \pi_{0}=1
$$

$P_{0}$ follows then from $P_{0}+\ldots+P_{n}=1$.# Example A7.9 

For the 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with one repair crew of Examples A7.6 and A7.7, i. e. for $v_{0}=2 \lambda, v_{1}=\lambda, \theta_{1}=\theta_{2}=\mu, U=\left\{Z_{0}, Z_{1}\right\}$ and $\vec{U}=\left\{Z_{2}\right\}$, give the asymptotic \& steady-state value $P A_{S}$ of the point availability and the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and $M T T F_{S 1}$.

## Solution

The asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability is given by (Eqs. (A7.131), (A7.151))

$$
P A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}=\left(\pi_{0}+\pi_{1}\right) P_{0}=\frac{1+2 \lambda / \mu}{1+2 \lambda / \mu+2 \lambda^{2} / \mu^{2}}=\frac{\mu^{2}+2 \lambda \mu}{2 \lambda(\lambda+\mu)+\mu^{2}}
$$

as per Eq. (6.87) with $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$. The system's mean time to failure follows from Eq. (A7.126), with $\rho_{01}=\rho_{0}=2 \lambda, \rho_{12}=\lambda, \rho_{10}=\mu$, and $\rho_{1}=\lambda+\mu$, as solution of

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T F_{S 0}=1 / 2 \lambda+M T T F_{S 1} \\
& M T T F_{S 1}=\frac{1}{\lambda+\mu}+\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu} M T T F_{S 0}
\end{aligned}
$$

yielding

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{3 \lambda+\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}} \quad \text { and } \quad M T T F_{S 1}=\frac{2 \lambda+\mu}{2 \lambda^{2}}
$$

## Example A7.10

A computer system consists of 3 identical CPUs. Jobs arrive independently and the arrival times form a Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$. The duration of each individual job is distributed exponentially with parameter $\mu$. All jobs have the same memory requirements $D$. Give for $\lambda=2 \mu$ the minimum size $n$ of the memory required in units of $D$, so that in the stationary case (asymptotic \& steady-state) a new job can immediately find storage space with a probability $\gamma$ of at least $95 \%$. When overflow occurs, jobs are queued.

## Solution

The problem can be solved using the following birth and death process



In state $Z_{i}$, exactly $i$ memory units are occupied. $n$ is the smallest integer such that in the steadystate, $P_{0}+\ldots+P_{n-1}=\gamma \geq 0.95$ (if the assumption were made that jobs are lost if overflow occurs, the process would stop at state $Z_{n}$ ). For steady-state, Eq. (A7.127) yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 0=-\lambda P_{0}+\mu P_{1} \\
& 0=\lambda P_{0}-(\lambda+\mu) P_{1}+2 \mu P_{2} \\
& 0=\lambda P_{1}-(\lambda+2 \mu) P_{2}+3 \mu P_{3} \\
& 0=\lambda P_{2}-(\lambda+3 \mu) P_{3}+3 \mu P_{4} \\
& \quad \vdots \\
& 0=\lambda P_{i}-(\lambda+3 \mu) P_{i+1}+3 \mu P_{i+2}, \quad i>2
\end{aligned}
$$The solution leads to

$$
P_{1}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu} P_{0} \quad \text { and } \quad P_{i}=\frac{\lambda^{i} P_{0}}{2 \cdot 3^{i-2} \mu^{i}}=\frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda / \mu}{3}\right)^{i} P_{0} \quad \text { for } i \geq 2
$$

Considering $\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{i=0}^{n} P_{i}=1$ (Eq. (A7.150)), $\frac{\lambda}{3 \mu}=\frac{2}{3}=a<1 \& \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{i=2}^{n} a^{i}=\frac{a^{2}}{1-a}$ it follows that

$$
P_{0}\left[1+\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\sum_{i=2}^{\infty} \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda / \mu}{3}\right)^{i}\right]=P_{0}\left[1+\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\frac{3(\lambda / \mu)^{2}}{2(3-\lambda / \mu)}\right]=1
$$

and thus,

$$
P_{0}=\frac{2(3-\lambda / \mu)}{6+4 \lambda / \mu+(\lambda / \mu)^{2}}
$$

The size of the memory $n$ can now be determined from

$$
\frac{2(3-\lambda / \mu)}{6+4 \lambda / \mu+(\lambda / \mu)^{2}}\left[1+\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\sum_{i=2}^{n-1} \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda / \mu}{3}\right)^{i}\right] \geq \gamma
$$

For $\lambda / \mu=2$ and $\gamma=0.95$, the smallest $n$ satisfying the above equation is $n=9\left(P_{0}=1 / 9\right.$, $\left.P_{1}=2 / 9, \quad P_{i}=2^{i-1} / 3^{i}\right.$ for $\left.i \geq 2\right)$, yielding $\left.P_{0}+P_{1}+\ldots+P_{8}=0.961\right)$.

As shown by Example A7.9, reliability applications of birth and death processes identify $v_{i}$ as failure rates and $\theta_{i}$ as repair rates. In this case

$$
v_{j} \ll \theta_{j+1}, \quad j=0, \ldots, n-1
$$

holds in practical applications, with $v_{j}$ and $\theta_{j+1}$ as in Fig. A7.9. Assuming

$$
\max \left\{v_{j} / \theta_{j+1}\right\}=r, \quad 0<r<1, \quad j=0, \ldots, n-1
$$

the following relationships for the steady-state probability $P_{j}$ can be obtained (Example A7.11)

$$
P_{j} \geq \frac{1-r}{r\left(1-r^{n-j}\right)} \sum_{i=j+1}^{n} P_{i}, \quad 0<r<1, \quad j=0, \ldots, n-1
$$

Thus, for $r \leq 1 / 2$, i. e. $2 v_{j} \leq \theta_{j+1}(j=0, \ldots, n-1)$, it follows that (Example A7.11)

$$
P_{j}>\sum_{i=j+1}^{n} P_{i}, \quad 2 v_{j} \leq \theta_{j+1}, \quad j=0, \ldots, n-1
$$

Equation (A7.157) states that for $2 v_{0} \leq \theta_{1}, \ldots, 2 v_{n-1} \leq \theta_{n}$, the steady-state probability in a state $Z_{j}$ of a birth and death process described by Fig. A7.9 is grater than the sum of steady-state probabilities in all states following $Z_{j}, j=0, \ldots, n-1$ [2.50(1992)]; property useful in developing approximate expressions for system availability (however, the condition $\max \left\{v_{j} / \theta_{j+1}\right\} \leq 1 / 2$, satisfied in all reliability applications, can be weakened for arbitrary birth and death processes).# Example A7.11 

Assuming Eq.(A7.155), prove Eqs. (A7.156) and (A7.157).

## Solution

Using Eq. (A7.151),

$$
\frac{\sum_{i=j+1}^{n} P_{i}}{P_{j}}=\frac{\sum_{i=j+1}^{n} \pi_{i}}{\pi_{j}}=\sum_{i=j+1}^{n} \frac{\pi_{i}}{\pi_{j}}=\frac{v_{j}}{\theta_{j+1}}+\frac{v_{j} v_{j+1}}{\theta_{j+1} \theta_{j+2}}+\ldots+\frac{v_{j} \cdots v_{n-1}}{\theta_{j+1} \cdots \theta_{n}}
$$

Setting $\max \left\{v_{i} / \theta_{i+1}\right\}=r$ for $0<r<1$ and $i=j, j+1, \ldots, n-1$, it follows that

$$
\sum_{i=j+1}^{n} P_{i} / P_{j} \leq r+r^{2}+\ldots+r^{n-j}=r\left(1-r^{n-j}\right) /(1-r)
$$

and then Eq. (A7.156). Furthermore, $0<r<1 \&(n-j) \in\{0,1, \ldots, n\}$ give $\left(1-r^{n-j}\right)<1$, and $r \leq 1 / 2$ leads to $r /(1-r) \leq 1$; thus, $r \leq 1 / 2$ yields $r\left(1-r^{n-j}\right) /(1-r)<1$ and Eq. (A7.157).

## A7.6 Semi-Markov Processes with a Finite Number of States

The striking description of Markov processes given in Appendix A7.5.2 (pp.501-02) allows a straightforward generalization to semi-Markov processes (SMP). In a semiMarkov process, the sequence of consecutively occurring states forms an embedded time-homogeneous Markov chain (as for Markov processes). The stay (sojourn) time in a given state $Z_{i}$ is a random variable $\tau_{i j}>0$ whose distribution depends on $Z_{i}$ and on the following state $Z_{j}$, but in contrast to time-homogeneous Markov processes it can be arbitrary (not exponential). Related to semi-Markov processes are Markov renewal processes $\left(\left\{N_{i}(t)=\right.\right.$ number of transitions to state $\left.Z_{i} \text { in }(0, t]\right\}$ [A7.23]).

To define semi-Markov processes, let $\xi_{0}, \xi_{1}, \ldots$ be the sequence of consecutively occurring states (sequence of random variables taking values in $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}$ ), and $\eta_{0}, \eta_{1}, \ldots$ stay times between consecutive states (sequence of random variables $>0$ ). A stochastic process $\xi(t)$ with state space $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}, 0<m<\infty$ is a semi-Markov process in continuous time $(t \geq 0)$ with a finite number of states, if for $n=0,1,2, \ldots$, arbitrary $i, j, i_{0}, \ldots, i_{n-1} \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$, and arbitrary $x, x_{0}, \ldots, x_{n-1}>0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \cap \eta_{n} \leq x\right) \mid\right. & \left(\xi_{n}=Z_{i} \cap \eta_{n-1}=x_{n-1} \cap \ldots \cap \xi_{1}=Z_{i_{1}} \cap \eta_{0}=x_{0} \cap \xi_{0}=Z_{i_{0}}\right)\} \\
& =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \cap \eta_{n} \leq x\right) \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\}=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)^{*)
\end{aligned}
$$

holds. $\xi(t)=\xi_{0}$ for $0 \leq t<\eta_{0}, \xi(t)=\xi_{n}$ for $\eta_{0}+\ldots+\eta_{n-1} \leq t<\eta_{0}+\ldots+\eta_{n}(n \geq 1)$ is a jump process, as shown in Fig. A7.10.
$Z_{j}$ is the next state to be visited after $Z_{i}$, and the semi-Markov transition probabilities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$, also known as one-step transition probabilities, are defined only for $j \neq i \quad\left(\mathrm{Q}_{i i}(x) \equiv 0\right)$.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{*}$ A semi-Markov process with states $Z_{0}, Z_{1} \& \mathcal{P}_{01}=\mathcal{P}_{10}=1$ is an alternating renewal process (p.523).

Figure A7.10 Possible realization for a semi-Markov process ( $x$ starts by 0 at each state change)

Setting, as refinement of pp. 500-02

$$
\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(\infty)=\mathcal{P}_{i j}, \quad j \neq i, \quad \mathcal{P}_{i i} \equiv 0
$$

and, for $\mathcal{P}_{i j}>0$,

$$
\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x) / \mathcal{P}_{i j}, \quad j \neq i, x>0, \mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

leads to

$$
\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)=\mathcal{P}_{i j} \mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x), \quad j \neq i, x>0, \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
$$

with (Example A7.2)

$$
\mathcal{P}_{i j}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+1}=Z_{j} \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\}=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(\infty), \quad \mathcal{P}_{i i} \equiv 0, n=0,1,2, \ldots, \sum_{j=0, j \neq i}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{i j}=1
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\eta_{n} \leq x \mid\left(\xi_{n}=Z_{i} \cap \xi_{n+1}=Z_{j}\right)\right\}, \quad \begin{aligned}
& j \neq i, n=0,1,2, \ldots, \\
& \mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathcal{P}_{i i}=0$ is mandatory for Markov processes with a finite number of states and for semi-Markov processes used in reliability analysis. However, $\mathcal{P}_{i i}>0$ must be accepted for a semi-Markov process embedded in a semi-regenerative process (see footnote on p. 526). The interpretation of the quantities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ given by Eqs. (A7.99) - (A7.101) on p. 502, is useful for practical applications (see pp. 222-23 and Eqs. (A7.182) - (A7.184a) on pp. 527-29); however, by assuming that for an SMP all $\tau_{i k}(k \neq j)$ not exponentially distributed are truncated (as per Eq. (A6.33a) with $a=0, b=\tau_{i j}$ ) at state change to $Z_{j}$, to make $Z_{j}$ a regeneration state as required by Eq. (A7.158). In fact, Eq. (A7.158) holds for any $j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$, and thus
all states of a semi-Markov process are regeneration states, implying that at each state change all "running times" must be exponentially distributed, see also the footnote on p. 386 (for time-homogeneous Markov processes, all running times are exponentially distributed at each $t \geq 0$ (pp.501-03)).The initial distribution, i. e. of the vector $\left(\xi_{0} \equiv \xi(0), \xi_{1}, \eta_{0}^{\circ}\right)$, is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{A}_{i j}^{\circ}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(0)=Z_{i} \cap \xi_{1}=Z_{j} \cap \text { residual sojourn time } \eta_{0}^{\circ} \text { in } Z_{i} \leq x\right\} \\
&=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\} \varphi_{i j} \mathrm{~F}_{i j}^{\circ}(x),
\end{aligned}
$$

with $p_{i j}$ as given by Eq. (A7.162) and $\mathrm{F}_{i j}^{\circ}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ residual sojourn time $\eta_{0}^{\circ}$ in $Z_{i} \leq x \mid$ $\left.\left(\xi(0)=Z_{i} \cap \xi_{1}=Z_{j}\right)\right\} ; \xi(0)$ is used here for clarity instead of $\xi_{0}$.

Considering that the semi-Markov process is memoryless only at the transition points from one state to the other, to have $t=0$ as a regeneration point, the initial condition $\xi(0)=Z_{i}$, sufficient for time-homogeneous Markov processes,
must be reinforced by $Z_{i}$ is entered at $t=0$.
The sequence $\xi_{0} \equiv \xi(0), \xi_{1}, \ldots$ is a Markov chain, embedded in the semi-Markov process, with transition probabilities $\varphi_{i j}$ and initial distribution $A_{i}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{0}=Z_{i}\right\}$, $i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$ (Eqs. (A7.162), (A7.72)). $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)$ is the conditional distribution function of the stay time in $Z_{i}$ with consequent jump to $Z_{j}\left(1-e^{-\varphi_{i} x}\right.$ for a Markov process).

A two state semi-Markov process is the alternating renewal process given in Appendix A7.3 $\left(Z_{0}=u p, Z_{1}=\right.$ down, $\left.\mathcal{P}_{01}=\mathcal{P}_{10}=1, \mathcal{P}_{00}=\mathcal{P}_{11}=0, \mathrm{~F}_{01}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)\right.$, $\mathrm{F}_{10}(x)=\mathrm{G}(x), \mathrm{F}_{0}^{\circ}(x)=\mathrm{F}_{A}(x), \mathrm{F}_{1}^{\circ}(x)=\mathrm{G}_{A}(x) \mathrm{P}_{0}(0)=p, \mathrm{P}_{1}(0)=1-p)$.

In many applications, the quantities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$, or $\mathcal{P}_{i j}$ and $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)$, can be calculated using Eqs. (A7.99) - (A7.101), as shown in Appendix A7.7 and Sections 6.3-6.6.

For the unconditional stay (sojourn) time in $Z_{i}$, the distribution function is

$$
\mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\eta_{n} \leq x \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\}=\sum_{j=0, j \neq i}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{i j} \mathrm{~F}_{i j}(x)=\sum_{j=0, j \neq i}^{m} \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)
$$

with $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ as per Eq. (A7.161) \& $\mathrm{Q}_{i}(\infty)=1$, and the mean

$$
T_{i}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(1-\mathrm{Q}_{i}(x)\right) d x<\infty
$$

For practical applications, one can assume the existence of

$$
\mathrm{q}_{i j}(x)=d \mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x) / d x
$$

Consider first the case in which the process enters the state $Z_{i}$ at $t=0$, i.e. that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t) \text { enter } Z_{i} \text { at } t=0\right\}=1 \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{F}_{i j}^{\circ}(x)=\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)
$$

The transition probabilities

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{j} \mid Z_{i} \text { is entered at } t=0\right\}
$$

can be obtained by generalizing Eq. (A7.120),

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)=\delta_{i j}\left(1-\mathrm{Q}_{i}(t)\right)+\sum_{k=0, k \neq i}^{m} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{q}_{i k}(x) \mathrm{P}_{k j}(t-x) d x, \quad t>0, \mathrm{P}_{i j}(0)=\delta_{i j}
$$

with $\delta_{i j} \& \mathrm{Q}_{i}(t)$ per Eqs. (A7.85) \& (A7.165). Note that in $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x), Z_{j}$ is the next state visited after $Z_{i}$, but this is not the case for $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$. The state probabilities follow as

$$
\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{j}\right\}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{Z_{i} \text { is entered at } t=0\right\} \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t), \quad t>0
$$with $\mathrm{P}_{j}(t) \geq 0, i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$, and $\mathrm{P}_{0}(t)+\ldots+\mathrm{P}_{m}(t)=1$. If the state space is divided into the complementary sets $U$ for the up states and $\bar{U}$ for the down states, as in Eq. (A7.107), the point availability follows from Eq. (A7.112)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t) \in U \mid Z_{i} \text { is enterd at } t=0\right\}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U} \mathrm{P}_{i j}(t), \quad \begin{aligned}
& i=0, \ldots, m<\infty, t>0 \\
& \mathrm{PA}_{S i}(0)=1 \text { for } Z_{i} \in U
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ per Eqs.(A7.168) \& (A7.169), see also the remark at the bottom of p. 511. The probability that the first transition from a state in $U$ to a state in $\bar{U}$ occurs after the time $t$, i. e. the reliability function, follows from Eq. (A7.122) as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(x) \in U \text { for } 0<x \leq t \mid Z_{i} \text { is entered at } t=0\right\} \\
& =1-\mathrm{Q}_{i}(t)+\sum_{Z_{j} \in U, j \neq i} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{q}_{i j}(x) \mathrm{R}_{S j}(t-x) d x, \quad Z_{i} \in U, t>0, \mathrm{R}_{S i}(0)=1
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\mathrm{Q}_{i}(t) \& \mathrm{q}_{i j}(x)$ per Eqs. (A7.165) \& (A7.167). The mean of the stay (sojourn) time in $U$, i. e. the system mean time to failure given $Z_{i}$ is entered at $t=0$ follows from Eq. (A7.172) as solution of ( $T_{i} \& \mathcal{P}_{i j}$ per Eqs. (A7.166) \& (A7.162))

$$
M T T F_{S i}=T_{i}+\sum_{Z_{j} \in U, j \neq i} \mathcal{P}_{i j} M T T F_{S j}, \quad Z_{i} \in U
$$

Calculation of the interval reliability is laborious, because the semi-Markov process is regenerative only at a state change, and a case-by-case evaluation is necessary. However considering Eq. (A7.180), $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{IR}_{S i}(t, t+\theta) \approx \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(\theta), \theta>0$, can often be used in practical applications.

Consider now the case of a stationary semi-Markov process. Under the assumption that the embedded Markov chain is irreducible (each state can be reached from every other state with probability $>0$ ), the semi-Markov process is stationary if and only if the initial distribution (Eq. (A7.164)) is given by [6.3, A7.22, A7.23, A7.28]

$$
\mathrm{A}_{i j}^{*}(x)=\frac{\mathcal{P}_{i} \mathcal{P}_{i j}}{\sum_{k=0}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{k} T_{k}} \int_{0}^{x}\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{i j}(y)\right) d y=\frac{P_{i} \mathcal{P}_{i j}}{T_{i}} \int_{0}^{x}\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{i j}(y)\right) d y
$$

In Eq. (A7.174), $\mathcal{P}_{i j}$ are the transition probabilities (Eq.(A7.162)) and $\mathcal{P}_{i}$ the stationary distribution of the embedded Markov chain; $\mathcal{P}_{i}$ are the unique solutions of

$$
\mathcal{P}_{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{i} \mathcal{P}_{i j}, \quad \text { with } \mathcal{P}_{i i} \equiv 0, \mathcal{P}_{i j}=\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(\infty), \mathcal{P}_{j}>0, \sum_{j=0}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{j}=1, j=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

The system given by Eq. (A7.175) must be solved by replacing one (arbitrarily chosen) equation by $\Sigma \mathcal{P}_{i}=1$. It differs from that of Eq. (A7.74) because of $\mathcal{P}_{i i} \equiv 0$. For the stationary semi-Markov process (with irreducible embedded Markov chain), the state probabilities are independent of time and given by [6.3, A7.22, A7.23, A7.28]

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i}(t)=P_{i}=T_{i} / T_{i i}=\mathcal{P}_{i} T_{i} \int_{k=0}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{k} T_{k}, \quad t \geq 0, T_{i}<\infty, i=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$with $T_{i}$ per Eq. (A7.166) and $\mathcal{P}_{i}$ from Eq. (A7.175). $P_{i}$ per Eq. (A7.176) and $\mathrm{A}_{i j}^{\circ}(x)$ per Eq. (A7.174) are thus the initial conditions at $t=0 . \quad T_{i i}$ is the mean time between two consecutive occurrences of the state $Z_{i}$ (in steady-state). These time points form a stationary renewal process with renewal density

$$
h_{i}(t)=h_{i}=1 / T_{i i}=\mathcal{P}_{i} / \sum_{k=0}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{k} T_{k}, \quad t \geq 0, i=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

$h_{i}$ is the frequency of consecutive occurrences of state $Z_{i}$. In Eq. (A7.176), $P_{i}$ can be heuristically interpreted as $P_{i}=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}\left\{\left(t / T_{i i}\right) T_{i}\right\} / t=T_{i} / T_{i i}$ or as ratio of the mean time in which the embedded Markov chain is in state $Z_{i}$ to the mean time in all states $P_{i}=\mathcal{P}_{i} T_{i} / \sum \mathcal{P}_{k} T_{k}$. Similar is for $\mathrm{A}_{i j}^{\circ}(x)$ in Eqs. (A7.174), considering also Eq. (A7.35). The stationary (asymptotic and steady-state) value of the point availability $P A_{S}$ and average availability $A A_{S}$ follows from Eq. (A7.176) as

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in U} P_{i}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in U} \mathcal{P}_{i} T_{i} / \sum_{k=0}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{k} T_{k}
$$

Similarly as Markov processes, the system mean up time, mean down time, and failure \& repair frequencies are given by (Eqs.(A7.141)-(A7.146),(A7.103),(A7.181))

$$
M U T_{S}=\frac{P A_{S}}{f_{u d S}}, \quad M D T_{S}=\frac{\left(1-P A_{S}\right)}{P A_{S}} M U T_{S}, \quad f_{u d S}=f_{d u S}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in U, Z_{i} \in \bar{U}} P_{i} \mathcal{P}_{j i} / T_{j}
$$

For any $i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m<\infty\}$, an irreducible embedded Markov chain and finite sojourn times are sufficient for the existence of [6.3, A7.22, A7.23, A7.28]

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{i}(t)=Z_{i} \cap \text { next transition in } Z_{j} \cap \text { residual sojourn time in } Z_{i} \leq x\right\} \\
& =\frac{P_{i} \mathcal{P}_{i j}}{T_{i}} \int_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{i j}(y)\right) d y=\frac{\mathcal{P}_{i} \mathcal{P}_{i j}}{\sum_{k=0}^{m} \mathcal{P}_{k} T_{k}} \int_{0}^{3}\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{i j}(y)\right) d y=\mathrm{A}_{i j}^{\circ}(x) \\
& \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{i}(t)=Z_{i}\right\}=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{P}_{i i}(t)=P_{i}=\frac{T_{i}}{T_{i i}}, \text { and } \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S i}(t)=P A_{S}=\sum_{Z_{i} \in U} P_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

Except for investigations on the reliability function (see footnote on p.513), an irreducible embedded Markov chain can be assumed in reliability applications. For such cases, according to Eqs. (A7.176) and (A7.180),
asymptotic \& steady-state can be used for stationary (see e.g. also pp. 187, 488, 493, 495 \& 514 as well as p.530).

For the alternating renewal process (Fig. A7.3, $Z_{0}=u p, Z_{1}=$ down) it holds that $\mathcal{P}_{00}=\mathcal{P}_{11}=0, \mathcal{P}_{10}=\mathcal{P}_{01}=1 \rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{0}=\mathcal{P}_{1}=1 / 2$ (embedded Markov chain), $T_{0}=M T T F$, $T_{1}=M T T R, T_{00}=T_{11}=T_{0}+T_{1}$, and Eqs. (A7.176) leads to $P_{0}=M T T F /(M T T F+M T T R)$;
this example shows best the basic difference between $\mathcal{P}_{i}$ as stationary distribution of the embedded Markov chain and the limiting state probability $P_{i}$ in state $Z_{i}$ of the original process (roughly stated, $P_{i}$ is related to stay time in $Z_{i}, \mathcal{P}_{i}$ to state changes to $Z_{i}$, see e.g. discussion to Eq. (A7.188)).For a stationary time-homogeneous Markov process (Appendix A7.5.3.3), Eqs. (A7.166), (A7.165), (A7.102) \& (A7.177), (A7.176) \& (A7.103), (A7.104), (A7.174) yield (for $i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m<\infty\}$ )

$$
T_{i}=1 / \rho_{i}, \quad h_{i}(t)=h_{i}=1 / T_{i i}=P_{i} \rho_{i}, \quad \mathrm{~A}_{i j}^{\mathrm{o}}(x)=\left(1-e^{-\rho_{i} x}\right) P_{i} \rho_{i j} / \rho_{i}
$$

# A7.7 Semi-regenerative Processes with a Finite Number of States 

As pointed out in Appendix A7.5.2, the time behavior of a repairable system can be described by a time-homogeneous Markov process
if all involved random times (failure-free, repair, or other) are exponentially distributed (constant rates during the stay time in each state, with possible stepwise change at a state transition, e.g. for load sharing).

Except for Erlang distributions (p. 461), non exponentially distributed failure-free and/or repair times lead in some few cases to semi-Markov processes (Sections 6.2, $6.3 .2,6.3 .3,6.8 .4,6.10,6.11$ ), but in general to processes with only few regeneration states (Figs. 6.10, A7.11-A7.13) or to nonregenerative processes (Tab.6.1 on p.171).

Example A7.12 (Fig. A7.11) shows the case of a process with states $Z_{0}, Z_{1}, Z_{2}$ in which only states $Z_{0}$ and $Z_{1}$ are regeneration states. $Z_{0} \& Z_{1}$ form a semi-Markov process embedded in the original process, on which investigations can be based;
processes with an embedded semi-Markov process ( $\geq 2$ states) with irreducible Markov chain are called in this book semi-regenerative processes.

Their investigation can become time-consuming and has to be performed on a case-by-case basis, often using a time schedule. ${ }^{+)}$

## Example A7.12

Consider a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy as in Fig. A7.4a with constant failure rates $\lambda$ in operating $\& \lambda_{r}$ in reserve state, arbitrarily distributed repair time ( $>0$, density $\mathrm{g}(x), \mathrm{g}(0)=0$ ), and only one repair crew. Give the transition probabilities for the embedded semi-Markov process.

## Solution

As Fig. A7.11a shows, only states $Z_{0}$ and $Z_{1}$ are regeneration states. $Z_{2}$ is not a regeneration state because at transition points in $Z_{2}$ a repair with arbitrarily distributed repair time is running. Thus, the process involved is not a semi-Markov process. However, states $Z_{0}$ and $Z_{1}$ form an

Figs. A7.11-A7.13, 6.10, 6.14 \& 6.16 give examples as how to operate.

Figure A7.11 a) Possible time schedule for a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with constant failure rates $\left(\lambda, \lambda_{r}\right)$, arbitrarily distributed repair time $(>0$, density $\mathrm{g}(x), \mathrm{g}(0)=0)$, one repair crew, and ideal failure detection \& switch (repair times greatly exaggerated); b) State transitions diagram for the embedded semi-Markov process with states $Z_{0} \& Z_{1}$ (regeneration states) ( $\mathrm{Q}_{12}^{-}$is not a semiMarkov transition probability, and during a transition $Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2} \rightarrow Z_{1}$ the embedded Markov chain (on $Z_{0}, Z_{1}$ ) remains in $Z_{1} ; Z_{2}$ down state (absorbing for reliability calculation); holds also for a k-out-of-n warm redundancy with $n-k=1$ and no further failures at system down, see p. 219 for $n=3$ )
embedded semi-Markov process on which investigations can be based. The transition probabilities of the embedded semi-Markov process (on $Z_{0}, Z_{1}$ ) are (Fig. A7.11, Eqs. (A7.99)-(A7.101))

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Q}_{01}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{0}(x)=1-e^{-\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right) x}, \quad \mathrm{Q}_{121}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~g}(y)\left(1-e^{-\lambda y}\right) d y \\
& \mathrm{Q}_{10}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \mathrm{~g}(y) e^{-\lambda y} d y=\mathrm{G}(x) e^{-\lambda x}+\int_{0}^{x} \lambda e^{-\lambda y} \mathrm{G}(y) d y
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{Q}_{121}(x)$ is used to calculate the point availability (Eqs. (6.106), (6.109)). It accounts for the transitions throughout the nonregeneration down state $Z_{2}$. During a transition $Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2} \rightarrow Z_{1}$, the embedded Markov chain remains in $Z_{1}$ (Fig. A7.11a, footnote on p.526), and for the embedded Markov chain it holds that $\mathcal{P}_{00}=0, \mathcal{P}_{01}=1, \mathcal{P}_{10}=\widehat{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda), \mathcal{P}_{11}=1-\widehat{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ with $\widehat{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{\lambda} \mathrm{g}(x) e^{-\lambda x} d x$ $=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{\text {failure-free }}>\tau_{\text {repair }}\right\}$. This is important to calculate $\mathrm{Q}_{1}(x)$, see below. $\mathrm{Q}_{12}^{-}(x)$ is not a semi-Markov transition probability; however, $\mathrm{Q}_{12}^{-}(x)$, expressed as (Fig. A7.11a)

$$
\mathrm{Q}_{12}^{-}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \lambda e^{-\lambda y}(1-\mathrm{G}(y)) d y=1-e^{-\lambda x}-\int_{0}^{x} \lambda e^{-\lambda y} \mathrm{G}(y) d y
$$

yields

$$
\mathrm{Q}_{1}(x)=\mathrm{Q}_{10}(x)+\mathrm{Q}_{12}^{-}(x)=1-(1-\mathrm{G}(x)) e^{-\lambda x}
$$

Supplementary results: Section 6.4.2 investigates reliability \& availability. $k \lambda$ instead of $\lambda$ in Eqs. (A7.182), (A7.182a) yields results for a $k$-out-of-n warm redundancy with $n-k=1$, one repair crew, and no further failure at system down.

As a second example, let's assume that for the 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy of Fig. A7.11, a travel time $(>0$, density $\mathrm{w}(x), \mathrm{w}(0)=0)$ must be considered before a repair for a failure in state $Z_{0}$ can be made Figure A7.12 gives a possible time schedule and the state transitions diagram of the involved semi-regenerative process. States $Z_{0}, Z_{1}, Z_{1}$, are regeneration states, and constitute an embedded 3 states semi-Markov process. $Z_{2}$ is not a regeneration state. The transition probabilities of the embedded semi-Markov process are (Fig. A7.12, Eqs. (A7.99) - (A7.101))

$$

Approximations use Eq. (6.113).Following considerations on semi-regenerative processes refine those given in Appendix A7.4 for general regenerative processes. A pure jump process $\xi(t), t \geq 0$, with state space $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}$ is semi-regenerative, with regeneration states $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{k}$, $(0<k<m<\infty)$, if the following holds: Let $\zeta_{0}, \zeta_{1}, \ldots$ be the sequence of consecutively occurring regeneration states and $\varphi_{0}, \varphi_{1}, \ldots$ the random time intervals between consecutive occurrence of regeneration states, assumed continuous, $>0$ with finite mean. Then, Eq. (A7.158) with $\zeta_{n}, \varphi_{n}$ instead of $\xi_{n}, \eta_{n}$ must be fulfilled; in other words,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \zeta(t) \text { as given by } \zeta(t)=\zeta_{0} \text { for } 0 \leq t<\varphi_{0} \text { and } \zeta(t)=\zeta_{n} \text { for } \varphi_{0}+\ldots+\varphi_{n-1} \leq t \\
& <\varphi_{0}+\ldots+\varphi_{n}, n \geq 1, \text { is a semi Markov process with state space } Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{k} \text { embedded in the original process } \xi(t) \text { with state space } Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m} \quad(0<k<m)
\end{aligned}
$$

The piece $\xi(t), \varphi_{0}+\ldots+\varphi_{n-1} \leq t<\varphi_{0}+\ldots+\varphi_{n}, n \geq 1$, of the original process is a cycle (p. 494). Its distribution depends on the regeneration state involved. The epochs at which a state $Z_{i}, 0 \leq i \leq k$, occurs are regeneration points and form a renewal process, belonging to $Z_{i}$, embedded in $\xi(t)$ (see e.g. Fig. A7.3 on p. 491 for a basic situation).

In reliability applications, the set of regeneration states is in general a subset of the system up states. The procedure used to develop Eqs. (A7.182)-(A7.184a) can help to find the transition probabilities involved (see also footnote on p. 526).

An irreducible embedded Markov chain (p. 497) on $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{k}$, continuous $\mathrm{F}_{i j}(x)$, $x>0, i, j \in\{0, \ldots, k\} \&$ finite mean cycle lengths for the embedded semi-Markov process are sufficient for the existence of limiting state probabilities $P_{e}[$ A7.9, A7.24, 6.3]

$$
P_{e}=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{e}\right\}, \quad e=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

Denoting by $T_{i}<\infty$ the mean stay time in state $Z_{i}, i=0, \ldots, k$, and by $T_{i i}<\infty$ the mean time between two consecutive occurrences of $Z_{i}$, it holds that

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}=P_{i}=T_{i} / T_{i i}, \quad i=0, \ldots, k
$$

Consecutive cycles of same type are possible, yielding transitions to a same state for the embedded Markov chain if the cycle contains only nonregeneration states (e.g. $Z_{1} \rightarrow Z_{2} \rightarrow Z_{1}$ in Fig. A7.11a). However, as for Markov and semi-Markov processes, an irreducible embedded Markov chain cannot be assumed for investigations on the reliability function (see footnotes on pp. 513, 526).

For the 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy of Fig. A7.11 it holds for the embedded Markov chain $\mathcal{P}_{00}=0, \mathcal{P}_{01}=1, \mathcal{P}_{10}=\mathrm{Q}_{10}(\infty)=\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda), \mathcal{P}_{11}=1-\mathcal{P}_{10}=1-\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$, and thus $\mathcal{P}_{1}=1 /(1+\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)) \geqq 1 / 2 \& \mathcal{P}_{0}=1-\mathcal{P}_{1}=\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda) /(1+\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)) \leqq 1 / 2 ;$ furthermore, $T_{0}=1 /\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)$, $T_{1}=(1-\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)) / \lambda, T_{00}=1 /\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+M T T R / \widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda) \& T_{11}=M T T R+\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda) /\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)$ yields (Eq. (A7.188)) $P_{0}=T_{0} / T_{00}, P_{1}=T_{1} / T_{11}$, and $P A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}$ as per Eq. (6.110) [ $T_{0} \& T_{1}$ follow from Eq.(A7.166) with $\mathrm{Q}_{0}(x), \mathrm{Q}_{1}(x)$ per Eqs.(A7.182), (A7.182a); $T_{00} \& T_{11}$ are obtained from Fig. A7.11a considering $T_{11}=\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)\left(M T T R+1 /\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\right)+(1-\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)) M T T R, T_{00}=$ $\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)\left(M T T R+1 /\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\right)+(1-\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)) \widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)\left(2 M T T R+1 /\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\right)+(1-\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda))^{2} \widetilde{\mathrm{~g}}(\lambda)\left(3 M T T R+1 /\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\right)+\ldots$, $1+2 x+3 x^{2}+\ldots=1 /(1-x)^{2} ; \widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{\infty} \widetilde{\mathrm{g}}(x) e^{-\lambda x} d x=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{\mathrm{op}}=\tau_{\mathrm{rep}}\right\} ;$ use of Eq. (A7.176) right not allowed].# A7.8 Nonregenerative Stochastic Processes with a Countable Number of States 

The assumption of arbitrarily (non exponentially) distributed failure-free and repair (restoration) times for the elements of a system, already leads to nonregenerative stochastic processes for simple series or parallel structures. After some general considerations, nonregenerative processes used in reliability analysis are introduced.

## A7.8.1 General Considerations

Solutions for nonregenerative stochastic processes are often problem-oriented. However, as a possible general method, transformation of the given stochastic process into a Markov or a semi-Markov process by a suitable state space extension can be used in some cases by one of the following ways:

1. Approximation of distribution functions: Approximating the involved distribution functions (for repair and/or failure-free times) by an Erlang distribution allows a transformation of the original process into a time-homogeneous Markov process through introduction of additional states (pp.193-95).
2. Introduction of supplementary variables: Introducing for each element of a system as supplementary variables the failure-free time since the last repair and the repair time since the last failure, the original process can be transformed into a Markov process with state space consisting of discrete and continuous parameters. Investigations usually lead to partial differential equations which have to be solved with corresponding boundary conditions.
The first method is best used when repair and/or failure rates are monotonically increasing from zero to a final value, its application is easy to understand (Fig. 6.6). The second method is general [A7.4 (1955)], but often time-consuming.

A further method is based on the general concept of point process. Considering the sequence of jump times $\tau_{n}^{+}$and states $\xi_{n}$ entered at these points, an equivalent description of the process $\xi(t)$ is obtained by a marked point process $\left(\tau_{n}^{+}, \xi_{n}\right)$, $n=0,1, \ldots$. Analysis of the system's steady-state behavior follows using Korolyuk's theorem $\operatorname{Pr}\left[\right.$ jump into $Z_{i}$ during $\left.(t, t+\delta t]\right]=\lambda_{i}^{h} \delta t+o(\delta t)$, with $\lambda_{i}^{h}=E[$ number of jumps in $Z_{i}$ during the unit time interval], see e.g.[A7.11, A7.12]. As an example, consider a repairable coherent system with $n$ totally independent elements, p.61. Let $\zeta_{i}(t), \ldots, \zeta_{n}(t)$ and $\zeta(t)$ be the binary processes with states 0 (down) \& $1(u p)$ describing elements and system, respectively. If the steady-state point availability of each element

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{PA}_{i}(t)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\zeta_{i}(t)=1\right\}=P A_{i}=\frac{M T T F_{i}}{M T T F_{i}+M T T R_{i}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

exists, then the steady-state point availability of the system (assumed coherent, p. 58) is given by Eq. (2.48) and can be expressed as (see e. g. [6.3, A7.10])$$
P A_{S}=M T T F /(M T T F+M T T R)
$$

( $M T T F \equiv M U T_{S}$ and $M T T R \equiv M D T_{S}$ for systems described by Markov \& semi-Markov processes, pp. $516 \& 525$ ). However, investigation of the time behavior of systems with arbitrary failure and/or repair rates can become time-consuming. In these cases, approximate expressions (Sections 6.7, 6.9.7) or Monte Carlo simulations (Section 6.9.6.2) can help to get results.

# A7.8.2 Nonhomogeneous Poisson Processes (NHPP) 

A nonhomogeneous Poisson process is a point process with independent Poisson distributed increments; i. e. a sequence of points on the time axis, whose count function $v(t)$ has independent increments (in nonoverlapping intervals) and satisfy

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t)=k\}=\frac{(\mathrm{M}(t))^{k}}{k!} e^{-\mathrm{M}(t)}, \quad t>0, k=0,1, \ldots, v(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

$v(t)$, assumed right continuous with unit jumps (Fig. A7.1 on p.480), gives the number of events in $(0, t] . \mathrm{M}(t)$ is the mean of $v(t)$, called mean value function,

$$
\mathrm{M}(t)=\mathrm{E}[v(t)], \quad t>0, \mathrm{M}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

and it holds that (Eqs. (A6.127) \& (A6.128), Example A6.21)

$$
\operatorname{Var}[v(t)]=\mathrm{E}[v(t)]=\mathrm{M}(t), \quad t>0, \mathrm{M}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

$\mathrm{M}(t)$ is a nondecreasing, continuous function with $\mathrm{M}(t)=0$ for $t \leq 0$, often assumed strictly increasing, unbounded, and absolutely continuous. If

$$
\mathrm{m}(t)=d \mathrm{M}(t) / d t \geq 0, \quad t>0, \mathrm{~m}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

exists, $\mathrm{m}(t)$ is the intensity of the NHPP. Eqs. (A7.193) and (A7.191) yield

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t+\delta t)-v(t)=1\}=\mathrm{m}(t) \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t), \quad t>0, \delta t \downarrow 0
$$

and no distinction is made between arrival rate and intensity. Equation (A7.194) gives the unconditional probability for one event (e. g. failure) in $(t, t+\delta t] . \mathrm{m}(t)$ corresponds to the renewal density $\mathrm{h}(t)$ (Eq. (A7.24)) but differs basically from the failure rate $\lambda(t)$, see remark on pp. 390-91. Equation (A7.194) also shows that an NHPP is locally without aftereffect. This holds globally (Eq.(A7.195)) and characterizes the NHPP. However, memoryless, i. e. with independent and stationary increments, is only the homogeneous Poisson process (HPP), for which $\mathrm{M}(t)=\lambda t$ holds.

Nonhomogeneous Poisson processes have been greatly investigated in the literature, see e.g. [6.3, A7.3, A7.12, A7.21, A7.25, A7.30, A8.1]. This appendix introduces some important results useful for reliability analysis. These results hold for HPPs $(\mathrm{M}(t)=\lambda t)$ as well, and most of them are a direct consequence of the independent increments property. In particular, the number of events in a time interval $(a, b]$$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { events in }(a, b] \mid H_{\mathrm{a}}\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { events in }(a, b]\}=\frac{(\mathrm{M}(b)-\mathrm{M}(a))^{k}}{k!} e^{-(\mathrm{M}(b)-\mathrm{M}(a))}, \\
k=0,1, \ldots, a \leq 0<b,
\end{aligned}
$$

and the rest waiting time $\tau_{R}(t)$ from an arbitrary $t>0$ to the next event

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R}(t)\right. & \left.>x \mid H_{t}\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { no event in }(t, t+x] \mid H_{t}\} \\
& =\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { no event in }(t, t+x]\}=e^{-(\mathrm{M}(t+x)-\mathrm{M}(t))}, \quad t, x>0, \mathrm{M}(0)=0,
\end{aligned}
$$

are independent of the process development up to time $t$ (history $H_{a}$ or $H_{t}$ ); i. e. the Poisson process is a process without aftereffect (memoryless if homogeneous). The mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{R}(t)\right]$ is thus also independent of the process development up to time $t$

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{R}(t)\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(\mathrm{M}(t+x)-\mathrm{M}(t))} d x
$$

Let now $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\tau_{2}^{*}<\ldots$ be the occurrence times (arrival times) of the event considered (e.g. failures of a repairable system with negligible repair times), measured from $t=\tau_{0}^{*}=0$ and taking values $0<t_{1}^{*}<t_{2}^{*}<\ldots$. * Furthermore, let $\eta_{n}=\tau_{n}^{*}-\tau_{n-1}^{*}$ be the $n$th interarrival time $(n \geq 1)$. Considering $\mathrm{M}(0)=0$, and assuming $\mathrm{M}(t)$ derivable, strictly increasing $(\mathrm{m}(t)>0)$, and unbounded $(\mathrm{M}(\infty)=\infty)$, the following holds:

1. The occurrence times (arrival times) $\tau_{1}^{*}, \tau_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ have joint density

$$
\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right) e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{i-1}^{*}\right)\right)}=e^{-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right), t_{0}^{*}=0<t_{1}^{*}<\ldots<t_{n}^{*}
$$

(follows from Eqs. (A7.194) \& (A7.195)), and marginal distribution function

$$
\mathrm{F}_{i}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i}^{*} \leq t_{i}^{*}\right\}=1-\sum_{k=0}^{i-1} \frac{\mathrm{M}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)}=\int_{0}^{\mathrm{M}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)} \frac{x^{i-1}}{(i-1)!} e^{-x} d x, \quad i=1,2, \ldots
$$

with density $\mathrm{f}_{i}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)=\mathrm{m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right) \mathrm{M}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)^{i-1} e^{-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)} /(i-1)!\&$ mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}^{*}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mathrm{f}_{i}(x) d x$ (events $\left\{\tau_{i}^{*} \leq t_{i}^{*}\right\}$ and $\left\{\right.$ at least $i$ events have occurred in $\left.\left(0, t_{i}^{*}\right]\right\}$ are equivalent).
2. The quantities

$$
\psi_{1}^{*}=\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{1}^{*}\right)<\psi_{2}^{*}=\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{2}^{*}\right)<\ldots
$$

are the occurrence times in an HPP with intensity one $(\mathrm{M}(t)=t)$ (follows from $\left.\mathrm{V}_{\psi^{*}}(\mathrm{M}(t))=\mathrm{V}_{\tau^{*}}(t) \rightarrow \mathrm{V}_{\psi^{*}}(t)=\mathrm{v}_{\tau^{*}}\left(\mathrm{M}^{-1}(t)\right) \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{V}_{\psi^{*}}(t)\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{\tau^{*}}\left(\mathrm{M}^{-1}(t)\right)\right]=\mathrm{M}\left(\mathrm{M}^{-1}(t)\right)=t\right)$.
3. The conditional distribution functions of $\eta_{n+1} \& \tau_{n+1}^{*}$ given $\eta_{1}=x_{1}, \ldots, \eta_{n}=x_{n}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\eta_{n+1} \leq x \mid \eta_{1}=x_{1}, \ldots, \eta_{n}=x_{n}\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\eta_{n+1} \leq x \mid x_{1}+\ldots+x_{n}=t_{n}^{*}\right\} \\
& =1-e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}+x\right)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right)\right)}=1-e^{-\int_{t_{n}^{*} m}^{t_{n}^{*}+x} m(y) d y}=1-\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { no event in }\left(t_{n}^{*}, t_{n}^{*}+x\right]\right\},
\end{aligned}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    *) * is used to explicitly show that $t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ are points on the time axis and not independent observations of a random variable $\tau$ (e. g. as in Figs. 1.1, 7.12, 7.14); see also footnote on p. 542.and

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{n+1}^{*} \leq t \mid x_{1}+\ldots+x_{n}=t_{n}^{*}\right\}=1-e^{-(\mathrm{M}(t)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right))}, \quad n \geq 1, t>t_{n}^{*}
$$

(both follow directly from Eq. (A7.196)).
4. For given (fixed) $t=T$ and $v(T)=n$ (time censoring), the joint density of the occurrence times $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T$ under the condition $v(T)=n$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*} \mid n\right)=n!\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T), \quad 0<t_{1}^{*}<\ldots<t_{n}^{*}<T, n=1,2, \ldots
$$

(see Eq. (A7.210)), and that of $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T \cap \mathrm{v}(T)=n$ is

$$
\begin{array}{r}
\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*}, n\right)=\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*} \mid n\right) \frac{\mathrm{M}(T)^{n} e^{-\mathrm{M}(T)}}{n!}=e^{-\mathrm{M}(T)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right) \\
0<t_{1}^{*}<\ldots<t_{n}^{*}<T, n=1,2, \ldots
\end{array}
$$

(follows from Eqs. (A7.203) and (A7.190)). From Eq. (A7.203) one recognizes that for given (fixed) $t=T$ and $v(T)=n$, the occurrence times $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T$ have the same distribution as if they where the order statistic of $n$ independent identically distributed random variables with density

$$
\mathrm{m}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T), \quad 0<t<T
$$

\& distribution function $\mathrm{M}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T)$ on $(0, T)$ (compare Eqs.(A7.210), (A7.211)).
5. Furthermore, for given (fixed) $t=T$ and $v(T)=n$, the quantities

$$
0<\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{1}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)<\ldots<\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{n}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)<1
$$

have the same distribution as if they where the order statistic of $n$ independent identically distributed random variables uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$ (follows from Point 2 above (Eqs. (A7.200) \& (A7.213))). For failure censoring (test stopped at $t_{n}^{*}$ ), Eqs. (A7.203) - (A7.206) and (A7.210)-(A7.213) hold, taking $T=t_{n}^{*}-0$ and multiplying over $n-1$ instead of $n$.
