6. The quantity

$$
(v(t)-\mathrm{M}(t)) / \sqrt{\mathrm{M}(t)}
$$

has for $t \rightarrow \infty$ a standard normal distribution (follows form the central limit theorem for renewal processes (Eq. (A7.34)) and Eqs. (A7.191) \& (A7.192)).
7. The sum of $n$ independent NHPPs with mean value function $\mathrm{M}_{i}(t)$ and intensity $\mathrm{m}_{i}(t)$ is an NHPP with mean value function and intensity

$$
\mathrm{M}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{M}_{i}(t) \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{m}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i}(t), \quad \mathrm{M}_{i}(t)=\mathrm{m}_{i}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

respectively (follows from the independent increments property of NHPPs and Eq. (A7.190), see Eq. (7.27) for HPPs).From the above properties, the following conclusions can be drawn:

1. For $i=1$, Eqs. (A7.199) \& (A7.193) yield

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}^{*} \leq t\right\}=1-e^{-\mathrm{M}(t)}=1-e^{-\int_{0}^{t_{1}} \mathrm{~m}(x) d x}
$$

thus, comparing Eqs. (A7.209) \& (A6.26) it follows that
the intensity of an NHPP is equal to the failure rate of the first occurrence time $\eta_{1}=\tau_{1}^{*}$.
2. Moreover, Eqs. (A7.201) \& (A6.26) show that the failure rate referred to the interarrival time $\eta_{n+1}=\tau_{n+1}^{*}-\tau_{n}^{*}$ given $\tau_{n}^{*}=t_{n}^{*}$ is independent of the process development up to $t_{n}^{*}$ and is equal to the failure rate at time $t_{n}^{*}+x$ referred to the first interarrival time $\eta_{1}$ or arrival time $\tau_{1}^{\prime}\left(\eta_{1}=\tau_{1}^{\prime}\right)$; i.e. for $n \geq 1, \lambda_{\eta_{n+1}}\left(x \mid t_{n}^{*}\right)=$ $\mathrm{m}\left(t_{n}^{*}+x\right)=\lambda_{\eta_{1}}\left(t_{n}^{*}+x\right)$ as per Eqs. (A6.27) \& (A6.28). This leads to the concept of as-bad-as-old, used in some considerations on repairable systems subjected

# Example A7.13 

Show that for given (fixed) $T$ and $v(T)=n$, the occurrence times $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T$ in a non homogeneous Poisson Process with intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)$ have the same joint density as the order statistic of $n$ independent identically distributed random variables with density $\mathrm{m}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T)$ on $(0, T)$.

## Solution

For an NHPP with intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)$, the occurrence times $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T$ given $T$ (fixed) and $v(T)=n$ have joint density (Eqs. (A7.190), (A7.194) \& (A7.195))

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*} \mid n\right)=\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*}, n\right) /\left(\mathrm{M}(T)^{n} e^{-\mathrm{M}(T)} / n!\right)=\mathrm{m}\left(t_{1}^{*}\right) e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}\left(t_{1}^{*}\right)\right.} \mathrm{m}\left(t_{2}^{*}\right) e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}\left(t_{2}^{*}\right)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{1}^{*}\right)\right)} \ldots \\
& \mathrm{m}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right) e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n-1}^{*}\right)\right)} e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}(T)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right)\right)} /\left(\mathrm{M}(T)^{n} e^{-\mathrm{M}(T)} / n!\right)=n!\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

which prove Eq. (A7.203). On the other hand, considering that for a set of $n$ realizations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of a given random variable $\tau$ there are $n$ ! permutations giving the same order statistic $t_{(1)}, \ldots, t_{(n)}$, the joint density of the order statistic of $n$ independent identically distributed random variables with density $\mathrm{m}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T)$ on $(0, T)$ is given by (Eq. (A6.57), remark on p. 542)

$$
\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)=n!\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)\right) \quad \text { on }(0, T)
$$

Supplementary results: For a homogeneous Poison Process, Eqs. (A7.42) \& (A7.210) yield

$$
\mathrm{m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)=1 / T \& \mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots, t_{n}^{*} \mid n\right)=n!/ T^{n} \text { on }(0, T)
$$

Furthermore, considering $\tau_{i}^{*} / T$, Eq. (A7.211) and point viii in Example A6.18 on p. $464\left(C=1 / T\right.$ applied to $\left.\mathrm{m}\left(t_{i}\right)\right)$ it follows that

$$
T \cdot \mathrm{~m}(T \cdot t) / \mathrm{M}(T)=T \cdot \lambda / \lambda T=1 \& \mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)=n!\text { on }(0,1)
$$

(same with Eq. (A7.210)). Thus, for given (fixed) $T$ and $v(T)=n$, arrival times $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T$ of an HPP have the same distribution as if they where the order statistic of $n$ indep. identically uniformly distributed random variables on $(0, T)$; on $(0,1)$ for $0<\tau_{1}^{*} / T<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*} / T<1$.to minimal repair (only failed parts are restored to as-good-as-new, pp. 138-39). However, if the restored part has a time dependent failure rate, the system failure rate cannot, after repair, be the same as just before failure ( $\approx$ in (i) on p. 443).
3. From Eq. (A7.202), the distribution of the occurrence time $\tau_{n+1}^{*}$ depends only on $t_{n}^{*}$; thus, $\tau_{1}^{*}, \tau_{2}^{*} \ldots$ is a Markov sequence.
4. From Eq. (A7.198) one can obtain Eq.(A7.204) when considering that $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\right.$ no event in $\left.\left(t_{n}^{*}, T\right\}\right\}=e^{-(\mathrm{M}(T)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right))}$, and vice versa.
5. Equations (A7.198) and (A7.199) show that for an NHPP, occurrence (arrival) times are not independent; the same is for interarrival times, which are neither independent nor identically distributed.

Thus, the NHPP is not a regenerative process. On the other hand, the homogeneous Poisson processes (HPP) is a renewal process, with independent interarrival times distributed according to the same exponential distribution (Eq. (A7.38)) and independent Erlang (Gamma) distributed occurrence times (Eqs. (A7.39) \& (A6.102)). However, because of independent increments, the NHPP is without aftereffect (memoryless if HPP) and the sum of Poisson processes is a Poisson process, both in homogeneous and non-homogeneous case (Eq. (7.27)). Convergence of a point process to an NHPP or to an HPP is discussed in Appendices A7.8.3 and A7.8.5. Finally,
although appealing, the assumption of independent increments, mandatory for Poisson processes (HPP and NHPP), can limit the validity of models used in practical applications (Sections 4.6.2, 5.3.4, 7.6, 7.7).

Nevertheless, the properties given in Points 1-7 above (in particular Eqs. (A7.200) and (A7.206)) are useful for statistical tests on NHPPs, as well as for Monte Carlo simulations. Results for exponential distributions or for HPPs can be used and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test holds with $F_{0}(t)=M_{0}(t) / M_{0}(T) \& \tilde{F}_{n}(t)=v(t) / v(T)$. Equation (A7.205) is useful to generate realizations of an NHPP: generate $k$ for given $T$ and $\mathrm{M}(T)$ (Eqs. (A7.190), (6.306)) and then $k$ random variables with density $\mathrm{m}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T)$, the ordered values are $k$ occurrence times of the NHPP on $(0, T)$. Same is for a homogeneous Poisson process, using $\mathrm{m}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T)=1 / T$ (see p. 291)).

# A7.8.3 Superimposed Renewal Processes 

Consider a repairable series system with $n$ totally independent elements (pp. 52, 280) and assume that repair times are negligible and that after each repair (renewal) the repaired element is as-good-as-new. Let $M T T F_{i}$ be the mean time to failure of element $E_{i}$ and $M T T F_{S}$ that of the system. The flow of system failures is given by the superposition of $n$ independent renewal processes, each of them related to an element of the system. If $v_{S}(t)$ is the count function at system level giving the number of system failures in $(0, t]$ and $v_{i}(t)$ that of element $E_{i}$, it holds that for a system with elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$$$
v_{S}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} v_{i}(t), \quad t>0, v_{i}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

$v_{i}(t)$ is a random variable, distributed as per Eq. (A7.12). Thus, for the mean value function at system level $\mathrm{Z}_{S}(t)$ it follows that (Eqs. (A6.68) and (A7.15))

$$
Z_{S}(t)=\mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{S}(t)\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{i}(t)\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{H}_{i}(t), \quad t>0, \mathrm{Z}_{S}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

yielding for the failure intensity at system level $z_{S}(t)$ (Eq. (A7.18))

$$
z_{S}(t)=d \mathrm{Z}_{S}(t) / d t=\sum_{i=1}^{n} d \mathrm{H}_{i}(t) / d t=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~h}_{i}(t), \quad t>0, z_{S}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

In Eqs. (A7.215) and (A7.216), $\mathrm{H}_{i}(t)$ and $\mathrm{h}_{i}(t)$ are the renewal function and renewal density of the renewal process related to element $E_{i}$. However, the point process yielding $v_{S}(t)$ is not a renewal process. Simple results hold for homogeneous Poisson processes (HPP) only, whose sum is an HPP (Eq.(7.27)) and thus a renewal process. Also the sum of nonhomogeneous Poisson processes (NHPP) is an NHPP, but an NHPP is not a renewal process.

For independent renewal processes, it can be shown that :

1. The sum of $n$ independent stationary renewal processes is a stationary point process with intensity (Eq. (A7.216))

$$
\mathrm{z}_{S}(t)=z_{S}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} h_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{M T T F_{i}}, \quad t \geq 0
$$

and distribution of the forward recurrence time (Eqs. (A7.37) \& (A6.78)) given by $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R S}(t)>x\right\}=\prod_{i=1}^{n} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{R i}(t)>x\right\}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1-\int_{0}^{t}\left(1-F_{i}(y)\right) d y / M T T F_{i}\right), t \geq 0, x>0$.
2. For $t \rightarrow \infty, v_{S}(t)$ is normally distributed (Eqs. (A7.214), (A7.34), Example A6.17 on p. 463).
3. For $n \rightarrow \infty$, the sum of $n$ independent renewal processes with very low occurrence ( 1 occurrence of any type and $\geq 2$ occurrences of all types are unlikely) and for which $\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{v_{i}(t)-v_{i}(a)=1\right\}=\mathrm{M}(t)-\mathrm{M}(a)$ holds for any fixed $t$ and $a<t$, converge to an NHPP with $\mathrm{E}[V(t)]=\mathrm{M}(t)$ for $t>0$ (Grigelionis [A7.14], see e. g. also [A7.11, A7.12, A7.30]); furthermore, if all renewal densities $\mathrm{h}_{i}(t)$ are bounded at $t=+0$, the sum converge for $n \rightarrow \infty$ to an HPP [A7.14].
4. For $t \rightarrow \infty$ and $n \rightarrow \infty$, the sum of $n$ independent renewal processes with low occurrence (one occurrence of any type is unlikely) converge to an HPP with renewal density as per Eq. (A7.217) [A7.17], see also [A7.8, A7.12, A7.30].

# A7.8.4 Cumulative Processes 

Cumulative processes [A7.24 (1955), A7.4(1962)], also known as compound processes [A7.3, A6.7 (Vol.II), A7.21], are obtained when at the occurrence of each eventin a point process, a random variable is generated and the stochastic process given by the sum of these random variables is considered. The involved point process is often limited to a renewal process (including the homogeneous Poisson process (HPP), yielding a cumulative or compound Poisson process) or a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP). The generated random variable are independent, if not otherwise stated, and can have arbitrary distribution. Cumulative processes can be used to model some practical situations; for instance, the total maintenance cost for a repairable system over a given period of time or the cumulative damage caused by random shocks on a mechanical structure (assuming linear damage superposition). If a subsidiary series of events is generated instead of a random variable and the two types of events are indistinguishable, the process is a branching process [A7.3, A7.21, A7.30], discussed e.g. in [6.1, A7.4(1968)] as a model to describe failure occurrence when secondary failures are triggered by primary failures.

Let $v(t)$ be the count function giving the number of events (on the time axis) of the involved point process (Fig. A7.1), $\xi_{i}$ the generated random variable at the occurrence of the $i$ th event, and $\xi_{t}$ the sum of $\xi_{i}$ over $(0, t]$

$$
\xi_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{v(t)} \xi_{i}, \quad v(t)=1,2, \ldots, t>0, v(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0, \xi_{t}=0 \text { for } v(t)=0
$$

The stochastic process of value $\xi_{t}(t \geq 0)$ is a cumulative process.
Assuming that the random variables $\xi_{i}$ are $>0$, mutually independent, independent from $v(t)$ and distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)$, it is not difficult to recognize that $\xi_{t}$ is distributed as the total repair time (total down time) for failures occurred in a total operating time (total up time) $t$ of a repairable item, and is thus given by the work-mission availability (Eq. (6.32)).

In the following, results are given for the case in which the involved point process is an HPP with parameter $\lambda$ and the generated random variables are mutually independent, independent from $v(t)$, and have the same exponential distribution with parameter $\mu$. Equation (6.33) with $T_{0}=t$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{t} \leq x\right\}=\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}(t, x)=e^{-\lambda t}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!} e^{-\lambda t}\left(1-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\mu x)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\mu x}\right)\right] \\
& =1-e^{-(\lambda t+\mu x)} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\mu x)^{k}}{k!}\right], \quad t>0 \text { given, } x>0, \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{t}=0\right\}=e^{-\lambda t}
\end{aligned}
$$

Mean and variance of $\xi_{t}$ follow as (Eqs. (A7.219), (A6.38), (A6.45), (A6.41))

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=\lambda t / \mu \quad \text { and } \quad \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=2 \lambda t / \mu^{2}
$$

Furthermore, for $t \rightarrow \infty$ the distribution of $\xi_{t}$ approaches a normal distribution with mean and variance as per Eq. (A7.220) (see the discussion to Eq. (6.33) on p. 181). Moments of $\xi_{t}$ can also be obtained using the moment generating function (Table A9.7a) or directly by considering Eq. (A7.218), yielding (Example A7.14)$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=\mathrm{E}[v(t)] \mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right] \quad \& \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=\mathrm{E}[v(t)] \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{i}\right]+\operatorname{Var}[v(t)] \mathrm{E}^{2}\left[\xi_{i}\right]
$$

Of interest in practical applications (e.g. cost optimizations) can also be the distribution of the time $\tau_{C}$ at which the process $\xi_{t}(t>0)$ crosses a give (fixed) barrier $C$. For the case given by Eq. (A7.219), in particular for $\xi_{i}>0$, the events

$$
\left\{\tau_{C}>t\right\} \quad \text { and } \quad\left\{\xi_{t} \leq C\right\}
$$

are equivalent. Form Eq. (A7.219) it follows then ( $C$ has dimension of $\mu^{-1}$ )

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{C}>t\right\}=1-e^{-(\lambda t+\mu C)} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\mu C)^{k}}{k!}\right], \quad C>0 \text { given, } t>0
$$

# A7.8.5 General Point Processes 

A point process is an ordered sequence of points on the time axis, giving for example the failure occurrence of a repairable system. Poisson and renewal processes are simple examples of point processes. Assuming that simultaneous events cannot occur (with probability one) and assigning to the point process a count function $v(t)$ giving the number of events occurred in $(0, t]$, investigation of point processes can be performed on the basis of the involved count function $v(t)$. However, arbitrary point processes can lead to difficulties, and results are known only for particular situations (low occurrence rate, stationary, regular, etc.). In reliability applications, general point processes can appear for example when investigating failure occurrence of repairable systems by neglecting repair times. In the following, only some basic properties of general point processes will be discussed, see e.g. [A7.10, A7.11, A7.12, A7.30] for greater details.

## Example A7.14

Prove Eq. (A7.221).

## Solution

Considering $\xi_{i}>0$, identically distributed, (mutually) independent, independent of $v(t)$, and with finite mean \& variance, Eq. (A7.218) yields, for given (fixed) $v(t)=n$ (Eqs. (A6.68) \& (A6.70))

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{t} \mid v(t)=n\right]=n \mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right] \quad \text { and } \quad \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{t} \mid v(t)=n\right]=n \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{i}\right]
$$

From Eq. (A7.224) it follows then (considering $v(t)=1,2, \ldots$ )

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \operatorname{Pr}[v(t)=n] \mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{t} \mid v(t)=n\right] & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \operatorname{Pr}[v(t)=n] n \mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right] \\
& =\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n \operatorname{Pr}[v(t)=n]=\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right] \mathrm{E}[v(t)]
\end{aligned}
$$

For $\operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{t}\right]$, it holds that (Eq. (A6.45)) $\operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{t}\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{t}^{2}\right]-\mathrm{E}^{2}\left[\xi_{t}\right]$; from which, considering $\xi_{i}^{2}=\left(\xi_{i}+\ldots+\xi_{v(t)}\right)^{2}$ and Eqs. (A7.225), (A6.68), (A6.69) \& (A6.45),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{t}\right] & =\mathrm{E}[v(t) \cdot \xi_{i}^{2}+v(t)(v(t)-1)) \cdot \xi_{i} \xi_{j}]-(\mathrm{E}[v(t)] \mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right])^{2} \\
& =\mathrm{E}[v(t)] \mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}^{2}\right]+\mathrm{E}\left[v^{2}(t)\right] \mathrm{E}^{2}\left[\xi_{i}\right]-\mathrm{E}[v(t)] \mathrm{E}^{2}\left[\xi_{i}\right]-(\mathrm{E}[v(t)] \mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right])^{2} \\
& =\mathrm{E}[v(t)] \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{i}\right]+\operatorname{Var}[v(t)] \mathrm{E}^{2}\left[\xi_{i}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$Let $v(t)$ be a count function giving the number of events occurred in $(0, t]$, assume $v(0)=0$ and that simultaneous occurrences are not possible. The underlying point process is stationary if $v(t)$ has stationary increments (Eq. (A7.5)), and is without aftereffect if $v(t)$ has independent increments (Eq. (A7.2)). The sum of independent stationary point processes is a stationary point process. The same holds for processes without aftereffect. However, only the homogeneous Poisson process (HPP) is stationary and without aftereffect (memoryless).

For a general point process, a mean value function

$$
\mathrm{Z}(t)=\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)], \quad t>0, \mathrm{Z}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

giving the mean (expectation) of the number of points (events) in $(0, t]$ can be defined. $\mathrm{Z}(t)$ is a nondecreasing, continuous function with $\mathrm{Z}(0)=0$, often assumed increasing, unbounded, and absolutely continuous. If

$$
\mathrm{z}(t)=\frac{d \mathrm{Z}(t)}{d t}=\frac{d \mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)]}{d t} \geq 0, \quad t>0, \mathrm{z}_{S}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

exists, $\mathrm{z}(t)$ is the intensity of the point process. Equations (A7.228) \& (A7.227) yield

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{v(t+\delta t)-v(t)=1\}=\mathrm{z}(t) \delta t+\mathrm{o}(\delta t), \quad t>0, \delta t \downarrow 0
$$

and no distinction is made between arrival rate and intensity. $\mathrm{z}(t) \delta t$ gives the unconditional probability for one event (failure) in $(t, t+\delta t] . \quad \mathrm{z}(t)$ corresponds thus to $\mathrm{m}(t)$ (Eq. (A7.193)) and $\mathrm{h}(t)$ (Eq. (A7.24)), but differs basically from the failure rate $\lambda(t)$ (Eq. (A6.25)) which gives (as $\lambda(t) \delta t$ ) the conditional probability for a failure in $(t, t+\delta t]$ given that the item was new at $t=0$ and no failure has occurred in $(0, t]$. This distinction is important also for the case of a homogeneous Poisson process (Appendix A7.2.5), for which $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ holds for all interarrival times (with $x$ starting by 0 at each renewal point) and $\mathrm{h}(t)=\lambda$ holds for the whole process. Misuses are known, in particular when dealing with reliability data analysis (see e.g. [6.1, A7.30] and comments on pp. 390-91 \& 393, Appendix A7.8.2, and Sections 1.2.3, 7.6, 7.7). Thus, as a first rule to avoid confusion,
for repairable items, it is mandatory to use for interarrival times the variable $x$ starting by 0 after each repair (renewal), instead of $t$.

Some limits theorems on point processes are known, in particular on the convergence to an HPP, see e. g. [A7.10, A7.11, A7.12].

In reliability applications, $\mathrm{z}(t)$ is called failure intensity [A1.4], ROCOF (rate of occurrence of failures) in [6.1]. $\mathrm{z}(t)$ applies in particular to repairable systems when repair (restoration) times are neglected. In this case, $v_{S}(t)$ is the count function giving the number of system failures occurred in $(0, t]$, with $v(0)=0$, and

$$
\mathrm{z}_{S}(t)=\frac{d \mathrm{Z}_{S}(t)}{d t}=\frac{d \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{v}_{S}(t)\right]}{d t} \geq 0, \quad t>0, \mathrm{z}_{S}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0
$$

is the system failure intensity.# A8 Basic Mathematical Statistics 

Mathematical statistics deals basically with situations which can be described as follows: Given a population of statistically identical and independent elements with unknown statistical properties, measurements regarding these properties are made on a (random) sample of this population, and on the basis of the collected data, conclusions are made for the remaining elements of the population. Examples are the estimation of an unknown defective probability $p$ or of the distribution function parameters of an item's failure-free time $\tau$, as well as a decision whether the mean of $\tau$ is greater than a given value. Mathematical statistics thus goes from observations (realizations) of a given (random) event in a series of independent trials to search for a suitable probabilistic model for the event considered (inductive approach). Methods used are based on probability theory and results obtained can only be formulated in a probabilistic language. Risk minimization for a false conclusion is an important objective in mathematical statistics. This Appendix provides the tools necessary for the quality and reliability tests given in Chapter 7. It is a careful introduction to mathematical statistics, consistent from a mathematical point of view but still with reliability engineering applications in mind (demonstration of established theorems is referred, and for all other propositions or equations, sufficient details for complete demonstration are given). Emphasis is on empirical methods, parameter estimation, and testing of hypotheses. To simplify the notation, sample is used for random sample (taken from a very large, homogeneous lot, if not otherwise stated), mean for expected value, and independent for mutually, statistically, stochastically independent (p.435). Estimated (or empirical) values are marked with ${ }^{\wedge}$. Selected examples illustrate the practical aspects.

## A8.1 Empirical Methods

Empirical methods allow a quick and easy evaluation/estimation of the distribution function and of the mean, variance, and other moments characterizing a random variable. These estimates are based on the empirical distribution function and have a great intuitive appeal. An advantage of the empirical distribution function, when plotted on an appropriate probability charts (probability plot papers) is to give a simple visual rough check as to whether the assumed model seems correct (see p. 545-48 for an introduction, and pp. 585-87 for lognormal, Weibull and normal distribution probability charts).# A8.1.1 Empirical Distribution Function 

A sample of size $n$ of a random variable $\tau$ with the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ is a random vector $\vec{\tau}=\left(\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}\right)$ whose components $\tau_{i}$ are assumed mutually independent and identically distributed random variables with $\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i} \leq t\right\}$, $i=1, \ldots, n$. For instance, $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ are the failure-free times (used in this book for failure-free operating times ) of $n$ items randomly selected from a lot of statistically identical items with a distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ for the failure-free time $\tau$. The observed failure-free times, i.e. the realization of the random vector $\vec{\tau}=\left(\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}\right)$, is a set $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of independent real values ( $>0$ in the case of failure-free times). Distinction between random variables $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ and their observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ is important from a mathematical point of view. ${ }^{+)}$

When the sample elements (observations) are ordered by increasing magnitude, an order statistic (also known as order sample) $t_{(1)}, \ldots, t_{(n)}$ is obtained. In life tests, observations constitute often themselves an order statistic. It is not difficult to recognizes that the joint density $\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)$ of an order statistic of $n$ observations on independent, identically distributed random variables with density $\mathrm{f}(t)$ has the simple form $\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)=n!\Pi_{i} \mathrm{f}\left(t_{i}\right)$ (consider Eq. (A6.57) and that permutation of the $n$ observations yields the same order statistic).

With the purpose of saving test duration and cost, life tests can be terminated (stopped) at the occurrence of the $k$ th ordered observation ( $k$ th failure) or at a given (fixed) time $T_{\text {test }}$. If the test is stopped at the $k$ th failure, a type II censoring occurs. A type I censoring occurs if the test is stopped at $T_{\text {test }}$. A third possibility is to stop the test at a given (fixed) number $k$ of observations (failures) or at $T_{\text {test }}$ whenever the first occurs. The corresponding test plans are termed $(n, \bar{r}, k),\left(n, \bar{r}, T_{\text {test }}\right)$, and $\left(n, \bar{r},\left(k, T_{\text {test }}\right)\right)$, respectively, where $\bar{r}$ stands for "without replacement / renewal". In many applications, failed items can be replaced (for instance in the case of a repairable item or system); in these cases, $\bar{r}$ is changed with $r$ in the test plans.

For a set of ordered independent observations $t_{(1)}, \ldots, t_{(n)}$ of a random variable $\tau$, the right continuous step function

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } t<t_{(1)} \\ \frac{i}{n} & \text { for } t_{(i)} \leq t<t_{(i+1)}, \\ 1 & \text { for } t \geq t_{(n)}\end{cases} \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n-1
$$

is the empirical distribution function (EDF) of the random variable $\tau$, see Fig. A8.1 for a graphical representation. $\widehat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ expresses the relative frequency of the event $\{\tau \leq t\}$ in $n$ independent trial repetitions, and provides a well defined estimate of

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$The investigation of statistical methods and the discussion of their properties can only be based on the (random) sample $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$. However, in applying the methods for a numerical evaluation (statistical decision), the observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ have to be used. For this reason, the same equation (or procedure) can be applied to $\tau_{i}$ or $t_{i}$ according to the situation.

Figure A8.1 Example of an empirical distribution function $\left(t_{1}=t_{(1)}, \ldots, t_{n}=t_{(n)}\right.$ is assumed here)
the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}$. The symbol $\wedge$ is used in this book to denote an estimate of an unknown quantity. As stated in the footnote on p. 542, when investigating the properties of the empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ it is necessary in Eq. (A8.1) to replace the observations $t_{(1)}, \ldots, t_{(n)}$ by the sample elements $\tau_{(1)}, \ldots, \tau_{(n)}$.

For given $\mathrm{F}(t)$ and any fixed value of $t$, the number of observations $\leq t$, i. e. $n \hat{\mathrm{~F}}_{n}(t)$, is binomially-distributed (Eq. (A6.120)) with parameter $p=\mathrm{F}(t)$, mean

$$
E\left[n \hat{\mathrm{~F}}_{n}(t)\right]=n \mathrm{~F}(t)
$$

and variance

$$
\operatorname{Var}\left[n \hat{\mathrm{~F}}_{n}(t)\right]=n \mathrm{~F}(t)(1-\mathrm{F}(t))
$$

(Eqs. (A6.122) \& (A6.123)). Moreover, application of the strong law of large numbers (Eq. (A6.146)) shows that for any given (fixed) value of $t, \hat{\mathrm{~F}}_{n}(t)$ converges to $\mathrm{F}(t)$ with probability one for $n \rightarrow \infty$. This convergence is uniform in $t$ and holds for the whole distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$. Proof of this important result is given in the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem [A8.4, A8.14, A8.16], which states that the largest absolute deviation between $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ and $\mathrm{F}(t)$ over all $t$, i. e.

$$
D_{n}=\sup _{-\infty<t<\infty}\left|\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)-\mathrm{F}(t)\right|
$$

converges with probability one toward 0

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} D_{n}=0\right\}=1
$$In life tests, observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ constitute often themselves an order statistic. This is useful for statistical evaluation of data, and will be tacitly assumed in the following. However, if the test is stopped at the occurrence of the $k$ th failure or at $T_{\text {test }}$, and $k$ or $T_{\text {test }}$ are small, the homogeneity of the sample can be questionable and the shape of $\mathrm{F}(t)$ could change for $t>t_{k}$ or $t>T_{\text {test }}$ (e.g. because of wear-out, see e.g. the remark on p.354).

# A8.1.2 Empirical Moments and Quantiles 

The moments of a random variable $\tau$ are completely determined by the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}$. The empirical distribution $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ introduced in Appendix A8.1.1 can thus be used to estimate the unknown moments of $\tau$.

The observed values $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ having been fixed, $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ can be regarded as the distribution function of a discrete random variable with probability $p_{k}=1 / n$ at the points $t_{k}, k=1, \ldots, n$. Using Eq. (A6.35), the corresponding mean is the empirical mean (empirical expectation) of $\tau$ and is given by

$$
\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}
$$

Taking into account footnote on p. 542, $\hat{\mathrm{E}}\{\tau\}$ is a random variable with mean

$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]]=\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}\right]=\frac{1}{n} n \mathrm{E}[\tau]=\mathrm{E}[\tau]
$$

(Eq. (A6.68)) and variance (Eqs. (A6.70), (A6.46))

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]]=\operatorname{Var}\left[\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}\right]=\frac{1}{n^{2}} n \operatorname{Var}[\tau]=\frac{\operatorname{Var}[\tau]}{n}
$$

Equation (A8.7) shows that $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]$ is an unbiased estimate of $\mathrm{E}[\tau]$, see Eq. (A8.18). Furthermore, from the strong law of large numbers (Eq. (A6.147) on p. 472) it follows that for $n \rightarrow \infty, \hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]$ per Eq. (A8.6) converges with probability one toward $\mathrm{E}[\tau]$

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}\right)=\mathrm{E}[\tau]\right\}=1
$$

The exact distribution function of $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]$ is known in a closed simple form only for some particular cases (normal, exponential, Gamma distributions). However, the central limit theorem (Eq. (A6.148)) shows that for large values of $n$ the distribution of $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]$ can always be approximated by a normal distribution with mean $\mathrm{E}[\tau]$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}[\tau] / n$.Based on $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$, Eqs.(A6.43)\&(A8.6) provide an estimate of the variance of $\tau$ as

$$
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}-\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}-\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]\right)^{2}
$$

This estimate is biased $\left(\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}-\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)^{2}\right]=\operatorname{Var}[\tau](n-1) / n\right)$; so that as empirical variance of $\tau$ one use often

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}[\tau]=\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}-\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{n-1}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{2}-\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}\right)^{2}\right]
$$

which is unbiased, i. e.

$$
\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}[\tau]]=\operatorname{Var}[\tau]
$$

The empirical higher-order moments (Eqs. (A6.41) and (A6.50)) can be estimated with

$$
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{k} \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}-\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]\right)^{k}
$$

The empirical quantile $\hat{t}_{q}$ is defined as the $q$ quantile (p. 450) of the empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$

$$
\hat{t}_{q}=\inf \left\{t: \hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t) \geq q\right\}
$$

# A8.1.3 Further Applications of the Empirical Distribution Function 

Comparison of the empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ with a given distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ is the basis for several non-parametric statistical methods. These include goodness-of-fit tests, confidence bands for distribution functions, and graphical methods using probability charts (probability plot papers).

A quantity often used in this context is the largest absolute deviation $D_{n}$ between $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ and $\mathrm{F}(t)$, defined by Eq. (A8.4). If the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ of the random variable $\tau$ is continuous, then the random variable $\mathrm{F}(\tau)$ is uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$. It follows that $D_{n}$ has a distribution independent of $\mathrm{F}(t)$. A.N. Kolmogorov showed [A8.20] that for $\mathrm{F}(t)$ continuous and $x>0$,

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\sqrt{n} D_{n} \leq x \mid \mathrm{F}(t)\right\}=1+2 \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k} e^{-2 k^{2} x^{2}}
$$

The series converges rapidly for $\mathrm{x}>1$, or $y=x / \sqrt{n}>1 / \sqrt{n}$, so that $k=1$ yields

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{D_{n} \leq y \mid \mathrm{F}(t)\right\} \approx 1-2 e^{-2 n y^{2}}
$$Table A8.1 Values of $y_{1-\alpha}$, for which $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{D_{n} \leq y_{1-\alpha} \mid \mathrm{F}(t)\right\}=1-\alpha$

| $n$ | $a=0.2$ | $a=0.1$ | $a=0.05$ |
| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
| 2 | 0.684 | 0.776 | 0.842 |
| 5 | 0.447 | 0.509 | 0.563 |
| 10 | 0.323 | 0.369 | 0.409 |
| 20 | 0.232 | 0.265 | 0.294 |
| 30 | 0.190 | 0.218 | 0.242 |
| 40 | 0.165 | 0.189 | 0.210 |
| 50 | 0.148 | 0.170 | 0.188 |
| for $n>50$ | $\leqq 1.07 / \sqrt{n}$ | $\leqq 1.22 / \sqrt{n}$ | $\leqq 1.36 / \sqrt{n}$ |

The distribution function of $D_{n}$ has been tabulated for small values of $n$ [A8.2, A8.27], see Table A9.5 and Table A8.1. From the above it follows that,
for a given continuous distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$, the band $\mathrm{F}(t) \pm y_{1-\alpha}$ overlaps the empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ with probability $1-\alpha_{n}$ where $\alpha_{n} \rightarrow \alpha$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$, with $y_{1-\alpha}$ defined by

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{D_{n} \leq y_{1-\alpha} \mid \mathrm{F}(t)\right\}=1-\alpha
$$

and given in Table A9.5 or Table A8.1.
From Table A8.1 one recognizes that the convergence $\alpha_{n} \rightarrow \alpha$ is good (for practical purposes) for $n>50$. If $\mathrm{F}(t)$ is not continuous, it can be shown that with $y_{1-\alpha}$ from Eq. (A8.15), the band $\mathrm{F}(t) \pm y_{1-\alpha}$ overlaps $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ with a probability $1-\alpha_{n}^{\prime}$, where $\alpha_{n}^{\prime} \rightarrow \alpha^{\prime} \leq \alpha$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$.

The role of $\mathrm{F}(t)$ and $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ can be reversed (see also pp. 475, 558, 559), yielding, the random band $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t) \pm y_{1-\alpha}$ overlaps the true (unknown) distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ with probability $1-\alpha_{n}$, where $\alpha_{n} \rightarrow \alpha$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$,
see Example A8.1 for an application. This last consideration is an aspect of mathematical statistics, while the former one (in relation to Eq. (A8.15)) was a problem of probability theory; both agree only because of $n \rightarrow \infty$. One has thus
the possibility to estimate an unknown continuous distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ on the basis of the empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ (Figs. 7.12 \& 7.14).

# Example A8.1 

How large is the confidence band around $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ for $n=30$ and for $n=100$ if $\alpha=0.2$ ?

## Solution

From Table A8.1, $y_{0.8} \approx 0.19$, for $n=30$ and $y_{0.8} \approx 0.107$ for $n=100$. This leads to the band $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t) \pm 0.19$ for $n=30$ and $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t) \pm 0.107$ for $n=100$.To simplify investigations, it is often useful to draw $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ on a probability chart (probability plot paper). The method is as follows,
the empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ is drawn in a system of coordinates in which a postulated type of continuous distribution function is represented by a straight line; if the underlying distribution $\mathrm{F}(t)$ belongs to this type of distribution function, then for a sufficiently large value of $n$ the points $\left(t_{i}, \hat{\mathrm{~F}}_{n}\left(t_{i}\right)\right)$ will approximate to a straight line (a systematic deviation from a straight line, particularly in the domain $0.1<\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)<0.9$, leads to rejection of the type of distribution function assumed); however, a mixture of distribution functions (pp.349, 444) can apply in some cases.

This can also be used as a simple rough visual check as to whether an assumed model $(\mathrm{F}(t))$ seems correct. In many cases, estimates for unknown parameters of the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ can be obtained from the estimated straight line for $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$. Probability charts for Weibull (incl. exponential), lognormal and normal distribution functions are in Appendix A9.8, applications in Section 7.5 (Figs. 7.12-14).

The following is a derivation of the Weibull probability chart. The function

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda t)^{\beta}}
$$

can be transformed to $\log _{10}(1 /(1-\mathrm{F}(t)))=(\lambda t)^{\beta} \log _{10}(e)$ and finally to

$$
\log _{10} \log _{10}\left(\frac{1}{1-\mathrm{F}(t)}\right)=\beta \log _{10}(t)+\beta \log _{10}(\lambda)+\log _{10} \log _{10}(e)
$$

In the system of coordinates $\log _{10}(t)$ and $\log _{10} \log _{10}(1 /(1-\mathrm{F}(t)))$, the Weibull distribution function given by $\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda t)^{\beta}}$ appears as a straight line, see Fig. A8.2 for $\beta=1.5 \& \lambda=1 / 800 \mathrm{~h}$. As shown by Fig. A8.2, $\beta \& \lambda$ can be obtained graphically (e.g. for a statistical evaluation of data, as in Example 7.15 on pp. 347-348),

- $\beta$ is the slope of the straight line, it appears on the scale $\log _{10} \log _{10}(1 /(1-\mathrm{F}(t)))$ if $t$ is changed by one decade (e.g. from $10^{2}$ to $10^{3} \mathrm{~h}$ in Fig. A8.2),
- for $\log _{10} \log _{10}(1 /(1-\mathrm{F}(t)))=\log _{10} \log _{10}(e)$, i. e. on the dashed line in Fig. A8.2, one has $\log _{10}(\lambda t)=0$ and thus $\lambda=1 / t$.

The Weibull probability chart also applies to the exponential distribution $(\beta=1)$.
For a three parameter Weibull distribution $\left(\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda(t-\psi))^{\beta}}, t>\psi\right)$ one can operate with the time axis $t^{\prime}=t-\psi$, giving a straight line as before, or consider the concave curve obtained when using $t$ (see Fig. A8.2 for an example). Conversely, from a concave curve describing a Weibull distribution (for instance, in the case of an empirical data analysis) it is possible to find $\psi$ using the relationship $\psi=\left(t_{1} t_{2}-t_{m}^{2}\right) /\left(t_{1}+t_{2}-2 t_{m}\right)$ existing between two arbitrary points $t_{1}, t_{2}$ and $t_{m}$ obtained from the mean of $\mathrm{F}\left(t_{1}\right)$ and $\mathrm{F}\left(t_{2}\right)$ on the scale $\log _{10} \log _{10}(1 /(1-\mathrm{F}(t)))$, see Example A6.14 on p. 459 for a derivation and Fig. A8.2 for an application with $t_{1}=400 \mathrm{~h}$ and $t_{2}=1000 \mathrm{~h}$, yielding $t_{m}=600 \mathrm{~h} \& \psi=200 \mathrm{~h}$. In a statistical evaluation of data, $t^{\prime}=t-\bar{\psi}$ can be used to estimate $\beta \& \lambda$ from the approximated straight line.

Figure A8.2 Weibull probability chart: The distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda t)^{\beta}}$ appears as a straight line (continuous line for $\lambda=1 / 800 \mathrm{~h}$ and $\beta=1.5$ ); for a three parameter distribution $\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda(t-\psi))^{\beta}}(t>\psi)$, one can use $t^{\prime}=t-\psi$ (yielding a straight line) or operate with a concave curve (dashed curve for $\lambda=1 / 800 \mathrm{~h}, \beta=1.5$, and $\psi=200 \mathrm{~h}$, see the remark at the bottom of p. 547 for a graphical evaluation of data)# A8.2 Parameter Estimation 

In many applications it can be assumed that the type of distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ of the underlying random variable $\tau$ is known. This means that $\mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}\left(t, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)$ is known in its functional form, the real-valued parameters $\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}$ having to be estimated. The unknown parameters of $\mathrm{F}(t)$ must be estimated on the basis of the mutually (statistically) independent observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of the random variable $\tau$. A distinction is made between point and interval estimation.

## A8.2.1 Point Estimation

Consider first the case where the given distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ only depends on a parameter $\theta$, assumed hereafter as an unknown constant. ${ }^{+)}$A point estimate for $\theta$ is a function

$$
\hat{\theta}_{n}=\mathrm{u}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)
$$

of the observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of the random variable $\tau$ (not of the unknown parameter $\theta$ itself). The estimate $\hat{\theta}_{n}$ is

- unbiased, if

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\hat{\theta}_{n}\right]=\theta
$$

- consistent, if $\hat{\theta}_{n}$ converges to $\theta$ in probability, i. e. if for any $\varepsilon>0$

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left|\hat{\theta}_{n}-\theta\right|>\varepsilon\right\}=0
$$

- strongly consistent, if $\hat{\theta}_{n}$ converges to $\theta$ with probability one

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \hat{\theta}_{n}=\theta\right\}=1
$$

- efficient, if

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\left(\hat{\theta}_{n}-\theta\right)^{2}\right]
$$

is minimum over all possible point estimates for $\theta$,

- sufficient (sufficient statistic for $\theta$ ), if $\hat{\theta}_{n}$ delivers the complete information about $\theta$ (available in the observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ ); i. e. if the conditional distribution of $\vec{\tau}$ for given $\hat{\theta}_{n}$ does not depend on $\theta$.

[^0]
[^0]:    +) Bayesian estimation theory (based on the Bayes theorem (Eq. (A6.18) \& note to Eq. (A6.58)), which considers $\theta$ as a random variable and assigns to it an a priori distribution function, will not be considered in this book (as a function of the random sample, $\hat{\theta}_{n}$ is a random variable, while $\theta$ is an unknown constant). However, a Bayesian statistics can be useful if knowledge on the a priori distribution function is well founded, for these cases one may refer e. g. to [A8.24, A8.25].For an unbiased estimate, Eq. (A8.21) becomes

$$
\mathrm{E}\left[\left(\hat{\theta}_{n}-\theta\right)^{2}\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\left(\hat{\theta}_{n}-\mathrm{E}\left[\hat{\theta}_{n}\right]\right)^{2}\right]=\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat{\theta}_{n}\right]
$$

An unbiased estimate is thus efficient if $\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat{\theta}_{n}\right]$ is minimum over all possible point estimates for $\theta$, and consistent if $\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat{\theta}_{n}\right] \rightarrow 0$ for $n \rightarrow \infty$. This last statement is a consequence of Chebyschev's inequality (Eq. (A6.49)). Efficiency can be checked using the Cramér - Rao inequality, and sufficiency using the factorization criterion of the likelihood function. Other useful properties of estimates are asymptotic unbiasedness and asymptotic efficiency, see e. g. [A8.1, A8.23].

Several methods are known for estimating $\theta$. To these belong the methods of moments, quantiles, least squares, and maximum likelihood.

The maximum likelihood method is often used in engineering applications. It provides point estimates which under general conditions are consistent, asymptotically unbiased, asymptotically efficient, and asymptotically normally distributed. Furthermore, if an efficient estimate exists, then the likelihood equation (Eqs.(A8.23) \& A8.24)) has this estimate as a unique solution; finally,
an estimate $\hat{\theta}_{n}$ is sufficient if and only if the likelihood function can be written in two factors, one depending on $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ only, the other on $\theta$ and $\hat{\theta}_{n}=\mathrm{u}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)$ only,
see e. g. [A8.1, A8.8, A8.15, A8.19, A8.23] for greater details. The maximum likelihood method was developed 1921 by R.A. Fisher [A8.15] and is based on the following idea,
maximize, with respect to the unknown parameter $\theta$, the probability (Pr) that in a sample of size $n$, exactly the values $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ will be observed (i.e., maximize the probability of observing that record); this by maximizing the likelihood function $(\mathrm{L} \sim \operatorname{Pr})$, defined as

$$
\mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}, \theta\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{p}_{i}(\theta), \quad \text { with } \quad \mathrm{p}_{i}(\theta)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau=t_{i}\right\}
$$

in the discrete case, and as

$$
\mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}, \theta\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{f}\left(t_{i}, \theta\right), \quad \text { with } \mathrm{f}\left(t_{i}, \theta\right) \text { as density function }
$$

in the continuous case.
Since the logarithmic function is monotonically increasing, the use of $\ln (\mathrm{L})$ instead of $L$ leads to the same result. If $\mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}, \theta\right)$ is derivable and the maximum likelihood estimate $\hat{\theta}_{n}$ exists, then it will satisfy the equation

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}, \theta\right)}{\partial \theta}\right|_{\theta=\hat{\theta}_{n}}=0
$$or

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \ln \left(\mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}, \theta\right)\right)}{\partial \theta}\right|_{\theta=\hat{\theta}_{n}}=0
$$

The maximum likelihood method can be generalized to the case of a distribution function with a finite number of unknown parameters $\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}$. Instead of Eq. (A8.26), the following system of $r$ algebraic equations must be solved

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \ln \left(\mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)\right)}{\partial \theta_{i}}\right|_{\theta_{i}=\hat{\theta}_{i n}}=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, r
$$

The existence and uniqueness of a maximum likelihood estimate is satisfied in most practical applications.

To simplify the notation, in the following the index $n$ will be omitted for the estimated parameters. Examples A8.2-A8.5 illustrate the use of the maximum likelihood method.

# Example A8.2 

Let $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ be independent observations of an exponentially distributed failure-free time $\tau$. Give the maximum likelihood estimate for the unknown parameter $\lambda$ of the exponential distribution.

## Solution

With $\mathrm{f}(t, \lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t}$, Eq. (A8.24) yields $\mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}, \lambda\right)=\lambda^{n} e^{-\lambda\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)}$, from which

$$
\hat{\lambda}=\frac{n}{t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}}
$$

This case corresponds to a sampling plan with $n$ elements without replacement, terminated at the occurrence of the $n$th failure. $\hat{\lambda}$ depends only on the sum $t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}$, not on the individual values of $t_{i} ; t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}$ is a sufficient statistic and $\hat{\lambda}$ is a sufficient estimate $\left(\mathrm{L}=1 \cdot \lambda^{n} e^{-n \lambda / \hat{\lambda}}\right)$. However, $\hat{\lambda}=n /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)$ is a biased estimate, unbiased is $\hat{\lambda}=(n-1) /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)$, as well as $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau]=\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right) / n$ given by Eq. (A8.6).

## Example A8.3

Assuming that an event $A$ has occurred exactly $k$ times in $n$ Bernoulli trials, give the maximum likelihood estimate for the unknown probability $p$ for event $A$ to occur.

## Solution

Using the binomial distribution (Eq. (A6.120)), the likelihood function (Eq. (A8.23)) becomes

$$
L=p_{k}=\binom{n}{k} p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k} \quad \text { or } \quad \ln L=\ln \binom{n}{k}+k \ln p+(n-k) \ln (1-p)
$$

This leads to

$$
\hat{p}=k / n
$$

$\hat{p}$ is the observed relative frequency, it is unbiased and depends only on $k$, i. e. on the number of events occurred in $n$ independent trials; $k$ is a sufficient statistic and $\hat{p}$ is a sufficient estimate $\left(L=\binom{n}{k} \cdot\left[p^{\hat{p}}(1-p)^{(1-\hat{p})}\right]^{n}\right)$.# Example A8.4 

Let $k_{\mathrm{P}} \ldots, k_{n}$ be independent observations (in $n$ trials, $n=1,2, \ldots, k_{i}=0,1, \ldots$ ) of a random variable $\zeta$ distributed according to the Poisson distribution defined by Eq. (A6.125). Give the maximum likelihood estimate for the unknown parameter $m$ of the Poisson distribution.

## Solution

Using Eq. (A6.120), the likelihood function becomes

$$
L=\frac{m^{k_{I}}+\ldots+k_{n}}{k_{1}!\ldots k_{n}!} e^{-n m} \quad \text { or } \quad \ln L=\left(k_{I}+\ldots+k_{n}\right) \ln m-n m-\ln \left(k_{I}!\ldots k_{n}!\right)
$$

and thus

$$
\hat{m}=\frac{k_{1}+\ldots+k_{n}}{n}
$$

$\hat{m}$ is unbiased. It depends only on the sum $k_{1}+\ldots+k_{n}$, not on the individual $k_{i} ; k_{1}+\ldots+k_{n}$ is a sufficient statistic and $\hat{m}$ is a sufficient estimate $\left(L=\left(1 / k_{1}!\ldots k_{n}!\right) \cdot\left(m^{n \hat{m}} e^{-n m}\right)\right)$.

## Example A8.5

Let $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ be independent observations of a Weibull distributed failure-free time $\tau$. Give the maximum likelihood estimate for the unknown parameters $\lambda$ and $\beta$.

## Solution

With $\mathrm{f}(t, \lambda, \beta)=\beta \lambda(\lambda t)^{\beta-1} e^{-(\lambda t)^{\beta}}$ (Eq. (A6.90)), it follows from Eq. (A8.24) that

$$
\mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}, \lambda, \beta\right)=\left(\beta \lambda^{\beta}\right)^{n} e^{-\lambda^{\beta}\left(t_{1}^{\beta}+\ldots+t_{n}^{\beta}\right)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\beta-1}
$$

yielding (Eq. (A8.27) and considering $a^{x}=e^{x \ln a}$ )

$$
\hat{\beta}=\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\hat{\beta}} \ln t_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\hat{\beta}}}-\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln t_{i}\right]^{-1} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\lambda}=\left[\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\hat{\beta}}}\right]^{1 / \hat{\beta}}
$$

The solution for $\hat{\beta}$ is unique and can be found using Newton's approximation method (the value obtained from the empirical distribution function can give a good initial value, see e. g. Fig. 7.12).

Due to cost and time limitations, the situation often arises in reliability applications in which the items under test are run in parallel and the test is stopped before all items have failed. If there are $n$ items, and at the end of the test $k$ have failed (at the individual failure times (times to failure) $t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots<t_{k}$ ) and $n-k$ are still working, then the operating times $T_{1}, \ldots, T_{n-k}$ of the items still working at the end of the test should also be accounted for in the evaluation. Considering a Weibull distribution as in Example A8.5, and assuming that the operating times $T_{1}, \ldots, T_{n-k}$ have been observed in addition to the failure-free times $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{k}$, then

$$
\mathrm{L}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{k}, \lambda, \beta\right) \sim\left(\beta \lambda^{\beta}\right)^{k} e^{-\lambda^{\beta}\left(t_{1}^{\beta}+\ldots+t_{k}^{\beta}\right)} \prod_{i=1}^{k} t_{i}^{\beta-1} \prod_{j=1}^{n-k} e^{-\left(\lambda T_{j}\right)^{\beta}}
$$

leads to (Eq. (A8.27) and considering $a^{x}=e^{x \ln a}$ )$$
\hat{\beta}=\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} t_{i}^{\hat{\beta}} \ln t_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-k} T_{j}^{\hat{\beta}} \ln T_{j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{k} t_{i}^{\hat{\beta}}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-k} T_{j}^{\hat{\beta}}}-\frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \ln t_{i}\right]^{-1}, \quad \hat{\lambda}=\left[\frac{k}{\sum_{i=1}^{k} t_{i}^{\hat{\beta}}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-k} T_{j}^{\hat{\beta}}}\right]^{1 / \hat{\beta}}
$$

Calculation method for Eq. (A8.32) applies for any distribution function, yielding

$$
\mathrm{L}=\Pi_{i} \mathrm{f}\left(t_{i}, \theta\right) \cdot \Pi_{i}\left(1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{j}, \theta\right)\right)
$$

where $i$ sums over all observed times to failure, $j$ sums over all failure-free times, and $\theta$ can be a vector. For the exponential distribution $(\beta=1)$, Eq. (A8.32) leads to

$$
\hat{\lambda}=\frac{k}{\sum_{i=1}^{k} t_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-k} T_{j}}
$$

For a test described by Eqs. (A8.32)- (A8.34), following two cases must be distinguished:

1. $T_{1}=\ldots=T_{n-k}=t_{k}$, i. e. the test is stopped at the (random) occurrence of the $k$ th failure (failure or type II censoring).
2. $T_{1}=\ldots=T_{n-k}=T_{\text {test }}$ is the given (fixed) test duration (time or type I censoring).

The 2 situations are basically different and this must be considered in data analysis.
If the test is stopped at the occurrence of the $k$ th failure, as per case 1 above, $T_{1}=\ldots=T_{n-k}=t_{k}$ holds in general, and the quantity $T_{r}=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) t_{k}$ is the random cumulative operating time over all items during the test. This situation corresponds to a sampling plan with $n$ elements without replacement (renewal), censored at the occurrence of the $k$ th failure. For the case of constant failure rate, the memoryless property of the Poisson process (Eqs. (7.26) and (7.27)) leads to $T_{r}=n t_{1}+(n-1)\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)+\ldots+(n-k+1)\left(t_{k}-t_{k-1}\right)=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) t_{k}$ (Eq. (7.23)). It can be shown that $\hat{\lambda}=k / T_{r}$ is biased, unbiased is (for $k>1$ )

$$
\hat{\lambda}=\frac{k-1}{t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) t_{k}}
$$

If the test is stopped at the fixed time $T_{\text {test }}$, as per case 2 above, Eq. (7.25) yields $T_{r}=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) T_{\text {test }}$. In this case, $T_{\text {test }}$ is given (fixed) but $k$ as well as $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{k}$ are random. This situation corresponds to a sampling plan with $n$ elements without replacement, censored at a fixed test time $T_{\text {test }}$. Also in this case, for constant failure rate, $\hat{\lambda}=k / T_{r}$ is biased.

However, important for practical applications is the
case with replacement (renewal) of failed elements, for which unbiased estimates can be easily found for failure censoring (Eq.(7.24)) \& time censoring (Eq. (7.28) or (A8.46)) samples (see also remarks on pp. 554 \& 559).# A8.2.2 Interval Estimation 

As shown in Appendix A8.2.1, a point estimation has the advantage of providing an estimate quickly. However, it does not give any indication as to the deviation of the estimate from the true parameter. More information can be obtained from an interval estimation. With an interval estimation, a random interval $\left[\hat{\theta}_{l}, \hat{\theta}_{u}\right]$ is asked such that it overlaps (covers) the true value of the unknown parameter $\theta$ with a given probability $\gamma .\left[\hat{\theta}_{l}, \hat{\theta}_{u}\right]$ is the confidence interval, $\hat{\theta}_{l}$ and $\hat{\theta}_{u}$ are the lower and upper confidence limits, and $\gamma$ is the confidence level. $\gamma$ has the following interpretation,
in an increasing number of mutually (statistically) independent samples of size $n$ (used to obtain confidence intervals), the relative frequency of the cases in which the confidence intervals $\left[\hat{\theta}_{l}, \hat{\theta}_{u}\right]$ overlap (cover) the unknown parameter $\theta$ converges to the confidence level $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$.
$\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ are the error probabilities related to the interval estimation. If $\gamma$ cannot be reached exactly, the true overlap probability should be near to, but not less than, $\gamma$.

The confidence interval can also be one-sided, i. e. $\left[0, \hat{\theta}_{u}\right]$ or $\left[\hat{\theta}_{l}, \infty\right)$ for $\theta \geq 0$. Figure A8.3 shows some examples of confidence intervals.

The concept of confidence intervals was introduced independently by J. Neyman and R. A. Fisher around 1930. In the following, some important cases for quality control and reliability tests are considered.

## A8.2.2.1 Estimation of an Unknown Probability $p$

Consider a sequence of Bernoulli trials (pp. 465-66) where a given event $A$ can occur with constant probability $p$ at each trial (as for a sample with replacement or taken from a very large, homogeneous lot). The binomial distribution

$$
p_{k}=\binom{n}{k} p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}
$$



Figure A8.3 Examples of confidence intervals for $\theta \geq 0$gives the probability that the event $A$ will occur exactly $k$ times in $n$ independent trials. From the expression for $p_{k}$, it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{k_{1} \leq \text { observations of } A \text { in } n \text { trials } \leq k_{2} \mid p\right\}=\sum_{i=k_{1}}^{k_{2}}\binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i}
$$

However, in mathematical statistics, the parameter $p$ is unknown. A confidence interval for $p$ is asked, based on the observed number of occurrences of the event $A$ in $n$ Bernoulli trials. A solution to this problem has been presented 1934 by Clopper and Pearson [A8.6]. For given $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$ the following holds,
if in $n$ Bernoulli trials the event $A$ has occurred $k$ times, there is a probability nearly equal to (but not smaller than) $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}$ that the confidence interval $\left\{\hat{p}_{l}, \hat{p}_{u}\right\}$ overlaps the true (unknown) probability $p$, with $\hat{p}_{l} \& \hat{p}_{u}$ given by

$$
\sum_{i=k}^{n}\binom{n}{i} \hat{p}_{l}^{i}\left(1-\hat{p}_{l}\right)^{n-i}=\beta_{2}, \quad \text { for } 0<k<n
$$

and

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{n}{i} \hat{p}_{u}^{i}\left(1-\hat{p}_{u}\right)^{n-i}=\beta_{1}, \quad \text { for } 0<k<n
$$

for $k=0$ take

$$
\hat{p}_{l}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{p}_{u}=1-\sqrt[n]{B_{1}}, \quad \text { with } \quad \gamma=1-\beta_{1}
$$

and for $k=n$ take

$$
\hat{p}_{l}=\sqrt[n]{B_{2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{p}_{u}=1, \quad \text { with } \quad \gamma=1-\beta_{2}
$$

Considering that $k$ is a random variable, $\hat{p}_{l}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}$ are random variables. According to the footnote on p. 542, it would be more correct (from a mathematical point of view) to compute from Eqs. (A8.37) \& (A8.38) the quantities $p_{k l}$ and $p_{k u}$, and then to set $\hat{p}_{l}=p_{k l}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}=p_{k u}$. For simplicity, this has been omitted here. Assuming $p$ as a random variable, $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ would be the probabilities for $p$ to be greater than $\hat{p}_{u}$ and smaller than $\hat{p}_{l}$, respectively (Fig. A8.3).

The proof of Eqs. (A8.38) is based on the monotonic property of the function

$$
B_{n}(k, p)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i}
$$

For given (fixed) $n, B_{n}(k, p)$ decreases in $p$ for fixed $k$ and increases in $k$ for fixed $p$ (Fig. A8.4). Thus, for any $p>\hat{p}_{u}$ it follows that

$$
B_{n}(k, p)<B_{n}\left(k, \hat{p}_{u}\right)=\beta_{1}
$$

For $p>\hat{p}_{u}$, the probability that the (random) number of observations in $n$ trials will

Figure A8.4 Binomial distribution as a function of $p$ for $n$ fixed and two values of $k$
take one of the values $0,1, \ldots, k$ is thus $<\beta_{1}$ (for $p>p^{\prime}$ in Fig. A8.4, the statement would also be true for a $K>k$ ). This holds in particular for a number of observations equal to $k$ and proves Eq. (A8.38). Proof of Eq. (A8.37) is similar.

To determine $\hat{p}_{i} \& \hat{p}_{u}$ per Eqs.(A8.37) \& (A8.38), a Table of the Fisher distribution (Appendix A9.4) or of the Beta function ([A9.1]) can be used. However, for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$, one of the following approximate solutions can often be used in practical applications:

1. For large values on $n(\min (n p, n(1-p)) \geq 5)$, a good estimate for $\hat{p}_{i}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}$ can be found using the integral Laplace theorem. Taking $\varepsilon=b \sqrt{n p(1-p)} / n$ and considering $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \delta_{i}=k$ (or rearranging Eq. (A6.149)), Eq. (A6.150) yields

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\frac{k}{n}-p\right)^{2} \leq \frac{b^{2} p(1-p)}{n}\right\}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{0}^{b} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x
$$

The right-hand side of Eq. (A8.41) is equal to the confidence level $\gamma$, i. e.

$$
\frac{2}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{0}^{b} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x=\gamma
$$

Thus, for a given $\gamma$, the value of $b$ can be obtained from a table of the normal distribution (Table A9.1). $b$ is the $1 / 2+\gamma / 2=(1+\gamma) / 2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution $\Phi(t)$, i. e. $b=t_{(1+\gamma) / 2}$ giving e. g. $b \approx 1.64$ for $\gamma=0.9$. On the left-hand side of Eq. (A8.41), the expression

$$
\left(\frac{k}{n}-p\right)^{2}=\frac{b^{2} p(1-p)}{n}
$$

is the equation of the confidence ellipse. For given values of $k, n$, and $b$,confidence limits $\hat{p}_{l}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}$ can be determined as roots of Eq. (A8.42)

$$
\hat{p}_{l, u}=\frac{k+0.5 b^{2} \pm b \sqrt{k(1-k / n)+b^{2} / 4}}{n+b^{2}}, \quad \beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2
$$

see Figs. A8.5 \& 7.1 for a graphical presentation and Example A8.6 for an application. Alternatively, the Poisson approximation can be used (Eq. (A6.129) or Fig. 7.3 on p. 317).
2. For small values of $n$, confidence limits can be determined graphically from the envelopes of Eqs. (A8.37) and (A8.38) for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$, see Fig. 7.1 on p. 313 for $\gamma=0.8$ and $\gamma=0.9$ (for $n>50$, the curves of Fig. 7.1 practically agree with the confidence ellipses given by Eq. (A8.43)).
One-sided confidence intervals can also be obtained from the above values for $\hat{p}_{l}$ and $\hat{p}_{u}$. Figure A8.3 shows that

$$
0 \leq p \leq \hat{p}_{u}, \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{p}_{l} \leq p \leq 1, \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{2}
$$

# Example A8.6 

Using confidence ellipses, give the confidence interval $\left[\hat{p}_{l}, \hat{p}_{u}\right]$ for an unknown probability $p$ for the case $n=50, k=5$, and $\gamma=0.9$.

## Solution

$n=50, k=5$, and $b \approx 1.64$ in Eq. (A8.43) yields the confidence interval [0.05, 0.19], see also Fig. 8.5 or Fig. 7.1 for a graphical solution.
Supplementary results: Corresponding one-sided confidence intervals would be $p \leq 0.19$ or $p \geq 0.05$ with $\gamma=0.95$.


Figure A8.5 Confidence limits (ellipses) for an unknown probability $p$ with a confidence level $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}=0.9$, here with $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}$, and for $n=10,25,50,100$ (according to Eq. (A8.43))The role of $k / n$ and $p$ can be reversed, and Eq. (A8.42) can be used (as consequence of Eq. (A8.41)) to solve a problem of probability theory, i. e. to compute, for a given probability $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}$ with $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}$, the limits $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ of the number of observations $k$ in $n$ independent trials for given (fixed) values of $p$ and $n$ (e.g. the number $k$ of defective items in a sample of size $n$, as per Eq. (A8.36); see also remarks on pp. 475, 546, 559)

$$
k_{1,2}=n p \pm b \sqrt{n p(1-p)}
$$

As in Eq. (A8.43), the quantity $b$ in Eq. (A8.45) is the $(1+\gamma) / 2$ quantile of the normal distribution (e. g. $b \approx 1.64$ for $\gamma=0.9$ from Table A9.1). For a graphical solution, Fig. A8.5 can be used, taking the ordinate $p$ as known and by reading $k_{1} / n$ and $k_{2} / n$ from the abscissa. An exact solution follows from Eq. (A8.36).

# A8.2.2.2 Estimation of the Parameter $\lambda$ for an Exponential Distribution: Fixed Test Duration (Time Censoring), Instantaneous Replacement 

Consider an item having a constant failure rate $\lambda$ and assume that at each failure it will be immediately replaced by a new, statistically identical item, in a negligible replacement time (Appendix A7.2). Because of the memoryless property (constant failure rate), the number of failures in $(0, T]$ is Poisson distributed and given by $\operatorname{Pr}\{k$ failures in $(0, T] \mid \lambda\}=(\lambda T)^{\lambda} e^{-\lambda T} / k$ ! (Eq (A7.41)). The maximum likelihood point estimate for $\lambda$ follows from Eq. (A8.30), with $n=1$ and $m=\lambda T$, as

$$
\hat{\lambda}=\frac{k}{T}, \quad k=0,1, \ldots
$$

( $k / T$ is unbiased, see the discussion to Eq. (A8.30)).
Similarly, estimation of the confidence interval for the failure rate $\lambda$ can be reduced to the estimation of the confidence interval for the parameter $m=\lambda T$ of a Poisson distribution. Considering Eqs. (A8.37) and (A8.38) and the similarity between the binomial and the Poisson distribution, the confidence limits $\hat{\lambda}_{1}$ and $\hat{\lambda}_{u}$ can be determined for given $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$ from

$$
\sum_{i=k}^{\infty} \frac{\left(\hat{\lambda}_{i} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\hat{\lambda}_{1} T}=\beta_{2}, \quad \text { for } k>0
$$

and

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\hat{\lambda}_{u} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\hat{\lambda}_{u} T}=\beta_{1}, \quad \text { for } k>0
$$

for $k=0$ takes

$$
\hat{\lambda}_{1}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\lambda}_{u}=\frac{\ln \left(1 / \beta_{1}\right)}{T}, \quad \text { with } \quad \gamma=1-\beta_{1}
$$Based on the relationship to the chi-square ( $\chi^{2}$ ) distribution (Appendix A9.2 or, for Eq. (A8.48), $k=n-1=v / 2-1$ and $\chi_{\mathrm{v}, 1-\beta_{1}}^{2} / 2=\lambda T$ in Eqs. (A6.102) \& (A6.103)), the values $\hat{\lambda}_{l} \& \hat{\lambda}_{u}$ given by Eqs. (A8.47) \& (A8.48) follow from the quantiles of the chi-square distribution as

$$
\hat{\lambda}_{l}=\frac{\chi_{2 k, \beta_{2}}^{2}}{2 T}, \quad \text { for } k>0
$$

and

$$
\hat{\lambda}_{u}=\frac{\chi_{2}^{2}(k+1), 1-\beta_{1}}{2 T}, \quad \text { for } k>0
$$

$\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$ is frequently used in practical applications. Fig. 7.6 on p. 331 gives the results obtained from Eqs. (A8.50) and (A8.51) for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$.

One-sided confidence intervals are given by

$$
0 \leq \lambda \leq \hat{\lambda}_{u}, \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{1}, \quad \text { and } \quad \lambda \geq \hat{\lambda}_{l}, \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{2}
$$

The situation considered by Eqs. (A8.46) - (A8.52) corresponds to that of a sampling plan with $n \geq 1$ elements immediately replaced at failure, each of them with failure rate $\lambda$, terminated at a fixed test time $T_{\text {test }}=t / n$ (footnote on p.330); situation basically different from that presented by Eqs. (A8.34), (A8.35), (A8.58).

# A8.2.2.3 Estimation of the Parameter $\lambda$ for an Exponential Distribution: Fixed Number $\boldsymbol{n}$ of Failures (Failure Censoring), no Replacement 

Let $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ be independent random variables distributed according to a common distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i} \leq t\right\}=1-e^{-\lambda t}, i=1, \ldots, n$. From Eq. (A6.102),

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n} \leq t\right\}=1-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\lambda t)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda t}=\frac{1}{(n-1)!} \int_{0}^{\lambda t} x^{n-1} e^{-x} d x
$$

and thus

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{a<\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n} \leq b\right\}=\frac{1}{(n-1)!} \int_{a \lambda}^{b \lambda} x^{n-1} e^{-x} d x
$$

Setting $a=n\left(1-\varepsilon_{2}\right) / \lambda$ and $b=n\left(1+\varepsilon_{1}\right) / \lambda$ it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\frac{1-\varepsilon_{2}}{\lambda}<\frac{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}}{n} \leq \frac{1+\varepsilon_{1}}{\lambda}\right\}=\frac{1}{(n-1)!} \int_{n\left(1-\varepsilon_{2}\right)}^{n\left(1+\varepsilon_{1}\right)} x^{n-1} d x
$$

Reversing the role of $\lambda \& \hat{\lambda}=n /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)$, i. e. considering $\hat{\lambda}$ given and $\lambda$ as random variable, Eq. (A8.54) can be used to compute the confidence limits $\hat{\lambda}_{l}$ and $\hat{\lambda}_{u}$ (see also pp.475, 546, 558). For $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$, this leads to

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(1-\varepsilon_{2}\right) \hat{\lambda}<\lambda \leq\left(1+\varepsilon_{1}\right) \hat{\lambda}\right\}=\frac{1}{(n-1)!} \int_{n\left(1-\varepsilon_{2}\right)}^{n\left(1+\varepsilon_{1}\right)} x^{n-1} e^{-x} d x
$$i. e.

$$
\hat{\lambda}_{l}=\left(1-\varepsilon_{2}\right) \hat{\lambda} \quad \& \quad \hat{\lambda}_{u}=\left(1+\varepsilon_{1}\right) \hat{\lambda}, \quad \text { with } \hat{\lambda}=n /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)
$$

and $\varepsilon_{1}, \varepsilon_{2}$ given by (see also Fig. A8.3 with $\theta=\lambda$ )

$$
\frac{1}{(n-1)!} \int_{n\left(1+\varepsilon_{1}\right)}^{\infty} x^{n-1} e^{-x} d x=\beta_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{1}{(n-1)!} \int_{0}^{n\left(1-\varepsilon_{2}\right)} x^{n-1} e^{-x} d x=\beta_{2}
$$

Using the definition of the chi-square distribution (Eq. (A6.103), Appendix A9.2), it follows that $1+\varepsilon_{1}=\left(\chi_{2 n, 1-\beta_{1}}^{2}\right) / 2 n$ and $1-\varepsilon_{2}=\left(\chi_{2 n, \beta_{2}}^{2}\right) / 2 n$ and thus

$$
\hat{\lambda}_{l}=\frac{\chi_{2 n, \beta_{2}}^{2}}{2\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\lambda}_{u}=\frac{\chi_{2 n, 1-\beta_{1}}^{2}}{2\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)}
$$

$\varepsilon_{2}=1$ or $\varepsilon_{1}=\infty$ lead to one-sided confidence intervals $\left[0, \hat{\lambda}_{u}\right]$ or $\left[\hat{\lambda}_{l}, \infty\right)$. Figure A8.6 gives the graphical relationship between $n, \gamma$, and $\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon_{2}=\varepsilon$ (Example A8.7).

The case considered by Eqs. (A8.53) to (A8.58) corresponds to the situation described in Example A8.2 (sampling plan with $n$ elements without replacement, terminated at the $n$th failure), and differs basically from that in Section A8.2.2.2.


Figure A8.6 Probability $\gamma$ that the interval $(1 \pm \varepsilon) \hat{\lambda}$ overlaps the true value of $\lambda$ for the case of a fixed number $n$ of failures $\left(\hat{\lambda}=n /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right), \operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}=1-e^{-\lambda t}, \bullet\right.$ for Example A8.7)# Example A8.7 

For the case considered by Eqs. (A8.53) to (A8.58), give for $n=50$ and $\gamma=0.9$ the two-sided confidence interval for the parameter $\lambda$ of an exponential distribution as a function of $\hat{\lambda}$.

## Solution

From Figure A8.6, $\varepsilon \approx 0.24$ yielding the confidence interval $[0.76 \hat{\lambda}, 1.24 \hat{\lambda}]$.

## A8.2.2.4 Availability Estimation (Erlangian Failure-Free and / or Repair Times)

Considerations of Section A8.2.2.3 can be extended to estimate the availability of a repairable item (described by the alternating renewal process of Fig. 6.2) for the case of Erlangian distributed failure-free and /or repair times (Appendix A6.10.3), and in particular for the case of constant failure and repair rates (Appendix A6.10.1).

Consider a repairable item in continuous operation, new at $t=0$ (Fig. 6.2), and assume constant failure and repair rates $\lambda(x)=\lambda, \mu(x)=\mu$ ( $x$ starting by 0 at the beginning of each operating or repair time, respectively). For this case, point and average unavailability rapidly converge (Table 6.3) to the asymptotic \& steady-state value $1-P A_{S}=1-A A_{S}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$, given as $\overline{P A}=\overline{A A}$ to simplify the notation

$$
\overline{P A}=1-P \mathrm{~A}=1-A A=\overline{A A}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)
$$

$\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$ is a probabilistic value and has his statistical counterpart in $D T /(U T+D T)$, where $D T$ is the down (repair) time and $U T=t-D T$ the up (operating) time observed in $(0, t]$. To simplify considerations, it will be assumed in the following $t \gg$ MTTR $=1 / \mu$ and that at the time point $t$ a repair is terminated and $k$ failure-free and repair times have occurred $(k=1,2, \ldots)$. Furthermore,

$$
\overline{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu \quad \text { instead of } \quad \overline{P A}=\overline{P A}_{a} /(1+\lambda / \mu) \approx \overline{P A}_{a}(1-\lambda / \mu)
$$

will be used here, yielding the counterpart $D T / U T \quad\left(\overline{P A}_{a}-(\lambda / \mu)^{2}<\overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{a}\right)$. Considering that at the time point $t$ a repair is terminated, it holds that

$$
U T / D T=\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}\right) /\left(t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{k}^{\prime}\right)
$$

where $t_{i} \& t_{i}^{\prime}$ are the observed values of failure-free and repair times $\tau_{i} \& \tau_{i}^{\prime}$, respectively. According to Eqs. (A6.102)-(A6.104), the quantity $2 \lambda\left(\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{k}\right)$ has a $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $v=2 k$ degrees of freedom; same is for the repair times $2 \mu\left(\tau_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{k}^{\prime}\right)$. From this, it follows (Appendix A9.4, footnote on p. 542) that

$$
\overline{P A}_{a} \cdot \frac{U T}{D T}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu} \cdot \frac{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{k}}{\tau_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{k}^{\prime}}=\frac{2 \lambda\left(\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{k}\right) / 2 k}{2 \mu\left(\tau_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{k}^{\prime}\right) / 2 k}
$$

is distributed according to a Fisher ( $\boldsymbol{F}$-) distribution with $v_{1}=v_{2}=2 k$ degrees of freedom ( $U T / D T$ is a random variable, $\overline{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu$ is regarded as an unknown parameter)

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\overline{P A}_{a} \frac{U T}{D T} \leq t\right\}=\frac{(2 k-1)!}{\left[(k-1)!\right]^{2}} \int_{0}^{t} \frac{x^{k-1}}{(1+x)^{2 k}} d x
$$Having observed for a repairable item described by Fig. 6.2 with constant failure rate $\lambda$ and repair rate $\mu \gg \lambda$, an operating time $U T=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}$ and a repair time $D T=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}$, the maximum likelihood estimate for $\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu$ is

$$
\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a}=(\lambda / \mu)=D T / U T=\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}\right) /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}\right)
$$

(Eq. (A8.25) with $L\left(U T / D T, \widehat{P A}_{a}\right) \sim\left[(U T / D T)^{k-1} \widehat{P A}_{a}^{k}\right] /\left(1+(U T / D T) \widehat{P A}_{a}\right)^{2 k}$ per Eq. (A8.61)); $D T / U T$ is biased, unbiased is $(1-1 / k) D T / U T, k>1$ (Example A8.10).

With the same considerations as for Eq. (A8.54), Eq. (A8.61) yields

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\frac{D T}{U T}\left(1-\varepsilon_{2}\right)<\widehat{P A}_{a} \leq \frac{D T}{U T}\left(1+\varepsilon_{1}\right)\right\}=\frac{(2 k-1)!}{[(k-1)!]^{2}} \int_{1-\varepsilon_{2}}^{1+\varepsilon_{1}} \frac{x^{k-1}}{(1+x)^{2 k}} d x
$$

and thus to the confidence limits $\widehat{P A}_{a_{l}}=\left(1-\varepsilon_{2}\right) \widehat{P A}_{a}$ and $\widehat{P A}_{a_{u}}=\left(1+\varepsilon_{1}\right) \widehat{P A}_{a}$, with $\widehat{P A}_{a}$ as in Eq. (A8.62) and $\varepsilon_{1}, \varepsilon_{2}$ related to the confidence level $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}$ by

$$
\frac{(2 k-1)!}{[(k-1)!]^{2}} \int_{1+\varepsilon_{1}}^{\infty} \frac{x^{k-1}}{(1+x)^{2 k}} d x=\beta_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{(2 k-1)!}{[(k-1)!]^{2}} \int_{0}^{1-\varepsilon_{2}} \frac{x^{k-1}}{(1+x)^{2 k}} d x=\beta_{2}
$$

From the definition of the Fisher ( $\boldsymbol{F}$-) distribution (Appendix A9.4), it follows that $\varepsilon_{1}=\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{1}}-1$ and $\varepsilon_{2}=1-\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, \beta_{2}} ;$ and thus, using $\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}, \beta_{2}}=1 / \boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{2}, \mathrm{v}_{1}, 1-\beta_{2}}$,

$$
\widehat{P A}_{a_{l}}=\widehat{P A}_{a} / \boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \widehat{P A}_{a_{u}}=\widehat{P A}_{a} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{1}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{2}} \& \boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{1}}$ are the $1-\beta_{2} \& 1-\beta_{1}$ quantiles of the Fisher ( $\boldsymbol{F}$-) distribution with $2 k$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.4). Figure 7.5 gives confidence limits for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$, useful for practical applications. $\widehat{P A}_{a_{l}} / \widehat{P A}_{l} \approx \widehat{P A}_{a_{u}} / \widehat{P A}_{u}$ $\approx \widehat{P A}_{a} / \widehat{P A}=1+\lambda / \mu \approx 1$ can often be used, yielding

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \widehat{P A} \approx \widehat{P A}_{a}=D T / U T \\
& 0 \leq \widehat{P A} \leq \widehat{P A}_{u}=\widehat{P A}_{a_{u}} \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{1} \text { and } \widehat{P A}_{a_{l}} \approx \widehat{P A}_{l} \leq \widehat{P A} \leq 1 \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

for point estimate and one sided confidence intervals of $\widehat{P A}$ (see Example A8.8 for an application). Corresponding values for the availability follow from $P A=1-\widehat{P A}$.

If failure free and/or repair times are Erlangian distributed (Eq. (A6.102)) with $\beta_{\lambda}=n_{\lambda} \& \beta_{\mu}=n_{\mu}, \boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{2}}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k, 2 k, 1-\beta_{1}}$ have to be replaced by $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k \cdot n_{\mu}, 2 k \cdot n_{\lambda}, 1-\beta_{2}}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 k \cdot n_{\lambda}, 2 k \cdot n_{\mu}, 1-\beta_{1}}$, for unchanged MTTF \& MTTR, see Example A8.11 on p. 571 $\left(\widehat{P A}_{a}=D T / U T\right.$ remains valid, $\left.\widehat{P A}_{a}=\left(\lambda^{*} n_{\mu} / \mu^{*} n_{\lambda}\right)=(\lambda / \mu)\right)$. Results based on the distribution of DT (Eq. (7.22)) are not parameter free (Section 7.2.2.3).

# Example A8.8 

For the estimation of an availability $P A, U T=1750 \mathrm{~h}, D T=35 \mathrm{~h}$ and $k=5$ failures and repairs have been observed. Give for const. failure \& repair rates the $90 \%$ lower limit of $P A$ (Fig.7.5, $\gamma=0.8$ ). Solution
From Eqs.(A8.62),(A8.65),(A8.66) \& Tab. A9.4a follows $\widehat{\widehat{P A}}_{a} \approx 2 \% \cdot 2.323$ and thus $P A>95.3 \%$. Suppl. results: Erlangian distr. times yield $\widehat{P A}_{u} \approx 2 \% \cdot 1.819$ for $n_{\mu}=3$ and $\approx 2 \% \cdot 1.61, n_{\mu}=n_{\lambda}=3$.# A8.3 Testing Statistical Hypotheses 

The objective when testing a statistical hypothesis is to solve the following problem, from one's own experience, the nature of the problem, or simply as a basic hypothesis, a specific null hypothesis $H_{0}$ is formulated for the statistical properties of the random variable considered; asked is a rule (test plan) which allows rejection or acceptance of $H_{0}$ on the basis of the mutually (statistically) independent realizations of this random variable in a suitable sample.

If $R$ is an unknown item's reliability, following null hypotheses $H_{0}$ are possible:
1a) $H_{0}: R=R_{0}$,
1b) $H_{0}: R>R_{0}$,
1c) $H_{0}: R<R_{0}$.
