To test whether the failure-free time of an item is distributed according to an exponential distribution $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)=1-e^{-\lambda t}$ with unknown $\lambda$, or $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)=1-e^{-\lambda_{0} t}$ with known $\lambda_{0}$, the following null hypotheses $H_{0}$ can be formulated:

2a) $H_{0}$ : the distribution function is $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$,
2b) $H_{0}$ : the distribution function is different from $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$,
2c) $H_{0}: \lambda=\lambda_{0}$, provided the distribution is exponential,
2d) $H_{0}: \lambda<\lambda_{0}$, provided the distribution is exponential,
2e) $H_{0}$ : the distribution function is $1-e^{-\lambda t}$, parameter $\lambda$ unknown.
It is usual to subdivide hypotheses into parametric (1a, 1b, 1c, 2c, 2d) and nonparametric ones ( $2 \mathrm{a}, 2 \mathrm{~b}$, and 2 e ). For each of these types, a distinction is also made between simple hypotheses (1a, 2a, 2c) and composite hypotheses (1b, 1c, 2b, 2d, 2e). When testing a hypothesis, two kinds of errors can occur (Table A8.2):

- type I error, when rejecting a true hypothesis $H_{0}$; the probability of this error is denoted by $\alpha$
- type II error, when accepting a false hypothesis $H_{0}$; the probability of this error is denoted by $\beta$ (to compute $\beta$, an alternative hypothesis $H_{1}$ is necessary; $\beta$ is then the probability of accepting $H_{0}$ assuming $H_{1}$ is true).

If the sample space is divided into two complementary sets, $\mathcal{A}$ for acceptance and $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ for rejection, the type I and type II errors are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \alpha=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { sample in } \overline{\mathcal{A}} \mid H_{0} \text { true }\} \\
& \beta=\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { sample in } \mathcal{A} \mid H_{0} \text { false }\left(H_{1} \text { true }\right)\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Both kinds of error are possible and cannot be minimized simultaneously. Often $\alpha$ is selected and a test is asked so that, for a given $H_{1}, \beta$ will be minimized. It can beTable A8.2 Possible errors when testing a statistical hypothesis

|  | $H_{0}$ is rejected | $H_{0}$ is accepted |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| $H_{0}$ is true | false $\rightarrow$ type I error $(\alpha)$ | correct |
| $H_{0}$ is false $\left(H_{1}\right.$ is true) | correct | false $\rightarrow$ type II error $(\beta)$ |

shown that such a test always exists if $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ are simple hypotheses [A8.22]. For given alternative hypothesis $H_{1}, \beta$ can often be calculated and the quantity $1-\beta=\operatorname{Pr}\{$ sample in $\left.\bar{\lambda} \mid H_{1} \text { true }\right\}$ is referred as the power of the test.

The following sections consider some procedures for quality control and reliability tests, see Chapter 7 for refinements and applications. Such procedures are basically obtained by investigating suitable quantities observed in the sample.

# A8.3.1 Testing an Unknown Probability $p$ 

Let $A$ be an event which can occur at every independent trial with the constant, unknown probability $p$. A rule (test plan) is asked which allows testing the hypothesis

$$
H_{0}: p<p_{0}
$$



The type I error should be nearly equal to (but not greater than) $\alpha$ for $p=p_{0}$. The type II error should be nearly equal to (but not greater than) $\beta$ for $p=p_{1} .{ }^{+)}$ Such a situation often occurs in practical applications, in particular in

- quality control, where $p$ refers to the defective probability or fraction of defective items ${ }^{+*)}$
- reliability tests for a given fixed mission, where it is usual to set $p=1-R$ ( $R=$ reliability).

In both cases, $\alpha$ is the producer's risk and $\beta$ the consumer's risk. The two most frequently used procedures for testing hypotheses defined by (A8.69) and (A8.70), with $p_{1}>p_{0}$, are the simple two-sided sampling plan and the sequential test (one-sided sampling plans are considered in Appendix A8.3.1.3).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{+)}$Considering the visualization given with Eqs. (A8.69) \& (A8.70), $H_{0}$ is true for $p<p_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ is true for $p>p_{1}$; between $p_{0}$ and $p_{1}$ both hypothesis are false.
    ${ }^{\text {++) }}$ No distinction is made in this book between defect and nonconformity (except pp. 388, 394, 395); however, defect has a legal connotation and has to be used when dealing with product liability.# A8.3.1.1 Simple Two-sided Sampling Plan 

The rule for the simple two-sided sampling plan (simple two-sided test) is:

1. For given $p_{0}, p_{1}>p_{0}, \alpha \& \beta(0<\alpha<1-\beta<1)$, determine the smallest integer $c$ and the value $n$ satisfying (see example 7.2 on p. 316)

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p_{0}^{i}\left(1-p_{0}\right)^{n-i} \geq 1-\alpha
$$

and

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p_{1}^{i}\left(1-p_{1}\right)^{n-i} \leq \beta
$$

2. Perform $n$ independent trials (Bernoulli trials), determine the number $k$ in which the event $A$ (component defective for example) has occurred, and

- reject $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$, if $k>c$,
- accept $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$, if $k \leq c$.

As in the case of Eqs. (A8.37) and (A8.38), the proof of the above rule is based on the monotonic property of $B_{n}(c, p)=\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i}$, see also Fig A8.4. For known $n, c$ and $p, B_{n}(c, p)$ gives the probability of having up to $c$ defectives in a sample of size $n$. Thus, assuming $H_{0}$ true $\left(p<p_{0}\right)$, it follows that the probability of rejecting $H_{0}$ (i. e. the probability of having more than $c$ defectives in a sample of size $n$ ) is smaller than $\alpha$

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { rejection of } H_{0} \mid H_{0} \text { true }\right\}=\sum_{i=c+1}^{n}\binom{n}{i}\left.p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i}\right|_{p<p_{0}}<\alpha
$$

Similarly, if $H_{1}$ is true $\left(p>p_{1}\right)$, it follows that the probability of accepting $H_{0}$ is smaller than $\beta$

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { acceptance of } H_{0} \mid H_{1} \text { true }\right\}=\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i}\left.p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i}\right|_{p>p_{1}}<\beta
$$

The assumptions made with Eqs. (A8.71) and (A8.72) are thus satisfied. As shown by the above inequalities, the type I error and the type II error are for this case $<\alpha$ for $p<p_{0}$ and $<\beta$ for $p>p_{1}$, respectively. Figure A8.7 shows the results for $p_{0}=1 \%, p_{1}=2 \%$, and $\alpha=\beta \leq 20 \%$. The curve of Fig. A8.7 is known as the operating characteristic curve (OC). If $p_{0}$ and $p_{1}$ are small (up to a few \%) or close to 1, the Poisson approximation (Eq. (A6.129))

$$
\binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i} \approx \frac{m^{k}}{k!} e^{-m}, \quad m=n p
$$

is generally used.

Figure A8.7 Operating characteristic curve (acceptance probability curve) as a function of the unknown probability $p$ for fixed $n \& c\left(p_{0}=1 \%, p_{1}=2 \%, \alpha=\beta=0.185, n=462, c=6\right.$ as per Tab. 7.3)

# A8.3.1.2 Sequential Test 

Assume that in a two-sided sampling plan with $n=50$ and $c=2$ per Appendix A8.3.1.1, a 3rd defect, i. e. $k=3$, occurs at the 12 th trial. Since $k>c$, the hypothesis $H_{0}$ will be rejected as per procedure (A8.73), independent of how often the event $A$ will occur during the remaining 38 trials. This example brings up the question of whether a plan can be established for testing $H_{0}$ in which no unnecessary trials (the remaining 38 in the above example) have to be performed. To solve this problem, A. Wald proposed the sequential test [A8.33]. For this test, one element after another is taken from the lot and tested. Depending upon the actual frequency of the observed event, the decision is made to either

- reject $H_{0}$
- accept $H_{0}$
- perform a further trial.

The testing procedure can be described as follows (Fig. A8.8),
in a system of Cartesian coordinates, the number $n$ of trials is recorded on the abscissa and the number $k$ of trials in which the event $A$ occurred on the ordinate; the test is stopped with acceptance or rejection as soon as the resulting staircase curve $k=\mathrm{f}(n)$ crosses the acceptance or the rejection line given in the Cartesian coordinates for specified values of $p_{0}, p_{1}, \alpha$, and $\beta$.

The acceptance and rejection lines are
Acceptance line: $k=a n-b_{1}$,
Rejection line: $\quad k=a n+b_{2}$,
with

Figure A8.8 Sequential test for $p_{0}=1 \%, p_{1}=2 \%$, and $\alpha=\beta=20 \%$

$$
a=\frac{\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}, \quad b_{1}=\frac{\ln \frac{1-\alpha}{\beta}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}, \quad b_{2}=\frac{\ln \frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}
$$

Figure A8.8 shows acceptance and rejection lines for $p_{0}=1 \%, p_{1}=2 \%, \alpha=\beta \leqq 20 \%$. Practical remarks to sequential tests are given in Sections 7.1.2.2 and 7.2.3.2.

# A8.3.1.3 Simple One-sided Sampling Plan 

In many practical applications only $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ or $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ are specified; i. e. one want to test $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$ against $H_{1}: p>p_{0}$ with given type I error $\alpha$, or $H_{0}: p<p_{1}$ against $H_{1}: p>p_{1}$ with given type II error $\beta$. For these cases, only Eq. (A8.71) or Eq. (A8.72) can be used and the test plan is a pair $c, n$ for each selected value of $c=0,1, \ldots$ and calculated value of $n$. Such plans are termed one-sided sampling plans.

Setting $p_{1}=p_{0}$ in the relationship (A8.69)-(A8.70) or in other words, testing

$$
H_{0}: p<p_{0}
$$

against

$$
H_{1}: p>p_{0}
$$

with type I error $\alpha$, i. e. using one $(c, n)$ pair (for $c=0,1, \ldots$ ) from Eq. (A8.71) and the test procedure (A8.73), the consumer's risk can become very large and reach the value $1-\alpha$ for $p=p_{0}$. Depending upon the value selected for $c=0,1, \ldots$ and that calculated for $n$ (the largest integer $n$ which satisfies inequality (A8.71)), different plans (pairs of $(c, n)$ ) are possible. Each of these plans yields different consumer's risks. Figure A8.9 shows this for some $c$ values (the consumer's risk

Figure A8.9 Operating characteristics curve (acceptance probability curves) as a function of the unknown probability $p$ for $p_{0}=A Q L=1 \%$, producer risk $\alpha=0.1$ and $c=0(n=10), c=1(n=53)$, $c=2(n=110), c=3(n=174)$ and $c=\infty(n=\infty)$ as per Fig. 7.3
(type II error) is the ordinate of the operating characteristic curve for $p>p_{0}$ ). In practical applications, it is common usage to define

$$
p_{0}=\mathrm{AQL}
$$

where AQL stands for Acceptable Quality Level. The above considerations show that with the choice of only $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ (instead of $p_{0}, p_{1}, \alpha$, and $\beta$ ) the producer can realize an advantage if small values of $c$ are used.

On the other hand, setting $p_{0}=p_{1}$ in the relationship (A8.69)-(A8.70), or testing

$$
H_{0}: p<p_{1}
$$

against

$$
H_{1}: p>p_{1}
$$

with type II error $\beta$, i. e. using one $(c, n)$ pair (for $c=0,1, \ldots$ ) from Eq. (A8.72) and the test procedure (A8.73), the producer's risk (type I error) can become very large and reach the value $1-\beta$ for $p=p_{1}$. Depending upon the value selected for $c=0,1, \ldots$ and that calculated for $n$ (the smallest integer $n$ which satisfies inequality (A8.72)), different plans (pairs of $(c, n)$ ) are possible. Considerations here are similar to those of the previous case, where only $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ were selected. For small values of $c$ the consumer can realize an advantage. In practical applications, it is common usage to define

$$
p_{1}=\text { LTPD }
$$

where LTPD stands for Lot Tolerance Percent Defective. Further remarks on one-sided sampling plans are in Section 7.1.3 on pp. 318-19.# A8.3.1.4 Availability Demonstration (Erlangian Failure-Free and/or Repair Times) 

Considerations of Section A8.2.2.4 on availability estimation can be extended to demonstrate the availability of a repairable item (described by the alternating renewal process of Fig. 6.2) for the case of Erlangian distributed failure-free and / or repair times (Appendix A6.10.3). In particular thus, for the case of constant failure and repair rates (exponentially distributed failure-free and repair times).

Consider a repairable item in continuous operation, new at $t=0$ (Fig. 6.2), and assume constant failure and repair rates $\lambda(x)=\lambda, \mu(x)=\mu$ ( $x$ starting by 0 at the beginning of each operating or repair time, respectively). For this case, point and average unavailability rapidly converge (Table 6.3) to the asymptotic \& steady-state value $1-P A_{S}=1-A A_{S}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$, given as $\overline{P A}=\overline{A A}$ to simplify the notation

$$
\overline{P A}=1-P \mathrm{~A}=1-A A=\overline{A A}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)
$$

$\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$ is a probabilistic value and has his statistical counterpart in $D T /(U T+D T)$, where $D T$ is the down (repair) time and $U T=t-D T$ the up (operating) time observed in $(0, t\}$. From Eq. (A8.83) it follows that

$$
\frac{\overline{P A}}{1-\overline{P A}}=\frac{\overline{P A}}{P A}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}
$$

As in Appendix A8.2.2.4, it will be assumed that at the time point $t$ a repair is terminated, and exactly $n$ failure free and $n$ repair times have occurred. However, for a demonstration test, $P A$ or $\overline{P A}$ will be specified (Eqs. (A.8.88) - (A8.89)) and $D T / U T$ observed. Similar as for Eq. (A8.60), the quantity (see footnote on p. 542)

$$
\frac{P A}{\overline{P A}} \cdot \frac{D T}{U T}=\frac{\mu}{\lambda} \cdot \frac{\tau_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{n}^{\prime}}{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}}=\frac{2 \mu\left(\tau_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{n}^{\prime}\right) / 2 n}{2 \lambda\left(\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}\right) / 2 n}
$$

is distributed according to a Fisher ( $\boldsymbol{F}$-) distribution with $v_{1}=v_{2}=2 n$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.4). From this (with $D T / U T$ as a random variable),

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\frac{P A}{\overline{P A}} \cdot \frac{D T}{U T} \leq t\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\frac{D T}{U T} \leq t \frac{\overline{P A}}{P A}\right\}=\frac{(2 n-1)!}{\{(n-1)!\}^{2}} \int_{0}^{t} \frac{x^{n-1}}{(1+x)^{2 n}} d x
$$

Setting

$$
\delta=t \cdot \overline{P A} / P A
$$

Eq. (A8.85) yields

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\frac{D T}{U T} \leq \delta\right\}=\frac{(2 n-1)!}{\{(n-1)!\}^{2}} \int_{0}^{\delta \cdot P A / \overline{P A}} \frac{x^{n-1}}{(1+x)^{2 n}} d x
$$

Considering $D T / U T=\left(\tau_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{n}^{\prime}\right) /\left(\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}\right)$, i. e. the sum of $n$ repair times divided by the sum of the corresponding $n$ failure-free times, a rule for testing

$$
H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0}
$$against the alternative hypothesis

$$
H_{1}: \overline{P A}>\overline{P A}_{1} \quad\left(\overline{P A}_{1} \geq \overline{P A}_{0}\right)
$$

can be established (as in Appendix A8.3.1.1) for given type I error (producer risk) nearly equal to (but not greater than) $\alpha$ for $\overline{P A}=\overline{P A}_{0}$ and type II error (consumer risk) nearly equal to (but not greater than) $\beta$ for $\overline{P A}=\overline{P A}_{1}$ (Table A8.2)

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left.\frac{D T}{U T}>\delta \right\rvert\, \overline{P A}=\overline{P A}_{0}\right\} \leq \alpha \quad \text { and } \quad \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left.\frac{D T}{U T} \leq \delta \right\rvert\, \overline{P A}=\overline{P A}_{1}\right\} \leq \beta \text {. (A8.90) }
$$

From Eqs. (A8.87) \& (A8.90), and considering the Fisher ( $\boldsymbol{F}$-) distribution (Appendix A9.4), it follows that $\delta \cdot P A_{0} / \overline{P A}_{0} \geq \boldsymbol{F}_{2 \mathrm{n}, 2 \mathrm{n}, 1-\alpha}$ and $\delta \cdot P A_{1} / \overline{P A}_{1} \leq \boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, \beta}$. Eliminating $\delta$ (using $\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}, \beta}=1 / \boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{2}, \mathrm{v}_{1}, 1-\beta}$ and taking the sign $=$ for $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 \mathrm{n}, 2 \mathrm{n}, 1-\alpha}$ or for $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, \beta}$ ), the rule for testing $H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0}$ against $H_{1}: \overline{P A}>\overline{P A}_{1}$ follows as (see also [A8.29, A2.6 (IEC 61070)]):

1. For given $\overline{P A}_{0}, \overline{P A}_{1}, \alpha \& \beta(0<\alpha<1-\beta<1)$, find the smallest integer $n$ which satisfy

$$
\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\beta} \leq \frac{\overline{P A}_{1}}{\overline{P A}_{0}} \cdot \frac{P A_{0}}{P A_{1}}=\frac{\left(1-P A_{1}\right) P A_{0}}{\left(1-P A_{0}\right) P A_{1}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\beta}$ are the $1-\alpha$ and $1-\beta$ quantiles of the $\boldsymbol{F}$-distribution with $2 n$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.4), and compute the limiting value

$$
\delta=\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha} \overline{P A}_{0} / P A_{0}=\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha}\left(1-P A_{0}\right) / P A_{0}
$$

2. Observe $n$ failure free times $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n} \&$ corresponding repair times $t_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, t_{n}^{\prime}$, and

- reject $H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0}, \quad$ if $\quad \frac{t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{n}^{\prime}}{t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}}>\delta$
- accept $H_{0}: \overline{P A}<\overline{P A}_{0}, \quad$ if $\quad \frac{t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{n}^{\prime}}{t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}} \leq \delta$,
see Example 8.9. Results for the availability follows from $P A=1-\overline{P A}$.
If failure free and / or repair times are Erlangian distributed (Eq. (A6.102)) with $\beta_{\lambda}=n_{\lambda} \& \beta_{\mu}=n_{\mu}, \boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\alpha}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n, 2 n, 1-\beta}$ have to be replaced by $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n \cdot n_{\mu}, 2 n \cdot n_{\lambda}, 1-\alpha}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_{2 n \cdot n_{\lambda}, 2 n \cdot n_{\mu}, 1-\beta}$, for unchanged MTTF \& MTTR, see Example A8.11. Results based on the distribution of DT (Eq. (7.22)) are not parameter free (Section 7.2.2.3).

# Example A8.9 

For the demonstration of an availability $P A$, customer and producer agree the following parameters: $\overline{P A}_{0}=1 \%, \overline{P A}_{1}=6 \%, \alpha=\beta=10 \%$. Give for the case of constant failure and repair rates $(\lambda(x)=\lambda$ and $\mu(x)=\mu \gg \lambda)$ the number $n$ of failures and repairs that have to be observed and the acceptance limit $\delta$.

## Solution

Eq. (A8.91) \& Table A9.4a yields $n=5\left(\left(\boldsymbol{F}_{10,10,0.9}\right)^{2} \approx 2.32^{2}<\left(6 \cdot 99 / 1 \cdot 94\right)<2.59^{2} \approx\left(\boldsymbol{F}_{8,8,09}\right)^{2}\right)$, see also Tab. 7.2. $\delta=\boldsymbol{F}_{10,10,0.9} \overline{P A}_{0} / P A_{0} \approx 2.32 \cdot 1 / 99=0.0234$ follows from Eq. (A8.92).
Suppl. result: Erlangian distr. repair times with $n_{\mu}=3$ yields $n=3, \delta \approx 0.0288(2.85 \cdot 2.13<6.32)$.# Example A8.10 

Give an unbiased estimate for $\overline{P A}_{\alpha}=\lambda / \mu$.

## Solution

From Eq. (A8.61) one recognizes that $\lambda U T / \mu D T$ has a $\boldsymbol{F}$ - distribution with $v_{1}=v_{2}=2 k$. Thus (Table A9.4), $\mathrm{E}\{\lambda U T / \mu D T\}=k /(k-1), k>1$. Considering now $\lambda / \mu$ as a random variable

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\frac{\lambda}{\mu} \leq t\right\}=\frac{(2 k-1)!}{\{(k-1)!\}^{2}} \int_{0}^{t U T} \frac{x^{k-1}}{(1+x)^{2 k}} d x
$$

and this leads to

$$
\mathrm{E}\{\lambda \hat{\prime} \mu\}=\frac{D T}{U T} \cdot \frac{k}{k-1}, \quad k>1
$$

$\lambda \hat{\prime} \mu=D T / U T$ is biased; unbiased is $(1-1 / k) D T / U T, k>1$.

## Example A8.11

Give the degrees of freedom of the $\boldsymbol{F}$-distribution for the case of Erlangian distributed failure-free \& repair times with parameters $\lambda^{*}, n_{\lambda} \& \mu^{*}, n_{\mu}$, respectively; with $\lambda^{*}=\lambda n_{\lambda} \& \mu^{*}=\mu n_{\mu}$ because of the unchanged $M T T F=1 / \lambda=n_{\lambda} / \lambda^{*} \& M T T R=1 / \mu=n_{\mu} / \mu^{*}$ as per Eqs. (A6.84) \& (A6.99).

## Solution

Let $\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{k}$ be the exponentially distributed failure-free times with mean $M T T F=1 / \lambda$. If the actual failure-free times are Erlangian distributed with parameters $\lambda^{*}, n_{\lambda}$ and mean $M T T F=n_{\lambda} / \lambda^{*}=1 / \lambda$, Eqs. A(6.102) - (A6.104) show that the quantity

$$
2 \lambda^{*}\left(\tau_{11}+\tau_{12}+\ldots+\tau_{1 n_{\lambda}}+\ldots+\tau_{k 1}+\tau_{k 2}+\ldots+\tau_{k n_{\lambda}}\right)
$$

corresponding to the sum of $k$ Erlangian ( $\lambda^{*}, n_{\lambda}$ ) distributed failure-free times, has a $\chi^{*}$-distribution with $v=2 k n_{\lambda}$ degrees of freedom (Eq. (A6.104)). Similar is for the repair times $\tau_{i}^{\prime}$. Thus, the quantity (Eq. (A8.60))

$$
\overline{P A}_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{U T}{D T}=\frac{\lambda^{*} / n_{\lambda}}{\mu^{*} / n_{\mu}} \cdot \frac{U T}{D T}=\frac{2 \lambda^{*}\left(\tau_{11}+\tau_{12}+\ldots+\tau_{1 n_{\lambda}}+\ldots+\tau_{k 1}+\tau_{k 2}+\ldots+\tau_{k n_{\lambda}}\right) / 2 k n_{\lambda}}{2 \mu^{*}\left(\tau_{11}^{\prime}+\tau_{12}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{1 n_{\mu}}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{k 1}^{\prime}+\tau_{k 2}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{k n_{\mu}}^{\prime}\right) / 2 k n_{\mu}}
$$

obtained by considering $\lambda=\lambda^{*} / n_{\lambda}, \mu=\mu^{*} / n_{\mu}$ (to conserve $M T T F=1 / \lambda=n_{\lambda} / \lambda^{*}, M T T R=1 / \mu=n_{\mu} / \mu^{*}$ ), has a $\boldsymbol{F}$-distribution with $v_{1}=2 k \cdot n_{\lambda}$ and $v_{2}=2 k \cdot n_{\mu}$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.4). Similarly (Eq. (A8.84)),

$$
\frac{P A}{\overline{P A}} \cdot \frac{D T}{U T}=\frac{\mu^{*} / n_{\mu}}{\lambda^{*} / n_{\lambda}} \cdot \frac{D T}{U T}=\frac{2 \mu^{*}\left(\tau_{11}^{\prime}+\tau_{12}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{1 n_{\mu}}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{n 1}^{\prime}+\tau_{n 2}^{\prime}+\ldots+\tau_{n n_{\mu}}^{\prime}\right) / 2 n n_{\mu}}{2 \lambda^{*}\left(\tau_{11}+\tau_{12}+\ldots+\tau_{1 n_{\lambda}}+\ldots+\tau_{n 1}+\tau_{n 2}+\ldots+\tau_{n n_{\lambda}}\right) / 2 n n_{\lambda}}
$$

has a $\boldsymbol{F}$-distribution with $v_{1}=2 n \cdot n_{\mu}$ and $v_{2}=2 n \cdot n_{\lambda}$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.4).

## A8.3.2 Goodness-of-fit Tests for Completely Specified $\mathbf{F}_{0}(t)$

Goodness-of-fit tests have the purpose to verify agreement of observed data with a postulated (completely specified or only partially known) model, see e. g. [A8.9]. A typical example is as follows: Given $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ as $n$ independent observations of a random variable $\tau$, a rule is asked to test the null hypothesis

$$
H_{0}: \text { the distribution function of } \tau \text { is } F_{0}(t)
$$

against the alternative hypothesis$H_{1}$ : the distribution function of $\tau$ is not $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$.
$\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ can be completely defined (as in this section) or depend on some unknown parameters which must be estimated from the observed data (as in the next section). In general, less can be said about the risk of accepting a false hypothesis $H_{0}$ (to compute the type II error $\beta$, a specific alternative hypothesis $H_{1}$ must be assumed). For some distribution functions used in reliability theory, particular procedures have been developed, often with different alternative hypotheses $H_{1}$ and investigation of the corresponding test power, see e. g. [A8.1, A8.9, A8.23]. Among the distribution-free procedures, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramér-von Mises, and chi-square ( $\chi^{2}$ ) tests are frequently used in practical applications to solve the goodness-of-fit problem given by Eqs. (A8.94) \& (A8.95). These tests are based upon comparison of the empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$, defined by Eq. (A8.1), with a postulated distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$.

1. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test uses the (supremum) statistic

$$
D_{n}=\sup _{-\infty<t<\infty}\left|\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)-\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\right|
$$

introduced in Appendix A8.1.1. A. N. Kolmogorov showed [A8.20] that if $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is continuous, the distribution of $D_{n}$ under the hypothesis $H_{0}$ is independent of $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$. For a given type I error $\alpha$, the hypothesis $H_{0}$ must be rejected for

$$
D_{n}>y_{1-\alpha}
$$

where $y_{1-\alpha}$ is defined by

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{D_{n}>y_{1-\alpha} \mid H_{0} \text { is true }\right\}=\alpha
$$

Values for $y_{1-\alpha}$ are given in Tables A8.1 and A9.5. Figure A8.10 illustrates the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test with hypothesis $H_{0}$ not rejected. Because of its graphical visualization, in particular when probability charts are used (Appendix A8.1.3, Section 7.5, Appendix A9.8), the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is often used in reliability data analysis.
2. The Cramér-von Mises test uses the statistic

$$
W_{n}^{2}=n \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)-\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\right]^{2} d \mathrm{~F}_{0}(t)
$$

As in the case of the $D_{n}$ statistic, for $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ continuous the distribution of $W_{n}^{2}$ is independent of $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ and tabulated (see for instance [A9.5]). The Cramér von Mises statistic belongs to the so-called quadratic statistic defined by

$$
Q_{n}=n \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)-\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\right]^{2} \psi(t) d \mathrm{~F}_{0}(t)
$$

Figure A8.10 Kolmogorov-Smirnov test $(n=20, \alpha=20 \%)$
where $\psi(t)$ is a suitable weight function. $\psi(t) \equiv 1$ yields the $W_{n}^{2}$ statistic and $\psi(t)=\left[\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\right)\right]^{-1}$ yields the Anderson - Darling statistic $A_{n}^{2}$. Using the transformation $z_{(i)}=\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(t_{(i)}\right)$, calculation of $W_{n}^{2}$ and in particular of $A_{n}^{2}$ becomes easy, see e. g. [A8.10]. This transformation can also be used for the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, although here no change occurs in $D_{n}$.
3.The chi-square $\left(\chi^{2}\right)$ goodness-of-fit test starts from a selected partition $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right),\left(a_{2}, a_{3}\right], \ldots,\left(a_{k}, a_{k+1}\right]$ of the set of possible values of $\tau$ and uses the statistic

$$
X_{n}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{\left(k_{i}-n p_{i}\right)^{2}}{n p_{i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{k_{i}^{2}}{n p_{i}}-n, \quad \sum_{i=1}^{k} k_{i}=n, \sum_{i=1}^{k} p_{i}=1
$$

where (Eq. (A8.1))

$$
k_{i}=n\left(\hat{\mathrm{~F}}_{n}\left(a_{i+1}\right)-\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}\left(a_{i}\right)\right)
$$

is the number of observations (realizations of $\tau$ ) in $\left(a_{i}, a_{i+1}\right]$ and

$$
n p_{i}=n\left(\mathrm{~F}_{0}\left(a_{i+1}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i}\right)\right)
$$

is the expected number of observations in $\left(a_{i}, a_{i+1}\right]$; obviously, $k_{1}+\ldots+k_{k}=n$ and $p_{1}+\ldots+p_{k}=1$. Under the hypothesis $H_{0}$, K. Pearson [A8.28] has shown that the asymptotic distribution of $X_{n}^{2}$ for $n \rightarrow \infty$ is a $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $k-1$ degrees of freedom. Thus, for given type 1 error $\alpha$,

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\mathrm{X}_{n}^{2}>\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2} \mid H_{0} \text { true }\right\}=\alpha
$$

holds, and the hypothesis $H_{0}$ must be rejected if

$$
\mathrm{X}_{n}^{2}>\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}
$$

$\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $k-1$ degrees offreedom (Table A9.2). The classes $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right],\left(a_{2}, a_{3}\right], \ldots,\left(a_{k}, a_{k+1}\right]$ have to be chosen before the test is performed, in such a way that all $p_{i}$ are approximately equal. Convergence is generally good, even for relatively small values of $n\left(n p_{i} \geq 5\right)$. Thus,
by selecting the classes $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right], \ldots,\left(a_{k}, a_{k+1}\right]$ (before test begin) one should take care that all $n p_{i}$ are almost equal and possibly $\geq 5$.

Example A8.12 shows an application of the chi-square test.
When in a goodness-of-fit test, the deviation between $\hat{F}_{n}(t)$ and $F_{0}(t)$ seems abnormally small, a verification against superconform (superuniform if the transformation $z_{(i)}=\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(t_{(i)}\right)$ is used) can become necessary. Tabulated values for the lower limit $l_{1-\alpha}$ for $D_{n}$ are e.g. in [A8.1] (for instance, $\alpha=0.1 \rightarrow l_{1-\alpha} \approx 0.57 / \sqrt{n}$ instead of $\approx 1.22 / \sqrt{n}$ as per Table A8.1).

# Example A8.12 

Accelerated life testing of a wet Al electrolytic capacitor leads to the following 13 ordered observations of lifetime: $59,71,153,235,347,589,835,913,1185,1273,1399,1713$, and 2567 h . Using the chi-square test and the 4 classes ( 0,200$],(200,600],(600,1200],(1200, \infty)$, verify at the level $\alpha=0.1$ (i. e. with a type I error $\alpha=0.1$ ) whether or not the capacitor's failurefree time $\tau$ is distributed according to the Weibull distribution $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}[\tau \leq t]=1-e^{-\left(10^{-3} t\right)^{1.2}}$ (hypothesis $H_{0}$ ).

## Solution

The given classes yield number of observations of $k_{1}=3, k_{2}=3, k_{3}=3$, and $k_{4}=4$. The numbers of expected observations in each classes are, according to Eq. (A8.103), $n p_{1} \approx 1.754$, $n p_{2} \approx 3.684, n p_{3} \approx 3.817$, and $n p_{4} \approx 3.745$. From Eq. (A8.101) it follows that $X_{13}^{2} \approx 1.204$ and from Table A9.2, $\chi_{\frac{2}{3} 0.9}^{2} \approx 6.251 . \quad H_{0}: \mathrm{F}_{0}(t)=1-e^{-\left(10^{-3} t\right)^{1.2}}$ cannot be rejected because $X_{n}^{2}<\chi_{k-\mathrm{L} 1-\alpha}^{2}$.

## A8.3.3 Goodness-of-fit Tests for a Distribution $\mathbf{F}_{0}(t)$ with Unknown Parameters

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and the tests based on quadratic statistic can be used with some modification when the underlying distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is not completely known (unknown parameters). The distribution of the involved statistic $D_{n}, W_{n}^{2}, A_{n}^{2}$ must be calculated (often using Monte Carlo simulation) for each type of distribution and can depend on parameter values [A8.1]. For instance, in the case of an exponential distribution $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t, \lambda)=1-e^{-\lambda t}$ with parameter $\lambda$ estimated as per Eq. (A8.28) $\hat{\lambda}=n /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)$, the values of $y_{1-\alpha}$ for the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test have to be modified from those given in Table A8.1, e. g. from $y_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.36 / \sqrt{n}$ for $\alpha=0.05$ and $y_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.22 / \sqrt{n}$ for $\alpha=0.1$ to [A8.1]

$$
\alpha=0.05 \rightarrow y_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.09 / \sqrt{n} \quad \text { and } \quad \alpha=0.10 \rightarrow y_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.0 / \sqrt{n}
$$Also a modification of $D_{n}$ in $D_{n}^{\prime} \approx\left(D_{n}-0.2 / n\right)(1+0.26 / \sqrt{n}+0.5 / n)$ is recommended [A8.1]. A heuristic procedure is to use half of the sample (randomly selected) to estimate the parameters and continue with the whole sample and the basic procedure given in Appendix A8.3.2 [A8.11, A8.32].

The chi-square $\left(\chi^{2}\right)$ test offers a more general approach. Let $\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(t, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)$ be the assumed distribution function, known up to the parameters $\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}(r<k-1)$. If

- the unknown parameters $\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}$ are estimated according to the maximum likelihood method on the basis of the observed frequencies $k_{i}$ using the multinomial distribution (Eq. (A6.124)), i.e. from the following system of $r$ algebraic equations (Example A8.13)

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{k_{i}}{p_{i}\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)} \cdot\left.\frac{\partial p_{i}\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)}{\partial \theta_{j}}\right|_{\theta_{j}=\hat{\theta}_{j}}=0, \quad j=1, \ldots, r
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{i}=\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i+1}, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i}, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)>0 \\
& p_{1}+\ldots+p_{k}=1
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
k_{1}+\ldots+k_{k}=n
$$

- $\frac{\partial p_{i}}{\partial \theta_{j}}$ and $\frac{\partial^{2} p_{i}}{\partial \theta_{j} \partial \theta_{m}}$ exist $(i=1, \ldots, k ; j, m=1, \ldots, r<k-1)$,
- the matrix with elements $\frac{\partial p_{i}}{\partial \theta_{j}}$ is of rank $r$,
then the statistic

$$
\hat{\mathrm{x}}_{n}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{\left(k_{i}-n \hat{p}_{i}\right)^{2}}{n \hat{p}_{i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{k_{i}^{2}}{n \hat{p}_{i}}-n
$$

calculated with $\hat{p}_{i}=\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i+1}, \hat{\theta}_{1}, \ldots, \hat{\theta}_{r}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i}, \hat{\theta}_{1}, \ldots, \hat{\theta}_{r}\right)$, has under $H_{0}$ asymptotically for $n \rightarrow \infty$ a $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $k-1-r$ degrees of freedom (R. A. Fisher [A8.15 (1924)]), see Example 7.18 for a practical application. Thus, for a given type I error $\alpha$,

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\hat{\mathrm{X}}_{n}^{2}>\chi_{k-1-r, 1-\alpha}^{2} \mid H_{0} \text { true }\right\}=\alpha
$$

holds, and the hypothesis $H_{0}$ must be rejected if

$$
\hat{\mathrm{x}}_{n}^{2}>\chi_{k-1-r, 1-\alpha}^{2}
$$

$\chi_{k-1-r, 1-\alpha}^{2}$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $k-1-r$ degrees of freedom. Calculation of the parameters $\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}$ directly from the observations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ can lead to wrong decisions.# Example A8.13 

Prove Eq. (A8.107).

## Solution

The observed frequencies $k_{1}, \ldots, k_{k}$ in the classes $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right],\left(a_{2}, a_{3}\right], \ldots,\left(a_{k}, a_{k+1}\right]$ result from $n$ trials, where each observation falls into one of the classes $\left(a_{i}, a_{i+1}\right]$ with probability $p_{i}=\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i+1}, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{0}\left(a_{i}, \theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right), i=1, \ldots, k$. The multinomial distribution applies. Taking into account Eq. (A6.124),

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { in } n \text { trials } A_{1} \text { occurs } k_{1} \text { times, } \ldots, A_{k} \text { occurs } k_{k} \text { times }\right\}=\frac{n!}{k_{1}!\ldots k_{k}!} p_{1}^{k_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{k_{k}}
$$

with
$k_{1}+\ldots+k_{k}=n$ and $p_{1}+\ldots+p_{k}=1$,
the likelihood function (Eq. (A8.23)) becomes

$$
\mathrm{L}\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k}\right)=\frac{n!}{k_{1}!\ldots k_{k}!} p_{1}^{k_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{k_{k}}
$$

or

$$
\ln \mathrm{L}\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k}\right)=\ln \frac{n!}{k_{1}!\ldots k_{k}!}+k_{1} \ln p_{1}+\ldots+k_{k} \ln p_{k}
$$

with

$$
p_{i}=p_{i}\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{r}\right), \quad p_{1}+\ldots+p_{k}=1, \text { and } k_{1}+\ldots+k_{k}=n
$$

Equation (A8.107) follows then from

$$
\frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \theta_{j}}=0 \text { for } \theta_{j}=\hat{\theta}_{j} \text { and } j=1, \ldots, r
$$

which complete the proof. A practical application with $r=1$ is given in Example 7.18.# A9 Tables and Charts 

## A9.1 Standard Normal Distribution

Definition: $\quad \Phi(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x, \quad-\infty<t<\infty$
Parameters: $\mathrm{E}[\tau]=0, \quad \operatorname{Var}[\tau]=1, \quad$ Modal value $=\mathrm{E}[\tau]$
Properties: $\quad \bullet \Phi(0)=0.5, d \Phi(t) / d t \sim e^{-t^{2} / 2} \rightarrow$ symmetric about $t=0 \rightarrow \Phi(-t)=1-\Phi(t)$

- For $\mathrm{E}[\tau]=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}[\tau]=\sigma^{2}, \quad(\tau-m) / \sigma$ has distribution $\Phi(t)$, i.e.

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{-\frac{(y-m)^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}} d y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{(t-m) / \sigma} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x=\Phi\left(\frac{t-m}{\sigma}\right)
$$

Chara cteris tic function: $\varphi(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{E}\left[e^{i t \tau}\right]=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\int e^{i t y}-\frac{(y-m)^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}} d y=e^{i t m-(\sigma t)^{2} / 2} \quad \begin{array}{c}((y-m) / \sigma=z+i t \sigma \\ i=(-1)^{k 2})\end{array}$

Examples: $\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq 2.33\} \approx 0.9901 ; \operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq-1\}=1-\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq 1\} \approx 1-0.8413 \approx 0.1587$# A9.2 $\chi^{2}$-Distribution (Chi-Square Distribution) 

Definition: $\quad \mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\chi_{\mathrm{v}}^{2} \leq t\right\}=\frac{1}{2^{\mathrm{v} / 2} \Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2}\right)} \int_{0}^{t} x^{\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2}-1} e^{-x / 2} d x=\frac{1}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2}\right)} \int_{0}^{t / 2} y^{\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2}-1} e^{-y} d y$,

$$
t>0(\mathrm{~F}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0), \quad v=1,2, \ldots(\text { degrees of freedom })
$$

Parameters: $\quad \mathrm{E}\left[\chi_{\mathrm{v}}^{2}\right]=v, \quad \operatorname{Var}\left[\chi_{\mathrm{v}}^{2}\right]=2 v, \quad$ Modal value $=v-2 \quad(v>2)$
Relationships: $\quad$ Normal distribution: $\chi_{\mathrm{v}}^{2}=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}} \sum_{i=1}^{v}\left(\xi_{i}-m\right)^{2}, \xi_{1}, \ldots, \xi_{v}$ independent (see also Appendices A9.4, A9.6 \& [A9.1]) normal distrib. with $\mathrm{E}\left[\xi_{i}\right]=m, \operatorname{Var}\left[\xi_{i}\right]=\sigma^{2}$

- Exponential distrib.: $\chi_{2 n}^{2}=2 \lambda\left(\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}\right), \tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ indep.exp.distrib.
- Poisson distribution: $\quad \sum_{i=0}^{v / 2-1} \frac{(t / 2)^{i}}{i!} e^{-t / 2}=1-\mathrm{F}(t), \quad v=2,4, \ldots$
- For $\chi_{\mathrm{v} 1}^{2}, \ldots, \chi_{\mathrm{v} n}^{2}$ independent, it holds that $\chi_{\mathrm{v} 1}^{2}+\ldots+\chi_{\mathrm{v} n}^{2}=\chi_{\mathrm{v} 1+\ldots+\mathrm{v} n}^{2}$

Examples: $\mathrm{F}\left(t_{16,0.9}\right)=0.9 \rightarrow t_{16,0.9}=\chi_{16,0.9}^{2}=23.542 ; \quad \sum_{i=0}^{8} \frac{13^{i}}{i!} e^{-13}=1-\mathrm{F}(26)=0.10 \quad(\mathrm{v}=18)$# A9.3 $\boldsymbol{t}$-Distribution (Student Distribution) 

Definition: $\quad \mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\boldsymbol{t}_{\mathrm{v}} \leq t\right\}=\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{v} \pi \Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2}\right)}} \int_{-\infty}^{t}\left(1+\frac{x^{2}}{\mathrm{v}}\right)^{-(\mathrm{v}+1) / 2} d x,-\infty<t<\infty$,

$$
v=1,2, \ldots(\text { degrees of freedom })
$$

Parameters: $\quad \mathrm{E}\left[\boldsymbol{t}_{\mathrm{v}}\right]=0 \quad(v>1), \quad \operatorname{Var}\left[\boldsymbol{t}_{\mathrm{v}}\right]=\frac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v}-2} \quad(\mathrm{v}>2), \quad$ Modal value $=0$
Properties: $\quad \mathrm{F}(0)=0.5, \mathrm{f}(t) \sim\left(\mathrm{v}+t^{2}\right)^{-\eta} \rightarrow$ symmetric about $t=0 \rightarrow \mathrm{~F}(-t)=1-\mathrm{F}(t)$
Relationsships: - Normal distribution and $\chi^{2}$-distribution : $\boldsymbol{t}_{\mathrm{v}}=\xi / \sqrt{\chi_{\mathrm{v}}^{2} / \mathrm{v}}$
(see also [A9.1]) $\xi$ is normal distributed with $\mathrm{E}[\xi]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}[\xi]=1 ; \chi_{\xi}^{2}$ is
$\chi^{2}$ - distributed with $v$ degrees of freedom, $\xi$ and $\chi_{\mathrm{v}}^{2}$ independent

- Cauchy distribution: $\mathrm{F}(t)$ with $\mathrm{v}=1$

Examples: $\mathrm{F}\left(t_{16,0.9}\right)=0.9 \rightarrow t_{16,0.9}=\boldsymbol{t}_{16,0.9}=1.3368 ; \mathrm{F}\left(t_{16,0.1}\right)=0.1 \rightarrow t_{16,0.1}=\boldsymbol{t}_{16,0.1}=-1.3368$# A9.4 $\boldsymbol{F}$ - Distribution (Fisher Distribution) 

Definition: $\quad \mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}} \leq t\right\}=\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mathrm{v}_{2}}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}_{1}}{2}\right) \Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}_{2}}{2}\right)} \mathrm{v}_{1}^{2} \mathrm{v}_{2}^{2} \int_{0}^{t} \frac{x\left(\mathrm{v}_{1}-2\right) / 2}{\left(\mathrm{v}_{1} x+\mathrm{v}_{2}\right)\left(\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mathrm{v}_{2}\right) / 2} d x$,

$$
t>0 \quad(\mathrm{~F}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0), \quad \mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}=1,2, \ldots(\text { degrees of freedom })
$$

Parameters: $\quad \mathrm{E}\left[\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}}\right]=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{2}}{\mathrm{v}_{2}-2} \quad\left(\mathrm{v}_{2}>2\right), \quad \operatorname{Var}\left[\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}}\right]=\frac{2 \mathrm{v}_{2}^{2}\left(\mathrm{v}_{1}+\mathrm{v}_{2}-2\right)}{\mathrm{v}_{1}\left(\mathrm{v}_{2}-2\right)^{2}\left(\mathrm{v}_{2}-4\right)} \quad\left(\mathrm{v}_{2}>4\right)$,
Modal value $=\mathrm{v}_{2}\left(\mathrm{v}_{1}-2\right) / \mathrm{v}_{1}\left(\mathrm{v}_{2}+2\right) \quad\left(\mathrm{v}_{1}>2\right)$
Quantiles : $\quad t_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}, \alpha}=\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}, \alpha}=1 / t_{\mathrm{v}_{2}, \mathrm{v}_{1}, 1-\alpha}=1 / \boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{2}, \mathrm{v}_{1}, 1-\alpha}$
Relationships: $\quad \boldsymbol{\ell}^{2}$-distribution: $\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}}=\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{v}_{1}}^{2} / \mathrm{v}_{1}}{\chi_{\mathrm{v}_{2}}^{2} / \mathrm{v}_{2}} \cdot \quad \chi_{\mathrm{v}_{1}}^{2} \cdot \chi_{\mathrm{v}_{2}}^{2}$ independent $\chi^{2}$ distributed (see also $[A 9.1])$

- Binomial distribution: $\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i}=\mathrm{F}\left(\frac{(1-p)(k+1)}{p(n-k)}\right)$

$$
\text { with } \mathrm{v}_{1}=2(n-k) \text { and } \mathrm{v}_{2}=2(k+1)
$$

- Beta distribution: $\boldsymbol{B}_{\mathrm{v}_{1} / 2, \mathrm{v}_{2} / 2}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{1} \boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}}}{\mathrm{v}_{2}+\mathrm{v}_{1} \boldsymbol{F}_{\mathrm{v}_{1}, \mathrm{v}_{2}}}=\chi_{\mathrm{v}_{1}}^{2} /\left(\chi_{\mathrm{v}_{1}}^{2}+\chi_{\mathrm{v}_{2}}^{2}\right)$
$\boldsymbol{B}_{a, b}$ has a Beta distribution with density $\mathrm{f}(t)=\frac{t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}}{\Gamma(a) \Gamma(b) / \Gamma(a+b)} \cdot 0<t<1$

Definition: $\quad \Gamma(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{z-1} e^{-x} d x, \quad \operatorname{Re}(z)>0$ (Euler's integral), solution of $\Gamma(z+1)=z \Gamma(z)$ with $\Gamma(1)=1$

Special values: $\quad \Gamma(0)=\infty, \quad \Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\sqrt{\pi}, \quad \Gamma(1)=\Gamma(2)=1, \quad \Gamma(\infty)=\infty$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \Rightarrow \int_{0}^{\infty} x^{-1 / 2} e^{-x} d x=2 \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-y^{2}} d y=\sqrt{\pi}, \text { Poisson's integral }\right. \\
& \left.\operatorname{yielding} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-a^{2} t^{2}} d t=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2 a} \text { and, using } \frac{d}{d a} \cdot \int_{0}^{\infty} t^{2} e^{-a^{2} t^{2}} d t=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{4 a^{3}}, a>0\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Factorial: $\quad n!=1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot \ldots \cdot n=\Gamma(n+1)$

$$
=\sqrt{2 \pi} n^{n+1 / 2} e^{-n+\theta / 12 n}, \quad 0<\theta<1 \quad \text { (Stirling's formula) }
$$

Relationships: $\quad$ Beta function: $\quad \mathrm{B}(z, w)=\int_{0}^{1} x^{z-1}(1-x)^{w-1} d x=\frac{\Gamma(z) \Gamma(w)}{\Gamma(z+w)}$

- Psi function: $\psi(z)=d(\ln \Gamma(z)) / d z=(d \Gamma(z) / d z) / \Gamma(z)$
- Duplication: $\Gamma(2 z)=(2 \pi)^{-1 / 2} 2^{2 z-1 / 2} \Gamma(z) \Gamma(z+1 / 2)$
- Incomplete Gamma function:

$$
\gamma(z, t)=\int_{0}^{t} x^{z-1} e^{-x} d x=\Gamma(z)-\int_{t}^{\infty} x^{z-1} e^{-x} d x, \quad \operatorname{Re}(z)>0
$$

- $\chi^{2}$-distribution $(\mathrm{F}(t)$ as in Appendix A9.2): $\gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2}, \frac{t}{2}\right)=\mathrm{F}(t) \Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2}\right)$

Definition: $\quad \tilde{\mathrm{F}}(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-s t} \mathrm{~F}(t) d t \quad \mathrm{~F}(t)$ defined for $t \geq 0$, piecewise continuos, $|\mathrm{F}(t)|<A e^{B t} \quad(0<A, B<\infty)$
Inverse transf.: $\quad \mathrm{F}(t)=\frac{1}{2 \pi i} \int_{C-i \infty}^{C+i \infty} \tilde{\mathrm{~F}}(s) e^{s t} d s \quad$ exists in the halfplan $\operatorname{Re}(s)=C>B, \quad i=\sqrt{-1}$
Moment gener. $\quad$ Considering $\mathrm{f}(t)$ as density of $\tau>0$, it follows (under weak conditions) that ating function:

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-s t} \mathrm{f}(t) d t=E\left[e^{-s \tau}\right]=E\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-s)^{k} \tau^{k}}{k!}\right]=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{s^{k}}{k!}(-1)^{k} E\left[\tau^{k}\right]
$$

thus, exept for the sign, the $k$ th coefficient of the MacLaurin expansion of $\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)$,
or $\left.\frac{d^{k} \tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{d s^{k}}\right|_{s=0}$, is $E\left[\tau^{k}\right]\left(\mathrm{f}(t)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t} \Rightarrow \tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)=\frac{\lambda}{s+\lambda}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{s^{k}}{k!}(-1)^{k} \frac{k!}{\lambda^{k}} \Rightarrow E\left[\tau^{k}\right]=\frac{k!}{\lambda^{k}}\right)$;
for arbitrary $\tau$, the characteristic function $E\left[e^{i t \tau}\right]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{i t x} \mathrm{f}(x) d x$ applies

A distribution function appears as a straight line when plotted on a probability chart belonging to its family. The use of probability charts (probability plot papers). simplifies the analysis and interpretation of data, in particular of life times or failure-free times (failure-free operating time). In the following the charts for lognormal, Weibull, and normal distributions are given.

## A9.8.1 Lognormal Probability Chart

The distribution function (Eq. (A6.110), Table A6.1)

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{0}^{t} \frac{1}{y} e^{-\frac{(\ln y \lambda)^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}} d y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\frac{\ln (\lambda t)}{\sigma}} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x, \quad \begin{aligned}
& t>0 ; \lambda, \sigma>0 \\
& (\mathrm{~F}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0)
\end{aligned}
$$

appears as a straight line on the chart of Fig. A9.1 ( $\lambda$ in $\mathrm{h}^{-1}$ for $t$ in h ), see Fig. 7.14. $\mathrm{F}(t)=0.5$, yielding $\lambda=1 / t_{0.5}$, and $\mathrm{F}(t)=0.99$, yielding $\ln \left(t_{0.99} / t_{0.5}\right) / \sigma \approx 2.33$, can be used for a graphical estimation of $\lambda$ and $\sigma$ (Eq. (7.44)-(7.46))


Figure A9.1 Lognormal probability chart (see Fig. 7.14 for an example with $\lambda=0.5 \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \& \sigma=0.4$ )# A9.8.2 Weibull Probability Chart 

The distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda t)^{\beta}}, t>0(\mathrm{~F}(t)=0$ for $t \leq 0), \lambda, \beta>0$ (Eq. (A6.89), Table A6.1) appears as a straight line on the chart of Fig. A9.2 ( $\lambda$ in $\mathrm{h}^{-1}$ for $t$ in h, see Fig. A8.2). On the dashed line, $\lambda=1 / t$; furthermore, $\beta$ appears on the scale $\log _{10} \log _{10}\left(\frac{1}{1-\mathrm{F}(t)}\right)$ when $t$ is varied by one decade (Figs. A8.2, 7.12, 7.13).


Figure A9.2 Weibull probability chart (see Fig. A8.2 for an example with $\lambda=1 / 800 \mathrm{~h} \& \beta=1.5$ )# A9.8.3 Normal Probability Chart 

The distribution function (Eq. (A6.105), Table A6.1)

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{-\frac{(y-m)^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}} d y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{t-m} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x=\Phi\left(\frac{t-m}{\sigma}\right), \quad-\infty<t, m<\infty, \sigma>0
$$

appears as a straight line on the chart of Fig. A9.3. $\mathrm{F}(t)=0.5$, yielding $m=t_{0.5}$, and $\mathrm{F}(t)=0.99$, yielding $\sigma \approx\left(t_{0.99}-t_{0.5}\right) / 2.33$, can be used for a graphical estimation of $m$ and $\sigma$. However, it is often more useful to calculate $\hat{m} \& \hat{\sigma}$ per Eqs. (A8.6) $\&(\mathrm{A} 8.10)$ and to operate with $\Phi\left(\frac{t-\hat{m}}{\hat{\sigma}}\right)$.


Figure A9.3 Normal probability chart (standard normal distribution)# A10 Basic Technological Component's Properties

For a repairable system (with negligible repair times), following arrival times $t_{i}^{*}$ of consecutive failures have been observed during $T=3^{\prime} 000 \mathrm{~h}: 450,800,1^{\prime} 400,1^{\prime} 700,1^{\prime} 950,2^{\prime} 150,2^{\prime} 450,2^{\prime} 600,2^{\prime} 850 \mathrm{~h}$. Test the hypothesis $H_{0}$ : the underlying point process is an HPP, against $H_{1}$ : the underlying process is an NHPP with increasing density. Fit a possible M $(t)$. (Hint: Use results of Section 7.6.3.)# Problem A6.1 

Devices are delivered from sources A with probability $p$ and B with probability $1-p$. Devices from source A have constant failure rate $\lambda_{A}$, those from source B have early failures and their failure-free time is Gamma distributed (Eq. (A6.97)) with parameters $\lambda_{B}$ and $\beta<1$. The devices are mixed. Give the resulting distribution of the failure-free time and the MTTF for a device randomly selected.

## Problem A6.2

Show that only the exponential distribution (Eq. (A6.81)), in continuous time, and the geometric distribution (Eq. (A6.131)), in discrete time, possess the memoryless property. (Hint: Use the considerations in Appendices A6.5 and A7.2.)

## Problem A6.3

Show that the failure-free time of a series-system with independent elements $E_{\mathrm{I}}, \ldots, E_{\mathrm{n}}$, each with Weibull distributed failure-free times with parameters $\lambda_{i}$ and $\beta$, is distributed according to a Weibull distribution with parameters $\lambda^{\prime}$ and $\beta$, give $\lambda^{\prime}$. (Hint: Consider Appendix A6.10.2.)

## Problem A6.4

Show that the probability to have exactly $k$ failures in the operating time $T$ of a system with constant failure rate $\lambda$, repaired as-good-as-new at each failure, is given by $(\lambda T)^{k} e^{-\lambda T} / k$ !

## Problem A6.5

Prove cases (i), (iii), and (v) given in Example A6. 18 (p. 464).

## Problem A6.6*

Show that the sum of independent random variables (r. v.) having a common exponential distribution are Erlangian distributed. Same for Gamma distributed r. v., giving a Gamma distribution. Same for normal distributed r. v., giving a normal distribution.

## Problem A6.7*

Show that the square of a standard normal distributed random variable (Eq. (A6.109)) is $\chi^{2}$ distributed with $v=1$. (Hint: Use $\mathrm{f}_{\eta}(t)$ per Eq. (A6.31), $\mathrm{u}(t)=t^{2} \&$ consider $-\infty<\tau<\infty \& 0<\eta=\tau^{2}<\infty$.)

## Problem A6.8*

Show that mean \& variance of a lognormally distributed random variable are given by Eqs. (A6.112), (A6.113). (Hint: Use $x=(\ln \lambda t) / \sigma \sqrt{2}$ and then $y=x-\sigma / \sqrt{2}$ for mean, $y=x-\sigma \sqrt{2}$ for variance.)

## Problem A7.1

Prove that for a homogeneous Poisson process with parameter $\lambda$, the probability to have $k$ events (failures) in $(0, T]$ is Poisson distributed with parameter $\lambda T$.

## Problem A7.2

Determine graphically from Fig. A7.2 (p. 484) the mean time to failure of the item considered in Case V of Example A7.1. (Hint: Consider Eq. (A7.30).) Compare this result with that obtained for Case V with $\lambda_{w}=0$, i. e., as if no early failures where present. Same for Case IV, and compare the result with that obtained for Case IV with $\psi \rightarrow \infty$, i. e., as if the wear-out period would never occur.

## Problem A7.3

Prove Eq. (A7.33) for the mean of the forward recurrence time $\tau_{R}(t)$ in a renewal process for $t \rightarrow \infty$. Show that for a homog. Poisson process it holds that the mean of $\tau_{R}(t)$ is independent of $t$ and equal the mean of the consecutive interarrival times $(1 / \lambda)$. Explain the waiting time paradox (p.486).# Problem A7.4 

Prove Equation (5.3) and give an explication for the validity of Eq. (5.4). (Hint: for Eq. (5.3) use results of Section 2.3.5 with $v_{i}=(n-i) \lambda, i=0,1, \ldots, n-1$; for Eq. (5.4), consider a 1-out-of- $n$ active redundancy, or a series model, with $E_{1}=\ldots=E_{n}$.)

## Problem A7.5

Prove that for a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) with intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)=d \mathrm{M}(t) / d t$, the probability to have $k$ events (failures) in the interval $(0, T]$ is Poisson distributed with parameter $\mathrm{M}(T)-\mathrm{M}(0)$.

## Problem A7.6

Investigate the cumulative damage caused by Poisson distributed shocks with intensity $\lambda$, each of which causes a damage $\xi>0$ exponentially distributed with parameter $\eta>0$, independent of the shock and of the cumulated damage. (Hint: Consider Appendix A7.8.4.) Same by assuming that $\xi>0$ is Gamma distributed.

## Problem A7.7

Investigate the renewal densities $\mathrm{h}_{n d}(t)$ and $\mathrm{h}_{d n}(t)$ (Eqs. (A7.52), (A7.53)) for the case of constant failure and repair (restoration) rates $\lambda$ and $\mu$. Show that they converge exponentially for $t \rightarrow \infty$ with a time constant $1 /(\lambda+\mu) \approx 1 / \mu$ toward their final value $\lambda \mu /(\lambda+\mu) \approx \lambda$. (Hint: Use Table A9.7b.)

## Problem A7.8

Let $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\tau_{2}^{*}<\ldots$ be the occurrence times (failure times of a repairable system with negligible repair times) of a nonhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)=d \mathrm{M}(t) / d t>0$ (from the origin $\left.t=\tau_{0}^{*}=0\right)$; show that the quantities $\psi_{1}^{*}=\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{1}^{*}\right)<\psi_{2}^{*}=\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{2}^{*}\right)<\ldots$ are the occurrence times in a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity one, i. e with $\mathrm{M}(t)=t$. (Hint: Consider the remarks to Eq. (A7.200).)

## Problem A7.9

Let $\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T$ be the failure times (arrival times) in the interval $(0, T]$ of a repairable system with negligible repair times. Assuming a nonhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)=d \mathrm{M}(t) / d t>0$, show that for given (fixed) $T$ and $v(T)=n$, the quantities $0<\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{1}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)<\ldots<\mathrm{M}\left(\tau_{n}^{*}\right) / \mathrm{M}(T)<1$ have the same distribution as if they where the order statistics of $n$ independent identically distributed random variables uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$. (Hint: Consider the remarks to Eq. (A7.206).)

## Problem A7.10*

Prove the equations for $\mathrm{Q}_{123}^{\prime}(x), \mathrm{Q}_{2^{\prime} 3}^{\prime}(x) \& \mathrm{Q}_{1}(x)$ related to the model of Fig. A7.13 on p. 529.

## Problem A7.11*

Prove Eq. (A7.220). (Hint: Use Eqs. (A6.38) and (A6.45).) Verify the proof of Eq. (A7.226).

## Problem A7.12**

Prove the conclusion for the 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy of Fig. A7.11 given at the bottom of p. 530.

## Problem A7.13**

Prove Eqs. (A7.185) \& (A7.186), and for $\mathrm{g}(x)=\mu e^{-\mu x}$ verify the results of Eq. (A7.185) \& (A7.186) in Tab. $6.8(n-k=2)$.# Problem A8.1 

Prove Eqs. (A8.10) and (A8.11).

## Problem A8.2

Give the maximum likelihood point estimate for the parameters $\lambda$ and $\beta$ of a Gamma distribution (Eq. (A6.97)) and for $m$ and $\sigma$ of a normal distribution (Eq. (A6.105)).

## Problem A8.3*

Investigate mean and variance of the point estimate $\hat{\lambda}=k / T$ given by Eq. (7.28).

## Problem A8.4*

Investigate mean and variance of the point estimate $\hat{\lambda}=(k-1) /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) t_{k}\right)$ as per Eq. (A8.35). Same for $\hat{\lambda}=n /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)$ given by Eq. (A8.28).

## Problem A8.5*

Prove Eq. (A8.32). (Hint: Use Eq. (A8.27).)

## Problem A8.6*

Prove Eq. (A8.62). (Hint: Use Eqs. (A8.61) \& (A8.25).) Same by assuming Erlangian distributed (Eq. (A6.102)) failure free and repair times with $\beta_{\lambda}=n_{\lambda} \& \beta_{\mu}=n_{\mu}$, for unchanged MTTF and MTTR.

## Problem A8.7*

Develop the procedure (Eqs. (A8.91) - (A8.93)) for the demonstration of an availability $P A$ for the case of constant failure rate and Erlangian distributed repair times with parameter $\beta_{\mu}=n_{\mu}$.# Acronyms
